11214114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11214114.value: Nuclear energy is derived from the kinetic energy of fission or fusion neutrons, which unfortunately also creates damage to the functional and structural materials making up the nuclear reactor. A good model of the damage accumulation processes is essential to mitigating reactor materials problems created this way, which bears direct consequence to issues that affect the cost of nuclear energy and public safety in a major way. Rate theory models based on a continuum description of the evolution kinetics of the generation and recovery of irradiation damage have dominated the scene since the early years. These have been very useful in describing, via parametrization, macroscopic effects due to microstructure changes resulting from irradiation damage production. However, due to the continuum approach adopted, mesoscopic details are necessarily neglected, such as the quantum statistics associated. Use of model parameters to account for such omissions may lead to oversimplifications that compromise the reliability of the model for predictive or interpretative purposes. This underpins the need of mesoscopic modelling efforts to bridge the vast gap between the atomistic and microstructure scales. The present project achieves a big step forward in the mesoscopic modelling efforts in this area.

11214814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11214814.value: A major task in gene expression data analysis is to find coherent patterns, which involve subsets of but not all samples in each dimension. For example, we may want to detect a subset of genes that are co-regulated under a subset of conditions during a subset of time points. This requires co-clustering techniques, which perform clustering in all directions simultaneously in multidimensional data. We have recently discovered that after an M-th order tensor is factorized using high order singular value decomposition (HOSVD), we can convert an M-dimensional co-clustering problem to the analysis of two-dimensional (2D) data with M singular matrices. The coherence in the tensor data is reflected in the hyperplanar relations among the singular vectors. The 2D data analysis problem can be solved using hyperplane detection algorithms. In this project, we will develop novel methods for co-clustering tensor data based on these useful properties. We will investigate effective procedures to detect different hyperplanar co-clusters, study robust methods to reduce the influence of noise and outliers, design efficient computer algorithms, and apply our techniques to real-world multidimensional data analysis problems. Our approach will have several advantages in comparison with existing methods. For example, our algorithm will be able to model different types of co-cluster patterns using the same formulation. Some commonly studied co-clusters can be viewed as special cases of our model. In many cases, tensor decomposition provides significant data reduction. In addition, HOSVD decomposes a co-cluster so that we can study it in individual dimensions. Our technique will also establish useful links between co-clustering and linear algebraic relations among singular vectors. In our method, HOSVD can be used to reduce the noise effect by separating tensor data into signal subspace and noise subspace and we only need to consider the singular vectors in the signal subspace. Our model can also incorporate several other powerful noise reduction techniques, such as generalized projections, relaxation labeling and data imputation and restoration procedures. Our work will lead to a new class of robust methods for co-clustering tensor data, which is an important problem but is difficult and often considered intractable mathematically and computationally. We will provide a systematic strategy to design robust computer algorithms for the detection of hyperplanar co-cluster patterns. The techniques developed in this project will find many practical applications, such as in genomic sequence, gene expression and image data analysis, and disease diagnosis such as cancer type and sub-type identification.

11214814.label: Realisation of objectives
11214814.value: Due to the rapid development of electronic and communications systems and biotechnologies, the amount of data is increasing at a rapid pace. For example, the pictures taken in the world every day would be in the order of billions. Much of the data are multidimensional and can be represented as a data array of multiple indices. Although a dataset can be very large, it is possible that meaningful and coherent patterns embedded in the data are much smaller in size. For example, to recognize facial expression, we only need to extract features around the person’s mouth and eyes. Other parts of the image, such as hair and clothes would not be important. In genomic data, we may want to find a subset of genes that co-express under a sub-set of conditions. In this project, we have developed advanced co-clustering algorithms for solving the coherent pattern detection problem. We have proposed a co-clustering technique based on hyperplane detection in singular vector spaces (HDSVS) is proposed. Specifically in this method, high-order singular value decomposition (HOSVD) transforms a tensor into a core part and a singular matrix along each mode, whose row vectors can be clustered by a linear grouping algorithm (LGA). Meanwhile, hyperplanar patterns are extracted and successfully supported the identification of multi-dimensional coclusters. To validate HDSVS, a number of synthetic and biological tensors were adopted. The synthetic tensors attested a favorable performance of this algorithm on noisy or overlapped data. We have studied the performance of HDSVS with respect to different noise levels and overlapped degrees in tensors. Our method showed a robust performance on noisy tensors, due to the selection of singular vectors by the truncated HOSVD. Meanwhile, the applications of HDSVS to two biological tensors, namely the gene x patient x time tensor and the gene x descendant x founder tensor, validated its reliability in dealing with real-world applications. Especially, the genes in the detected co-clusters were significantly enriched in biologically verified pathways and GO terms. In addition, comparisons between HDSVS and other popular methods on 2D synthetic data and 2D yeast gene expression data further showed the robustness and stability of HDSVS. The experiment results show that HDSVS is an efficient method for cocluster identification in high-order tensors. Experiments with gene expression data and lineage tracing data of embryonic cells further verified the reliability of HDSVS to practical problems. Moreover, the detected coclusters are well consistent with important genetic pathways and gene ontology annotations. We have employed co-clustering methods to analyze and predict protein secondary structures. We first selected 3,000 non-redundant proteins from the protein databank (PDB) and obtained their secondary structures from the Dictionary of Protein Secondary Structure (DSSP). According to the DSSP classification, 8 types of secondary structures are defined. We made a statistical analysis of the amino acids for each type of the secondary structures and then paid our attention to two most common regular structures α-helix and β-strand. We analyzed the amino acids and their neighbors of the chains in detail. Moreover, hydrogen bond patterns were studied for the α-helices. We conducted co-clustering analysis of the α-helix and β-strand chain-feature matrices, and used the co-clusters to predict the secondary structures of unseen samples. Results show that testing accuracies of β-strand and long α-helices are very high. As the prediction did not work well for short α-helices, we employed amino acid feature vectors to solve the problem. By comparing the angles between the testing vector and training vectors in a co-cluster, we can predict the structure of the testing chain. The testing accuracy of short α-helices can reach 96% when using vectors. Gabor wavelets are useful for facial expression recognition, but the number of features is very large as compared to the number of available samples. Among these overwhelming number of features only a small fraction may be needed. Feature selection in this regard improves the scalability (defying the curse of dimensionality) and reduces the identity bias when specific regions are located. In this project, a novel method for feature selection in facial expression recognition based on co-clustering is proposed. Our method is able to reveal the saliency of face regions by selecting a small number of dominant features from Gabor wavelets features. Experiments have been conducted on widely used benchmark facial expression image databases. With the JAFFE and MMI databases, we achieved recognition rates of 95.31% and 94.09% respectively using SVM on reduced feature sets. With the CK+ database, we obtained the accuracy of 96.05% by using only 20% of the features. An interesting aspect of this work is that when a feature set containing as little as 0.9% of the entire feature data were used, we could still obtain an accuracy of 90.23%. Several other feature selection approaches were also considered to detect prominent features in comparison with co-clustering based feature selection (CCFS). The feature selection methods based on feature ranking analyze the features separately and perform selection one after another. This might be undesirable in multiclass recognition, where different features have different strength on discriminating different classes. As comparison with other approaches, CCFS achieves better results, which indicates that the local structures in the feature matrix are more crucial for discriminant feature selection and is a better way to analyze class features jointly. Making use of the discriminating ability of CCFS in terms of recognizing facial expressions in frontal view images, we can extend our work on data captured in the wild, in order to test and improve the robustness of proposed method on spontaneous, non-posed and multi-view images. Performance on cross databases, variations in expressions within the same classes and face occlusions are the main challenges that need to be addressed. We can fuse geometric and appearance features along with feature selection to tackle these problems. Co-clustering provides classifications simultaneously in all directions of a multidimensional data array. It can be used to detect coherent patterns that are embedded in a large matrix or tensor and contain a subset of elements in each direction. It can be performed effectively in singular vector spaces based on hyperplane detection. We expect that co-clustering will gain more and more applications to feature selection, noise filtering, and coherent pattern detection in machine learning, pattern recognition, and big data analytics.

11214814.label: Major findings and research outcome
11214814.value: We have three discoveries that are proven mathematically [Publication 1]: (1) single co-cluster patterns as matrices have rank 1 or 2. Using singular value decomposition (SVD), we will then only have 1 or 2 non-zero singular values. (2) When there are more than one co-clusters in a matrix, then the matrix rank can be large than 1. However, points in the co-clusters will be located on hyperplanes and points not in the co-clusters will be off the hyperplanes. If there is noise, the rank can also be larger than 1. In noisy data, points in the co-clusters will be located close to the hyperplane. Such property is crucial for designing our linear grouping based algorithm for co-cluster detection. (3) We can convert the detection of a higher-order co-clusters to the detection along each mode of the tensor data and then combine the results. This property is crucial for the analysis of multi-way data arrays based on higher-order SVD (HOSVD). Based on the above three properties, we have developed a co-clustering technique based on hyperplane detection in singular vector spaces (HDSVS). Our method has the following advantages compared with existing ones. (1) We can remove small singular values in SVD to reduce the noise influence. (2) We can detect different types of co-clusters, such as constant, additive or multiplicative ones. (3) We can deal with a data array of arbitrary order (arbitrary number of indices). Co-clustering has many applications to big data analysis, in which we would like to search for small subsets of coherent patterns. In this project, we have find useful biomedical applications, including gene expression analysis and cancer subtyping [1-4, 6]. Recently we have found a very interesting application of co-clustering for selecting Gabor wavelet features of images for facial expression classification [7]. Through the analysis of co-clusters, we can retain relevant features for a facial expression and discard all other features. With only 20% of the features selected this way, we have obtained an even higher classification rate than that from the entire set of features [7]. The reason for the improved performance is that through co-clustering, we can remove irrelevant and noisy features and enhance the feature quality. To our best knowledge, we are the first to propose a robust feature selection procedure using co-clustering. We expect our work on co-clustering will lead to powerful techniques for solving many image and video analysis problems.

11214814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11214814.value: Co-clustering has many other applications, some of which are listed below [from discussions in publication 5]: - Analysis of consumer spending patterns to discover a subset of consumers who like to purchase products from a subset of companies, - Analysis of financial data to find a subset of sectors that have similar economic growth patterns in a subset of regions, - Analysis of chemical components in food to determine a subset of components (nutrients or toxicants) in a subset of food types, - Analysis of web documents to search for a subset of documents that contain a subset of keywords in a subset of locations, and - Analysis of training data in machine learning to extract a subset of features that are relevant to a subset of features, such as in image and video analysis. We have used co-clustering algorithms in gene expression data analysis [2-4], cancer subtyping [6], and human facial expression recognition [7]. More applications will studied in the future.

11214914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11214914.value: Like many other types of glasses, metallic glasses inevitably relax over time towards a lower energy state owing to their non-equilibrium nature. Therefore, for a long time, structural relaxation in metallic glasses has been used as an effective means to control/optimize their mechanical/physical properties. On the other hand, there is a surge of interest in recent years to improve the mechanical properties of monolithic metallic glasses by nucleating secondary crystalline phases to form metallic-glass matrix composites. However, as of today, little is known yet on how the ‘composite’ approach could possibly alter the relaxation behavior of the metallic-glass matrix in the pursuit of the superior mechanical properties in the glasses. In this project, we aim to characterize and understand the relaxation behavior of metallic glasses and their composites across the size scales ranging from ~1 nm to ~1 mm and the time scales from ~1E-5 s to ~10 s by fully exploiting the recently developed nano-scale dynamic mechanical analysis (NanoDMA) and atomic force microscopy techniques as combined with the conventional DMA. To achieve our goal, metallic-glass samples in different forms (bulk, foil and fiber) will be prepared with the controlled chemical composition and thermal/mechanical history; afterwards, we will systemically investigate the effects of chemical composition, plastic deformation and cooling rate on the global/local structural relaxation behavior of the metallic glasses and metallic-glass matrix composites. The successful implementation of this project will unfold, in a comprehensive manner, how the local structural relaxation process in metallic glasses and their composites are affected by the various external factors, such as size, cooling rate, plastic deformation, which finally leads to the global structural relaxation behavior and the resultant mechanical/physical properties typically seen in bulk metallic glasses. From the scientific perspective, the proposed research could deepen our understanding of the structural origin of the relaxation process in metallic glasses; from the application viewpoint, our research could provide the most needed information on the most efficient way for the control and optimization of the mechanical properties of bulk metallic glasses and their composites through structural relaxation. Furthermore, since sample size is the factor to be investigated in our proposed research, the outcome of our project is also very valuable to the development of metallic-glass based nano- and micro-systems, which is an emerging high-tech area recently showing great technological promise in micro- and nano-scale manufacturing, sensing and actuation, biotechnology and energy harnessing. 和許多玻璃一樣，由於非平衡物質的本質，金屬玻璃隨著時間流逝無可避免的會結構弛豫到一個更低的能量狀態。因此，在很長的一段時間裡面，結構弛豫被工程界用作一種有效的手段去改變金屬玻璃的機械物理特性。另外一方面，以金屬玻璃為基體的複合材料在近年來被用作一種有效手段去改良金屬玻璃的力學性能。然而，對於引入新的第二象會如何改變金屬玻璃基體的弛豫特性還是一個未知之謎。本項研究的目的是充分利用已建立的多尺度力學平台去研究金屬玻璃在不同尺度和不同時間下的弛豫行為，進而為生成性能卓越的金屬玻璃以及相關的複合材料提供實驗方案和準則。

11214914.label: Realisation of objectives
11214914.value: Objective 1: To fabricate Zr-Cu-based metallic-glass samples in the forms of bulk and thin foil, and to tune their internal structures through sub-Tg thermal annealing and mechanical deformation This objective was achieved through the fabrication of Zr-Cu based bulk metallic glasses with arc melting and thin foil metallic glass or metallic glass ribbons through melt spinning. These samples were thermally annealed and used in the subsequent studies for objectives 2 to 4. Objective 2: To characterize the global and local atomic structure of the metallic-glass and composite samples across different length scales and before/after structural relaxation. At the macroscopic scale, two secondary relaxation processes were identified in 2015 in different metallic glasses rather than one secondary relaxation as reported before. When we first observed this phenomenon in La-based metallic glass, we thought that it was because our metallic glass contains a variety of mobile atomic pairs due to the combination of the very mobile with immobile elements, multiple local relaxation processes arise because of the distinction in the different onset temperatures for secondary relaxations. As a result, this facilitates the detection of the very subtle and much localized relaxation process in the metallic glass with an activation energy of ~0.5 eV, being as low as that for the individual thermal activation process. On the basis of our findings, we proposed a physical picture which describes how mechanical relaxation is initiated and progresses in metallic glasses. At a low temperature, relaxations are initiated and centred in the very local sites where the most mobile atoms reside. As the temperature increases, the relaxations spread out to their surroundings and include less mobile atoms; however, during this stage, these relaxations are still local and confined by the overall elastic ‘matrix’ of glass. However, through a more thorough experimental study, we later found in 2017 that the fast beta relaxation we observed previously is common to a variety of MGs. Compared to the slow beta relaxation that is generally related to chemical bond breakage, STZ activation and yielding in MGs, the fast beta relaxation correlates with a more confined inelasticity process activated at a much lower energy. This subtle relaxation process is more sensitive to the local atomic packing variation than the chemical bonding in the amorphous structure of MGs, therefore insensitive to the corresponding glass transition temperature. By fully activating the fast beta relaxation, multiple shear banding can be triggered in different MGs near a temperature being much lower than the glass transition point but close to the peak temperature for the fast secondary relaxation. These interesting findings unfold an intrinsic correlation between relaxation and mechanical deformation in MGs. At the nano-scale, by using the dynamic atomic force microscope as an “imaging” as well as a “forcing” tool, we unfold a real-time sequence of structural evolution occurring on the surface of an Au-Si thin film metallic glass. In sharp contrast to the common notion that plasticity comes along with mechanical softening in bulk metallic glasses, our experimental results directly reveal three types of nano-sized surface regions, which undergo plasticity but exhibit different characters of structural evolution following the local plasticity events, including stochastic structural rearrangement, unusual local relaxation and rejuvenation. As such, yielding on the metallic-glass surface manifests as a dynamic equilibrium between local relaxation and rejuvenation as opposed to shear instability in bulk metallic-glasses. Our finding demonstrates that plasticity on the metallic glass surface of Au-Si metallic glass bears much resemblance to that of the colloidal gels, of which nonlinear rheology rather than shear instability governs the constitutive behavior of plasticity. Objective 3: To establish correlations between the structure and relaxation behavior of the metallic-glass and metallic-glass composite samples across different size/time scales and at different energy states Based on our experimental findings, we contended that the fast beta relaxation we discovered should result from reversible atom inelastic motion in an elastic matrix, which could be a universal character related to the topological heterogeneity in MGs. Furthermore, we also demonstrated that the fast beta relaxation shares a similar activation energy with anelasticity in MGs. Since anelasticity is the precursory process of yielding, these recent new findings thus deliver a strong message, that is, it is the fast beta relaxation that triggers plasticity in MGs. Very recently, our collaborator, Ouyang et al. obtained the activation energy for anelasticity in a variety of MGs, which showed the similar trend of chemical insensitivity as the fast beta relaxation. More importantly, we found that plastic MGs, such as Pd-, Zr- and Cu-based, tend to possess a lower ratio of Eβ’ /E than the brittle ones, such as Ce-, Mg- and La-based. There seems a demarcation line E’ = 0.41E that separates the plastic from brittle MGs. This phenomenon can be easily rationalized since the smaller is the ratio of E’/E the easier is to initiate local plasticity before yielding sets out in MGs. Quantitatively, we showed that the fast beta relaxation in the plastic MGs contains a smaller number of but more mobile atoms than those in the brittle MGs. Notably, the triggering role of the fast beta relaxation could be further substantiated through mechanical tests. We further demonstrated an unusual brittle-to-ductile transition at a medium temperature in MGs, which can be keyed to the fast beta relaxation profile. Objective 4: To reveal the structural origin of relaxation in the metallic-glass and metallic-glass composite samples through experiments, atomistic simulations and theoretical modeling Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were used in combination with the theoretical modeling to understand the mechanisms of relaxation and the resultant cyclic loading induced elastic softening in the Cu50Zr50 MG. Our results clearly show that, while cyclic loading causes atomic bond breaking even in the normal elastic regime, part of the elastic softening at the lower stress rate is more due to the viscoelasticity resulting from the activation of “liquid-like” atomic clusters. Since yielding in MGs is strain controlled, fundamentally being correlated with the glass transition temperature or the elastic modulus, the continuous elastic softening in MGs with cyclic loading can ultimately lead to yielding even for an applied stress lower than the quasi-static yielding strength. Through the Eshelby theory, we established a quantitative link between overall elastic properties and local structural heterogeneities in MGs. General formulas for elastic moduli were derived from characteristics of structural hetergeneities from the Eshelby's theory. Our theoretical modeling is verified by the experimental data obtained from various MGs annealed to different degrees. Particularly, we revealed that upon annealing, the Poisson's ratio decreases upon annealing of MGs if the shear softening dominates the behavior of the local soft regions, or increases if pressure softening becomes dominant. The degrees of the bulk and shear modulus softening in local soft regions are extracted for different MGs, and is found to closely correlate with their ductility. The aging dynamics during the annealing process is also quantitatively studied based on the relations between the local elastic heterogeneities and overall elastic constant properties. The implication of our results were also discussed with regard to the Poisson's ratio effect on the ductility and liquid fragility of MGs. Given the generality of Eshelby's theory, the intrinsic correlations herein discovered should be applicable to a wide range of elastically heterogeneous solids.

11214914.label: Major findings and research outcome
11214914.value: Major findings: (1) A fast beta relaxation common to a variety of MGs is identified for the current research. Compared to the slow beta relaxation that is generally related to chemical bond breakage, STZ activation and yielding in MGs, the fast beta relaxation correlates with a more confined inelasticity process activated at a much lower energy. This subtle relaxation process is more sensitive to the local atomic packing variation than the chemical bonding in the amorphous structure of MGs, therefore insensitive to the corresponding glass transition temperature. By fully activating the fast beta relaxation, multiple shear banding can be triggered in different MGs near a temperature being much lower than the glass transition point but close to the peak temperature for the fast secondary relaxation. These interesting findings unfold an intrinsic correlation between relaxation and mechanical deformation in MGs. (2) The surface plasticity behavior of the Au-based TFMG by directly probing stress-induced structural evolution. Through in-situ DAFM observations, we observed the nano-sized regions which exhibit unusual characteristics of structural evolution immediately after the local plasticity. Unlike BMGs, whose plasticity is governed by local softening and shear instability, the Au-based TFMG surface exhibits gel-like plasticity similar to those occurring in soft glassy materials, such as colloidal gels and suspensions. These interesting findings suggest a nonuniform glassy structure near the surface of the Au-based TFMG, which can be further explored for important applications, such as nanoscale lubrication and self-healing. (3) metallic glasses (MGs) are a homogeneous solid at the macroscopic scale; they contain nano-scale elastic heterogeneities. On the basis of Eshelby's theory, we reveal that the properties of the local elastic heterogeneities are correlated with the measurable overall elastic properties of MGs, such as shear/bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio. Upon annealing, the Poisson's ratio decreases if shear softening dominates the behavior of local soft regions or increase if pressure softening becomes dominant in MGs. Research outcome: Through the GRF support, we have published 13 SCI papers, including those in the first rate journals, such as Nature Communications, Materials Today, Acta Materialia, Scripta Materialia, National Science Review, Journal of Applied Physics and etc. We also presented our work in several international and national conferences. Part of the GRF funding was used to support two PhD students, i.e. Dr. Ye Yifan who graduated in 2017 and received the prestigious Humboldt research fellowship and Dr. Lu Yumiao who also graduated in 2017 and is now a research staff in Chinese Academy of Science.

11214914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11214914.value: Through the GRF support, we have discovered a very interesting while more complicated through normally expected relaxation behavior in metallic glasses. The molecular dynamics simulations and theoretical modeling we performed constitute the first attempt to understand the physical origin of such an interesting phenomenon. More sophisticated models and simulations could be developed in future and extended to metallic glasses other than Zr-Cu metallic glass. More importantly, we should ask themselves: what can we do with the stress relaxations? Can we make a better metallic glass (more plastic or more tough) by tuning or controlling the stress relaxation behavior. This would be left for future research.

11214914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11214914.value: Metallic glasses are commonly known as “frozen liquids” because of their thermodynamically metastable nature. While they may behave overall like a solid under normal loading conditions, metallic glasses contain local liquid like sites which can easily relax the local mechanical stress. This stress relaxation behavior can be correlated with shear/bulk modulus, Poisson’s ratio and even the post-yielding (plastic versus brittle) behavior of the whole glass. Understanding such a unique behavior of metallic glasses may help us design new and better metallic glasses in future.

11215314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11215314.value: Fire phenomena involve complicated and highly non-linear interactions between parameters. Currently, computer simulations by use of numerical methods applying on mathematical models - zone and field modelling techniques in form of differential equations have been widely adopted for predicting results of fire phenomena. While the accuracy of the prediction is highly relying on the accuracy of the mathematical models applying on the fire phenomena, the latter also involves extremely expensive computations. This research explores the use of the artificial neural network (ANN) to simulate the behaviour of the enclosure fire growth phenomena. The ANN is an information processing system similar to the human judgment mechanism and has been considered effective in recognizing and judging a situation with “fluctuating” and “obscure” factors. In fact, it is a complicated mathematical tool for data regression. In this research study, in order to address to these issues, a novel and unique ANN model suitable for enclosure fire growth and fire risk analysis (FRA) will be developed based on General Regression Neural Network (GRNN) and Fuzzy ART (FA) Algorithms. The former is extremely powerful for the identification of highly non-linear characteristics of a system, while the latter will enhance the model by clustering of data into representative kernels. As the kernels formulated by FA cannot be directly used with the GRNN, a new compression technique will also be developed based on the k-nearestneigbourhood theory to provide a closure to this approach. For training and validations of the ANN fire model, the CFD models shall be used to provide simulation results including transient smoke layer height and temperature, time to flashover and flow through openings, etc. Also, experimental results from enclosure fire tests will be used for training and validations of the model. When applied to complicated studies of fire scenarios in buildings, the new ANN model will be relatively much faster and computationally economical than its counterparts (i.e. zone or field models). The results of this research study is expected to shed new lights to further enhance applications of ANN techniques for fire engineering predictions including flame and smoke spread and the fire risk assessment for buildings. The new GRNN-FA model will offer a much efficient and economic means for fire safety analysis in buildings which may be adopted in the Performance-Based Fire Engineering approach or Codes in Hong Kong and other countries internationally.

11215314.label: Realisation of objectives
11215314.value: Objective 1: Development of ANN Fire Model - GRNNFA A new, unique General Regression Neural Network Fuzzy ART (GRNNFA) model for fire studies had been developed. In this new model, the Fuzzy ART algorithm (FA) for creating prototypes with the training data were compressed to representative kernels for the nonlinear regression by the GRNN model. Also, a newly developed compression scheme in which the prototypes were converted to a set of representative kernels for the GRNN had been developed. It has been possible to remove the noise content of the data of the same prototype by projecting the centroid of the data points on the input and output domains to obtain the representative kernel input and output respectively. The K-nearest-neighbour (kNN) algorithm to assist the GRNN model to construct the regression surface over the whole input domain by tuning the kernel widths was formulated. A new online training mechanism was developed for the GRNNFA model. The Monte-Carlo simulation was adopted to deal with the embedded uncertainties in the training samples. Distributions were built in each dimension of the collected samples. Samples were extracted from the distributions for model training. Therefore, the model was made capable of characterisation of the general behaviour of the system from the collected samples. Objective 2: Training and validation of GRNNFA Model with Computational Data The experimental data obtained from Steckler et al. [1] was employed for training and evaluation of the GRNNFA. In this reported works, a total numbers of 55 steady state full scale fire experiments had been carried out in a single compartment. The multiple inputs consisted of opening size and location, fire size and location, ambient temperature. The multiple outputs consisted of locations of neural plane and thermal interface, air mass flow rate, average temperature of the lower and upper gases layers, maximum mixing rate and velocity and temperature profiles at the opening. In model training, the well-known conventional approach of “Leave-one-out cross-validation” (as frequently used for ANN model training and subsequent validation) was applied to evaluate the performance of prediction. The training of GRNNFA model had been further carried out with simulation fire field data using the computational fluid dynamics model for fire – Fire Dynamics Simulator (NIST) [2]. The typical single compartment with single fire source had been considered. The multiple inputs for the enclosure fire growth consist of sizes, dimensions and locations of the vents and also the room dimensions. The multiple outputs will be the time to flashover, transient temperature, smoke concentration, smoke layer heights, etc. The predicted results were compared with the experimental data to ascertain the degree of accuracy and the stability of the network performance. The model parametric sensitivity study had been carried out to confirm the setting of the parameters. The “Leave-one-out cross-validation” as discussed above had been applied. To increase the amount of the quality experimental data for the training and evaluation of the GRNNFA model, the experiments conducted in a reduced scale (2/5 ISO 9705 room) enclosure (RSE) [3] with various fuel sources had been employed with the above approach for training and evaluation of the GRNNFA model. Since the training of [2] had been used to provide the adequately large set of data for training purposes. Also, the FIRE3D developed by the PI had also been employed to give further data supplement. The typical single compartment with single and multiple fire sources had been considered. The multiple inputs for the enclosure fire growth consisted of sizes, dimensions and locations of the vents and the room dimensions. The multiple outputs were the time to flashover, transient temperature, smoke concentration, smoke layer heights, etc. The “Leave-one-out cross-validation” as discussed above had also been applied. Objective 3: Validation of the new GRNNFA fire model for fire scenario predictions The GRNNFA model was validated by the well-known ANN benchmarking problems: Ozone, Friedman#1 and Two-intertwined-spirals problems which were particularly designed for noisy data regression and classification. The performance of the GRNNFA had been compared with other ANN models to confirm the significance in noise removal. Experimental fire data was also employed for validating the performance of the GRNNFA in the prediction of real fire scenarios. Experimental data reported by Steckler [1] for single compartment fire had been used. The established GRNNFA fire model performed satisfactorily in fire scenario predictions. 11215314.label: Major findings and research outcome
11215314.value: It has been well-recognized in the fire research community that the interactions between the physical and chemical processes involved in building fires are extremely sophisticated and complicated in nature. Also, the available data for ANN model development has been very rare and highly sparse. In this research study, in order to address to these issues, a novel and unique ANN model - General Regression Neural Network Fuzzy ART (GRNNFA) model had been developed based on the GRNN and the FA Algorithms. The former is extremely powerful for the identification of highly non-linear characteristics of a system, while the latter will enhance the model by clustering of data into representative kernels. As the kernels formulated by FA cannot be directly used with the GRNN, a new compression technique was formulated based on the k-nearest-neigbourhood theory to provide a closure to this approach. Also, unlike some of the ANN models, this model has been capable of on-line training (i.e. easily adaptable to newly available fire data). Therefore, it is suitable for fire modelling where continuous data, though rare, may be made available from time to time due to fire incidences and related studies reported. In the current research, both experimental and computational data were used to train this GRNNFA model. The new developed GRNNFA model was validated against also both by available experimental and computational data. The model can be used to assess and predict fire risk levels due to various fire scenarios including multiple fire origins in fire safety enclosure.

11215314.value: Potentially, the newly developed GRNNFA model in the current research can be further developed to become an overall framework for analysis of building fire risk. In longer terms, this model will be able to offer a much efficient and economic means for fire safety analysis in buildings which may assist in the enhancement of the Performance-Based Fire Codes in Hong Kong and other countries internationally.

11215614.value: 本項目在基於顯微視覺的光誘導介電泳平台上，採用瞬態運動分析方法，實現非侵入式、低成本的單細胞質量測量。 我們的研究團隊在基於顯微視覺的光誘導介電泳平台上，建立了生物細胞瞬態運動的一階系統瞬態響應模型。我們建立的系統瞬態響應函數可以很好的描述細胞在介電泳力場中的瞬態運動，並使用Raji細胞和紅血球細胞驗證我們提出的一階系統瞬態響應模型。我們通過測量細胞運動的初始速度和時間常數，實現了細胞運動軌蹟的精確建模。我們針對細胞在介電泳力場中瞬態運動的前期研究工作表明瞬態運動分析方法可以高效、靈活的應用於單細胞特性的研究。本項目的最終目標是在基於顯微視覺的光誘導介電泳平台上，結合微流控技術的光誘導介電泳芯片，實現細胞瞬態運動的快速分析與單細胞質量的測定。 為了實現本項目提出的非侵入式細胞質量測量的目標，我們需要研究以下幾個基本問題：1) 準確建立細胞在介電泳力場中瞬態運動的模型，並考慮電動現象與電致熱效應的相關影響；2) 開發基於顯微視覺的三維細胞運動跟踪算法，分析細胞在三維空間的平移和旋轉運動；3) 研究光誘導介電泳力與細胞瞬態運動響應的聯繫，進一步分析不同細胞的動力學特性；4) 優化光誘導介電泳實驗的相關參數，對細胞的運動軌跡進行仿真，根據細胞運動的最優軌跡參數，準確估算單細胞質量。本項目將通過嚴謹的科學實驗和數值分析仿真方法理解並解決以上這些基本問題，實現項目提出的研究目標。 項目主要的研究成果包括：a) 定制的光誘導介電泳平台用於自動單細胞質量測量；b)開發融合微流控技術的光誘導介電泳芯片，實現細胞在介質中的拋體運動；c ) 開髮用於自動識別並估算細胞體積的顯微視覺算法，並完成細胞三維運動的跟踪與分析；d) 通過科學實驗和數值仿真的交叉驗證，深入理解基於光誘導介電泳的瞬態運動相應。 本項目所開發的新技術將對單細胞質量及其特性的測定提供一個嶄新的思路，並相應的促進在細胞異質性的研究，癌細胞的識別，以及細胞生長等領域的潛在應用研發。

11215614.label: Realisation of objectives
11215614.value: All objectives of this projects were achieved, including the 1) development of an accurate model for single cell transient motion under an ODEP force field by transient motion analysis; 2) realization of a computerized algorithms to automatically isolate and calculate the transient motion of cells from microscope video-images in real-time; 3) experimental determination of ODEP system parameters for stimulation of transient motion of cells in different culturing medium with different fluidic permittivity and conductivity; and 4) experimentally determined the transient motion response of single cells and subsequently determined their mass through cross-validation with sedimentation theory. Using the method developed in this project, we measured the density and the mass values of 56 individual L1210 cells. Results showed that the densities of L1210 cells varied between 1.05 and 1.12g/ml, while the mass values were in the range of 350–1600pg. This result conforms in general with those obtained by the SMR (suspended microchannel resonators) method. This finding demonstrates that our method is practical for measuring the density and the mass of single cells. Although HL-60 cells have been widely investigated for many years, we could not find any relevant data on the density and mass of single HL-60 cell in the literature, therefore, we could not cross-check our experimental data as of now. In terms of finding the optimal parameters to induce the transient motion of cells in the ODEP platform, we have tried two different fluidic media, i.e., 0.1M and 0.2M sucrose solutions -- this allowed us to obtain a more generalized model for micro particles “sedimenting” in a microfluidics chip. In order to validate the developed particle trajectory model, polystyrene beads with diameters ranging from 5um to 25um were tested experimentally using the ODEP system. An image matching algorithm was used to analyze the image sequences of the 'sedimenting' microspheres and cells captured by the ODEP platform, and then the their trajectories and velocities were calculated. After the sedimentation velocity was obtained, a new correction factor for Stokes’ force in was calculated. The same sedimentation processing was used for the two kinds of cancer cells (i.e., L1210 and HL-60) with similar diameters (8–15lm) to determine the density and mass values of individual cancer cells. In developing the computerized program to automatically isolate and determine the transient motion of cells from videomicroscopy images, we used an image-matching-based algorithm capable of accurately determining the translational motion and self-rotational speed of cells. To automatically track a specific cell in a video featuring more than one cell, a background subtraction technique was used. To determine the rotational speeds of cells, a reference frame was automatically selected and curve fitting was performed to improve the stability and accuracy. Results show that the algorithm was able to accurately calculate the motion trajectories and self-rotational speeds of cells (up to ~150 rpm). Three key concepts were employed in this algorithm to make the speed extraction automatic, accurate, and reliable. (1) To achieve automated tracking of a cell, the cell is manually selected in the first frame of the video. It is then automatically tracked in the subsequent frames using the background subtraction technique. (2) A reference frame that is quite distinct from its adjacent frames is automatically selected according to the correlation coefficients between adjacent frames. (3) A parabolic curve is fitted for each peak of the maximum correlation coefficient sequence, which is calculated based on the maximum correlation coefficients between each frame of the video and the reference frame. We note that it is very difficult to determine the vertical velocity of a moving microsphere or cell from a top view just by using a single monocular microscope. However, we solved this problem by using an image matching method that could accurately track the vertical trajectories of the spheres/cells. When the microscope’s focal distance is fixed, the defocused images of a sphere/cell at different heights are unique. Because the diffractive light paths change the images depending on the sphere’s/cell's distance from the microscope lens, the standard defocused images were captured at different heights first. The location where a particle has the mostly clear image, i.e., a focused image, was set as the “zero height point” and the image obtained at this height was selected as the “zero height image.” Next, we let the microscope move its z-axis stage automatically towards the objective lens in 0.1um incremental steps while the microscope captured at each step an image of the static microsphere/cell. Once the falling microspheres had been captured in a video, the vertical position of each frame could be obtained by comparing them to these standard images. Both the standard images and the experimental images had to go through noise reduction, sphere/cell recognition, and feature extraction. Following feature correlation comparison between the standard and experimental images, it was straight forward to identify the most similar standard image with a known height. Combining the elapsed time information recorded in the video, a distance-time plot could be obtained from the sedimentation motion of a microsphere/cell. In summary, we have realized a rapid single leukemia cell density and mass determination method using an ODEP platform, which is based on a combination of computer vision, microparticle manipulation, and sedimentation theory principles. We have tested two kinds of mammalian leukemia cells and reported the results for the cellular mass and density values of 132 individual cancer cells. The results on L1210 are consistent with those from SMR tests (while there is no other existing data to compare our measured results for HL-60 cells), which demonstrate that our method is a practical, rapid, accurate, and multiplicative measurement technology for single cancer cell mass and density.

11215614.label: Major findings and research outcome
11215614.value: We have developed a non-invasive, inexpensive, and rapid method for measuring single cell mass on the basis of transient motion (sedimentary motion) analysis using an optically-induced dielectrophoresis (ODEP) and microvision-based platform. Our tests on mouse lymphocytic leukemia cells (L1210) and human leukemic cells (HL-60) have verified the practical viability of this method. The transient motion of microspheres and biological cells were proved to be first-order transient motion response in a microfluidic environment using an ODEP and microvision-based platform. A kernel function was derived to describe this transient motion. This function has been shown to matched to the experimental data for Raji cells, red blood cells (RBCs), and other suspended cancer cells from cell lines. The motions of the cells were induced by ODEP force, and a micro-vision algorithm was used to track the sedimentary trajectory of the cells -- which allowed us to determine the initial velocity and the transient time-constant of the cells. Our results indicate that transient motion analysis is an effective and flexible method for research into the physical properties of single cells. We have explored several fundamental issues related to this novel non-invasive measurement method: 1) Developed a model to predict suspended cells’ transient motion response, including electrokinetic phenomena and light-induced electrothermal forces under ODEP force field; 2) Developed microvision-based motion tracking algorithms to detect the cells' motion in 3D space, including translation and rotation, for microscopic image sequences analyses; (details of the algorithms are discussed in "Accurate Extraction of the Self-Rotational Speed for Cells in an Electrokinetics Force Field by an Image Matching Algorithm", Micromachnies, 8(9), 282, 2017); 3) Studied the relationships between ODEP force and the kinetic characteristics of cells for quantitative analysis of various cells, including HL-60 (human) and L1210 (mouse lymphocytic) leukemia cells; 4) Combined ODEP force, sedimentary theory, and micro-vision algorithms to successfully determined the mass and density of several types of cells, including Raji, L1210), and HL-60 cells. We believe that our work has shown the possibility of a new paradigm for the measurement of single cell mass and properties, which will in turn find potential applications in the fields of cellular heterogeneity research, cancer cell identification, and cell growth studies. We are also currently exploring how the ODEP-based cell manipulation technology developed in this project can be applied to cell-injection applications ("A Review of Automated Microinjection of Zebrafish Embryos", Micromachines, 2019, 10(1), 7).

11215614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11215614.value: We have shown through this project that the density and mass of micro-scale entities such as beads and cells could be rapidly determined using an ODEP platform, which is based on a combination of computer vision, microparticle manipulation, and sedimentation theory principles. Essentially, the falling trajectory and velocity of individual cells or micro beads could be tracked and calculated utilizing micro-vision processing techniques. We envisioned that the following research directions can be explored using the ODEP system developed in this project: 1) Conduct experiments to significantly improve the throughput of this technique, i.e., use ODEP force to induce the sedimentary motion of many cells parallelly in an ODEP chip and use vision-tracking algorithms to determine the velocity and consequently the mass and density of each cell; 2) Use the principle of ODEP to induce cell translational and rotational motions in order to determine the electric properties of cells, i.e., cell membrane capacitance, conductance, etc; 3) Use ODEP to manipulate multiple microspheres in order to create supler-resolution imaging lens arrays. We will continue to submit proposals to the RGC, NSFC, and ITF to secure funds to continue the research directions described above.

11215614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11215614.value: We have developed a method to rapidly (~20s) determine the density and mass of single cells using an optically induced dielectrophoresis (ODEP) platform. The technique combines sedimentation theory, computer vision, and micro particle manipulation techniques on an ODEP microfluidic platform to determine the mass and density of micron-scale entities in a fluidic medium. Our team has performed many experiments to determine an universal correction factor to Stokes’ equation in expressing the drag force on a microparticle (i.e., a sphere or a suspended cell) as it falls towards the substrate surface of a microchannel. A theoretical model for micron-sized spheres settling towards an infinite plane in a microfluidic environment was derived and which was validated experimentally using five different sizes of microspheres (with diameters ranging from 5um to 25um). The same experimental process was applied to two kinds of leukemic cancer cells in an ODEP platform, and their density and mass were determined accordingly. Our tests on mouse lymphocytic leukemia cells (L1210) and human leukemic cells (HL-60) have verified the practical viability of this method. Potentially, this new method provides a new way of measuring the volume, density, and mass of a single cell in an accurate, selective, and repeatable manner.

11216014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11216014.value: Reliability assessment plays an important role in engineering design and maintenance management. Current methods for reliability assessment of complex systems have fundamental flaws, due to their inability to keep pace with new technologies, and to account for complex usage profiles. Failures of systems are common due to their complexity (e.g., airplane crashes caused by failed electronics, power grid shutdowns caused by failed sensors, and financial shut-downs due to failed servers). The impact of these failures to the society on safety, availability, and cost is staggering. Newly improved modeling techniques are needed for reliability and degradation assessment, fault diagnostics, and prognostics (the real-time prediction of reliability and the remaining useful life) of complex systems. The proposed research approach is a radically new approach, which focuses on effective and efficient reliability prognostics and system health management (PHM) for complex systems based on integration of failure time and degradation data, physics of failure knowledge, and the information on the actual field operational conditions of the systems. The proposed research methods can be applied to a wide range of complex systems, including electronic-rich systems, critical automotive components, and power systems. In particular, we will investigate its application to the rechargeable batteries, a widely used power sources in many electrical and electronic systems today. There is a strong industry demand both in Hong Kong and China to raise quality and reliability to a new international level. The proposed PHM technologies and remaining useful life (RUL) estimation methods will meet this challenge. The main objective of this research is to develop an integrated modeling approach for accurately predicting system health that helps engineers and scientists understand and quantify the impact of risk and uncertainty in making reliability and maintenance decisions. In particular, we will (i) develop new classes of integrated models that combine failure time and degradation data together with dynamic usage information to predict malfunctions and remaining useful life for complex systems, with a particular emphasis on battery systems; (iii) develop model validation metrics and test cases for validating and assessing the proposed methods. 系統可靠性評估對於工程設計和系統的維護管理具有重要意義。由於缺乏對新技術的利用以及沒有考慮複雜的實際使用情況，目前針對複雜系統的可靠性評估方法存在根本性的缺陷。現代的工程系統具有高度複雜性，因此系統失效是常見的現象(例如電子系統故障導致飛機失事，傳感器故障導致電網斷電，伺服器故障引發金融系統崩潰等)。這些問題在安全、有效性以及成本方面對社會帶來的影響是巨大的。針對這些複雜系統，我們需要研究新的建模方法來對系統的可靠性和衰退情況進行評估，診斷及預測系統失效。我們在這裡提出一種高效的新方法來解決這個問題。針對複雜系統的可靠性預測和系統健康管理，我們的方法主要關注以下方面的集成信息建模：系統失效時間和衰退數據， 失效的物理機理，和系統的實際使用情況。這種方法可以廣泛應用於各種複雜系統，包括電子系統，車載系統，和電力系統等。由於可充電電池在各種電子電氣系統中越來越重要的地位，我們將會特別關注該方法在可充電電池上面的應用。在香港以及中國大陸，工業界對於提高產品質量與可靠性有強烈的需求。我們提出的系統健康管理以及剩餘壽命預測方法將會推動這方面的進步。 為幫助工程師和科學家理解並且量化在制定系統可靠性和維護策略中的風險以及不確定性，本項目的主要目標是發展一種可以精準預測系統健康狀況的集成建模方法。我們將會提出一種新型的基於失效時間、衰退數據和動態使用信息的集成模型。該模型將會被用於預測複雜系統的故障以及剩餘有效壽命，特別是電池系統。我們將提出模型的有效檢驗方法，並且通過實際案例來驗證我們所提出的方法。

11216014.label: Realisation of objectives
11216014.value: Objective 1: Develop new classes of integrated models that provide accurate remaining useful life and system health prediction, integrate hard and soft failures, and allow for assessment of dynamic environment and root cause failure analysis. We have conducted a comprehensive review on the topic of prognostics and health management. We surveyed most related papers in the field, with a particular interest on data-driven methods. This has laid a solid foundation for our later work. We investigated and compared the performance of some data-driven prognostic methods for rechargeable batteries with hard failures, based on their health indicator measurements such as internal resistance and capacity. Some problems of the existing methods have been identified and possible improvements have been looked into. One key aspect of the RUL prognosis is the construction of the best prediction interval for failure occurrence. The interval should have a reasonable length and yield the best prediction power. In this work, we propose a new scheme, the Maximum Power Interval (MPI), for estimating the interval with maximum prediction power. The MPI guarantees the best prediction power under a given interval length. Some technical challenges involved in the MPI method were resolved using the maximum entropy principle and truncation method. A numerical simulation study confirmed that the MPI has better prediction power than other prediction intervals. A case study using a real industry data set was conducted to illustrate the capability of the MPI method. Linear Brownian motion with constant drift is widely used in remaining useful life predictions because its first hitting time follows the inverse Gaussian distribution. State space modelling of linear Brownian motion was proposed to make the drift coefficient adaptive and incorporate on-line measurements into the first hitting time distribution. In previous studies, an underlying assumption used in the state space modelling was that in the update phase of Kalman filtering, the predicted drift coefficient at the current time exactly equaled the posterior drift coefficient estimated at the previous time, which caused a contradiction with the predicted drift coefficient evolution driven by an additive Gaussian process noise. To alleviate such an underlying assumption, a new state space model is constructed. As shown in the experiment result, in the update phase of Kalman filtering, the predicted drift coefficient at the current time evolves from the posterior drift coefficient at the previous time. Moreover, the optimal Kalman filtering gain for iteratively estimating the posterior drift coefficient at any time is mathematically derived. Objective 2: Develop high- fidelity degradation models and estimation methods for battery capacity in order to assess battery health conditions and make prediction for battery RUL. Battery remaining useful life prediction under soft failure mode (i.e., a failure threshold is given) has also been investigated. Based on the charging experiment from some lithium-ion batteries, we proposed a prognostic method based on battery capacity degrading to 80% of its initial value. A state space model for lithium-ion battery capacity is first constructed to assess capacity degradation. Then, a spherical cubature particle filter (SCPF) is introduced to solve the state space model. Degradation data of 26 lithium-ion battery capacities was analyzed to validate the effectiveness of the proposed prognostic method. The analytical results show that the proposed prognostic method is effective in prediction of RUL of lithium-ion batteries, compared to an existing PF based prognostic method. Some lithium-ion battery materials show two-phase degradation behavior with evident inflection points, such as lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (Li(NiMnCo)O2 or NMC) cells. A model-based Bayesian approach was proposed to predict remaining useful life (RUL) for these types of batteries. First, a two-term logarithmic model is developed to capture the degradation trends of NMC batteries. By fitting the battery degradation data, it is experimentally demonstrated that the developed model is superior to existing empirical battery degradation models. A particle filtering–based prognostic method is then incorporated into the model to estimate the batteries' possible degradation trajectories. Correspondingly, the RUL values of NMC batteries are expressed in terms of probability density function. The effectiveness of the developed method is verified with our collected experimental data. The results indicate that the proposed prognostic method can achieve higher predictive accuracy than the existing two-term exponential model. Additionally, we looked in to models based on Brownian motion with adaptive drift for prognostics problem. In this work, a prognostic method based on nonlinear-drifted Brownian motion with multiple hidden states was proposed and then it is applied to predict remaining useful life of rechargeable batteries. In practice, different discharge rates (DDRs) would affect both usable battery capacity and battery degradation rate. Consequently, it is necessary to take DDRs into consideration when a battery prognostic method is designed. We propose a discharge-rate-dependent battery prognostic method that is able to track usable battery capacity affected by DDRs in the process of battery degradation and to predict RUL at DDRs. An experiment was designed to collect accelerated battery life testing data at DDRs, which are used to investigate how DDRs influence usable battery capacity, to design a discharge-rate-dependent state space model and to validate the effectiveness of the proposed battery prognostic method. Results show that the proposed battery prognostic method can work at DDRs and achieve high RUL prediction accuracies at DDRs. Objective 3: Develop model validation metrics and procedures that allow designers to assess prediction capability and optimize engineering design. Evaluate and test the proposed methods and algorithms using simulated data, experimental data, and field data. In this topic, we mainly focused on extracting information from vibration signals measured from working systems such as cutting tools and bearings. Novel algorithms have been developed for information extraction, feature selection and parameter optimization. In the particular example of cutter wear estimation in a milling process and bearing fault diagnosis, our methods have demonstrated to be superior than existing ones. We investigated a joint modeling method for hard failures where both degradation signals and time‐to‐event data are available. The mixed‐effects model is used to model degradation signals, and extended hazard model is used for the time‐to‐event data. The extended hazard is a general model which includes two well‐known hazard rate models, the Cox proportional hazards model and accelerated failure time model, as special cases. A two‐stage estimation approach is used to obtain model parameters, based on which remaining useful life for the in‐service unit can be predicted. The performance of the method is demonstrated through both simulation studies and a real case study. Rolling element bearings are widely used in various machines to support rotating shafts. Due to harsh working environments, the health condition of a bearing degrades over time. To analytically model the bearing degradation process, two novel mixed effects models are proposed. Each of the two mixed effects models is able to simultaneously model Phases I and II of the bearing degradation process. Consequently, two different closed-form distributions of bearing remaining useful life are derived from the two mixed effects models via Bayes’ theorem once real-time bearing condition monitoring data are available.

11216014.label: Major findings and research outcome
11216014.value: Finding 1: Develop a maximum power for prediction of the failure interval We proposed a new scheme, the Maximum Power Interval (MPI), for estimating the interval with maximum prediction power. The MPI guarantees the best prediction power under a given interval length. Some technical challenges involved in the MPI method were resolved using the maximum entropy principle and truncation method. Finding 2: Develop a discrete differential evolution algorithm for feature selection of extreme learning machine We proposed a discrete differential evolution (DE) algorithm to select input features for the extreme learning machine (ELM), and a continuous DE algorithm is used for parameter optimization of the mixed kernel function for the ELM. The experimental results indicate that the proposed adaptive evolutionary ELM-based tool wear estimation model can effectively estimate the tool wear in high-speed milling process. Finding 3: Develop a Gauss–Hermite integration based Bayesian inference to optimize wavelet parameters for bearing fault diagnosis As shown in Wang et al (2016), we proposed a new Gauss–Hermite integration based Bayesian inference method to estimate the posterior distribution of wavelet parameters. The Gauss–Hermite integration is introduced to analytically predict and update moments of the joint Gaussian distribution. Two comparisons with the fast kurtogram are used to demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve better visual inspection performances than the fast kurtogram. Finding 4: Develop a spherical cubature particle filter for remaining useful life prediction of lithium-ion batteries We proposed a prognostic method to predict the remaining useful life (RUL) of lithium-ion batteries, see Wang et al (2016). A state-space model for the lithium-ion battery capacity is first constructed to assess capacity degradation. Then, a spherical cubature particle filter is introduced to solve the state-space model. The analytical results show that the proposed prognostic method is more effective in the prediction of RUL of lithium-ion batteries, compared with an existing particle filter-based prognostic method. Finding 5: Develop a Wavelet-based statistical approach for monitoring and diagnosis of rolling bearings Motivated by the problem of monitoring and diagnosis of compound faults in rolling bearings at the early stage, in Fan et al (2018), we proposed a new approach by using statistical signal detection method and wavelet transform to handle the fault signals. This work aims at monitoring vibration signals and diagnosing fault types. Our simulation results show the proposed approach outperforms existing methods, especially at an early stage.

11216014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11216014.value: Prognosis of the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of a unit or system plays an important role in system reliability analysis and maintenance decision making. One key aspect of the RUL prognosis is the construction of the best prediction interval for failure occurrence. The interval should have a reasonable length and yield the best prediction power. In current practice, the center-based interval and traditional confidence internal are widely used. Although both are easy to construct, they do not provide the best prediction performance. In the future, we will continue to improve our existing methods on RUL prediction, with various industrial applications such as batteries, bearing, gearboxes. In particular, We will apply the MPI method to the recently developed RUL prognostic models and investigate its performance. We plan to study along these lines and will report the results in the future. Besides, we expect to develop an enhanced algorithm for the battery RUL prediction under hard failure mode. Methods will all be tested using comprehensive simulations and real data sets.

11216014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11216014.value: Reliability assessment plays an important role in engineering design and maintenance management. Current methods for reliability assessment of complex systems have fundamental flaws, due to their inability to keep pace with new technologies, and to account for complex usage profiles. Failures of systems are common due to their complexity. The impact of these failures to the society on safety, availability, and cost is staggering. Newly improved modeling techniques are needed for reliability and degradation assessment, fault diagnostics, and prognostics (the real-time prediction of reliability and the remaining useful life) of complex systems. The proposed research approach is a radically new approach, which focuses on effective and efficient reliability prognostics and system health management (PHM) for complex systems based on integration of failure time and degradation data, physics of failure knowledge, and the information on the actual field operational conditions of the systems. The proposed research methods can be applied to a wide range of complex systems, including electronic-rich systems, critical automotive components, and power systems. In particular, we will investigate its application to the rechargeable batteries, a widely used power sources in many electrical and electronic systems today.
