11402814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11402814.value: Anti-corruption agencies and scholars alike agree that successful corruption prevention strategies are greatly facilitated by securing active public support. Yet the implementation of an anti-corruption community relations strategy is invariably constrained by the need to devote limited financial resources to the more immediate tasks of investigating, prosecuting and preventing corrupt activities. In many countries, as a consequence, the community relations strategy consists of little more than top-down sermons on the evils of corruption. Hong Kong’s Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is an exception. Over nearly forty years of community interaction through its decentralized local offices, it has successfully won public support for zero tolerance of corruption, defined as bribery. Yet, for two reasons, this strategy may now need refinement. First, perceptions of what constitutes corruption are changing rapidly from traditional notions of bribery to more sophisticated conflicts of interest, deferred advantages, money-laundering, other forms of cross-border corruption, and electoral fraud. Second, while the ICAC strongly emphasizes and communicates a generic message of zero tolerance of corruption to the public, its strategy is not specifically tailored to combat socially-embedded attitudes which might promote corruption in some groups but not in others. The ICAC’s original in-house research between 1977 and 1986 and our more recent research, which includes a small pilot survey of two districts, suggest that there are significantly different attitudes towards corruption, broadly defined, among various socio-economic groups in Hong Kong. The pilot survey gives us confidence that we can measure these differences among socio-economic groups on three cross-checking dimensions. We will ask our respondents how they perceive and define corruption; their willingness to tolerate corruption judged by their reactions to scenarios in which behavior might be suspected to be corrupt; and their willingness to report corruption. Our present proposal is to extend the pilot survey to 1,000 respondents. From the results, we will obtain a more comprehensive picture of corruption perceptions which will enable us to accomplish three important research objectives: to provide a composite disaggregated picture of the experience and perceptions of corruption of different socio-economic groups across Hong Kong; to aid in the formulation of more targeted and evidence-based policy by providing information on changing public perceptions of corruption; and to help in the development of more sophisticated methodologies for assessing perceptions of corruption. 摘要 反腐機構和反腐學者一致認為，成功的預防腐敗策略在很大程度上得益於它能夠獲得公眾的支持。然而，實施反腐敗的社區關係策略不可避免地受到財力的制約，因為有限的財政資源需要優先分配給包括調查、起訴以及預防腐敗等活動在內的更緊迫的任務。正因為如此，在許多國家，把社區關係作為反腐策略的實際意義僅僅停留在對腐敗危害性的自上而下的說教而已。在這方面，香港廉政公署是個例外。香港廉政公署通過其分設與各區的社區關係處，擁有將近四十年的與社區互動經驗，成功地贏得了公眾對腐敗行為（指賄賂）的零容忍。 然而，出於如下兩個原因，香港的社區關係策略需要進一步優化。首先，對於什麼是腐敗的認知在迅速變化。傳統的觀念認為腐敗就是賄賂，而現在的腐敗概念則包括更為複雜的利益衝突，延後的利益兌現，洗錢和其它形式的跨境腐敗，以及賄選行為等。第二，儘管廉政公署努力強調並向公眾推廣對腐敗的零容忍，但其策略並未具體地針對嵌入社會深層的特定社會群體的態度。 廉政公署於1997年到1986年間開展的入戶調查以及我們近期在兩個居民區所作的一個初步調查發現，不同的社會經濟群體對腐敗（廣義而言）的態度存在着很大分別。我們的初步調查結果促使我們從三個可以相互檢驗的維度來測量社會經濟群體之間的認知差異。我們會詢問受訪者對腐敗的認知和定義；考量他們在某些場景下遇到可能涉嫌腐敗的行為時會採取何種行動，以此來判斷他們容忍腐敗的程度；最後是測量他們舉報腐敗行為的意願。 我們計劃在先前初步調查的基礎上將受訪者擴展到1000位。從調研的結果中，我們試圖勾畫出一幅更為全面的腐敗認知的圖景，這將有助於我們實現三個重要的研究目標：提供一個香港各社會經濟群體在有關腐敗的經歷和認知方面既全面而又細化的圖景；通過分析公眾對腐敗認知的變化為制定更有針對性和更以事實為基礎的廉政政策提供有益的信息；最後，也期待對日益複雜的評估腐敗認知的研究方法作出貢獻。

11402814.label: Realisation of objectives
11402814.value: The success of the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) in Hong Kong has attracted considerable scholarly attention. However, the extent to which the public has contributed to Hong Kong’s anti-corruption effectiveness is understudied. Little is known about how the general public perceives corruption. Even less clear is how perceptions and attitudes towards corruption may vary among socio-economic groups. Our research was intended to address this issue. Specifically, our project aimed to examine how the public in Hong Kong responded to corruption historically and currently; how and to what extent public perceptions of corruption varied among the public and what might explain the variation; and how public attitudes towards corruption contributed or posed challenges to controlling corruption in Hong Kong and why. In addition to obtaining a disaggregated picture of the corruption perceptions of different socio-economic groups across Hong Kong, our research also aimed to aid in the formulation of more targeted and evidence-based policy by providing information on changing public perceptions of corruption. Last but not least, the project sought to address the question of whether corruption is measurable by developing valid and reliable methodologies to assess perceptions of corruption. The project fully achieved these objectives. To begin with, the research teams conducted extensive desk-based analysis of government documents, media reports and relevant scholarly works on perceptions of corruption. Special attention was given to the variation of perceptions and attitudes towards corruption among citizens. The detailed desk-based documentary analysis and literature review allowed us to develop hypotheses about the possible variation of attitudes in Hong Kong society and conceivable explanations of how these variations may have arisen. On this basis, we proceeded with data collection from three major sources. First, we obtained the raw data of the ICAC’s mass surveys from 1977 to 1986 and annual surveys from 1987 to 2017. This database gave us a general chronological picture of the patterns and characteristics of the public perceptions of corruption in Hong Kong. But it also indicated that there had been insufficient effort to disaggregate public attitudes to identify and explain the different attitudes among social groups. Consequently, and using the dataset as a backdrop, we conducted an original survey in 2015. In the survey, we employed three measurements to detect variations in public perceptions and attitudes towards corruption. The first was an assessment of respondents’ definitions and tolerance of corruption in general, in which we asked them to indicate their level of tolerance of corruption on a scale from 0 to 10 with 10 being the highest tolerance. Our second measurement consisted of scenarios designed to assess how respondents might react to different forms of corruption. Some forms of corruption might appear less harmful than others and hence might be perceived as acceptable. Lastly, we also examined people’s willingness to report corruption to see whether and to what extent they might take action to confront corruption. With the help of the Social Sciences Research Centre (SSRC) of Hong Kong University, we distributed the questionnaire using probability-based sampling methods and received a total of 1,025 valid responses which represented various socio-economic groups. We then supplemented the survey by conducting in-depth interviews with selected respondents and with retired and serving ICAC officials. The face-to-face interviews provided us with valuable qualitative information on social perceptions and attitudes towards corruption and on how the ICAC’s community relations strategy was successfully implemented to engage the public in controlling and preventing corruption. The successful data collection efforts provided us with a composite disaggregated picture of public perceptions of corruption in Hong Kong and led to important findings. We found, for example, that age and educational attainment have an important impact on people’s perceptions of corruption. We further identified two necessary conditions that might determine people’s propensity to report corruption when they were confronted with suspected cases: one is a lower level of tolerance of corruption and the other a higher level of trust in the government’ s anti-corruption effectiveness. Our chronological research showed that these two factors contributed greatly to Hong Kong’ s success in controlling corruption in the past four decades. Our research has strong policy implications for future corruption prevention in Hong Kong and possibly for other jurisdictions as well. We argue, based on the research findings, that controlling corruption should not only rely on institutional engineering in a top-down fashion, as seen in the efforts to establish the rule of law and effective anti-corruption agencies (ACAs), but should also strive to increase public awareness and social intolerance of corruption through bottom-up efforts. The effective interaction between top-down and bottom-up approaches to corruption prevention has enabled the Hong Kong society to remain clean.

11402814.label: Major findings and research outcome
11402814.value: The research findings of this project are manifest mainly in three areas. First, based on rich empirical evidence, we have identified a number of factors that are key to Hong Kong’s success in fighting corruption. Among them, the ICAC’s continuous efforts to change public attitudes towards corruption and the ensuing low social tolerance for corruption are particularly noticeable and contributed considerably to Hong Kong’s transition from a corrupt-prone society to a clean one. (See, for example, Scott & Gong, 2019; Gong & Xiao, 2017; Scott, 2016; Scott & Gong, 2015; Gong, Wang & Ren, 2015). Second, Hong Kong’s success in fighting corruption and the ICAC’s strategy towards changing social attitudes may be appealing to other regions which are facing corruption as a major challenge. Although devising a bottom-up approach to controlling corruption may draw on the Hong Kong model, there is no “one-size-fits-all” template. It is important to keep in mind that anti-corruption policies and measures should be tailor-made to fit specific social contexts. The findings of our comparative analysis of corruption and anti-corruption reforms in Hong Kong and Mainland China confirm this. (See, for example, Gong & Scott, 2017; Gong & Xiao, 2017; Li, Gong & Xiao, 2016; Gong & Scott, 2015; Scott; 2015; Gong, 2015) Third, our findings have confirmed that not only corruption is measurable, but we can also develop measurements for anti-corruption effectiveness. Toward that end, we have further distinguished people’s trust in an anti-corruption agency from their perceptions of its performance. We argue that perceived effectiveness in combatting corruption may lead to "generalised trust", but there is no necessary positive linear relationship between effectiveness and institutional trust because positive perceptions may be based on the agency’s previous achievement rather than its current performance. Our surveys in Hong Kong, Taipei and Changsha illustrate this (See, for example, Scott & Gong, 2019; Xiao, Gong, Yu, Zhuang & Yuan, under review). We have developed a new GRF proposal based on this finding to study the relationship between institutional trust and perceptions of effectiveness in corruption prevention. The research outcomes from this project are highly satisfactory. We published 2 books, 12 articles and book chapters in English and 5 articles in Chinese as a result of this project and other relevant research. We also made 8 presentations at international and regional conferences to disseminate the research findings.

11402814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11402814.value: We have found from conducting this project that the public perceptions of corruption and anti-corruption performance are multi-faceted. They include not only people’s assessments of the levels, causes and consequences of corruption, but also their trust in the anti-corruption agency and their satisfaction with its effectiveness. The relationship between institutional trust and perceptions of anti-corruption effectiveness is particularly complex, because these elements are not necessarily complementary. We have designed a new research project to explore how and why these two variables may deviate from each other and what explains the disparities between them. The new research has been submitted as a GRF proposal with the following objectives: to conduct a longitudinal analysis of institutional trust and perceptions of effectiveness with reference to the ICAC, drawing on its own survey data and our previous research; to conduct a new survey specifically designed to ascertain levels of institutional trust and perceptions of effectiveness in the ICAC; to analyze findings relevant to building social intolerance of corruption, particularly, public willingness to report corruption and effective resource allocation; and to explore the implications of the Hong Kong experience for other regions.

11402814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11402814.value: Successful anti-corruption strategies require active public support. Yet the implementation of an anti-corruption community relations strategy is invariably constrained by limited financial resources. In many countries, as a consequence, the community relations strategy consists of little more than top-down sermons on the evils of corruption. Hong Kong’s Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is an exception. It has successfully won public support for zero tolerance of corruption. However, this strategy may now need refinement. First, perceptions of what constitutes corruption are changing rapidly from traditional notions of bribery to more sophisticated forms. Second, while the ICAC strongly emphasizes and communicates a generic message of zero tolerance of corruption to the public, its strategy is not specifically tailored to combat socially-embedded attitudes which might promote corruption in some groups but not in others. We conducted an original survey of 1,025 respondents. From the results, we obtained a dataset of corruption perceptions which enabled us to accomplish three important research objectives: providing a composite disaggregated picture of corruption perceptions of different socio-economic groups across; aiding in the formulation of more targeted and evidence-based policies; and helping in the development of more sophisticated methodologies for assessing perceptions of corruption.

11403014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11403014.value: Recently there has been a resurgence of interest in Confucian political philosophy and numerous attempts to analyze ways in which it may contribute to a political philosophy for East Asia, how it may need to be modified to suit the contemporary context, and how it can contribute to a dialogue with Western political theories. However, Confucianism is only one school of thought from China’s long philosophical history, and there are numerous other political theories from China’s past that have the potential to make important contributions to contemporary debates. Furthermore, while it is acknowledged that Confucianism faces important challenges that must be overcome in order to profitably come into dialogue with Western political philosophy, there has been little recognition of the fact that it has long been challenged from within its own historical tradition, perhaps nowhere more strongly than by Han Fei. Furthermore, far from merely being a critic of Confucianism, Han Fei advances his own unique positive vision of political organization. However, his system has rarely been engaged with in an attempt to learn from it. As such, a deeper understanding of Han Fei’s political philosophy can lead to challenges to both Western political theories and Confucian political thought. By reconstructing Han Fei’s philosophy, I demonstrate that it has much to offer those interested in political theory, in Asia as well as in the world at large. He offers us a strong defense of the value of engaging in the history of political philosophy, a claim that is often questioned today. Furthermore, while he does not directly tackle many of the issues that are the central concerns of contemporary political philosophers, often we can, by reconstructing his philosophy and analyzing what his principles commit him to, determine how he would address numerous issues of contemporary interest. This project does not advocate a return to Han Fei’s Legalist political theory in its entirety. There are many areas in which Han Fei gets it wrong, and he seems to be blind to certain effective and appealing alternatives. However, by constructively engaging first with Han Fei himself and subsequently with important issues in contemporary political philosophy, this work will demonstrate not only that two vastly different political traditions can profitably be brought into dialogue but that regardless of our final analysis of the viability of Han Fei’s political philosophy, his arguments provide challenges that must be taken seriously by contemporary political philosophers. 近年儒家政治哲學重新受到關注。有許多研究嘗試分析儒家政治哲學如何能有助建立一套適合亞洲的政治哲學，儒家如何改變以適應當代的環境，以及儒家如何與西方政治理論對話。但其實儒家只是中國衆多哲學思想的其中一個學派，倘有許多其他的政治理論也能對當代的討論帶來幫助。而且儒家必須克服許多重要的挑戰才能與西方政治哲學作有效益的對話。 韓非對儒家不僅作出有力的挑戰，同時他也提出獨特的政治理念。可是這些挑戰與創見卻備受忽視，鮮有全面的研究。深入認識韓非的學說可以令我們反思儒家以及西方的政治思想。例如政治哲學史的價值在現代受到質疑，但是韓非卻維護政治哲學史的價值。儘管韓非沒有直接探討現代政治哲學的核心議題，可是只需要透過重建韓非的學説、分析他的主張，就可以估量韓非對這些議題的回應。 本研究計劃並非主張全盤接受韓非的學說。事實上韓非的學說也有錯漏，韓非無視其他可行的選擇。但是，透過重新審視韓非及現代政治哲學的核心議題，本研究計劃不僅展示兩個不同的政治傳統能進行有效益對話，而且無論最終我們如何評價韓非的思想，現代政治哲學家必須認真面對韓非的政治論述及其構成的挑戰。

11403014.label: Realisation of objectives
11403014.value: This project had three major objectives, and substantial progress was made in realizing all of them. The first objective was to deepen our understanding of the political philosophy of the great pre-Qin synthesizer and political philosopher Han Fei. This objective has been addressed and completed in a variety of ways. First, I presented several papers at conferences, and wrote several articles and a book directly addressing and elucidating Han Fei’s political philosophy. Each of these products furthered our understanding of various aspects of Han Fei’s political philosophy as well as providing groundwork upon which to address the second and third objectives of this project. In addition, by way of an article and a book on Han Fei’s predecessor, Shen Dao, I came to a better understanding of what underlay Han Fei’s political philosophy and how his ideas developed. While not ostensibly on the topic of “Han Fei’s Political Philosophy,” my book on Shen Dao provided vital background information necessary for further study and investigation of Han Fei’s own political philosophy and its similarities and divergences from that of Shen Dao. In particular, writing this book allowed me to extensively develop my understanding of Han Fei’s position on the role of the ruler, the establishment of fixed standards, and the source of the law. The second and third objectives of this project were hindered in part by the fact that the RGC decided not to allow funds to be used for the travel that my original project proposed as the basis for this research. Therefore, research trips to the United States to work with those more versed in the history of Western political philosophy and contemporary political philosophy than I had to be cancelled. However, I believe that I was able to overcome this and fulfill these objectives in my output. Nonetheless, the articles and books written do engage both with the history of Western political philosophy and with a range of issues in contemporary political philosophy. In particularly, they are all written from the perspective of an analytic philosopher and deal with a range of issues and topics that were both seen as central to the history of Western political philosophy and continue to be seen as central in contemporary political philosophy. Topics addressed include how to justify political authority, the role of human nature in the political realm, what undergirds and justifies legal punishment, what should be the role of morality in politics, and numerous others. Therefore, while I believe that there is much more work left to be done in bringing Han Fei into greater conversation with the Western world, I believe that a substantial amount of progress was made. While there were a range of important findings throughout this project, I highlight three major findings below: 1. The findings laid out in my book “The Shenzi Fragments: A Philosophical Analysis and Translation”. Here, I demonstrate that Shen Dao works with a conception of the natural world as fixed and following a set of regular patterns, a feature he wishes to replicate in the social and political realm. Just as an understanding of the natural world will allow it to be utilized for human benefit, so too will an understanding of aspects of human beings, in particular their dispositions, allow for the effective organization of the state. In particular, Shen Dao believes that there are three psychological dispositions that must be taken into account: people act based upon their own interests, their strengths and abilities vary, and feelings of resentment and expectation arise when decisions are seen to be subjectively determined. Shen Dao thinks that the ruler must implement a fixed set of standards and unfailingly adhere to them. While simply having fixed standards is better than the alternative, Shen Dao does believe that the content of these standards matter, as, in order to develop and preserve the order and strength of the state, it is important that these standards accord with the Way. And understanding the Way involves understanding the properties of the world around us and the disposition of all that we interact with, from the natural world to the human world. This allows us to better understand the starting point of much of Han Fei’s political philosophy as well as providing an entry point into investigations into Han Fei’s conception of the “Dao” and the role it plays in his political philosophy – which is the second major finding: 2. Han Fei’s conception of the “Dao” and its role in his political philosophy: This is the topic of my forthcoming chapter in the Oxford Handbook of Chinese Philosophy. There, I demonstrate that Han Fei lays out a well developed and integrated conception of the "dao" and its impact on both the natural and human worlds. Given the facts about the way that the universe actually is and the way that human beings actually are, it is necessary that members of communities act in particular ways as prerequisites for their survival and flourishing. The philosophy that Han Fei develops shows a keen awareness of the "dao" underlying all natural and human processes, and the various methods, laws, and techniques that he advises the ruler to take up and implement are all aimed at ensuring that the members of the community act in the ways that will best ensure the community’s survival, particularly in instances in which the members would otherwise be disinclined to so act. He uses his conception of the "dao" as the basis for constructing a mechanical bureaucratic and legal leviathan to which the ruler plays the role of the phantom oiler. Emulating the cosmic dao while at the same time tying all his tools back to this "dao," the ruler remains a mysterious figure, one whose image is made all the more awesome by the inevitability of his reactions to those within the state whose actions do not accord with his conception of the "dao". 3.The third set of findings come out in my book on Han Fei’s political philosophy, currently under review. In this book, I show that a) Han Fei begins from the perspective of the strength and stability of the state and justifies that state by reference to the order that only it can create and sustain. In addition, I demonstrate that Han Fei provides arguments that morality within the political sphere not only is not useful, it can be positively disastrous. These arguments are brought into conversation with opposing arguments raised by early Confucians as well as with contemporary arguments on the question of whether political philosophy is a subset of moral philosophy or whether it has its own normativity. I also demonstrate that Han Fei has a unique understanding of the justification of punishment that does not rely on notions of desert and demonstrate how an understanding of these features of his thought may be useful in certain contemporary debates. These findings lead to the final finding of the volume, which works to tie Han Fei’s conception of the “dao”, as elucidated in point 2 above and Shen Dao’s understanding of the law as elucidated in point 1 above into a deeper understanding of Han Fei’s own understanding of the law and its role and limits.

11403014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11403014.value: The "Han Feizi" is such a diverse and rich text that opportunities for engaging with and learning from it are almost unlimited. I am currently working on two projects that expand on the work done in this one. The first is a book project entitled "Explaining & Illustrating the Laozi: A Translation and Analysis of the Earliest Commentaries on the Laozi". This book, written with Prof. Eric L. Hutton, examines the two earliest commentaries on the "Laozi", which are chapters of the "Han Feizi". We will submit our proposal to a publisher in the next few months. A second book project, co-edited with Prof. Henrique Schneider, is collection of essays entitled "Adventures in Realism". This volume attempts to take insights from Han Fei and other early Chinese Realists and apply them to contemporary moral and political issues. We shall be submitting this volume in the next six months.

11403014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11403014.value: Recently there has been a resurgence of interest in early Chinese political philosophy and analyses ways in which it may contribute to political philosophy, how it may need to be modified to suit the contemporary context, and how it can dialogue with Western political theories. However, the focus has primarily been on Confucianism, and little work has been done analyzing the potential contributions of other early Chinese thinkers. Han Fei provides strong challenges to Confucian political theory and advances his own unique positive vision of political organization. A deeper understanding of Han Fei’s philosophy thus leads to challenges to both Western political theories and Confucian political thought. By reconstructing Han Fei’s philosophy, I demonstrate it has much to offer those interested in political theory. He offers us a strong defense of the value of engaging in the history of political philosophy, a claim that is often questioned today. Furthermore, while he does not directly tackle many of the issues that are the central concerns of contemporary political philosophers, often we can, by reconstructing his philosophy and analyzing what his principles commit him to, determine how he would address numerous issues of contemporary interest.

11403114.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11403114.value: 中国的“血汗钱”和协商正义

11403114.label: Co - Investigator(s)
11403114.value: Dr Ng, Kwaihang Prof Peerenboom, Randall

11403114.label: Project Objectives
11403114.value: Different from previous studies that rely on court archive, legal regulations, sporadic interviews, published judgments, media reports, and anecdotal accounts to study criminal justice in China, in this Project we will employ a new method – by directly examining the dynamics of the criminal trial and reconciliation processes. It will examine two categories of factors that affect the process and outcome of criminal reconciliation: social norms of the offenders and victims toward the relationship between economic compensation and justice; political and bureaucratic considerations on social stability, petitions, avoidance of appeal, and backlog of cases. They will form the basis to understand the developing norms on justice and the operational patterns of Chinese criminal practice. China’s criminal justice has long been regarded as repressive. The Project seeks to understand, through the interactions in the process of criminal reconciliation, how criminal justice is negotiated. It will explore not just the bargaining between the victim and the defendant, but also the role of the courts. Specifically, by looking at the varied interpretations on money and justice of victims and defendants, and political, economic, and bureaucratic pressures the courts are subject to, we will depict a more dynamic yet comprehensive picture of this negotiated process. Criminal reconciliation has been hailed for achieving efficiency and social harmony in China’s criminal justice (Song ed. 2011, Chen 2008). This Project explores the extent to which criminal reconciliation may undermine the rights of certain types of defendants or victims, especially those are pressured by the courts to reconcile. It will shed light on the hidden problems created by a system that values conciliation over adjudication and the delivery of justice. It thus raises important questions with regard to the policies on China’s criminal law procedures. Policy recommendations will be generated for reforms. Through examining how criminal justice is negotiated in China, this Project will provide a story on the relationship between law, money, and politics in China’s context. It is widely regarded as illegitimate or immoral to compare, bargain for, and manipulate the assigned monetary values, as if they were market prices (Carruthers 2010: 59), for subject matters such as life (Posner and Sunstein 2005), child (Zelizer 1985), or intimacy (Zelizer 2005). Why exchanges between life, justice, and money have been well received and even promoted in contemporary China? Exploring the forces underneath the interactions in criminal conciliation in China, it will enrich the literature of comparative studies on money and justice, which has most drawn from the experience of other countries.

11403114.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11403114.value: Despite the fact that criminal reconciliation is key to understand the current policy “Balancing Leniency and Severity” in China’s criminal justice, the existing literature has rarely examined the factors that affect its process and outcome. To fill the gap, this Project will expand our preliminary study to six courts with their representative profiles of different levels of caseload, court hierarchy, economic and institutional development, political pressures, and judicial professionalism. Drawing upon court ethnography and interviews with relevant judges, victims, defendants, and their family members, this Project will explore the impact of two categories of factors—social and political—on the operation of China’s criminal justice. The findings of this Project are critical to understand how criminal justice is exercised in Chinese courts. This focus on actual criminal court practices in turn allows us to explore how the patterns of criminal law practice affect the realization of legal rights and the underlying social and political forces shaping it. The Project will not only generate policy recommendations for reforms to the criminal procedure in China, but also provide evidence for broader theoretical debates about the relationship between law, money, politics, and perception of justice. 本研究通过“血汗钱”来理解中国刑事和解的过程和结果。通过对法院和当事人的访谈，揭示刑事过程中对钱的理解的文化含义以及政治在这一过程中的作用。

Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11403114.value: Legal commensuration is a complex mechanism of valuation. It entails social exchanges among parties in the litigational context. The way the law evaluates the unevaluable is guided by many specific facts about the parties and is influenced by its own institutional priorities. The criminal reconciliation process in China is used as a real-world empir- ical illustration. Drawing mainly on data collected from fieldwork in- vestigation of two basic-level courts, this article identifies two factors that affect the process and outcome of legal commensuration: institu- tional interests promoting reconciliation and the cultural meanings of money. Political considerations play a decisive role in incentivizing judges to facilitate reconciliation. But the cultural meanings of money also shape judicial outcomes. In particular, blood money is valued both for its certainty and its symbolic value as a token of apology. Through a brief comparison of the Chinese and U.S. courts, we show that our emphasis on process can generate a more socially grounded understanding of legal commensuration.

11403514.label: Project Objectives
11403514.value: The study aims at investigating the effectiveness of dialogic reading techniques with bilingual creative text in developing verbal creativity of young children. 11403514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11403514.value: This study aims to examine the effectiveness of dialogic reading techniques with creative texts in kindergartens using a quasi-experimental design. It also aims at documenting the grammatical profile in both Chinese and English of young children between 3 and 6 years old by using the Edmonton Narrative Norms Instrument for English and the Cantonese - Language Assessment, Remedial and Screening Procedure. We hypothesize that verbal creativity and syntactic complexity of young children will be enhanced in the experimental group compared to the control group. We also hypothesize that young children's grammatical profile will be more advanced after exposing to dialogic reading techniques for two years in the experimental group compared to the control group. Two types of language data will be collected by audio or video recording: composing a story, and free conversation. The study will contribute to developing effective reading instruction and promoting creativity in language education for young children. The ultimate goal is to prepare students for becoming both creative individuals and proficient language users. 是項研究透過一個擬實驗法的設計，探討採用對話式閱讀方法閱讀創意繪本的成效。研究亦會記述三至六歲幼兒的中文及英文的語法概況。我們假設實驗組幼兒的語文創造力和句法的複雜性較控制組幼兒發展佳。經過兩年以對話式閱讀方法培育，實驗組幼兒的語法概況亦較控制組幼兒發展為前。我們亦會透過錄音、錄影方式，搜集幼兒創作的故事和日常對話為廣東話和英語發展的語料，進行比較。是項研究希望為幼兒語言發展、創造力培訓和有效閱讀學法教提供實證，以兒童能成為有創意和精通雙語的個體為最終目標。

11403514.label: Realisation of objectives
11403514.value: The study aimed at investigating the effectiveness of dialogic reading techniques in kindergartens in enhancing young children’s Chinese and English language skills and verbal creativity. Two studies were conducted in 2014-2015/2015-2016 and . Study 1 was a pre-test and post-test quasi-experimental with a longitudinal design for 31 kindergarten children aged from 3 to 4 in both two K1 classes and two K2 classes from a local kindergarten (15 in the experimental group and 16 in the control group) to investigate their performance of language skills and verbal creativity after twice 4-week 12-session dialogic reading techniques respectively in Chinese. After a year, a follow-up study was conducted to see long-term changes. Study 2 was a pre-test and post-test quasi-experimental design on demonstrating the effect of dialogic reading with creative texts in English language and creativity performance for 89 kindergarten children aged from 4 to 5 years old in both three K2 classes and three K3 classes from same kindergarten (43 in the experimental group and 46 in the control group) after twice 4-week 12-session dialogic reading techniques respectively. Two-way ANOVA and One-way repeated measures ANOVA were used to analyze the cross sectional and longitudinal data provided by participants in both the experimental and control groups.

11403514.label: Major findings and research outcome
11403514.value: In the study of using Chinese creative text, there were significant differences in interaction effect in several variables (Receptive vocabularies, STT, Dependent Clause, and complexity index). Furthermore, the research has done the follow up test to investigate the lasting effect of the dialogic reading technique, 31 students could finish the whole four times testing, 15 experimental group and 16 control group, the results showed that there were significant differences of interaction effect on receptive vocabulary, STT, complexity index, AN, Story Grammer Unit, which suggested that the effect of dialogic reading technique can help experimental students to maintain or improve their Story telling and Chinese sentence complexity. In the study of using English creative text, there were also significant differences in interaction effects in several variables (Independent Clause, Dependent Clause, Complexity index, Clause unit and mean length of communication units). 11403614.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11403614.value: 弱势群体的联合：中国城乡交界处的污染抗争

11403614.label: Co - Investigator(s)
11403614.value: Dr Lora-Wainwright, Anna Dr Lu, Jixia

11403614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11403614.value: This project examines scale shifts and the formation of rural-urban environmental coalitions in China through a study of resistance against waste incineration. Many parts of rural China suffer from severe pollution (Lora-Wainwright 2013b), and the siting of waste incinerators in the countryside threatens to add to this burden (Balkan 2012). Since 2006 an anti-incinerator coalition—comprising sceptical experts, environmental NGO activists, academics, lawyers, and journalists—has formed in Beijing. NGO documents and our own pilot research reveal linkages between this urban coalition and rural communities opposed to incinerators. However, this remains unexplored by the literature. Activist coalitions promote diffusion of information and strategy between previously unconnected sites (Givan et al 2010). Through “frame bridging” and “brokerage,” they can have the important effect of “scaling-up” environmental campaigns from localised affairs to broader social movements (Rootes 2009; McAdam & Boudet 2012). This occurred in the United States, where networked anti-incinerator activism promoted more environmentally sustainable ways of treating waste and rejuvenated a green movement heavily oriented towards institutionalised lobbying (Szasz, 1994; Gottlieb 2002). Yet the processes through which localised environmental campaigns develop coalitions and form larger movements remain poorly understood (McAdam & Boudet 2012: 134). Our research would examine how Chinese rural dwellers—often assumed to be “isolated” from intermediary support from outside activists (Van Rooij 2010)—form coalitions with networked urban environmentalists, and how this affects campaign processes and outcomes. It addresses several questions: how do rural-urban anti-incinerator coalitions form, and how are tensions overcome? How do coalitions affect campaign tactics and outcomes, and participants’ perceptions of the issue? Why do Chinese urban environmental activists—previously assumed to shun linkages with pollution victims in favour of an approach “embedded in the state” (Ho 2007)—cooperate with rural anti-incinerator campaigners? What do these cases reveal about the potential, and obstacles, for movement expansion in an authoritarian state? Our project would adopt a top-down and bottom-up approach in studying rural-urban anti-incinerator coalitions in China. It would examine anti-incinerator activism in three villages, in Hebei, Jiangsu, and Sichuan provinces. Following Mertha (2008), sites are selected based on outcomes, with one “success,” one “failure,” and one “mixed outcome.” We would conduct in-depth qualitative research in these three locations to better understand how rural dwellers fight pollution, and how they form linkages with wider networks. We would also interview participants in the Beijing-based anti-incinerator coalition to examine urban-rural networks from a top-down perspective. 该项目通过抵抗垃圾焚烧的案例，研究中国城乡环境联合的规模转变和形成。 中国农村许多地区倍受重污染损害(Lora-Wainwright 2013b),在农村建造垃圾焚烧炉成为加重污染负担的威胁(Balkan 2012)。2006年，一个反垃圾焚烧的联合体在北京形成，其中包括持怀疑态度的专家，民间环保组织的积极分子，学者，律师以及记者。民间组织的记录以及研究者自行的试点研究均揭示了该城市联合体同反对垃圾焚烧的农村社区之间的联系。然而，该联系仍无文献研究。 积极分子的联合促进了先前孤立的各个地点之间的信息和策略的传播(Givan et al 2010)。通过“框架搭桥”(“frame bridging”)和 “居间联络” (“brokerage”),无论是在地方事务还是在更宽泛的社会运动方面，他们都能够取得扩大环保运动规模(“scaling-up”)的重要影响(Rootes 2009; McAdam & Boudet 2012)。美国已经有此经历，它的反垃圾焚烧的积极分子相互联系，找到了更多环保的可持续的垃圾处理方法，并且为一场着重制度化游说的绿色运动重新注入了活力(Szasz, 1994; Gottlieb 2002)。然而，地方环保运动产生联合以及形成更大规模运动的过程却很少被了解(McAdam & Boudet 2012: 134)。 中国农村居民通常被认为得不到外界积极分子的中间支持(Van Rooij 2010)，此项目旨在研究他们是如何与城市中交互联系的环保人士形成联合的，及其对运动过程和结果的影响。研究的问题包括：城乡反垃圾焚烧联合是如何形成的、紧张氛围是如何缓解的？不同的联合对运动的策略和结果有什么影响、参与者对该问题持怎样的观点？之前有观点认为中国城市环保积极分子倾向于与政府合作而避免与污染受害者打交道(Ho 2007)，他们为什么又会同农村反垃圾焚烧的运动者合作呢？这些案例反映出一个专制国家中运动扩展的哪些潜力和障碍？ 该项目采取自上而下和自下而上的方法来研究中国城乡反垃圾焚烧联合，研究的对象为河北省、江苏省和四川省三个村庄中的反垃圾焚烧积极分子。参照Mertha (2008)，研究选址以结果为依据，分别为一“胜”，一“败”，一“混合结果”。研究者将在上述三个地点进行深度定性研究，以期更好地了解农村居民如何抵抗污染、如何与更宽泛的人际网形成联系。研究者也会采访在北京的反垃圾焚烧联合的参与者，来自上而下地研究城乡人际网。

11403814.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11403814.value: 民主完美主義：自由主義與儒家的觀點

11403814.label: Project Objectives
11403814.value: (1) Construct a robust normative concept and political theory of democratic perfectionism as distinct from both liberal perfectionism and political liberalism (2) reconceive constitutionalism, social justice and political leadership (in a liberal society) from the perspective of democratic perfectionism (3) construct a normative political theory of Confucian perfectionism from the perspective of democratic perfectionism without the wholesale embrace of the liberal element associated with the latter (4) expand Confucian democratic perfectionism to the areas of Confucian constitutionalism, Confucian social justice and Confucian political meritocracy.

11403814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11403814.value: Over the past two decades, political theorists and philosophers in East Asia and beyond have been struggling with a non-liberal mode of political regime and practice related to East Asia’s Confucian philosophical and societal context. As a result, Confucian political theory has emerged as an important sub-field in political theory. For instance, although Western political scientists such as Samuel Huntington once called ‘Confucian democracy’ a contradiction in terms, no informed scholar nowadays would subscribe to such a presumption not least because of the successful democratic transitions of East Asian, and historically Confucian, countries such as South Korea and Taiwan but also because of the collective endeavours of scholars to advance a normatively compelling and sociopolitically practicable mode of democracy in East Asia distinct from Western-style democracies – namely, Confucian democracy. Given the impressive diversity of Confucian political theories in terms of style, political orientation, interpretive angle and methodology, it is difficult to single out the most distinctive feature(s) that these theories have in common as Confucian political theory per se. Nevertheless, it appears that most Confucian political theories hold some shared perfectionist assumptions in common, namely: (1) Confucian ethics is a kind of perfectionist ethics that assumes the existence of the objectively good life and thus aims at the moral perfection of the people; (2) given the inseparability of Confucian ethics and politics, the supreme goal of Confucian politics lies in promoting the objectively good life and securing the socioeconomic conditions that enable such a life; and therefore (3) the state in a Confucian polity is morally authorised to promote a particular (Confucian) conception of the good life. The underlying argument is that democracy is either only instrumentally valuable or unimportant provided that the perfectionist ends are promoted by the state. In this book project, I will attempt to theorise a form of Confucian perfectionism that is fully compatible with the intrinsic value of democracy. To do so, I will first construct a robust normative concept and political theory of democratic perfectionism by critically engaging with liberal perfectionist theory while testing its practical plausibility in the areas of constitutionalism, distributive justice and political leadership. Then, from the perspective of democratic perfectionism thus constructed, I will explore a normatively attractive theory of Confucian perfectionism that is robustly democratic and culturally relevant in East Asia and equally test its plausibility in a contemporary Confucian cultural and societal context. 在過去的二十年裡，東亞及其他的政治理論家和哲學家一直努力在東亞的儒家哲學及社會脈絡中，探討一個非自由主義的政治制度和的它相關的實踐。正因如此，儒家政治理論已經成為政治理論中一個重要的環節。例如，即使西方政治學家，如塞繆爾•亨廷頓，曾經指出“儒家民主”是個自相矛盾概念，但現在相關領域的學者再不贊同此等假設。這不單是因為東亞傳統的儒家國家，如韓國和台灣，已成功完成民主化過程，同時亦因為不少學者正努力發展一套原則上有說服力，社會政治上具可行性，以及與西方民主制度相異的民主模式―─儒家民主。 即使不同的儒家政治理論在風格上，政治取向上，詮釋角度上和方法上有多樣性，但是我們仍不能從這些理論中尋找出這些儒家政治理論共同並且最鮮明的特點。儘管如此，似乎大多數的儒家政治理論都共同擁有一些完美主義的假設，包括：（1）儒家倫理是一種完美主義的道德理論，它認為客觀的美善人生是可能的，所以它以成就人類完美的道德情操作為目標；（2）基於儒家倫理與政治的不可分割性，儒家政治的最高目標在於推動客觀的美善人生和確保社會和經濟的條件可促成美善人生；（3）在儒家政治制度下的政府有道義的權責宣揚此特定的儒家式的美善人生。這背後有一隱藏的論點：國家所宣揚的完美主義是一種目標，在這目標下，民主只有工具性的價值，而其他特點並不重要。 在此書的項目中，我會嘗試把儒家完美主義的概念理論化，並把它整合成一種與民主本質價值完全相符的一種理論。要做到這一點，我會先研究自由完美主義理論，同時測試其在憲政，平等正義和政治領導等領域的實際可行性；從而建構一個在道德概念上和政治理論上健全穩固的民主完美主義理論。接著，我會由我所建構的民主完美主義的角度出發，探索出一套理論上有吸引力儒家完美主義。此理論不單具民主的特徵，同時合適東亞文化背景。最後我會測試此理論於當代儒家文化和社會合理性。

11404214.label: Realisation of objectives
11404214.value: 本計劃題為《群經平議》斠正，訂正此書之失，是計劃核心。本研究全面檢討《群經平議》每一條的說法，而為了讓學界明瞭俞說之失，本研究利用文字學、音韻學、訓詁學、語法學、校讎學等方法，就有問題的條目作學理上的分析，並提出較為確當的結論。此對治經學者，或治訓詁學者當有助益。 本研究計劃先後撰寫了十餘篇論文，論文不單指陳俞樾訓釋之誤，更釐凊相關問題的爭議，提出新的解釋，如《左傳》隱公元年“大叔完聚” 一語，自《杜注》、《孔疏》後，注家大致同意“完” 與“聚” 為二事。“完”指“完城郭” ，鮮有質疑，“聚” 指 “聚人民” 或“聚禾黍” 則有異議。俞樾讀“完”為“捖”，捖聚猶言摶聚。從語法言之，這是同義複詞，並無賓語，所“聚” 者何，殊難定奪。“捖聚”乃自鑄新詞，於義不通。俞氏先以“完”為“捖” 之借，再將“摩括”義之“捖” 釋“團聚”之“摶”，實過迂迴。遍考先秦兩漢文獻，作動詞用之“完”、“聚”，未嘗不帶賓語者，“大叔完聚” 之 “完” ，是用作動詞，為“完成” 義。 “聚” 為“聚糧” ，與“完” 為動賓結構。這個研究突頗傳統說法相信可為“大叔完聚” 的爭議劃上句號。 另一例子是俞樾《孟子平議》“申之以孝悌之義”。 俞樾解“申” 為“約束” 。當今最為權威的字典--《漢語大字典》“申” 字下亦收錄俞樾的說法，可見俞說影響之大。然而，先秦兩漢文獻“申之以”句式的文例，“申”皆是加重、一再申明之意，並無約束含義。俞說非是，而《漢語大字典》亦誤。 以上兩例反映本研究既能指出《群經平議》的錯誤，亦能解決一向以來的經籍疑難。這證明本計劃的目標得到充分實踐。

11404214.label: Major findings and research outcome
11404214.value: 俞樾是晚清樸學大家，徐世昌《清儒學案‧曲園學案》曰：「曲園之學，以高郵王氏爲宗。發明故訓，是正文字而務爲廣博，旁及百家，著述閎富，同、光之間，蔚然爲東南大師。」《群經平議》乃其代表作。此書既是經學鉅著，又是訓詁典範，學者研治相關典籍，多從俞氏意見，而權威工具書如《漢語大字典》、《漢語大詞典》採用俞說者甚多，故是書對學術界影響甚大。然而，細檢其書，發現錯誤的地方實在不少，為免貽誤後學，糾正《群經平議》之誤，是十分逼切的。本計劃正是從文字、音韻、語法、訓詁各方面探討俞書致誤的緣由，並搜羅證據，平息所有異議，進而解決相關問題。本研究計劃先後撰寫十餘篇論文，內容涵蓋《詩經》、《尚書》、《周易》、《左傳》、《禮記》、《論語》、《孟子》、《國語》等典籍；另一篇關於《周書》的論文亦將送審。這些論文訂正了《群經平議》中的諸多錯誤，並詳加論證，為相關論題提出合理解釋，相信已為歷來爭議劃上句號。

11404214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11404214.value: 《群經平議》對先秦經典文獻疑難問題，詳加探析，體大思精，是一部經學鉅著。然而，其立論有不少錯誤的地方。本計劃除發表了十餘篇論文之外，亦斠正了該書引書、行文的一些錯誤，並蒐集了不同學者對相關經典問題的說法。這部份的資料達二十餘萬字(詳見以下連結) ，相信這會為將來對經典研究帶來助益。 https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B1K4Woc8F8d8STFxUDRjV1B5ckk/view?usp=sharing

11404214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11404214.value: 德清俞樾是晚清樸學大家，所著《群經平議》，針對先秦至西漢經部典籍的疑難問題作深入的探討，是儒家經典訓釋的鉅著，亦是從事經學研究者不可或缺的參考著作。然而，檢查《群經平議》一書，發覺其中不少可議之處，如誤釋詞義、輕言假借、昧於語法等。是書既是權威之作，更須詳加檢討，訂正其誤，俾能有益於典籍訓解，亦可免於貽誤後學。本計劃正是要對《群經平議》作徹底檢討，從文字、音韻、訓詁、語法、校讎等方面糾正書中錯失。

11404614.value: to cover a rich field of local screen practices long left out in the story of HK cinema; to reinstate the role of film theory in qualifying and informing artistic practice, especially experimental actions; to contextualize Expanded-Future Cinema in HK based on intensive field work: interrelation between mainstream and expanded cinema, activation of audience space, intermedia methods and technical innovations; to qualify the local media-art community: who the practitioners are, modes of practice, institutional and social resources, cultural capital, career trajectories; to represent the technical, black-boxed aspects of Expanded Cinema to a non-technical audience; and to practice "media archaeology" as an art history method.

11404614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11404614.value: This research project is about rarely studied screen practices in Hong Kong, including lens-less moving image, multiple screen narrative, immersive environments, interactive systems, moving-image archives, projections and found footage as performance. These activities constitute the rich field of contemporary screen practices in HK, which can be grouped under the term “Expanded Cinema” (EC). Existing accounts of “HK cinema” has long been confined to commercial exhibitions. They have simplified the actual field of cultural production and rendered many on-going activities absent, invisible, or unworthy for discussion. The history of cinema is in ways that of technological experiment. As the dawn of the digital age has seen the relationship between technology and the end-user/viewer of a work transformed, we must acknowledge the need for a more sophisticated understanding of the technological apparatus hidden behind artworks. Media art’s demand on art history is to have a better understanding of how technology forms the core aesthetics of art by opening up the “black box”. (Rodriguez, n.d.) Although EC is not a new concept, the footprints and doings of our own HK-EC and the public resources already deployed are yet to be traced. The sidelined EC activities contain critical facts of local artistic practices, institutional mentalities, continuities and disruptions within fields of cultural production, and desires embodied in our visual culture. As a researcher of art/media history and a practicing new media artist, I will write these long overdue stories to offer a fuller view of HK Cinema. This project will strive for detailed knowledge about the technical workings of mediation inside the “black box” to shed light on the social-cultural dimension of our screen culture. A key contribution of this project to local history and media/art scholarship lies in its method “media archaeology.” “Expanded Cinema” refers to moving image practices that cross over with other existing art forms with transformed reception apparatuses. Media archaeology facilitates the unraveling of these aspects as it, by definition, attends to the multiple technological lineages that cut through a medium, and the many linkages a work may have with non-technological aspects of everyday living. This project will chart key local players and works, describe digital components to a non-technological audience, and turn individual media works into multi-lateral stories – object-based, personal-biographical, locational, experimental, technical, cultural-historical and discursive – to venture beyond textual or semantic analysis of their works into the material and technological realities of creation. 此研究項目聚焦於香港較少人涉獵的活動影像實踐，包括不需鏡頭拍攝的動態影像、多螢幕敘事、沉浸式虛擬環境、互動系統、動態影像檔案庫、投影和現成影像的表演等，這些活動構成「香港當代活動影像實踐」的豐富範疇，並可歸類為「膨脹電影」或「延展電影」。關於「香港電影」的既有討論總是局限於商業銀幕的大電影，因過度簡化文化生產的實際領域而令許多一直在進行的創作活動看似缺席、無形、或是沒有討論價值。如果我們肯定電影史本質上同時是技術實驗的歷史，就自然注意到數碼時代的來臨已經大大改變了技術與終端用戶／觀眾之間的關係。這使得我們必須更透徹地瞭解隱藏於藝術品背後的技術設備。媒體藝術要求藝術史研究者打開「黑盒子」，理解技術如何構成藝術品的核心美學（羅海德）。「膨脹電影」並非新概念，但它於香港迄今的歷程以及用於此領域的公共資源始終有待回溯。被忽視的膨脹電影活動包含許多關鍵史實，從中可窺見關於本地藝術實踐的種種、文化生產領域的連續性與斷裂、機構操作背後的心態和視野，以及本地視覺文化體現的欲望。作為藝術／媒體歷史的研究員及新媒體藝術家，我將記述這些遲來的故事，藉此豐富人們對香港活動影像的想像，跳出「香港電影」的框框。透過這個研究項目，我將詳細認識打開「黑盒子」後內裡的技術原理，在社會文化層面上闡明本地的活動影像實踐。以「媒體考古學」為方法是項目對本地歷史與媒體／藝術的重要學術貢獻：媒體考古學探究特定媒體的繁雜技術譜系以及作品與日常生活非技術層面之間的連繫，起步点就是观赏与接收工具的拆解及至影像创作的翻新。此項目將羅列重要的本地實踐者及其作品，向一般受眾描述數碼組件，超越作品的文本或語義分析，轉而描畫創作的物質性與技術性現實，並把個別媒體作品轉化成以物件、地理位置、個人傳記、實驗、技術、文化歷史、論述為本的多邊故事。

11404614.label: Realisation of objectives
11404614.value: In addressing the six objectives, my research process was increasingly marked by a multi-strategy approach. In terms of primary research, i.e. to furnish the documentary descriptions of what happened, who the players are and why they do what they do, my coverage ranges from profiling individuals, repeated interviews of individual players, case analysis, and the making of chronologies to the engagement with specific individuals in tailor-made collaborative projects. Thus I went through a trajectory of investigation that begins with field study through discourse analysis to a feminist practice-based participatory action research to performative moments of challenging established categorization and institutional organization by inserting myself as the engaged artist and/or advocate curator. My activist turn has taken me one step further beyond an observer/investigator (researcher) or a stake-holder (as an artist) to land on a critical re-grounder (to re-define and re-classify the practice of cinema). Field work was conducted within a one-year time frame to exhaust media art events in as many venues as possible. Photographs and fact sheets were prepared to maximize the descriptive power of the documents to contain “ambience” as an inevitable element. Gradually, I realized “knowledge transfer” opportunities that came to me in my research process were essential. They were occasions such as workshops, seminars, guest lectures and workshops where important themes and concepts were shared. In some of these occasions, I gathered new research subjects and collaborators. This allowed me to move more in the direction of action research, by the definition of which, designing activities to take purposeful actions is not only for data collecting, but also an end in itself. There were notably several curatorial projects I have initiated, following from my action-research direction. Curatorship is a highly integrated activity. I interacted with different levels of stakeholders in deep conversations. I need to theorize through research, work analysis and writing to conceptualize. I did not play the role of an ordinary museum or gallery curator. I did not just program screenings, but enforced less attempted objectives as an advocate. The role of an advocate curator also challenged me to be sharp in reasoning and shrewd in communication. As an established moving image practitioner myself, I naturally moved between advocate curatorship and recent-creation. In all of my solo and group shows/screenings, I engaged in writing, exchanging views in interviews, and meeting with experts and the general audience to bring my theoretical position to tests and trials. The final year of the research turned even more towards an activist note, especially through organizing experimental workshops, to systematically present my historical research and conceptual defense for ethical practices in moving image, and to make works and “write” with them. A 140-page “manifestos” on one’s videographic practices grounded in theory and history, using additional funds from the Hong Kong Arts Development Council (HK ADC) is one primary example among others. There is a gradual switch of role on my part from researcher to researcher as stakeholder, and to researcher as experimenter and re-grounder of the terms for moving image practices. In terms of academic research, theoretical and history writing, my activist turn found my recent writings and talks more on the ethical imperative to turn movie-image practices into the very location of better against total consumerism. The question of what one should do with image-making tools, art of not, is increasingly critical to me. (See publications and activist projects in 2017-2018.) In completing Project Objectives (POs) (1), I also advanced in POs (2), in my writing, my own video experiments, advocate curatorship as well as my activist projects. Beyond a historicist account of Expanded Cinema as it was initiated by Gene Youngblood and his contemporaries in the 1960s and 1970s, my thorough engagement with local practitioners and stake-holders argue for a media art/video art historical account unique to Hong Kong., which is my POs (3) and (4). The black box and black-boxing issues, i.e. POs (5), are not easy. They embrace both Critical Theory and specialist knowledge in coding, electronics and hardware computing, which is not “naturally” the training of someone in the humanities, including most artists. But I have tackled this more in describing what is beyond the work. The two Writing Machine Collective exhibition series (2014, 2018) are addressing this problem. “Media Archaeology,” POs (6), is a broad that requires heavy contextualization. In this research, it informs how I write the survey history of video art in Hong Kong, my micro-excavation of video diaries by non-experts made in 1997-1998. It also pushes me to think of media art and moving image not so much as mediums and machines, but more as human desires and the urge of technics to extend our physical capability. I thus look for the place of light and smoke, shadow and figures, and the arrival of electricity in Hong Kong as several tangential nexus to help imagining a different genealogy to build in my future research.

11404614.label: Major findings and research outcome
11404614.value: (1) Diary films have predominantly informed local videographers' moving image experiments. The impulse to write one’s sentiments and to record important moments of everyday life remains the driving force of non-mainstream cinema practices. (2) There is also a growing attention to how digital videos and videography are closely linked to archiving possibilities. There is a growing attention to the "shot," a fragment of a whole work, a sequence and other sub-narrative units and their epistemological potential. (1) and (2) both point to video images’ function in alternative historiography. (3) Expanded Cinema (EC) in the digital age is beyond activating the spectators' space. There is a stronger attention to the low-level elements such as light, heat, image and shadow, ambience and fabricated sound, waves, and methods to play with them. Projection practices that alert spectators of the artificiality of image practices seem to have given way to total immersion. My critical response is the need to revisit the question of attention economy. (4) A huge gap exists between those who consider video as a writing tool (the diary film camp) and those who are after medium-specific exploration, such as thinking of electronic signals, the magnetic make-up of a tape, and, recently, software, digitality and computing as artistic raw material. The gap is partly due to an educational paradigm in which the humanities and the sciences are segregated. My research partly focused on seeking those artists who can understand technology as raw material and could describe what they are doing by partially “opening the black box” without giving up cinema as human communication. (5) In following through my gradual shift from just investigating and writing to action research and critical participation, I have not only involved young artists to provide themselves with the grounds and reasoning for videography, but I also challenged my own experimental video practice on the conceptual level. Along this line of pursuit, I have grown more in the direction of a materialist approach to moving image (Gidel, McGrice, Deleuze), in search of ways to contemplate and use images beyond signification, but more into the potentiality of images in ascribing a new sense of time to us. (6) By and large, my conceptual, philosophical research only makes sense when it is tied to a Critical Theory orientation by which videography is far from just an aesthetic activity – art and aesthetics are the very core of control in marketing-oriented capitalism. Emotions and aesthetics are precisely where control takes place, With that in mind, the experimental edge of videography is also critical.

11404614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11404614.value: This research has produced a lot of material that should form a book manuscript for a comprehensive view of non-mainstream sight and sound practices: (1) Unpublished: media art event list in Hong Kong 1973-2015 (2) Unpublished: 8 detailed interview profiles of key players in sight-and-sound related media art in HK (3) Unpublished: several cases on documentation as a response to black-boxing (5th and 6th editions of the Writing Machine Collective) and programs that gather unpublished video diaries (C & G) (4) All published essays provide survey views of multiple orientations. On the theoretical side, Bernard Stiegler’s “organology” remains a critical conceptual instrument to establish the intricate and complex relations between different organs of society. This opens up a de-centralizing model of image culture by which the critical significance of imaging practice required more than one overarching paradigm. An organological is an important supplement to Marx’s base-superstructure model, Adorno’s view of culture industry’s tempering public taste, Althusser’s view of media functioning as state apparatus, Bourdieu’s map of fields of production and so on. Organology opens up more “basis” of control, from government, policy, a place of discipline, consumer behavior, to beauty, individual desires and sentiments in general, as the central point of investigation.

11404614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11404614.value: I have thoroughly studied several kinds of screen practices in HK outside mainstream cinema, flourishing, but under-represented in existing literature. I have uncovered many players and daily practices. I found video diaries a key impetus in democratizing moving images, starting with the countdown years to 1997. Diary-mode videos facilitated social activism and answered the cry for a history of everyday life by which personal sentiments and doings are centred. They stand in contrast with the ubiquitous presence of screens in the city space and the growing availability of imaging tools. Digital technologies are consumed, not understood. Experiments in 1960s-70s in the West, called “Expanded Cinema” (EC), aimed at re-activating the spectators’ space “frozen” by mainstream cinema. EC takes on very different meanings in the digital age in HK. Taking moving-image out of the cinema is only the first step. Multifarious methods to “move” images result in “black-boxing” the media deployed. I therefore focus on artists who are concerned with opening the black box. In media art, what one sees is not what the artists "write": software can result in the users’ loss of knowledge. My concern is how not to leave spectators in the dark to be blind consumers.

11405314.label: Project Objectives
11405314.value: Present a thorough and balanced synthesis of the best practices of computer game analysis and interpretation. While there are multiple models of game analysis and interpretation focusing on different aspects of computer game play, the field lacks a thorough synthesis of these models, mapping their overlaps and focus areas. It is expected that a synthetic meta-model would be very useful to computer game scholars and critics not least as providing a common ground for debates. Describe the experience of single-player computer game play in relation to existentialist ideas of freedom and responsibility in e.g. Sartre's account of being in the world. This allows exploring new ground in philosophy of computer games: using insights from existentialist philosophy (e.g. Satre, Fink, Solomon) for the purpose of describing the game/player relationship. To clarify the concepts used to describe phenomena related to single-player computer games by drawing on post-phenomenological philosophy of technology. This allows bringing in material sensibilities that recognize the material affordances that make up 'playability', and thus seeing not only how 'playability' can leak into other media forms and technologies, but also how computer games can inform the conceptual trajectories of interactive art and media-archaeology, and vice versa. This contribution can inform game design and encourage innovative approaches to what computer games could be. To provide an account of the conditions under which single-player computer games can be described as constraining their interpretations. This amounts to describing how interpretation of computer games differs from interpretation of narrative and interactive media, and, is epistemological groundwork immediately useful for game analysis and scholarship beyond this project. It can also be used to inform public policy (e.g. content rating systems). Designers of entertaining, serious, and artistic games and game-like media applications will find that this contribution can help them to convey messages using playable media.

11405314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11405314.value: Computer games have entered the mainstream of contemporary mediaculture, questioning the assumptions about a pastime of adolescent males only. Last decade has seen for example yoga-games and cooking simulations alongside adaptations of film noir aesthetics. In 2010 the global revenue generated by computer game sales surpassed that of cinema box offices. As media audiences accustomed to playability mature, we begin to find game-like interactivity in a variety of ‘serious’ fields of new media and digital technology, such as training, education and journalism. Computer games are an expressive medium and an artform. They can offer experiences as profound as those offered by film, theatre and literature. This calls for establishing an aesthetics specific to computer games and seeing value in informed readings and critiques of them. The ways in which narrative media like cinema are experienced as significant are already well-theorised. In last decades, focus of many media and culture scholars shifted to “interactive” media, which due to its seemingly empowering user position was hailed as a cause for paradigm shift. Due to fundamental differences between the ways in which narrative, interactive, and playable media engage their audiences, the theories and methodologies which apply on narrative or interactive media cannot simply be transferred to understand signification in playable media. Underlying the attempts of analysing and critiquing computer games, designing attractive computer games, using them for education, or creating artistic computer games, is a fundamental question that has not been fully answered yet: how interpretation of single-player computer games can be possible in the first place? The goal of this project is to answer this question by theorising the interpretation of single-player computer games based on a synthesis of current game analysis practices, comparative close-playing analyses of computer game artefacts, and typology creation. This project will break new ground in game studies and philosophy of computer games by using insights from existential philosophy and post-phenomenological philosophy of technology to address the relationship between, freedom, responsibility, technological materiality, and interpretation. The project will shed light on the ways single player computer games appear as meaningful to their players. It describes how the experience of meaningful play consists of individual elements present in solitary game-playing experience, including narrative structures, game-play incentives, audiovisual elements like graphics and sounds, and external rewards such as the “achievement badges”, and, how these elements relate to the core dynamic of playability. 電腦遊戲已經成為當代媒體文化主流的一部份，並且被視為一種表達的媒介與藝術形式。為此，我們須要建立一套專門針對電腦遊戲的美學觀，並從與此有關的論述與批評中找到價值。現時已有很多理論，探討觀眾如何認真看待諸如電影之類的敘事媒體，但對於詮釋與電腦遊戲的理論卻十分稀少。透過探討當今遊戲分析、詮釋與批評的最佳範例，本計劃旨在綜合出一個存在主義對電腦遊戲的觀點，以填補上述的理論空隙。

11405314.label: Realisation of objectives
11405314.value: The project has looked at a number of approaches to the topic of interpretation in computer games, and, brought these perspectives together by using ideas concerning drawn from existentialist philosophy. The project has demonstrated how computer games can be conceptualized as ‘worlds’, or, computer game play as phenomenologically similar to ‘being in the world’. This has cast new light on hermeneutic paradigms that presuppose the nature of the object ‘as’ something, e.g. as a ‘game’, as a 'story', as ‘computer software’, as ‘virtual space’, as ‘simulated embodiment’, as ‘art’, or as ‘object of emotions’, etc. They now all appear to be sustainable only in a very benevolent sense: nothing in the materiality of the so-called computer game necessitates these modes of description. The “playability” of the so-called computer game objects does not depend on these, but, rather, on the dynamic of freedom and responsibility: that we are responsible for our own freedom as players of the game. This is the same dynamic which, according to the existentialists, characterizes our being in the world in general. Thus, it appears that this ‘worldness’ of computer games prevails as a sustainable paradigm for the interpretation, analysis, and critique of computer games. The ways in which computer games offer themselves to be interpreted by players can be described as a function of their worldness: there is content that is absolutely critical for player’s persistent being as a player of the game (i.e. survival), and, content, which is in this respect trivial. By making some of the content critical and some trivial, the game can constrain the player’s possible interpretations of the game. As this mechanism depends on there being the possibility of the player surviving or not surviving, we cannot describe it in how films, TV, and other traditional media offer themselves to be interpreted by their audiences. Thus, interpretation in computer games differs from interpretation in other media. Furthermore, regarding the relationship between playability and interpretation, there is a significant difference also between traditional analogue ‘games’ and the so-called computer games. The previously described mechanism is hard-coded in the technological materiality of the game, and transcends individual players and playings: i.e. it does not depend on the player’s attitudes or preconceptions toward the object. Regardless of whether we approach Tetris ‘as a game’ or ‘as a technology’, the same mechanism constraining our interpretation prevails. Thus, in the interpretation of computer games, the technological materiality takes precedence over any ‘gameness’. Same cannot be said of a group of found objects which may be used to play a game: Mahjong tiles, for example, have their in-game meaning only if being benevolently used for a game of mahjong. This casts critical light on the paradigm of ‘transmediality’ as used in computer game studies, referring to the assumption that games can effortlessly move between media.

rows: Present a thorough and balanced synthesis of the best practices of computer game analysis and interpretation. While there are multiple models of game analysis and interpretation focusing on different aspects of computer game play, the field lacks a thorough synthesis of these models, mapping their overlaps and focus areas. It is expected that a synthetic meta-model would be very useful to computer game scholars and critics not least as providing a common ground for debates.

Describe the experience of single-player computer game play in relation to existentialist ideas of freedom and responsibility in e.g. Sartre's account of being in the world. This allows exploring new ground in philosophy of computer games: using insights from existentialist philosophy (e.g. Satre, Fink, Solomon) for the purpose of describing the game/player relationship.

To clarify the concepts used to describe phenomena related to single-player computer games by drawing on post-phenomenological philosophy of technology. This allows bringing in material sensibilities that recognize the material affordances that make up 'playability', and thus seeing not only how 'playability' can leak into other media forms and technologies, but also how computer games can inform the conceptual trajectories of interactive art and media-archaeology, and vice versa. This contribution can inform game design and encourage innovative approaches to what computer games could be.

To provide an account of the conditions under which single-player computer games can be described as constraining their interpretations. This amounts to describing how interpretation of computer games differs from interpretation of narrative and interactive media, and, is epistemological groundwork immediately useful for game analysis and scholarship beyond this project. It can also be used to inform public policy (e.g. content rating systems). Designers of entertaining, serious, and artistic games and game-like media applications will find that this contribution can help them to convey messages using playable media.

11405314.label: Major findings and research outcome
11405314.value: This project has demonstrated that the artifacts we previously called computer games are not best described as "games", as we know the concept from traditional play theory. 'Playable artifacts' would be a much better term. This is because their technological-material nature constrains interpretation in ways which we cannot describe in traditional games. While some playable artifacts can be interpreted 'as games', (e.g. football on PlayStation), this is by no means necessary across the full range of playable artifacts. Different playable artifacts afford different 'levels', of interpretation and knowledge-discovery. (See the paper in the proceedings of Philosophy of Computer Games 2016). This has a number of repercussions. Conceptualising playable artifacts as 'games' still prevails as the paradigm within computer game studies. It is understandable given how the field has evolved, but appears not only romantic but also dangerously misguided. First: it can give us only a partial description of the ways in which computer games are meaningful. Second: it overlooks the ways in which playable artifacts and their players are intertwined in the structures of neoliberal society. A free-to-play clicker "game" is a cash-extracting machine with questionable material morality, inasmuch as it can be played as-a-game. An aspiring electronic sports athlete playing LoL concerns herself with self-fashioning and acquiring social capital as much she does with entertainment and pleasure. (see the paper in proceedings of Philosophy of Computer Games 2014, and the article published in Journal of Gaming & Virtual Worlds) Furthermore, through a comparative study of various kinds of Mahjongs, the project demonstrated that the technological materiality of playable artifacts is multistable: it affords a range of projects among which 'playing the game' is only one. (see the article published in Games & Culture, and the paper in the proceedings of Philosophy of Computer Games 2015) The project also looked at computer games interpreted not by players themselves, but by observers and onlookers, by drawing on the study of performances. Playable artifacts appear not only as objects which can be used in a performance, or as 'stages' for a performance, but they also provide the existential baseline for experiencing empathy toward the performer, which, in traditional performance is derived from the fact of both the performer and audience being humans. To be able to appreciate a gameplay performance, we must know what is it like to 'be in' that game. (See the paper in proceedings of Philosophy of Computer Games 2017 conference)

11405314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11405314.value: The project has already sparked two funded GRF projects, which both build on the findings of this project. First of these is a project on gamification. It seeks to find out whether the 'worldness', and the associated mechanism of constraining interpretation, which are characteristic to computer games, can be found in reportedly successful applications of gamification, and, what this tells us about the nature of applications of 'gamification' as games. This provides a critical perspective on gamification and allows us to discuss its true potential among all the marketing hype. Second of these is a comparative study of competitive computer game play in game arcades, and, in the context of electronic sports (eSports). It builds directly on the findings pertaining to the relationship between freedom and play from this project (PoCG 2014, JVWG article), and, on the questions of interpreting other people's gameplay (PoCG 2017 paper). Among other things, this new project seeks to find out whether it is feasible to describe the activity in game arcades as 'play', and, that in eSports contexts as 'work'.

11405314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11405314.value: This project sought to describe how interpretation works in computer games. Traditional games and computer games have a number of similarities,but also significant differences. Not least of the differences is the presence of narrative in computer games. Thus, it is not surprising that computer games are often described as some kinds of hybrids, inviting us to interpret them simultaneously as 'games' and as 'stories'. This, however, appears somewhat accidental: why just these two domains and not others? Computer game players, not unlike humans in the world, discover objects, events, and encounters, some of which are important to their lives than others, and which leave lasting memories. Their experiences cannot be reduced to either the game-like logic of interpretation relying on winning or losing, or, the narrative logic relying on empathy toward the characters: the 'hybrid' approach to game interpretation alone is not viable. We sought to complement it by using existentialist philosophy and examining the similarities between 'being in the world' and 'playing a computer game'. We found out that by considering computer games 'as worlds', it is possible to fuse together the sometimes conflicting paradigms of computer game interpretation, and, describe how players interpret computer games.
