12403714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12403714.value: In modern society, religion has been widely conceived as one of the sources for social conflicts. But it is interesting that almost every religion teaches its believers to seek a just and peaceful personal life through their religious quest. Against this background, a better understanding of the concepts of social justice in religious thought and their social implications occupy an important place in the well-being of humankind. This research aims to study the concept of social justice of two foreign religions in China—Protestant Christianity and Islam in the first half of the twentieth century. Through studying their publications, this research investigates how they understood social justice, and the social implications of this understanding. Four important periodicals, Association Progress, The True Light Review, Qingzhen Duobao, and YueHua, will be used as the basic research materials. The key research questions are: 1. How do Chinese Christians and Hui Muslims understand and articulate social justice with their religious resources? 2. What are the characteristics of these discourses compared with the general understanding of social justice in the respective religious tradition and contemporary non-religious Chinese? 3. How do these discourses establish a contemporary relevance between religious and social life? Finally, this research critically assesses the differences and similarities, and the merits and shortcomings of these discourses in helping these two foreign religions to develop reciprocal adaptations between themselves and China. The methodology of this research is textual-hermeneutical analysis. An understanding of the concept of social justice among Chinese Christians and Muslims will be achieved by the following steps: 1. Identify important public issues and religious practices related to social justice that were addressed by the periodicals. 2. Analyze the religious texts and concepts have been employed in their discourses. The analysis will cross-examine the similarities and differences in interpretations and hermeneutical steps of the texts and concepts between the mainstream religious traditions and Chinese believers. 3. Compare the convergence and divergence between the religious and general public understanding, and Christian and Muslim understanding of the social justice. The interactions between religions and the society will be studied. 4. Critically investigate the social implications of the understanding and practice of social justice among the Chinese Christians and Muslims. 5. Finally, proposals for promoting reciprocal adaptations between Chinese public and her foreign religions will be suggested. Three articles and one monograph will be generated for promoting the mutual understanding and positive interaction between religions and society. 宗教於現代社會裡常被視為社會衝突的根源。但有趣的是，幾乎每一宗教皆教導其信眾追求正直及和平的人生。因此，理解宗教的社會公義概念及其影響，乃與人類的福祉有著重要關係。本研究旨在考察民國時期兩個中國外來宗教──基督新教及伊斯蘭教的刊物裡，如何陳述社會公義概念，及其社會影響。本研究會首先選取四種重要雜誌：《青年進步》、《真光》、《清真鐸報》及《月華》作為分析對象。本研究主要的研究問題為：1. 中國基督徒及穆斯林如何運用他們的宗教資源來理解與闡述社會公義概念？2. 從非宗教論述比較宗教論述對社會公義的理解有何特點？3. 這些論述如何將宗教及社會生活關連起來？4. 批判分析這些論述的相同及相異之處，並評析它們對幫助自身宗教與中國社會互動調適的優點與不足。本研究將採取文本－詮釋分析為研究方法，以此找出中國基督徒及穆斯林對社會公義概念的理解。

12403714.label: Realisation of objectives
12403714.value: 1. The objective of enumerating the characteristics of the discourses on social justice of Chinese Protestant Christians and Hui Muslims in their religious periodicals from 1911 to 1949 has been achieved through documenting and indexing the articles that discussed the related social issues. After making index tables, keywords are generated to chart out the characteristics. I have selected the Sino-Japanese War, religious dialogue between Christianity, Islam and Confucianism, the reform of education system, discussion of the political change of the Republican China, and the anti-religious movements as issues to further enumerate the characteristics. In the study, the following main characteristics of social justice in the religious discourses are identified: a) Social justice in religious discourses gets along with expected common desirable benefit of the country, if the issues are not directly related to the religion. b) When the religions are directly involved in the issues (usually being considered as negative factors for non-religious believers), the religious discourses attempt to show how they can contributive positively to the welfare of the nation, and why the criticisms towards their religions are not valid. c) Religious authority (e.g., the Bible or Quran) is the basis and foundation of the religious social justice discourses. It is quite difficult to differentiate the whether the authors borrowed the religious resources to support a particular social standpoint, or the religious resources can naturally lead to the standpoint. But, one can figure out if the religious discourses are thick description and have ample supports from the religious traditions or a kind of proof-texting. d) The religious discourses followed the main stream public opinion to understand social justice for the Republican China as modernization and national salvation. e) Active participation of religious leaders and religious believers with high social and political status in the public discussion helped an integration of opinions on particular social issues and religious viewpoints. f) the division between the non-religious public and religious believers on social issues can be resolved by reducing attack to religious beliefs while seeking common social goal of both groups. g) Different political camps would draw support from religious believers. In our case, the religious believers followed the majority view of Chinese society for their social justice endeavors. Even when someone used the tension between religious identity and national identity to seek their support for an agenda against majority public opinion (e.g., Japanese aggression of China), our discourses showed that Muslims and Christians do not opt for the position that may sacrifice the welfare of the wider community. h) If there are tensions between an explicit theological position and common public opinion, we can find that the discourses will sort to explain the merits of religious doctrines to the issue, or find out other doctrines to explain the possibility for a convergence with the public opinion. Unless the public opinion is religiously hostile, we can find that the accommodation occurs across the issues. 2. The objective of analyzing the similarities and differences of these discourses with the general understanding of social justice in the respective religious tradition in China has been achieved through the case study. Regarding the general principles of social justice, the research finds that they tend to be generic. They usually point to vague concepts of good, charity, equality, equity and fairness. These concepts are heavily loaded with religious expositions of the holy texts, models of religious leaders and the history of the religious community. When we turn to the religious discourses of the case study, one will find that they will extend the general concepts of social justice to become specific implementations or policies that they were discussing. In these circumstances, the general principles are warrants for concrete standpoints or actions. In the course of applying general doctrines to specific issues, the research finds that they may turn out to become something new to the original traditional position in meeting with the challenge of contemporary issues. 3. The objective of scrutinizing nuances of the reciprocal adaptations between the foreign religions, and the state and general public in China during the period from 1911 to 1949 has also achieved through case study. The research finds that the religious believers were quite keen to adapt themselves with the general public opinion. Conversely, the study of anti-religious movements showed that the public opinion of the concerned discussion has shown a greater adaptation in the interaction with Islam than Christianity. The research suggests that it is due to Christianity was considered as a tool of the Western Imperialism, while Islam only an unscientific and backward religion. But, the baptism of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek and the break out of the Sino-Japanese War made changes of public impression towards Christianity. They also led to a better adaptation of non-religious public to Christianity. The change showed that the general public evaluated the religious bodies with concepts of social justice such as national salvation, modernization, and affinity with Chinese nation. Especially national salvation, it was the key factor that affected the mutual adaptations between the foreign religions, and the state and general public in the Republican China period. 4. The objective of critically assessing the relative merits and shortcomings of these historical attempts of reciprocal adaptations for promoting a positive interaction between foreign religions, and the state and general public in China has been achieved by the case study. In terms of the merits, the research finds that the religious discourses attempted to be religiously faithful and socially just. In the midst of great crises of the Republican China, Islam and Christianity as foreign religions did not act as bystanders of the crises. The discourses showed that there are resources and strategies for religious believers to achieve a greater consensus with non-religious public in understanding justice in society. For the shortcomings, the research finds that the mechanism for an incontestable religious teaching on social justice in issues is still vague. The research finds that a thick description of the doctrines and the religious tradition is vital and important. But, it also finds that the contemporary social atmosphere and the religious identity can affect the direction of understanding social justice. In other words, the religious discourses cannot solve the problem of identity politics. When the tension between religious groups and non-religious public is huge, or when the public opinion is highly divided in a particular issue; the religious discourses do not have much resources in achieving a better understanding of social justice of the society. 5. In the case study, the research achieved a critical analysis of the religious contributions to the good of the society during the period from 1911 to 1949. The research finds that both Chinese Muslims and Christians supported modernization of education, a government of national salvation, equality and democracy, resistance of Japanese aggression, and a positive integration of their religions and Chinese culture. Though, as I have pointed out in the above paragraph, the problem of identity politics still exists in the discourses, the research points out a direction for a future positive interaction between religions and the society.

12403714.label: Major findings and research outcome
12403714.value: The research identifies that though Islam and Christianity were considered as foreign religions by some people in the Republican China period, the understanding of social justice of Chinese Christians and Muslims is in line with common public opinion. The main concern of social justice for the Republican China is modernization and national salvation. Modernization brings the hope of improvement of life and well-being of Chinese people. The urge of national salvation indicates a concern of international political equality and justice. Religious believers want to show that they are both religiously devoted and patriotic. The research also finds that religious believers need evidences from religious texts and tradition as the foundation of their social justice endeavors. For religious believers, they are keen to have a religious rationale for their participation of social justice project. In other words, religious and social identities are undergoing a process of integration in the discourses. The research also finds that role of religious leaders and high social status religious believers are important for promoting a positive integration of religious belief with general understanding of social justice. Unfortunately, the general public opinion towards religions are quite negative in the Republican China period. Religions are considered as unscientific and unpatriotic. In meeting the challenge of anti-religious discourses, the research finds that Chinese Muslims and Christians on the one hand repudiating the anti-religious arguments are biased, on the other hand, the religious believers attempt to show their faith can contribute good things for national salvation and modernization. The research suggests that a better interaction between religious groups and general public can been achieved through religious friendly attitude and seeking the common good of the society. The research generated four journal articles and four conference papers. One monograph is being prepared for publication.

12403714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12403714.value: The potential of having further research is high. The research can extend to an investigation of Buddhism and Taoism. Buddhism and Taoism are highly indigenized religions, but have been severely repressed by the National government for it considered them superstitious. . The further research can explore if they had differences from Islam and Christianity on understanding the social justice in the Republican period. Another possible research area is to further study the mechanism of how religious believers utilize the religious authority to orchestra their discourses on social justice. For the it is highly technical in doctrinal exposition, the research should be done by a group of Islamic and Christian scholars. The third possible topic for future research is to chart out interaction between religious leaders and religious believers with high social and political status. The present research identifies that there is a positive reciprocal relationship between religious leaders and religious believers with high social and political status. How the relationship builds up and what are the factors for the relationship are important future research topics.

12403814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12403814.value: 本研究旨在對中國南京城區的985位高中生進行第四次生命歷程轉變的探索性追蹤調查。在經濟改革前, 年青人的生命歷程往往受到國家政策影響。如在大躍進及文化大革命期間，由於入讀大學的機會減少和上山下鄉運動，結果令當時很多城市年青人的生命歷程受到局限和脫離原來的軌跡。隨著1970年代末期，中國進行經濟改革，年青人在教育、工作及家庭等方面，有較多的選擇。然而，現時的文獻主要是著重經濟改革前的年青人生命過渡的規律和變化，有關在經濟改革全面實施時期成長的年青人的生命歷程研究，則非常少。 在各種年青人的生命過渡轉變中，以從學校過渡到職場的轉變過程最受學者關注；這是因爲這個過程對年青人日後的生命歷程，如結婚、生育、居住安排(如離開父母獨立居住或自置居所)和職業生涯等，有着重要的影響；而這些生命歷程又會影響個人社會地位、代際社經地位差異、個人福祉及代際之間的關係。 是次研究是一個針對中國城市年青人從學校進入職場過程的試驗性研究。1990年代，中國的高等教育擴張，增加了年青人上大學的機會，同時也推遲了他們進入職場的過程。本研究將探討年青人大學畢業後進入職場的過程，主要目的有三：（一）描述年青人由學校進入職場的路徑、（二）探討家庭背景、學校及個人志向對此過程的影響，及（三）評估此過程對日後個人福祉及社會網絡的影響。 第一期調查的數據是在2010年初，即受訪者讀高二(讀大學前一年)時搜集的。這些數據為是次研究提供了基礎資料，包括家庭背景、校園經驗、個人志向、父母期望、家庭文化資本及個人社會資本等。第二期及第三期的資料搜集則在他們完成高中後進行，主要是關於他們的學業成就、工作、社交、個人志向及社會資本與文化資本的累積。是次研究將會進行第四期調查，集中受訪者完成高等教育後的生命歷程轉變及這些轉變對他們的個人福祉及社會網絡的影響。 本研究希望透過是次調查，闡明在中國城市年青人從學校過渡到職場的過程中，社會結構與個人能動性如何互相影響，在社會優勢跨代傳遞、學校分層對工作成就的影響及年青人的生命歷程等三方面的研究範疇作出貢獻；並能作為將來同類的大型全國性追蹤調查的參考。

12403814.label: Realisation of objectives
12403814.value: This GRF project is part of a panel study on the life transitions of young people in urban Nanjing, which was first launched in 2010. To achieve the two project objectives, two online surveys were conducted on 989 respondents, who were randomly selected from 11 senior high schools at different rankings in 2010, to collect information about the respondents’ college experiences and job search process. We conducted two surveys instead of one to take into account of the different graduation years of respondents in 3-year junior colleges and 4-year universities. The first survey (2014 Survey) ran from November 2014 to January 2015, 4-6 months after junior college respondents graduated, whereas the second survey (2015 Survey) ran from December 2015 to April 2016. Both surveys were administered to all the respondents in the original panel, regardless of their study / employment status, and received responses from 754 respondents, or 76% of the original panel (989 respondents). About 86% (647) and 80% (599) of the respondents in the 2014 and 2015 surveys respectively participated in all the previous waves of data collection. The two surveys asked similar questions, except that some questions were specifically designed for junior college graduates or university graduates. The survey questions cover family background, educational experiences since the last survey in 2013, social networks, family relations, career aspirations, the job search process, life planning, and health. The use of online survey has posed two major challenges to us. While the online survey enables us to reach our respondents over geographical distances, we have limited control over the motivation of respondents to participate in the survey and data quality. To overcome these problems, in addition to economic incentives, we tried hard to cultivate “guanxi” with our respondents to enhance their willingness to participate and cooperate. This is particularly important for the current project because our respondents have already participated in several rounds of survey since 2010 and might thus experience fatigue and refuse to continue to cooperate with us. We hired a group of research assistants, who were graduate students in Nanjing University. Each RA was assigned to a certain number of respondents. They sent festival greetings and encouragement e-messages to respondents via social media from time to time over the years. RAs were also responsible for tracking down the respective respondents during the data collection period. With the hard work of our RAs, we managed to successfully retain 76% of the original panel. However, we found more missing data and inconsistent data in the two surveys compared to the previous ones, probably due to survey fatigue. RAs were sent back to verify the information with the respondents via telephone or social media. After checking back and forth with the respondents, most of the data discrepancies were adjusted. Data discrepancies that could not be verified were treated as missing. The data cleaning process took more than one year to complete, much longer than we had expected. To address the two research objectives, data from the two surveys were linked to the information on personal background and educational experiences collected in the previous waves. Since a vast majority of the respondents transitioned to higher education after high school, data analyses focused on the college/university experiences (including extra-curricular participation, changes in network size, access to social capital, family relations, and dating relations), job search process (use of job search methods and characteristics of the job found), life plan, psychological well-being. 1. To identify the pathways of the school-to-work transition taken by a cohort of young people in urban Nanjing We applied descriptive statistics to examine the patterns of transition after college/university (looking for jobs or furthering studies) and job search methods. We also examined group differences by family backgrounds (indicated by parental education), institutional types (elite vs. non-elite), gender, and migration status (studying in Nanjing vs. studying elsewhere). About 80% of the respondents (n=599) in the 2015 Survey participated in all the previous waves of data collection. Of the 599 respondents, 0.7% of them terminated their education at high school, 16.4% graduated from junior college, 47.8% graduated from university, 21.2% went on to graduate study, 13.4% had not yet graduated from junior college or university, and the remaining 0.6% were preparing for further studies. Unfortunately, less than 30% of respondents who were no longer in school provided information about job search or further study, despite our RAs’ persistent efforts to motivate them to provide data. As such, we resorted to collecting qualitative data to shed light on the process (details to be given below). 2. To examine the effects of family origin, school, and personal aspirations on the transition Extensive research literature has shown a relationship among family background, education, and labor market outcomes. Yet, relatively less attention is placed on young people’s actual experiences in the higher education setting, its relationship with family background, and impact on the outcomes, particularly in the Chinese context. The Western experience informs that attainment of higher education per se cannot explain persistent social inequality and suggests a shift of research attention to quality of education, for example, extra-curricular participation as a strategy to enhance labor market success. Further, in the case of China, the persistent importance of guanxi use for job search and labor market mobility is documented. We analyzed first the relative impacts of family background, institutional types, gender, and migration status on extra-curricular participation and social ties developed in college/university, and then the impacts of these relevant variables on job search. We undertook additional works that were not initially included in the research proposal but could enrich the project. During the project preparation stage, we noticed that in addition to getting a job, getting married was an important life goal for university students after graduation. We thus decided to include dating behaviors as an additional project focus. We also examined the psychological impacts of university experiences for young people because of the intense competition on the university campus and in the labor market. Moreover, we conducted 16 in-depth interviews with survey respondents, some of whom went to university outside of Nanjing and returned to Nanjing for employment. Further, a Ph.D. student under PI’s supervision interviewed 31 university students in Tianjin, who came from Tianjin, other cities, or rural areas. Adopting a mixed method approach, she used the survey data collected for this GRF project and the interview data to examine the contingent impact of social capital on labor market outcomes of university graduates by migration status. These interviews, though not part of the original GRF project, were deemed helpful for us to understand young people’s life course transition in the era of educational expansion.

12403814.label: Major findings and research outcome
12403814.value: Respondents report an increase in network size after transitioning to college, regardless of institutional prestige. Participation in extra-curricular activities helps expand social network, which in turn, facilitates the access to social capital (measured by contacts’ occupational prestige) via friends and friends’ parents. However, respondents report a reduced access to social capital through non-kin ties compared to their report given in high school. The social diversity of the college population may increase personal distance among students and respondents thus have limited knowledge about their peers’ family background. Students of elite universities enjoy double advantages in social capital access in the college setting through extra-curricular participation and a high concentration of students from privileged families in elite universities. They are more actively involved in extra-curricular activities than their non-elite counterparts, probably due to the greater opportunities for extra-curricular participation provided by elite institutions. The competitive culture in elite universities may also prompt students to strategize their positions for future employment through involvement in extra-curricular activities. Being in elite institutions provide men with greater access to social capital. Participation in extra-curricular activities facilitates women’s access to social capital but not men’s. Men and women report a similar level of extra-curricular participation but join different types of student clubs. Club membership tend to be more exclusive for women (fine arts) than for men (sports). Students attending college outside of Nanjing report a lower level of social capital compared to their counterparts. Qualitative data show that migrant students tend to experience barriers in developing resourceful ties with local students. Respondents use both formal and informal means for job search. Family and relatives are the most active ties. University ties provide job information and influence the hiring process. Family background, elite institutions, and access to university social capital are positively associated with the use of social ties for job search. Respondents are more likely to get a job via formal means than informal means. The use of social ties does not result in significantly better jobs than the use of formal means, in terms of monthly salary and job satisfaction. Compared to migrant students, local students are better able to mobilize university-based social capital in job search, which also brings better jobs for them. Access to social capital comes with a psychological cost. Compared to women, men with better access to social capital report a higher level of distress, particularly men from better socioeconomic background.

12403814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12403814.value: Our panel study has collected data from 2010 to 2016 to explore the life course transition from high school to college and beyond among a group of young people in urban Nanjing. Future studies may investigate other life course changes, such as job mobility, family formation, home-ownership, and residential changes. However, respondents have shown signs of fatigue. To capture future transitions, future studies will have to adopt a mixed-method approach where a short online survey collects basic information and intensive interviews with selected respondents uncover the dynamics in the transition process. Although our data come from one Chinese city and in no doubt, cannot represent China, unlike the municipalities and cities in the special economic zones, Nanjing is an “average” Chinese city, which is less prone to the fluctuations of state policies. Our data can thus inform the youth experiences in many other Chinese cities. Yet, similar panel studies can be conducted in cities at various scales and levels of development to provide comparative data. The time dimension can be extended back to primary school or even pre-school to fully understand the origin of social inequality.

12403814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12403814.value: This GRF project is part of the panel study that explores the life course transition from high school to college and beyond among a group of young people in urban Nanjing. Built upon data collected between 2010 and 2013, the present study aims to (1) identify the pathways of the school-to-work transition and (2) examine the effects of family origin, school, and personal aspirations on the transition. Two online surveys were administered to 989 respondents, who were randomly selected from 11 senior high schools, in 2014 and 2015 respectively. Both surveys reached 76% of the original panel. Qualitative data via in-depth interviews were collected to illuminate the interpretation of survey findings. Our findings demonstrate the intergenerational transmission of social advantages on university experiences and its subsequent impacts on labor market attainment and well-being of young people. Although our data come from one Chinese city and cannot represent China, Nanjing is an “average” Chinese city, which is less prone to the fluctuations of state policies in municipal cities and the special economic zones. Our data can thus inform the youth experiences in many other Chinese cities. Built upon the panel data, follow-up studies can be done on subsequent life course changes.

12403914.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12403914.value: 階級與跨國流動夢想：對中國大陸小留學生家庭的多選址研究

12403914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12403914.value: China’s study abroad fever has been steadily gaining momentum. Since 2000, the number of Chinese students abroad has been increasing 20 percent annually (People’s Daily Online, 2011). In addition to traditional student migrants who travel abroad to pursue Master’s or PhD degrees, there is a rising number of younger students who go abroad for high school or undergraduate education. With the expansion of China’s middle class population, and the increasing participation of less-wealthy families, studying abroad at a young age is no longer a privilege for the rich and the elite, but a popular alternative for Chinese families from various social and economic backgrounds (Zeng 2013). Existing Chinese media reports on young overseas students mainly focus on their problematic behaviors and failure stories and little is known about the pre-migration decision making process within the family. Following scholars who treat migration as a family strategy (Salaff et al 2010), this research interprets young Chinese students’ educational migration as a family project that is loaded with financial, emotional, and even political investments from the parents. According to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the number of Chinese students in private American high schools increased from 65 in 2005 to 23,795 in 2012 (Zhao 2013). Another source shows that there was a 43 percent increase in Chinese undergraduates in the U.S. in 2012 (Cross 2013). The decrease of age in overseas Chinese students and the amazingly fast growth in their number prompted one educational agent to predict that by 2014 these younger students would make up 70 percent of the Chinese study abroad population (People’s Daily Online, 2011). Scholars have noted the key role of consumption practices in shaping people’s class identity and lifestyle (Freeman 2000; Mills 1999; Zhang 2008). This study treats the study abroad projects of Mainland Chinese families as a special type of educational consumption that is marked by class distinctions. I am interested in how parents’ investments in their children’s transnational mobility dreams are burdened by their own feelings of insecurity or anxiety about political instability, social unrest, and class disparities in Chinese society. Building on literature on transnational split families in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and South Korea, this research also examines the relationship between international education and class reproduction, namely, how Mainland Chinese parents and children’s participation in the study abroad projects impacts or transforms their class positions and subjectivities in China’s new social order. 中國的“出國留學熱”壹直在持續升溫。自2000年以來，中國海外留學人數每年的增長率為20%（People’s Daily Online, 2011)。 除了那些到國外攻讀碩士與博士學位的傳統意義上的留學生外，到國外就讀高中或大學的小留學生也逐漸增多。隨著中國中產階級的增長及工薪階層家庭的參與，低齡留學已不再是富人與精英的特權，而是來自不同社會經濟背景的中國家庭的壹種熱門選擇（Zeng，2013)。目前國內媒體對小留學生的報道主要集中在他們在海外的負面行為及失敗的經歷，對此類家庭如何作出跨國留學決定的過程卻知之甚少。參考有關學者將跨國遷移看做壹種家庭決策的思路（Salaff et al 2010)，本研究將小留學生以受教育為目的的跨國遷移解析為壹種家庭決策，這種決策註入了父母在金錢上，情感上，甚至政治上的諸多投資。 根據美國國土安全部的報告，美國私立高中的中國留學生人數從2005年的65人上升到2012年的23795人（Zhao，2013）。另有數據顯示，2012年赴美攻讀學士學位的中國留學生人數上升了43% (Cross 2013)。中國留學生人數的飛速增長以及低齡化趨勢促使某留學機構人員預測： 到2014年小留學生將占整個中國海外留學人數的70%（People’s Daily Online, 2011)。有學者指出消費行為在塑造階級身份與生活方式方面的重要作用（Freeman 2000;Mills 1999; Zhang 2008)。本研究把中國大陸家庭的出國留學計劃看作是壹種特殊的，帶有階級差別的教育消費形式。作者旨在探討父母對於孩子跨國流動夢想的投資如何反映出他們自己對於中國大陸政治不穩定，社會動蕩，階級差別所產生的焦慮和不安。基於對香港，臺灣以及韓國的跨國分離家庭的文獻回顧，本研究有意考察國際教育與階級再生之間的關系，即中國大陸父母和孩子對出國留學計劃的參與如何影響或改變他們在中國社會新秩序中的階級地位和主體性。

12404514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12404514.value: The major goal of this research project is to investigate the art and cultural, socio-economic-political aspects of 18th and 19th century China (namely the late Qing period) through the study of visual images, including paintings, drawings, prints and photographs that were produced during this period. As a cross-cultural and inter-disciplinary research topic, this study focuses on the landscapes depicted in the late Qing China coast specifically Canton, Hong Kong, Macao, and Shanghai. These places were open to foreigners during the late Qing period, first for trading and later for political reasons due to the decline of the Imperial Court. Landscapes produced in the form of paintings and photographs related to these places, by Chinese and Western professional artists, travellers or amateurs, were well received by foreigners, hence they were produced in large numbers in the last two centuries. Interestingly, the making of these landscapes changed over time, indicating the rise and fall of the significance of a certain place. The artistic representation of these landscapes also changed during different stages of development, showing that both the Chinese and Westerners had different ways of seeing China over time. Thus, to investigate the topographical depictions of the China coast not only enables us to understand the changing perceptions of the artists and patrons towards the places, it at the same time unveils the current socio-economic-political situation hidden in the landscape, thus allowing us to understand and interpret the subject from different perspectives. Visual images play an increasingly important role in historical study nowadays, widening our scope by providing an alternative to the conventional use of textual evidence. The study of visual representations of the late Qing China coast is intended to be interdisciplinary in nature since it covers not only the arts and cultures of both the Chinese and the West, but also knowledge about topography, tourism, social customs, politics, commerce and so on. Through such a cross-cultural study, the principal investigator hopes to explore the potential and possibility of visual arts study in the realm of Chinese art as well as to strengthen the efficient use of visual information in the academic field.

12404614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12404614.value: This 36 months project aims to explore teaching approaches for school mathematics with mathematics teachers designing teaching tasks making use of concrete tools and manipulatives. In traditional Hong Kong school mathematics classrooms, the teaching and learning of mathematics mainly follow a teacher-centred approach. Teachers often present known abstract mathematical facts to students that are symbolic in nature, and students use these facts to solve problems. Even though this approach may be effective to enable students to prepare for examination and can be conducive to train students’ thinking, it does not motivate students to realize that mathematics can actually be experienced personally through handling of concrete objects and that abstract ideas can be acquired through an inquiry process. Research has shown that mathematical experiences can be mediated through tools and tools are commonly considered as resources susceptible of enhancing the teaching-learning activity. We interpret tools here as physical or virtual objects that have the potential to mediate between mathematical experience and mathematical understanding. For examples, wooden unit blocks or abacus-like tool helps children develop arithmetic, and interactive ICT platforms enhance students’ understanding of geometry. Through designing teaching and learning tasks with appropriate integration of tools, students are opened to learning environments where they can experience and make sense of abstract mathematical concepts. Using tools in the teaching and learning of mathematics has been shown to greatly empower students’ mathematical ability. In this connection, teachers play a complex and critical role to exploit the pedagogical potentials of the tools. Therefore, the starting point of exploration should focus on how teachers design tool-based teaching tasks. This project is grounded on teaching and learning theories of tool mediation and task design. Selected Hong Kong primary and secondary mathematics teachers will be engaged in workshops, lesson planning and trial teachings with appropriately chosen tools to design teaching and learning tasks. It aims to develop a tool-based mathematics task design model that is practical for teachers to use and serves as a frame for theoretical study. Currently the Hong Kong New Senior Secondary Mathematics Curriculum is under review and one area of discussion is on how to design assessment task to be used for teaching and learning. Hopefully this project will contribute to this area of discussion. 這為期36個月的研究項目是要探討數學老師怎樣運用具體教學工 具設計數學教學課業。香港學校傳統的數學教學方向往往採取以 教師為中心的模式。教師一般會先把抽象的數學觀念及符號闡述 傳遞給學生，然後學生運用這些觀念及符號去解決課程中要求的 數學問題。雖然這種教學取向對於協助學生應付考試及培養思考 有一定的效用，它卻未能引導學生透過處理具體物件去親身體驗 數學，並通過探究過程獲取抽象數學概念。教學研究已表明工具 可作為汲取數學經驗的媒介，因此工具已被視為可提高教學活動 效能的一種資源。在這研究中，我們視工具為任何對數學經驗與 數學理解有仲介潛質或功能的實物或虛擬物件。例如，數粒或算 柱可幫助兒童發展運算能力。資訊科技的互動功能可提升學生對 幾何的理解。通過設計融合工具的課業可以開啟一個讓學生經驗 及意識到抽象數學概念的學習環境。教學研究已有證據顯示利用 工具輔助數學教學可提升學生的數學能力。而老師怎樣運用這些 工具的教學潛質扮演著複雜且關鍵的角色。因此，研究的起點應 集中探討老師如何設計以工具為本的課業。這個研究項目建基於 工具仲介學習理論及課業設計理論。參與這個研究項目的香港小 學及中學數學教師將會參與工作坊，選取合適的工具去設計課業 及教學方案，並進行試教。這個研究項目的目的是要探究發展一 個切合老師實際需要，且可作為日後理論研究框架的工具為本數 學課業設計模型。現時香港新高中數學課程正值檢討中，而其中 一個討論焦點是如何設計可用於教與學的評估課業，期望這次研 究計劃能對這方面的討論有所貢獻。

12404614.label: Realisation of objectives
12404614.value: The purpose of the project was to investigate the roles of using concrete (physical or digital) tools in the teaching and learning of school mathematics. In contrast to the traditional pedagogical mode where teaching mathematics is by teacher-directed transmission of knowledge, a tool-based pedagogy requires students to explore mathematics concepts hands-on using tools designed or chosen by the teacher, or even by the students themselves. Well-chosen tools create a learning environment where both teachers and students co-construct mathematical knowledge under a carefully designed pedagogical sequence. The project was conducted via the formation at the start of the project a Learning Circle composed of a group of 4 primary and 7 secondary school mathematics teachers, three project investigators and a project manager who was a PhD student trained under the project. The Learning Circle created a platform to promote and cultivate a collaborative lesson design culture among teachers from different schools whereby diverse pedagogical experiences from the teachers and the researchers stimulate the task design process, and consequently instrumented to explore how Hong Kong school mathematics teachers design pedagogical tasks using tools in the teaching of school mathematics (Objective 1). The Learning Circle met regularly at the beginning phase of the project when the teachers and the project investigators shared and discuss the pedagogical roles of different tools and tool-based task design. Teachers designed their tool-based lessons together or individually through peer-planning processes where teachers and researchers shared freely their comments and critiqued on each other’s task designs. Teachers tried to design and/or choose their own tools that could fit the mathematics topics to be taught. The designs and choices were usually neither easy nor obvious because teachers had to design how tools could play epistemic mediation role between the learners and the mathematics to be learnt. Therefore, during the project, how teachers design and implement tool-based lessons became a reflective process where multiple factors had to be taken in consideration. Workshops were organized for teachers and researchers to present their tool-based (concrete and digital) pedagogical experiences. These activities involved how teachers integrate different tool environments (for example, ICT environment) into mathematics classrooms in designing tool-based teaching tasks for specific mathematic topics (Objective 2). Each teacher implemented his/her tool-based lessons under the supervision of a project investigator who monitored the lesson implementation via lesson observation, teacher interviews and provision of suggestions for improvement. A major finding was that the tools themselves do not play a pedagogical role without teacher-designed meaningful tasks that engage students to explore mathematical ideas based on how to use the tools in progressively epistemic ways. Thus the tools themselves take a transformative epistemic role during the pedagogical process. This tool transformation aspect task constitutes a critical element in forming a model of tool-based task design (Objective 3). With respect to the above process, the project objectives were achieved in a concerted way where the concerns raised in the research questions enlightened each other. The following is a summary of a tool-based pedagogical task design process that captures the objectives of the project: To design a tool-based mathematics lesson, one start with the object of learning which is the intended mathematics topic to be taught and learnt. Once this is decided, the teacher has to design a sequence of tool-based activities using suitable tools starting with the following basic considerations: 1.The tools have potential to represent in some way the intended mathematics concept to be taught. The representation can be crude or sophisticated, it depends on how the teacher understands the tools and design appropriate activities using them. 2.Multi-tool or single tool, physical and/or digital tool environment are pedagogical decisions to ensure coherent and faithful representations of mathematical concepts. 3.Students need to know how to use the tools, if not, they need to be trained to do so. 4.The tools should afford hands-on exploration for students to foster a student-centered pedagogical approach. The teacher either design and make his/her own tools or gets the tools from different resources. During the project, teachers and researchers shared their favored tools with each other. The design of the tool-based task sequence was the most critical component of the whole process when different pedagogical theories can be employed to frame the task designs. The fundamental idea of a tool-based task design is to the bridge the epistemological gap between tool-based experiences gained and formal mathematical concepts (e.g. as presented in textbooks) intended to be learnt. The task sequence should be progressively designed from creating physical concrete sensual experiences by using the tools to gradually transforming those experiences into more abstract mathematical ideas. How the teacher guides the students throughout the tool-based activities usually determines the success of the lesson. Studying the interactions occur between the students, the teacher, the tools and the mathematics knowledge in the lesson implementation and its further refinement provides valuable data to develop practical pedagogical approach for tool-based task design. This process sets up a foundation to develop a model of task design using tools for school mathematics which teachers can use practically in the classroom In the project, data from 10 lessons were collected that reflected fully or partially the task design process mentioned above, some of which were analyzed in detail resulting in major scholastic work. Therefore, the objectives of the project were achieved to initial research on the possibility of a tool-based pedagogical orientation in Hong Kong’s mathematics classroom and beyond.

12404614.label: Major findings and research outcome
12404614.value: Findings One Two new theoretical constructs Didactical Interactions and Tool-Task Dialectic were proposed for tool-based pedagogy based on the idea of Didactical Cycle in the theory of semiotic mediation. They were empirically developed from the project teachers’ tool-based task design cases where pragmatic manipulations of tools by the students and the teachers’ orchestration provided strong evidence to illustrate meaningful pedagogical interplays between tools and tasks. The analysis identified new transitional directions of critical phases grounded on the theory of Didactical Cycle. These new theoretical constructs contribute novice ideas to mathematics tool-based pedagogy research. They were supported by an international authority in this field of study via the PhD Oral Defense of the trained PhD student of the project. Findings Two This concerns the implementation of tool-based mathematics lesson based on the theoretical concept of Duo of Artifacts. Duo of Artifacts is constituted by a physical (i.e., concrete) tool and a digital counterpart (i.e., technological) of the physical one. They play different roles in the tool-based learning environment where students develop mathematics senses with interplays of the tools. In analyzing a project lesson, it was found that the two types of tools could be considered as a whole. A modified idea Compounded Tool was proposed consisting of duo parts of physical and digital representations. Students critically manipulate either the material part or the digital part of the Compound Tool to legitimate the functions of the other part. Tool-based task design should consider a balance between the orchestration of the physical and digital parts of the Compound Tool according to the critical and relational features of the tools. This Compound Tool idea contributes a novice research approach on combining the use of physical and digital tools simultaneously and meaningfully in the mathematics classroom. It was presented in an international conference in New Media for Educational Change. Findings Three Inquiry-based learning, mathematical modeling, and tool-based pedagogy provides a possible integrated pedagogical framework for mathematics and science. One of the project lesson sequence explored such an integrated pedagogy and consequently an inquiry-based modeling pedagogical cycle was proposed. The lesson sequence conducted a scientific experiment on the mathematics topic of estimation using a multi-tool environment in the school’s science laboratory. Pedagogical features that characterize a tool-based problem-solving integrated pedagogical approach were identified. This proposal was published in a rank A international journal in mathematics education and has already been cited and referenced in other publications.

12404614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12404614.value: The major findings of this project suggest that a tool-based and problem-solving based pedagogy is conducive to implementing a student-directed classroom where teachers, students and the tools actively interacting with each other in meaningful and epistemic ways. This approach can be extended to STEM education. Major findings 3 mentioned above has already initiated a research in this direction. STEM education involves the use of tools to engineer and to reason. What were learnt in this project could be transferred to researching STEM classroom teaching and learning fore-fronting problem-solving and tool-based strategies acting as a bridge to cross the pedagogical boundaries between the STEM disciplines. This would expand the study of tool-based task design to a more generic setting and thus promote the use of tool as an important epistemological means in school education. A GRF proposal has been submitted for this purpose.

12404614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12404614.value: This project begins a significant research in how tools, physical or virtual, are regarded as pedagogical resources in the mathematics classroom. Specifically, tools are used as exploration means for students to experience mathematical ideas in the process of formation of mathematics concepts. The project explores how Hong Kong school teachers design pedagogical tasks to foster such student-directed tool-based learning environment. This new teaching and learning approach in the Hong Kong context opens up possibilities and potentials for experiential learning in mathematics education and beyond. The findings of the project suggest that the interactive influences between the teachers, the students and the tools under well-designed tasks play a critical role in fostering students understanding of mathematical concepts. Furthermore, a multi-tool environment consisting both physical and digital tools could create inter-related representations that enrich and deepen students’conceptual understanding. This tool-based pedagogical approach can be extended to problem-based learning like that in STEM education where the use of tools to engineer a problematics situation is a common pedagogical practice. The value of the project is its transferability to a larger educational context whenever tools, in its broadest sense, are involved.

12405414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12405414.value: 晚清至民國時期，大英聖書公會、美華聖經會與蘇格蘭聖經會是基督新教最重要的中文聖經出版及發行機構。三家聖經公會自成立以還，皆以出版及發行「不加注釋或評論」的聖經為宗旨，以免注釋或評論的內容挑起神學爭端，影響跨宗派的合作與支持。然而，中國並非基督教國家，中國人的文化、宗教生活於多方面皆與聖經所描述的有所不同。因此，在華傳教士認為，聖經公會應容許中文聖經附有解釋聖經時代的文化習俗、宗教特色之注解，以免中文聖經讀者因誤解聖經而抗拒基督教。由於堅持己見，雙方為此爭持不下凡數十載。聖經公會應否出版及發行附加注解的中文聖經，或可視為自「聖號譯名問題」(The Term Question) 之後，基督新教在華傳教事業所面對的又一難題。 是項研究計劃將以分散英、美兩地的檔案資料為基礎，旨在探討十九世紀基督新教中文聖經注釋問題的來龍去脈，藉此說明基督新教來華不但是聖經自西徂東的旅程，也是西方基督教世界省思其宗教傳統的契機。首席研究員將會考察傳教士與聖經公會在中文聖經注釋問題上所持的立場及其理據，以及基督新教在華傳教事業中雙方的互動及權力關係，進而剖析為何聖經公會最終願意作出讓步，出版及發行附有簡注的中文福音書單行本。首席研究員亦會分析該等注解所反映的文化調適策略。是項研究計劃的成果不但有助填補中文聖經翻譯與出版史的空白，亦會加深我們對於基督教傳播史的了解。

12405414.label: Realisation of objectives
12405414.value: The project has achieved all the revised objectives. The Principal Investigator (PI) conducted archival research in several overseas archives, including the archives of the British and Foreign Bible Society (BFBS) in Cambridge University Library, the archives of the American Bible Society (ABS) in New York, the archives of the National Bible Society of Scotland (NBSS) at the Scottish Bible Society in Edinburgh and the archives of the United Bible Societies China Partnership in Singapore. The PI discovered and collected primary sources relevant to the ‘annotation question’ of the Chinese Protestant Bible. These sources include the minutes of the decision-making bodies and sub-committees of the three Bible societies in late Qing and early Republican China, namely the BFBS, the ABS and the NBSS, the correspondence between the Bible societies and Protestant missionaries in China, the Bible societies’ reports on their work in China and their annotated Chinese Bible editions. Having critically examined the aforementioned primary sources and compared them with relevant published materials such as reports of the General Conferences of Protestant Missionaries of China and contemporary missionary journals, the PI was able to shed light on the origin of the annotation question and the controversy over the question between the three Bible societies and Protestant missionaries in China. It is found that after the Treaties of Tianjin and the Convention of Beijing were signed in 1858 and 1860 respectively, Protestant missionaries gradually extended their work into the inner parts of China. Having more personal, direct contact with the Chinese people, they found that cultural and religious discrepancies between Chinese society and the societies depicted in the Bible made it difficult for a Chinese to understand the Bible simply from its plain text. Such experience challenged the view on the self-sufficiency of the Bible that was popular among western missionaries and held by the three Bible societies, i.e. the Bible needs no annotations since the Bible’s main messages are sufficiently clear to its unprejudiced readers; the Bible’s clearest passages provide all the light necessary to illuminate more obscure verses. While more and more missionaries had urged the Bible societies to publish and distribute Chinese Bibles with readers’ helps since the 1870s, it was not until the 1890s that the missionaries’ appeal began to be seriously considered. The major reason was that the Bible societies insisted on publishing Chinese Bibles without annotations owing to their constitutional, long-established ‘without note or comment’ principle, which helped them to solicit interdenominational support by avoiding sectarian or theological controversy. However, through studying the minutes of the decision-making bodies and sub-committees of the three Bible societies, the PI gained insights into the power relationship between the missionaries and the Bible societies in the context of the China mission field. In respect of Chinese Bible translation and circulation, they were interdependent: The missionaries relied on financial support from the Bible societies to produce Chinese Bibles while the latter needed the former’s linguistic expertise and assistance in supervising colporteurs. This contributed to the NBSS’s and BFBS’s fine-tuning of their stance as regard their publishing policies in China, when the missionaries there persistently and strongly demanded annotated Chinese Bibles from Bible societies. The two Bible societies eventually agreed to publish annotated editions of the Chinese Bible in 1892 and 1910 respectively by re-interpreting their ‘without note or comment’ principle for the sake of the China mission field. The collection of annotated Chinese Bibles held by the Cambridge University Library offered the PI the texts for his study of the annotation practices adopted by the Protestant missionaries whom the NBSS and the BFBS entrusted to prepare annotations for use in their Chinese Bible editions. Having compared the draft annotations for and the annotations eventually published in the annotated Chinese Bible editions of the NBSS and the BFBS, the PI was able to show the differences between the annotation practices endorsed by the two Bible societies. Since the BFBS strongly believed in the Bible’s self-explanatory power and an individual’s ability to interpret the Bible, the annotations in the BFBS’s annotated Chinese Bible editions contain very brief information or, sometimes, simply a reference to a particular biblical verse. The BFBS thought that such kinds of annotations provided adequate explanation of something completely unfamiliar to Chinese Bible readers. By contrast, the NBSS, being more attentive to the unfamiliarity of the Bible to the Chinese, allowed some explanations of the biblical text with reference to other religions in China and conflicts between biblical and Confucian teachings to be included in its annotated Chinese Bible editions. Moreover, the NBSS adopted the Chinese practice of presenting annotations in the form of interlinear notes printed in a smaller font, placing them in the biblical text. The BFBS, however, placed annotations in the margin above the biblical text, which indicates that annotations do not belong to the biblical text.

12405414.label: Major findings and research outcome
12405414.value: The findings of the project were presented at four international academic conferences and formed the basis of three scholarly articles. The PI also prepared a tentative bibliography of the annotated Chinese Protestant Bible editions published by Bible societies in late Qing and republican China. The major findings are summarized as follows: The conflicting views on the self-sufficiency of the Bible held by Bible societies and Protestant missionaries in late Qing and early Republican China were the main reason for the controversy over the annotation question of the Chinese Protestant Bible. However, the interdependence between Protestant missionaries and Bible societies in respect of Chinese Bible translation and circulation contributed to the NBSS’s and BFBS’s fine-tuning of their stance as regard their publishing policies in China, when the missionaries there persistently and strongly demanded annotated Chinese Bibles from them. The two Bible societies eventually agreed to publish annotated editions of the Chinese Bible in 1892 and 1910, as they interpreted the ‘without note or comment’ principle as a principle not excluding all notes or comments but the doctrinal or sectarian ones from the Chinese Bible editions published by them. However, the influence of the aforementioned power relationship between Protestant missionaries and Bible societies was not overwhelming, as indicated by the ABS’s insistence on not publishing any annotated Chinese Bible editions. Both the NBSS and the BFBS published annotated editions of the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles in Chinese. However, the exciting discovery of the NBSS’s annotated Proverbs in the Mandarin Union Version published in 1933 indicates that the NBSS expanded the scope of its annotated Chinese Bible series by including an edition of an Old Testament book. While the BFBS and the NBSS relied on Protestant missionaries to prepare annotations for their annotated Chinese Bible editions, they set up ad-hoc committees to exercise control over the contents and extent of the annotations, so that they would comply with the ‘without note or comment’ principle. The two Bible societies adopted different annotation practices. For example, the BFBS only prepared a relatively small number of explanatory readings for the Chinese Bible and included minimal explanatory information about the Bible in its annotations, which were called ‘translational helps’. In contrast, the NBSS allowed some explanations of the biblical text with reference to other religions in China and conflicts between biblical and Confucian teachings to be included in its annotated Chinese Bible editions.

12405414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12405414.value: The findings of the project lay a foundation for further research into the history of Chinese Bible publishing. One of the potential future research projects could be a comparative study of the annotations in the annotated Chinese Bibles published by Bible societies and other Christian publishing houses in late Qing and Republican China. It would further contribute to our understanding of how biblical annotations facilitated the spread of Christianity in China by explaining biblical teachings and ideas in reference to socio-cultural context of the Chinese people. Another potential future research project is to study the impact of the annotation question on the development of the three Bible societies’ work in Republican China. Issues to be examined include whether the Bible societies’ different positions on publishing annotated Chinese Bibles were an obstacle to their collaboration in the China mission field. The PI has done some preliminary work in that regard and will present his findings at the 11th International Convention of Asia Scholars in Leiden in July.

12405414.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12405414.value: Provoked by the ‘without note or comment’ principle of Bible societies, the ‘annotation question’ of the Chinese Protestant Bible (i.e. whether the Chinese Protestant Bible needed to be published with annotations explaining the biblical world to Chinese readers) was heatedly debated between Protestant missionaries and Bible societies in China for most of the second half of the 19th century. This project investigated the origin of and the controversy over the annotation question, as well as the annotation practices adopted by Protestant missionaries and endorsed by Bible societies for their annotated Chinese Bible editions published in late Qing and Republican China. The findings of the project shed light on the implications of the power relationship between different Protestant groups for the dissemination of Christianity in China. They also provide fresh insights into the historical process by which Christianity was spread in the non-Christian world by showing that the experience of the Protestant mission in China challenged the traditional Western understanding of the Bible’s self-sufficiency and an individual’s ability to interpret the Bible, which resulted in a change of Bible societies’ publishing policies that had far-reaching impacts on the history of Chinese Bible publishing.

12405514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12405514.value: This project investigates the philosophical reflections of German-educated Chinese thinkers on the problem of modernity and the state during the 1930s when the Nanjing Government’s (1927-1937) nation-building programme was in full swing. Since the mid-nineteenth century, the impact of modernity in China has been highly visible: industrialism, rationalization, consumerism and scientific intervention crawled into various aspects of Chinese life, bringing about transitions in urban life, health and medicine, popular culture and significantly, the political reform of Republican China. Jiang Jieshi, inspired partly by a simplistic understanding of Germany, looked to reproduce a centralized industrial and military machine in China fueled by a culture of pragmatism. As a result, the Nanjing Decade witnessed an attempt in fabricating a strong state of nation-wide authority, complemented by an immense economic and industrial capacity that would further China’s modernization. Contradistinctive to Jiang’s idea, an influential group of Chinese philosophers, poets and political thinkers expressed concern over the future of China under the clockwork of modernity. The intellectuals- Zong Baihua (1897-1986), Feng Zhi (1905-1993), Zhang Junmai (1887-1969) and He Lin (1902-1992) studied at German universities and experienced first-hand the woes of the Weimar Republic. Seeing beyond the surface of modernity a crisis from creeping political transformation and excessive innovation, the intellectuals noted the peril of creating a China hanging merely unto an empty shell: stripped of inner essence, modern men end up isolated and soulless, strolling aimlessly in modern techno-poleis, as was confirmed by Hitler’s use of an almighty state apparatus to govern a society of helpless individuals. Convinced that China dangerously traced the footsteps of the German experience, the intellectuals began in the 1930s to assess the power and evils of a rapidly ongoing modernity. As a resolution to the withering of spiritual wellbeing, the traditional German cultural ideals of Innerligkeit (inwardness) and Bildung (forming of the soul) were put forth, calling for a new Chinese culture which could afford the transformations and pressure of a modern Chinese state. Working as the Chinese counterparts of Innerligkeit and Bildung, Feng’s solitude and meditation, He’s “inner sageliness,” Zong’s aesthetics and Zhang’s integration of democracy and social statism sought equilibrium in modernization through an enlightening reform for the Chinese mind, particularly in exploration of the relations between: material progress and cultural growth; spiritual interiority and modern life; self and collectivity and individual and state, eventually kicking off the search for an alternative approach to China’s future development.

12405514.label: Realisation of objectives
12405514.value: This project has succeeded in addressing during its duration the following five objectives： 1. To study the Chinese intellectuals’ response to modernity in the time frame Mainstream interpretations of the May Fourth Movement oversimplify China’s intellectual spectrum in the 1920s by emphasizing the confrontation between the “all-out Westernization” stream led by Wu Shi and the traditionalists with the national essence school (guocui) and the neo-traditional Confucians as representatives. For decades scholars in relevant fields see the former as a progressive force that sought to remove outworn values, ethics and social practices so as to inject into Chinese culture modern values such as equality, science, democracy and rationalism, and the latter as conservatives who strove to defend the traditional ways of life at any cost. Focusing on the thoughts of four German-educated thinkers in the interwar years, namely Zong Baihua (1897-1986), Feng Zhi (1905-1993), Zhang Junmai (1887-1969) and He Lin (1902-1992), this project reveals how the German cultural ideals of Bildung (self-cultivation), Innerlichkeit (inwardness) and sensibilities and spirituality join forces to facilitate a reassessment of modernity. Inspired by German great minds such as Goethe, Schiller and Hegel, they began as early as in the 1920s to challenge scientism, materialism and urban life which were byproducts of modern society. Feng Zhi, for instance, highlighted in his poems men’s anomie, loneliness and solitude in urban societies that isolated them from nature. In contradistinction to the Westernizers and the traditionalists, Zong Baihua devoted his energy to rediscovering different dimensions of men’s souls. For him, if fully developed, they could form well-rounded and self-sustained personalities that survived modernity. 2. To explore their conceptualization of the relations between the individual, state, modernization and modernity Zhang Junmai and He Lin’s early writings, which this project investigates, reexamined the above concepts. For many non-Western developing nations, including China under Jiang Jieshi, modernity is perceived as an end worthy of investment. With military and industrial prowess, an authoritarian state is instrumental in delivering the mission of modernization that benefited all. Standing on an alternate lane, the German-educated thinkers regarded mental gist as the foundation of nation-building. Influenced by Hegel, Zhang Junmai and He Lin saw civil society in which free and complete personalities confronted, negotiated and cooperated as a key stage toward an ethical state. It was upon organic interaction between individuals and communities that modern states emerged. 3. To examine how the problems within Weimar Germany led to Chinese intellectual concerns My papers published over these years converge on the point that the four German-educated Chinese thinkers’ intellectual sojourn in Weimar Germany, instead of lighting up their imagination of modernity, pushed them further deep into the realm of spiritual interiority. Amazed by the charms of Berlin in the 1920s, many saw the German capital, which swiftly rose from the ruins of war, as a symbol of modernity. In fact, it soon became the most populated and industrialized of all German cities, featuring large scale urbanization, tremendous technological innovations (trains, automobiles, and telephones as well as photography, photojournalism, and film), mass cultural entertainment, etc. However, the German-educated Chinese thinkers that this project examines, showed in their works in the interwar years the gloomy side of modernity. Zong Baihua, who found himself a loner in Berlin, looking always for peace and silence in the dark night of this vociferous city. It was also in Berlin plagued by excessive consumerism and social inequality that He Lin reflected on the values of morality and aesthetic values. 4. To project the proposition and reinterpretation of Innerlichkeit to fill in the spiritual vacuum caused by modernization and the intellectuals’ reflections on spirit and self; collectivity and state The project has fully addressed the above issues as all the four German-educated Chinese thinkers dealt with them in different degrees and in different manners. Zong Baihua urged men in his works to return to their hearts, asking them to feel, intuit, imagine, and idealize things surrounding them, and then to frame and organize their own life. Just like breathing, men should inhale a great variety of rational, cultural, and spiritual ingredients which underwent a process of catharsis (cleansing or purifying) in the heart, then came out through exhale activities and expressions in beautified forms. An active life was for him an ever-improving process and active lives joined forces to create a better world. Feng Zhi, having personally experienced life’s takebacks and explored the melancholy of German Romanticism, expressed in his artistic works the imminence of moral ethics and traditional ideals that had been disparaged in 1920s China. Notably, he as a poet illuminated how heart, mind and soul must be substantially and harmoniously redeemed at a time when the inner self are oftentimes lost in science, reason and materialism. Being a political philosopher who centered his attention in his early years on the creation of a new constitution for China, Zhang Junmai envisioned in his On Constitution a distortionless political condition that enabled public consensus created by free and mature citizens to direct rational politics. From a metaphysical perspective, He Lin envisioned the interconnectedness of self and nation in the movements of world history. 5. to investigate how these ideas provided an overall critique of and alternative option for China’s development The four thinkers’’ education and personal experience of the darks and bright sides of modernity led them to reflect on the contradiction of material progress and emotional vacuum in modern society at a time when the Chinese political reformers and leading educated elite tried hard to push China onto the fast track of modernization. Instead of blindly defending the Chinese heritage or stubbornly resisting Western civilization, they called for the rebuilding of the Chinese people’s personality and spiritual interiority. Behind their works lie a crucial message that reminds of the need to humanize by embracing one’s sensibilities, individuality and the natural world. Though accused of being too metaphysical and impractical, they showed forcefully clear-minded criticisms of the clockwork-like modern society and the one-dimensional modern men. Their renewed appreciation of the Confucian social order, in which knowledge and spirituality as well as individuals and collectivity, all harmoniously existed in wholeness as the accumulation of the active Chinese souls, also demonstrated the common intellectual concerns of modern Chinese and German philosophers.

12405514.label: Major findings and research outcome
12405514.value: The conference presentations in the last three years have turned into four papers that have been or will soon be published. 1. The Search for Spiritual Inwardness in Modern Society: Zong Baihua’s (1897–1986) Aesthetic Vision in the 1920s and 1930s This paper demonstrates that Zong Baihua’s early aesthetic vision resulted from not only the German cultural resources that he adapted, but also his renewed interests in Confucianism. While the German cultural ideals of “Bildung” (forming of the soul) and “Innerlichkeit” (inwardness) inspired him in the 1920s to search for a complete personality founded upon a balanced development of intellectuality and sensibilities, he completed his theoretical body after his German sojourn drawing on Confucianism which was a life-centric system that harmoniously integrated knowledge and morality, and individuals and the collective. 2. Unraveling China’s Progress through German Romanticism: Feng Zhi’s Critique of Modernity and Proposition of Aesthetics Unlike most works that see Feng Zhi as a poet, this paper, focusing on Feng Zhi’s works on Rilke, Novalis and Schiller from the late 1920s to the late 1930s, explains how he put forward through these works a life strategy that enabled one to bridge the gap between reason and spirit, achieving a self-enlightened, optimistic and all-rounded personality that could withstand the perils of modernity. 3. 張君勱（1887—1969）的《國憲議》：求個人、社群和國家的有機發展 Zhang Junmai’s（1887—1969） On Constitution: The Organic Interaction of Individuals, Communities and the State It was a mission of liberal educated elite in Republican China to design a new constitution that guaranteed individuals’ rights and duties, regulated the relationship between regional and central governments, and encouraged citizen participation in public affairs. Zhang Junmai, this paper points out, saw the rebuilding of Chinese people’s characters as the first step toward China’s political renewal. For him, it was upon Chinese people’s civic awareness and power of self-governance that a new Chinese government could be founded. 4. 往返東西：二次大戰前賀麟（1902-1992）的思想漫遊 From the East to the West: He Lin’s（1902-1992）Spiritual Wandering in the Interwar Years This paper traces how Westernized education in China admitted He Lin to science and democracy, and how life experience and postgraduate training in the USA and Germany led him back to Confucianism. He Lin criticized in the 1920s traditional Chinese ways of life utilizing high sounding ideals and crude scientific methods, but his encounter with the excesses of modernity awakened him to the diversity of men’s spiritual capacity. Following the footstep of Hegel, he reassessed the values of aesthetics, history and moral philosophy that later formed his philosophy of mind.

12405514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12405514.value: German-educated Chinese thinkers and the transmission of German cultural ideals to China are two major themes that deserve our attention. Stemming from them are range of topics, including (1) literary clubs, association and magazines to which German-educated intellectuals contributed, such as “shaonian zhongguo xuehui” (Young China Society) and “chenzhong she” (Sunken Bell Association), (2) German cultural elements embedded in curriculums of German studies in major Chinese universities such as Tongji University, Peking University and Nanjing University since the 1910s, (3) German classics by Heinrich Heine, Friedrich Hölderlin, Kant and Hegel that were translated into Chinese and were introduced in different forms, (4) German romantic novels, plays and dramas that were popularized up to the early 1940s, (5) the cultural uniqueness of neglected German-educated Chinese thinkers such as Yang Bingchen (1892-?), Chen Quan (1903-1969), Li Shicen (1892-1934), and Zhang Mingding (1904-1979), and (6) the alternative weltanschauung and strategy for cultural renaissance these works and people presented, all of which merit systematic exploration. A new GRF entiteld "Unrevealed Charms of the Soul: German Romanticism in Republican China," was submitted last year to address the above issues. It scored 3.5 and will be revised for resubmission this year.

12405514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12405514.value: This project, by highlighting four German-educated Chinese thinkers’ yearn for sensibilities, spiritual interiority, natural beauty, all-rounded development of personalities etc., draws a broader picture of the cultural spectrum that the so-called “May Fourth Paradigm” fails to fully cover. Rather than seeking a formula that could reproduce advanced Western nations’ industrial successes or reassuring the values of traditional Chinese culture, they sought a new pathway to the completeness of personality, complementing reason with feeling and intuition of aesthetic experience. Zong Baihua’s aesthetic studies, Feng Zhi’s poems, Zhang Junmai’s political treatises and He Lin’s philosophical works joined forces to present an idealized person. That person was an artist of life who could transform in his mind, heart and soul everyday encounter with the reality into feelings and sentiments, by means of which he or she recreated the world through his or her works, no matter whether poetry, painting or natural sciences. The works of this idealized person, in a sense, were the unity of ideal and reality, subjective and objective, and this idealized person represented the future of China.

12405614.label: Project Objectives
12405614.value: To fill a chapter in Hong Kong visual art history relating the spiritual and the artistic impacts of the New Ink Movement in the 1960s to the case studies of the selected local artists and their later artistic development in the 1970s. To investigate the spiritual legacy of the New Ink movement in Hong Kong and how its meaning of “adaptation” was manifested by the selected artists in building the local art scene in the 1970s. To critically review some of the representative discourses on “Hong Kong art” by referring to the analysis and the findings of this project, which are the artistic attempts of the selected local artists, and the proposition in post-colonial theories that artists living under colonial power have taken on a hybrid artistic identity.
