12405614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12405614.value: The proposed project aims to investigate the development of local art via case studies of six Hong Kong artists who had their artistic developments nurtured during and after the significant New Ink art movement in the 1960s. In the 1960s, Lu Shoukun launched the “New Ink Movement”. He believed that by combining the artistic development and technology in the West with the spiritual temperament and ink brush strokes of the Chinese tradition, one could create new visual experience that will be regarded as “Hong Kong art”. He regarded the artistic attempt as an important form of existential “adaptation” of local painters living in the ex-colony which should originate from artists’ self-understanding. The project intends to investigate Lu’s notion of “adaptation” in the visual arts of Leung Kui Ting 梁巨廷, Aser But畢子融, Kan Tai Keung 靳埭強, Choi Yan Chi 蔡仞姿, Lui Chun Kwong呂振光 and Kong Kai Ming江啟明. Leung, But and Kan were active during the New Ink Movement and were under the influence of Lu. Choi, Lui and Kong were individual artists who followed their own artistic directions in the post-New Ink era. Though they are making visual arts in various forms and media, they have been pushing forward important artistic innovations as forms of “adaptation” that Lu suggested. They are involved in a liberation process in the colonial territory that emerged during the period of significatory or representational undecidability in Hong Kong in the 1970s. The study aims to fill a chapter in the Hong Kong visual art history which reviews the revelation of the New Ink Movement and the artistic attempts of representative Hong Kong artists after the significant movement. It recognizes their contributions to the multiplicity of visual art styles in Hong Kong and reviews their own artistic “adaptation” against the social and cultural backgrounds of the colonial Hong Kong in the 1970s. It then critically reviews current discourses on Hong Kong art with the empirical findings of the project. This is an interdisciplinary research using methods of interview, oral history, art analysis and critical practice. It utilizes theories of art history, aesthetics, social studies and post-colonial studies. The research outcomes of the project will be presented in both local and international conferences and published in reputable academic venues. 此計劃乃旨在研究於一九六零年代新水墨運動在香港推行以後，視覺藝術語言的發展。本計劃以六位本地藝術家的作品為個案研究，見出新水墨運動精神的影響及其變奏。 一九六Ｏ年代，呂壽琨先生提出在香港從事藝術創作，一方面得秉承中國傳統藝術的精神，一方面需要「順」與「適」，以能在香港安心立命。其順適的觀念，包括把中國傳統跟西方現代藝術加以融合，以發展全新的視藝經驗。呂壽琨繼而掀起了重要的「新水墨運動」，其影響力一時無倆。 本計劃擬深入研究一九七Ｏ年代於「新水墨運動」後冒起的六位藝術家，包括梁巨廷、畢子融、靳埭強、蔡仞姿、呂振光與江啟明。他們並非全是呂壽琨的跟從者，與新水墨運動亦非全體支持，有幾位且與之保持距離，唯他們皆於一九七Ｏ年代開始即全情投入創作及藝術教育，並發展自己獨特的藝術語言，在某種意義上實踐著呂壽琨先生所說的「順」與「適」。 此計劃希望對香港視覺藝術史作出一九七Ｏ年代的補遺，並檢視於一九七Ｏ年代新水墨運動所曾作出的多元影響，同時肯定這六位藝術家的藝術成就與貢獻。研究方法包括個案研究法、口述歷史、訪談紀錄、藝術史方法及藝術語言分析，並加進考察香港殖民時代社會及政治的場域研究，是真正的跨學科研究實踐，且同時檢討近年對香港藝術史論述的一些濫調。

12405614.label: Realisation of objectives
12405614.value: 1. To fill a chapter in Hong Kong visual art history relating the spiritual and the artistic impacts of the New Ink Movement in the 1960s to the case studies of the selected local artists and their later artistic development in the 1970s. This study outcome, which turns out to be a monograph with 6 chapters, has succeeded in filling the gap in Hong Kong visual art history. The interviews that the PI has conducted with individual artists, tell common stories about their encounter with the pioneers of the New Ink Art Movement in the 1960s, and the impacts they have received from these artists, directly or indirectly. The names of the important people in art education and art arena in the 1970s are identified, as well as the artistic deeds they have done, the education courses they have taught and the art events they have organized, which have led to the discussion and practices in creating the artistic identity of Hong Kong. Besides common names of the people and the art societies that were mentioned in each interview, the study has also noted the psychological process, artistic experiments and struggles of the 6 visual artists, and the changes throughout their creative developments which are oriented from the 1970s. 2. To investigate the spiritual legacy of the New Ink movement in Hong Kong and how its meaning of “adaptation” was manifested by the selected artists in building the local art scene in the 1970s. The study has also reviewed the representative work of the 6 artists and the stages of their artistic development, which has noted some common influences, e.g. from hard edge art and graphic design, and how these Western modern artistic attempts were incorporated into individual artists’ work, especially in those who have merged traditional Chinese landscape painting with these new Western art movements. The study demonstrates how they have met the mission raised by Lu Shou-kun, who claimed that Chinese artists in Hong Kong should be “adaptive” in terms of living and creating in the ex-colony. The findings of this study illustrate how the broad meaning of adaptation is manifested in various artistic attempts taken by the 6 artists individually. For example, in the case of Kan Ti Keung, it is his “geometrical landscape” which becomes his signature style through the transition of “hard edge” to symmetrical placement of landscape. He admits that it is the graphic design that has incorporated into the method of Chinese landscape painting in his work which dominated his artistic attempt in the 1970s. The popular practice of graphic design was to meet the rapid economic and industrial developments in Hong Kong in the 1970s, and the work of Kan has built a way to adopt the practice. 3. To case study individual artistic development of the selected visual artists who have their artistic styles and languages nurtured in the 1970s during the post-New-Ink movement era, and to recognize their ‘adaptive” contributions to the establishment of Hong Kong art. The case studies of Choy Yan Chi and Lui Chun Kwong are two examples which demonstrate how young artists like Choy and Lui were under the influences of Lu Shou-kun directly or indirectly in experimenting their own artistic styles during the 1970s. Choy was in close contact with Lu and has carried with her strong cultural identity when she studied art in the US. She then departed from “New Ink Art” and expanded her artistic ideas into the installation art she introduced after she returned to Hong Kong. Lui Chun Kwong has no direct contact with the “New Ink Movement”, but adopted similar attitude which led him to evolve from realistic painting to minimalism, which last throughout his later painting. 4. To study in contextual tactic the relation of the artistic development of the selected artists and the social and cultural changes in Hong Kong in the 1970s, including the dialectical relationship between the expectations of the British colonizers and the impulse to construct an independent artistic identity among the selected artists.. The findings regarding this objective were established from the oral histories provided by the 6 artists during interviews, when they described the life growing up or living in the ex-colony and the situation of art education and the support that has given to them in the 1970s. 5. To conduct an interdisciplinary research, utilizing theories of art history, art and aesthetics, social studies and post-colonial studies. This objective was only met to a certain extent in the way that not many post-colonial theories were applied to individual studies nor the philosophical aesthetics theories. The interdisciplinary attempt was made in the conclusion chapter though. 6. To critically review some of the representative discourses on “Hong Kong art” by referring to the analysis and the findings of this project, which are the artistic attempts of the selected local artists, and the proposition in post-colonial theories that artists living under colonial power have taken on a hybrid artistic identity. Yes, this objective was met to a good extent in all the individual studies which comes up to the 6 chapters. Analysis or reading of the representative work of the 6 artists during the era demonstrates the richness and the variety of the hybrid artistic identity.

12405614.value: The outcome of this study, which turns out to be a monograph with 6 chapters, has succeeded in filling a gap in Hong Kong visual art history, which relates the spiritual and the artistic impacts of the New Ink Movement in the 1960s to selected local artists' artistic developments in the 1970s.. The interviews that the PI has conducted with individual artists tell common stories about their encounter with the pioneers of the New Ink Art Movement in the 1960s and the impacts they have received from these artists, directly or indirectly. The names of the important people in art education and art arena in the 1970s are identified, as well as the influential artistic deeds they have done, the education courses they have introduced and the art events they have organized which have led to the discussion and practices in creating the artistic identity of Hong Kong. Besides common names, events and the art societies that were mentioned in each interview, the study has also noted the psychological process, artistic experiments and struggles, and changes throughout the creative developments of the 6 artists which are oriented from the 1970s. The study has also reviewed the representative work of the 6 artists and the stages of their artistic development, which has noted some common influences, e.g. from hard edge art and graphic design to geometrical landscape, and how these Western modern artistic attempts were incorporated into individual artists’ work, especially in those who have merged traditional Chinese painting and materials with these new Western artistic attempts, to their later developments which became their signature styles. The findings of this study illustrate how the broad meaning of adaptation is manifested in various artistic attempts taken by the 6 artists. Their artistic languages are analyzed and described, and their links to personal history and art history are also traced. The study demonstrates how the artistic attempts of the 6 local artists have met the mission raised by Lu Shou-kun, that is to be “adaptive” in terms of living and creating in the ex-colony. It has also demonstrated study in contextual tactic the relation of the artistic development of the selected artists and the social and cultural changes in Hong Kong in the 1970s.The biographical notes reflect impulse to construct an independent artistic identity among the selected artists, and how their living under colonial power have taken on hybrid artistic styles.

12405614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12405614.value: 1. The current study has only dealt with 6 cases, which is far from the ideal representability in exploring the subject. With more cases, it could help to critically review some of the representative discourses on “Hong Kong art”, and the proposition in post-colonial theories that artists living under colonial power have taken on a hybrid artistic identity. 2. This study has identified art schools, camps and artistic beliefs that are different from the “New Ink Art” movement initiated in the 1960s. There were disagreements, debates and exclusivities among them, as well as distortions, which are related to different political standpoints and beliefs in what art can and should do. The backgrounds of the artists should be further traced down, and more should be done to conduct an interdisciplinary research, utilizing theories of art history, art and aesthetics, social studies and post-colonial studies. 3. This research helps to understanding the continuous impacts of the important “New Ink Movement” in Hong Kong from 1960s to 1980s, and the process of the making of Hong Kong art in the 1970s. It has laid a foundation for further analysis, reading and dialogues regarding developments of Hong Kong art history in the mentioned eras.

12405614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12405614.value: The study aims to fill a chapter in the Hong Kong visual art history which reviews the cultural and the artistic impacts of the New Ink Movement and its later variations. It investigates its heritage and spiritual legacy and sees how it has influenced individual artistic development. It also recognizes the contributions of the selected artists to the multiplicity of visual art forms in Hong Kong. The project cross studies local artistic development and the social and cultural changes of the colonial Hong Kong in the 1970s. It is an interdisciplinary research using methods of interview, oral history, art criticism and critical practice, and it utilizes theories of art history, aesthetics, social studies and post-colonial studies. The visual artists the project has studied are LEUNG Kui Ting 梁巨廷, Aser BUT畢子融, KAN Tai Keung 靳埭強, CHOI Yan Chi 蔡仞姿, LUI Chun Kwong呂振光 and KONG Kai Ming江啟明. They nurtured and strengthened their artistic languages in the 1970s. They were either the followers of Lui Shou-Kun, the pointeer who initated the "New Ink Art Movement" in the 1960s, or those who distanced from the movement, and are all influential art educators.

12406114.label: Project Objectives

12406114.label: Realisation of objectives
12406114.value: Our project objectives have been advanced during the second half of our research project and the following year due to the main efforts of the PI, since the Research Fellow left HKBU to return to Europe in July 2016, and so refocused his attention on obtaining a new position, and added nothing more to the project from that point on. Though this was a major obstacle to overcome, the PI continued to work with the materials at hand, and was able to produce six articles (one in Chinese (translated by others) and five in English, two of those in English to appear in volumes edited by others, and three to appear as chapters in a book contracted with Lexington Press authored by the PI and to appear in 2019. (Please see output report.) To his credit, the Research Fellow did produce one small article that appeared in Sinological News. (Please see output report.) In addition to these published and forthcoming outputs, there were eight conference presentations or university lectures presented by the PI from 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2018 that dealt with various aspects of the goals for this research project. Another factor that undoubtedly affected the under-achievement of this research project was that the PI officially retired from HKBU as of 1 September 2017, and so in preparation for that major transition, there was very much to do both at the university and with international institutions in order to fully move out from Hong Kong and return to a new home base in the USA. One consequence of that movement was that materials and books had to be boxed and prepared for shipping as early as April 2017, and those materials related to some of the research materials collected in Vanve, Lyon, and elsewhere did not arrive in our home base until November 2017. Although the PI retained access to some of the main published works of Couvreur and Wieger during this period, and so could advance research on those items, the unpublished materials were not accessible. In addition, the overall situation with post-retirement conditions ended up involving an adjunct position with my department that included specific guidance with PhD students I had before my retirement. This involved more time in reviewing all the dissertation related materials that were produced during this time, which I reviewed diligently for the sake of those students. Now I have only one more PhD student to see complete his dissertation. While all of these matters brought some degree of hindrance to completing the project objectives, my beloved wife and I have been able now to endure our first full year in post-retirement living in our new American home, and are anticipating a fruitful New Year in 2019 related to continued research, writing, editing, publishing, lecturing, and mentoring. During this past year much has been done to review and articulate the "Jesuit cross-cultural hermeneutics" employed in the "old Jesuit mission in China" (lasting from 1580 till 1775) and its contrast with the "modern / new Jesuit mission" in which Couvreur and Wieger had a significant part. Along with this has been a continual exploration of the various canon-in-translation of foreign language renderings of Ruist and Daoist canonical literature, broadening the research scope related to "missionary-scholars" to include work by one Russian Orthodox abbot (Iakinf or Nikita Y. Bichurin (1777-1853), a number of key Protestant figures (James Legge, Ernst Faber, Richard Wilhelm), and other Jesuit figures residing in some part of China (Angelo Zottoli and Joachim Angelico de Jesus Guerra). This has created a much larger and more explicit historical and cultural context that can now serve as a hermeneutic basis for identifying the contributions and complications in both Couvreur's and Wieger's prolific published works. What needs to be done to make one of the final goals possible -- that is an outline of a full volume devoted to the life and works of Couvreur and Wieger -- are the following issues: (1) A systematic review of all the previously collected unpublished materials, in order to integrate what is learned from those documents into the final versions of the chronologies for both Courveur and Wieger. (2) Obtaining copies of Wieger's works published about the post-traditional Chinese cultural situations (published after 1911 and starting in the 1920s as an annual "report" to portray the general situation in the Republic of China, as far as he was able to discern it). (3) Continuing to work through comparative analyses of Ruist ("Confucian") canonical texts produced by Couvreur that have not yet been thoroughly reviewed and compared with Legge, Wilhelm, and (as a result of new discoveries) Guerra and possibly Zottoli. What has already been done is a thorough analysis of his French and Latin versions of The Four Books (Les quatres livres), and some portions of his work in the Shijing (The Book of Odes/Poetry) and the Liji (The Record of Rites). This leaves more to do with both of the latter two works, but also his versions of the Shangshu, the Chunqiu and its Zuozhuan Commentary, and his version of the Yili. (4) More work needs to be done in understanding how Couvreur and Wieger learned about contemporary and classical Chinese languages, and how these are reflected in their own works. Once these four tasks are completed, the PI will be able to complete an informed outline for a major monograph dealing with these two major modern Jesuit "savant missionaires".

12406114.label: Major findings and research outcome
12406114.value: (1) New unpublished materials from the Vanve Archive of French Jesuits and the Lyon Municipal Library (including French Jesuit published materials) has revealed much about both the institutional context of the Xianxian French Jesuit mission compound as well as the personal characteristics of both Couvreur and Wieger that have never before been documented and confirmed. (2) Documentation of the international status of Couvreur (the only three time recipient of the Stanislas Julien Prize to this date) and Wieger (one time recipient of the Stanislas Julien Prize and major figure in modern studies of Chinese language) has been advanced, refined, and confirmed. (3) Couvreur's immense contributions in producing French and Latin versions of the whole of Ruist ("Confucian") canonical texts has been given a more precise descriptive account, along with a thorough evaluation of his versions of The Four Books (Les quatres livres) in comparison with similar renderings made by Legge and Guerra, with some references to Zottoli and Wilhelm. (4) Wieger's critical analysis of the impact of Zhu Xi's major role in the development of so-called "Neo-Confucianism" has been seen to anticipate the similarly negative analyses presented in Richard Wilhelm's history of Chinese philosophy and Guerra's categorization of Zhu Xi as the "second major heretic of Ruist traditions". (5) Visits to the location of the former French Jesuit Xianxian mission realized in the Spring of 2016 made possible a completely new and concrete documentation of details about how and where Couvreur and Wieger lived and died. No one previously had documented this information with such thoroughness, and brought it up to date in terms of how that former mission now survives in a contemporary Chinese Catholic institutional form.

12406114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12406114.value: As outlined in 5.3 above, there are four major steps to take in order to bring this project to the point of being ready to produce an informed outline for a major monographic study focused on the lives and works of Couvreur and Wieger. These are the matters for further development that the PI will seek to pursue with a few scholars who have adequate French background and are competent in Chinese. Though this can no longer be pursued as a research project under the aegis of the HKBU, because the PI has retired as of 1 September 2017, there is another institutional and funding possibility for pursuing these goals. The PI is actively seeking to establish a new intellectual/spiritual retreat center in the Colorado Rockies in the USA where both Chinese and Christian studies will form the basis for a wisdom-based method of learning and research. If this institution can be established within 2019 as the Hephzibah Mountain Aster Academy (which is the current plan), philanthropic support can be sought to provide funding to realize these remaining research tasks with appropriate research personnel.

12406114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12406114.value: This research project has sought to identify and reveal the unusual character of the prolific output produced by two modern Jesuit missionary-sinologists, Seraphin Couvreur (1835-1919) and Leon Wieger (1856-1933). Their work has never before been systematically reviewed and evaluated, especially from the angle of their own Jesuit spirituality and its institutionalization within the context of the French Jesuit mission in the town of Xianxian in Hebei Province. Through the production of seven articles (six by the PI and one by an associated Research Fellow), major steps have been taken to raise awareness of the strengths and weaknesses of the published materials produced by these two prolific "savant missionnaires" (French for "sagely missionaries"). Though our research has not been able to complete all the previously conceived research goals, the advances made have set new precedents that are already receiving attention among Chinese scholars interested in these persons and their works.

12406714.value: To provide a detailed account of China's urbanization pathways with a focus on rehousing arrangements for former villagers driven by top-down zoning and bottom-up segregation when their land and housing were taken away or demolished, follow the evolution of different rehousing projects, and examine their sustainability. To examine the impacts of different rehousing projects on community rebuilding, in terms of living environment and community governance.

12406714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12406714.value: Despite China’s promotion of the free market since 1978, the land property system remains ambiguous and split between urban and rural areas, and villagers have collective claim to the use of the land for residential, farming and related purposes. The new national strategy to develop Western China has led to the revisit of arguments on how to compensate and relocate villagers after land expropriation. From the top-down zoning perspective, both local governments and developers have engaged in rehousing projects. For local governments, they have multiple goals in mind such as to obtain revenues from development projects, to construct the “harmonious society” and to balance the development of affordable and expensive housing. For developers, they participate in the zoning practice as the partner of local governments to invoke the requisition process, to overcome the problem of fragmented property rights, and to make a deal with a county or village. Previous studies emphasize the consequent economic loss and destructive effects on traditional rural life for former villagers, but do not examine in detail how they are relocated, which has complicated implications for property (re)distribution and community rebuilding. From the bottom-up segregation perspective, some villagers and grassroots collectives have undertaken informal housing development when the urban expansion encroaches into surrounding villages. Furthermore, some “compensation land” was ceded back to villages by governments to smooth the development process. In a form of village corporatism, grassroots collectives colluded with local villagers to construct their own rehousing projects. The consequent bottom-up segregation constitutes a new means of property (re)distribution in which insiders’ rights are prioritized, and an alternative path of community rebuilding that may alter the living environment and restructure community governance. The research site, a village in Ningxia, witnessed two pathways to rehouse villagers in the face of urbanization. In the first pathway, governments and developers have constructed and assigned housing communities for former villagers. In the second pathway, villagers and grassroots collectives managed to get a piece of “compensation land” and constructed a collective neighborhood of single-family houses to accommodate indigenous residents. This project will generate a qualitative dataset of 100 relocated village households and 10 local “planners” (officials and developers). Via a systematic examination of homeownership, housing values, living environment and community governance, this study will follow the evolution of different rehousing projects, examine their sustainability, and explore their implications for property (re)distribution and community rebuilding. 中國1978年以來的經濟體制改革大大推動了市場的擴張，但是土地所有權依然是一個富有爭議的領域，城鄉之間依然存在著產權的斷裂，其中農村居民只能在集體土地上進行居住和耕種等活動。國家的西部大開發戰略重又引發了土地開發後如何對農民的土地進行補償和安置的討論。從自上而下的規劃角度看，地方政府和開發商參與了安置專案的構建，從中地方政府要實現多重目標，如從開發專案中獲利，構建“和諧社會”，以及平衡普通和高檔住宅的發展。對開發商來說，他們與當地政府合作參與地區規劃以順利達成土地徵用，處理各種所有權問題，以及與縣或村達成徵用協定。過去的研究強調了土地開發給傳統鄉村生活和經濟帶來的負面作用，但沒有詳細考查村民如何被安置，而這對資產（再）分配和社區重建有著複雜而深遠的影響。自下而上的角度來看，當城市擴張侵入周邊農村，一些村民或者基層集體以非正規的開發作為對抗的手段。而政府為了清除開發過程中的障礙，也劃給村民一些“補償用地”。在村莊共同體的形式下，基層集體與村民得以合議建設他們自己的安置專案。這種自下而上的局部區隔化造就了一種新的資產（再）分配方式以優先照顧“自己人”。相對應地，這還可能造成社區重建的新模式，從而影響居住環境和社區管治的重塑。 本研究以寧夏某村莊為例考察城市化過程中村民安置的兩種方式。第一種方式是由政府和發展商主導，為村民建設並分配居住社區。第二種方式是由村民和基層集體主導，在“補償用地”上為本地居民建設獨棟房子組成的集體居住區。本研究計畫訪問100個安置村民家庭和10個本地“規劃者”（官員和開發商）。本研究將通過系統考查住房所有權、房屋價值、居住環境和社區管治，根據不同安置方案的進展來檢視它們的可持續性，並探索其對資產（再）分配和社區重建的啟示。

12406714.label: Realisation of objectives
12406714.value: The present work involves a three-fold analysis of urban expansion of Yinchuan City, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, in China’s lagging northwestern territories, where rural villages have been absorbed into the urban areas since the late 1990s. Data are derived from extensive fieldwork conducted in 2014 and 2015. The first part of the study focuses on the changing resource structures of those relocated peasant-communities, i.e. former villages, engulfed under the expanding city, and is primarily concerned with Objective 1. The findings reveal significant differentiation within and between communities, and such inequalities derive not only from the compensation policies but also from the resource distribution prior to development. In addition to the impacts of policy changes that favour more recently developed communities, stratification in resource holding prior to land development within given communities is also important. Different from the general impression that egalitarian communities are disturbed and reshuffled by urbanization, stratification in compensation and relocation is shaped by self-financing capabilities in property management, which are based on pre-existing inequalities in resource distribution, and affected by the bargaining power and grassroots strategies. The second part which corresponds largely with Objective 2 examines in greater detail former peasants’ transition to urban workers. It reveals increase in unemployment rate and changing distribution of job categories. The findings highlight the importance of age, gender, and education after land expropriation when agriculture ceases to function as a “safety net,” and illustrate the significant effect of pre-expropriation employment as well as compensation from land development. Specifically, jobs available for older and less educated peasants are mostly unstable and low-end work in construction and service sectors. For those who had prior market experiences and financial capabilities to start private businesses, or who received better education, there are opportunities, albeit limited, the conversion to formal urban residents enable them to establish and develop their career. The study thus illustrates emerging entrepreneurship and economic mobility irrespective of prevalent segregation and discrimination against former peasants in the labour market. But gender bias is obvious: men are more active in pursuing private businesses and formal white-collar jobs by pooling together family resources; whereas women are under-represented in both sectors. The third part of the study, which corresponds to Objective 3, further explores the issue of prejudice against landless villagers by making reference to the media and public discourses on chaiqian baofahu or people getting rich overnight due to demolition and relocation compensation, and sushi or quality. Urbanisation and urban development have brought people from diverse groups to live together. The urbanites, especially those who were laid off due to the reform of state-owned enterprises, have a ready comparison: the landless villagers receiving “handsome” compensations and relocated to urban neighbourhoods. As such, they feel aggrieved about their loss of superiority. The rapid socio-economic change and economic inequality have created an anxiety about deprivation. Both lay-off workers and landless villagers harbour feelings of insecurity and injustice: the former highlight housing inequality whereas the latter emphasise the lack of salary parity and social security. In China, prejudice against peasantry is deeply engrained in complex historical, economic and political processes. When the division between urban and rural residents is so clear and the society is dominated by prejudiced values, it is difficult to change intergroup attitudes through intergroup contact.

12406714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12406714.value: The ancient silk road, which is to be revived under the Belt and Road Initiative, traverses Northwestern China. Economic and urban growth along the Hexi Corridor is destined to accelerate further. The present study lays down the ground work for analysing how phenomenal urban transformation particularly land and hukou conversion in this part of the country affects individual communities and people on rural-urban fringes. A natural extension of the project is to examine other major cities, such as Urumchi and Xian, along the corridor. So far our analysis has been restricted to Han Chinese. Thus, another avenue of research is bring the issue of ethnic minorities such as the Hui People in Yinchuan who feature quite prominently in the area to the fore.

12406714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12406714.value: Under the national strategy of “developing the west”, Northwestern China have witnessed massive land development and urban sprawl. This study examines the consequent relocation process on the outskirts of the Municipality of Yinchuan. It reveals significant differentiation within and between communities, and such inequalities derive not only from the compensation policies but also from the resource distribution prior to development. The findings also highlight the importance of age, gender, and education in transiting to urban employment after land expropriation and illustrate the significant effect of pre-expropriation employment as well as compensation from land development. Gender bias is obvious: men are more active in pursuing private businesses and formal white-collar jobs by pooling together family resources; whereas women are under-represented in both sectors. In the relocated neighbourhoods where both landless peasants and workers laid off by state enterprises co-locate, both groups harbour feelings of insecurity and injustice: the former highlight housing inequality whereas the latter emphasise the lack of salary parity and social security. In China, prejudice against peasantry is deeply ingrained in complex historical, economic and political processes. It is difficult to change intergroup attitudes through intergroup contact.

12406814.label: Project Objectives
12406814.value: By comparing leading newspapers of differing ideological persuasions in the U.S., Britain, and France, we shall engage seriously with—and contribute to—the literature in international communication studies. We seek to “detotalize” the “western” press by empirically evaluating media frames from three cases (the U.S., Britain, France) on one issue (China’s rise). Hallin and Mancini (2004) characterize the U.S. media as embodying the liberal model, the French media as a case of the “polarized pluralist model,” whereas the British media is defined as a liberal model that incorporates polarized pluralist elements. The three cases differ in the mix of journalism “genres,” authorial voices, and topical “schemes of departmentalization” (Barnhurst & Nerone, 2001, p. 3). We shall examine how these structural media characteristics and journalistic traditions influence the framing of China’s rise. The focus on comparative frames will enable us to examine both the media-system contrasts in international news-making and the differences attributable to ideologies operating within each country's press. It is often assumed that international news coverage is “indexed” to the vantage points of national interest, as crystallized by foreign policy (Bennett, 1990; Lee, 2002). We intend to test this hypothesis across three countries. The U.S. media might be expected to highlight negative implications of China’s rise to America’s superpower status and global interests—often in the universal names of democracy and human rights. Britain, while being a junior partner to the U.S., has its own national interest; the British media may be more likely to focus on the implications of China’s rise to British interests in Asia. France's media are commonly regarded as a major western antithesis to American political and cultural hegemony, thus colliding and colluding with the U.S. media on various issues. We maintain that there will be a high degree of consistency and continuity in media framing of China’s rise across various administrations during the study period. Having said this, we will take account of how the press reflects elite divisions within the bounds of "legitimated controversy" (Hallin, 1986) over the issues concerning China’s rise in each country. It has been argued that the exercise of indexing and counter-framing is facilitated when actors link problems to broader cultural repertoires, which typify a society within a particular historical period and go unchallenged in intra-elite debate (Gans, 1979; Said, 1981). For example, compared with western Europeans, Americans continue to regard individualism as far more important than the role of the state (Pew Research Center, 2011). We seek to understand how different cultural repertoires would play out in shaping the media prisms of China’s rise. We hope to produce conference papers, journal articles, and a full-length monograph. We will catalogue research materials online for public access after we complete our analysis.

12406814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12406814.value: This project seeks to compare how leading newspapers across the ideological spectrum in three major western countries—namely, the U.S., Britain, and France—“frame” the rise of China from 2001 to the present. In the post-cold war, neoliberal global order, China’s emergence as a world power has been greeted internationally both as a threat and as an opportunity. We seek to “detotalize” the “western” press by empirically evaluating media frames from three countries (the U.S., Britain, France) on one issue (China’s rise). If the U.S. media embody the liberal model and the French media represent the “polarized pluralist model,” the British media can be characterized as a liberal model with polarized pluralist elements. Furthermore, the rise of China may present markedly different national interest considerations for the U.S., Britain, and France. By focusing on comparative frames, we shall examine both the media-system contrasts in international news-making and the differences attributable to ideologies operating within the press in each country. It is often assumed that international news coverage is “indexed” to the vantage points of national interest, as crystallized by foreign policy. We shall be able to test this hypothesis across three countries. Moreover, we would like to examine how the enduring “cultural repertoires” in the three countries play out in the shaping of press prisms. We hope to contribute to the advancement of international communication studies by systematically assessing press frames across national contexts, and by seriously engaging with media theories that attempt to account for the relationship between press frames and national interest. We also seek to enhance policy understanding by investigating how “opinion leaders” in the western press interpret the significance and implications of China’s rise to each of their countries and to the global system in general. 本研究旨在比較西方國家(美國、英國和法國)各意識形態陣營的領軍報紙從2001年至今如何「架構」中國崛起這一議題。冷戰結束后，在新自由主義的全球秩序下，中国崛起是威胁还是机遇成為了全世界廣泛關注的问题。 我們試圖對三個國家（美國、英國和法國）在同一議題（中國崛起）上的報道框架展開實證分析，從而「解構」西方媒體。 如果說美國媒體代表了自由模式，而法國媒體代表了「極化多元模式」，那麼英國媒體則兼備兩種模式的部分特征。此外，美國、英國和法國對中國崛起都有各自顯著不同的國家利益考量。 我們通過對三個國家報道框架的比較研究,可以考察媒介體制差異和不同意識形態對國際新聞產制的影響。 一般都會認為國際新聞拘泥于官方既定的狭隘视野之内, 以外交政策為「索引」。 我們希望可以藉此檢驗這個假設。 本研究也將考察三個國家的恆久文化價值觀對媒體報導角度的影響。我們將試圖歸納各國媒體的報導框架，系統梳理媒介框架與國家利益兩者關係的相關理論，進一步推進國際傳播研究。同時，我們將解析西方媒體中的「意見領袖」如何詮釋中國崛起對本國及世界的意義與影響，藉此提升對政策的理解。

12406814.label: Realisation of objectives
12406814.value: This project has successfully addressed all seven objectives through a range of empirical studies. A comparison of leading newspapers in the US, UK and France across different time periods enables a nuanced analysis of media images of China’s rise in Western countries. Although the newspapers of these three countries all belong to the broad category of “Western”press, they exemplify different state-media relations, journalistic cultures, media systems, and the “enduring values”embedded in each of the societies (Gans, 1979). These differences in structural characteristics, cultural repertoire and particularly national interests reflect upon different media perceptions of China’s rise. This project provided a corrective to many of previous studies that characterize Western media systems by the use of aggregate summary measures. Specifically, our analysis identified various types of causal conditions—the event environment, media organization, the media system, and the political system—and sought to calibrate the influence of each level of ideological discourse (Objective 1). Notably, our findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the concept "political parallelism" in the comparison of Western media systems and its news-making mechanisms. Although different newspapers exhibit different ideological positions within each country, our findings suggest that intra-national differences are much less significant than between-country differences. Our analysis paid considerable attention to their cultural and historical specificity in an attempt to relativize Western values and premises (Objective 2). Our longitudinal comparison addressed objective 3 and 4 by tracing the differences attributable to press ideologies, cultural repertoire, and the vantage points of national interest as crystallized by foreign policy. China’s rise has posed a threat not only economically but also geopolitically to the US superpower status, while China’s rise is seen as having brought about considerable economic opportunities to the declining UK and France. All three countries show a high degree of continuity in media framing of China’s rise across different administrations, but there were also fluctuations within the bounds of what Hallin (1986) calls “legitimated controversy.” Our analysis expanded on the concept of “established pluralism” (Lee, 2000) to show how media images of China’s rise are indexed to “elite-cum-official consensus” in the US, UK and France (Objective 4) . This project not only used a computer-assisted quantitative approach to analyze the large datasets of news texts, but also employed discourse analysis to analyze news texts with reference to ideological packages, news values, reporting strategies, attitudes and stance (Objective 5). All three countries' newspapers were found to apply the topoi of liberal democracy in viewing China’s rise. French press highlights the value of equality while the US press highlights the values of individualism and responsible capitalism in its criticism of China’s rise. We linked our analysis of these frames and ideological packages to the broader cultural repertoire that typifies intra-elite debate (addressing Objective 5). We have thus far published four journal articles (including three SSCI-listed journals) and a couple of conference papers. More papers are under review. We are also preparing a book manuscript which expands on the published articles with an emphasis on a comparative perspective (Objective 6). We have established a database composed of research findings and press corpuses (addressing Objective 7). Once we get our work under review published and clarify the copyright issues with the publisher, we will open this database for public access.

It has been argued that the exercise of indexing and counter-framing is facilitated when actors link problems to broader cultural repertoires, which typify a society within a particular historical period and go unchallenged in intra-elite debate (Gans, 1979; Said, 1981). For example, compared with western Europeans, Americans continue to regard individualism as far more important than the role of the state (Pew Research Center, 2011). We seek to understand how different cultural repertoires would play out in shaping the media prisms of China’s rise.
We hope to produce conference papers, journal articles, and a full-length monograph.
We will catalogue research materials online for public access after we complete our analysis.

12406814.label: Major findings and research outcome
12406814.value: This longitudinal study compared how leading newspapers in US, UK and France framed the rise of China from 2001 to the present. From 2001 to 2007, US newspapers’ perception of China’s rise was primarily framed in terms of strategic, economic, and political considerations that impinge on the U.S. as a global power. The British newspapers in general reported on the rise of China in a relatively neutral tone, and mainly focused on the economic impact of China’s rise and its geopolitical implications for U.S.-China relations. The French newspapers were much less politically minded than their US and UK counterparts, and much more economically focused. From 2008 to 2011, the US newspapers placed an increasing emphasis on the links between economic issues and the political equilibrium. The UK newspapers were attentive to what China means to global trade and European market. French newspapers consistently focused on the economic rise of China. From 2012 to 2017, the US newspapers shifted their focus to the political dimension in China’s rise, and similar changes were also found in the UK press. The French press, however, still focused on GDP and price issues. Previous comparative research has explored the decreased weight of nation-states in the international news-making with the impact of globalization and digitalization. Our findings suggest that national filters remain resilient and explain the differences in media framing cross-culturally (Song & Lee, 2016, 2017; Zeng & Song, 2018). Compared with the remarkably distinct cross-national differences, the intra-national differences in press framing of China's rise are trivial (Song, Lee & Huang, 2016). All three countries' newspapers acknowledged China's rise as an established fact, and discussed it in terms of economic progress and geopolitical influence, but from the vantage point of their perceived national interest. The US press is conventionally regarded as more internally pluralist, while the French is considered more partisan with the British falling in between. But this study found that the US newspapers are characterized by more polarized elements in their coverage of China’s rise (Song & Lee, 2015). This points towards the importance of taking the “event environment” into account along with system-level factors in explaining international news making. Rather than seeing the influence of different levels (e.g., the event environment, the media organization, the media system, and the political system) as independent, comparative communication research should view them as a coherent whole and seek to calibrate the influence of each level.

12406814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12406814.value: There is great potential to extend the project into investigating how the Chinese newspapers frame China’s rise for a broader comparison with Western press prisms. This is also a comparison of the interplay between the insider’s view and the outsider’s view. Such an addition would provide an alternative to the West-centric framework of comparative international communication research. We have already conducted a comparative analysis of British, US and Chinese press coverage of China's rise from 2008 to present. The paper is under review. Secondly, future research should include a larger number of newspapers per country and incorporate analysis of online platforms. That would serve to extend the empirical database and lay the groundwork for further theorizing and refinement of a framework for comparing coverage of international affairs. As a pilot study, we have published an article examining the Twitter accounts of journalists working for the China beat at leading US, UK and French news organizations (Zeng & Song, 2018). More journal papers are being prepared. Internet media technologies, and notably social media sites, are playing increasingly important roles in global news production and consumption. Further research on the representation of China on new media platforms is definitely needed.

12406814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12406814.value: China’s rise has been widely recognized as one of the defining events in international politics, not only from the perspective of global wealth redistribution but also for its potential import to end the unipolar international system. This longitudinal project compares how leading newspapers in the US, UK and France covered China's rise across different time periods. The perception of China’s rise is not only a concern for western journalists and policymakers, but also matters to China’s soft-power efforts. Theoretically, this study examines both the media-system contrasts in international news making and the differences attributable to different features of the events reported and of the political environment. This study has explored how these differing structural characteristics influence the press framing, with what implications for media outcomes. This study takes exception to the argument that the role of nation-states is as important in the era of globalization and digitalization. In fact, "national filter" remains as a powerful determinant of cross-cultural press prisms. Methodologically, this study combines computer-assisted quantitative linguistic analysis with qualitative discourse analysis.

12406914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12406914.value: This project has the main objective of analyzing the relationship between what journalists say about their roles and their performance of those roles. It will examine how gaps and convergences between the two phenomena are related to media structures. The project will investigate journalism in the different media systems of Hong Kong and mainland China. It is anticipated that journalists in the two places will give different self-conceptions and that the practices of journalism will be different. The project will provide comparative insights into how media structures influence journalists’ self-conceptions, their practical activity, and the relationship between the two. The project consists of two main components. The first is a content analysis of representative newspapers in Hong Kong and mainland China. The aims are first to record the key characteristics of news stories and, second, to identify the journalists who produced them. The second component involves a survey of the journalists producing substantial amounts of the analysed material to discover their conceptions of the roles. The project will analyze the continuities and disjunctures between role conception and role performance identified by the field research and situate these within the different media systems involved. The project constitutes the Chinese section of a broader international comparative research effort titled `Journalistic Role Performance Around the Globe.' This comparative project will research the connections between journalists' conceptions of their professional roles and what the same actually journalists produce. The project consists of a network of experienced researcher in 27 different countries. In addition to the active researchers, the project has an advisory committee of 12 scholars, including some of the most distinguished names in the field. The participation of the team from Hong Kong and mainland China will enrich this project by bringing data derived from the situation in two parts of the country to an international audience. In turn, the situation of the project within a broader perspective will enable to distinctive features of the national experience to be brought more sharply into focus. Further details of the project can be obtained from the website: http://www.journalisticperformance.org. As well as working on the development of the theoretical grounding of the project and conducting the field work in Hong Kong and the mainland, the investigators will publish work both of a scholarly and more journalistic nature on their findings. They will produce work both specific to China and participate in the broader dissemination of the findings.

12406914.label: Realisation of objectives
12406914.value: Objectives 1-5 have all been completely achieved within the context of this project. The analysis of the overall results of the comparative project, now involving 19 countries, is currently underway. Preliminary findings will be presented at the Annual Conference of the International Communication Association in May 2017 and at the 2017 Annual Conference of the Association for Education in Journalism and Mass Communication. In addition, a book proposal for this overall analysis is under discussion. The conduct of the content analysis was unproblematic since it deals with material that is in the public domain and, generally, readily available. Access to the Hong Kong data required a visit to the only library which holds the complete records of the chosen newspapers but this was a problem easily resolved. The questionnaire proved somewhat more difficult. Gaining access to the staff of three of the mainland papers required some negotiation but was relatively easily obtained. Gaining access to the staff of People's Daily proved slightly more difficult but, through the use of contacts gained in previous research, it proved possible to recruit a collaborator employed by the paper's research department who was able to circulate and collect the questionnaire. Two of the Hong Kong papers were relatively easy to approach, although their editorial policies did not allow the exact identification of the authors of particular articles, so the data here is for their overall national reporting staff rather than, as in the mainland Chinese case, at the individual level. Since it has, so far, not been an issue for the analysis of the data, we do not believe that this will represent a serious problem for the project. The third Hong Kong newspaper's relevant material, we determined, was in fact produced by mainland journalists and we were able to obtain responses from them. It is interesting to note that the content analysis of this material demonstrates that its character is much closer to that of the mainland papers overall than to the other two Hong Kong papers. While the team was able to produce the required material well within the international time frame, other national teams experienced some difficulties. There was no international funding for this project and each team had to find their own support. This part of the project was relatively very well funded compared with some other efforts and, indeed, some were obliged to withdraw due to financial and other difficulties. As a consequence of these factors, the collection of the international data was somewhat delayed, and the analysis is only now underway. In addition, the number of countries able to complete the provision of data declined to 19. This remains a large number of participants, with material from North and South America, Europe, Asia and Africa. It will therefore be possible to draw at least some valid international comparisons from the work of the project. Objective 6 has been partly achieved. Papers have been presented at conferences of the International Communication Association and the International Association for Media and Communication Research disseminating the results for Hong Kong and mainland China. Two papers have been published in English with findings from the mainland content analysis (details in Section C below). One paper with an overall account of the content analysis in Chinese is in press. A further paper on the mainland content analysis is under review. One paper comparing the findings of the mainland and Hong Kong content analysis is currently nearly complete. Two further papers detailing the analysis of the questionnaires completed by journalists are currently in production. The data sets for Hong Kong and mainland China, together with an introduction, the research instruments, and top-level results, have been made publicly available on the HKBU library website, in English and both traditional and simplified Chinese characters. Objective 7 has been completely achieved. The close study of mainland and Hong Kong journalists revealed that, while very considerable attention has been given to issues like the impact of the press market, professional attitudes etc., there was relatively little concrete attention to the daily practice of journalism, particular in the context of the development of digital media. As a consequence, a project was developed comparing the impact of new media on the mainland Chinese media with the international experience. (Members of the team had previously investigated this issue in the Hong Kong case, which proved to be something of an international outlier give the extraordinary development of free newspapers in the city.) The findings demonstrated that while the impact of digital media had been relatively late in mainland China it had recently begun to intensify dramatically. Compared with other countries, notably the USA, the process was much more concentrated and and its consequences are very intense. On the basis of this project, a further application for funding, including for a GRF, was developed investigating the consequences of these developments for the daily practice of journalists. We may say, in summary, that the work of data gathering in the project was successfully completed in Hong Kong and the mainland, and has eventually been completed in other countries, giving a total of 19 cases for analysis. (Hong Kong and the mainland being treated as two different cases.) The process of analysis of the data for Hong Kong and mainland has been completed and is underway for the international comparative dimension of the project. The process of dissemination for the Hong Kong and mainland findings has begun and is continuing. The process of dissemination for the international comparative dimension of the project is underway but remains at an early stage with no published outputs.

12406914.label: Major findings and research outcome
12406914.value: The major findings of the Hong Kong and mainland project may be summarized in the following points: 1. The conventional division of the mainland Chinese press into "market oriented" and "politically oriented" press is an oversimplification. In fact, there four significantly different strategies within our sample. While there is clearly a market oriented press, this is significantly differentiated with regard to the extent to which it engages in what may be summarized as "critical reporting." While there is also clearly a party oriented press, the two titles here were significantly differentiated by the degree to which they employed popular journalistic techniques. These overall findings were detailed in the article in the Asian Journal of Communication recorded in Part C. 2. One of the party papers, China Youth Daily, was significantly and very clearly differentiated from all of the other mainland titles by its use of many of the techniques of popular journalism. While these techniques did not amount to anything resembling "tabloidization" as evidenced in Hong Kong or Europe, they did mark the title out from other mainland papers and it might approximate to what is neologistically termed a "broadloid" paper. The detailed findings are presented in the article in Journalism recorded in Part C. 3. While overall the Hong Kong and mainland papers were significantly different, once one discussed individual titles these distinctions broke down. One of the Hong Kong titles was closer in content to the majority of the mainland titles than to its local neighbours. Further, the "broadloid" mainland paper and the unquestionably "tabloid" Hong Kong paper displayed some marked similarities. These findings are detailed in a forthcoming article currently being completed. 4. Similarly, while there are some marked differences in aggregate between the Hong Kong and the mainland journalists, in the international comparison they fall together on key issues as being clearly differentiated from other titles in the international spectrum. These findings form the substance of the paper being presented at the 2017 ICA and AEJMC conferences. 5. The common differentiation between a "liberal" wing of the Chinese press (exemplified by Nanfang Dushi Bao) and a "party" wing (exemplified by Renmin Ribao) can be shown to exist even at the time of our sample, but they are less differentiated than some commentators have claimed. In fact, particularly in their handling of investigative reporting, both titles display a great deal of caution. These findings are discussed in a paper currently under review.

12406914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12406914.value: There are three ways in which the research on Hong Kong and the mainland could be developed: 1. While the Hong Kong sample is arguably representative, the sample of mainland titles was very small. There is no way of knowing whether the findings (for example, the popular nature of China Youth Daily) are isolated instances or represent a current within the mainland press. A content analysis with a larger sample could answer this question. 2. The analysis is of a sample from two consecutive years within two changing environments. A longitudinal analysis would allow the identification of trends in the two press systems, in particular whether there has been a decline in the amount of critical journalism in the mainland press since the late 1990s, and whether there has been convergence in the coverage of the mainland and Hong Kong presses. 3. The categories in this analysis paid no attention to the "political" content of the journalism, and the sample was restricted to national news in both cases. A fresh analysis, perhaps with a broader sample, which addressed both of these issues would provide a more detailed picture of similarities and differences between the two systems.

12406914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12406914.value: This project analysed the national news content of eight newspapers, five in the mainland and three in Hong Kong. A representative sample of editions was drawn from the years 2012 and 2013. The project was the local element in an international study that gathered and analyzed data from 19 cases. The main findings of the local study were as follows: 1. The eight titles do not naturally fall in to two groups based on locality. On the contrary, at least one of the Hong Kong titles displays stronger similarities with other mainland titles than with its Hong Kong neighbours. 2. The mainland press is more differentiated than scholars have believed in the past. In particular, one of the titles, China Youth Daily, publishes journalism of a markedly "popular" kind. 3. The difference between the most "liberal" and most "party-minded" newspapers in mainland China is narrower than many scholars have thought. 4. Although there are differences in the professional attitudes of mainland and Hong Kong journalists, on important issues like their readiness to investigate powerful institutions they display marked similarities compared with journalists from other countries. These findings provide quantitative evidence of the performance of the Hong Kong and mainland press that was not previously available.

12407314.label: Project Objectives
12407314.value: To investigate what has/has not been translated in the field of foreign literature in the PRC under its censoring system, and what kind of discourses were especially affected by censorship, including censorship on the internet; how and why. To develop a database both for the study of censorship and translation in the PRC with contrastive data from Taiwan/HK and as a service for other researches on PRC translations/censorship in translation. To analyse selected translations with regard to censorship-related omissions, changes, ‘non-’/‘zero’ translations and paratexts (i.e. translators’ prefaces, editorial notes, etc.), to find out how and why translations have been affected by censorship across different periods. To study what has and/or what has not changed in censorial policies and practices in the PRC over the past 60-odd years, how and why. To draw insights through the PRC case on what locations there are (political, cultural, linguistic, etc.) at which censorship may meet translation in a given society, and how studying different patterns of censorship and translation may contribute to our understanding of the cultural politics of translation at large.

To analyse selected translations with regard to censorship-related omissions, changes, ‘non-’/‘zero’ translations and paratexts (i.e. translators’ prefaces, editorial notes, etc.), to find out how and why translations have been affected by censorship across different periods.
To study what has and/or what has not changed in censorial policies and practices in the PRC over the past 60-odd years, how and why.

To draw insights through the PRC case on what locations there are (political, cultural, linguistic, etc.) at which censorship may meet translation in a given society, and how studying different patterns of censorship and translation may contribute to our understanding of the cultural politics of translation at large.

12407314.label: Realisation of objectives
12407314.value: 1) This project has studied how censorship, as a form of institutional (e.g. government, editorial, publishers’) as well as the translator’s own control of the circulation of information and ideas, regulates translation in the China. It has covered 60 and more years from the founding of the PRC in 1949 till mid-2017 when the project was concluded. The translation and publication of foreign fictions and novels, works on human science and social science, biographies and documentaries, as well as other types of writings varied with the times and the changing political and social conditions within the country. The project has found that the history of publication of translated foreign works in the PRC can also be seen as a history of censorship – state/government/institutional regulations, whether or not overtly articulated, on which works were allowed to be imported, whether and how they were to be translated, and on what range and scale they could be published. 2) The research has made full use of the HKBU library as well as online portals and websites such as Baidu Baike (i.e. Baidu Encyclopedia) and Wikipedia, search engines such as Baidu and Google, web tools such as Baidu Reading and Google Books, library catalogues of major colleges and universities around the world, Harvard, Cambridge, HKU. Other related internet portals which have contributed to the research include government official websites such as legal department of the US, General Administration of Press and Publication of the PRC, the information office of Russia, etc. 3) Comprehensive data has thus been obtained through an in-depth survey via the university library system at HKBU including its all its databases and interlibrary connections, as well as via all accessible online search engines (i.e. google, Baidu, etc.), on books published/not published in the Mainland of China, with special regard to whether and/or how they might have been affected by censorship/censorship in translation. Information on books published in Hong Kong and Taiwan was collected and analysed mainly as comparison to the data on related books published in the Chinese mainland. 4) Basic information on the books covered in the research is listed in alphabetical order in the tables of information on published translation (affected as well as non-affected by censorship). Altogether, the study has covered and collected information on a total of some 2400 works of translation that have been published in the PRC with some parallel entries from the Taiwan and Hong Kong contexts, which are classifiable into three kinds, i.e. ‘Full/Near Full’ translation (which may be described as basically not affected by censorship); ‘Partial’ translations (which may be described as partially affected by censorship); and ‘Non-translations’ (referring to ‘translations’ that have not been made, or that do not at all exist, because the potential source texts are so sensitive politically, ideologically, morally, etc. that they are totally forbidden to be translated in the context of the PRC. 5) Overall, the project has investigated what major foreign literature has or has not been translated and published in the PRC since its founding in 1949 under the country’s censoring system. Apart from sketchy discussions of such censorship-affected translation as those of Hilary Clinton’s Living History, Robert Kuhn’s The Man Who Changed China: the Life and Legacy of Jiang Zemin and Peter Hessler’s contemporary China trilogy, in-depth case studies have been made of Vladimir Nabokov’s Lolita, George Orwell’s Animal Farm, and Ezra F. Vogel’s Deng Xiaoping. Henry Kissinger’s On China, Pearl Buck’s The Good Earth. 5 papers have been written 4 of which have already come out in reputable journals (3 in major international English-language journals and 1 in a foreign language-culture core journal in the Chinese mainland). The how and why issues on translational censorship and self-censorship have been addressed in good detail and in depth across those 5 papers. In addition, the findings thus presented via these papers have also made their prior appearances as well as invited a good deal of discussions/responses at three important conferences (one in Canada, one in China and a third in Japan). Hence, it can said that the findings of the project have been quite widely and adequately disseminated in the field; that this GRF project has been brought to a successful conclusion; and that its research outcomes have quite positively contributed to the relevant field of knowledge and research.

12407314.label: Major findings and research outcome
12407314.value: 1) Important findings have been obtained from the research. All these were presented in the five major papers (see attached articles for detail), as well as in the three conference papers, which were disseminated to international audiences (one conference in Canada, another in Japan, and the third in China). 2) Four of papers were already published in refereed, major international translation studies journals (3 in English and one in Chinese). The fifth article, also submitted to an international English-language journal, is being reviewed. The reception of the research findings was positively reflected in the number of downloads of the publications. According to statistics from the HKBU Institutional Repository, a total of 40 new downloads have been made in 2017 across some 20 countries and regions, which can in some way serve as an indicator of the interest the paper have roused in the field of censorship and translation research. (See also Supplementary Research Report attached to Part C.)

12407314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12407314.value: Further research is possible in several areas. For example, the time range of related research can be narrowed down to 10 years or so, to study the trend on books selected to be translated and published – whether they are the result of political/ideological consideration or for economic purposes, etc. The 10-year period of translation and publication during the Cultural Revolution could be a good example to study in depth, because it was a time when readers were told not only what translations to read but also how to read them. Further research focused on one particular book could also be done, for example the translation of Lolita or Lady Chatterley’s Lover, etc., to look on the changes/modulations/omissions found in the translations as well as the implementation and operation of state policies and regulations on translated works involving censorship. (See also Supplementary Research Report attached to Part C.)

12407714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12407714.value: 時在公元八世紀的盛唐詩歷來公認是中國以至世界文明其中最燦爛的一頁，然而英語學術界對這段期間的研究卻意外地非常貧乏，且多集中在某一詩人的個案研究。本計劃希望重新對盛唐詩作一番追源工作，勾勒出它與六朝詩之間的關係，並將重點放在佛學與道教對詩學的影響上。過去數十年學者對六朝詩學的重新梳理無疑讓本研究得以審視盛唐詩在技巧、文辭以至表達模式等多方面如何借鑑六朝詩。不過，如此肯定六朝對後代詩學的貢獻也帶來了一個問題，即盛唐詩學相較其六朝傳統而言，有甚麽特質？本研究將探索普遍認為乃唐代獨有成就的文化資源，即自六朝至初唐發軔的所謂思想轉型。當中最突出的就是印度佛教中國化與佛教新學派的開創，而道教在中國佛教興盛之際順時建立則為另一重要方面。本計劃將會在已有的研究之上查看佛教與道教如何建構盛唐詩學的思想框架，包括時空觀、自我與世界、宏觀與微觀等。

12407714.label: Realisation of objectives
12407714.value: Thanks to the help of this GRF grant, I was able to complete several interrelated studies of the topic "Ideological Origins of High Tang Literature." The primary work consisted of translating, interpreting, and contextualizing a number of relatively obscure Tang dynasty texts, as well as relating them to more prominent pieces by Tang writers. The texts I worked on crossed over disiplinary boundaries, particularly between religion and literature, but also extending beyond the bounds of the Tang empire to certain Chinese works produced in Japan during the same period. Overall, the project has been sucessfully completed but has raised even more new questions than it resolved, and has provided the foundation for several new projects I will continue to work on in the future. As my research progressed, the nature of the research did shift considerably. In particular, my original plan had involved a certain amount to synthesis of previous scholarship. As I understood it, the influence of Buddhism on Tang poetry had already been discussed extensively by numerous scholars, so I expected to be able to build on this previous work. Much to my surprise, though, I quickly discovered that English-language scholarship has long misrepresented and undervalued the role of Buddhism in Tang poetry. This greatly increased the challenge of my project, but also its potential significance. Thus the primary achievement of my GRF grant is a research article forthcoming in the journal CLEAR which illuminates new aspects of Wang Wei's Buddhist poetry that had previously been overlooked, especially by Western scholars. Simultaneously, I discovered that some of the most interesting case studies in the interaction of religion and literature during the Tang period actually relate to Nara and Heian Japan. Certain unusual genres, like the prayer text (yuanwen), became more prominent in Japan than in contemporary Tang China, and shed new light on the role of Buddhism in contemporary culture. I completed a study of Nara poet Yamanoue no Okura, whose works are full of references to relatively obscure religious texts from contemporary China, as well as a study of the "Pure Land" that focuses on medieval China but also broadens its scope of inquiry to contemporary China.

12407714.label: Major findings and research outcome
12407714.value: Overall, my project has successfully illuminated new aspects of Buddhist and other religious ideology in the development of Tang dynasty poetry. Li Bai, who is often misrepresented as a free-spirited writer unconcerned with grander issues of state or philosophy, actually wrote a number of pieces that are rich in political and philosophical ideas. My article on his "Rhapsody on the Hall of Light" has focused attention on one of these pieces and offered the first translation into English of one of his most substantive compositions. Wang Wei is general recognized as a poet strongly influenced by Buddhism, but Western scholars over the past several decades have quixotically attempted to deflect attention from this aspect of his poems and misrepresent him as primarily a secular, court poet. While Chinese scholars have been much more balanced in their treatment, they can be too fixated on the role of Chan Buddhism, even though it had not really developed fully in Wang Wei's day. My study shows that Wang Wei's poetry is actually inspired much more by traditional Mahayana concepts of nonduality. Finally, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism were simultaneously influential in Nara and Heian Japan, but Japanese writers adapted these influences in original ways, for instance transforming the concept of the Pure Land. These adaptations had long-lasting implications for the development of Japanese literature and culture.

12407714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12407714.value: My research project has inspired a number of new avenues of research. Just to point out two of these: 1) The role of Buddhism in medieval Chinese poetry remains grossly neglected in English-language scholarship. Most of Wang Wei's relevant compositions have not even been translated into English, not to mention those of many of his contemporaries. This is a huge field of research, not just the subject of a single research project, but I plan to continue to work in this area, focusing on the development of regulated verse and its ideological presuppositions. 2) Chinese-language (kanbun or kanshi) writings in classical Japan were not just a major part of the literary output of their time, but also shed light on contemporary developments in China. Japanese writers were careful readers of classical Chinese literature who brought a new perspective to these texts. Thus my next GRF project, I hope, will be a study of the intersecting influences of Buddhist thought and Chinese rhetoric in Heian Japan.

12407714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12407714.value: Tang poetry has long been appreciated as an important contribution to world civilization, but relatively little attempt has been made to explain why it achieved its special form and expressive power. This project has shed light on Buddhist and other ideological influences, tracing them back to Han and Six Dynasties cultural developments, as part of an explanation for how the crystalline compactness of Tang poetry manages to convey so much about the world. The project involved focused studies of works by two key Tang poets, Li Bai and Wang Wei, while touching on a vast range of materials (Tang writings in numerous different genres, Buddhist scriptures, works from throughout the literary tradition, contemporary Japanese poems, etc.).
