14101514.label: Major findings and research outcome
14101514.value: Our epidemiological studies indicated that natural amino acid variation K93R within HPV-52 E6 might confer a higher association with cancer risk when compare to its prototype and other natural variants. In order to verify our epidemiological findings, we performed a series of phenotypic and molecular assays to compare the oncogenic properties of HPV-52 E6 K93R (V1) with prototype and other common natural variants, namely E14D/V92L (V2) and K93R/N122 (V3). From our phenotypic assays using primary BRK cells that express HPV-52 E6 prototype and variants constitutively, we found that these cells possess a similar growth pattern and proliferation with no obvious sign of senescence and crisis. Moreover, HPV-52 E6 prototype and variants can induce immortalization, transformation, migration and invasion of these cells. Intriguingly, HPV-52 E6 V1 possess a greater immortalization and invasion ability when compare to its prototype and other variants. At molecular level, all HPV-52 E6 prototype and variants share a similar ability in binding to p53 and E6AP. In addition, they can degrade p53 and PDZ proteins, including Dlg and MAGI-1 equally well. It is worth noticing that HPV-52 E6s can degrade p53 better than HPV-16 E6AA in cells of p53-null background. However, their ability in targeting PDZ proteins is weaker than HPV-16 and -18 E6. On the other hand, we found that all the HPV-52 E6 prototype and variants protein turn-over rates are similar, and that amino acid variation within HPV-52 E6s does not affect their protein cellular localization. Taken all together, our results showed that in line with our epidemiological findings, HPV-52 E6 V1 has a greater ability in inducing immortalization and invasion when compare to prototype and other variants. Even though V1 can degrade p53 and PDZ proteins at a similar extent as its other counterparts, its higher oncogenicity might occur through manipulating other cellular pathways. This awaits further investigation.

14101514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14101514.value: Using our current experiment settings, we found that HPV-52 E6 prototype and variants share a similar ability in promoting cancer phenotypes. This is potentially contributed by their similar molecular and biochemical properties, particularly in targeting the major tumor suppressors, including p53 and PDZ proteins for degradation. As observed from our epidemiological studies that HPV-52 infection harboring natural E6V1 might possess a higher association to cancer risk, it is highly possible that E6V1 exerts its oncogenicity through other cellular pathways. This can be addressed by performing mass spectrometry to analyze other potential strong target protein of HPV-52 E6V1, and followed by further validation through a series molecular and phenotypic assays. In addition, as HPV induces carcinogenesis through combined activity of E6 and E7, future studies should include E7, in combination with HPV-52 E6 prototype and variants. Similarly, their oncogenic properties can be further validated through a series of phenotypic and molecular assays. Most importantly, the assays should be performed using primary keratinocytes originated from Hong Kong population. This will allow us to have a comprehensive understanding on the role of HPV-52 in inducing carcinogenesis under a physiologically relevant condition.

14101514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14101514.value: Cancer arising from uterine cervix is the fourth most common cancer affecting women worldwide. It has been well-established that Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection contributes to majority of cervical cancer cases and increasing findings nailing its causative role in head and neck cancers. Upon HPV infection, the virus produces 2 major proteins contributing to cancers, namely E6 and E7. Among the cancer-causing HPV types, HPV-52 has an unexpectedly high prevalence among Eastern Asian populations, including Hong Kong. From clinical findings, we identified that HPV-52 harboring natural mutation within E6, designated as V1, pose a higher association to cancer risk. In order to further understand the underlying mechanism, we performed a series of assays aiming to elucidate and compare the role of HPV-52 E6 prototype and natural variants in cancer progression, their expression pattern and stability, ability in deactivating key tumor suppressors commonly targeted by HPV E6, including p53 and PDZ proteins. We found that indeed cells with HPV-52 E6V1 can divide infinitely and invade better than other HPV-52 E6s. Our study helps to understand why HPV52 poses a higher disease burden in East Asia and possible clinical intervention designing in future.

14101814.label: Major findings and research outcome
14101814.value: Objective 1: To study the performance of the droplet digital PCR assay for detection and quantification of KIT and PDGFRA mutations in plasma of patients with GIST. Results: - For detection of PDGFA exon 18 D842V mutation and KIT exon 9 AY insertion, corresponding FAM probe is designed to cover the mutant area, while a wild-specific VIC probe is designed to bind DNA without the mutations. Following ddPCR, positive FAM signal and negative VIC signal indicates the presence of PDGFRA exon 18 D842V mutations or KIT exon 9 AY insertion (Figure 1a) - For detection of KIT exon 11 deletion and point mutations, FAM probe is designed to cover the wild-type area of interest while another reference VIC probe is designed to cover areas known to be not containing mutations/deletions. The purpose of VIC probe is to ensure amplification of DNA and avoidance of false-negativity. Following ddPCR, the dual positive FAM and VIC signals indicate the presence of corresponding mutations or point deletions in KIT exon 11 (Figure 1b) Objective 2: To analyze the tumor-associated mutations of KIT or PDGFRA in plasma and tissue samples in a prospective cohort of patients with GIST - The 18 samples had tumor harboring mutation in the KIT gene with different mutations type summarized in Table 1. One of them had mutation in the PDGFRA (Table 1) and 4 had no mutations in either KIT or PDGFRA gene. - The TNGS analysis showed that 98.7% (35 out of 39) concordance with Sanger sequencing for detection of mutations in exon 11 of KIT gene in FFPE tissue samples. - Amongst these 18 samples, ddPCR identified 12 samples correction as mutation positive. TNGS was therefore performed to analyze the 6 plasma samples with negative ddPCR results. It was found that TNGS could identify 4 out of 6 samples. The remaining two samples with both negative ddPCR and TNGS results belonged to wild type according to Sanger sequencing on tumor samples. - Markers for monitoring of clinical outcomes: Amongst the cohort, the serial plasma samples of 3 patients who underwent surgery and 6 patients who underwent imatinib treatment showed reduction in fractional concentration after surgery or imatinib treatment. For examples, for PW016 whereas a deletion of KIT gene was identified, the fractional concentration of mutant DNA was 1.32% and 0.08% at baseline and one-month after imatinib treatment. Subsequent imaging showed that the patient had partial responsewith the treatment. For details, please refer to enclosed pdf file (page 42-49 Section 11 Part C) .

14102014.label: Realisation of objectives
14102014.value: 1.1 Generation of fractionation-then-sequencing RNA-seq datasets using HCC cell model To achieve comprehensive assessments of lncRNA subcellular distributions in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), we sequenced cytoplasmic and nuclear RNA obtained from 8 patient tissue-derived HCC cell lines developed in Prince of Wales Hospital, Hong Kong. The cells were subjected to subcellular fractionation for cytoplasmic and nuclear RNA extraction. qPCR were then conducted to quantitate the relative enrichments of cytoplasmic marker genes (RPS14, GAPDH) and nuclear marker genes (U6 snRNA, MALAT1) in respective RNA extracts. Results indicated 8 to 12-fold enrichment of cytoplasmic markers in cytoplasmic RNA extracts, and 3 to 15-fold enrichment of nuclear markers in nuclear RNA extracts. The findings confirmed effective separation of the two fractions. The RNA extracts were successively depleted of rRNA and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform in strand-specific, pair-end configuration. The numbers of clean reads obtained from cytoplasmic RNA ranged from 59.8 to 99.2 million, where the effective sequencing depth was estimated between 11.4x and 17.3x. In contrast, transcript diversity in the nuclear fraction was significantly higher and required doubling the sequencing throughput. The final number of clean reads obtained from nuclear RNA ranged from 95.9 to 171.2 million, where the effective sequencing depths were estimated between 3.8x and 7.1x. 2.1 Acquisition of TCGA-LIHC RNA-seq datasets We submitted a request to The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database to obtain data access to restricted, raw RNA-seq data derived from Caucasian HCC patient tissue samples in TCGA Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma (TCGA-LIHC) cohort. Notably, the dataset included RNA-seq data from 50 pairs of tumor/tumor-adjacent tissue samples. The dataset enabled us to identify un-annotated, novel lncRNAs via ab initio transcriptome assembly, and to pinpoint lncRNA specifically deregulated in HCC via differential expression analysis. 2.2 Comparative analysis of transcript characteristics in the nuclear/cytoplasmic fraction For both protein coding genes and lncRNA genes, it was found that reads assigned to their intronic and 3’ downstream regions took up a significant portion of mapped reads in the nuclear fraction. Nevertheless, these intronic and 3’downstream reads were depleted in the cytoplasmic fraction. The observation indicated effectiveness of rRNA-depletion protocol in capturing nascent and incompletely spliced transcripts that were not polyadenylated. By evaluating the distribution splice-junction reads, it was found that the vast majority of lncRNA transcripts were poorly spliced in the nuclear fraction, while some lncRNA transcripts in the cytoplasmic fraction were also incompletely spliced. In contrast, protein-coding genes were nearly completely spliced in both fractions. The observation was also consistent across all 8 cell samples. Results suggested that incompletely spliced lncRNA transcript maybe overlooked by conventional poly-A RNA-seq protocol, and splicing might not be necessary for lncRNA function especially if they reside in the nucleus. 3.1 Novel metric scheme to describe fraction enrichment bias of genes To describe the fraction enrichment bias of genes, we calculated the log2 ratios of normalized expression levels between the cytoplasmic fraction and the nuclear fraction for all genes. Indicated by a negative median log2 ratio, the population of lncRNA genes were seemingly biased towards the nuclear fraction. To select the most confident fraction-enriched subset of lncRNA genes, a list of 3,804 RNA-seq-derived human housekeeping genes was downloaded. Of these, 3,544 (93.1%) genes were consistently expressed (FPKM>0.1) in both the nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions of all 8 cell samples. The mean log2 ratios of these housekeeping genes were then assumed a reference range for normal variations in fraction bias. This implied that only genes with a substantially negative or positive log2 ratio values would be considered fraction-enriched. Based on this assumption, the 5th and 95th percentiles of the reference range (-1.278, 3.056) were selected as the cutoffs for detecting nuclear-enriched and cytoplasmic-enriched genes. Asymmetry in the cutoff values was consistent with the general knowledge that mRNAs are predominantly enriched in the cytoplasmic fraction, which is also the site of protein translation. 3.2 Generation of lncRNA transcriptional map in HCC Using both reference-based and de novo approaches, we produced 216 unique ab initio transcriptome assemblies from 108 datasets (8 from HCC cell lines, 100 from 50 pairs of TCGA HCC tumor/tumor-adjacent samples). The assemblies were intersected to obtain a high-consensus, strand-specific cancer transcriptome shared among the cell samples and the TCGA samples. The consensus transcriptome included 506 GENCODE(v27)-annotated lncRNA transcripts (444 genes) and 450 high-quality predicted, unannotated lncRNA transcripts (411 genes). 3.3 Identification of nuclear-enriched lncRNA with HCC disease characteristics To identify deregulated lncRNAs with possible involvements in the HCC tumorigenesis, we first conducted differential expression (DE) tests of the TCGA-LIHC tumor and tumor-adjacent samples. Overall, 87 and 117 deregulated lncRNA transcripts were identified in the annotated and unannotated lncRNA sets, respectively. Of the 204 deregulated lncRNAs, 81 annotated and 45 unannotated lncRNA transcripts were upregulated in and assembled exclusively within tumor samples. Based on fractionation-then-sequencing data and our proposed cutoff scheme, a subset of 28 transcripts corresponding to 26 lncRNA genes further exhibited stable nuclear-enrichment in ≥4 HCC cell samples. Remarkably, the list of genes included PXN-AS1, which was experimentally validated to interact with the nuclear-localized splicing factor MBNL3 and could promote liver and lung cancer progression. The finding strongly suggests a connection between lncRNA nuclear enrichment phenotype and lncRNA-driven biological mechanisms residing within cell nucleus. These lncRNA transcripts were further characterized in a non-exclusive manner for stem cell histone marks on active promoters and correlations with poor patient survival and embryonic tissue expression. The analysis suggested that the HCC-associated lncRNA identified in our bioinformatics pipeline shared the characteristics of other experimentally support HCC-prognostic lncRNA and may also possess cancer-driving capabilities. 4.1 Functional validation of novel nuclear-enriched HCC-deregulated lncRNA Based on characterization analysis outcomes and qPCR results, we selected a representative HCC-associated lncRNA gene MHCC.15406 for functional validation. MHCC.15406 was a novel lncRNA unannotated in GENCODE. It was detected by PCR in all 8 HCC cell lines. Importantly, MHCC.15406 was enriched in the nuclear fraction and could also significantly affect survival outcome of early (I/II) stage HCC patients. siRNA knockdown of MHCC.15406 in HKCI-4 cell line significantly impacted cell viability in WST and BrdU assays. Moreover, co-expression analysis revealed that MHCC.15406 and reported HCC-driving lncRNA PXN-AS1 was significantly co-expressed with a common set of reported cancer-driving protein coding genes. There are ongoing efforts to further elucidate the underlying cellular mechanisms behind the proposed candidate HCC-associated lncRNA by, and to identify more potential HCC-associated lncRNA based on the implications of our bioinformatic analysis by experimental means.

14102014.label: Major findings and research outcome
14102014.value: 1. Elucidating the subcellular distribution landscape of transcripts We performed fractionation-then-sequencing in an assortment of HCC cell models. Employing a novel metric scheme, the subcellular distribution bias for expressed genes were systematically evaluated. We confirmed previous research findings where the population of lncRNA genes are more nuclear-biased, while the population of protein-coding genes has no apparent bias towards either nuclear or cytoplasmic fraction. Additionally, we newly report that the distribution bias of transcripts are stable across different cell samples, which suggested that the tight regulation of subcellular transcript abundances might be crucial for the maintenance of cellular homeostasis in both healthy and cancerous cells. 2. Connecting subcellular enrichment status with lncRNA biology Recent studies reported associations between many lncRNAs with biased subcellular distribution patterns and HCC. In our study, a new catalogue of HCC-associated lncRNAs and their respective fraction enrichment bias were constructed by an integrative analysis of our fractionation-then-sequencing datasets and TCGA-LIHC RNA-seq datasets. To further select the most confident fraction-enriched subset of lncRNA genes, a reference for normal variations in subcellular transcript distributions were defined using a reported list of housekeeping genes. Results indicated that since cellular transcript levels might be subjected to temporal fluctuations due to mechanisms such as burst transcription, only genes with a substantial distribution bias should be considered fraction-enriched. 3. Discovery of nuclear-enriched lncRNAs with HCC disease characteristics Within the catalogue of HCC-associated lncRNAs, we identified a subset of 26 lncRNA genes that exhibit stable nuclear-enrichment and are specific to tumor samples. Remarkably, the list of genes included PXN-AS1, which was experimentally validated to interact with the nuclear-localized splicing factor MBNL3 and could promote liver and lung cancer progression. The finding strongly suggests a connection between lncRNA nuclear enrichment phenotype and lncRNA-driven biological mechanisms residing within cell nucleus. Additionally, the other lncRNA genes including 6 novel genes also shared the characteristics of other experimentally supported HCC-prognostic lncRNA and may possess cancer-driving capabilities. This work is currently under review (manuscript available in Part C). 4. Collaborative efforts to elucidate underlying biology of RNA localization In the motivation to obtain novel insights and ground knowledge for further elucidating the phenomenon of RNA subcellular localization, we explored relevant RNA regulatory mechanisms and sequence elements in join efforts with other research groups across different disciplines and achieved solid outcomes. Our bioinformatics know-how stemmed from this project has extended to benefit these studies, which are in part enabled by this RGC funding support along with other research grants .

14102014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14102014.value: 1. Dissecting isoforms of nuclear-exclusive lncRNA genes High number of intronic reads in nuclear RNA-seq data limited its application in de novo transcriptome assembly, and hindered identification of some lncRNAs that reside exclusively in the nucleus. We propose to conduct additional sequencing experiments of nuclear RNA with PacBio Iso-seq technology, which could provide full-length transcript isoform information in an assembly-free manner. Existing Illumina short reads will be applied for providing accurate locations of splice junctions and correcting sequencing errors in PacBio long reads. 2. Elucidating landscape of lncRNA gene transcription in cell nucleus Gene transcription in eukaryotic nucleus was hypothesized to undergo in pervasive manner, where many genomic loci were transcribed but only a subset of transcripts gets processed and exported from nucleus. Consequentially, the large number of intergenic reads in nuclear RNA-seq data may indicate novel loci where pervasive transcription occur, among which some might be corresponding to undiscovered lncRNA genes. We propose for further exploration using our established cancer models and via orthogonal approaches such as ATAC-seq and GRO-seq. These techniques would enable detection of accessible chromatin regions and nascent transcripts, and could provide additional evidences for pervasive transcription phenomenon.

14102014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14102014.value: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a prevalent type of cancer and notorious for a rapid progression and poor prognosis. A dysregulation of non-protein-coding, regulatory RNA expression profile in liver cells was reported to facilitate HCC progression. While some hallmark cancer-driving non-protein-coding RNAs have been suggested localizing and functioning within the cell nucleus, there has not yet been systematic attempts to resolve sub-cellular localization landscape of RNAs and associate with their cancers-driving properties. In this study, we subjected cancer cells obtained from HCC patients to subcellular fractionation and independently sequenced RNAs from the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments. The information enabled us to establish a novel catalogue of potential regulatory, non-protein-coding RNAs that are stably enriched in the cell nucleus among a population of HCC cell samples. With the integration of other public datasets, we revealed strong connections between nuclear-enrichment phenotype and nuclear regulatory mechanisms of non-protein-coding RNAs. We further identified novel HCC-associated non-protein-coding RNA candidates that may serve as clinical biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets in HCC diagnosis and treatment. Our fractionation-then-sequencing approach could be widely applicable to other studies into the disease etiologies of non-protein-coding RNA.

14102214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14102214.value: The enteric nervous system (ENS) is the complex network of neurons and glia within the bowel that regulates many essential functions, including peristalsis, secretion and blood flow. Abnormal development of the ENS during embryogenesis can lead to disorders of gut functions ranging from chronic constipation to other more serious motility problems. Importantly, the hindgut, the distal portion of the embryonic colon, is a common site of congenital ENS abnormalities such as Hirschsprung’s disease and intractable constipation, disorders which can be life-threatening or even lethal. Thus, there is a need to better understand the development of the ENS within the hindgut in order to gain insights to the mechanisms underlying enteric neuropathies, and to improve our ability to develop effective programmes for prevention, diagnosis and therapy of enteric neuropathies that affect this gut region. Within the wall of the hindgut, the intrinsic neurons and glia that comprise the ENS are derived from the neural crest during embryonic development. While the majority of neural crest cells (NCCs) that form the hindgut ENS has been known to originate from the vagal (cervicothoracic) level, a smaller but significant contribution coming from the sacral level of the neuraxis has been recently established in the mammal. However, it is still unknown how these sacral NCCs interact and then mingle with vagal NCCs to form the complex network of enteric ganglia and what types of enteric neurons sacral NCCs differentiate into following the early formation of the ENS network. We hence hypothesize that in collaboration with vagal NCCs, sacral NCCs form an integral part of the ENS and contribute to certain neuronal subtypes of the hindgut ENS. To prove this hypothesis, we propose to (1) elucidate the cell-cell interaction of sacral and vagal NCCs within the developing hindgut during the formation of the network of interconnected neural crest-derived cells, (2) determine the subsequent differentiation and contribution of sacral NCCs to the hindgut ENS, and finally (3) ascertain the ability of sacral NCCs to form different subtypes of neurons by transplanting them to the aganglionic hindgut segment of mouse models of aganglionosis. Results of this study will give us information on the early formation of the neuronal network in the hindgut, the contribution of sacral NCCs to the hindgut ENS and the feasibility of restoring the normal development of the ENS by transplanting sacral NCCs to aganglionic gut segments.

14102214.label: Realisation of objectives
14102214.value: Three objectives have been set as follows: Objective one: To elucidate the cell-cell interaction of sacral neural crest cells during the formation of the complex network of interconnected neural crest-derived cells within the hindgut by time-lapse live cell imaging This objective has been fully achieved, and the following methods were developed to acheive the objective: (a) A cell labelling method to simultaneously label two types of neural crest-derived cells in the developing gut: The enteric nervous system (ENS) is exclusively derived from neural crest cells (NCCs) from both vagal and sacral levels. Vagal and sacral NCCs are morphologically and molecularly similar, and no specific cell markers so far have been found to distinguish these two groups of NCCs, making studies on cell-cell interactions among NCCs difficult. In this study, we used two transgenic markers to label separately vagal and sacral NCCs. One of these was Ednrb-hKikumeGR which labelled specifically all enteric NCCs (including vagal and sacral NCCs), and its encoded proteins could be changed from green to red fluorescent on irradiation with ultraviolet light. By selective photo-conversion, labelled single cells or a small group of labelled vagal NCCs were changed to red fluorescent, and their interactions with neighboring cells which were all green fluorescent were investigated. Another marker was EGFP which was driven by the CMV-IE enhancer/chick β-actin/rabbit β-globin hybrid promoter, and expressed in all nucleated cells. (b) Time-lapse live cell imaging on individual enteric cells: We coupled confocal microscopy with the previously established organ culture system where small segments of mouse hindgut at E11.5 to E13.5 (around 3-4 mm in length and 0.2-0.4 mm in diameter) were cultured ex vivo for up to 10 days. Serial confocal images were taken from the gut culture at fixed time intervals with computer software, and video-recordings on the dynamic changes of migrating cells were reconstructed from these serial images. (c) Recombination of pelvic ganglia with hindgut explants ex vivo: The exact location of pelvic ganglia at E12.5-E13.0 was first mapped with 3-dimensional computer reconstruction of hundreds of confocal images on serial cross sections of mouse embryos after the sections were stained with specific triple immunofluorescence staining for the expression of enteric NCC markers Sox10, p75 and Phox2b. With guidance of these computer images, pelvic ganglia were accurately isolated, and one pelvic ganglion was recombined with one hindgut segment explanted at E12.5-E13.0. The hindgut explant was cultured ex vivo for up to 4 days. During this culture period, sacral NCCs genetically labelled with EGFP migrated from the pelvic ganglion and entered the hindgut explant for further migration in the explant as what they did in vivo, while vagal NCCs, which were labelled with Ednrb-hKikumeGR, also migrated along the hindgut. With this recombination approach, dynamic cell-cell interactions between vagal and sacral NCCs were investigated. Objective two: To determine the enteric phenotypes and contribution of sacral NCCs to the enteric nervous system in the mouse hindgut by ex vivo culture and exo utero transplantation This objective has also been fully achieved with the following experimental methods: (a) Immunofluorescence localization of various neuronal subtypes of the hindgut ENS: To determine the spatiotemporal development of various neuronal subtypes in the hindgut as the first step toward a better understanding of the contribution of sacral NCCs to the ENS, we developed specific double and triple immunofluorescence methods with various antigen retrieval protocols for both whole-mount and section preparations using antibodies against different cell markers including Sox10, p75, Phox2b, TuJ1, PGP9.5, Hu, serotonin, CGRP, ChAT, calbindin, NOS, B-FABP, GFAP and SMA. 3-dimensional confocal images were reconstructed from serial cross sections using in-house computer software. (b) Transplantation of genetically labelled sacral NCCs to the hindgut explant ex vivo: EGFP-labelled sacral NCCs were isolated from pelvic ganglia of EGFP/B6 transgenic embryos at E12.5, and transplanted by microinjection to hindgut explants at E12.5. Alternatively, pelvic ganglia genetically labelled with EGFP were recombined with hindgut explants at E12.5. The hindgut explants transplanted with sacral NCCs or recombined with pelvic ganglia were cultured ex vivo for up to 6 days to study the differentiation and contribution of sacral NCCs to the ENS. (c) Exo utero transplantation of genetically labelled sacral NCCs to pelvic ganglia: For studies of longer-term differentiation of sacral NCCs in vivo, a more sophisticated and technically demanding surgical technique - exo utero transplantation - was developed. After pregnant mice at E13.0 were deeply anesthetized, the abdomen was incised, and the uterus was open to expose the embryonic sacs inside which live embryos were located. With the guidance of a series of computer images, EGFP-labelled sacral NCCs were transplanted to the pelvic ganglia of the embryos inside the embryonic sacs by direct microinjection through the embryonic membranes. The abdominal wall was then sutured, and the pregnant mice were allowed to recover. The mice were sacrificed one or two days before full term, and the differentiation and distribution of transplanted cells in the embryos were analyzed after immunofluorescence staining. Objective three: To ascertain the ability of sacral NCCs to form different neuronal subtypes in the aganglionic hindgut segment by cell transplantation This objective has also been fully achieved with the following experimental methods: (a) Dominant megacolon (Dom) mice as the animal model of aganglionosis: The hindgut of embryos homozygous for Dom shows total aganglionosis, and thus this mutant was used as the animal model of aganglionosis. Skin fibroblasts isolated from both wild-type and homozygous Dom embryos were reprogrammed into wt-iPSCs and Dom-iPSCs, respectively, with four Yamanaka transcription factors Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc. (b) Gene correction with CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing: CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing with homology directed repair was used to re-introduce a correct Sox10 sequence to Dom-iPSCs to become Dom-corrected iPSCs before cell transplantation. This method, instead of the originally proposed TALEN (transcription activator-like effector nuclease) gene editing platform, was used because it is technically simpler with higher efficiency. DNA sequencing confirmed the correction of the Sox10 mutation in Dom-corrected iPSCs. (c) Expansion of cells in vitro for cell transplantation: Six cell types including (1) sacral NCCs, (2) vagal NCCs, (3) enteric neural crest stem cells (ENCSCs) from E14.5 embryonic guts, (4) wt-iPSCs, (5) Dom-iPSCs and (6) Dom-corrected iPSCs were expanded in vitro in different culture media to obtain enough cells for transplantation. (d) Transplantation of cells to hindgut explants cultured ex vivo: Hindgut segments from wild-type and homozygous Dom embryos at E12.5 were explanted ex vivo. Each of the aforementioned 6 cell types labelled with EGFP was transplanted by microinjection to the outer wall of the hindgut segments which were then cultured ex vivo for up to 6 days, and the distribution and differentiation of the transplanted cells in the hindgut segments were analyzed. (e) Transplantation of cells to the descending colon of postnatal mice after laparotomy: The best surviving cell type in the hindgut explant, i.e. ENCSCs, was selected and transplanted to the normoganglionic descending colon of wild type postnatal (P7 to P14) mice and to the hypoganglionic segment of the descending colon of heterozygous Dom postnatal (P7 to P14) mice. Under deep anesthesia, the distal part of the descending colon was exposed after laparotomy. Neurospheres which contained about 6x106 EGFP-labelled ENCSCs were transplanted by microinjection to the descending colon. The abdominal wall was then sutured, and the mice recovered. 7 to 14 days later, the mice were sacrificed, and the distribution and differentiation of transplanted cells in the colon were analyzed after immunofluorescence staining.

14102214.label: Major findings and research outcome
14102214.value: With the two-color cell labelling system coupled with time-lapse live cell confocal imaging, we showed that sacral NCCs interacted extensively with vagal NCCs in the distal hindgut at E13.5 to form a complex cellular network of the early enteric nervous system (ENS). Four days after sacral NCCs were transplanted to the outer wall of E13.5 hindgut explants ex vivo, sacral NCCs were able to migrate to the myenteric plexus to form the cellular network with endogenous vagal NCCs of the hindgut explant, and differentiated into early enteric neurons immunoreactive to TuJ1 and PGP9.5. To confirm the contribution of sacral NCCs to the early ENS in vivo, a sophisticated exo utero surgical transplantation method was developed for transplanting cells directly to the pelvic ganglia of live embryos inside the embryonic sac. Four days after exo utero transplantation, transplanted sacral NCCs from pelvic ganglia migrated to the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, and some of these NCCs differentiated into early enteric neurons. Results of the 3-dimenional reconstruction of computer images after extensive immunofluorescence localization of different cell markers in the hindgut at E14.5 to E17.5 indicated that most neuronal subtypes, particularly those in the submucosal plexus, were not detected before birth despite that early neurons expressing neuronal markers PGP9.5 and HuC/D were already identified throughout the entire hindgut at E14.5. In a separate set of experiments where the potential of different cell types to differentiate into enteric neurons was examined, enteric neural crest stem cells (ENCSCs) isolated from E14.5 embryonic guts were found to be able to form myenteric neurons 4 days after transplanted to the hindgut explant ex vivo and one week after transplanted to the descending colon of early postnatal mice in vivo. Similar observations were made when ENCSCs were transplanted to the descending colon of mutant postnatal mice which showed deficiency of enteric neurons, indicating that ENCSCs might be a promising cell type in the cell-based therapy for enteric aganglionosis. However, iPSCs reprogrammed from skin fibroblasts of normal embryos or embryos with aganglionosis (embryos carrying a Sox10 mutation) or iPSCs with the Sox10 mutation corrected by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing were unable to survive in the hindgut explant ex vivo. We concluded that sacral NCCs are a distinctive group of migratory cells which are able to differentiate into enteric neurons both ex vivo and in vivo, and that ENCSCs are a potential cell source in the cell therapy for enteric aganglionosis.

14102214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14102214.value: In this study, we found that sacral NCCs are a distinctive group of migratory cells which can form both enteric neurons and glia. Thus, one of the directions for future studies may focus on the use of sacral NCCs in the cell-based therapy for congenital enteric neuropathies including Hirschsprung’s disease where deficiencies of enteric neurons (aganglionosis) in varying lengths of distal bowel are identified. The differentiation potentials of sacral NCCs may first be examined in different differentiation culture media or by transplanting them under the kidney capsule. Then, they may be expanded in vitro and tested for their therapeutic potentials by transplanting them to the descending colon with aganglionosis or hypoganglionosis. We also found in the present study that enteric neural crest stem cells derived from embryonic guts could be another cell source in cell therapies. iPSCs reprogrammed from mouse skin fibroblasts were however unable to survive in the hindgut, but our preliminary studies show that they can survive much better and form enteric neurons in the hindgut if they are induced to form NCC-like cells in vitro before cell transplantation. Thus, the induction of NCCs from fibroblast-derived iPSCs for autologous cell transplantation can be another direction for future studies.

14102214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14102214.value: Enteric nervous system (ENS) is the intrinsic innervation of the gastrointestinal tract, and derived exclusively from neural crest cells (NCCs) at vagal and sacral levels during embryonic development. The aim of this project was to determine the contribution of sacral NCCs to the ENS. With a combination of advanced experimental techniques including time-lapse live cell imaging, specific immunofluorescence localization of different neuronal types, gene editing, embryonic gut culture and cell transplantation to live embryos and to the descending colon of postnatal mice, we found that sacral NCCs migrated from pelvic ganglia toward the embryonic hindgut, then entered the hindgut and migrated to the myenteric and submucosal plexuses to form enteric neurons. At birth, sacral NCCs had not yet differentiated to all different types of enteric neurons found in adulthood. Enteric neural crest stem cells isolated from embryonic guts also formed enteric neurons after transplanted to the descending colon of early postnatal mice, indicating the potential application of this cell type in the cell therapy for deficiencies of enteric neurons. We conclude that sacral NCCs are migratory cells which can form enteric neurons of the hindgut ENS, and that enteric neural crest stem cells possess the potential to form enteric neurons.

14102314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14102314.value: Background: The level of patient safety and outcomes accomplished depend on the quality of care provided. Previous studies found that nurse-to-patient ratio, practice environment, and nursing education were significant predictors of patient outcomes. However, the outcomes measured in previous studies were mainly inpatient mortality and failure-to-rescue rates, and few nurse-sensitive patient outcomes have been measured that quantify nurses’ contribution to patient care. Selecting appropriate outcomes that reflect the clinically relevant effect of nursing care is important. Moreover previous studies were largely cross-sectional and retrospective. These research designs are limited in their ability to explain the casual links between the variables examined. Aim: The proposed study will be the first to determine the associations among staffing levels, the skill mix of baccalaureate-prepared registered nurses, and the practice environment on nurse-sensitive outcomes for medical and surgical patients in public hospitals in Hong Kong using a prospective design. Methods: This study will adopt a multi-method research design. The hospital sample will be collected from nine major public hospitals that offer 24-hour accident and emergency services. The clinical wards selected will include medical and surgical wards. Multiple responses from registered nurses who work in the study wards will be collected over 12 months to examine their individual characteristics and perceptions of the practice environment. A 12-month prospective observational study will be carried out to determine the association between nurse staffing levels, the practice environment, and nurse-sensitive patient outcomes including pressure ulcers, falls and restraint prevalence, urinary catheter-associated urinary tract infections, central line catheter-associated bloodstream infections, and smoking cessation counselling for acute myocardial infarction, pneumonia and heart failure patients. Multilevel Cox proportional hazards models will be employed to examine the association between these patient outcomes and the explanatory nursing factors of primary interest (nurse staffing levels, education composition, and practice environment), with adjustment for all patient-, ward- and hospital-level potential confounders (age, sex, diagnosis, comorbidities, level of surgical invasiveness, mortality, length of stay, and type of admission). Significance: It is anticipated that knowledge of the association between nurse staffing levels, the practice environment, and nurse-sensitive outcomes will inform the provision of quality and timely patient care. This study will provide a landmark report that is of relevance and importance to patients and to hospital stakeholders and managers, health policy makers, nurses, and educators who advocate patient benefits. 背景：住院病人的安全及其護理相關的結果跟護理的質素是息息相關的。研究文獻指出護理相關的病人結果的重要預測因素包括護士與病人的比例、護士的工作環境和護理教育程度。然而這些研究大部份只量度住院病人死亡率和搶救失敗率，較少量度可衡量護士對病人照護貢獻的護理相關的病人結果。選擇合適的結果以反映臨床照護的影響是十分重要的。而且過去的研究文獻大多是橫斷性和回顧性研究，這些研究設計對解釋所有檢測因素之間的因果關係存在著一定的局限性。 目的：本研究是香港首個以前瞻性研究設計，探討香港公立醫院內科及外科病房的護士人力配置、混合技術護理模式中入職時已擁有本科學位註冊護士的比例，和護士工作環境對護理相關的病人結果的相關性。 方法：本研究將採用多元方法，研究樣本包括本港九間提供二十四小時急症服務的公立醫院，研究會在內科及外科病房內進行。我們會於十二個月內收集數次所有在這些病房內工作的註冊護士的資料及他們對工作環境的意見。我們亦會進行一項為期十二個月的前瞻性觀察性研病人結果包括壓瘡、跌倒及使用約束衣的流行率、導尿管相關的泌尿道感染、中心導管相關的血流感染，以及為患有急性心肌梗塞、肺炎和心臟衰竭病人提供的戒煙輔導服務。本研究將採用多層Cox比例風險模式，檢測以上的病人結果與主要的解釋性護理因素（包括護士人力配置、教育程度的混合和護士工作環境）之間的相關性。數據檢測會從病人、病房和醫院的層面對可能的干擾因素（包括年齡、性別、醫學診斷、共病、外科手術的創傷性、死亡率、住院時間及入院類別）作出調整。 重要性：我們希望透過此研究了解護士人力配置、護士工作環境與護理相關的病人結果的相關性，研究結果將有助提供高質素及適切的病人護理。本研究的報告將會是相關研究課題的新里程，對病人、乃至醫院出資者及管理層、醫療政策決策者、護士、及為病人倡議權益的教育工作者具有相關性和重要性。

14102314.label: Realisation of objectives
14102314.value: The three objectives of the study have been achieved. The nurse-sensitive patient outcomes of interest of the study included 1) pressure ulcers identified at 48 hours after admission to the hospital or ward, 2) incidence of fall, 3) use of physical restraint, 4) incidence of catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI), and 5) central line catheter-associated bloodstream infections (CLCABI). We have analysed the study outcomes as aggregated monthly data nested in ward level in the forms of number of patients with pressure ulcers, number of fall incidence, number of patients with physical restraints, number of patients with CAUTI, and number of patients with CLCABI, given that only aggregated monthly data of the study outcomes were available for the participating wards. Since the number of patients with CLCABI was not routinely reported in many wards of the four study hospitals, analysis for this outcome was not possible in the present study. The explanatory variables of interest of the study included patient-to-nurse ratio, proportion of registered nurses with a Bachelor’s or higher degree upon entry to the profession, and practice environment. The average monthly number of patients and nurses in the three shifts of duty in each ward were used to derive the monthly average patient-to-nurse ratio in each ward in each month. The tri-monthly surveys on the participating wards were used to estimate the proportion of registered nurses with a Bachelor or higher degree upon entry to the profession and quantify the practice environment using the composite score of the Practice Environment Scale of the Nursing Work Index (PES-NWI) in the study wards. The ward-level monthly data of these proportion and practice environment variables were projected from the four tri-monthly survey data. For example, the explanatory variables estimated for April, May and June were the same and based on the survey done on April. A random slope mixed-effects model was used to examine the associations between each of the outcomes and each of the explanatory variables. Specifically, there were two levels in the model with the twelve sets of aggregated monthly data as level one and the participating wards as level two. This model can account for the possibly intra-correlated aggregated monthly data nested within each ward and allow for varying strengths of association between the underlying outcome and explanatory variables across different wards. The effect of hospital was adjusted as a level 2 fixed-factor in each of the mixed-effects model for each of the outcomes concerned. The outcomes of number of patients with pressure ulcers, number of fall incidence, and number of patients with CAUTI were all square root transformed before being entering into the mixed-effects models. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS release 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC). All statistical tests involved were 2-sided with level of significance set at 0.05.

14102314.label: Major findings and research outcome
14102314.value: Surveys about practice environment The total number of nurses surveyed ranged from 604 to 865 over the four tri-monthly surveys. Over 90% of the participants were aged 55 years old or below. Majority of them were registered nurses (>80%) while the remaining were advanced practice nurses (13%), nursing officers, nurse specialists, ward managers or nurse consultants (4%). The median years of working experience as a registered nurse was 5.0-5.7 years. The participants had an averaged 76% or more of their working time spent on direct patient care. Nearly 50% obtained a Bachelor’s degree upon entry to the nursing profession. The highest educational attainment included Bachelor’s (60%) and Master’s (about 25%) degrees. The results showed that the nurses’ satisfaction with their practice environment was consistently fair over the four waves of survey. The mean of the composite score of the Practice Environment Scale of the Nursing Work Index (PES-NWI) ranged from 2.63 (SD 0.33) to 2.64 (SD 0.35). Three of the five domains (‘Nursing foundations for quality of care’, ‘nurse manager ability, leadership and support of nurses’, and ‘collegial nurse-physician relations’) consistently showed the highest score (mean range: 2.77 (SD 0.42) to 2.81 (0.31)). The mean score of the domain ‘Staffing and resource adequacy’ was the lowest (mean range: 2.10 (SD 0.54)-2.20 (SD 0.57)). Nurse staffing level and educational level The average monthly patient-to-nurse ratio per ward (n=71) was 9.0 (SD 2.6; inter-quartile range: 7.4–9.9). The average monthly percentage of registered nurses with a Bachelor’s or higher degrees per ward was high (Mean 82.8, SD 14.9). Associations with nurse-sensitive patient outcomes The average monthly number of nurse-sensitive patient outcomes including: 1) patients with pressure ulcers per ward was 0.7 (SD 1.2), 2) fall incidence per ward was 0.6 (SD 0.9), physical restraints per ward was 125.1 (SD 83.9), and patients with CAUTI per ward was 1.1 (SD 1.9). The results showed that patient-to-nurse ratio was significantly associated with the number of patients with physical restraints (B: 9.72, 95% CI 6.19-13.25, p<0.001). There was also a significant association between nurses’ perception of practice environment and number of patients with pressure ulcers (B: -0.010, 95% CI -0.019 to -0.001, p=0.033). No significant association was found between the percentage of registered nurses with a Bachelor’s or higher degrees upon entry to the profession with the nurse-sensitive patient outcomes.

14102314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14102314.value: This study identified two key findings which included significant associations between nurse staffing level and the number of patients using physical restraints, and perception of practice environment and number of patients with pressure ulcers. Use of physical restraints and presence of pressure ulcers can be associated with poor patient outcomes but are preventable. Future directions of our research are to continue examine and test effective strategies to promote positive practice environment that encourages nurse participation in hospital affairs, enhances quality of nursing care, promotes support to nurses, increases nurse staffing and resources, and promotes nurse-physician relations. Furthermore, more research on devising strategies to deploying nurses and resources more effectively to address the patient needs and hence reduces the use of physical restraints in patients is needed. Follow-up longitudinal and experimental studies could be initiated with the study hospitals to further enhance the quality of nursing care and nurses’ perception of their practice environment.

14102314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14102314.value: The longitudinal study is the first of its kind in Hong Kong to examine the associations between nurse staffing level, educational level and practice environment, and the nurse-sensitive patient outcomes including pressure ulcers, falls, physical restraints, catheter-associated urinary tract infections and central line catheter-associated bloodstream infections. The study results showed that there were significant associations between patient-to-nurse ratio and the number of patients with physical restraints; and nurses’ perception of practice environment and the number of patients with pressure ulcers. The results supported the importance of ensuring adequate patient-to-nurse ratio and a positive practice environment on patients’ outcomes. Future directions of research include testing effective strategies to promote a practice environment that is supportive and encourages nurse participation in hospital affairs, and deploying adequate nurses and resources for enhanced quality of nursing care.

14102714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14102714.value: Our aim is to functionally characterize tumor suppressor long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) associated with human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Critical PDAC-associated proteins including Kras, P16, P53 and Smad4 have been well characterized, but current therapies for PDAC are still ineffective and the prognosis is dismal. Novel therapeutic targets are therefore urgently in demand. LncRNAs possess key biological functions including histone-codes establishment, genomic imprinting and dosage compensation. Accumulating evidence suggests that lncRNAs play critical roles in cancer by regulating gene expression. However, the role of lncRNAs in PDAC remains largely unexplored. The novel lncRNA Ak311005 was frequently downregulated in PDAC tumor tissues and cell lines, and had important role during PDAC development as reduction of its expression was detected in precursor lesion of PDAC. AK311005 played tumor suppressor roles as depletion of AK311005 in non-tumor human pancreatic ductal epithelial (HPDE) cells significantly promoted cell growth and induced cell cycle progression. By gene expression microarray, we identified a subset of gene upregulated upon depletion of AK311005 RNA in HPDE cells. They included aniline Anillin (ANLN), Aurora Kinase A (AURKA), Disc, Large (Drosophilla) Homolog Associated-Protein 5 (DLGAP5) and kinesin family member 23 (KIF23) that participated in cell cycle, mitotic division and cell growth. SiRNAs knockdown of them significantly inhibited the growth of PDAC cells, while measurement of their expression in human PDAC tissues showed clinical significance. They suggested that these proteins were critical downstream targets of AK311005. Bioinformatics analysis suggested that AK311005 interacted with a gene silencing protein complex DREAM. By RNA immunoprecipitation, we showed the physical interaction between AK311005 and the core members of DREAM complex. Analysis of promoter elements of AK311005 targets showed that majority of them harbored DREAM complex binding elements. Knockdown of the core DREAM complex member and inhibition of histone deacetylase increased the level of AK311005 targets. Taken together, our preliminary data prompted us to believe that AK311005 is a driver lncRNA with critical roles in the development of PDAC by silencing cancer associated genes. Based on our promising preliminary results, we intend to 1) characterize the role of AK311005 in PDAC; 2) identify PDAC-associated AK311005 targets; 3) reveal the silencing mechanism of AK311005 gene regulatory pathway. Knowledge gained from this project will improve our understanding to PDAC biology and prompt the development of new therapeutic strategies. 本課題的目的是要對與胰腺導管腺瘤相關的長鏈非編碼RNAs（lncRNAs）進行功能表征。雖然胰腺導管腺瘤與Kras, P16, P53 及 Smad4等基因的關係已廣為人知，但是目前仍然缺乏有效的治療方法，其預後極差。因此，迫切需要尋找新的治療靶標。LncRNAs在基因調控中起了非常重要的作用。然而，lncRNAs與胰腺導管腺瘤的關係仍然很不明確。我們鑒定了一個新的lncRNA Ak311005。Ak311005在胰腺導管腺瘤中表達顯著下調，並具有潛在的腫瘤抑制作用。 基於我們的前期研究結果，本課題計畫中進行如下研究：1）表徵AK311005在胰腺導管腺瘤中的作用；2）鑒定在胰腺導管腺瘤相關的靶分子；3）解析AK311005調控基因表達的分子機制。本課題研究結果將有助於研發新的治療胰腺導管腺瘤的方法。

14102714.label: Realisation of objectives
14102714.value: To identify the lncRNA that had tumor suppressor functions in PDAC, we analyzed the expression profiles of lncRNAs by microarray in 4 pairs of PDAC tumor and paired non-tumor tissues (Arraystar Inc. http://www.arraystar.com/). Our selection criteria were a) fold change ≥ 2 and b) decreased in all patients. A novel lncRNA annotated as AK311005 was downregulated in all 4 tissue pairs. In turn, we searched for public dataset that measured AK311005 expressions in PDAC tissues. In GSE57144 dataset, the levels of AK311005 were relatively lower in PDAC tissues compared to normal pancreas tissue. We next measured AK311005 transcript level in a cohort of PDAC clinical specimens (n=20). qRT-PCR results showed that AK311005 level was frequently reduced in PDAC tumors compared to adjacent non-tumor tissues. qRT-PCR showed that AK311005 level was low or barely detected in PDAC cancer cells compared to non-tumorigenic HPDE cells. In turn, we attempted to study the role of AK311005 during the transformation of PDAC. We conducted in situ hybridization of AK311005 RNA using an LNA-based ribonucleotide probe (Exiqon) on pancreatic in situ neoplasia (PanIN) tissues, the precursor lesion of PDAC. We showed that AK311005 the expression of AK311005 RNA was downregulated in PanIN (n=5), while it was readily detected in non-tumor pancreatic ductal epithelia. To show that AK311005 regulated PDAC cell growth and cell cycle in vitro, we transiently transfected the siRNAs targeting AK311005 into PDAC cell lines, and measured the knockdown efficiency by qRT-PCR. Knockdown of AK311005 RNA by siRNAs was able to promote cell proliferation in HPDE, CAPAN2 and SW1990 cells. Cell cycle analysis showed that inhibition of AK311005 in HPDE cells accelerated the progression of cell cycle, prompting an increased cell population to enter S phase. We also established permanent knockdown of AK311005 by transducing lentivirus carrying shRNAs in HPDE cells. Knockdown of AK311005 by shRNAs also promoted the growth of HPDE cells. Lentivirus carrying shRNAs that targeted AK311005 lncRNA was transduced into HPDE cells. Wound healing assay showed that inhibition of AK311005 led to the complete closure of the wound, while only about 50% of the wound was closed in control cells. To show that AK311005 suppresses target genes critical in cell growth and cell cycle, we identified the downstream targets regulated by AK311005. We first inhibited AK311005 level in HPDE cells by siRNAs. In turn, total RNA was extracted for genome-wide gene expression microarray analysis (GeneChip Human Genome U133 Plus 2.0 Array, Affymetrix). Gene ontology analysis showed that AK311005 regulated genes that participated in cell cycle process, cell division and microtubule-based process. Microarray analysis showed that there was a subset of genes differentially expressed that are highly associated with cancer cell growth. Knockdown of AK311005 by siRNAs could upregulate the RNA expressions of the targets. In addition, we knocked-down AK311005 by shRNAs, and showed that ANLN was upregulated after depletion of AK311005. More importantly, depletion of AK311005 could upregulate the protein expression of both ANLN and KIF23 levels. To show that AK311005 targets exhibit important functions and clinical relevance in PDAC, we unravel the full length of AK311005 by rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE, First Choice RLM-RACE Kit, Ambion) and then further cloned it into our established lentiviral vector and a doxycycline inducible vector pTRE-3G (Tet-on® 3G Inducible Expression System, Clontech). To confirm the putative target of AK311005, the level of potential AK311005 targets were detected in AK311005 overexpressed PDAC cells. Upon AK311005 overexpression by lentiviral transduction, the expression levels of Anillin (ANLN), Aurora Kinase A (AURKA), Disc, Large (Drosophilla) Homolog Associated-Protein 5 (DLGAP5) and kinesin family member 23 (KIF23) were reduced. We then measured the transcript levels of ANLN, AURKA, DLGAP5 and KIF23 in a panel of PDAC cell lines by qRT-PCR, and showed that they were frequently upregulated compared to HPDE cells. Knockdown of both DLGAP5 and KIF23 inhibited the cell proliferation of CFPAC1 cells, which suggested that they played a role in promoting PDAC cell growth. In addition, we illustrated the clinical relevance of AK311005 pathway in PDAC tissues. We showed that the level of AK311005 RNA in human PDAC tissues was correlated with that of ANLN (p=0.0005) and AURKA (p=0.0223). We also studied the abundance of DLGAP5 and KIF23 proteins in human paired tissues by immunohistochemical staining (IHC), and showed that both were overexpressed in PDAC tumor tissues. To further studied the effect of AK311005 restoration to the cell proliferation rate of PDAC cells, full length AK311005 was cloned into a doxycycline-inducible plasmid, and stable PANC1 cells were established that carried the AK311005 inducible gene. Doxycycline treatment on the inducible PANC1 cells could effectively induce AK311005 expression in PANC1 cells. Induced AK311005 expression by treating PANC1 cells with doxcycline could inhibit cell proliferation of PANC1 cells. In turn, we would like to study the effect of AK311005 overexpression to its downstream target genes in PDAC cells. Stable SW1990 cells with inducible AK311005 transgene was treated with doxycycline. Doxycycline treatment could also inhibit the expression of ANLN and AURKA RNA expression in SW1990 cells. In addition, we established a doxycycline-inducible AK311005 CFPAC1 cells. Overexpression of AK311005 could readily downregulate the expression of ANLN in CFPAC1 cells. To identify the silencing mechanism of AK311005, we first analysed the DNA elements present in AK311005 targets’ promoters. AURKA, DLGAP5 and KIF23 harbored cell cycle gene homology region (CHR) promoter element that is recognized by DREAM complex. Bioinformatic tool lncPro showed that AK311005 potentially interacted with most members of the DREAM complex. To note, AK311005 RNA had high interactive value with the core members Lin37, MYBL1/2 and RBL2, as well as catalytic proteins HDAC1/2. To show the physical association of AK311005 RNA with DREAM complex, we carried out RNA-binding Protein Immunoprecipitation (RIP, Magna RIPTM, Millipore) using antibody that immunoprecipitated DREAM complex members LIN37 and MYBL2 in PANC-1 cells. The two members were selected owning to their high predicted interactive value. RIP showed that AK311005 RNA was enriched with the both proteins. To study the effect of AK311005-DREAM complex, we inhibited a core DREAM member E2F4 by siRNAs in HPDE cells and measured the level of AK311005 targets. Knockdown of E2F4 significantly upregulated AK311005 targets. DREAM complex suppressed target gene expression via the recruitment of histone deacetylase (HDAC) and induction of histone H4 deacetylation. Upon TSA treatment, the expression level of AK311005 targets was significantly upregulated. To show that the targets of AK311005 were regulated by DREAM complex, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay was performed to study the occupancy of DREAM complex core members at the promoter regions of the targets. We showed that the core members were frequently observed in the promoter regions of DLGAP5, ANLN, KIF23 and AURKA. We then measured the enrichment levels of the DREAM complex by qPCR and compared them between HPDE and PANC1 cells. We showed that DREAM complex members B-myb, E2F4 and P130 were frequently lower at the promoter region of DLGAP5, ANLN, KIF23 and AURKA in PANC1 cells compared to HPDE cells. By ChIP assay, we showed that H4 acetylation level was frequently higher at the promoter region of DLGAP5, ANLN, KIF23 and AURKA in PANC1 cells compared to HPDE cells. It suggested that the loss of AK311005 may contribute to the activation of its target genes through the increase of H4 acetylation.

14102714.label: Major findings and research outcome
14102714.value: We have identified a novel lncRNA AK311005 that contributed to the tumorigenesis and progression of human PDAC. AK311005 was frequently downregulated in four human PDAC tissues compared to their corresponding adjacent non-tumor tissues . AK311005 was also downregulated in PDAC cell lines compared to non-tumor ductal epithelial cells. We also showed that AK311005 was downregulated in the PanIN, the precursor of PDAC, suggesting that loss of AK311005 could be an early and critical event to the carcinogenesis of PDAC. Depletion of AK311005 contributed to the malignant phenotypical changes of PDAC. AK311005 regulated cell proliferation, cell cycle progression and cell migration that may contribute to the development and progression of PDAC. Gene ontology analysis showed that loss of AK311005 heavily affected critical steps of cell cycle, as it induced the alteration of genes that regulated cell cycle process, cell division, microtubule-based process, M phase of mitotic cell cycle, M phase, mitotic cell cycle, cell cycle phase and mitotic prometaphase. We further showed AK311005 regulated the expression of ANLN, AURKA, DLGAP5 and KIF23 in PDAC cells. These AK311005 target genes may play important roles in PDAC, as we showed that their expressions were frequently increased in PDAC cell lines compared to non-tumor HPDE cells, and in human PDAC tissues compared to adjacent non-tumor tissues. AK311005 was the upstream regulator of ANLN, AURKA, DLGAP5 and KIF23 in PDAC cells as inhibition of AK311005 promoted their expressions while overexpression of AK311005 inhibited their expressions. Bioinformatic analysis showed that AK311005 could interact with histone deacetylase members HDAC1 and HDAC2. We showed that AK311005 coupled with DREAM complex and had physical interaction with the core members Lin37, MYBL2/B-Myc, E2F4 and RBL2/P130. AK311005 may recruit DREAM complex to the promoter of its target genes, and led to the downregulation of target genes through the deacetylation of the histone H4 at their promoter regions.

14102714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14102714.value: We believe that loss of AK311005 played a critical role in the initiation of the precursor lesions PanIN, and subsequently the development of PDAC. In order to study the role of AK311005 in the initiation of PDAC tumor, transgenic mice with knock-out of AK311005 will be establish. The occurrence of lesions in the pancreas will be closely monitored. We can crossbred the AK311005 KO mice with other transgenic mice that harbor critical mutation such as KRAS and p53 mutation. The incidence and time to the development of PDAC from precursor lesions are monitored. As such, we can study the role of AK311005 in the initiation of PDAC. The underlying mechanism of the downregulation of AK311005 was not explored. Characterization of molecular mechanism leading to the suppression of AK311005 could allow a better understanding of the critical event leading to suppression of tumor suppressor lncRNAs. Promoter region of AK311005 will be identified by promoter reporter assays. Potential aberration on epigenetic regulation such as DNA methylation or histone modification will be studied. In addition, the regulating elements on the promoter region of AK311005 will also be identified by promoter assays. Critical elements that contributed to loss of AK311005 expression will be revealed.

14102714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14102714.value: We have shown that the abundance of AK311005 RNA was low in PDAC tumor tissues compared to non-tumor tissues. AK311005 RNA contributed to the development and progression of PDAC by promoting the growth of PDAC cells and enhancing the migration ability of PDAC cells. More importantly, restoration of AK311005 could result in anti-cancer effect to PDAC cells. We have also unraveled the protein expressing genes that were regulated by AK311005 RNA, which included ANLN, AURKA, DLGAP5 and KIF23. We showed that AK311005 functioned to suppress the expression of these genes. Consistent to the reduced AK311005 level, we found that the abundance of these genes were high in PDAC tissues compared to non-tumor tissues. We showed that increased expression levels of these protein genes may be the underlying reason for the increased of cell growth upon loss of AK311005 RNA in PDAC. Lastly, we discovered that AK311005 RNA could physically bind with a complex called DREAM complex. DREAM complex functions to lower the expression of genes by removing the acetylation from histone H4 on chromatin. AK311005 RNA brought the DREAM complex to its target protein genes which resulted in the inhibition of their expressions.

14102914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14102914.value: 肝細胞癌（HCC）是全世界最常見及致死率最高的癌症之一，男性患者發病率顯著居多，尤其在乙型肝炎流行區域更為明顯。雄激素受體（AR）是一種調控發育和維持男性性徵的配體激活型核受體。在男性發病率高的癌症中，異常激活的AR信號被認為能導致癌症的惡化。人類HCC基因組測序研究已發現多個重要的突變基因，但對HCC表觀遺傳學上的異常改變和影響，目前仍未完全明瞭。多硫蛋白成員EZH2可通過組蛋白H3第27位的賴氨酸三甲基化，導致抑癌基因的表達沉默，在腫瘤發生中起關鍵作用。 AR和EZH2都被認爲可導致HCC的致癌基因，但二者在HCC發展過程中的相互調節和交叉效應卻仍然不明。 綜上所述及初步數據，我們假設AR信號異常，特别是受AR直接控制的細胞周期相關性激酶(CCRK)，可引起EZH2介導的一系列表觀遺傳及基因轉錄的異常改變，進而促進HCC的發生和發展。我們提議，通過分析AR如何導致EZH2磷酸化的分子機理，以及使用全基因組關聯綜合分析，研究表觀遺傳及基因轉錄的異常改變，應可發現在AR引發HCC發展過程中，之前未爲人所知的表觀遺傳調控基因的功能和作用。本研究結果不僅可進一步揭露HCC發病率上性別差異的分子水平機理，同時亦可提供一個新的核受體調控癌症表觀遺傳的範例。對於AR/CCRK/EZH2調控網絡細節的研究， 亦可望爲研發通過抑制癌症特異性信號通路的靶標療法提供指引。

14102914.label: Realisation of objectives
14102914.value: Epigenetic dysregulation represents a major oncogenic mechanism in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), which can be triggered by a number of risk factors including hepatitis B virus (HBV) and androgen receptor (AR) signaling in males. At molecular level, we have demonstrated that AR can transcriptionally activate cell cycle-related kinase (CCRK), which in turn phosphorylates GSK3β to up-regulate β-catenin/TCF signaling, resulting in EZH2/p-EZH2 overexpression and histone mark modifications. Intriguingly, AR-stimulated EZH2 can both activate pro-tumorigenic genes and inhibit tumor-suppressive genes through associations with H3K27me3 and H3K4me3, respectively. Such deregulated AR/CCRK/EZH2 axis is recapitulated in a HBV X protein (HBx) transgenic (TG) mouse model, as well as HBV-related HCC patients. Of clinical relevance, activation of AR/CCRK/EZH2 axis correlates with worse survivals of patients. We therefore aimed to investigate the underlying mechanisms and functional consequences in comprehensive manners. For objective 1, we have dissected the mechanistic regulations of AR signaling on EZH2. We employed the LO2 and SK-Hep1 cell models to monitor the changes of signaling cascades by Western blot following overexpression/knockdown of molecules in the AR/CCRK/EZH2 axis. In parallel, we introduced ectopic CCRK, AKT and EZH2 mutants into the cells for comparisons. Furthermore, we applied luciferase reporter assays to examine gene promoter activities, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and PCR to examine nuclear factor/histone mark occupancy at gene promoters, and co-immunoprecipitation to examine protein-protein interactions. Our final results consolidated the parallel actions of two positive feedback loops comprising AR/CCRK/GSK3β/β-catenin/E2F1/EZH2 and AR/CCRK/p-AKT/p-EZH2 responsible for epigenetic deregulations in the liver cells. For objective 2, we have investigated the effects of AR signaling on the epigenomes and transcriptomes of liver cells from cell lines, mouse models and human specimens. This was achieved by examinations of the genome-wide bindings of EZH2, H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 using nano-ChIP-seq, followed by the comparisons of gene expression levels using RNA-seq. These seq data were subjected to a series of bioinformatic and statistical analyses. Moreover, similar omics data obtained from other cell/patient samples and published in TCGA databases were also used for comparisons. Collectively, these integrated data revealed that the occupancies of activating histone mark (e.g. H3K4me3) and suppressive histone mark (e.g. H3K27me3) at specific genomic loci are facilitated by the co-bindings of different nuclear factors such as EZH2, p-EZH2, YY1, etc., which thereby regulate the expression of not only a myriad of tumor suppressor genes/oncogenes (e.g. IGFBP4, FOXA1, HNF1A, HNF4A, UBE2C, PLK1, etc.), but also novel microRNAs (e.g. miR-9) to reinforce hepatocarcinogenesis. For objective 3, we have characterized the functional roles of individual AR-dependent and epigenetically regulated genes (e.g. CCRK, EZH2, IGFBP4, YY1, etc.) in HCC. This was achieved by up-/down-regulations of target genes through transfections of multiple liver cell lines, examinations of downstream signaling cascades by Western blot, analyses of cell cycle progressions by flow cytometry, assessments of cell growths by proliferation and colony formation assays, evaluations of tumorigenic potentials by induction of tumors in mouse models, etc. In addition, we also performed qRT-PCR, Western blot and immunohistochemistry staining to examine the expression of these epigenetically regulated genes, together with their associated upstream regulators and downstream effectors (e.g. AR, GSK3β, β-catenin, E2F1, AKT, etc.) in HCC patients, followed by statistical analyses to determine the correlations of epigenetically regulated genes with patient survivals and clinicopathological features. In summary, we have completed all three objectives, and also extended our research beyond the scopes described in the proposal. Collectively, we have published our findings in multiple international conferences and journals (as attached, including “Journal of Hepatology”, “Gut”, “Pharmacology & Therapeutics”, “Journal of Pathology”, etc.).

14102914.label: Major findings and research outcome
14102914.value: By manipulating the AR, CCRK and EZH2 expression in liver cell lines and mouse models, we demonstrated that these molecules form positive feedback circuits. Specifically, AR induces the transcription of CCRK, which in turn phospho-inactivates GSK3β to stimulate β-catenin/E2F1 signaling, resulting in upregulation of EZH2 that inhibits Wnt antagonists. In parallel, the induced CCRK also promotes AKT phosphorylation, which thereby phosphorylates EZH2 and enhances its binding with AR at the CCRK promoter for continuous activation. This CCRK-EZH2 circuitry is activated in human HCC tissues, and significantly correlates with poor patient survivals (Feng et al., J Hepatol 2015). Besides, we also identified the oncogenic CCRK/STAT3/AR signaling pathway in obesity-related HCCs (4/2016/New Orleans). Using ChIP to determine the genome-wide binding loci of H3K27me3 in HBV-related liver cell lines and mouse models, we discovered that the transcription factor YY1 interacts with EZH2 to achieve epigenetic silencing. Among the YY1- and H3K27me3-occupied genes, at least 15 are microRNAs with tumor-suppressive properties. Functionally, we demonstrated that ablation of YY1 suppresses HCC growth through NFκB signaling at both in vitro and in vivo levels (Tsang et al., J Pathol 2016). Moreover, our ChIP-seq analyses identified IGFBP4 as a novel tumor suppressor in the liver that takes part in the AKT-EZH2 epigenetic cascades (3/2017/Taiwan), and provided important insights into the differential regulations of activating/suppressive histone marks (e.g. H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, etc.) on different genomic elements in HCCs (4/2016/New Orleans; 3/2017/Taiwan). As for translational potential, we identified that the CCRK-EZH2 oncogenic signaling increases IL-6 production through NFκB signaling, leading to increased immunosuppression, and hence suggesting that CCRK inhibition coupled with immune-checkpoint blockade may represent an effective therapeutic strategy (Zhou et al., Gut 2018). Moreover, we also found that inhibition of HDAC8, responsible for genome-wide histone deacetylation, can be combined with immunotherapy for HCC suppression (3/2017/Taiwan). Of interest, our collaborative study showed that Bufalin, a major digoxin-like component in the Chinese medicine Chansu, is a potential therapy of HCC based on its effective suppression of oncogenic CCRK/β-catenin/TCF signaling (Yu et al., Sci Rep 2018). Finally, we have published multiple reviews on crucial epigenetic regulators (e.g. CUL4B, CCRK, β-catenin, HDAC8, etc.) in HCC-relevant contexts (Mok et al., J Pathol 2015; Tian et al., Cancers 2016; Cheung et al. Front Genet 2016; Wong et al., Book chapter in Handbook of Nutrition, Diet, and Epigenetics 2017; Mok et al., Pharmacol Ther 2018), and also presented an overview in international conference (10/2015/Nagoya).

14102914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14102914.value: One of our major findings concerns the AR/CCRK-dependent oncogenic signaling in HCCs that links the liver epigenome and transcriptome to not only HBV, but also obesity-related fatty liver disease, which has emerged to be the major risk factor of HCC in the next decades. In addition to a solid rationale for the development of CCRK inhibitors for HCC treatment, our current studies showed that existing epigenetic drugs, immune-checkpoint blockers and specific Chinese medicine may possess synergistic effects on HCC suppression. Future studies are warranted to optimize their dose-dependent effects in vivo, and most importantly, determine their mechanistic effects at molecular levels. Moreover, our integrative and comprehensive epigenomic analyses of HCCs have identified the loci-dependent effects of multiple histone marks and their interactions with different nuclear factors on novel genomic elements, for instance, gene enhancers. Future follow-up studies will help dissect the mechanistic interplays of epigenetic regulators on gene enhancers, and their respective downstream effects on specific liver phenotypes and individual HCC subtypes. The anticipated results will shed light on the potential of applying enhancer-targeted inhibitors as a novel approach for HCC treatment.

14102914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14102914.value: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a male-predominant disease independent of the risk factors, in which the male hormone-responsive androgen receptor (AR) is a major factor driving the tumorigenesis through complex molecular pathways. In this project, we delineated two parallel positive feedback circuits comprising GSK3β/β-catenin/E2F1/EZH2 and p-AKT/p-EZH2 that fuel continuous AR-dependent stimulation of the oncogenic cell cycle-related kinase (CCRK). Moreover, we demonstrated that CCRK promotes IL-6 production, through EZH2/NFκB signaling, to establish an immunosuppressive microenvironment for HCC formation. By examining the HCC genomes, we comprehensively profiled the epigenetic defects mediated by multiple nuclear factors and histone marks, and experimentally confirmed that overexpressed EZH2/YY1 coupled with H3K27me3 can silence tumor suppressive microRNAs to promote hepatocarcinogenesis. In addition, EZH2/H3K27me3 also ablates IGFBP4 which functions to regulate AKT activity and suppress HCC growth. All these deregulated molecular pathways are significantly associated with human HCCs. Of translational potential, our findings showed that Bufalin, a component in Chinese medicine, is effective in targeting CCRK signaling. Furthermore, CCRK/HDAC8 inhibitors and immune-checkpoint blocker have synergistic effects in suppressing HCCs. Collectively, these data provide mechanistic insights into the epigenomic dysregulation in HCCs, and suggest that CCRK/EZH2/HDAC8-targeted inhibitors and immunotherapy are potentially novel approaches for HCC treatment.

14103014.label: Realisation of objectives
14103014.value: Engineered nucleases called transcription activator-like (TAL) effectors nucleases (TALENs) were successfully employed to knockout specific genes in zebrafish. In order to establish an efficient gene knockout platform for routine use, we have adapted and modified a set of TALENs plasmids originally designed for use in yeast and plants for our application in zebrafish. Compared with previous reports, the mutation efficiency achieved by our system is much higher. Using this modified TALENs method established in our laboratory, we have successfully mutated the two ligands (Lh and Fsh) and the two receptors (Lhr and Fshr) in zebrafish systemically in the single gene knockout lines as well as in the double gene knockout lines by exploiting all the possible combinations.
