14105814.label: Major findings and research outcome
14105814.value: Project 1: Bone Morphogenic Protein 4-Smad-Induced Upregulation of Platelet-Derived Growth Factor AA Impairs Endothelial Function. We generated Ad-Bmp4 to overexpress Bmp4 and Ad-Pdgfa-shRNA to knockdown Pdgfa in mice through tail intravenous injection. SMAD4-shRNA lentivirus, SMAD1-shRNA, and SMAD5 shRNA adenovirus were used for knockdown in human and mouse endothelial cells. We found that PDGF-AA impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation in aortas and mesenteric resistance arteries. BMP4 upregulated PDGF-AA in human and mouse endothelial cells, which was abolished by BMP4 antagonist noggin or knockdown of SMAD1/5 or SMAD4. BMP4-impared relaxation in mouse aorta was also ameliorated by PDGF-AA neutralizing antibody. Tail injection of Ad-Pdgfa-shRNA ameliorates endothelial dysfunction induced by Bmp4 overexpression (Ad-Bmp4) in vivo. Serum PDGF-AA was elevated in both diabetic patients and diabetic db/db mice compared with nondiabetic controls. Pdgfa-shRNA or Bmp4-shRNA adenovirus reduced serum PDGF-AA concentration in db/db mice. PDGF-AA neutralizing antibody or tail injection with Pdgfa-shRNA adenovirus improved endothelial function in aortas and mesenteric resistance arteries from db/db mice. The effect of PDGF-AA on endothelial function in mouse aorta was also inhibited by Ad-Pdgfra-shRNA to inhibit PDGFRα. Project 2:Inhibition of endothelial Smad4 suppresses endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and atherosclerosis We demonstrated that Smad4 expression confined to endothelial cells is required for vascular inflammation and vascular dysfunction by inducing oxidative stress and ER stress pathways, leading to expression of inflammatory chemokines and adhesion molecules, accompanied by reduction of NO production. The key findings of our study include: (1) deletion of endothelial Smad4 attenuated vascular dysfunction and blood pressure increase in hypertensive mice after AngII infusion; (2) deletion of endothelial Smad4 reduced atherosclerotic plaque formation in mice on ApoE knockout background; and (3) Smad4 is involved in AngII induced increase of ROS production, followed by induction of ER stress signalling pathway, leading to vascular inflammation and diminished NO production in endothelial cells. In summary, we showed that endothelial Smad4 is required for vascular dysfunction and inflammation in both mouse models of hypertension and atherosclerosis. Smad4 activation is involved in ROS production, ER stress responses, and reduced NO production in endothelial cells. We are now preparing a manuscript for submission within next three months to a journal of American Heart Association.

14105814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14105814.value: We have extended some research along the similar direct to investigate how patterns of shear stress impact BMP4-Smad signaling pathway in endothelial cells and its link to vascular calcification, a common feature in human atherosclerotic plagues. We also explore the possibility of targeting this signaling axis with small molecules to alleviate vascular inflammation in rodent models of vascular diseases.

14105814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14105814.value: Cardio-metabolic disease is a complex disorder involving multiple pathological processes in multiple organs. Endothelial cell dysfunction participates in initiation and progression of cardiovascular diseases. Several studies have revealed the role of BMP4 in hypertension and atherosclerosis. Intracellular signal transducers Smad1/5/8 are activated by BMP receptors and mediate BMP signals; and thereby form complex with the common mediator co-Smad (Smad4) for translocation into nucleus, regulating the transcription of target genes. However, the detailed underlying mechanism of BMP4 and Smad signaling on vascular dysfunction associated with metabolic disease is poorly understood. Our preliminary results support the contributory role of BMP4 in induction of endothelial dysfunction. By employing tissue-specific transgenic mouse models of leptin receptor deficient db/db mice and endothelial-specific Smad KO, and the diet-induced obesity model, we have investigated (1) whether BMP4-Smad signaling pathway contributes to vascular dysfunction and vascular insulin resistance associated with diabetes and obesity; and (2) whether deletion of endothelial cell-specific Smad1/5 and Smad4 ameliorates vascular dysfunction in diabetic and obese mice. We have provided a clearer picture profiling the functional role of BMP4-Smad in endothelial dysfunction and inflammation, and help us further understand how and why endogenous metabolic stress initiates and facilitates development of vascular complications in diabetes.

14106014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14106014.value: Osteoarthritis (OA) affects 30 % of the world population with typical symptoms as pain and loss of mobility. The incidence increases with advancing age and OA of the knee is particularly common among Hong Kong older Chinese people. Currently there is no cure for OA. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) provide pain relief, but it cannot stop disease progression. Antioxidant dietary supplements are claimed to have anti-aging effects, although their therapeutic efficacies on aged-assoicated OA need to be further confirmed. It follows that combined anti-inflammatory and antioxidative actions may have good therapeutic effects for OA. Quercetin is a natural compound that possesses both anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative activities. It is considered highly safe for pharmacological use. In a pilot study, we found that quercetin could reduce OA pain and degenerative changes in a rat model. It suggests that quercetin has good potential to be developed into a medication for OA. Because absorption of oral quercetin is very low, local administration will be more favorable. It can be injected into joints similar to the current practice of viscosupplementation (i.e. hyaluronic acid). To enhance a longer stay of quercetin in the joint and to reduce the need for repeated injections, we propose to develop a controlled drug delivery system by nanoparticle encapsulation of quercetin. The effectiveness of the encapsulated quercetin to modify knee pain and degenerative changes in knee joints will be evaluated and compared with oral-supplementation of quercetin in animal models of primary and post-traumatic knee OA. This research project will contribute to the exploration of sustained drug delivery for novel therapeutic strategies of OA. 骨關節炎是一種關節疾病，症狀包括關節痛而且關節活動受限。現時全球大概有30%人口受此疾病影響，多見於中老年人。隨著香港人口老化，患有膝關節炎的人數亦隨著上升，但到目前亦没有能治愈關節炎的藥物。市面上有不同針對改善關節炎症狀的藥物及產品，例如非類固醇消炎止痛藥（non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, NSAIDs)，能舒緩疼痛但不能夠減慢疾病惡化。各種抗氧化營養補充品聲稱有抗衰老作用，但對於退化性骨關節炎的治療效果還有待驗證。槲皮素（Quercetin）是具有抗炎及抗氧化活性的天然化合物，常見於水果、蔬菜和穀物等植物中。它已被認定為一種安全度高的營養補充品。在老鼠模型的初步研究中，我們發現槲皮素可以減輕關節炎的疼痛及退化，因此槲皮素可能開發成爲治療骨關節炎的藥物。由於身體吸收口服槲皮素的能力比較低，局部注射的效果可能較好。為了延長槲皮素在關節内逗留的時間和避免重複注射， 我們希望研發藥物調控釋給系統（controlled delivery system）把槲皮素包在納米顆粒 (nanoparticle) 内，並參考現有透明質酸的注射方法，直接在膝關節内注射。我們將利用退化性骨關節炎及創傷性骨關節炎的動物模型，評估控釋槲皮素能否改善骨關節炎引起的疼痛和退化，並與口服槲皮素作比較。此研究項目將有助探索持續釋放藥物作為治療骨關節炎的新方法。

14106014.label: Realisation of objectives
14106014.value: The experiments listed for the two objectives of this proposal have been completed. The first objective focuses on characterising the drug delivery system, monomethoxypoly(ethylene glycol)-L-poly(Alanine) (mPEG-PA). The thermosensitive hydrogel, mPEG-PA, was synthesized via ring-opening polymerization of N-carboxy anhydride of L-alanine on α-methoxy-ω-amino poly(ethylene glycol). The molecular composition of mPEG-PA polymer was determined using 1H NMR (Varian Uniytinova-500 MHz spectrometer). Based on the two peaks at 1.5-1.8 ppm and 3.8-4.0 ppm, which represent the methyl group of alanine and ethylene glycol group of PEG respectively, the molecular weight of mPEG-PA was determined to be 2000-2650 Da. Aqueous solutions of mPEG-PA (1.5 – 5 wt%) were prepared at 4 °C. The sol-gel transition of mPEG-PA polymer was determined using the test-tube inverting method. Polymer solutions of 1.5 - 5 wt % mPEG-PA underwent sol-to-gel transition between <15 - 46°C, with a higher concentration of polymer demonstrate a lower transition temperature. Solutions of mPEG-PA at 4 wt%, which has a transition temperature at 17°C, was used in this study. For the cell viability assay, human chondrocytes were collected and cultured from patients underwent total knee arthroplasty according to previously published protocol. The collection of human samples was approved by the Joint Chinese University of Hong Kong – New Territories East Cluster Clinical Research Ethics Committee Clinical Research Ethics Committee (Reference number: 2013.248). Chondrocytes at passage 1 were seeded onto 96-well plate overnight and treated either with medium (Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium: Nutrient Mixture F-12, 10% Fetal bovine serum, 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin-Neomycin (PSN) Antibiotic Mixture) or medium supplemented with various concentrations of mPEG-PA hydrogel (4 mg/mL or 0.4 mg/mL) for 24, 48 and 72 hours. At 4 h prior to complete incubation, 10 µL of alamarBlue® reagent (Bio-Rad, CA, USA) was added to each well. The absorbances at wavelength 570 nm and 600 nm were measured (μQuant™, BioTek Instruments, Inc., NE, USA). To study the release of Que loaded mPEG-PA hydrogel in vitro, quercetin (Que) dihydrate (Sigma Aldrich, Cat no.: Q0125, 1mg/mL) suspension was prepared in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) at 4 °C and mixed with mPEG-PA polymer. The mixture was vortexed until all mPEG-PA polymer was dissolved. The Que loaded mPEG-PA was gelated at 37 °C in a 96-well plate (n=6). Pre-warmed PBS was added to each well and replaced at pre-determined time intervals (Time: Baseline, 4 hours, 1 day, 2 days, 3 days, 7 days, 14 and 28 days). At each sampling time point, an aliquot of the supernatant (50 µL) was mixed with ethanol (100%, 50µL). The absorbance was measured at 380 nm (μQuant™, Biotek® Instruments, Inc., NE, USA). The second objective of this proposal was to evaluate the therapeutic effects of mPEG-poly(Ala) encapsulated with Que as compared to oral supplemented-Que on OA-associated pain and structural changes in animal models of primary and post-traumatic OA. All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics and Experimentation Committee of the Chinese University of Hong Kong (Reference No: 13/015/GRF). For the post traumatic osteoarthritis model in rats, unilateral post-traumatic OA was surgically induced in the right knees of 48 12-week old, female Sprague Dawley rats. Briefly, under anaesthesia, the right knee of each rat was shaved and disinfected. A medial para-patellar incision was made and the patella was dislocated to expose the intra-articular space. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) was transected with microscissors and confirmed by anterior drawer test. The patella was relocated, and the joint capsule and skin were closed sequentially with absorbable suture (Ethicon US). Free cage activity was allowed after the operation. At 24 weeks post-operation, when OA had been developed, rats were randomly assigned to 6 different groups for either an IA injection in the knee or oral supplementation. For IA injection, rats would receive either (1) 0.9% saline, (2) hydrogel only, (3) hydrogel with Que (50 µg) or (4) hydrogel with Que (500 µg) in the operated knee under isoflurane anaesthesia. For oral supplements, rats would receive oral galvage of either (5) water or (6) Que (30 mg/mL) five times on every other day. IA injections were performed through the patellar tendon using a 50 μL syringe with a 26G removable needle (Hamilton Company, Reno, NV, USA). For spontaneous osteoarthritis guinea pigs, 24 guinea pigs were randomly assigned to 3 different groups to receive 100 μL bilateral injections of either (1) 0.9% saline, (2) hydrogel only or (3) hydrogel with Que (100 µg). Gait analysis were performed both in rats and guinea pigs. Gait data were collected at pre ACLT, 24 (pre-treatment), 28 (4 weeks post IA injection), 32 (8 weeks post IA injection) and 36 weeks (12 weeks post IA injection) post-operation in rats, and at 7 (pre-treatment), 8 (4 weeks post IA injection), 9 (8 weeks post IA injection) and 10 (12 weeks post IA injection) months old in guinea pigs using Catwalk XT 9.0 system (Noldus Information Technology, Wageningen, the Netherlands). Animals were placed onto a glass walkway and allowed to walk voluntarily back and forth. For rats, the OA-associated pain was analysed and indicated by the Limb Idleness Index (LII) according to our published protocol. The LII measures the gait adaptation to OA pain in rats with unilateral knee OA by taking into the account on three parameters, the ratio of target print (hind limbs) intensity, anchor print (front limbs) intensity and swing duration of the hind limbs. For guinea pigs, the base of support of the hind limbs were measured to investigate OA associated gait changes. At 12 weeks post injection, all animals were sacrificed. The hind limbs were collected for histopathological assessments. In brief, knee samples were fixed in 10% buffered formalin solution for 3 days and decalcified in 9% formic acid for 4 weeks. Joints were cut into two approximately equal halves along the medial collateral ligament in the frontal plane. The anterior and posterior halves were embedded in paraffin. Sections of 5 m at 200 m interval were cut and a minimal of three intervals were collected for toluidine blue and hematoxylin and eosin staining. The OA severity of the most severe section was evaluated using the Osteoarthritis Research Society International (OARSI) score for rats and the recommended guidelines from the OA histopathological initiatives for guinea pigs. The synovial inflammation was evaluated using the Krenn scoring system at the site with most pathological changes. Histological scoring was performed by two raters (SWM and YCC). In cases of discrepancies, discussions were held until consensus had been reached. All statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 24 (IBM, Armonk, New York, U.S.). All data were checked for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk Test. Parametric tests were used for normally distributed data, otherwise, a nonparametric equivalence was used. Repeated measure ANOVA was used to analyze cell viability. Friedman test was used to compare gait data with respect to temporal changes. To compare the difference in LII between pre- and post-treatment, and histological scoring between the control and treatment groups, Kruskal-Wallis H test with pairwise comparison was used. Signifiance values were adjusted with Bonferonni correction for multiple tests. All statistical significance was accepted at α = 0.05.

14106014.label: Major findings and research outcome
14106014.value: In vitro cytotoxicity assay demonstrated chondrocytes treated with or without hydrogels (0.4 mg/mL or 4 mg/mL) were viable and proliferated after 24, 48 and 72 hours of incubation with mPEG-PA hydrogel. In vitro release kinetics Que from mPEG-PA hydrogel could be sustained for over 28 days, which approximately 30% of Que remained in the hydrogel on day 28. From the gait analysis, the LIIs of all rats were significantly increased at 24 weeks post ACLT (p=0.003, paired t-test). Group 3 rats showed the largest reduction in LIIs at both 4 and 8 weeks post injection and lasted through 12 weeks post IA injection study period. Group 4 rats also showed a reduced LII at 4 and 12 weeks post IA injection. Group 1 and 2 rats showed a minimal reduction in LIIs, and gradually increased throughout the 12-week post IA injection. However, the differences between groups were insignificant at each time point (p>0.05, Kuskal-Wallis test). Furthermore, oral administration of Que did not lead to a significant reduction in pain up to 12 weeks post treatment (p=0.600), and no difference was observed between oral administration of quercetin and saline at all time points. Severe cartilage degradation was found in the posterior compartment of the medial tibial plateau in the operated knees of all rats. Group 1 rats had the highest median OARSI score of 23, while Group 3 rats had the lowest median OARSI score of 19 and was significantly different from group 1 (p=0.006, Kruskal Wallis H test). Furthermore, most rats had low-grade synovitis but there was no difference between groups (p=0.192, Kuskal-Wallis test). In GPs, there was a slight increase in BOS of GPs which received hydrogel loaded with Que at 4 weeks post-injection, while all GPs demonstrated a decrease in BOS relative to pre-injection. However, the differences were insignificant between all groups at both 4 and 12 weeks post injection (p=0.381 and 0.995). The weight bearing region of the tibia plateau was scored in each GP. Fissures and/or loss of cartilage extending to the deep zone or calcified cartilage could be seen in all three groups, with the most severe complete loss of cartilage found in the control group. The loss of proteoglycan content was also present in all three groups as shown by toluidine blue staining. However, the total score between groups were insignificant (p=0.260, Kruskal Wallis H Test).

14106014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14106014.value: In PTOA rats, our findings suggest the Que formulation is both anti-nociceptive and chondroprotective. Further studies should investigate the potential anti-nociceptive mechanism of Que on osteoarthritic pain and chondroprotection. For example, Que could modulate inflammatory pain by reducing inflammatory cytokines. Que may also be able to protect the articular cartilage by reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and downstream factors such as matrix metalloproteinases to prevent cartilage degradation. We were unable to demonstrate the same significant effect of Que in OA GPs. OA in GPs are bilateral and symmetrical, while studies on OA related gait changes in other OA animal models mostly focus on unilateral OA which allow the injured limb to transfer loading to the other three uninjured limbs. In addition, most gait analysis investigated the walking gait instead of stance. Hence, the measurement of the BOS to reveal OA related gait changes may not be sensitive enough for OA in GPs. Furthermore, the current histopathological assessments did not take into the account of other OA features, such as the severity of synovitis. Future improvements should include exploring other gait parameters and OA histological features, and the dosage of Que to further confirm the efficacy of Que for spontaneous OA.

14106014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14106014.value: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease and one of the major causes of disability that severely affects the quality of life of the patients. There is currently no effective cure for OA, which the recommended pharmoacological treatments can only provide temporary symptomatic relief and have their associated deleterious side effects. Quercetin (Que) is both anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative and has been used as an oral supplement for osteoarthritis (OA) with inconsistent findings due to a low bioavailability. We encapsulated Que in a thermosensitive drug delivery system, mPEG-polyalanine (mPEG-PA), to prolong its bioactivity in osteoarthritis animal models. The therapeutic effect of quercetin loaded mPEG-PA was investigated in OA animals. This study investigated three aspects of osteoarthritis in terms of pain, cartilage degradation and synovial inflammation. Our findings suggested this formulation was able to reduce pain and cartilage degradation. Hence, the current approach to delay the progression of OA by localizing and sustained delivery of a bioactive component in a drug delivery system is promising. Currently, there are other oral SYSADOA in the market which their efficacy in treating OA were demonstrated to be inconsistent. Therefore, it may be meaningful to investigate their true efficacy using similar approach.

14106614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14106614.value: Adequate antibiotic therapy is critical for survival in critically ill patients with sepsis. In the Intensive care unit (ICU), patients with severe infections requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT) are at risk of receiving inadequate antibiotic therapy because the administration of RRT can differ greatly between ICUs, causing significantly different pharmacokinetics. Current dosing guidelines are ineffective for this reason. The development of an evidence-based antibiotic dosing guideline for different modalities of RRT is of international significance and essential to improve the outcome of infected ICU patients requiring RRT. The study aim is to develop improved antibiotic guidelines for ICU patients undergoing RRT with life-threatening infection. Specifically guidelines that adjust for patient characteristics and the type of RRT that is prescribed. This will be achieved through the following: 1. Detailed description of the demographic, clinical, RRT characteristics, and plasma antibiotic concentration-time data in a large ICU patient cohort undergoing RRT. 2. Analyze the detailed pharmacokinetic, clinical and statistical data collected to develop a preliminary, but comprehensive and accurate prediction algorithm for antibiotic dosing. The study is a prospective multi-national pharmacokinetic study of ICU patients requiring RRT who are prescribed Vancomycin, Piperacillin-Tazobactam, and/or Meropenem. The international cohort will require 450 patients (150 patients for each antibiotic). Hong Kong will recruit and study 15 patients in each group. Detailed pharmacokinetic sampling will occur on study day 1-2 and repeated at a dosing interval between days 3-6, over an 8-12 hour period on each occasion. Whole blood samples will be taken from the RRT filter ports or a pre-existing arterial line. Urine collection samples and filter effluent, when relevant, will also be collected on these 2 study days. Data collection will include: demographic data, residual renal function, filter age, and RRT settings and 28-day mortality. An electronic case report form (eCRF) will be developed. Whole blood samples will be frozen, and transported for processing at The University of Queensland, Australia. Data analysis, pharmacokinetic and statistical analysis for development of antibiotic dosing algorithms will be undertaken at The University of Queensland, Australia, and CUHK, Hong Kong. 14106614.label: Realisation of objectives
14106614.value: OBJECTIVE 1. The study protocol was published in March 2016. Patient recruitment was closed in March 2017, with 133 patients recruited from 26 participating ICUs internationally, and 15 from the grant centre in Hong Kong. Because of difficulty with recruitment internationally, identical data sets from patients entered into previous single centre studies were used to complete the dataset. This was reported to the RGC in the interim report. This resulted in 384 patients with sufficiently complete datasets as described in the protocol (final dataset completed and verified, August 2018), and allowed detailed demographic description of a substantial cohort as stated in the objective. This dataset was described in paper 2 (Completed, awaiting central endorsement by the ANZICS Clinical Trials Group for submission to Intensive Care Medicine Journal, IF 15, Attached under peer reviewed output section). The main findings were: 1. Highly varied antibiotic dosing and renal replacement therapy (RRT) prescribing practices result in antibiotic concentrations that fail to meet therapeutic targets in many patients. 2. Increasing estimated total renal clearance (eTRCL), calculated by adding measured creatinine clearance of residual urine output and effluent flow rate, is associated with lower trough antibiotic concentrations, although variability remains substantial. 3. No significant associations were observed between sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores and trough concentrations, or between albumin and trough concentration for any of the tested antibiotics The markedly variable trough antibiotic concentration results have been presented at the Asia Pacific Association of Critical Care Medicine Conference in December 2018 (Attached). In conclusion, this paper strongly implies the need for improved individualised dosing techniques in critically ill patients receiving RRT for AKI. OBJECTIVE 2. Statistical pharmacokinetic (PK) parameter distributions in patients receiving continuous modes of dialysis (CRRT) were evaluated using the concentration-time data for each antibiotic in plasma, CRRT effluent and urine. Data was fitted using non-parametric population pharmacokinetic software (Pmetrics for R, Los Angeles, USA). The stepwise modeling procedure started with a 2-compartment model including pre- and post-filter plasma concentrations with a common distribution volume. With this basic model, each step included the addition of one excretory compartment (RRT effluent then Urine and non-renal CL). The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) were used to discriminate the best structural model. In accordance with the model’s complexity, each model was tested using a two-step approach using a parametric and a non-parametric algorithm. A Bayesian iterative two-stage (IT2B) algorithm was used in order to estimate the PK parameter ranges. Then, a non-parametric adaptive grid (NPAG) algorithm was performed to estimate AIC and PK parameters. Once the structural model was found, parameter ranges were adjusted in order to improve the visual predictive checks (VPCs) of outputs. Modeling reports were compiled on 187 patients receiving Meropenem, 160 patients receiving Piperacillin, 101 receiving Tazobactam and 60 receiving Vancomycin (Respective sampling occasions 303, 260, 159 and 109; comprising 3698, 2602, 2082 and 1001 individual sample concentrations; and utilizing a 5, 5, 5, and 4 compartment models respectively). Population PK modeling confirms a wide variability of antibiotic clearance and Vd. Briefly the models show high variability of CL (note that total CL is the sum of the three clearance parameters in each model) and Vd: 1. Appropriate dose ranges based on the modeled PK parameters were simulated using dosing prediction formulae previously published by our group (Crit Care Med 2009; 37:2268 –2282), and EUCAST defined target MICs i.e. 1xMIC and 4xMIC for typical ICU organisms (Abstract 1). Selected examples for continuous-infusion and intermittent dosing at common dose intervals: 1. Meropenem (target concentration 8mg/L) Continuous Infusion: Loading dose 170mg-400mg followed by infusion rate 16-31mg/h respectively. Intermittent dosing: Loading dose 350mg-1500mg followed by maintenance dose of 200mg-1400mg 8-hourly respectively. 2. Piperacillin (target concentration 64mg/L) Continuous Infusion: Loading dose 1250mg-3200mg followed by infusion rate 110-200mg/h respectively. Intermittent dosing: Loading dose 2500mg-8250mg; followed by maintenance dose of 1250mg-7000mg 8-hourly respectively. 3. Vancomycin (target concentration >15mg/L) Continuous Infusion: Loading dose 300mg-600mg followed by infusion rate 16-40mg/h respectively. Intermittent dosing: Loading dose 600mg-4400mg, followed by maintenance dose of 300mg-4000mg 12-hourly respectively. Given the potentially wide dosage range identified for each antibiotic, a method for informing individualised dosage is of key importance. OBJECTIVE 3. To determine the effect of patient characteristics and eTRCL on PK parameters, we constructed directed acyclic graph (DAG) diagrams and performed GEE equations, adjusted for centre, to establish the significance of patient characteristics on eTRCL. A relationship between eTRCL (adjusted for total sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score at occasion 1 sampling) and estimated drug clearance from population PK modelling in CRRT patients, by antibiotic was confirmed. (A) meropenem (n=139 from 16 centres; P=0.003), (B) piperacillin (n=112 from 16 centres; P<0.001), (C) tazobactam (n=83 from 14 centres; P=0.022) and (D) vancomycin (n=27 from 8 centres; P=0.908). However, no associations were found between total SOFA score (adjusted for SOFA renal score, SOFA hepatic score and albumin at occasion 1 sampling) and estimated drug Vd. We estimated the proportion of total variance explained by the model (R2) and the relative importance of each factor using linear regression with Shapley and Owen decomposition of R-squared method (“rego” package, STATA 15.0 software, StataCorp, College Station, TX). For antibiotic clearance, the variables included were age, eTRCL, SOFA liver, SOFA cardiovascular and albumin. For drug Vd, variables included were age, gender, weight, height, SOFA renal, SOFA liver and albumin. In a sensitivity analysis, Vd/body weight was considered a dependent variable and independent variables were age, gender, height, SOFA renal, SOFA liver and albumin. The final multiple regression models were adjusted for centre effect, and the variance inflation factor was used to check for presence of multicollinearity. For meropenem, only SOFA (cardiovascular component, P=0.001), and for tazobactam, and vancomycin (SOFA, renal component, P=0.017 and P=0.02), were significantly associated with CL or Vd. The relative contributions (%) to overall R2 of the models was low (20-40%). After sensitivity analysis, independent variables were non-significant for all antibiotics. Thus, the data set obtained from objective one and modeled PK parameters derived from objective 2 were systematically explored, however robust associations were not observed. OBJECTIVE 4. While objectives 1-3 were completed, and therefore the basis for this step has been achieved, the lack of robust and consistent associations between dose, RRT prescription, and key patient characteristics with relevant PK parameters, or trough antibiotic concentrations, has meant that this objective cannot be reached with the original methods described. Despite the lack of consistent associations observed, attempts to apply novel complex statistical and mathematical modelling will be attempted by a team with appropriate expertise, led by Prof. SJ Paul, Chair in Clinical Epidemiology, Biostatistics and Health Services Research, University of Melbourne, Melbourne EpiCentre, under the supervision of the international project leadership, Prof Jason Roberts. It is expected that results will be available before late 2019. (Word count 1158)

14106614.label: Major findings and research outcome
14106614.value: As hypothesised, in the largest multi-national cohort of ICU patients receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT) to date, we showed that highly varied antibiotic dosing and RRT prescribing practices resulted in antibiotic blood concentrations that failed to meet therapeutic blood concentration targets in many patients. Achieving therapeutic target blood concentrations in patients is critical as inappropriately low concentrations result in increased mortality and promote resistance, and inappropriately high concentrations cause toxicity. This data strongly implies the need to develop improved individualized dosing techniques in this population (See conference paper, Part C). Secondly, increasing estimated total renal clearance (eTRCL), the sum of measured creatinine clearance and effluent flow rate, was associated with lower trough antibiotic concentrations, although variability remains substantial. This new finding suggests appropriate dose adjustments, potentially individualised on the basis of eTRCL would facilitate consistent therapeutic target blood concentrations (See paper under review, Part C). Thirdly, no significant associations were observed between sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores, or serum albumin concentration and trough concentrations for the tested antibiotics, suggesting that the relationship between severity of illness, the acute phase reaction and organ failure in critically ill patients receiving RRT is more complex than previously hypothesised, and requires detailed exploration. (See paper under review, Part C). Fourthly, population pharmacokinetic (PK) modelling of the large dataset confirmed the hypothesis that the key variables of volume of distribution (Vd) and total clearance (CL) for all studied antibiotics were highly variable in this population, and simulated dose ranges to achieve clinically important target blood concentrations were thus also large (2-3 fold depending on antibiotic). The results provided the basis for exploring the individual effect-relationship of RRT and patient factors with CL and Vd, to inform required dosing in individual patients. Fifthly, RRT dose, and particularly the parameter eTRCL, was shown to correlate with antibiotic CL, adjusted for confounding factors, but this correlation was not precise. Multivariable logistic regression, and sensitivity analyses adjusting for body weight, assessing known factors affecting PK parameters in ICU patients, while revealing some significant associations, failed to show sufficiently precise associations between these factors and Vd or CL. Thus, while developing individualised dosing algorithms was not feasible, the findings remain important to inform the understanding of the effect of antibiotic dosage, RRT dose, and key patient characteristics on antibiotic blood concentrations. To date this is the only large multi-national cohort to have systematically assessed these relationships in this population.

14106614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14106614.value: As descried above, the results strongly imply the need for individualised antibiotic dosing in this population (Abstract 1, and Paper 1 completed). The population pharmacokinetic modelling results confirmed high variability of PK parameters in this population (Abstract 2 and paper 2 in preparation). While the exploration of associations between RRT mode, ultimate RRT dose, and factors known to affect PKs in critically ill ICU patients with key PK factors did not reveal robust associations, the results are important and will advance knowledge relating to the relationship between critical illness, antibiotic PK parameters and therapeutic trough concentrations (Abstract 3 and paper 3 in preparation). Although the observed relationships above prevented planned development a robust and clinically useful dosing algorithm in the first instance, sufficient data has been collected to allow attempts to apply novel complex statistical and mathematical modelling, to explore the possibility of developing predictive models. This will be led by an international team with appropriate expertise, Prof. SJ Paul, Chair in Clinical Epidemiology, Biostatistics and Health Services Research, University of Melbourne, Melbourne EpiCentre, under the supervision of the multi-national SMARRT collaboration, led by Prof. Jason Roberts. It is expected that results will be available before late 2019.

14106614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14106614.value: ICU patients are severely ill, and often develop failure of some critical organs, including the kidneys. These organs are often supported by artificial means. This research examines ICU patients with severe illness, and kidney failure requiring dialysis, to see how the body responds to commonly used antibiotics. Most importantly it was shown in hundreds of patients treated in ICUs all over the world, that doctors are not able to consistently choose antibiotic doses that result in blood concentrations that are high enough to kill bacteria effectively and save lives, but not so high as to be toxic to the patient. We showed that ICU patients have dialysis prescribed and delivered in ways that vary widely in effectiveness, affecting how the antibiotic is removed from the body by the dialysis-machine, and therefore blood concentrations are very often lower or higher than anticipated, and unpredictable. Other factors examined – like prescribed dose, heart and liver dysfunction and illness severity were not consistently linked to blood concentrations, so predictive formulae for dose choice in individual patients could not be developed. However, our understanding of how critical illness affects patients has increased substantially by this study and future dose advice algorithms may therefore be possible.

14106914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14106914.value: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) impose major health burden in rapidly aging populations including Hong Kong. The causes of these diseases remain enigmatic and the choices of treatment are limited. There is urgent need to elucidate the mechanisms of pathogenesis and explore novel treatment strategies. In this project, we will unravel the relationship between the process of neuroinflammation and the accumulation of brain iron, two features commonly observed in specific brain regions, and generally believed to be important in neuronal death, in these diseases. Taking advantage of both inflammation-based and traditional animal models of AD and PD, we emphasize the detection of early events in neuroinflammation that predispose abnormal iron mobilization and accumulation. Specifically, we will (1) investigate whether inflammation is the major contributor of iron accumulation at early stage of AD and PD; (2) identify the key inflammatory mediators that cause iron dysregulation in neurons in these diseases, and (3) decipher the key pathways underlying the effects of the inflammatory mediators on iron accumulation. The results will help clarify the causal relationship between neuroinflammation, iron accumulation and neuronal degeneration, and also the key roles played by various cytokines, oxidative stress and iron transport proteins in these processes. In addition, since the currently available therapeutic options for these disorders are not disease-modifying in nature and there are still no effective cures, the results of the current project will provide the scientific basis for the much needed direction of neuroprotective strategies. 因人口快速老化，神經退行性疾病，如阿茲海默氏症和帕金森氏症，在香港以至全球已成為主要的健康問題。這些疾病的病因大都未明，現時也沒有根治的方法。闡明發病機制對探索新治療策略至關重要。炎症和鐵積聚常見於神經退行性疾病受影響的腦區，並被認為是神經元死亡的重要原因，但兩者之間的因果關係卻不清楚。在這個項目中，我們將利用阿茲海默氏症和帕金森氏症傳統及炎症動物模型，找出病發前或早期可能促進鐵異常積聚的炎症過程。期間我們將（1）確定炎症是否早期阿茲海默氏症和帕金森氏症鐵積聚的主要因素，（2）找出引起神經元鐵異常的炎症因數及（3）其導致鐵積聚的機制。這些實驗結果將幫助闡明神經炎症、鐵聚集及神經退化之間的因果關係，以及不同細胞因數、氧化應激和鐵轉運蛋白在其過程中的關鍵角色，最終為從根本治療神經退行性疾病的方向提供依據。

14106914.label: Realisation of objectives
14106914.value: Overall, we have completed experiments to address the 3 main objectives of the proposal, namely 1) to determine if inflammation is a major contributor of iron accumulation at early stages of Parkinson's disease, 2) to identify the key inflammatory mediators that cause iron dyshomeostasis in neurons in these diseases, and 3) to decipher the key intracellular pathways underlying the effects of the inflammatory mediators on iron accumulation. Under objective 1, we have provided evidence supporting that inflammatory responses precede iron accumulation in an LPS model. Under objective 2, after some intensive efforts, we have identified the HMGB1 protein as a probable key inflammatory mediator that leads to accumulation of iron in the LPS model. Significantly, based on a traditional model of Parkinson's disease, the role of HMGB1 is confirmed. For objective 3, as expected, we found evidence for a role played by reactive oxygen species in the process of LPS-induced iron accumulation. But the most significant findings are the identification of HMGB1-mediated changes in iron transport proteins DMT1+, DMT1- and transferrin receptor as the key cellular processes underlying the effects of the inflammatory mediators on iron accumulation in LPS and Parkinson's disease model. The planned experiments have been completed and a full paper describing the results are in preparation. Also, some results stemming from the experiments of the present work have been incorporated and published in 2 papers.

To decipher the key intracellular pathways underlying the effects of the inflammatory mediators on iron accumulation.

14106914.label: Major findings and research outcome
14106914.value: The most important results are summarised as follows: (1) Under Objective 1 in determining if inflammation is a major contributor of iron accumulation at early stages of Parkinson's disease, we found that microglia were activated 6 hrs after LPS injection, as revealed by increased CD11b signal and morphological change of microglia. The microglia activation was also accompanied by increased ED1 signal in the SN. At the same time, astrocytes were also activated 6h after LPS injection, revealed by increased GFAP signal. Importantly, no tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (TH+) neuronal loss and iron accumulation were found in the SN 6h after LPS injection. In parallel with the above findings, we revealed that LPS injection for 1 day caused iron accumulation before TH+ neuron loss. While the total iron contents were increased in SN 1 day after LPS injection, TH+ neurons were lost significantly not until 3 days post-injection. (2) To search for key mediators linking inflammatory response to iron dyshomeostasis under Objective 2, we identified the high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) protein as a candidate molecule. HMGB1 is a secreted by immune cells and known to play a role in inflammation. We found that LPS induced HMGB1 over-expression and also release before iron accumulation. More specifically, HMGB1 was overexpressed and translocated from cell nucleus to cytoplasm for releasing in the SN 6h after LPS injection. The majority of HMGB1 overexpressing neurons in the SNc were not TH+. Furthermore, HMGB1 was depleted in the SN 1 day after LPS injection. In a parallel set of experiments on 6-OHDA induced Parkinson’s disease model in which iron accumulation has been consistently found, anti-HMGB1 neutralizing antibody ameliorated 6-ODA-induced asymmetry of forelimb use and decrease in locomotor activities. Consistently, Anti-HMGB1 neutralizing antibody repressed 6-OHDA- induced dopaminergic neuronal loss. 3) To decipher the key intracellular pathways underlying the effects of the inflammatory mediators on iron accumulation under Objective 3, we focused on the roles played by iron transport proteins. We found that DMT1+, DMT1- and Tfr, but not ferroportin, were overexpressed in TH+ neurons in the SN 1 day after LPS injection as detected by immunofluorescence. Consistently, HMGB1 neutralization suppressed 6-OHDA-induced overexpression of DMT1 in the SN. Thus, modulation of the expression of iron transport proteins are key pathways in the pathogenic process. In addition to a couple of publications on works related to this project, a manuscript reporting the major findings of the present project is currently underway.

14106914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14106914.value: The present project have confirmed a key role of inflammatory response and a key molecule in the pathogenic process of excessive iron accumulation happening in major neurodegenerative disease such as the Parkinson's disease. Therefore, further work could be directed to further dissect out the role of other inflammatory mediators in similar processes, and the possibility of applying the knowledge to early diagnosis of these diseases.

14106914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14106914.value: There is evidence that elevated iron level in the brain is a major common pathway leading to neuronal damage in neurodegenerative disorders. On the other hand, neuroinflammation is a commonly observed phenomenon in neurodegenerative diseases. In this study, we have addressed the hypothesis that there is a causal relationship between neuroinflammation and abnormal iron mobilization and accumulation that finally lead to damage and degeneration of neurons. To test this hypothesis, we have performed a series of experiments to dissect out the key processes underlying inflammation-induced iron homeostasis dysfunction, and their role in neurodegeneration. We emphasized the detection of early events that predispose abnormal iron mobilization and accumulation. We have shown inflammation is a major contributor of iron accumulation, especially at the early stage of neurodegeneration, and that a particular inflammatory molecule like the inflammatory response to iron accumulation, and via the modulation of iron transport protein expression. Since this process could be common to many neurodegenerative diseases, the results will have widespread implication and significance in the prevention and treatment of this group of important disorder.

14107014.label: Project Objectives
14107014.value: To document the findings on APT images of benign and malignant tumours of the head and neck. To determine if changes in APT of head and neck carcinoma can be detected during treatment with chemoradiotherapy.

To determine if changes in APT of head and neck carcinoma can be detected during treatment with chemoradiotherapy.

14107014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14107014.value: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides excellent anatomical images of head and neck tumours and the surrounding complex normal structures in this region of the body, and as such MRI plays an important role in image-based management of patients with head and neck cancer. However, more advanced MRI techniques are being developed that can also probe the microstructure and function of these cancers. Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (CEST) is one such new molecular MRI technique that offers novel image contrast based on the chemical exchange process between physiology relevant macromolecules and free water. Amide proton transfer (APT) imaging, which investigates the proton exchange between free water and endogenous mobile amide protons found in cellular proteins and peptides of cancers, has shown great potential for various clinical applications. APT imaging is now ready for application in human subjects, where it could have widespread clinical applications because it is non-invasive, easily incorporated into current MRI cancer assessment protocols, and does not require an injection of intravenous contrast. Currently, APT-imaging has not been applied to human head and neck cancers, but according to our preliminary investigation we believe APT imaging, using MRI detectable amide as a cancer biomarker, has the potential to improve many aspects of image–based management of head and neck cancer. In this study we wish to document the findings in APT imaging of benign and malignant head and neck tumours, and document changes in APT imaging of cancers during chemoradiotherapy. The results of this study will show whether this new molecular imaging technique has the potential to characterise head and neck tumours and assess early cancer treatment response.

14107014.label: Realisation of objectives
14107014.value: Objective 1. To document the findings on APT images of benign and malignant tumours of the head and neck. 1). Patients with four groups of head and neck tumours were recruited and APT imaging was analysed in 85 patients according to the planned sample size. The objective was achieved. APT mean, median, maximum, minimum, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis were documented in 30 patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), 25 patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), 10 patients with non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) and 20 patients with salivary gland tumours (SGT) (appendix Table 1) 2). In addition to the planned objective we were able to perform an analysis to compare differences in APT values between malignant tumours and normal tissues, between malignant tumours and benign tumours, and between different groups of malignant tumours (appendix Table 2). Our analysis included a comparison of the results of APT imaging with those of diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) which is a well-established functional MRI technique in the head and neck. Objective 2. To determine if changes in APT of head and neck carcinoma can be detected during treatment with chemoradiotherapy in patients with head and neck carcinoma 1). Patients with head and neck undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma were recruited and underwent pre-treatment APT imaging according to the planned sample size of 30 patients. Because of a change in planned treatment or side effects of chemoradiotherapy during treatment data for analysis was performed in 21 patients. The objective was still achieved. Two weeks after the start of treatment changes in APT could be detected in all primary tumours when comparing absolute change (∆) and % change (%∆) between pre-treatment and the two-week intra-treatment APT levels. Results are shown for undifferentiated carcinoma (appendix Table 3) and squamous cell carcinoma (appendix Table 4). 2). In addition to the planned objective, an analysis was performed in patients with undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma to determine whether the change in APT levels at two weeks intra-treatment could predict outcome (responders vs non-responders) at 6 months after treatment. We also analysed the change in tumour volume at the same time point. The results for change in tumour APT levels and change in tumour volumes are shown (appendix Table 5 and Figure 1)

14107014.label: Major findings and research outcome
14107014.value: Objective 1. To document the findings on APT images of benign and malignant tumours of the head and neck. 1). APT imaging is a feasible imaging technique in the head and neck and APT levels were documented in undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma and salivary gland tumours. 2). APT imaging has the potential to distinguish malignant tumours from normal tissues, and malignant tumours from benign tumours. APT mean and APT median were significantly higher in malignant tumours (undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma and malignant salivary gland tumours) compared to normal tissues (brain and muscle) and benign tumours (benign salivary gland tumours). 3). APT imaging may not be able to distinguish between different groups of malignant tumours. 4). In addition, APT imaging has the potential to provide complementary information to diffusion weighted imaging , APT having lower sensitivity but higher specificity for tumour characterisation than diffusion weighted imaging. Objective 2. To determine if changes in APT of head and neck carcinoma can be detected during treatment with chemoradiotherapy in patients with head and neck carcinoma When compared to pre-treatment APT levels, changes in APT levels can be detected two weeks after the start of treatment in all patients with head and neck cancer (undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma). Early intra-treatment APT imaging has the potential to predict treatment response. In patients with undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma the ∆ and %∆ APTmean showed a significant difference between responders and non-responders, responders showing a decrease In APT levels and non-responders showing an increase in APT levels. Summary of research outcome 1). APT imaging is a new functional MRI technique which can be successfully applied to the head and neck and shows promise in the assessment of head and neck tumours. 2). APT imaging has the potential to distinguish between benign and malignant tumours which would help MRI in the characterisation of tumours that do not have a histological diagnosis. Our publication in Radiology (Law BKH et al. Radiology, 2018) is the first to show the value of APT imaging in head and neck tumour characterisation and the complementary role of APT imaging to diffusion weighted imaging. 3). APT imaging has the potential to monitor and predict treatment response early during treatment which would allow treatment regimens to be modified and tailored to the patient. Our publication in European Archives of Otorhinolaryngology (Qamar S. et al. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol, 2019) is the first to show the value of APT imaging in head and neck cancer treatment assessment and is one of only a handful of early reports in cancer research.

14107014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14107014.value: 1. Performance of pre-treatment APT imaging in predicting long-term treatment response in patients with undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma. The results from this initial observational study are promising and we have increased the recruitment of patients with undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma to investigate whether the pre-treatment APT values alone can predict outcome and treatment response to radiotherapy and chemoradiotherapy.

14107014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14107014.value: APT imaging is a new non-invasive functional MRI sequence that can image the amide protons of proteins and peptides inside cancers. This functional MRI sequence provides new cancer data that could be of additional value to the current MRI sequences that depict anatomy and probe the cancer microenvironment. This is one of the first studies to assess APT imaging in the head and neck which is a region of the body that can be technically challenging for functional MRI. Our study shows that APT imaging can be performed successfully, and the information obtained could aid the management of patients with head and neck tumours. Firstly, we extracted and documented APT values from a range of different head and neck tumours. This is the first study to show that APT values differ between tumors. This data has the potential to distinguish between benign and malignant tumours which would help MRI to characterise a tumour when there is no histological diagnosis. Secondly, we found the changes in APT levels in cancer of the nasopharynx, a common head and neck cancer in Hong Kong, can be detected early in a course of chemoradiotherapy and the change can be used to predict response at the end of treatment. This is the first head and neck cancer study to show that APT imaging provides a marker for early monitoring of treatment response. APT markers have the potential to allow treatment regimens to be modified and tailored to the patient in the future.

14107514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14107514.value: Our long-term goal is to re-construct the fruiting body development kinase signaling pathways. This is important because kinases are master switches of development. The specific aims are to (1) validate in silico identified kinases putatively involved in fruiting body development in Coprinopsis cinerea by gene knockdown analyses, (2) construct knockout mutants of the putative kinases and (3) characterize the mutants to delineate the functional roles of the kinases by their developmental morphological changes and gene expression profiles. Inhibitor intervention will also be performed to support the knockout studies. C. cinerea is a model organism in studies of homobasidiomycetes biology because of its short life cycle and established genetic manipulation methods. The initiation and development of the mushroom fruiting body are regulated by environmental signals such as temperature, nutrient, and light-dark cycle. We know little about the regulation of development program and signal transduction pathways in mushroom-forming fungi. Supported by recent achievements in fungal genomics, there are increasing studies on the regulation of mushroom initiation and development. Our laboratory has studied fruiting body development for more than 15 years and we have recently obtained Serial Analysis of Gene Expression (SAGE) and microarray gene expression profiles of developmental stages of C. cinerea. Based on these knowledge and datasets, this study proposes to (a) validate kinases identified by in silico investigation as putatively involved in C. cinerea fruiting body development by gene knockdown studies to show that they cause abnormal fruiting body development, and (b) knockout the genes of these kinases to see whether the knockouts change in morphology and expression profiles of genes. Protein kinases hypothesized to be important in mushroom developmental processes have been selected for the studies. They are, PKA, PKB/Akt, PKC, Erk, and GSK3β. This study would be one of the few functional studies on the functional roles of kinases in signaling in fruiting body development of mushroom-forming fungi. Identification and functional characterization of regulators in fruiting body development will contribute to our understanding of this important process. With a better understanding of the relationship between external stimuli and fruiting body initiation and development, the mushroom growers can optimize the cultivation of various basidiomycetous mushrooms more systematically and effectively. 本項目的長遠目標是重新構建影響子實體發育過程的激酶信號傳導通路。由於激酶是調節發育進程的主開關，對激酶的研究具有承上啟下的重要意義。此項目將會實現的具體目標包括：1. 用生物信息方法選定的候選激酶，並通過基因抑制（Gene Knockdown）手段來驗證其是否參與灰蓋鬼傘菌(Coprinopsis cinerea)的子實體萌發發育過程；2. 構建不含有候選激酶基因的敲除（Gene Knockout）菌株；3. 通過比較基因敲除菌株的發育形態變化和基因表達譜，研究候選激酶的功能特性。激酶抑製劑將用於補充驗證基因敲除菌株的敲除效果。灰蓋鬼傘菌是研究同擔子菌綱的模型生物，它不但有較短的生命週期，而且適用於很多發展成熟的基因研究技術。其子實體的萌發和發育受到外部環境因子的嚴格控制，包括溫度、養分和光暗週期。但是外部環境因子如何調節控制這一過程（如信號傳導通路、發育進程控制機制）仍是未解之謎。 近年來，真菌界生物基因組的研究有了很大的進展，并延伸應用于對蘑菇子實體萌發和發育的研究。我實驗室有長達15年的子實體發育研究經驗，最近我們還取得了對灰蓋鬼傘菌不同發育時期的基因表達連續分析數據（SAGE，Serial Analysis of Gene Expression）和微陳列基因表達譜。利用這些數據和其他其他相近物種的基因組分析，我們計劃在此項目中：a）用現有數據選出潛在的控制灰蓋鬼傘菌子實體發育的激酶，並用基因抑制法驗證其作用，最後篩選出相關基因抑制令菌株出現畸形發育的激酶；b）上述步驟中篩選出的激酶將會被用於構建基因敲除菌株，畸形發育記錄及基因表達譜將會被用於找出信號通路中的其他蛋白。 我們已經挑選了一些對蘑菇子實體發育有重要但未經證實作用的蛋白激酶，包括 蛋白激酶A（PKA），蛋白激酶B（PKB/Akt），蛋白激酶C（PKC），细胞外调节蛋白激酶（Erk），和糖原合成激酶3β（GSK3β）。目前，關於激酶在蘑菇子實體發育信號傳導通路的功能性研究還很少，找出調節這一過程的關鍵控制子并對其功能性狀進行研究，將幫助我們更好地理解子實體萌發和發育過程與外部環境影響因子之間的關係。這些知識更可以令擔子菌食用菌的種植者系統有效地開發出優化的培育方法。

14107514.label: Realisation of objectives
14107514.value: 1. To validate, by transient knockdown, in silico selected putative regulatory kinases in fruiting body development signaling in C. cinerea. We used RNA interference method to knockdown those in silico selected putative protein kinase genes such as GSK3, PKA and AKT. We synthesized small RNA of 21 bps which matched to RNA of target protein kinase to stop the translation and lead to degradation of that mRNA. When C. cinerea mycelium reached the edge of agar plates, they were transferred to incubator with 12hr/12hr light dark cycle and 28 oC which are conditions favorable for fruiting body development. Until primordium formed, we used needle to inject small RNA to selected primordium. 74% of primordium injected with small RNA targeting to GSK3 transcript were stopped in primordial stage and retarded the fruiting body development. To validate the efficiency of RNA interference, we used quantitative real time PCR to determine the expression of target genes in those small RNA treated samples. The GSK3 small RNA treated samples had 85% of reduction in GSK3 gene expression. However, for samples treated with small RNA targeting other protein kinases, they could still grow into fruiting body and autolyzed finally. 2. To generate knockout mutants of the selected kinases. Sophisticated genetic editing method-CRISPR- Cas9 was used to knockout GSK3 gene. We inserted CRISPR Cas 9 ribonucleoprotein (Cas9-RNP) and sgRNA into protoplasts of C. cinerea and sgRNA brought Cas9-RNP to GSK3 target site. Then the protoplasst were regenerated and = grown in YMG agar plates. At first, the regenerated protoplasts were selected and consistently grown into mycelial stage. Then we extracted DNA from the mycelium to validate any gene editing by sanger sequencing. However, no change in the target site of GSK3 gene was found. Therefore, we may need to further verify gene mutation by using other approaches. We have used forward genetics with ultra-violet irradiation to generate mutants with phenotypic screening and obtained over 50 mutants. We sequenced the genomes of 5 mutants and found three with potential GSK3 deletions. These mutants have basic phenotype as the wild type under inhibitor interventions. We will confirm the existence of these deletions. 3. To characterize the morphology and gene expression profile changes of the knockout mutants and inhibitor interventions. Application of a GSK3 inhibitor Lithium chloride (LiCl) induced enhanced mycelial growth and inhibited fruiting body formation in C. cinerea. RNA-Seq of LiCl-treated C. cinerea resulted in a total of 14128 unigenes. There were 1210 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the LiCl-treated samples and control samples in the mycelium stage (first time point), whereas 1402 DEGs were detected at the stage when the control samples formed hyphal knots and the treatment samples were still in mycelium (second time point). Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genome (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis of the DEGs revealed significant associations between the enhanced mycelium growth in LiCl treated C. cinerea and metabolism pathways such as “biosynthesis of secondary metabolite” and “biosynthesis of antibiotics”. In addition, DEGs involved in cellular process pathways, including “cell cycle-yeast” and “meiosis-yeast”, were identified in C. cinerea fruiting body formation suppressed by LiCl under favorable environmental conditions. We did not have enough time to characterize the mutants by transcriptomics. We will use our own resources to carry out the remaining experiments.

14107514.label: Major findings and research outcome
14107514.value: We have used RNA interference to knockdown glycogen synthase kinase 3 gene and retarded 74% of primordium to developed into fruiting body. The efficiency of knocking down glycogen synthase kinase 3 gene was determined by quantitative real time PCR and showed a significant reduction of expression by 85%. Moreover, we used glycogen synthase kinase 3 inhibitor- lithium chloride to treated C. cinerea mycelium. By inhibiting the glycogen synthase kinase 3 activity, C. cinerea mycelium grew faster and fruiting body development retarded. We analyzed the transcriptome profile of lithium chloride-treated C. cinerea and identified 1210 and 1402 differentially expressed genes associated with the glycogen synthase kinase activity and mycelium growth, as well as fruiting body formation respectively. Our findings suggest that GSK3 activity is essential for fruiting body formation as it affects the expression of fruiting body inducing genes and genes in cellular processes. Further functional studies of GSK3 in basidiomycetous fungi may help understanding the relationships between environmental signals and fruiting body development.

14107514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14107514.value: Based on RNA interference in C. cinerea primordium and inhibitor intervention in C. cinerea mycelium, the role of GSK3 in C. cinerea was associated with mycelium growth and fruiting body development. Inactivating glycogen synthase kinase enhanced mycelium growth and inhibited the fruiting body formation. By first transcriptome profiling of GKS3 inhibited C. cinerea, we characterized the role of GSK3 in C. cinerea mycelium growth and fruiting body formation. Up-regulated genes were determined and the enriched metabolic pathways, such as “biosynthesis of secondary metabolites” and “biosynthesis of antibiotics”, explained the enhanced mycelium growth.. Besides, the down-regulated genes in the cellular process pathways, including “cell cycle-yeast” and “meiosis-yeast” were identified in the C. cinerea suppressed by LiCl under conditions favorable for fruiting. In the future, the differentially expressed genes involved in environmental response will be subject to study on the signal transduction between different pathways. In this way, further studies on the phosphorylation of GSK3 with external environmental signals will facilitate the understanding of how environmental factors induce fruiting body development.

14107514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14107514.value: To characterize the functional role of protein kinase in the signaling of fruiting body development in mushroom-forming fungi, we carried out gene knockdown and inhibitor intervention of glycogen synthase kinase 3(GSK3). We also sequenced the transcriptome of the protein kinase inhibited samples by RNA-sequencing. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first transcriptome profiling of the role of GSK3 in C. cinerea fruiting formation. By transcriptional analysis, there were 1210 and 1402 differentially expressed genes detected in mycelium growth and fruiting body formation respectively. Most of differentially expressed genes involved in metabolism pathways and cell process pathways, indicating that the activity of GSK3 was associated with those pathways and regulating the mushroom development. Intervention of the activity of this protein kinase can be a useful tool to control the growth and development of mushroom.

14108014.label: Realisation of objectives
14108014.value: (1) To analyze the interactions between soybean accessions with Rfg1 or rfg1 genotypes and Sinorhizobium fredii strains. We have built two models of S. fredii strains to facilitate in-depth analyses of this species and its interactions with soybean. Full de novo genomes of two S. fredii strain CCBAU25509 (incompatible with Rfg1 type soybean) and CCBAU45436 (compatible with Rfg1 type soybean) were built. By comparative genomics, core and accessory genes subsets were identified. Based on the reference genomes, transcriptome analysis identified 42 and 77 genes down-regulated and up-regulated, respectively, in CCBAU45436 bacteriods within soybean accession C08 (Rfg1 type) nodules compared to those in soybean accession W05 (rfg1) nodules. From these differentially affected genes, two genes, znuA and mdtA were found to be essential for host adaptation and their mutants showed significant changes in nodulation phenotype. We identified that metabolic flux is important for soybean-rhizobium interaction. Although nitrogen-fixing bacteroids are no longer growing, they are metabolically active and heavily reply on the host. We constructed metabolic models of CCBAU45436 bacteriods in both W05 and C08 based on the bacteria genome and transcriptome data generated in this work. Out of 541 genes in the model, 141 genes were found to have influence on symbiotic process, where 121 genes were predicted as essential and the remaining as having a partial effect. These models reconcile our previous study that bacteriods within the cultivated soybean host is able to fix more nitrogen than in the wild soybean. We carried out extensive transcriptomic study of the plant hosts under the influence of the two S. fredii strain. From the differentially expressed gene, we found that key components in defense response pathway of the host soybean plants have been compromised during the nodulation process. (2) To identify the alleles of Rj2/Rfg1 in the wild soybean accessions and correlate them with their compatibility toward S. fredii. In additional to the 3 previously reported allele (Rj2/rfg1, rj2/rfg1 and rj2/Rfg1) defined by 7 amino acid polymorphisms (2 for Rj2 and 5 for Rfg1), we identified an additional allele with unreported combination of amino acids polymorphism at the Rj2 region (E452, R490). Through nodulation test, it is found that the this uncharacterized Rj2 allele (E452, R490) behaved as rj2. Interestingly, a natural Rj2/Rfg1 mutant W10 which carries Rfg1 allele based on the five amino acid polymorphisms however can be nodulated with CCBAU25509 was discovered. Sequencing of the W10 Rj2/Rfg1 gene found that there are one deletion (6bp) and two insertions (35bp and 25bp) in the gene which disrupted the function Rj2/Rfg1 protein from W10 to restrict CCBAU25509. The new allele of Rj2 (E452, R490) and W10 allele of Rj2/Rfg1 indicated that the previously reported polymorphism may not be sufficient to distinguish all the Rj2/Rfg1 allele. To look at a bigger accession collection, amino acid consensus of 302 re-sequenced soybean accessions at these positions were retrieved from previous study. After removing accessions with ambiguous SNPs, either missing or heterozygous, 147 accessions showed clear allele types remained. Surprisingly, none of these 147 accessions bear the well-defined Rj2 allele (E452 and I490). All of them carry rj2 allele (either K452, R490 or E452, R490) For Rfg1 genotype, 101 out of 147 accessions have the Rfg1 allele. 45%, 58% and 80% of wild soybean, landrace and improved cultivars are having Rfg1 allele, respectively. This may suggest that Rfg1 allele is more favorable during soybean improvement. (3) To identify and characterize the S. fredii nodulation outer proteins that interact with the soybean Rj2/Rfg1 protein. As proposed, we have attempted to use Rj2/Rfg1 fragments as baits to screen for direct interacting S. fredii protein using bacterial two-hybrid system and screen for soybean protein that may bridge the interaction between Rj2/Rfg1 and S. fredii protein using yeast two-hybrid system. Nevertheless, after several rounds of screening, no potential interacting partner was identified. Alternatively, we adopted the high-through proteomics strategies to compare the secretome between CCBAU25509 and CCBAU45436. We have identified 7 and 8 Nodulation Outer Proteins (Nops) from the secretome of CCBAU25509 and CCBAU45436, respectively. NopX is missing in CCBAU25509 secretome, although the intact gene can be found in the genome of CCBAU25509. A mutant defective in the type-3 secretion system in CCBAU25509 is not able to secrete the remaining Nops except NopA. This mutant can nodule incompatible soybean containing the Rfg1 allele suggesting that secreted Nop proteins are playing key roles in the host specificity. We compared the sequence of Nops between Rfg1 compatible and incompatible S. fredii strains including CCBAU45436 and CCBAU25509. Protein sequences of most Nops were either completely identical between the two strains (NopA, NopC, and NopL) or showing no host-specific sequence conservation (NopB, and NopX). The NopP sequences in restrictive Sinorhizobial strains are invariable while there are some random non-synonymous changes in non-restrictive strains. Meanwhile, NopI of restrictive strain and non-restrictive strains is only differ in one amino acid (Y72C). Thus, the host-specific sequence conservation of NopP and NopI are highly possibly be the culprit of host incompatibility. We attempted to investigate if there is direct interaction between the Rfg1 and the Sinorhizobial NopI or NopP using yeast- 2-hybrid. The results suggested that there is no direct interaction between Rfg1 to either NopI or NopP. NopI or NopP may bind to an unknown decoy in soybean which mediates the restriction functions of Rfg1.

14108014.label: Major findings and research outcome
14108014.value: To harness the importance of biological nitrogen fixation, this study aimed to understand the interaction between Sinorhizobium fredii and soybean mediated by the host R gene Rfg1. CCBAU25509 (restricted) and CCBAU45436 (not restricted) are two S. fredii strains showing distinctive host specificity toward soybean plant carrying different Rfg1 alleles. We have successfully built two models for S. fredii by providing two complete genomes, comprehensive transcriptomes, proteomes, and secretomes (Outputs #1 and 5). By analyzing the differentially expressed genes, two genes, znuA and mdtA were found to be essential for host adaption and mutations of these genes can significantly alter the nodulation pattern (Output #1). By analyzing the differentially expressed genes, two genes, znuA and mdtA were found to be essential for host adaption and mutations of these genes can significantly alter the nodulation pattern (Output #1). The interactions between bacteroids and plant cells were put to a perspective of interaction and regulation of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus metabolism in root nodules of legumes (Outputs #2 and #3). Based on the genome and transcriptome, metabolic models of CCBAU45436 bacteroids were built which precisely predicted that bacteroid within cultivated soybean host can fix more nitrogen than in wild soybean (Output #4). Using data from this work and public datasets, we confirmed that there are 3 major allelic types of the Rj2(Rfg1) protein that function to restrict some B. diazoefficiens and some S. fredii strains (Output #5). To identify the Rfg1 mediated effector triggering immunity of the plant host, we carried out secretome analysis of CCBAU25509, CCBAU45436 and a T3SS mutant in CCBAU25509 background. Seven and eight Nodulation Outer Proteins (Nops) were identified from the secretome of CCBAU25509 and CCBAU45436, respectively. Instead, probably by disrupting Nops secretion, the T3SS mutant is able to bypass the immunity and nodulate the otherwise incompatible soybean carrying the rj2/Rfg1 allelic type. Thus, the secreted Nops by CCBAU25509 proteins are playing key roles in the host specificity. The allelic forms of NopP and NopI in S. fredii are associated with the restriction imposed by Rfg1. However, no direct interaction between either NopP or NopI with Rfg1 could be observed (Output #5).

14108014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14108014.value: We have built two important models for S. fredii by completing two full genomes, comprehensive transcriptomes, proteomes, and secretomes. We will make these datasets available to everyone in the field and therefore expedite the research in bacteria-plant interaction of S. fredii. A web server for data visualisation is under construction. We have also successfully identified Nops that are associated with the host restriction due to the allelic type of the Rj2(Rfg1) protein. Since there is no direct interaction between Nops and Rj2(Rfg1), the interactions may involve multiple components such as decoys. We have established collaboration with Profs. Kiwamu Minamisawa and Masayuki Sugaward of the Tohoku University (experts of Nops study) to continue to resolve this interacting protein complexes. We have built the first metabolic model of S. fredii in nodules. In collaboration with Prof. Siu-Hung Chan, we will continue to build the metabolic model on the plant side, which will be much more complicated.

14108014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14108014.value: Biological nitrogen fixation of nodule formed between soybean and Sinorhizobium fredii could be important component of sustainable agriculture. Rj2(Rfg1) is the resistance protein of soybean controlling the specificity of S. fredii strains to form root nodules. Using genomics, transcriptomic, proteomics analysis, and metabolic modeling, we have compared the interaction between soybean carrying different allelic types of the Rj2(Rfg1) versus compatible and incompatible S. fredii strains. Large omics datasets at different biological levels have been generated to expedite the research of this field. We have identified important bacterial genes that are essential for host adaptation. Metabolic models that showed high predictive power for host-symbiont interaction were built. Allelic types of the Rj2(Rfg1) protein based on amino acid polymorphism was confirmed using multiple soybean germplasms. Through high-throughput proteomics study, we have identified S. fredii secretory proteins that are highly possibly be the candidates that genetically interacting with the Rj2(Rfg1) protein and determine the host specificity.
