14402114.label: Major findings and research outcome
14402114.value: Major findings can be summarized as two. Firstly, the relationship between the philosophy of life and the leftist theories is highly complicated. Zhang Junmai (張君勱) delivered a lecture entitled “The Philosophy of Life” at Tsinghua University in 1923. This lecture sparked off the debate on scientism versus metaphysicism. This debate is an important turning point of the Chinese intellectuals’ reception of Bergson. Hereafter, Bergson’s philosophy of life has been categorized as metaphysicism and associated with Neo-Confucianism. At the same time, Chinese Communists considered Marxism as scientism and began to criticize Bergson’s philosophy of life. This debate split Marxism and Bergsonism into two opposing sides, and influenced studies of the Chinese reception of Bergson later on. Therefore, most of these studies are mainly focused on the relationship between Bergson’s philosophy and Neo-Confucianism. Our research identified nine major Chinese leftist intellectuals who are obviously related to Bergson and the philosophy of life. We collected, listed and analyzed 1056 works by these nine intellectuals which are related to the philosophy of life. We try to challenge the dominant binary opposition of Bergsonism/Marxism by placing the Chinese leftist intellectuals’ reception of Bergson in the foreground. Secondly, Chinese leftist intellectuals, such as Li Dazhao, Qu Qiubai, Zhu Qianji and Taixu (太虛法師), made the important contribution to reinterpret Bergson’s philosophy of life by their efforts to connect the philosophy of life with anarchism, socialism, Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism. They referred to both Western theories and traditional Chinese thought when they discussed the philosophy of life. For the Chinese leftist intellectuals, the philosophy of life was not just referred to Bergson’s thinking, but also the thought from Buddhism, Daoism and Zhou yi (周易). In consequence, they radically rewrote and transformed the theoretical formation of both Western thought and traditional Chinese thought.

14402114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14402114.value: In late Meji and Taisho (early twentieth century), Japanese intellectuals received the new ideas and theories from the West. They reconnected and reconstructed Bergson’s philosophy of life, Emerson’s transcendentalism, evolutionism, Ellen Key’s feminist thought and Peter Kropotkin’s theory of Mutual Aid as a new discursive formation. SUZUKI Sadami (鈴木貞美) calls this new discourse as “Taisho Vitalism.” (大正生命主義) The PI found that this new discourse was finally circulated to the Republican China, and the Chinese intellectuals further transformed the discursive formation of “Taisho Vitalism” in the process of translation and reception. The PI proposed the new concept of “East Asian Vitalism” (東亞生命主義) for conceptualizing this process of traveling theory. The PI proposed this new concept in his conference presentation in Seoul on 24th November, 2018. The PI’s research has been extended to a further study of “East Asian Vitalism.” His paper on Ding Ling (丁玲)’s early fictions, which will be published in Reviews and Research on Chinese Literature (《現代中文學刊》), is the first research output of this new research direction. Several papers related to this new direction are in preparation.

14402114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14402114.value: This research studies modern Chinese literature and intellectual history from the perspectives of Cultural Studies. The research project considers the “Bergson Fever” in modern China as a part of the transcultural site and currents across Europe and Asia in early twentieth century. We attempt to highlight the complexity of modern Chinese intellectuals’ thinking, and the transcultural and hybrid nature of Chinese modernity. The research also tries to challenge the dominant binary oppositions of left/right, local/global, literary writing/philosophical thinking, East/West and tradition/modernity. The project paves way for further study not only on Chinese leftist intellectuals’ reception of Henri Bergson’s philosophy of life, but also the creative transformation of traditional Chinese thought and culture.

14402414.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14402414.value: 十八世紀中期至十九世紀初期蘇州與重慶的商事習慣及商業十八世紀中期至十九世紀初期蘇州與重慶的商事習慣及商業訟案

14402414.label: Project Objectives
14402414.value: To delve into how the legal factors functioned in the middle eighteenth and early nineteenth century Chinese economy. To trace and compare the evolution of commercial custom both in Suzhou and Chongqing. To scrutinize the rulings in commercial lawsuits and pinpoint the legal reasoning deployed by the officials. To find out how merchant groups functioned in the commercial disputes and what were their contributions and limitations during the process of adjudication in the commercial lawsuits.

14402414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14402414.value: As the long-distance trade advanced in the 18th century China, both Suzhou and Chongqing became centers of commerce and industry. As many merchants made their fortunes in Suzhou, Chongqing and other cities, how commerce contributed to society was the pertinent issue and subject of increasing discussions at that time. Many officials had witnessed that ordinary people suffered more when merchants were not active in a specific county where the inhabitants lacked of either the basic necessities for survival or silver to pay their taxes. Protecting merchants was thus acknowledged as one effective means for bettering the material life of ordinary people at least since the 18th century. It was, to some extent, a time of change in economic mentality that prevailed in those cities along the long-distance trade routes. Trade proceeded with the evolution of various commercial customs, and inevitably more disputes and lawsuits occurred. How did Qing officials adjudicated commercial disputes brought to their courts? What were the pertinent statutes, provincial regulations, and other kinds of legal orderings, that informed their decisions? How were the commercial customs in different business accommodated or rejected by the ruling? And what kind of strategies did the litigation masters hired by merchants most often resort to? These questions all merit further inquiry. This project compares Suzhou in the economically advanced Lower Yangtze area and Chongqing in the relatively less prosperous but also important economic center in the Upper Yangtze region; I shall delve into the question of how various commercial customs interacted with the extant codified law in the middle 18th and early 19th century China. 隨著18世紀中國長程貿易的進展，蘇州與重慶都成為商業與手工業的中心，當許多商人在蘇州重慶與其他城市經商營業的同時，社會上也有愈來愈多的官員與士大夫開始關注與討論商業如何有益於社會的各項議題。許多官員觀察到，如果商人無法踴躍到達本地州縣經商的話，則本地居民將會缺乏維生所需的糧食以及繳稅所需要的白銀，百姓便會因此而生活窘困。至少從18世紀開始，保護商人也被視為是一種改善百姓生活的有效方法。從某個意義上說，這是一種沿著當時長程貿易沿線城市而發展出來的一種經濟心態的轉變。 商業貿易隨著各式各樣的商業習慣的演化而不斷擴展，同時也不可避免地引發了商業糾紛與訴訟。清代官員到底如何審酌裁決呈控到衙門的種種商業糾紛？既有的相關律例、審例以及其他種類的法律命令如何牽動官員的裁決？不同行業的商業習慣如何受到官員裁決的承認或否決？由商人聘請的訟師最常使用何種策略來協助進行商業訟訴？這些問題都值得深入探究。 本計劃分別比較當時位於中國長江下游，長江上游兩個經濟最發達的蘇州和重慶，探究18世紀中期到19世紀初期，中國不同的商業習慣究竟如何與既有的法律相互影響？

14402414.label: Realisation of objectives
14402414.value: 1. In exploring the legal factors influencing the economy of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century China, I attempt to explain why Qing officials did not display concepts or theories related to modern European-style “private law, commercial law, and merchant law” or their specific forms of legal reasoning or legal rhetoric. I argue that this is not only related to their ability but also to their willingness. With the help of private secretaries and litigation masters, who worked in the background, and through their collective efforts, the legal reasoning adopted in some commercial cases silently entered into various kinds of legal rhetoric, and by this means was incorporated into the Da Qing luli (大清律例, Statutes and Sub-statutes of the Great Qing Dynasty), the “Provincial Statutes” of each province and the “Established Precedents” of localities. This legal evolution is not only closely related to the development of long-distance trade and a national market between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, but is also tied to the growth in numbers of legal specialists in eighteenth-century China. 2. As to comparing how commercial customs evolved in the two cities of Chongqing and Suzhou, I have written two papers. The first paper focuses on the changes in regulations governing weights and measures and related commercial customs. The system of weights and measures had its origins not only in the rules proclaimed by the government but also developed in close interaction with the commercial customs prevailing in particular markets. The system of weights and measures was an important factor influencing the commercial practices adopted in each market; it was also in some sense a result of how market transactions influenced local commercial practices. It was thus a crucial link in shaping local market systems. I selected relevant Suzhou stele inscriptions from the perspective of transaction costs, as well as finding examples from the Ba Xian Archives related to dou hang (斗行, brokers in charge of weights and measures), in order to examine more closely how the regulations governing weights and measures in the Da Qing lüli and the local commercial customs of Suzhou and Chongqing collectively impacted and changed their respective market systems. The second yet-unpublished paper delves into the role of consultant managers (known as gushi賈師) in Suzhou’s cotton industry. Acquiring knowledge about dyeing was a way for gushi to defeat persistent cheating on the part of “cunning” workers; it helped gushi to scrutinize the dyeing quality, and accordingly to calculate a fair wage per piece of cotton cloth produced. This reduced workers’ complaints and also satisfied the bosses of the firms, who paid gushi a very good salary. Possessing knowledge allowed the gushi to maintain his reputation as perfectly capable (in the eyes of the boss) and very fair (in the eyes of workers). The text Bujing (Classic of Cloth) interweaved this passionate pursuit of capability and reputation; one of its authors even portrayed the relationship between a gushi and his boss as that between a revered prime minister and a sage emperor (shengjun xianxiang 聖君賢相). Where the cotton industry was under the management of gushi there seems to have been little place for merchant guilds to intervene. Compared to the role that gushi and related commercial customs played in Suzhou’s cotton industry, the regulations of guilds involved in the Chongqing cotton industry seem to have had more power. Moreover, the local government of Ba Xian seems to have been more willing to endorse the monopoly claimed by merchant guilds. This is an interesting feature that needs further investigation. 3. I inquire into the legal reasoning that informed state handling and adjudication of commercial lawsuits mainly involving strikes and wage negotiations in Suzhou and Chongqing. Primarily in the interests of maintaining public order, local governments in Suzhou repeatedly intervened in the industry through legal amendments specifying wage standards. Scrutinizing Suzhou stele inscriptions from the early Qing, we can find economic legislation related to wage disputes and see that in the process by which they formulated standards for wages, officials proceeded from considerations of public order to regulate both merchants and artisans. The local Suzhou government in its wage legislation seems to have had set priorities: maintaining the stability of currency flow between copper money and silver ingots, and assisting in stabilizing currency circulation through a “bankers’ guild hall” (qianye gongsuo錢業公所). Local government in Chongqing, however, seems to have faced little pressure from laborers; strikes occurred less frequently and were weaker in their impact. 4. Regarding the fourth objective—looking comparatively at the similarities and differences in the roles played by commercial organizations in Chongqing and Suzhou in commercial lawsuits—I have written two papers. Based on several lawsuits from the Ba Xian Archives, I found that in the process of hearing cases concerning commercial debt or partnership in nineteenth-century Chongqing, not only was the documentary evidence provided by merchants from both sides important in how officials decided the case; but the leaders of commercial organizations such as the kezhang (客長, leader of migrant and/or commercial organizations) and basheng kezong (八省客總, general leader of the eight migrant and/or commercial organizations) also played an important role in helping officials examine various sorts of commercial documents like account books, contracts and correspondence that were submitted as evidence, and in acting as mediators to resolve the dispute. Compared to Chongqing, Suzhou in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries was even more a major urban center with a dense population and flourishing commerce and industry. What is surprising, however, is that in the extant Suzhou inscriptions recording commercial disputes and judicial proceedings involving huiguan or gongsuo, it is very difficult to find any examples of the leaders of migrant and/or commercial organizations being appointed by officials to investigate or mediate commercial lawsuits. Commercial guidebooks in the Qing dynasty urged merchants to avoid any litigation because officials and clerks tended to take advantage of them. Nonetheless, historical records show that in Suzhou and Chongqing, where commerce and industry flourished in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, an increasing number of merchants actively resorted to litigation to protect their rights. I delve into the paradoxical gap between the stricture to avoid litigation in the commercial guidebooks and the existence of numerous commercial lawsuits. How did local merchants utilize imperial law to justify their entitlements? This phenomenon demonstrates that the merchants were struggling to balance the risks of business and politics. From the perspective of business, it might be better for merchants to avoid litigation, because resorting to law would probably incur extortion by clerks, runners and even officials in the local courts. But from the perspective of politics, merchants seem to have realized that resorting to litigation would protect their thwarted interests and might avert further damage to their rights. Based on both Suzhou steles and Ba Xian lawsuits, I offer a framework for understanding the dynamics of the imposition of law and of resistance to law when merchants faced various menaces and hence had to balance risks.

14402414.label: Major findings and research outcome
14402414.value: Three publications and three conference papers derive from this project. Most were presented in conferences held separately in Hong Kong, Beijing, Taipei, Kyoto, Frankfurt and Berlin; discussions with colleagues led me to accordingly revise and even reconsider my arguments. “Constructing ‘Commercial Law’ in Eighteenth-Century China” addresses my first research objective of exploring the legal factors influencing the economy of Qing China. Analyzing many commercial lawsuits from Suzhou and Chongqing contributes more pertinent cases to understand better the complex interaction between economy and law. A journal article,〈《大清律例》如何影響商業習惯——試析18、19世纪蘇州的度量衡訴訟〉[How Did the Qing Code Affect Commercial Customs? Lawsuits Pertaining to Weights and Measures in Eighteenth- and Nineteenth-Century Suzhou], and paper “What Made Suzhou the Center of the Cotton Industry in Eighteenth-Century China? From the Perspective of Acquiring and Monitoring Dyeing Skills for Cotton Cloth” speak to the second research objective of comparing how commercial customs evolved in Chongqing and Suzhou. Another paper, 〈十八世紀蘇州的工資糾紛與地方政府經濟立法〉[Disputes over Wages and Related Economic Regulations Issued by Local Government in Eighteenth-Century Suzhou], was accepted in 2017 and will be published this year. It takes up the third objective of investigating the legal reasoning that informed state handling and adjudication of commercial lawsuits, highlighting the different tropes of legal reasoning deployed by local governments in Suzhou and Chongqing. This difference merits prudent consideration. As for the fourth objective—comparing the roles played by commercial organizations in Chongqing and Suzhou in commercial lawsuits—I have published a book chapter 〈十九世紀前重慶城的債務與合夥訴訟〉[Lawsuits over Debt and Partnership in Early Nineteenth-Century Chongqing] and delivered one conference paper 〈平衡商業與政治風險：十八、十九世紀蘇州和重慶的商業訴訟〉[Balancing Risk between Business and Politics: Commercial Lawsuits in Eighteenth- and Nineteenth-Century Suzhou and Chongqing]. These tentatively explain the similarities and differences in the roles played by merchant communities in mediating commercial lawsuits in each city. The strategies adopted show interesting patterns and deserve further exploration.

14402414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14402414.value: By the early nineteenth century, the strategies that merchants in Suzhou and Chongqing had adopted in dealing with commercial lawsuits already manifested some interesting differences and similarities. Such differences and similarities are likely to have constituted an important aspect of the operations of commerce, of judicial proceedings, and even of urban life both in Chongqing and Suzhou. Delving into these commercial lawsuits from these two prosperous cities engaged in the long-distance trade along the Yangze River will shed light on the character of economic development and legal norms in late imperial China. I was fortunate to have valuable opportunities to discuss my project with several experts on European legal history during my two-month visit to the Max Planck Institute for European Legal History (MPIeR) in 2016. Their feedback on my conference paper greatly illuminated the issues and benefits my current research on Chinese economic and legal history. In particular, the book Companies and Company Law in Late Medieval and Early Modern Europe (2016), edited by Wim Decock, one of the commentators on my conference paper in MPIeR, provides a very useful framework for comparing the paths by which commercial law was constructed in Europe and China.

14402414.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14402414.value: Law is not the only source merchants could rely on to resolve their disputes. This observation certainly applied to the situation in eighteenth-century China. However, many scholars have cast doubts on the role of law in Chinese traditional business behaviors, and have contended that not only did merchants lack motivation to appeal to courts, but that Chinese law was basically the same across the Ming and Qing dynasties and was incapable of dealing with commercial lawsuits. In the last two decades, some scholars have questioned the opinions described above; their works all argue, on their own terms, against the “custom-law dichotomy.” Debates rage over factors such as key resources, basic definitions, and most of all the roadmaps different scholars have laid out for study. The debates are very likely to continue. But in the process they provide a crystal ball that allows readers to see into and unravel the mystery of the many forms of legal orderings, or the legal pluralism, that existed in Qing China. I hope to contribute to the discussion through my project focusing on the commercial customs and lawsuits in Suzhou and Chongqing in mid-eighteenth and early nineteenth century China.

14402614.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14402614.value: 夾縫之中: 大陸婚姻移民與香港的反移民政治

14402614.label: Project Objectives
14402614.value: To examine the gender dynamic underlying anti-immigration discourses e.g. how female marriage migrants have been constructed in these discourses and to what extent these discourses reflect particular concepts of manhood and contribute to the formation of specific forms of masculinity. To examine the discrepancies between anti-immigration discourses and lived realities of female marriage migrants, as well as how the direct and indirect effects of anti-immigration discourses affect the settlement process of female marriage migrants and their families through shaping the perceptions of people in their community, extended family and spousal networks. To understand how stigmatized female marriage migrants make sense of their situation, resist stigmatization by negotiating and constructing identity, and to explore the strategies they mobilize to cope with the direct and indirect consequences of stigmatization by anti-immigration discourses. In more general terms, to explore the political, social and cultural roots of the expanding gulf between the social realities of migration, the lived experiences of immigrants, and the increasingly restrictive immigration legislation, as well as how men’s and women’s positions at the macro and micro level produce and reproduce gender inequalities. Through examining the mechanisms responsible for the double marginalization of female marriage migrants from Mainland China in post-colonial Hong Kong, explore possible avenues for the ‘transformative politics’ (Piper, 2006) needed to change the stigmatization and social exclusion of these women and their families.

14402614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14402614.value: 自一九七零代起，本港開始產生一種反大陸「新移民」的情緒。九七回歸後，反新移民的情緒不但未有半點減退，還達到一個新的高峰。在政策上，香港社會對內地新來港居住人士的負面觀感充分反映在日漸收緊的移民政策及社會福利政策中；在社會層面，反移民的言論充斥媒體，針對新移民的歧視行為在社區中也愈益普遍。近年，反移民的情緒更產生了所謂「香港人優先」的運動，主張在政策及資源分配上均以土生土長香港人的利益為先。這種種反移民的情緒與行動，對因婚嫁來港的中國大陸新來港女性婚姻移民的影響尤為值得關注。自八十年代中開始，本港大部份的成年移民均是由內地來港與丈夫團聚的女性婚姻移民，在一九八六年，由香港男性與中國女性組成的跨境婚姻總數已達15,776宗。此後二十年來，跨境婚姻的數字不斷上升，並達到二零零六年的高峰28,145宗；二零一一年，由香港男性與中國女性組成的跨境婚姻佔香港的新登記婚姻約三成四。由於中國女性婚姻移民佔香港移民一個重大比數，因此反移民的論述亦包含性別成份──新移民女性被建構為野蠻、不擇手段及危險的人，不但對社會造成威脅，亦摧毀由本港男性及女性所組成的婚姻及家庭。結合多種定性研究方法，包括對媒體報導、公眾討論及移民福利政策的文本分析、與老、中及青年男性的焦點小組討論，以及對政黨人士、官員、新移民婦女及其家人的深入訪談，本研究希望回答以下問題： (1)香港反移民的論述如何污名化由中國大陸來港的女性婚姻移民？(2) 反移民的論述是否反映了特定的、對男性的文化期待，及是否被挪用以建構某種特定的男性氣概？(3)社會上反移民的情緒及論述如何影響由大陸來港的女性婚姻移民及其家人與社區人士的相處和互動？(4)由大陸來港的女性婚姻移民如何理解她們自身的處境？面對歧視時，她們採用何種應對策略？透過這些問題，本研究希望加深社會及研究者對反移民論述、國家主義及性別如何共同影響女性婚姻移民在香港的處境，延續及再製社區內及區域間的性別不平等。

14402614.label: Realisation of objectives
14402614.value: First and foremost, our findings suggest that the development of anti-migration sentiments in Hong Kong is a result of ‘the tension between prolonged political strain and accelerated economic integration between Hong Kong and China. Although politically residents of Hong Kong want to maintain their autonomy, economically the territory has been increasingly integrated with China. Economic integration has been accompanied by accelerated population mobility, which saw the rapid increase of mainland tourists visiting Hong Kong and of children being born in Hong Kong to non-Hong Kong resident mainland Chinese parents. Together with the great number of cross-border parallel traders, some Hong Kong residents have increasingly felt that the city’s basic infrastructure and resources were being stretched too thin to meet the demands of tourists and the needs of immigrants from mainland China. This popular dissatisfaction has fuelled nativist and anti-migration politics. Our findings suggest that since 2012 anti-immigration has become a central theme for political mobilisation and opposition politics against China’s rule. Immigrants from mainland China have increasingly been seen as part of China’s effort to ‘dilute’ local resistance and to colonialise Hong Kong. The rightist groups that emerged around this time put forward different political prospects for Hong Kong, including pro-independence, pro-city-state, permanent continuation of the Basic Law and constitution by all people, and China-Hong Kong demarcation. They, however, were unified in their position that the number of immigrants, including the mainland Chinese spouses and non-adult children of Hong Kong men in cross-border marriages, must be greatly reduced, and that immigrants’ access to social welfare should be restricted (Choi, Lai and Pang, forthcoming). Secondly, our findings delineate the gender dynamic underlying anti-immigration discourses. Our analysis shows that the cultural representation of immigrants as an inferior other, undeserving of full membership of society, represents an amalgam of sexist and classist ideologies. It is based on the misogynist perception that poor men are lesser men, and that poor women are merely sexual objects for male sexual gratification and consumption or use as weapons in political warfare between men. It is also founded on contempt for the socioeconomically disadvantaged, whose humanity is often denied in order to justify their marginalisation and exclusion. The Hong Kong case shows that racialisation does not depend on the existence of racial or ethnic differences. The key to racialisation is not race or ethnicity; it is the politics of exclusion and domination (Choi, 2017). Our findings further illustrate the discrepancies between anti-immigration discourses and lived realities of female marriage migrants, as well as how the direct and indirect effects of anti-immigration discourses affect the settlement process of female marriage migrants and their families. We found that an increasing number of immigrant women from mainland China had preferred living in Shenzhen to settling in Hong Kong. However, in order to allow their children to benefit from what they perceived as superior educational opportunities in Hong Kong, these migrant mothers have launched their children into becoming frequent cross-border students. This bordering strategy reflects the aspirations that these migrant parents have for their children and their determination to ensure that their children gain full cultural membership of Hong Kong society by learning and mastering the ‘authentic’ local way of being. The experiences of this group of hyper border-crossing children and their parents occur in a context in which Hong Kong society has increasingly stigmatized immigrants as unwelcome outsiders based on their cultural knowledge and practices, which are viewed by Hongkongers as inauthentic or inappropriate. Children’s frequent border crossing can be viewed as a strategy devised by their parents to prepare them for future immigration, successful integration, and the acquisition of full cultural membership (Chiu and Choi, 2018). Thirdly, our findings show how stigmatized female marriage migrants make sense of their situation, resist stigmatization by negotiating and constructing identity, and explore the strategies they mobilize to cope with the direct and indirect consequences of stigmatization by anti-immigration discourses. We develop a conceptual framework that decouples marriage migrants’ legal and spatial migration in order to capture the nuances and paradoxes that exist in the broader category of cross-border marriage migration. We examine the causes and consequences of two forms of decoupling: (1) wife migrates spatially before her legal status changes and (2) wife’s change in legal status is not accompanied by spatial migration. We argue that these two forms of decoupling have their origins in state policies, economic constraints and personal choices, and that their impact on the intimate and household dynamics of cross-border families is gendered. We show that a framework in which legal and spatial migration are decoupled offers a way of untangling the intricate nexus of relations between gender, power and space, as it illuminates the conditions under which marriage migration may bring about new forms of agency and empowerment or disempower women in cross-border marriages (Chiu and Choi, conditionally accepted). We also analyze the impact of anti-migration on the well-being of the so-called ‘double no’ children in Hong Kong and illustrate the agency of these children in navigating poverty, displacement and societal stigmatization (Choi, 2016). Together the above findings illustrate the various strategies immigrant women and their children mobilize to cope with the direct and indirect consequences of stigmatization caused by growing anti-immigration discourses and discrimination against immigrants. In addition to the micro-politics of migrant negotiation and strategizing, our papers also uncover the political, social and cultural roots of the expanding gulf between the social realities of migration, the lived experiences of immigrants, and the increasingly restrictive immigration legislation, as well as how men’s and women’s positions at the macro and micro level produce and reproduce gender inequalities. Finally, we identify various strategies to overcome the growing stigmatization of immigrants, including a better dissemination of information about the structural obstacles encountered by immigrants to counter fake news that often wrongly portray immigrants as predators or thieves of Hong Kong’s social welfare. Secondly, to reduce gendered oppression against immigrant women, we argue that it is of paramount importance that feminist scholars highlight and find ways to disseminate the theorisation of gender as a social structure or social system that is beyond immediate individual or interpersonal interactions to the general public. Thirdly, it is crucial that structural gender inequalities be made visible. Fourthly, more work needs to be done to communicate to the general public different pathways through which gender structures constrain and disadvantage immigrant women and simultaneously oppress some groups of men, e.g. single men who are squeezed out of the local marriage market in general, and the husbands and male children of immigrant women specifically. We argue that a transformative politics of empowerment and changed be built upon the recognition of the structural and intersectional constraints imposed on immigrant women and their strategies, agency, and humanity in navigating and overcoming these constraints.

14402614.label: Major findings and research outcome
14402614.value: Major Findings: 1. We argue that the development of anti-migration sentiments in Hong Kong is a result of the tension between prolonged political strain and accelerated economic integration between Hong Kong and China. 2. Although scholars generally agreed that anti-migration sentiment in Hong Kong existed as early as the late 1970s, our analysis suggests that it was only in 2012 that it became a central theme for political mobilisation and opposition politics against China’s rule. 3. Our findings illustrate the discursive strategies, gendered dynamics and intersecting nature of anti-migration politics, which represent an amalgam of sexist and classist ideologies. 4. Our findings suggest that in view of growing anti-immigrant sentiments, a growing number of immigrants have preferred living in Shenzhen to settling in Hong Kong. However, in order to allow their children to gain the cultural citizenship and to benefit from what they perceived as superior educational opportunities in Hong Kong, these migrant mothers have launched their children into becoming frequent cross-border students. 5. Our analysis also suggests the increasing decoupling of legal and spatial migration among immigrant women in cross-border marriages. The causes and consequences of two forms of decoupling were identified and analyzed. 6. We also documented the impact of anti-migration on the well-being of the so-called ‘double no’ children in Hong Kong and illustrated the agency of these children in navigating poverty, displacement and societal stigmatization. 7. In addition to documenting the micro-politics of migrant negotiation and strategizing, our papers also uncover the political, social and cultural roots of anti-migration politics. We argue that a transformative politics of empowerment and change must be built upon an understanding that links the macro and structural factors with the micro dynamics of negotiation and coping. Research Outcome: • Six SSCI journal articles (2 published, 1 accepted, and 3 under 2nd round of review after minor revision); • One international conference co-organized by the PI and researchers at National University of Singapore; • Two conference panels organized by the PI at the American Sociological Association Annual Meeting, and the XIX ISA World Congress of Sociology respectively. • One special issue lead-edited by the PI for a world leading journal on migration and mobility; • One award winning PhD thesis, winner of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s 2018 Young Scholar’s Thesis Award 2016; • One article in Hong Kong Council of Social Science Quarterly Journal; • Sixteen international and local conference presentations.

14402614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14402614.value: Based on the findings of this research, three surveys were conducted by the PI and her research team to further examine the links between migration, identity and politics in Hong Kong. The findings of one of the three surveys were published in an edited volume by Routledge (Choi, SYP and Fong E. (eds.) 2017. Migration in Post-Colonial Hong Kong. New York: Routledge). The other two surveys are currently being analyzed for journal article submissions. These surveys provide a wealth of quantitative data for the examination of how gender ideology is linked to anti-migration politics, and how social boundaries between locals and mainland Chinese immigrants in Hong Kong are being constructed, policed, crossed, and transformed over time; and how social groups vary in gender, age, social economic status, and identity perceive and understand immigration. In addition, a research team consisting of political scientists, geographers, sociologists, historians, demographers, and psychologists was formed by the PI to carry out a large collaborative research project on identity, migration and group dynamics in post-colonial Hong Kong. The group submitted a Collaborative Research Grant application, which was shortlisted in 2016. The PI would continue to revise the proposal and resubmit it.

14402614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14402614.value: By triangulating qualitative data collected through focus groups and in-depth interviews, and by analyzing published texts, such as government reports and cultural products related to migration, this research examines the gender and class dynamics of anti-migration politics in Hong Kong. It identifies the economic and political roots of anti-migration mobilization, and the gendered dimensions of anti-migration discourses. It also illustrates the gaps between the images of immigrants portrayed in these discourses and the lived realities of immigrants, particularly female immigrants in cross-border marriages and their children. By identifying the direct and in-direct effects of anti-migration politics on the lives of female marriage immigrants and their children, and by analyzing the multiple strategies immigrants mobilize to navigate and cope with the structural and cultural constraints imposed on them, this study draws attention to the agency and humanity of immigrants, and links macro politics with micro and interpersonal dynamics of being. Built upon this linkage, it highlights the intersecting constraints related to gender, class and migration status women in cross-border marriages face. It also demonstrates that any efforts to empower disadvantaged immigrants and change society must build upon an understanding of the link between macro constraints and micro dynamics of negotiation.

14402914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14402914.value: Comics are an important source of Hong Kong’s cultural identity and collective memory. Now, given that core elements of Hong Kong’s comic production—and of other creative industries, such as film and online gaming—have physically moved to mainland China, local people are consuming cultural products made by Hong Kong artists/producers residing in China that are mainly produced for the Chinese market. The question is this: What will the effect be on the Hong Kong identity, which the people of the Special Administrative Region of Hong Kong have long celebrated as being distinct from that of sovereign China? This proposed project thus aims to: (1) briefly map out the current comic industry as one of the core creative industries in Hong Kong; (2) examine the specificity of the Hong Kong-created-but-China-made cultural production; and (3) explicate how and in what ways this emerging China-made cultural production could change the cultural identities of Hong Kong. The project builds on the PI’s previous study of the game, music, and film industry in Hong Kong and China, and his longitudinal studies (with Eric Ma) relating to changing cultural identities in Hong Kong since 1996. Based on the proposed method of data collection (interviews with key comic artists, representatives of local publishing companies and professional bodies, and selected comic fans, together with the textual analysis of comic content), the project will map out the cultural image of people from Hong Kong and the mainland Chinese in contemporary comic texts given the current mode of production that hybridizes Hong Kong creativity and mainland Chinese culture. Drawing references from cultural studies—including studies of cultural identities, cultural industries, and policy—and specific studies about comics and related industries under the realm of cultural production, the project will shed light theoretically on the concept of creativity and creative workers, resistance, and negotiation (between Hong Kong and Chinese culture), and cultural hybridization in relation to the transformation of local cultural identities. At an audience level, the study will answer fundamental questions about changing cultural identities in relation to the consumption and interpretation of everyday culture and comics. Meanwhile, at the policy and industry level, this project will provide baseline findings for the development of Hong Kong’s comic industry and reveal implications relating to the role of Hong Kong in cultural production at local, national (China), and regional (Asia) levels.

14402914.label: Realisation of objectives
14402914.value: Overall, this study aims to study Hong Kong’s comic industry as one of the creative industries in Hong Kong and its changes in the face of the China market. It is by far the most comprehensive academic study of contemporary Hong Kong comics in that it covers fieldwork from the production side to the comic text (content) and comic consumption of readers/ fans. The significance of the study lies in revealing the transformation of cultural identities in relation to changes in cultural consumption/ production in this specific historical context. As to policy implication, the study of the model/ strategies of local comic industry and its relocation to mainland China also addresses the policy needed to facilitate the drastic changes of the industry. Throughout the entire study, there is no particular difficulty encountered, as local comic artists and industries are very united in promoting the industry. The fieldwork is assisted by members from Hong Kong Novelist Association and the Hong Kong Comics and Animation Federation. All the major actors in the field are identified and interviewed. The research team was welcome by various companies and researchers were invited to their companies for observations apart from interviews. The PI was invited time to time in their activities as judge for events and guest. Multiple and interdisciplinary methods are used to collect data in the two years’ research period. The PI hired an RA and trained a Mphil student for this project (with a thesis finished on the same topic). First Objective: To examine the content, model of production, distribution, and marketing strategies of the comics industry as one of the core creative industries in Hong Kong. Representatives of 25 major comic workers (17 in the first year and 8 in the second year), from owners and investors of companies, to distributors, marketers and artists were all interviewed. Because of the plunge of the revenues of the industry, apart from the focused interviews, the President of the Hong Kong Tradebook Publishers Association and the owner of Rightman Publisher (one of the largest Hong Kong comic book publisher now) and CEO of Culturecom, the largest listed comic company in Hong Kong, had a few more meetings with the PI to discuss the different kinds of business model and strategies for the Hong Kong comic industry to survive against the backdrop of China market. Details about (re)packaging of comic contents in various forms (including the sales of IPs) for China, and online distribution for local markets are two directions to go. Such discussion, together with selected interviews and analysis will be published in a forthcoming book, and the industry in fact welcomes this kind of knowledge transfer work as it also helps promote comics in Hong Kong. While the interviews become the core data of the publications needed, the PI also comes up with the industry policy recommendations for the industry. Second Objective: To study the changing contours of Hong Kong cultural identities in relation to the emerging China-made cultural production, and the consumption of cultural products, six focus groups (with 43 readers of different comics), together with at least 20 more individual interviews (as follow up interviews to enrich the data) were conducted in Hong Kong. We were able to receive help from the comic student association in the University and the online radio program ACrubbish focusing on ACG to recruit active comic readers into our focus groups. We were able to get a balanced composition of participants with equal representation on gender, age groups, and socio-economic status. During the focus group interviews, these active readers discussed a wide range of local comics and in particular, those readers who are loyal readers of Hong Kong’s classic comics and young online readers are able to conceptually draw up a relationship between Hong Kong cultural content and identities. The new reading habits of readers through and on social media/ apps are also discovered. Textual analysis of Hong Kong comics was largely based on the results of the focus group interviews. For the past year when journal articles were written for submission, content of specific comics were analyzed in conjunction with the analysis of the focus group results. In general, as seen in our published/ publishing articles, at least three main comics in Hong Kong were textually analyzed. Comic fans who are involved in secondary production (based on original comic) are also studied. The owner of HKACG, the annual comic/animation exhibition in Conventional Centre, actively helped our research team to give us VIP access to the exhibition and help distribute questionnaires to some of the exhibitors in Hong Kong. This is an additional fieldwork (on dual consumption/ production that are beyond the objectives) we did not expect we could achieve. Third Objective: To investigate how audience, comics artists, and owners of publishing companies perceive and understand the China-relocated Hong Kong comics production and content, the PI and the RA visited various Hong Kong comic artists and owners in Guangzhou, Hangzhou and Beijing, and the various China’s cultural clusters (or technology park) in which Hong Kong artists, investors and comic exhibitors are working. Because of the PI’s close relationship with the industry, in particular, the PI was given access to the Beijing National Creative Industry Expo in the end of 2015 to have private gatherings and interviews with the China’s counterparts. In May 2015, the PI also visited the largest comic publisher in Guangzhou and interviewed editors, publishers, and comic artists, including Hong Kong artists working there. In April 2015, because the PI was speaker for the Hangzhou Comic and Animation Expo, the largest comic exhibition in China, in one of the public seminars for exhibitors, he was then able to interview all the major players in China, and Hong Kong and Taiwan exhibitors as well. He was also invited as VIP for the Golden Dragon Award (for comics and animation) that was organized in conjunction with the Expo in Hangzhou. In the two years of studies, he visited and interviewed the owner and artists of the two China’s most well-known creative hubs for comics in Hangzhou. In all these cases, the PI was the only and the first international academic who was able to work closely with these industry personnel and interviewed them. In all these fieldwork, in particular for those Hong Kong comic artists in China, they are very willing to engage with the academics as they also want to make known to public the difficulties of Hong Kong creative workers residing in China. Based on the vicissitudes of all these Hong Kong comic artists and investors working in different positions/ collaboration in China, we are able to conceptualize the Hong Kong-relocated-China model, the precarity of creative labor in China, and the strategies of China’s comic industry in relation to Hong Kong and globalization. The findings not only inform theories on cultural industries, creative labor and cultural policy but also help formulate policy recommendation for the government and the industry.

14402914.label: Major findings and research outcome
14402914.value: Research outcomes are mainly in the form of publications. At this moment when this report is done, there are already 2 refereed journal articles, 5 book chapters and 1 monograph secured (as indicated in Part C8). Research findings were also presented in various international conferences on cultural studies and communication and conferences in China, as seen in Part C9. There are 3 more journal articles which are under review. The journal article ranges from comics as creative industries (article appearing on International Journal of Communication) to comics as anchor of cultural identities in Hong Kong (article published in Global Media and China, and the ones being reviewed in Social Identities and Media, Culture and Society). Our interviews also revealed that the representation of comics can take different forms such as cosplay and secondary production (where fans create new stories based on the original comics). These new findings become additional refereed book chapters in important volumes. As our project proceeds, it is made known to international scholars who invited us to contribute our research output to their edited volumes. Besides, this project becomes the seed for international collaboration. Based on interviews about comic industry in China, joint Sino-Japanese and Korean production was discovered, and this new discovery of joint Asian media collaboration is a rising concern in the field. A journal article has been written jointly with the data in this project and that from an Australian scholar who works in the area of Asian comics, and the article is under review by Media Industry Journal. Second, as the topic concerned is about Hong Kong comic industry, as promised in the original proposal, Chinese publications are to be delivered for the local industry and those interested in the local creative industry (as a form of knowledge transfer). A Chinese monograph under a renown local publisher (Zhong Hua) will be published in 2018. To further enhance the policy impact, a series of articles are published in comic magazine and a professional article written in layman language in Media Digest for media professional. Besides, since the inauguration of the project, the PI has promoted the project in various occasion as guest of honor and judge (e.g. in the Hong Kong Ani-Wave Comic Award) to create the local impact. Third, a local Mphil student is trained and he also publishes the findings with the PI. Now the Mphil student proceeds to PhD studies.

14402914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14402914.value: First, in terms of research, although comics in Hong Kong is understudied, comics as creative industry has been becoming a rising international academic area, given the popularity of DC Comic, Marvel and so forth, and the adaptation of IP of comics into movies and games. In other words, comics, which is put under the perspective of creative industries as one of the key value-chains requires further research (in conjunction with animation, movies and games). Second, in the course of development of this project, the PI has met international research team who study comics (and animation) in China, Japan and Korea. Toward the end of this project, the PI was asked to join them as partner investigator to submit an Australian National Research Discovery Grant on China’s creative industries, and now the grant is awarded Third, while the PI was working on this project, he was invited by CreateHK to conduct a commissioned project on digital entertainment industry in Hong Kong (where comics is one of the seven areas). The data shows that the comic industry shows sign of revival. The PI now continues to work with CreateHK as a second phrase of this policy study to enhance this creative industry.

14402914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14402914.value: This study theorizes comics as creative industry which is a rising field of study, and highlights the emergent China market in which Hong Kong has to cope with. Based on interviews with the industry workers, this project concludes that there are divided views on comic development. For those longing for a perpetual survival of the comic business, these workers choose to relocate the production base to Guangzhou, Hangzhou and Beijing because of the attraction from and the availability of cultural clusters (or technology parks) that offer them extra benefits. Second, Hong Kong comic artists actively sell to China comics as intellectual property (IP) that evolves into new cultural forms such as mobile/ online game, animation and movies. While the advantage of these strategies is the considerable expansion of Hong Kong comic industry in China, there is fear that those Hong Kong comics developed in China will lose creativity and the Hong Kong legacy. On the contrary, there are a group of relatively younger artists who decide to remain in Hong Kong to continually produce local comics and online comics that celebrate the Hong Kong identities vis-à-vis China. Practically, the project offers possible policies that could facilitate its growth and development.

14403014.label: Project Objectives
14403014.value: To examine whether age differences in visual attention toward happy and angry stimuli would be moderated by the instrumentality of emotion (i.e., the matching of anger with confrontation, and happiness with collaboration), negotiation partner (kin, close friend, casual friend) and levels of interdependence
rows: To examine whether age differences in visual attention toward happy and angry stimuli would be moderated by the instrumentality of emotion (i.e., the matching of anger with confrontation, and happiness with collaboration), negotiation partner (kin, close friend, casual friend) and levels of interdependence

14403014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14403014.value: The literature on aging is generally silent about whether emotion aging is universal. Yet, my own prior work has documented that while Americans have shown preferential cognitive processing (e.g., attention and memory) of positively-valenced stimuli over negatively-valenced stimuli with age (known as the age-related positivity effect), Chinese do not do so (Fung et al., 2008, 2010). One possible reason for these cultural differences may lie in the goals that different cultural groups seek. If different cultural groups seek different emotional goals in life, and each does so more with age, then it makes sense that emotion aging may differ across cultures. Meanwhile, in the general literature on emotion, there is a theory on the instrumental approach of emotions (Tamir, Mitchell, & Gross, 2008). The theory argues that individuals are motivated to regulate their emotions not only by hedonic goals (i.e. the desire to feel good), but also by instrumental goals (i.e., the desire to use the emotion to perform a certain behavior). Supporting the theory, several experiments (e.g., Tamir, et al., 2008; Tamir & Ford, 2012) revealed that although the emotion “anger” was generally unpleasant and seemed to go against the hedonic goals, college students would favor anger over happiness, and would actively engage in activities to elicit anger when they were asked to imagine a confrontational situation that required this emotion. Conversely, asking college students to imagine a collaborative situation made them favor happiness over anger, and actively engage in activities to elicit happiness. In the proposed project, I aim at clarifying when, to whom and why the age-related positivity effect occurs by applying the theory and methodology of the instrumental approach of emotions to study age differences in visual attention toward angry and happy stimuli. Attention (fixation time) will be measured by eyetracking technology. I hypothesize that adults would show the age-related positivity effect in visual attention when they are put in collaborative situations that make happiness more instrumental. In contrast, adults would not show the age-related positivity effect, or even show an age-related increase in attention toward angry stimuli, when they are put in confrontational situations that make anger more instrumental. In addition, the moderating roles of the levels of interdependence of the individual, and the social relationship between the negotiation partner and the individual (kin, close friend or casual friend) will also be examined. 老年的文獻對情緒老化是否普遍通常都不着筆墨。我自己的研究结果則有記錄，隨年齡增長，美國人認知偏好(如注意力和記憶力)於正面效價的刺激多於負面效價的刺激(稱作跟年齡有關的正向情緒影響)，但中國人卻不盡是如此。(Fung et al., 2008, 2010)。這些文化差異可能是由於不同文化對不同目標的追求。如果不同文化追求不同的情緒目標，而且隨着年齡增加，那情緒老化便順理成章地會有文化差異。 與此同時，情緒文獻中有一個關於情緒調節的工具性理論 (Tamir, Mitchell, & Gross, 2008) 。該理論提出個人調節情緒的動機除了有享樂主義的目標 (即是渴望自我感覺良好)外，還有工具性的目標 (即是渴望用情緒來執行某種行為)。數個支持這理論的實驗(e.g., Tamir, et al., 2008; Tamir & Ford, 2012)顯示雖然“憤怒”的情緒普遍來说會令人不安，亦跟享樂主義的目標相違背，但大學生偏好憤怒多於快樂，當他們被要求想像需要這種情緒的對立局面時，他們會積極參與會引發憤怒的活動。相反，當他們被要求想像協作的情況時，他們會傾向快樂過於憤怒，並積極參與會引發快樂的活動，以引發快樂。 在此實驗中，我們會透過應用情緒調節在工具性角度的理論與實驗來研究對憤怒跟快樂注意力的年齡差異，我們的目標是要澄清何時，對誰，還有爲何跟年齡有關的正向情緒影響會發生。注意力（固定時間）會用眼球追踪技術來量度。我們預計當成年人在協作的情況下，當快樂的情緒更有作用時，他們在視覺專注中會有跟年齡有關的正向情緒影響。相反，在對立的情況下，當憤怒的情緒更有作用時，成年人不會有跟年齡有關的正向情緒影響，針對憤怒的刺激時專注力更可能會有跟年齡有關的增加。再者，個人的獨立程度，以及協商合作夥伴與個人（親屬，親密朋友或普通朋友）之間的社會關係兩者之調節角色也將被查究。

14403014.label: Realisation of objectives
14403014.value: We conducted a study to address the objective. We examined whether age differences in visual attention can be shifted by the instrumentality of emotion, such that (1) when the instrumentality of anger was primed in a confrontation condition, older adults would pay more attention to angry relative to happy facial expressions than did younger adults; (2) conversely, when the instrumentality of happiness was primed in a collaboration condition, the traditional age-related positivity effect would occur. Older adults would pay less attention to angry relative to happy facial expressions than did younger adults. We also tested whether the types of negotiation partner, including relative, close friend and casual friend, would moderate these age differences in visual attention. Method Participants 250 younger adults (172 females, aged 17-35, M = 20.03, SD=2.64) and 277 older adults (201 females, aged 60-85, M = 66.91, SD=6.97) from Hong Kong were recruited. Younger participants were recruited from a local university campus through advertisement and undergraduate subject pool. Older participants were recruited from the local community. Course credit or monetary stipends were given for their participation. Participants were excluded if they could not be calibrated due to droopy eyelids, frequent winking or other eye problems, or if they were not successfully tracked for 20% of area of interests. After this screening process, a total of 242 younger adults and 203 older adults were included for analysis. Stimuli Attention stimuli were slides that depict facial expressions. In each trial, the slide presented a neutral facial expression next to an emotional facial expression: anger, happiness, sadness or fear. There were 16 facial expressions for each emotion and in total 64 trials. Anger and happiness were the foci of this study while the other two emotions were filters. These emotional expressions had been validated by Isaacowitz and colleagues (2006a) for Americans and Fung and colleagues (2008) for Chinese. Procedure After signing an informed consent form, younger and older participants were randomly assigned to three manipulation conditions. Manipulation. To evoke participants’ desirability for anger or happiness, an experimental paradigm used in Tamir and Ford (2012) was adopted. Participant was told to imagine that he/she was a landlord but a tenant had not paid rent in two months. Hence, he/she needed to either collaborate (to evoke desirability for happiness) or confront (to evoke desirability for anger) with the tenant in order to settle the rent situation. Participants in the confrontation condition were told that their goal was to get the money back immediately, while participants in the collaboration condition were told that their goal was to maintain a long-term relationship with their tenant. Previous research has demonstrated that under the collaboration condition, individuals seek happiness whereas under the confrontation condition, individuals believe that anger is more desirable. In the control condition, participants were simply told to settle the rental situation without specifying a goal. To vary the types of negotiation partner, the participants were asked to imagine that the tenant was one of their casual friends, close friends, or relatives. Attention task. After the manipulation, all participants did an attention task. They were told, “Before recording a voice message to the tenant, we have a separate task that is completely unrelated to the rent settlement. We would like you to watch some pictures.” In the attention task, all stimulus were presented trial by trial on a 15-inch computer monitor located approximately 20 inches from the head of participants. At the beginning of the task, participants were instructed to look at the monitor as naturally as possible while moving as little as possible. Participants’ attention (gaze) toward the stimuli was tracked by ASL EYE TRAC 6 Desktop Eye Tracker. In this study, each facial expression on each trial was defined as an area of interest (AOI). The total duration of fixation within AOIs were calculated and is the key variable that we are interested in.

14403014.label: Major findings and research outcome
14403014.value: We examined the four-way interaction between age group, condition, target type, and the perceived need for anger relative to happiness (the score on the need for anger minus the score on the need for happiness). The results revealed that although the four-way interaction was not significant (p > .25), there was a significant three interaction between age group, condition and perceived needs (p = .04). Dissecting the three-way interaction, it was found that there was a two-way interaction between age group and perceived needs under the confrontation condition (p = .002), and this interaction was not significant under the collaboration condition (p = .23) or the control condition (p > .25). , Whereas there was no age difference in attention in the collaboration condition or the control condition (ps > .25), older adults in the confrontation condition paid more attention towards angry faces compared to happy faces than did younger adults (b = 7.45, SE = 3.22, p = .02). This finding is consistent with our hypothesis that, under the confrontation situation when anger is believed as useful, older adults pay more attention to stimuli that can potentially give rise to this emotion compared to younger adults. In addition, this age difference was moderated by the individuals’ subjective perception about the instrumentality of anger relative to happiness (b = -.06, SE = .02, p = .002). The simple slope analysis revealed that, at all levels of the perceived needs for anger relative to happiness (-1SD below, mean level, and +1SD above), compared to younger adults, older adults paid more attention to angry faces relative to happy faces (ps < .05), which is consistent with the main finding we discussed above. However, the magnitude of such an age difference was slightly mitigated as individuals’ perceived needs for anger increased (at -1 SD level, b = 7.57; at mean level, b = 7.37; at +1 SD level, b = 7.17). The non-significant four-way interaction suggested that the above results were not moderated by the types of negotiation partner. Taken together, our findings provide partial support for the hypothesis that it is the instrumentality of emotion that drives the age-related positivity effect in cognitive processing. We did not find that older adults were more likely to pay attention to happy facial expressions in the collaboration condition where happiness is more useful. But we did find that older adults were more likely to pay attention to angry facial expressions in the confrontation condition where anger is more useful. We have written up the above results in a manuscript and submitted it to a journal. In addition, the moderating effect of the needs of anger vs. happiness was packaged with some of studies not supported by this grant into another manuscript. This manuscript, Lu, Yang, Fung and Tamamura (2019), commented that experiencing positive emotions in intergroup conflicts might be perceived as unacceptable and discomfort among non-dialectical individuals. When such a feeling is evoked, it would magnify the negative responses toward outgroup members. Dialectical thinkers, by contrast, accept contradictory emotions. For them, positive emotions could buffer against the oppositional consequences of intergroup provocations. The manuscript was accepted by Emotion. Moreover, although valuing happiness did not affect age-related attention, it was related to subjective wellbeing. Data collected from this study were used to examine the associations between valuing happiness, self-construal and subjective wellbeing among younger and older adults. Such findings were written up as a manuscript that was accepted by Journal of Happiness Studies. Wong, Gong and Fung (2019) found that interdependence mediated the relationship between valuing happiness and subjective wellbeing among older adults but not younger adults.

14403014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14403014.value: One puzzle in the findings reported above is why we did not find any age differences in visual attention in the collaboration condition. This is not consistent with the age-related positivity effect that is typically observed in the literature. One possible explanation is that collecting rent from a tenant who has not paid rent for a few months is not a happy task, no matter how we frame it. Although participants may find it useful to use happiness in the situation (thus our manipulation check was successful), they do not see the need to look at happy stimuli to increase their genuine happiness. They simply “fake” smiles to handle the situation. Older adults may do so to a greater extent than do younger adults if the age-related positivity effect occurs. We had video-taped participants’ facial expressions while they were engaging in the negotiation task. We had purchased a FaceReader software that could code facial expressions according to the Facial Action Coding System. We will examine whether the rate of “non-genuine” smiles is higher in the collaboration condition than the other two conditions and whether it is higher in older than younger adults. In addition, what the participants said during the negotiation task was also recorded. We will analyze age by condition differences on the content of the conversation to shed light on how perceived instrumentality of emotion may influence age-related behavior.

14403014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14403014.value: For a number of years, cognitive processing was believed to universally decline with age. Later, some studies found that cognitive processing for pleasant stimuli was the same, or sometimes even better, among older adults than younger adults. Yet, studies outside the United States, including our prior studies on Chinese, occasionally do not replicate these findings, raising the possibility that emotion aging may differ across cultures. Meanwhile, the instrumental approach of emotions states that we are motivated to regulate emotions not only by a desire to feel good, but also by a desire to use it to perform a certain behavior. Some prior studies revealed that although “anger” was unpleasant, individuals would favor anger over happiness in contexts in which anger was experimentally manipulated to be useful. In this project, we adopted this paradigm to study age differences in visual attention toward angry and happy stimuli. We found that in confrontation context when anger was believed to be useful, older adults paid more attention to angry stimuli compared to younger adults. This provides some support for the hypothesis that as we age, we selectively retain our cognitive processing for stimuli that are useful to us.

14403214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14403214.value: The aim of the proposed project is to develop and evaluate a state-of-the-art school-based intervention, designed specifically for the Hong Kong context, to increase students’ physical activity (PA) levels in and out of school. In-service physical education (PE) teachers will be trained to implement the interventions during PE classes at their schools. In line with global PE development trends, the Hong Kong Education Bureau initiated a series of PE curriculum reforms to indicate the importance of promoting fitness for schoolchildren aged 6 to 18 (Curriculum Development Council, 2002; Education Bureau, 2013). Schools are important institutions for promoting PA and fitness in young people (Centers for Disease Control & Prevention, 2011) and the initiatives suggest that PE curricula should focus on students’ individual differences and learning interests. However, Hong Kong students often find traditional fitness activities tedious and boring (Ha, Sum, Chan, & Ng, 2013). Therefore, a student-centered approach, focusing on moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) should be planned and incorporated in school PE. According to self-determination theory (SDT; Ryan & Deci, 2002), students are more likely to engage, and persist, in activities that 1) are fun and enjoyable, and/or 2) provide outcomes that are valued by the individual. Therefore, the intervention proposed in this study aims to introduce atypical activities, such as rope skipping, which students consider to be fun (Ha et al., 2013), that are suitable for the unique environments of Hong Kong, and are of moderate-to-high intensity. Based on SDT, teachers will be trained to create classroom environments which support students’ psychological needs, thereby supporting more PA engagement through lifestyle changes. In-service teachers will be trained to implement the interventions at their schools. Teachers will be invited to attend workshops to learn how to teach the activities. Using a protocol adapted from Cheon, Reeve, and Moon (2012), teachers will also be trained to teach in more supportive ways (e.g., providing choice and meaningful rationales for the activities). The intervention will be evaluated based on students’ objectively measured physical activity levels during PE classes and in their leisure time. As PA levels in childhood and adolescence are related to that in adulthood, the intervention may support and maintain physically active lifestyles of students throughout their lifespans. This could have important implication for public health, such as reducing health-related issues including obesity and diabetes. 與國際教育趨勢接軌，香港教育局近年進行了一系列之課程改革，目標是要增強學童的體適能水平。然而，香港學童普遍認為傳統體能課活動較沈悶，而未能積極參與，最終不能達至預期學習的效果。根據self-determination theory (SDT)理論解釋，學生如覺得活動的內容有趣、或能從中得益（例如因完成目標而獲得滿足感），他們亦較傾向踴躍參與這些活動，從而得到相應之效果。是項計劃目的，旨在從學生的角度出發，將鍛練體能的元素融入一些較有趣味性的活動當中 （例如花式跳繩），從而設計一套以學生為本的體適能課程。體育教師亦會根據SDT理論的原則提供一個合適的學習氣氛，讓學生能愉快地學習，增進每日的運動量，繼而投入活躍健康的生活模式。 本研究計劃將邀請本地體育教師，透過參與一系列嶄新的教學工作坊，有效地將體適能教學融入一般的體育課中，藉以增強本地學童的體質。研究團隊將使用運動計量器及有關之量化工具，收集學生在不同時段的運動量數據，從而驗証不同教學法對增進學童體能水平的成效。

14403214.label: Realisation of objectives
14403214.value: All objectives stated in the original application have been achieved. Additional information regarding these outcomes are listed below: Objective 1: Develop a school-based intervention guided by self-determination theory that can be implemented by school PE teachers We designed and implemented a school-based intervention guided by self-determination theory at local secondary schools. Teachers from 26 schools were trained to provide the intervention at their school during physical education classes. After receiving the training, teachers implemented the intervention during eight physical education lessons in at least one of the classes they taught. Objective 2: Evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention in terms of changes in PA participation during and outside school PE classes Using a clustered randomized controlled trial, we examined the effectiveness of the intervention in terms of physical activity behaviours. Multi-level regression analyses were conducted to account for the clustering nature of the measured data. Results suggested that the intervention was successful in increasing students’ moderate-to-vigorous physical activity during school physical education classes. However, no changes in terms of leisure-time activity was found. Objective 3: Examine changes in students’ perceived teaching autonomy support Results suggested the intervention had no significant effects on students’ perceived autonomy support from teachers. Objective 4: Examine changes in students’ need satisfaction, motivation, and psychological well-being We found decreases in boys’ need satisfaction and psychological well-being from pre- to post-intervention. These constructs for girls, by contrast, did not change over time. In terms of motivation, results suggested that girls’ autonomous motivation increased from pre- to post-intervention. However, there were no changes in boys’ autonomous motivation. Objective 5: Examine changes in students’ intention to engage in physical activity There were no changes in students’ intention towards physical activity. Objective 6: Identify the essential determinants that affect students’ PA behaviors, and test a structural equation model based on self-determination theory Qualitative interviews were conducted with participating teachers and students. Individuals from both roles claimed the intervention brought new knowledge, variety, and enjoyment to existing physical education. Gamification of fitness activities also increased students’ motivation and enjoyment in these classes. Using structural equation modelling methods, we also tested a process model based on self-determination theory. Results suggested that the hypothesized model was supported. Specifically, we found that perceived autonomy support promoted need satisfaction, which was in turn related to more autonomous motivation and psychological well-being.

14403214.label: Major findings and research outcome
14403214.value: Researchers and practitioners have suggested that students should spend 50% of total lesson time in moderate-to-vigorous forms of physical activity. Unfortunately, none of the classes included in the current study met this target, suggesting intervention is required. In this study, we found that a simple and scalable intervention (i.e., applying a novel tool to physical education classes and improving teachers' interpersonal styles) was successful in increasing students' physical activity levels, while students also perceived the lessons to be more enjoyable. Results also suggested that self-determination theory is an appropriate theoretical framework to guide school-based interventions. Specifically, results from the current study supported the positive effects of psychological need satisfaction on both behavioural (i.e., moderate-to-vigorous physical activity) and affective (i.e., psychological well-being) outcomes. Methods to support students' competence, autonomy, and relatedness are imperative, and should be incorporated in physical activity interventions.

14403214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14403214.value: In the current study, we found that the designed intervention was successful in increasing students' activity levels during school physical education, yet the effects did not appear to carry over to leisure-time activities. Since leisure-time activities contribute to a larger proportions of health-promoting physical activity accrual, future intervention should also target participants' out-of-class activities. To this end, we have submitted proposals to the RGC for self-determination theory-based, after-school interventions to increase the activity levels of both primary and secondary schools students. One of these projects was successfully funded, and the other is currently under review.

14403214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14403214.value: Fitness activities, despite being important to enhance students' health-related fitness, are often disliked by students because they require much effort but, in most cases, is not fun or enjoyable. To enhance students' experience in such activities, a simple and novel intervention was designed to increase students' participation in such activities during school physical education. Specifically, using a simple tool to gamify fitness activities, and providing training to teachers to improve their training behaviours, students' activity levels during physical education classes was increased. Students' also reported finding such classes more enjoyable than those using more traditional approaches. Since the intervention does not involve expensive equipment or require a high level of expertise to operate, it is scalable and can be applied to many facets of physical education or sports training.
