14403514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14403514.value: A major developmental challenge for children and adolescents is to master their regulation of emotional expression – flexibly suppressing, amplifying, and/or substituting emotional displays as required by social contexts. Extensive research has documented emotion regulation aimed at minimizing personal pain and maximizing pleasure, but has less often acknowledged that expressions of emotion must also be regulated in the service of interpersonal goals. This project will address key shortfalls in research about youth’s emotion expression regulation and its links with social relationships. A combination of longitudinal and experimental methods, utilizing self-report and objective measures, will investigate developmental, relational, and cognitive processes that hinder or promote children’s flexible use of different strategies to regulate emotion expression. Whereas prior research has mostly focused on effects of (dys)regulation upon peer (age-mate) relationships, peer influences on youth’s expressive regulation are understudied. Children gradually shift from parent to peer interactions, however, meaning that peers likely operate as a socializing force affecting children’s regulatory abilities. Experiences of peer rejection may be an especially disruptive force upon children’s control over their emotional behavior, as rejection tends to evoke strong negative feelings, reduced self-control, and temporary cognitive impairments. Understanding the ways in which peers interfere with youths’ ability to regulate their expressive behavior in order to achieve social goals thus represents a major gap in knowledge, and has critical implications for interventions at various ages. I propose a model of reciprocal influence, in which experiences of peer rejection or acceptance affect youths’ abilities to flexibly switch between different emotion-regulatory behaviors as required by the social context. Failures and successes in regulation, in turn, affect the quality of children’s peer relationships. Perceived rejection might especially lead to dysregulation and rigidity in patterns of emotional behavior, which subsequently create further social difficulties. I further propose that child personality characteristics can account for different patterns of dysregulated behavior in the face of peer rejection. This project examines children’s regulation of emotional expression in face-to-face interactions with peers. Insights gleaned from this research will be shared with educators, practitioners, and families through activities aimed at promoting flexibility in youths’ context-appropriate regulation of emotional behavior. Whether to help youths maintain friendships or cope with rejection, examining how youths control their emotional expressions in peer contexts can address crucial gaps in knowledge about children’s social lives and positive adjustment. 兒童青少年發展過程中的一個重大挑戰是學會對情緒的表達進行調節：根據社會情境的需求來靈活地控制、釋放、轉換情緒的表達。很多研究都涉及情緒調節，但目標僅在於降低個體的痛苦感受及提升個體的愉悅感，卻較少提及情緒表達在服務於人際目標時必須需要進行調節的事實。本課題將解決以往對於青少年情緒調節及其與社會關係的聯繫方面的研究的重要缺陷。研究將結合縱向測量和實驗方法，使用主觀報告和客觀測量，用以考察那些能促進或阻礙兒童靈活使用不同策略來調節情緒的發展性、關係性和認知性過程。 儘管以往的研究多有關注不良的調節對同伴關係的影響，但同伴對於青少年情緒調節的影響卻還未被研究。當兒童的互動逐漸從父母轉向同伴的同時，也意味著同伴可能作為一種社會化的力量影響兒童的調節能力。而同伴拒絕則尤其可能成為兒童控制其情緒性行為的一種破壞性力量，因為拒絕可能引發強烈的消極感受，降低自我控制能力，以及導致即刻性的認知受損。理解同伴如何影響青少年的情緒行為調節能力進而達到一種社會性的目標，在當前的知識上是一種空白，對於不同年齡段青少年的行為干預有重要意義。 本課題提出一個雙向影響模型，該模型認為同伴接納或拒絕會影響青少年在一定的社會情境下靈活轉換與情緒調節相關的行為的能力。調節的成功或失敗，反過來也會影響兒童的同伴關係品質。對同伴拒絕的感知尤其可能導致情緒性行為的失調和僵化，並進一步引發社會化方面的困難。同時，本研究進一步提出，面對同伴拒絕，兒童自身的人格特點也會對行為失調的模式產生影響。 本課題將考察兒童在與同伴面對面的互動中的情緒調節行為。研究所得到的成果將通過活動的方式分享給教育者、實踐者，以及家庭，這類活動旨在提高青少年在與情境適切的情緒性行為調節方面的靈活度。無論是為了幫助青少年維持友誼還是應對同伴拒絕，考察青少年如何在同伴情境下控制自己的情緒表達，都能填補兒童社會生活和積極適應方面的知識的重要缺口。

14403514.label: Realisation of objectives
14403514.value: As of the mid-term progress report, the project had experienced obstacles in participant recruitment. Despite the PI’s efforts to attract partnerships with HK schools, insufficient space for conducting the research and long testing sessions for each participant decreased local enthusiasm for collaboration. Fortunately, after obtaining permission to move the project to Mainland China, the PI quickly forged agreements with two elementary and two junior high schools to collect three waves of longitudinal data. Agreements were made with other Mainland middle schools for collecting experimental data. Thus, despite initial challenges, we successfully completed the major data collection within the final 18 months of the project. To date, the following findings and activities have helped to realize project objectives: Objective 1: This project is the first to examine the concept of flexibility in expressive regulation among child and adolescent populations. Whether flexibility could even be reliably measured/observed in these age groups, and whether it would indeed show meaningful links with psychosocial functioning, constituted major research questions that were successfully addressed by the project. The project succeeded in developing and validating both behavioral/observational (Publication 1, Presentation 3) and self-report instruments (Publication1, Presentations 1 and 5) to examine regulatory flexibility. Studies also successfully differentiated flexibility from rigid tendencies toward certain regulation strategies, thus demonstrating both the existence and predictive value of this construct. Efforts to communicate findings to educators and practitioners are still ongoing. The planned mid-point expert meeting was not feasible in the absence of data/results, due to aforementioned recruitment delays. However, the PI recently chaired a well-attended international conference symposium on youth’s flexible emotion regulation (Presentation 6), combining studies from Hong Kong, China, and the USA to draw greater attention to this construct. We have also communicated results to educators, practitioners, and researchers via five presentations at international conferences on child and adolescent development. These talks covered different aspects of regulatory flexibility (suppressing vs. amplifying expressions, congruent vs. incongruent facial responses), short-term and long-term correlates (psychological well-being, social adjustment), different measures (observational coding, fEMG, self-report), and longitudinal and experimental designs. Two additional conference submissions are being prepared for 2020. The PI’s team has delivered one presentation (in Chinese) at each of the participating Mainland schools. The presentations educated teaching, counseling, and administrative staff (25-50 attendees per meeting) about regulatory flexibility, highlighted its major indicators, and summarized preliminary findings. These staff are responsible for approximately 3000 students across the different schools, providing opportunities for knowledge about regulatory flexibility and peer relationships to inform a large number of staff-student interactions in diverse contexts. Follow-up presentations covering the full project results are currently being scheduled for early Fall 2019 (following the dissertation defense of the trained PhD student). These follow-up presentations to teaching, counseling, and administrative staff will include a pamphlet for audience members summarizing the major findings, as well as suggestions for implementing related exercises and activities in classrooms. Finally, comprehensive research presentations about the project have been delivered to researchers and practitioners at the Adolescent Development and Social Psychology Departments of Utrecht University and The University of Amsterdam, respectively. These presentations (held in 2019) have served as a springboard for the start of collaborations on cross-cultural extensions of the present findings. Objective 2: The question of whether peer relationships indeed predict youth’s flexibility in emotion regulation comprises the most important theoretical innovation of the project, and was successfully addressed across several studies. Our in-revision paper (Publication 2, Presentation 5) finds that youth’s emotion regulation predicts better psychological functioning (e.g., lower depression, delinquency) and healthier peer relationships across youth from 9 to 16 years. Our longitudinal study (Publication 1, Presentation 3) assessed students from Grades 4-8. Despite this broad range, we found no major age differences links between peer relationships and youth’s regulation. Across late childhood and early adolescence, peer difficulties predict later impairments in emotion regulation. Experimental work in preparation (Presentation 1), conducted with 7th Graders, also demonstrates that peer rejection has causal effects on emotion regulation. Importantly, these effects were typically stronger than effects from emotion regulation to later peer relations. Overall, the results suggest that the entire period from late childhood to early adolescence is a setting in which peer difficulties impact regulatory functioning. The consistent observation of this effect across several studies and different developmental periods fulfills a major conceptual goal of this project. Considering that prior literature as mostly emphasized effects of (dys)regulation upon peer relationships, it is important to note that our findings challenge conventional wisdom regarding the predominant direction of influence. Objective 3: We examined personality moderators in several studies, although permission was granted to omit Experiments 1c and 2c (which aimed to examine personality moderators of responses to rejection) from the revised proposal in order to bring the budget in line with funds allocated by the RGC. In both our longitudinal project and across several experiments, Ego Resiliency (our proposed personality moderator) did not predict differential responses to peer rejection. However, our experimental research (Publication 3, Presentation 4) has identified youth’s dispositional needs for interpersonal belonging as a factor that systematically shapes adolescents’ abilities to enact specific facial responses to peers’ friendly and hostile emotional expressions. A longitudinal study currently in preparation has also identified youth’s social anxiety as a personality-based moderator of the over-time link from adolescent’s self-regulation to later peer acceptance. Specifically, youth with lower social anxiety show stronger positive associations between their emotional regulation and later friendship quality. This is an important finding, because the strength of over-time associations from regulatory functioning to peer acceptance were generally lower than anticipated, and increase substantially when this moderator is considered. Thus, our experimental and longitudinal work successfully identified personality factors that predict the strength of associations both from peer friendliness/hostility to youth emotion regulation, and from youth emotion regulation to the quality of peer relationships. Objective 4: The project successfully utilized both experimental and longitudinal research designs, as well as various forms of measurement (self- and peer-report, observational coding, and psychophysiological methods), to clarify the relationships between youth’s regulation of emotional expressions and their relationships with peers. Our in-press longitudinal study (Publication 1, Presentation 3) used a combination of observationally-coded videos of youth’s expressive regulation, self-reported friendship quality, and peer-reported popularity. Our in-review paper (Publication 2, Presentation 5) linked observationally-coded videos with a newly-developed self-report measure of expressive regulation that can be used in future studies to quickly and efficiently measure this ability in adolescent populations, and showed that this measure held significant relationships with psychosocial functioning. Our in-review experimental paper (Publication 3, Presentation 4) showed that youth’s self-reported dispositional needs for social belonging predicted their abilities to mimic and counter-mimic the friendly and hostile emotional expressions of their peers, as measured by facial electromyography (fEMG). Another in-reparation experiment (Presentation 1) utilized both observational video coding and adolescent self-report to demonstrate bi-directional relationships between peer relations and expressive regulation. Perhaps the most overall important finding of our research -- the identification of effects from peer interactions (i.e., friendship quality, peer status, and youth’s dispositional orientations toward their relationships) to youth’s emotion regulation capabilities (measured through both observational coding and self-report) -- was consistently found across various separate studies that each used different combinations of measurements and research designs.

14403514.label: Major findings and research outcome
14403514.value: In contrast to extensive prior research examining youth’s regulation of internal feelings, this project focused on youth’s ability to regulate external emotional expressions in accordance with contextual demands. The ability to flexibly switch between suppressing and amplifying emotional displays in a socially appropriate manner predicts healthy psychosocial functioning among adults, but is not well-understood among youth. This project investigated youth’s flexible regulation of emotion expression and its links with social relationships. Across several studies, we demonstrated that this flexibility is reliably measurable via both behavioral observation (Publication 1, Presentations 1, 3, 4) and youth self-report (Publication 2, Presentation 5). Multiple longitudinal and experimental studies then investigated whether peer relationships predict children’s short- and long-term regulatory flexibility. Prior research has mostly emphasized impacts of (dys)regulation upon peer relationships, but such effects were somewhat modest across our studies, and often qualified by personality traits and the type of peer relationship examined. While youths’ abilities to suppress their expressive behavior indeed predicted greater peer acceptance over time (Publication 1, Presentation 3), the project also consistently found strong effects of peer interactions upon youth’s regulatory functioning. Healthier peer relationships predicted increased regulatory flexibility and among youth aged 9-16 years (Publication 2, Presentation 5). Across late childhood and early adolescence, peer difficulties predict later impairments in both suppressing and amplifying emotional behavior (Publication 1, Presentation 3). Peer rejection also had causal effects on 7th Graders’ abilities to clearly express emotions (Presentation 1). Furthermore, adolescents’ needs and expectations within their peer interactions helped to shape their responses to emotional expressions of their interaction partners (Publication 3, Presentation 4); Adolescents who have stronger needs for social belonging are better able to modify their own facial responses to peers’ hostile and friendly emotions in ways that might maximize their social acceptance. Overall, the results suggest that the entire period from late childhood to early adolescence is a setting in which peers operate as a socializing force upon youth’s regulation of emotional expressions. Within this period, peers difficulties appear to have detrimental effects on the flexibility with which youth can deploy various regulatory strategies. The combined evidence supported a model of reciprocal influence, in which peer relationships affect youths’ abilities to flexibly switch between different regulatory behaviors. Failures and successes in regulation, in turn, affect the quality of children’s peer relationships. Perceived rejection might especially lead to dysregulated, rigid patterns of emotional behavior, which subsequently create further social difficulties.

14403514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14403514.value: Project extensions fall into three main areas: Examination of personality factors predicting regulatory flexibility, cross-cultural comparisons, and parents’ roles in promoting emotion regulation. A collaborative paper between the PI and Utrecht University, currently in preparation, examines adolescents’ social anxiety as a personality moderator of links between emotion regulation and friendship quality. This collaboration is the launching pad for a more extensive cross-cultural comparison of Chinese and Dutch youth. Our finding that expressive suppression was more strongly associated with peer relations than expressive enhancement (Publication 1, Presentation 3) might result from Chinese society’s valuing of emotional inhibition. A cross-cultural study to address this interpretation will be completed in 2020. Finally, an additional finding arising from the longitudinal dataset is that parents continue to impact youth’s emotion regulation (Presentation 2). Two papers in preparation respectively show that family emotional climate and parental monitoring behaviors impact youth’s internal and external emotion regulation. The PI will then submit a small-scale development grant in 2020 to pilot a more extensive investigation of parental influences on adolescent emotion regulation. This will form the basis of a GRF submission within two years that directly examines the roles of parents versus peers in promoting youth’s emotion regulation abilities.

14403514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14403514.value: Youth must regulate their emotional behavior in order to achieve interpersonal goals. Because some situations require suppression of emotional behavior (to avoid making a scene in public) and other situations require amplification of expressions (pretending to like a disappointing gift), youth must develop flexibility in the strategies used to manage emotional behavior across different social contexts. This project examined associations between youth’s expressive regulation and their peer relationships. Although prior studies have often implied that adolescents’ successes or failures in emotion regulation have effects on the quality of their peer relationships, results from both longitudinal and experimental studies actually suggest bi-directional influences: Failures and successes in regulation affect the quality of youth’s relationships with peers, and the quality of these relationships, in turn, affects youths’ abilities to flexibly switch between different emotion-regulatory strategies. In some studies, these associations depended on adolescent personality characteristics, such as their levels of social anxiety and needs for social belonging. Notably, effects from peer relationships to youth’s regulatory abilities were stronger and more consistent than the reverse associations. This finding suggests that educators and practitioners aiming to improve young people’s regulation of emotional behavior should focus on helping them to build supportive relationships with age-mates.

14403714.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14403714.value: 当代中国的博物馆文化

14403714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14403714.value: This project is an interdisciplinary study of museums and exhibitionary culture in China from the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976) to the present. It examines three interrelated topics: the politicization and reinscription of art and history museums during the Cultural Revolution, as well as the use of exhibitions in Red Guard movements; the afterlives of Mao-era museums in the era of reform and opening-up; and the establishment of new museums, both by the state and by private individuals, in China today. This research begins by tracing the trajectory of museums during the political turmoil of the Cultural Revolution. It takes Shanghai as its case study and examines this history from two perspectives. On the one hand, it asks how the curators and workers in the Shanghai Museum responded to the Red Guards’ “Attack on the Four Olds,” ultimately continuing its work in preservation and exhibitions. On the other hand, it studies the phenomenon of Red Guards’ using short-term exhibitions as a technique for political struggle. From the theme of Mao-era politicization, the next topic focuses on the depoliticization of Cultural-Revolution-era museums in the 1980s. The example studied here is the Landlord Manor Museum and its Rent Collection Courtyard sculptural series in Anren Township, Sichuan Province. The Landlord Manor Museum, created during the late 1950s and employed for “class education,” was presented with two challenges: how to reform its exhibits in “seeking truth from facts” and how to adapt to the economic imperatives of the reform era. The final section covers the current museum-building boom, both by local governments and by private individuals. The phenomenon of individual collectors establishing their own museums has coincided with a deep ambivalence in Chinese society over whether and how to commemorate China’s recent past. The politics of today’s museum culture will provide a framework for understanding how people can and cannot address their collective history. This project seeks to re-frame the cultural history of museums in the People's Republic of China, highlighting their importance as texts and as spaces. Through an interdisciplinary examination of the museum as a text—from its architecture to its artifacts, from its narration by docents to its reception by visitors—this research shows how museums contributed to historical and political understanding. By analyzing the use of the museum as a space, including private counter-narratives and the inclusion of unapproved artifacts, this project studies the boundaries of contemporary discourse on the past. 这是一项关于文化大革命（1966-1976）至当代中国的博物馆以及展览文化的跨学科研究，主要考察了以下三个相关领域：文革期间，被“政治化”与“再书写”的艺术和历史博物馆以及“红卫兵运动”中展览的功用；改革开放后毛时代博物馆的命运；当代中国由官方或者私人建立的新型博物馆。 首先，本文回顾了文革政治动乱中博物馆的发展历程。以上海作为个案，我从以下两个方面展开讨论。一方面，我探究了上海博物馆的馆员以及工作人员如何回应红卫兵“破四旧”的口号，并最终得以继续保留文物和持续展览。另一方面，我也关注“红卫兵”如何利用短期展览来开展政治批斗。 以四川省安仁镇的地主庄院和它的“收租院雕塑”为例，我的下一个议题关注毛时代“政治化”的展览馆在八十年代“去政治化”的倾向。创建于五十年代后期的地主庄院，在当时主要用于“阶级教育”，在此刻却面临两大挑战：如何改变布展的方式以求“实事求是“ 以及如何适应改革后的经济环境。 最后一部分中，我关注当代中国展览馆（包括官方以及私人展览馆）纷纷兴建这一现象。 私人收藏家建立展览馆反映了当代中国社会对这段文革历史的矛盾态度：是否该去纪念这段历史，以及如何纪念这段历史？当代展览馆文化中的政治亦有助于理解中国人是如何谈论以及被禁止谈论他们的“集体记忆”的。 通过着重突出博物馆作为“文本”以及“空间”的重要性，此项研究意在重组中华人民共和国展览馆的文化史 。运用跨学科的视角，我将博物馆从建筑到展品、从讲解员叙述到观众观感的各方面视为“文本”，以展示博物如何参与构建历史与政治认识。将博物馆视为空间（其中包括对个人“反叙事” 以及未陈列展品的分析），我探问了博物馆的“当代话语”与“历史事实”之间的边界。

14404514.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14404514.value: 跨亞洲女性論壇：情色/色情媒介與文化情感

14404514.label: Project Objectives
14404514.value: The study contributes to feminist cultural studies by analyzing women's uses of digital media and sexually explicit media from a cross-cultural perspective. The study will initiate empirical research about female erotica users in Hong Kong and the USA. It will critically investigate how experiences with sexually explicit media are impacted by cultural values and media technologies. The study will promote a knowledge of women's attitudes within specific cultures and cross-culturally. Rather than relying on universalizing claims about the impact of sexually explicit media, it will conduct research about media usage within specific cultural environments. Since most discussions of pornography have been dominated by Western scholars, the study will be a platform to enhance East Asian and Chinese participation. The study will organize outreach activities and share information with non-academic communities about gender/sexuality alongside evolving cultural art forms, media technologies, and legislative proposals. The study will lead to a website and the publication of a journal issue about the topic of women and sexually explicit media. We will seek collaboration with a major journals such as Sexualities, Porn Studies, Participations, Inter-Asia Cultural Studies.

14404514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14404514.value: This study proposes a cultural studies framework for examining Hong Kong Chinese and American women’s experiences with sexually explicit media and digital media networks. The study will analyze how sexually explicit media are sensed and consumed within a post-cinematic and Trans-Asian framework of cultural affect. The post-cinematic framework allows women to access a wide range of sexually explicit media, to browse, select, archive and share movies produced within different cultures and media industries. But despite this ease of access, women's erotic agencies are also influenced by cultural affect--the feelings of fondness or aversion that they have towards local or global cultural aesthetics and values of social-political change. The study will analyze if and how women construct cultural affect around their digital agencies and preferences for sexually explicit media. The two cultures were chosen because of their different ways of implementing or resisting feminist/queer movements, and because of a high degree of interconnectivity through histories of migration, global media and commerce. The study also builds on a previously established thesis in the health sciences that women would adopt a "drifting gaze" around sexually explicit media. (Chivers, 2004) Women cannot easily identify with male-oriented sexually explicit media and their models of arousal, instead seeking out alternative products as well as novel ways of constructing affect. In a pilot study funded by a Direct Grant at Chinese University of Hong Kong, based on preliminary focus groups in Hong Kong and the USA, we found that Hong Kong Chinese and American women are searching for alternative products to hard-core pornography. It was made clear that they are seeking out women-friendly and queer erotica products, while also reorganizing strategies of gaining cognition and affect around these products. Additionally, it was found that women often refered to cultural aesthetics and social issues when explaining their erotic preferences. We would like to propose a long-term research project on women's porn/erotica cultures and strategies of cultural affect around digital media networks. The long-term goal study would be to involve a wide range of East-Asian and Western cultures and networks of feminist scholarship around art and sexually explicit media. In this regard, we would like to set up a Trans-Asian research network for academic communities and art/activist networks who are interested in discussing aspects of cultural/artistic representation as well as sexually explicit media, censorship and social change. 本研究在文化研究的框架下檢視香港、中國大陸和美國女性對情色/ 色情媒體和電子媒體網路的使用經驗。研究將會分析，在當下這個文化傳播受到後影像技術和跨亞洲網絡影響的時代，含有情色/ 色情內容的媒體如何受到審查又如何為受眾消費。 今天，由於後影像時代的發展和普及，女性可以接觸到大量含有情色/ 色情內容的媒介。她們能夠在不同的文化與媒體之間瀏覽、選擇、存儲和分享這些影視產品。然而，雖然女性已經可以輕易獲得這些產品，但她們的色情主體性同時也被文化情感影響——文化情感是指女性對於本土或全球文化審美取向和社會政治政治的認同或背離。這項研究著重分析女性面對情色 /色情內容時，是否及如何建立其媒介能動性和興趣偏好。我們選擇了中美兩種不同的文化，是因為它們在實施或抵抗女性主義/ 酷兒主義運動方面有一定差異；同時，由於移民、媒介和商務在兩國及全球範圍內的流動，中美兩種文化的連接也愈來愈緊密。 Meredith L. Chivers等健康科學領域的學者發現，女性觀看含有情色/ 色情內容的媒介產品是，往往會有一種“游移的凝視”：女性很難輕易認同男性導向的情色媒介及其呈現的性刺激模式，她們會自發尋找不同於男性導向型的替代媒介，也會探索她們自己在這方面建立文化情感的新鮮方式。在香港中文大學直接資助的一項研究中，我們在香港和美國兩地進行的焦點小組，發現兩地的女性都在搜尋非主流的情色 / 色情媒介來替代硬色情產品。研究清楚表明，女性會搜集取悅女性的色情內容和酷兒色情內容，並在觀賞這些內容時，在認知和情感上獲得滿足。另外，我們也發現女性闡釋自己對於情色內容的偏好時，常常會談論到相關的文化審美和社會議題。 本研究的長期目標是希望能夠觸及更多位於東亞和西方的文化群體，並且溝通和連接致力於色情媒介與藝術研究的女性主義學者。我們更計劃建立一個跨亞洲的研究網路，為學術社群和藝術家、社會活動家社群提供一個平台，協助他們就色情媒介、內容審查和社會文化變化等相關議題展開深入而廣泛的溝通和協作。 --

14404514.label: Realisation of objectives
14404514.value: In regards objectives 1. 2. and 3. the GRF study has made a contribution to feminist cultural studies by doing research about female-oriented pornographies and about women's usage of sexually explicit media within two different cultural environments, Hong Kong and the USA. At a first stage the study, as explained in a previous report, the study set out to examine cultural environments and cultural differences in regards to pornography usage and how women express states of affect around sexually explicit media. I conducted my fieldwork in San Francisco and Hong Kong and found that there are very different types of porn/sex industry and bodily aesthetics, but also different emotive reactions to mediated acts of sexualization. As I explained in greater detail in my book "The Afterglow of Women's Pornography in Post-Digital China "(Palgrave Macmillan 2015) women in Hong Kong and China rely on different cultural styles and media to understand and express fantasies around queer sexuality. Queer women and feminists in the USA have started participating in online porn industries and associated activist-oriented networks, where as queer women and feminists in Hong Kong are less enamoured with porn aesthetics and do not engage in a similar kind of sexual self-expression. Nonetheless, as I have further speculated in a forthcoming article "Women's Sex/Porn Sanctuaries and Political Activism in Hong Kong and San Francisco," each culture has asserted a need for female-focused and queer sex entertainment and has actualized different types of political activism around pornography. In regards to objective 4. 5. and 6, I would like to mention three important contributions. 1. There was an international academic event that I co-organized as part of the GRF study, which focused specifically on Sexualities and Sexualized Media in the East-Asia region. In May 2016 I held an international symposium "Gender/Queer Sexualities and Digital Activism," which focused on emerging technologies of feminism and queer activism in and around digital media and social networks. The symposium was a part of the International Symposium on Electronic Arts (ISEA) 2016 and took place at Art & Culture Outreach on 17 May 2016. (https://www.vcs.crs.cuhk.edu.hk/digital-sex).The symposium invited international and local scholars and activists to present critical views about the role of media and technological innovation in experiences with sexuality, gender and social activism. Scholars also presented papers sexually explicit media as a wide range of tools and media practices embedded within cultural environments. 2. Secondly, I started a collaboration with two other scholars of sexually explicit media, Alexandra Hambleton and Thomas Baudinette, in order to edit a forthcoming issue of the academic peer-reviewed Routledge journal Porn Studies. The issue will be devoted to East-Asian Pornographies and Online Porn Cultures and will include articles about feminist and queer pornography. We will start solliciting essay abstracts and papers in Spring 2018. We will invite authors to rethink the cultural impact of pornography as audio-visual and online media from an East Asian perspective. The issue will specifically focus on pornographies made and consumed in and across Japan, Korea, China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. The overall aim of the special issue will thus be to think through how the lived experience of producing and consuming various pornographies throughout East Asia may extend, nuance, challenge, or even affirm the dominant Euro-American understandings of pornography that are becoming increasingly axiomatic within pornography studies as an emerging interdisciplinary field of study. 3. In regards to objective 6, I worked with research assistants and web designers to develop and publish a major website www.womenspornographies.com. The website intends to make some aspects of the research available to wider audiences and to present it in a visually appealing manner. The website has an introductory video that explains the project, while there are several webpages that show samples of my fieldwork in San Francisco and Hong Kong. I also have developed several webpages that give background information about sex culture and pornography in Hong Kong and in mainland China. Finally there is a webpage with academic references and news articles about the topic of the GRF study.

14404514.label: Major findings and research outcome
14404514.value: 1. I have shown in my book "The Afterglow of Women's Pornography in Post-Digital China" (Palgrarve Macmillan, 2015) that women in Hong Kong and mainland China involved in porn production and consumption have started taking into account sexual differences, sex-positive feminisms and various developments towards queer aesthetics. Rather than thinking of pornography as male-oriented sexual entertainment based on neo-liberal reform, this book posits how and why women in Hong Kong and China are divulging social imaginaries around sexually explicit media and sex/gender politics. 2. One might think that social/political movements are divorced from changes in sex entertainment and porn industry, but the cross-cultural fieldwork in Hong Kong and San Francisco shows that the opposite could be the case. By surveying producers and consumers in Hong Kong and San Franscico, it is shown that porn innovation is indeed related to legacies of civil rights and democracy movements. I have further detailed this claim in my forthcoming publication "Women's Sex/Porn Sanctuaries and Social Movements in Hong Kong and San Francisco," which will be published in Porn Studies in Spring 2018, 3. In Hong Kong the study presents a network of sex innovators who are at the frontier of feminist sex retail and education and who also strongly believe in political activism. They talk about their mission to serve sexual minorities and diversify Chinese sex entertainment, but they are skeptical about the Euro-American aesthetics of queer pornography. Instead they are at the frontier of a new type of independent sex education in which pornography and sexualized media will play a major role. These young Chinese activists and sexperts testify about being burdened by restrictive bodily norms and tastes of the mainstream Chinese culture, and about how censorship practices are affecting local sex culture and porn retail. 4. The San Francisco advent of queer porn has grown out of decades of civil rights and anti-censorship activism and radical types of sex education involving pornographic self-representations and community outreach. At the same time it is shown that these advances in alternative sex culture have almost always been threatened or displaced by burgeoning corporate tech companies as well as overly adamant political opposition. These forces have intensely shaped the relative distribution of feminist and queer pornography while also proving to be highly stimulating topics of conversation.

14404514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14404514.value: This study and its research outcomes have launched a Chinese and East-Asian perspective on feminist and queer porn studies. The field of pornography studies has matured into a vigorous and interdisciplinary academic field with a peer-reviewed journal Porn Studies, which is owned and managed by the academic publisher Routledge. At the same time the field is still dominated by Euro-American scholarship and questions of online industry, feminism, sex activism and porn affect are most often not considered outside western cultural contexts. There is still a need for this kind of research to open up further to non-western cultures and their different types of sexually explicit art forms and media policies. To carry out this mission, I co-organized an international symposium on the topic of Gender/Queer Sexualities and Digital Activism in Hong Kong with a specific focus on sexually explicit media. I will now follow up with a themed-issues of the journal Porn Studies, entitled "East Asian Pornographies and Online Porn Cultures." A Call For Papers will be issued in January 2018 and we will sollicit and edit peer-reviewed essays to be published in 2019/2020.

14404514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14404514.value: This research study focuses on women's attitudes and states of affect around pornography within different cultural environments. It is often assumed that women are guided by cultural biases and negative states of affect, but the study has found that both both American and Hong Kong Chinese women have developed complex attitudes and a unique "pornosphere." One of the most important themes that was further explored is women's pornographies in relation to civil rights and social activism. In the USA women believe that porn and sex industries should be developed around questions of ethical labor and LGBTQ activism. In Hong Kong women believe less in the transformative power of porn industry, but they do profess a new sex-positive type of retail and sex education. As such women's participation in civil rights and feminist and queer sex culture will have a lasting impact on the future of pornography in Hong Kong, East Asia and the USA.

14404814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14404814.value: This study zooms into several villages and towns in northern Jiangsu and Anhui provinces in the 1940s and early 1950s to decipher how individuals and communities perceived and engaged with the momentous transformations of the time. This area was central to the contestation between several armed states (Nationalist, Communist, Japanese, Collaborators) because of its strategic significance to the control of the Lower Yangzi Delta; and the results of this conflict, some would contend, were crucial to the rise of the Communists. Yet, the aim of this study is not to re-kindle earlier debates about Communist success and “peasant revolution.” It is animated by a concern that the resulting justifiable skepticism about “the people” as a force in history and the historiographical turn away from rural China has led to a pervasive lack of interest in most people living in China at this time. This project will look for the history of common Chinese people during the mid-twentieth century era of war and revolution through an examination of the world as they saw it as members of their families, local village communities and social-environmental sub-regions. This was the era of the great process through which most of China – that is rural Chinese communities -- became integrated with the modern Chinese state that itself was in its formative period. Influenced by the historical anthropology studies and sub-regional religious studies of late imperial China and French micro-histories of rural society, this study seeks to illuminate processes of local state-society formation in village-centered history. The core question is: what was the experience and contribution of people in these local communities to the processes of their integration into the modern state? Aware of the common critiques of micro-history, this study considers vital local links to distant metropoles (Shanghai, Nanjing) and the role of multiple external players. Yet it retains a consistent focus on 1) competing local power-holders and social organizations (mainly lineages and religious societies) in specific socio-economic contexts, and 2) the specific cultural mentalities of villagers, their values and priorities, including their interest in defending their territories and patrimony from external human and spiritual forces. If the homogenized construct of “the people” was employed by the state to enforce power in the localities, there is also a history of local people contributing to the construction of power-relations between the locality and the modern Chinese state. 本研究以40年代和50年代初的江蘇北部和安徽省幾個鄉鎮為重點，分析個人和社區如何參與大變遷和對這些變遷的看法。 由於長江三角洲是一個重要戰略地區，因此江北區域是幾個武裝派別，亦即國民黨、共產黨、日本軍與汪偽政府之間的重要戰場。 有些學者可能會爭辯說，這場衝突的結果對共產黨的崛起至關重要。 然而，這項研究的目的並不是要重新辯論共產黨的成功和“農民革命”。 反而，因為由此產生了懷疑過“人民”作為一個歷史的力量，所以歷史學研究對中國農村普通民眾普遍缺乏興趣。本項目試圖應對這種趨勢，研究二十世紀中葉時期日常村民的歷史，以及他們作為當地農村宗族、協會、社區和社會環境的子區域的成員，如何在戰爭與革命中生活。 在40年代和50年代，中國大部分農村地區跟正在形成的現代國家治理系統成為一體結構。 這項研究受三個主要研究方法影響，包含歷史人類學研究、地方宗教研究與法國學派的微觀地方史研究。 因此，從村民的角度來看，本項目將考察當地國家政權與地域社會的關係的歷史形成過程。 核心問題是：什麼是經驗和人在這些地方社區的一體化進程到現代國家？意識到針對微觀地方史研究的共同批評，本研究考慮重要的地方連結到遙遠的大都市（上海，南京）和多個外部參與者。 然而，本研究保留了一貫注重 1 ）本地官方與社會組織（主要是宗族和宗教團體）之間的競爭發生在特定的社會經濟環境；2) 村民特定的文化心態，他們的根本信仰和優先事項，包括他們在捍衛自己的領土和遺產的興趣。 雖然國家政府為了在各種地方統一構建執行權力，利用了所謂“人民”範疇，其實我們也可以確定普通人民在當地與現代中國的權力關係的形成歷史作出了貢獻。

14404814.label: Realisation of objectives
14404814.value: From the standpoint of advancing my research agenda, this grant was enormously helpful and will result in a major monograph, several articles currently, and a subsequent book that synthesizes my scholarship with comparable cases, all of which are now in process. During the years of the grant, these funds made possible my multiple fieldwork and archival trips/visits that were at the basis of my fundamentally transforming my approach to historical research. In that sense, it was critical also to my training of multiple PhD students (currently 7 in process) in these methods, as well as to making possible my leading role in a major collaborative research project (including organizing, leading and producing papers for 3 workshops and 1 major conference), as well as an international trans-disciplinary symposium, and also the writing, compiling and editing of a research methods guide collected volume (contracted for publication in late 2019 or early 2020). I have also been invited to publish two of my conference papers in prominent international journals. Of course, in terms of what is to be reported in this form, it is a fact that I spent less than half of the grant funds and have no publications in print yet from this project. The reasons for the limited spending are that: 1) my multiple research trips cost less than anticipated, especially once I gained traction in northern Jiangsu; 2) I should have applied for teaching relief instead of other options -- I needed more time than money -- (though my administrative duties also limited that possibility); 3) other funds jointly applied for with my collaborators covered the costs of the workshops, conference, and symposium I organized. As to the publications, quite frankly, this kind of historical research with fieldwork and archives, not to mention writing a worthwhile book and articles with it, takes a lot of time and cannot be rushed if it is to be done properly. I have been invited to publish my work with prominent international publishers and journals, but do not wish to publish prematurely just for the sake of grant reports or annual assessments. Within the next few years, I will publish this work in a form that I hope will have lasting and widespread impact in my field, and I will thank the RGC.

14404814.label: Major findings and research outcome
14404814.value: The major findings extend far beyond my expectations. I have re-thought the original questions and the basis on which they were asked. I did so as I learned a new method and honed in on a specific core region of northern Jiangsu -- the Huaibei area-- that I have come to know increasingly well from the "ground up." A major realization in this kind of micro-study is the extent to which the generalizations to most historical characterizations about these areas are, in effect, caricatures produced by powerful outsiders for their own purposes. They tell us little about the understandings and experiences of, and consequences for, local people. My studies illuminate this phenomenon and seek to relate not only what happened in local communities, but how mentalities centered on the imaginative, moral, and social-relational concepts and logics of family, ancestor, territory, spirits, gods and nature in particularly challenging conditions produced and perceived sustained change at the local level during the tumult of the twentieth century. Trying to understand modern history without appreciating how people lived in their local way, the Huaibei way in this case, misses and distorts far too much. Current dominant narratives of war, modern-state building and revolution in modern Chinese history incorporate little of what is evident in these local histories. Whether it is the matter of the emergence of modern education and cultural forms, notably relating to the roles of women, youth and family, the external demands and ideological interventions of modern nation, state, and economy building, the crises of violence and catastrophe in the 1920s and 1940s, or the imposition of Maoist socialism in the 1950s, the local processes churning through varriations in ecology and district, tensions between and within clans and territorial alliances, rural villages and major towns, and the reasoning of everyday ethics, rituals, customs and social norms and practices produced multiple fissures and ultimately remade all these themes in locally relevant ways. Powerful outsiders had a part in this, but all conflicts, including the crisis of wartime occupation, played out in escalations of horrific internicine local warfare the devestating consequences of which have to be viewed at the family and village level. Adaptation for survival in such local communities is one of the least understood and consequential historical developments and engines of change. in the story of modern China.

14404814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14404814.value: The project has been and will be ongoing for several more years. I will be completing the revision of two papers for publication in the coming months. I continue to work on writing the major monograph that examines the Huaibei region from its rural core in Shuyang county from the late Qing to the 1970s. I plan to submit the manuscript to Yale University Press (which has first rights) before the end of 2020. As local historians of this topic continue to visit and work with me and invite me back to this area, I will likely produce further work on new research beyond the intitial monograph. But I have already begun a project to compare my explanation of local rural transformations in Huaibei (northern Jiangsu) with comparably "troubled" local areas researched by other scholars (mostly in China) along with some of my new research in northern Anhui, southwestern Henan and upland Hubei that I have begun at my own expense. This will result in a readable synthesis -a book of about 200 pages -- that places these "troubled lands" at the center of the narrative of the twentieth century incorporation of the rural into the modern Chinese nation-state.

14404814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14404814.value: On the basis of a meticulous local study of a "peripheral" rural region known largely for its "backwardness," "ungovernability," and "violence," this research brings to light the rich human complexity to the local Huaibei area rural people's struggle to live, adapt, and survive the tumult of China's twentieth century. Seen at this level of the local, the village, and the family and in their cultural terms, the fissures and fusions that formed modern China look entirely different from the well-known national, provincial or even broadly regional perspective. In regions like northern Jiangsu, the "people's history" of China was a local one, sorted out in local contexts in ways that have had long-term consequences for China even now in the twenty-first century.

14405114.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14405114.value: 改良道德、革新社會：民國時期耶穌會小說與戲劇研究(1912-1937)

14405114.label: Project Objectives
14405114.value: To make a pioneering investigation of the Chinese fictional and dramatic literature published by the Jesuit presses in the Republican period. To supplement a missing chapter in the history of Chinese Christian literature of the early twentieth century. To probe into the moral/religious dimensions and impacts of these Jesuit works against the background of the social/political movements in the Republican era, for instance, "renge jiuguo" (national salvation by character) in the 1920s. To stimulate scholarly discussion and further research in the field by publishing three or four academic articles.

To supplement a missing chapter in the history of Chinese Christian literature of the early twentieth century.

To probe into the moral/religious dimensions and impacts of these Jesuit works against the background of the social/political movements in the Republican era, for instance, "renge jiuguo" (national salvation by character) in the 1920s.
To stimulate scholarly discussion and further research in the field by publishing three or four academic articles.

14405114.label: Realisation of objectives
14405114.value: The current project has achieved all the four proposed objectives in the following manner: Firstly, this project constitutes the first critical and comprehensive attempt to investigate the Chinese fictional and dramatic literature published by the Jesuit presses during the Republican period. By taking research trips to several European and Chinese archives and libraries (including the Archives de la Province de France de la Compagnie de Jésus, Paris; Bibliothèque Municipale de Lyon, France; National Library of China; Peking University Library; Shanghai Library), the Principal Investigator has made exciting discoveries of the rare collections of primary materials consisting of three major types of texts: first, Chinese translations of French Catholic novels; second, original novels composed by Chinese Jesuits; and third, Catholic plays, which chiefly were dramatic adaptations of biblical narratives and hagiographies. Most intriguingly, some biblical tales were creatively represented in a variety of dramatic genres, including traditional Chinese opera, folk performing arts, and modern spoken drama. These performative texts were periodically put on stage in Catholic churches, schools, and orphanages during religious festivals and celebrations. The staging of biblical dramas performed important religious functions: dramatizing the history of salvation, providing edified entertainment, facilitating community building and transformation, and presenting the Catholic Church as a morally relevant and socially engaging community in the Republican Chinese society. New light has been shed on the Chinese reception and transformation of the Bible through dramatic texts, and the ritualistic function of dramatic performances. Secondly, this project has supplied an overlooked yet important chapter in the history of Chinese Christian literature. The Jesuit missionaries during the late Ming and early Qing era produced a substantial corpus of Chinese Catholic literature, which contributed to the introduction of Greco-Roman poetics and Chinese literary modernity. Our understanding of the history and literature of the Chinese Catholic Church, however, has long been dominated by the earlier period. Taking a broader perspective, the study of Chinese Christian literature in the late Qing and early Republican periods has chiefly focused on the Protestant works, leaving the examination of Catholic literature a largely missing chapter. In fact, the Catholic missions resorted to literary means for their proselytizing endeavours in the late Qing and Republican periods. By highligting the significance of Catholic literature in the Republican era, this project has balanced the overarching emphasis on the study of late-Ming/early-Qing Catholic literature and late Qing/early Republican Protestant literature. Thirdly, this project has broken new ground on the study of religious literature and its moral and social functions, particularly in the Chinese cultural context of the early twentieth century. With the collapse of imperial regime in 1911, the Republic of China saw an urgent need to establish new moral, social and political orders. With a vividly moralistic and religious emphasis, some Catholic novels intended to contribute to the construction of the new moral and social orders of the Republic of China by means of Catholic ethics and values. These novels, for example, Xiaonü jiufu (孝女救父 The Filial Girl Saves Her Father, 1917) and Nü junzi (女君子 A Noble Woman, 1923), attempted to infiltrate Catholic thoughts and virtues, in conjunction with traditional Chinese ones, such as chastity, filial piety, forgiveness and reconciliation, for the edification and moral transformation of the Chinese readers. The preface of Daozhen Lai Hua (道眞來華 Daozhen Comes to China, 1916), from the series of original novels, further elaborated the far-reaching impacts of fiction: “A work of moral fiction serves as an effective tool for social reform. Its enchanting narrative and elegant wording will not only enlighten the mind, but also touch the heart of the readers. Encountering the virtues of loyalty, filial piety, chastity and righteousness, the readers would imitate; perusing the stories of the wicked and malicious, they would detest. The gradual transformation of people’s mind and moral constitutes the key to national strengthening.” The social relevance and significance of these Jesuit works becomes more prominent when they are examined against the cultural, social and political landscape of the early Republican era, notably the May Fourth new literary and cultural movements, the advocacy of renge jiuguo (人格救國national salvation by character), and the anti-imperial/anti-Christian movements in the 1920s. Finally, the Principal Investigator has published one refereed monograph, one annotated volume of dramas, four refereed journal articles, and presented five conference papers/public lectures, much more productive than the original anticipated output of three to four articles. The in-depth examination of representative Chinese Catholic dramas and novels in the monograph and articles have helped to draw some theoretical observations for a deeper understanding of the Chinese reception and transformation of the Bible through fictional and dramatic texts; the ways in which Catholic thoughts and ethics conveyed and contextualized in these texts; and the Chinese Catholic writers’ approaches to resolve the cultural, moral, and religious conflicts in the literary endeavours. Furthermore, the annotated volume has made the rarely known works of Chinese Catholic dramatic texts readily accessible to the academic world. The republication of these priceless primary texts will be of considerable value to scholars of the history of Catholicism in China and of modern Chinese literature.

14405114.label: Major findings and research outcome
14405114.value: Published by Brill (Leiden) in their reputable Studies in Religion and the Arts series, my monograph "Sketching the Sacred: Literary Representations of Christianity in Late Qing and Republican China" argues for the “literary turn” in the study of Chinese Christianity by foregrounding the importance of literary texts, including the major genres of Chinese Christian literature (novel, drama, poetry and folkloric literature) of the late-Qing and Republican periods. By including both the Protestant and Catholic literature, this book has thrown some new lights on the emergence of different genres and different literary emphases within the Protestant and Catholic churches in China. It has supplemented an overlooked yet important chapter in the history of Chinese Christian literature by balancing the previous emphasis on the study of late-Ming/early-Qing Catholic literature and late Qing/early Republican Protestant literature. The pioneering volume 古聖若瑟劇本──民國天主教聖經戲劇選輯 (Gusheng Ruose Juben: An Annotated Anthology of Chinese Catholic Biblical Plays of the Republican Period) collected and elaborately annotated nine representative works of Chinese Catholic biblical plays published in the Republican era. This volume has made the invaluable primary texts much more accessible to scholars in the fields of Christianity in China and of modern Chinese literature, particularly the study of religious dramas. The four refereed journal articles have explored new research themes and approaches by doing a critical textual analysis of several pieces of under-researched Chinese Catholic dramas, for instance Majiabai’a zhuan 瑪加白阿傳 (The Story of the Maccabees, 1918). The Chinese playwright, well aware of the contesting moral values in the Chinese cultural contexts, adopted some dramatizing strategies to resolve the moral dilemma among most Chinese audiences in the process of rewriting the martyrdom narratives in the text. The dramatization of biblical and martyrdom stories in Chinese were employed as a tool of religious education in Catholic families and schools. The performing of the dramatic texts on martyrdom also contributed to the identity building of the Chinese Catholic community as a distinctive group on the borders of the mainstream Chinese society. From a broader perspective, the making of martyrdom in Chinese Catholic dramatic texts and the performance of martyrdom stories in China facilitated the “re-membering” of not only the Western saints into the Chinese church but also the Chinese martyrs into the universal Catholic Church.

14405114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14405114.value: On the basis of the substantial research findings of the current project, further research could be undertaken to examine the ways in which the Chinese Jesuit literature of the Republican era distinguish from, or inherit, that of the late-Ming and early-Qing periods, in terms of its literary features and religious discourse. In this connection, the Principal Investigator may explore the possibility of having academic collaboration with Prof. Wallace Sher-shiueh Li of Academia Sinica (Taiwan), who is the leading expert in the field of the Chinese Jesuit writings in the late-Ming and early-Qing periods. Li’s voluminous scholarly works have convincingly argued that the early Catholic missionaries engendered the introduction of Western poetics and Chinese literary modernity. A potential collaborative project with Prof. Li may further contribute to complementing, if not revising, traditional accounts about the spread of Catholicism in China, the development of new Chinese literary genres and vernacular language, through the lens of Chinese Catholic literature during the late-Ming, Qing and Republican periods.

14405114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14405114.value: This project has undertaken a pioneering investigation of the fictional and dramatic literature published by the Jesuits in China during the Republican era. The early Republican era could be considered a transitional period, when the imperial regime and political system had been dismantled, but the new cultural and social orders had not yet taken definite shape. The publication of several series of Chinese Jesuit fiction and drama, with a total of over 60 works, attempted to transform the religious landscape, morality and social order of Republican China by means of Catholic ethics and values. The project has made three major academic contributions. Firstly, it has filled in an overlooked yet crucial chapter in the history of Chinese Catholic literature by balancing the overarching emphasis on the study of late-Ming and early-Qing periods. Secondly, it has thrown new light on the broader issues relating to religiously inspired literature and its moral and social functions. Finally, the project has deepened our understanding of the history of Chinese literary modernity and intercultural communication. The academic implications of this project for both the modern Chinese literary, intellectual, and religious history are profound.

14405214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14405214.value: 基督宗教傳統上宣稱為對終極真理與拯救的唯一途徑，而此一宣稱在當代受到嚴重的挑戰。很多神學家嘗試在當代宗教分歧的脈絡中，重新考慮基督宗教與其他宗教的關係。事實上，宗教分歧不僅是一個神學或宗教的問題，因為它也涉及哲學、文化、實踐以及社會政治上的議題。 基督宗教在中國所面對的宗教分歧的問題，與在西方社會中所面對的有著重要的分別。基督宗教徒只佔中國人整體人口中的一小部份，而中國的宗教傳統似乎是以和諧並存，並且是正面地肯定宗教分歧。在這種宗教氣氛中，若對其他宗教作排斥性的宣稱，似與中國文化主流格格不入，並肯定會引起其他宗教人士的不滿。這更有可能是與中國政府倡導建立和諧社會的口號或政策相左。最後，任何對基督宗教作排他性的宣稱，更似是與當代中國的一些思潮脫節，當中一方面包括對外來事物的反感，而另一方面也包括對任何對真理的絕對宣稱皆採取相對主義、懷疑主義以至不可知論的態度。 本研究計劃嘗試研究當代中國基督宗教徒如何面對有關宗教分歧的課題，尤其如何處理他們的神學傳統與當代中國的文化、宗教、學思、社會及政治脈絡間的張力。本研究將依據他們的教會背景及神學傳統，分析他們對宗教分歧的論述，並識別當中具代表性的論述。之後，再探討這些中國基督宗教徒的論述有否及如何，有別於西方神學家對宗教分歧的論述，而如果有分別的話，這些分別又有甚麼成因。本研究也會審視中國基督宗教徒的論述，有否及如何受當代中國的脈絡所特定的因素影響，而這這些非神學性的因素與神學性的因素如何互動。最後，本研究將探索中國基督宗教徒的論述，是否展示出一種新的進路，對於在其他脈絡中的基督宗教徒面對宗教分歧的問題，也是值得慎重參考。 本研究可望有助豐富對當代中國的研究，尤其中國基督宗教徒如何回應傳統中國文化以及與宗教分歧有關的社會政治議題；此外，也會對中西文化的比較研究作出貢獻，尤其二者如何處理宗教分歧的問題。本研究計劃的成果將提供重要的資訊，有助提升華人社會中的社會和諧。

14405214.label: Realisation of objectives
14405214.value: Through digesting the primary and secondary sources related to the contemporary Chinese Christian discourses on religious diversity, the PI obtained an overview of the topic, including: identification of the representative positions, their relationship with the traditional religious culture, their relations with the discourses of previous generation, the relationship with their own intellectual as well as social and political contexts. Through presenting papers at different conferences, the PI presented his preliminary findings, compared the similarities and dissimilarities between the Chinese and Western discourses, and explored the possible significance of the Chinese discourses for the international discussion on the related topics. The final realizations are the 11 resultant publications.

14405214.label: Major findings and research outcome
14405214.value: The project finds that the contemporary Chinese Christian discourses on religious diversity were shaped not only by the traditional Chinese culture as well as the Chinese Christian discourses of the previous generation, but also the contemporary intellectual as well as social and political contexts. (These findings feature particularly in the publications items 2, 3 and 7 mentioned in Part C.) Regarding the cultural tradition, Confucianism has the greatest potentials to enrich the Christian approach to religious diversity and inter-religious dialogue. (These findings feature particularly in the publication items 6 and 9 mentioned in Part C.) Some of the Chinese Christian discourses were shaped by the positions of some western theologians and some of the western discourses, especially Karl Barth and Paul Tillich, remain useful in the contemporary Chinese context, including the dialogue with Buddhism. (These findings feature particularly in the publication items 1, 4, 5 and 10 mentioned in Part C.) However, in order to address the religious diversity in China in a more adequate way, it is necessary to reject the inclusivism-exclusivism-pluralism typology advocated by many western theologians, and to adopt a multi-dimensional understanding of salvation, which may help Chinese Christians to respond to the public issues in China in a better way. (These findings feature particularly in the publication items 8 and 11 mentioned in Part C.)

14405214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14405214.value: Based on the findings of the project, the contemporary Chinese Christian discourses on religious diversity address not only the Chinese Christians, but the general public as well. In other words, these Christian discourses are to a certain extent public discourses. There are two themes deserving to be further explored. One is how public theology is to be articulated in this religious pluralistic and yet politically totalitarian context. The other one is about the Chinese Christian discourses on salvation, especially how they interpret this seemingly religious concept in responses to their social and political contexts.

14405214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14405214.value: The project finds that the contemporary Chinese Christian discourses on religious diversity are shaped not only by the traditional Chinese culture as well as the discourses of the previous generation, but also the contemporary intellectual as well as the social and political contexts. These factors make the contemporary Chinese Christian discourses significantly different from their counterparts in the western world, and have the potentials to make distinctive contributions to the international discussion on related topics.

14405314.label: Project Objectives
14405314.value: To profile how parenting in Hong Kong has changed over the last half century; To understand generational shifts in ideology and practice of parenting; To analyze how contextual factors - cultural, social, demographic and economical – configured to shape the “ecology of parenthood” and parental goals and parenting practices; To examine discursive formations of dominant discourses that shape parenting beliefs and condition and constrain parenting practices; and To draw implications for policy formulation, service provision and future research direction.

14405314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14405314.value: The project aims to examine the historical trends of parenting and generational shifts in parental beliefs and practices in Hong Kong. Although the importance of historical perspective in understanding a phenomenon has been well-recognized, attempt to study generational shifts in parenting is meager and is almost non-existent in Hong Kong. Contemporary parenting is characterized as fraught with problems – anxieties about children, anxieties about one’ own adequacy as parents, and worries about adverse consequence of parenting on children. Rhetoric abounds such as irresponsible parenting, overprotective parenting, anxious parents, “helicopter parents”, and “monster parents” are terms frequently found in mass media sounding alarms over contemporary parenthood. However there is little study attempt to trace how contemporary parenthood has become characterized as such. In retrospect, there have been generational shifts in “themes” of parenthood in the history of Hong Kong as a modern city. The proposed study seeks to unravel these generational shifts in parenthood in Hong Kong, and investigates how the interplay between history, culture, and socio-demographic contexts provided the ground for these generational shifts to emerge. The study explores changing context for child-rearing over the past decades, and examines how contextual factors and dominant social and professional discourses shaped and re-shaped the “ecology of parenthood”. Specifically, the study aims to (1) profile how parenting in Hong Kong has changed over the last half century; (2) understand generational shifts in ideology and practice of parenting; (3) analyze how contextual factors - cultural, social, demographic and economical – configured to shape the “ecology of parenthood” and parental goals and parenting practices; (4) examine discursive formations of dominant discourses that shape parenting beliefs and condition and constrain parenting practices; and (5) draw implications for policy formulation, service provision and future research direction.

14405314.label: Realisation of objectives
14405314.value: Objectives and tasks stated in the project proposal were all successfully completed. The research project employed mixed methods including four components: Stage 1: Discourse analytic study mapping discourses embedded in parent education resource materials - Materials from the Family Life Education Resources Centre (FLERC) were extracted from its database. 1365 relevant items were selected for the sampling frame and grouped into 30 sub-categories. A purposeful sample of 48 items were methodically selected for in-depth discourse analysis. Discourse analysis arrived at 17 thematic domains. These thematic domains provoked a reflexive examination of professional role in shaping the ecology of parenthood. (b) Stage 2: Narrative inquiry of parenthood experience - 120 in-depth interviews, with 60 parents and each had participated into two individual interview, were completed. The participants spanned across five generational cohorts (from 70s and before to 2010s) with 6 fathers and 6 mothers in each cohort. A diverse sample in terms of socio-economic background and gender was obtained. Each interview lasted for approximately 1.5 hours. Interviews inquired people's experience of parenthood, meanings they conferred to parenthood and their parental identity construction. There would be an interviewer and a RA involved in each interview. Interviewing and reflective notes were prepared by each of them for triangulation purpose and the interviewing summary were shared with participants to ensure trustworthy of data. all interview were audio-taped and transcribed. Data were analysed with dominant themes identified. The findings uncovered generational shifts in parental beliefs, parenting practice and meaning of parenthood. Based in the findings, indigenous items for survey study were developed. (c) Stage 3: Survey study of parental ideologies, goals and beliefs, roles and responsibilities - Questionnaire was constructed by using existing scales and indigenous items developed based on the themes extracted from the in-depth interview in Stage 2. A non-random proportionate sample (N = 5,749 which was exceeding the original proposed sample of 4500) of 5 generational cohorts of parents (the earliest cohort being parents of young children in the 1970’s and before and the latest is parents with children born in the 2010s). A sample size of 0.1% of each respondent group was sampled based on the census data, with parenthood in the 70 and before estimated to be 1000 (N=1005), 80s to be 1000 (N=991), 90s to be 1000 (N=984), 2000s to be 1000 (N=1770), 2010s to be 500 (N=715), and with 242 with missing information responded. Indigenous scales developed were validated and published. The survey findings profiled societal trends in parenting in terms of parental beliefs, parenting practice and patterned changes overtime on "ecology of parenthood ". (d) Stage 4: focus group discussions among parents, parenting professionals and teachers - Focus group method has been applied as a form of participatory inquiry, and to further understand the results. A total of 10 focus group, including 5 parent inquiry group with a total of 43 parents and 5 parent professional groups with a total of 33 participants, has been conducted. The groups engaged parents and practitioners in a reflective knowing. Findings revealed that parenting is intensive these days and requires parental investment of resource and time, very much planning and decision-making, and learning expert knowledge and skills for proper parenting. Contemporary parenthood regards incompetent parenting as aversive to children’s well-being. Parents thus impose on themselves a much broader domain of parental responsibilities while self-blaming for faulty parenting. Participants reflected on the changing parental ideology and ecology of parenting and examines how contextual factors and discursive formations promoted by parenting professionals have shaped contemporary parenting. By using mixed research method and triangulating the findings collected in the four stages of data collection, the study was able to achieve its goals including profiling how parenting in Hong Kong has changed over the last five decades (see paper titled "Has parenting changed over past decades"); understanding generational shifts in ideology and practice of parenting (see paper Development and Validation of a Questionnaire on Chinese Parents’ Beliefs in Parental Roles and Responsibilities, Parents' expectations of familial elder care under the Neoliberal Hong Kong Society); analyzing how contextual factors shape the "ecology of parenting' (see paper titled "Has parenting changed over past decades and "Reflections of parents and parent work practitioners"), examine how dominant discourses shapes parenting beliefs and constrains parenting practices (see paper titled "Intensive parenting in a risk society"). There were journal publications generated from the findings. Findings has been presented in international, regional and local conference/agency seminars/workshops. It is hoped that by sharing the findings and promoting dialogue with different parities, there will be paradigm shift in our parent education policy and services.

14405314.label: Major findings and research outcome
14405314.value: (1) We developed and validated a culturally- and diachronically-sensitive quantitative measure of parental beliefs on parental roles and responsibilities. This emic quantitative measure provides a culturally-sensitive scale for studying parental beliefs about parental roles and responsibilities in a Chinese cultural context. (2) We unravelled generational shifts in parenthood in the recent history of Hong Kong by discourse analysis, life story interviews and focus group study. Our exploration explicates that: (2.1) Problematizing parenthood and expert domination: Indigenous publications and video resources converge on a negative focus of people’s parenthood experience. “Problematizing parenthood” discourse legitimized professional regulation of parenting, advanced the “market project” of parenting professionals and turned parenting into a pseudo-professional practice. Parent education is now a form of parent support as well as a tool of professional subjugation of parents. (2.2) Expanding scope of parental responsibility: Beginning from the 1980s parental responsibility gradually expanded to include all-round parental guidance and nurturance of children. The younger-generation parents (from the 1990s till now) talked about cultivation of children, arranging early training for children, enhancing children’s capacity in emotional management and tending to the quality of parent-child relationship. There were increasing self-imposed demands and, consequently, self-doubt and self-blame among younger-generation parents, as they held themselves chiefly responsible for children’s failure or success. (2.3) Parental nurturance determines child outcome: In comparison to older-generation parents, younger-generation parents exhibit a stronger awareness of their parental role and drive themselves harder to fulfil their parental responsibilities by more knowledge-informed practice. Contemporary generation of parents now subscribe to the “nurture” assumption of the “nature vs. nurture” debate in child development. (2.4) Parenting in Hong Kong can be meaningfully understood from the perspective of risk society. On the one hand, parents’ self-perception is shaped by the risk discourses; on the other hand, parents who are able to reconstitute their reflexive selves can create a space, no matter how tenuous, within which they can have a more positive view of themselves and their children. (3) We surveyed 5749 Chinese parents and found that (a) parents with lower family income or being unemployed tended to hold stronger traditional beliefs about roles and responsibilities in parenting than did high-income or employed parents; (b) while traditional gendered expectations about sons and daughters were gradually changing, a significant proportion of parents still subscribed to traditional gendered expectations; (c) although a more equalitarian gender attitude was noticed, gendered share of childcare responsibilities with mothers playing the main role in childcare largely persisted.

14405314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14405314.value: Regarding the scales of Chinese Parents’ Beliefs in Parental Roles and Responsibilities that this study has developed and validated, we can further assessed the scale’s construct validity. Indeed, there were indigenous scales developed (e.g. division of labor in parenting, gender expectation on son and daughter etc.) that can further study and validate. These scales can be validated in conjunction and to compare with existing, tested scales. Chinese parents in other Chinese societies, such as Macau, Taiwan, and mainland China, can be sampled for comparative studies. Qualitative in-depth interview of this study has generated meaningful data that can further analyse for more in-depth understanding. Also, parents in other Chinese societies can be interviewed to further understand the meaning of parenthood in different Chinese culture contexts. In our focus group study, while different generations of parents and practitioners working in different settings were recruited to capture the variations in their perceptions and experiences, a bigger sample can better capture the diverse view of parents and practitioners. In sum, rich and meaningful data has been obtained from this study that can further analysed. Now all the respondents were Hong Kong parents, the study can expand to cover parents in other Chinese societies.

14405314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14405314.value: Hong Kong has gone through dramatic socioeconomic changes since World War II. Against such backdrop, the parenting beliefs and practices of Hong Kong has also been evolving substantially. Despite the well-recognised importance of historical perspective in understanding this phenomenon, attempt to study generational shifts in parenting in Hong Kong is almost non-existent. This study has pioneered research effort along this theme, seeking to unravel the generational shifts in parenthood in Hong Kong, and has investigated how the interplay between history, culture and socio-demographic contexts provided the ground for these generational shifts to emerge. Our research has made its unique contribution to the understanding of how parenting in Hong Kong has changed over the last half century, how contextual factors configured to shape parental goals and parenting practices, and how professional discourses shaped and re-shaped parenting condition and constrain parenting practices. It represented a joint effort with well over 5000 parents and practitioners who participated in the research to various extent. The research outcome has helped us critically analyse and reflect upon the challenges and opportunities the Hong Kong parents are facing, and will draw implications for policy formulation, service provision and future research direction.
