14409814.label: Major findings and research outcome
14409814.value: The PI has been immensely productive in terms of generating and preparing research outcomes to disseminate the major findings of the project. The PI has (a) already published one article in an international peer-reviewed journal, (b) three chapters accepted for publication in leading international peer-reviewed collections, (c) a further three papers currently under review at international journals, (d) made substantial progress on a single-authored monograph (a sample chapter is included in part C), and (e) delivered or arranged for delivery ten paper presentations at leading international conferences and/or prestigious centers of academic excellence. There are, in addition, a number of chapters and papers in various stages of preparation, which will be the basis for subsequent international peer-review publications that will be properly acknowledged as financially supported by the RGC. The major findings of the project have been disseminated through a single-authored article, entitled ‘The Boundaries of a Deliberative System: The Case of Disruptive Protest', published in ‘Critical Policy Studies’. This article summarized the major findings of the project discussed in section 5.3, in particular: (a) the critique of deliberative systems, (b) the reformulation of deliberative systems, and (c) the deliberative typology of activist tactics. The venue for this research has been particularly useful for securing significant academic impact and international visibility, as it appeared in a special section devoted to the latest cutting-edge research on deliberative systems. The ideas contained within it have consequently been discussed in a commentary published in the same issue of the journal by a leading international expert in the field (John S. Dryzek, ‘Symposium Commentary: Reflections on the Theory of Deliberative Systems’). The article has also already been cited in a recently published critical study on deliberative systems (John Boswell and Jack Corbett, ‘Why and how to compare deliberative systems’, European Journal of Political Research 38, 2017). The scope for securing impact and visibility has also been enhanced by a number of placements in prestigious peer-reviewed collections, such as the forthcoming ‘Oxford Handbook of Deliberative Democracy’ and ‘Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Politics’ (both published by Oxford University Press). These collections are comprised of contributions by the world’s leading scholars, with the goal of setting the agenda for new research in their fields. The PI’s contributions enable him to draw attention to core themes of the project, such as its account of the communicative dimensions of political protest and the transnational applicability of deliberative systems theory.

14409814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14409814.value: The goal of bringing the literature on deliberative democracy into a constructive dialogue with the literature on social movements and contentious politics has opened up avenues for a further project, which explores the applicability of deliberative democracy to the internal organization of protest movements. This is distinct from the completed project in exploring a range of issues beyond its primary focus on the impact of protest on deliberative systems, such as power asymmetries among protesters, the merits of consensus-based decision-making, and the politics of prefiguration. It is, at the same time, a natural progression from the completed project, because it allows for a continuation of the dialogue between deliberative theory and social movement studies. There are, in particular, a number of empirical studies that offer much-needed guidance for normative evaluation of ‘enclave’ deliberation. These studies can be drawn upon to challenge theoretical assumptions that deliberation among activists is either not possible or not theoretically interesting, due to an alleged lack of diversity among participants. The PI has thus prepared and submitted an application to the GRF 2017-18 funding exercise, to support this research into an important dimension of the relationship between disruptive protest and deliberative democracy.

14409814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14409814.value: This research project has explored the nature, significance and value of disruptive protest for democratic politics. The primary focus has been on the ethical and political issues surrounding protest that obstructs everyday routines and activities, on a temporary or ongoing fashion, in order to compel society to hear the demands or grievances of protesters. Such protest is often seen as incompatible with important civic values, such as the duty to comply with law, to reach collective agreements through institutionalized procedures, and to avoid causing inconvenience and disruption to others. This project has defended disruptive protest against such objections, by showing how it often embodies civic virtues such as critical reflection, respect for others, and a willingness to engage in dialogue with opponents. It has also shown that disruptive protest performs a variety of important roles within democratic politics, such as drawing attention to marginalized persons or perspectives in the public realm. The broader goal of the project is to encourage societies to display greater toleration and respect for protest, which should be reflected in its institutions and practices. This includes law enforcement agencies, which should adopt progressive forms of protest policing and reject the use of militarized force against protesters.

14410714.label: Project Objectives
14410714.value: To use three national large-scale surveys of rural households to test how the number of migrants and its gender composition would impact on household economic and social well-being in China. To test whether the impacts of migration on household economic and social well-being is gender-sensitive. To examine the effect of household members’ migration on stay-behind and returned women’s power position, division of labor, as well as participation in off-farm and agriculture works. To collect ethnographic data from rural households in three selected sending areas (counties in Hunan, Shannxi and Anhui provinces) to supplement the interpretation of quantitative data analysis, to evaluate the consistency and gaps in national large-scale data and ethnographic data on the family processes related to migration decisions and gendered dynamics of well-being among household members in the sending communities.

14410714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14410714.value: This project will investigate two important questions in the intersection of migration and gender. First, what is the impact of the number of migrants and the gender composition of household migration stock on rural households’ economic and social well-being? Second, will household members’ migration and their characteristics influence the power position, division of labor and economic activities of those women who remained in households or who returned? In many developing countries, labor migrants maintain close connections with the households in the places of origin. This is particularly true in China’s large scale rural-to-urban labor migration, in which labor migrants lack a sense of long-term commitment to the places they are migrating due to China’s unique Hukou system. It was estimated that the number of such migrants has been beyond 200 million recently. The answers to these questions are fundamentally important to the understanding of migration as a household strategy affecting rural households’ economic and social well-being. The previous literatures in this line mainly see number of migrants as a monolithic entity; while largely ignore the role of gender in migration strategy-making processes. There is a necessity to consider the power and interest differentials that exist along gender within the household when considering the household as a resource-pooling unit. By incorporating the role of gender, this study will add nuances to mechanisms between migration and household development. Drawing on three national large-scale surveys including China Health and Nutrition Survey (CHNS), China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) and China Labor Force Dynamics Survey (CLDS), this project will be the first and foremost study to examine migration, gender and their intersecting consequences to rural households in a systematic way in China. All three surveys include detailed household members’ migration information and household information, and all of them are on-going panel surveys, which can overcome some of the methodological barriers in previous studies. The survey instruments from different surveys can complement each other well for the purposes of this study. In addition, we will also conduct an ethnographic study in selected migrants sending rural places to obtain qualitative data on the patterns of negotiation and interaction between household members that have led to specific migration decisions, as well as the nuanced implications of migration on the status, role taking, and power of stay-behind and returned women in the household. The ethnographic data will enable us to make more insightful interpretation for findings from quantitative approach. 本项目将要研究两个关于迁移与性别的重要问题。第一，家庭人口迁移的规模和性别组成是如何影响农村家庭经济与社会福利的？第二，家庭其他成员的迁移及其特征是否会影响留守和返迁女性的权利，劳动分工和经济活动？在大多数发展中国家，劳工迁移人口通常和原住家庭保持密切的联系，这一点在中国更加明显。在中国，因为户口的限制，农村到城市的迁移人口往往对城市缺乏归属感，导致他们与农村的原住家庭关系更加密切。据最新的估计，这种迁移人口在中国达两亿以上。基于此，对以上问题的研究于农村家庭迁移策略和农村家庭社会经济具有极其重要的意义。然而，以前的研究往往只是单纯考虑家庭人口迁移规模，而没有对性别在人口迁移和家庭经济策略中扮演的角色做进一步的研究。人口迁移作为一项家庭经济策略，起到重要的家庭资源重新汇聚和分配的作用，考虑到性别在人口迁移中不同的作用，此项研究会对迁移和家庭发展之间的机制作出增强了解。本研究将使用三个具有全国代表性的数据，包括中国营养与健康调查，中国家庭动态调查，以及全国劳动力动态调查。这三个数据都包括详细的家庭户人口迁移和家庭经济社会福利的数据，并且都是正在进行中的并会继续的大型追踪社会调查，所以能够克服很多以往类似研究的由数据问题造成的障碍。这三个数据的侧重点有所不同，所以它们之间也能够很好的互补。除此之外，我们也将会在湖南，陕西和安徽收集第一手的质性调查研究的数据，对量化研究进行经验性补充和理论解释上的启发，特别是在质性研究中，我们可以收集具体的性别协商，了解具体迁移决策制定过程，家庭相对社会地位，角色扮演以及女性的家庭地位和权利义务等信息。本研究将是第一个在中国对人口迁移与性别及它们的交叉性因素对原住家庭经济社会福利影响的全面性的研究。

14410714.label: Realisation of objectives
14410714.value: 5.3. We have largely achieved all the research objectives for this funded project. We have written three academic articles and two chapters of Phd thesis out of this project. I will explain it in more details. Objectives 1-3: To use three national large-scale surveys of rural households to test how the number of migrants and its gender composition would impact on household economic and social well-being in China; to test whether the impacts of migration on household economic and social well-being is gender-sensitive; to examine the effect of household members’ migration on stay-behind and returned women’s power position, division of labor, as well as participation in off-farm and agriculture works. The first three objectives have been largely achieved. We have written three papers and two PhD thesis chapters based on the quantitative analysis. The first paper is titled as “Migration, Livelihood Strategies and Agricultural Outcomes: A Gender Study in Rural China”. This paper examines whether the gender composition of migrants in rural households affects household economic strategies and agricultural productivity. This paper has been presented in the Annual Meeting of American Sociological Association (ASA) and seminar talk in Shanghai University. It has been submitted to Rural Sociology, a flagship journal of Rural Sociological Society. One round of “revise & resubmission” has been completed and it received a “minor revision” for publication in Rural Sociology. This paper has largely fulfilled the first objective on how migration and its gender composition affect household economic well-being. It also addressed the second objective on the gendered analysis. The second paper is titled as “Intimacy Lost or Autonomy Gained? Spousal migration and Left-behind Partners’ Psychological Well-being in Rural China”. It examines how spousal migration affected left-behind partners’ psychological well-being. Different version of this paper has been presented in the Annual Meeting of Population Association of America and a few other conferences. Seminar talk has also been made based on this paper. It has been submitted to Social Forces for publication. Unfortunately, despite a rather positive review in general, this paper has been declined by Social Forces for a nearly a year’s under review process. Since we do not want to rush to a different journal without improvement based on reviewers’ comments, we decided to hold it off to have further revision. Now we have used more waves of the data to improve the paper, and it will be ready for resubmission in about one month. We plan to submit to British Journal of Sociology. In this paper, we have examined how migration affects stay-behind women’s power position, division of labor, and how this affect their psychological well-being, which is the third objective of this paper, and gendered analysis is also addressed in this paper. The third paper is titled as “Migration and Rural Household Economic Status: The Heterogeneity of Demographic Profiles and Endowment of the Households in Rural China”. In this paper we used 1997-2011 China Health and Nutrition Survey (CHNS) house level data and fixed effect models, we examined how migration has affected the household economic status from both absolute net income and relative rank within community. Different of version of this paper has been presented in conference of European Society for Rural Society, International Union for the Scientific Study of Population as well as International Sociological Association Population and Family Section. It has also been presented in seminar talk such as University of Auckland. The paper still needs some final stage tone up before submission. We plan to submit to Population Studies. We expect it will be submitted in about one to two months. This paper has addressed all three objectives. In all these papers, gender has been one of most important perspective to the analysis. All three papers are led by PI. Training Phd students is one of important objectives out of research project, although it was not stated formally in the research objectives. Thanks to this research grant, I can support my Phd student in her last two years for her thesis work when she is helping me on the data preparation of this project. Given our common interest and her role as a part-time research assistant for this project, her thesis title is “What does Migration Bring to the Sending Communities and Households?: Macro and Micro Perspectives on Rural-Urban Migration in China”. In this Phd thesis, two chapters have used the same data sources of this project to study how migration impacts the sending communities. One of them examined how migration affects the economic inequality of rural community, and the other examines how adult children migration affects the health of rural older adults. The latter has been published in the journal of Population research, and the second one is under preparation of journal submission. Objective 4: To collect ethnographic data from rural households in three selected sending areas (counties in Hunan, Shannxi and Anhui provinces) to supplement the interpretation of quantitative data analysis, to evaluate the consistency and gaps in national large-scale data and ethnographic data on the family processes related to migration decisions and gendered dynamics of well-being among household members in the sending communities. This objective has been achieved. We have collected 90 household interview data, which provide valuable information for us to inform our quantitative analysis results. These valuable data will further inform our future study related to this area.

14410714.label: Major findings and research outcome
14410714.value: The major findings of this paper can be summarized in two aspects. One is migration and gendered consequences to the rural household in their economic well-being; the other on their social psychological well-being. First, in terms of economic well-being, we have found households with migrants are less likely to engage in agricultural activities or operate small businesses compared to households with no migrants. However, households with female migrants are less likely to engage in agricultural activities to a greater extent than those with male migrants, whereas the latter poses an obstacle to running small family businesses. This suggests that women may have to shoulder the burden of agriculture work when men migrate, whereas the presence of male migrants hampers households from engaging in local non-agricultural activities. Although the presence of male migrants does not significantly discourage households from continuing agricultural activities, it does reduce agricultural productivity. We also found that overall, migration is harmful to household economic status in rural China, although it could have been beneficial in early time of migration, despite that there are large heterogeneity in terms of migration influences on household economy based on their demographic profiles and household endowment. We have addressed this heterogeneity from perspectives of gender, life course, household human capital stock as well as amount of landholdings. Finally, the graduate thesis chapter on income inequality showed that when migration becomes more prevalent, household income inequality increases initially, but decrease eventually. Second, in terms of social well-being, we showed that prolonged spousal separation increased depressive symptom of left-behind spouses, and the detrimental consequences on left-behind spouses’ psychological well-being can be explained by the reduced level of emotional intimacy between husband and wife, and partially explained by women becoming the master of the household. Considering that being the master of the household is accompanied by elevated stress levels associated with increasing family responsibilities. Further examination showed that economic resources can buffer the negative effect associated with being the master of the household when spouse migrates. However, we did not find that time use is an effective mechanism to link spousal migration and left-behind spouses’ well-being. In the PhD thesis chapter on migration consequence to rural elderly, our study demonstrates that the migration of adult children is detrimental for rural elderly parent health. The negative effects on elderly parent health primarily result from a lack of emotional support due to the migration of adult children.

14410714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14410714.value: Based on this project, we have developed a new GRF application which is under review now. In this newly proposed project, we plan to further study how gender and life course affect rural people’s livelihood choice. This time, we will focus on mainly how migration affects individual people’s livelihood choices and what will be the consequences to them over a long time transition period in China. In particular, we will focus on their off-farm work choice.

14410714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14410714.value: Migration has been a population dynamic which impacts nearly everybody’s life. It not only affects those who migrate, but also those who are in migration destination and who are left behind. This project specifically focuses on migration’s impact in China’s rural sending community, which specifically exams how migration and its gender composition affect rural household’s economic and social well-being. Despite that migration remittances have been assumed to be beneficial to household economic status, we found that the consequence is mixed even from the perspective of economic benefit. We found that migration is harmful to household agricultural productivity, although it may not affects the household engagement of agricultural activity. It discourages household’s pursuit’s on non-farm activity such as family small business. We also found that migration’s influences on household economy differs by gender, where male migration has more profound effect than female migration on agricultural productivity, although it is not the case of engagement. In that process, traditional patriarchal cultural norm plays important role on who migrate and who stay, which has affected household economic outcome. Socially, we found that migration is harmful to left-behind members’ psychological well-being, although it might increase their decision making power.

14410914.label: Project Objectives
14410914.value: To look at how actors in government, advisory bodies and NGOs understand their roles in citizenship education before and after 1997. To identify the aims and the practices of citizenship education offered by NGOs. To compare the practices of citizenship education through various major NGOs from the local, national, and global levels, and to find out their commonalities and differences. 14410914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14410914.value: Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) have various important roles in social affairs and citizenship education, and these roles have been increasingly acknowledged by academics, policy-makers and practitioners. In Hong Kong, NGOs of various kinds have long been making important contributions, including service delivery, interest aggregation and articulation, policy advocacy, and civic participation. These have also been recognized in recent policy statements by the government because incorporating the third sector or civil society organizations in the governance scheme is seen to help enhance public governance. In Hong Kong, there is also a strong presence of NGO activities in the area of civic education. Over the years, different departments of the government and advisory bodies, together with many NGOs, have carried out various activities and projects to promote civic and national education with youngsters. Recently, the government has strongly encouraged NGOs to organize various youth activities and national education programmes to help strengthen the youngsters’ sense of national identity. The role of NGOs in providing “other learning experience” at senior secondary level, such as moral and civic education and community service, is also stressed in the ongoing curriculum reform. Proceeding with a 4-level analysis, and with specific reference to the field of civic education practices of the NGOs in Hong Kong, and based on the Civil Society Diamond model and Crick’s strands of citizenship education as an analytical framework, this study will examine the relative roles of NGOs and the government in shaping or supporting citizenship education for young people (aged 10–30) in Hong Kong, inside and outside schools. The project will begin in September 2014 and last for 28 months. Mixed research methods will be employed, involving documentary analysis, a survey, and in-depth case studies. In terms of policy implications, this project will bridge the gap between policy and practice in the field of citizenship education. Further, it will not only enhance our knowledge of the nature, constituents and roles of civil society in citizenship education, but also help develop practical measures which can strengthen civil society and enhance its impact as an agent for shaping people’s ideas and values, particularly with regard to citizenship. 非政府組織在社會事務和公民教育有各種重要的角色，並越來越為學者、政策制定者和從業者所肯定。在香港，各種非政府組織也早已在提供服務、利益匯集和表達、政策倡導和公民參與等多方面作出重要貢獻。這些貢獻也在政府近年的政策文件中承認，並將第三部門或公民社會組織納入治理計劃，以有利公共管治。 在香港，非政府組織在公民教育方面的活動一向顯著。多年來，不同的政府機構部門，各式諮詢機構，聯同眾多的非政府組織合作，開展各種活動和項目，向青少年推廣公民及國民教育。最近政府更大力鼓勵非政府組織舉辦各類青年活動和國民教育項目，以加強青少年的國家認同意識。當前的課程改革也強調非政府組織在高中階段提供「其他學習經歷」的作用，當中便涉及德育及公民教育，以及社會服務兩環。 針對非政府組織在香港的公民教育實踐領域，並基於公民社會鑽石模型和克里的公民教育為分析框架，本研究從四層次的架構出發，分析香港政府和非政府組織在塑造或支持以年輕人(10-30歲）為對象，在校園內外進行有關公民教育的各自角色。本計劃於2014年9月開始，為期28個月。將採用混合研究方法，包括文獻分析、調查，以及深入的案例研究。 在政策啟示上，本研究將填補在公民教育方面中政策與實踐間的差距。此外，它不僅將提高我們對公民社會在公民教育中的性質，構成和作用的認識，也有助於制定切實可行的措施，以強化公民社會和加強其塑造人的思想和價值觀的影響，特別是關於公民身份。

14410914.label: Realisation of objectives
14410914.value: The primary purpose of this project is to examine the relative roles of NGOs and the government in shaping or supporting citizenship education for young people (aged 10–30), both in school and out-of-school contexts. The project has gathered or generated the following materials: a) available reports on two major funding schemes and minutes of meetings of the key advisory body “the Committee on the Promotion of Civic Education” (CPCE) over the past 30 years; b) In-depth individual interviews with 23 CPCE’s members from a wide cross-section of the community; c) an archive of general background of active NGOs involved in citizenship education for young people over the years in light of newspaper dataset, websites and relevant documents and materials; c) a questionnaire survey of the views and work of some 120 NGOs active in citizenship education; and d) in-depth cases studies of 8 NGOs involved in a particular dimension of citizenship education for young people. Taken together, the data collected help delineate the socio-political surroundings in which the NGOs are located in Hong Kong as well as the state–civil society relations in the specific domain of civic education. As for the internal structure of civil society and the role of individual NGOs, considerations are given to their organizational structure, resources and capacity, aims and ideas, participants, autonomy, the network linking these NGOs, and the choices and strategies taken. And the values dimension considers the extent to which civil society promotes the values conducive to citizenship. Concerning the dynamics between the state and civil society, and among the NGOs themselves, we can examine how these NGOs interact with the state through their direct influence on public policy-making, oversight of governmental activities, and involvement in advisory bodies or meetings with officials. Also at stake is cooperation and competition among NGOs themselves. Functional analysis can be conducted with regard to the activities and achievements on the part of the state (e.g., funding, and regulation), and on the part of the NGOs (e.g., advocacy and service provision). Concerning the first specific objective stated in 5.1, the views of the stakeholders on their roles in citizenship education could be documented in the sources a) and c). As for the aims and the practices of citizenship education offered by NGOs, findings are mainly drawn from sources b), c) and d). The commonalities and differences of the practices of citizenship education through various major NGOs are examined through the general survey as well as the in-depth case studies. Finally, the over issues of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats concerning the NGOs working in relation to citizenship education could be addressed with all the sources of data above. In brief, many NGOs are flexible and proactive, and they meet social and educational needs with specialized services and innovative projects for citizenship education, including interactive workshops, award scheme, provision of materials for learning citizenship, as well as a wide range of service opportunities. The NGOs play a connectivity role within the citizenship education area, bridging the gap between formal and less formal education, or between schools and the community. Albeit with these accomplishments, the project also shows that the Hong Kong Government has attempted to manipulate and steer the Committee on the Promotion of Civic Education’s work in a number of ways, including through its terms of reference, the restructuring of the Committee, its activities, funding support and the appointment of members. As a result, the Committee has been constrained by its composition, powers and functions, and this has impaired its role as an advocate for civic education. For instance, with three NGOs as illustrations, they can help young people explore human rights issues in the relevant school subjects, as well as using experiential learning in extra-curricular activities. NGO’s contributions to human rights education are evident in terms of five major areas: provision of education resources, school talks, pedagogical innovations, school clubs and youth engagement in the community. There are several merits. The first is that many activities are free of charge or very affordable for the participants. Second, with their specific niches and advantages, these NGOs can easily reach their specific target groups with their services and activities and bringing the service-recipients, volunteers, sponsors, and other partners together. They can easily link up with different partners like community groups, the media, and the private sector to provide opportunities for adolescents in human rights education activities. Meanwhile, human rights education in Hong Kong is now a number of hurdles: 1) government’s stance of aloofness, 2) unfavorable school ethos, and; 3) lack of external support. As for practical suggestions, this project proposes that: 1. For a stronger state–civil society partnership, the ways of collaborations between NGOs and the government in citizenship education might need a rethink, including the operation of the official platforms like CPCE. The issues concerning the proper directions and objectives, relevant scope and topics, and suitable works of civic education are subject to wider public participation. 2. There is a pressing need to enhance the promotional work of CPCE itself, and to improve it visibility in the eyes of the public. Resources used and flexibility of the funding schemes for citizenship education projects also have some room for improvement. 3. Liaison activities with NGOs, and exchanging and popularizing good practices and successful project experiences in the field of citizenship education are to be encouraged.

14410914.label: Major findings and research outcome
14410914.value: Three crucial observations are made with regard to the project: 1. There have been changes in priorities in citizenship education accorded by the Government since the 1997 handover. There has also been changing partnership between the Government and different NGOs involved in citizenship education. As indicated by sources of funding and pattern of consultation, some NGOs are co-opted while others, marginalized. Please refer to the attachments in Part C for more details. 2. There are diversified notions of citizenship and the works of NGOs in citizenship education are dispersed in several dimensions, and citizenship education has been shaped by ideological and organisational factors, and ecological forces. While most patriotic NGOs follow the lines of the Government, some Christian organizations and international bodies adopt alternative civic education discourses and practices, exhibiting essential tension between the state and the civil society.This is well demonstrated in the responses of the local Christian communities to the official curriculum proposal in 2012 (details see Tse (2017) When Christian education meets patriotism: Christian organisations’ response to the introduction of Moral and National Education in Hong Kong schools. British Journal of Religious Education 39(3):257-268. [SSCI journal] in Part C ). 3. Some NGOs form an issue-based ad hoc alliance occasionally whereas frequent cooperation among most NGOs in citizenship education is still rare. With the data collected from the project, so far the PI has made 6 presentations respectively in international conferences: two dealing with global citizenship education and NGOs in Hong Kong, one about the contributions of NGOs in Hong Kong to human rights education, one about the work of civic education by the two largest local teachers' organisations, one about Hong Kong's NGOs' views on civic education, and another one about the role of CPCE’s Community Participation Scheme in funding projects for NGOs in Hong Kong’s citizenship education. A specific paper about local Christian organisations’ response to the Hong Kong Government’ plan of Moral and National Education has also been recently published by British Journal of Religious Education. Four papers generated out of the project are also under review for publications in four international journals. These papers together identify and explore some challenges and difficulties with civic education, as well as the opportunities and possibilities ahead. More details about the findings could be found in the attachments in Part C.

14410914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14410914.value: This project has demonstrated that the civil society in Hong Kong has long been making important contributions to civic education. It is hope that the findings and suggestions will be disseminated to the community through the newspapers or magazines. By stretching the focus from macro/meso to micro one, the involvement and gains of the beneficiaries in those NGOs’ civic education projects or activities is another significant line of enquiry in future studies. How the existing programmes can be improved so that the benefits on young people can be strengthened and extended to a larger population is also a strategic research topic to explore.

14410914.value: In Hong Kong, there is a strong presence of civil society in the area of citizenship education and NGOs of various kinds have vital roles in facilitating young people’s citizenship. Adopting a multi-level analysis and mixed research methods including documentary analysis, a survey, and in-depth case studies, this project examines the relative roles of civil society and the government in shaping or supporting citizenship education for young people in Hong Kong in and out of schools. It results in a comprehensive database of key NGOs and members in advisory bodies actively involved in this area. This robust enquiry into the roles of NGOs in citizenship education is crucial to our understanding of the character, the workings and functions of local civil society, and the contributions that it can make towards citizenship education as well as citizenship in Hong Kong in the days to come. Apart from knowing more about the nature and roles of civil society in citizenship education, this project is also crucial to policy formulation concerning citizenship education, including national education. The results help develop practical measures strengthening the civil society as an agent for shaping people’s values and competencies with regard to citizenship.

14411314.label: Project Objectives
14411314.value: Longitudinal Study of Second Language Learning of a Tone System:- An 18-month longitudinal study of the development of a non-native tone system during second language learning will be performed to provide empirical data by which to achieve the subsequent objectives. A target group of first language Mandarin speakers with no significant prior experience of speaking or listening to Cantonese will participate in the study. Each participant’s progress in learning the Hong Kong Cantonese tone system, both in terms of perception and production, will be tracked over a series of five experimental sessions comprising both behavioral and electroencephalographic components. Synchronic Analysis of Tone System States:- The synchronic data obtained from each experimental session of the longitudinal study will be analyzed to determine the degree of consistency between each participant’s tone systems for perception and production, and the degree of consistency across participants. Diachronic Analysis of Tone System Dynamics:- The dynamics of each participant’s tone system will be assessed by comparing the synchronic tone system states across experimental sessions. The resultant diachronic data will be examined to determine how the tone systems for perception and production co-evolve, and to determine how variability in the speech stimuli that learners are exposed to influences rate and accuracy of convergence toward the native Hong Kong Cantonese tone system. Determination of Tone System Representation:- The tone system dynamics that are observed empirically will be compared to the dynamics predicted by computational simulations of the abstract and exemplar-based models for tone system representation—and hybrid variants of them—to determine which model best reflects the empirical data. This will enable refinements to these models to be proposed to provide a clearer picture of the cognitive mechanisms involved in representing tone systems.

14411314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14411314.value: Many languages make use of distinct pitch patterns to indicate different words. Like all linguistic features, the resultant phonological categories, called lexical tones, tend to change over time, both in terms of the words that belong to each tone category and in terms of the pitch patterns that represent them. Much is known about the historical development of lexical tones in Chinese, but our understanding of the cognitive mechanisms by which lexical tones are learned and represented remains incomplete. Two sets of models provide contrasting hypotheses regarding the cognitive mechanisms by which phonological categories are represented. Abstract models hypothesize that, whenever an individual perceives speech, the speech input undergoes online computation and transformation into a single abstract representation of each phonological category that is not talker-specific. In contrast, exemplar-based models hypothesize that listeners maintain phonological categories via multiple episodic traces containing talker-specific details of past speech input. Depending on which hypothesis is correct—or, more likely, a hybrid of the two models—the dynamics by which phonological categories are learned and change will differ. Hence, by analyzing the dynamics of a phonological system during learning, we have a window with which to assess evidence for the cognitive mechanisms by which phonological categories are represented. In this project, we will investigate the learning, representation, and dynamics of a system of lexical tones by second language learners of Hong Kong Cantonese, both from a behavioral and a neuroscientific perspective. In particular, we will carry out an 18-month longitudinal study of 50+ first language Mandarin speakers with no prior experience of Cantonese. Starting within three months of their arrival in Hong Kong, participants will perform in a sequence of behavioral and electroencephalographic experiments to probe the states and dynamics of their tone systems, both in terms of perception and production. By comparing participants’ observed tone systems to those of native Cantonese-speaking participants, and by relating their dynamics to those predicted by computational simulations of the abstract and exemplar-based models for tone system representation, we aim to better understand the cognitive mechanisms by which lexical tones are represented. This project constitutes a case study for the more general question of how phonological categories are represented and learned, and how variability in the speech stimuli that learners are exposed to influences learning outcome. The findings of the project may, therefore, also assist educators to identify pedagogical methods that result in more effective language teaching. .很多語言都會使用不同的音高模式去代表不同的字詞。和其他所有語言特徵一樣，聲調會在每個聲調範疇的字詞和其所代表的音調上，隨著時間改變。我們對中文聲調的歷史與發展已經有一定的了解，但是我們對聲調的認知機制在學習和表示方面的認識仍然十分缺乏。 關於聲調認知機制的理論，大體上可分為兩套，有着不同的假設 。根據抽象理論﹐受話者在感知語音的時候，語音輸入會通過在線計算，轉化為一個不受講話者影響的抽象表示形式。與之相對，根據樣例理論﹐受話者會通過多種情節的跡象去保留講話者在語音中的信息。視乎哪個理論正確（更有可能是兩個理論的結合），語音範疇習得以及變化的機制會有所不同。因此﹐通過分析語音範疇習得的機制，我們可以進一步瞭解語音範疇在大腦中所運用的認知機制。 在本計劃中，我們將會從行為和神經科學的角度，探討以廣東話為第二語言的人在聲調學習、聲調表徵及聲調動態上的表現。特別是，我們將會對50個以上無廣東話經驗並以普通話為母語的受試者進行一個為期18個月的長期性研究。受試者將於到達香港的首三個月內進行一系列的行為和腦電波實驗，以探究他們的音調系統在感知和說話方面的表現。他們的實驗結果將會和以廣東話為母語的受試者進行比較。比較的結果將和抽象理論以及樣例理論相連結，藉此更深入地了解聲調的認知機制。 總括來話，本計劃構成一個案例研究，有助探討一些更廣泛的問題，例如：語音的類別在大腦中如何表示和習得，以及語音的變異如何影響學習的結果等。因此，本計劃的發現將會有助於教育者去尋找更有效的教學方法以提升語言學習的效率。

14411314.label: Realisation of objectives
14411314.value: In this project, we conducted a longitudinal study of second-language learning of a tone system, using the empirical data that is obtained to clarify how lexical tones are cognitively represented. We recruited 35 first language Mandarin speakers with no prior experience of Cantonese to learn Cantonese tones. Each Mandarin participant took part in a series of three experimental sessions dispersed by two training sessions: Experimental Session 1 (Pre-test) + Training Session 1 + Experimental Session 2 (Mid-test) + Training Session 2 + Experimental Session 3 (Post-test) Each test session compromised the same two tasks: the production task and the identification task. Before each test, subjects received written instructions and became familiarized with the experiment via a practice session. The auditory stimuli used in the practice session were different from those used in the tests. Stimulus presentations were controlled by E-Prime 2.0 in the test sessions. The Cantonese tone production task: Subjects’ productions were recorded with Adobe Audition in a sound-insulated booth. The characters used in the production task were the same as those used in training. In each trial, a traditional Chinese character, together with the corresponding Jyutping transcription and tone letter, was presented on screen. Subjects were instructed to read aloud the characters as naturally as possible, and were encouraged to correct or repeat their pronunciations whenever necessary. Each production task consisted of 108 trials (36 characters × 3 repetitions), which were mixed and played in a random order. After finishing 54 trials, subjects could take a one-minute break. This was a self-paced production task. Once subjects were satisfied with their pronunciation for each trial, they were required to press the space button to move on to the next trial. The Cantonese tone identification task: The test stimuli (36 tonal syllables × 5 repetitions) were mixed and played in a random order. In each trial, an auditory stimulus was played binaurally to subjects, and six traditional Chinese characters sharing the same base syllable but having distinct lexical tones were also shown on the screen at the same time. Subjects were instructed to press a button from 1 to 6 on the keyboard to indicate which tone they perceived. The maximum allowable response time was 2,500 milliseconds (ms). During the tone identification task, subjects' EEG signals were also recorded simultaneously. As for the training sessions, the speech shadowing paradigm was adopted to train Mandarin subjects’ Cantonese tone perception and production simultaneously. The stimulus presentation for training was controlled by Praat. In each trial, a training stimulus was played first and participants were instructed to imitate the recording they heard. The corresponding traditional Chinese character, its Jyutping transcription, and the tone letter of each stimulus were also shown on the screen for the learners’ reference. Each training set consisted of 576 stimuli (4 speakers × 36 tonal syllables × 4 samples; about 30 minutes). Stimuli from the same speaker were blocked and the 36 tonal syllables were played sequentially (i.e., /fɐn55/, /fɐn33/, /fɐn22/, /fɐn21/, /fɐn23/, /fɐn25/, /fu55/, …) within each block. Each training session comprised six training sets. Mandarin subjects were assigned to either the high variability (HV) or low variability (LV) training materials. They were asked to finish one training set every two days at a quiet place of their own choice using their own computers and headphones. In order to construct a baseline for each tone category, the native norm for each tonal category was calculated by averaging 29 native Cantonese speakers’ productions (12 informants recruited for speech recordings for preparing the testing stimuli and training materials and 17 subjects recruited as the control group) across all pronunciations with the same tone. Analysis of the production data: Subjects’ productions were analysed acoustically. The pitch trajectories of all the recordings obtained during the production task were characterized by two variables: the pitch height and pitch slope. The acoustic distance between each utterance (corresponding to a syllable) produced by Mandarin subjects and the native norm was calculated. The pitch slope, ranging between −0.2 and 0.2, was multiplied by 10 so that it was enlarged to the same range as the pitch height. Smaller distance means higher resemblance between a Mandarin subjects’ production and the native norm. Mandarin subjects’ learning results of Cantonese tone productions were evaluated based on the production improvement. The production improvement after the first training session was calculated as the mid-test distance minus the pre-test distance, and the improvement after the second training session was calculated as the post-test distance minus the mid-test distance. If subjects’ production improved after training, the production improvement would be a negative number. Therefore, the smaller the number obtained, the larger the production improvement achieved. Analysis of the perception data: The perception improvement was analysed to evaluate subjects’ learning results of Cantonese tone perception. In each trial, a tonal syllable was played to subjects. If subjects could correctly identify the tonal category of the stimulus they heard, the trial was counted as a correct one. Otherwise, it was regarded as wrong. Subjects’ perception accuracies in all three test sessions were calculated. The perception improvement after the first training session was defined as the mid-test accuracy minus the pre-test accuracy. Likewise, the perception improvement after the second training session was the post-test accuracy minus the mid-test accuracy. To further illustrate the detailed perceptual results, the confusion matrices of the identification task are also calculated. The confusion matrix shows how frequently a target tonal category was identified as each of the six Cantonese tone categories. Moreover, event-related potentials (ERPs) were calculated by averaging the EEG epochs time-locked to each target tone respectively. ERPs were compared synchronically across different tones within each sessions, and ERPs of the same tone were also compared diachronically across different testing sessions.

14411314.label: Major findings and research outcome
14411314.value: In the literature, the degree of speech variability has been controlled by the number of speakers involved in the training speech materials: small variability speech materials from a single speaker, and large variability speech materials from multiple speakers. Therefore, the variation involved includes both variation from relevant dimensions (e.g., pitch height and slope for tones) and that from irrelevant dimensions. Our study is the first one which investigates whether speech variability in the relevant dimensions affects L2 tone learning. Furthermore, our study is also the first one which looks at how tonal language speakers learn another non-native tone system. Speech variability in the present study showed a comparatively small effect on improving Mandarin speakers' learning of Cantonese tones (CT). High speech variability only facilitated Mandarin subjects' production of CT22 and CT33, the tones that were not mapped to any Mandarin tone (MT) categories, but did not promote their production of CT55, CT25, CT23, or CT21, which were mapped to their native MT55, MT35, and MT21 categories. Such a result indicates that the effect of speech variability on L2 lexical tone learning is constrained by subjects’ language backgrounds. Only when the L2 tonal categories are notably different from the tonal categories in learners’ L1 can speech variability facilitate tonal language speakers’ acquisition of L2 lexical tones. Besides, Mandarin subjects’ production, but not their perception, of CT22 and CT33 benefited from the HV training. Considering the well-acknowledged difficulty in perceiving the Cantonese level tones in isolation, the unequal results indicate that the effect of speech variability on improving L2 lexical tone learning is not robust and can be overwhelmed if the task is too difficult.

14411314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14411314.value: The native tone system and the non-native tone system may interact highly complicatedly. In order to tease apart the two factors: the influence of L1 tone system on tone learning and the influence of speech variability on tone learning, it is ideal to conduct the current research with two groups of non-tonal language speakers (one group to be trained with small variability speech materials, the other group trained with large variability speech materials). Without the influence from L1 tone system on tone learning, the picture of the influence of speech variability on tone learning would be clearer. My role was switched from the Co-I to the PI in the middle of the project. Moreover, the researcher who is skilled at computational simulations left the research team when I took over the PI role. With the remaining budget as well as the time, we failed to find another scholar who can help fully implement the Objective 4. However, it is an interesting research topic for us to purse in the future.

14411614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14411614.value: 結核病，尤其是近期出現的耐多藥和廣泛耐藥的結核病，已成為世界上對公共衛生危害最大的傳染病之一。結核病強大的傳染力和持續的感染能力使它成為長期威脅全球健康的疾病，並導致數以百萬的病例和死亡。現代科學的發展極大促進了對結核病的研究。如微生物學研究結核病基因上的演變，醫學地理學研究結核的時空聚集，流行病學家探討結核的流行和傳播因素。然而，細菌是如何在人群中穩定存在並持續傳播仍是一個未解之題。肺結核的傳播是十分活躍和高度複雜的，不能僅僅依靠一項領域求解。預防結核病的關鍵在於明晰疾病在空間和時間中的傳播模式，而且這些與人類活動息息相關。 本研究的目的是希望整合近期中國在不同研究領域得到6000多個結核病基因樣本資料庫，並且建立一個綜合各學科方法分析肺結核傳播的嚴格理論方法，本研究的科研成果將用於改善公共衛生實踐以及制定相關衛生政策。我們首先將從多種空間和時間尺度分析結核病，查明疾病在時空分佈中的異質性。第二，將利用中國疾病控制體系收集到大型結核病基因資料進行細菌演變的分析。第三，運用時空分析方法，我們能更好的理解結核病在微觀和宏觀上的傳播。中國擁有世界上最大的流動人口，這項研究也將會系統地探索人口遷移對肺結核傳播的影響。除此之外，研究將盡可能地結合人口因素、社會經濟學因素以及環境氣候因素（如陽光強度和照射時間、降雨、相對濕度、溫度）去綜合地闡述各種因素對結核病傳播的影響。最後，基於上述的研究分析，我們將提出一系列相關的衛生和疾病控制政策建議。本研究將為系統研究結核病和相關傳染病傳播機制打下堅實的科學基礎。

14411814.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14411814.value: 音符識別訓練與大腦視覺皮層活動變化之間的因果關係

14411814.label: Project Objectives
14411814.value: To investigate whether there is a causal relationship between note discrimination training and neural changes in the visual areas of the musical expertise network.
rows: To investigate whether there is a causal relationship between note discrimination training and neural changes in the visual areas of the musical expertise network.

14411814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14411814.value: ---Project Background--- Recent years have witnessed a surge of interest in the study of perceptual expertise for different object categories, such as faces, birds, dogs, fingerprints, letters and words. Recent studies have shown that fluent music readers also possess unique visual skills. For expert musicians, brain regions responsible for visual analyses show selectively higher activity to musical notes than to other visually similar patterns such as letters, pseudoletters and symbols. Novices do not show such selectivity. The engagement of the early visual areas and the ventral and dorsal visual pathways makes musical notes rather unique compared with other objects of expertise like faces and letters. An intriguing possibility is that brain activity changes as a result of an individual’s acquisition of expertise in recognizing musical notes. However, just like other research about real-world perceptual expertise, it is difficult to answer the causation question: Does the visual experience with musical notes establish some visual regions’ selectivity for notes? Or maybe those individuals who have a visual system better equipped for notes would more likely be engaged in music training and thus recognize musical notes more efficiently? ---Brief Project Description--- The objective of the project is to test the causal relationship between perceptual training and activity changes in the early visual cortex. Novices with no prior music training will learn to discriminate between note sequences in the laboratory for 30 sessions (45 minutes each). Before and after training, brain activity will be measured using ERP (event-related potential) and fMRI (functional magnetic resonance imaging). Results will show whether note discrimination training would cause selectively higher activity for musical notes compared with pseudoletters. ---Significance of Project--- The findings will identify the brain activity changes caused by the acquisition of perceptual expertise with musical notes. Theoretically this will allow further comparison between perceptual expertise with musical notation and other categories like faces, letters, etc. Practically, the training regimen will potentially help musicians overcome some of the bottlenecks of music reading, thus enhancing the efficiency of musical training. Results can also inform the treatment of musical alexia and agraphia, problems in reading and writing music. ---項目背景--- 近年科學界對不同領域如臉，鳥，狗，指紋，字母和詞語等的知覺專長的研究興趣激增。最近的研究顯示，看樂譜的能手也具有獨特的視覺技能。在善看樂譜的音樂人的大腦中，音符對視覺皮層的刺激較字母和符號等更高。生手則並無表現出這樣的選擇性大腦活動。早期視覺區以及腹側和背側視覺通路的參與，使音符成為知覺專長的一個特殊例子。一個有趣的可能性是，大腦活動的變化是對識別音符發展出專長的結果。然而，就像其他關於現實世界的感知專長的研究一樣，這涉及一個很難回答的因果關係問題：是識別音符的視覺訓練，引致視覺區域展現這種選擇性活動，還是那些視覺系統本身較適合識別音符的人，更可能從事音樂訓練，因而能更有效地識別音符？ ---項目簡介--- 這項目的目的是測試在音符感知訓練和早期視覺皮層活動的變化之間的因果關係。沒有受過音樂訓練新手將參與30次（每次45分鐘）的實驗室音符識別訓練。訓練前後實驗員將量度大腦對音符的反應變化。 ---項目的意義--- 研究結果將確定音符識別訓練和大腦活動變化的因果關係。從理論而言，這將允許把樂譜和其他如臉，文字等知覺專長作進一步比較。從應用而言，這種訓練或有助音樂家克服閱讀樂譜的瓶頸，從而提高音樂訓練的效率。

14411814.label: Realisation of objectives
14411814.value: The project initially planned to use both EEG and fMRI to address the question of whether early visual cortex activity would be changed after note discrimination training. We planned to test 20 novices before and after training, and also 20 musicians. Since the beginning of the project, it has become more and more difficult to secure time slots for conducing fMRI scans in local 3T scanners (including the ones at the HKU and at the Prince of Wales Hospital). While we have been relying on collaborators in the mainland and in Taiwan for scanning for other projects, this is not feasible for the current project since it involves visual training conducted in our laboratory in Hong Kong. This, together with the 20% cut of the funding, lead to our decision to give up the fMRI measures in this project. The change request was approved by the Research Committee of CUHK on 31 Aug, 2016 (please see attached). Twenty valid novice participants (3 more tested but data discarded due to EEG data quality issues) have taken part in the training study. Each participant went through 10-26 hours of computerized training spanning around 6 weeks, 1-2 hours each session, to acquire the visual skills to discriminate between briefly presented note patterns. Before and after training, participants went through behavioral and EEG pre-/post-tests to measure the changes to the neural activity in the visual areas responsible for shape analyses. It was found that our training successfully enhanced musical note discrimination performance in novices after training at a level comparable with that of fluent music readers in our own previous studies. Importantly, however, training caused changes in the responses of the higher-level visual areas to musical notation (N170), but not changes in earlier visual areas (as indicated by the C1 component). We concluded that visual training is enough for causing changes in the responses of the higher-level visual areas to musical notation while the engagement of the early visual areas may involve additional nonvisual factors. Despite the challenges, the main objective (to investigate whether there is a causal relationship between note discrimination training and neural changes in the visual areas of the musical expertise network) was still met, for the following reasons: 1. With ERP we can measure the ERP components (C1, P1, N170) which have been associated with brain processing at different points of the ventral visual streams responsible for visual shape analyses. The temporal resolution of the ERP techniques allow us to study different areas via the study of different time points when effects occur. While ERP cannot replace fMRI completely, arguably it is more useful than fMRI in this study in terms of studying the feedforward, bottom-up neural processing in the visual areas. In contrast, activations found in fMRI are often susceptible to explanations related to feedback from higher-level areas, which makes it hard to conclude if training results in changes in visual areas per se or if training results in changes of feedback of higher-level areas on the visual areas. With ERP we did see differential effects of our training, that occur for later visual areas (as indicated by the N170) but not the earlier ones (as indicated by the C1 and P1). 2. With the EEG data collection as the focus, we addd a repetition suppression paradigm besides the planned one-back repetition detection paradigm described in the proposal. While the one-back repetition detection paradigm allowed us to compare the general activation levels for different stimulus categories (e.g., musical notes, pseudo letters) before and after training, the additional repetition suppression paradigm allowed us to further look into the changes of ERP as a result of presenting the same vs. different stimuli (e.g., different musical notes). Thus the additional paradigm allowed us to go beyond studying activation differences between categories and look into sensitivity of the ERP to shape differences within categories. Indeed we found that training affected such sensitivity of the N170 component. The new paradigm resulted in a much longer EEG scanning time (e.g., >4 hours including the channel setup time, twice as long as planned). We therefore focused on testing the novices for twice as long a duration (before and after training), instead of testing both novices and musicians. 3. We spent a lot of time, energy, and effort to explore with a postdoc different analyis techniques to get the most out of the data. Most notably, we adopted the multivariate pattern analyses to analyse the single-trial EEG data, and found that the pattern of voltage across the scalp carried information about which stimulus category (musical notes, pseudoletters) are being viewed, and whether a musical note is the same as the previous one shown or not. The technique is also now being used to analyse the musician data of our 2014 ERP paper. While a paper has already been published on the ERP findings, another manuscript is being prepared to discuss the additional analyses showing that musicians (in the 2014 paper) demonstrated higher discriminability of EEG responses to different notes compared with novices at early processing stages, while novices (in the current project) did not show higher discriminability of EEG responses to different notes after training compared with before.

14411814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14411814.value: This project aimed to test whether training or experience can explain the higher responses of the visual system of the music readers to musical notation. We trained 20 novices who did not read music to visually discriminate between different musical note patterns for 10-26 hours. Brain activity (electroencephalogram) measures showed that training led to enhanced responses of the more advanced, higher-level visual areas, but the earlier, more primary visual areas did not change after training. The findings show the higher potential of changes in the more advanced regions of the sensory brain, and suggest that experience involving more modalities (e.g., vision, hearing, touch, motor) may be required for modifying the more primary portions of the sensory brain.

14411914.label: Realisation of objectives
14411914.value: This Database is a tailor-made electronic search tool, and is developed so as to allow the general public to get access to the information in the PI’s Greek-Chinese Lexicon by simply inputing the verse number. This product can help Chinese readers to overcome the languages barrier. The implementation of this project consists of five phases. Each phase focuses on a set of tasks and deliverables that can be measured to ensure consistency and progress throughout the project. The five phases are identified below: • Phase 1 – Project Preparation: The purpose of this phase is to provide detail planning and preparation for the project. • Phase 2 – Scope and Blueprint: The purpose of this phase is to create the scope and blueprint, which is a detailed documentation of the result gathered during requirements workshops including IT development objects and data requirements. Largely, the blueprint helps achieve a common understanding of how we intend to run the products by the end of the project. • Phase 3 – Realization: The purpose of this phase is to implement project requirements based on the blueprint. The key tasks of the realization phase are preparing, restructuring and converting the Microsoft Word Document of the PI’s Greek-Chinese lexicon into database file, which comprises more than 1400 pages, and finally developing the IT tools for end users. • Phase 4 – Final Preparation for go live: The purpose of this phase is to complete the final preparation, including testing of the end-product, and to plan and effect the go-live. • Phase 5 – Go live and Support: The purpose of this phase is to release the product to end user and provide support to achieve the Lexicon product stability. The final product could be accessed through following link (please download java programme before using this link): https://www.dropbox.com/s/hsmmyq4jdch3g8y/lexiconBrowser.zip?dl=0 Its users, whether they know Greek or not, can acquire the lexical information in Chinese about an individual Greek content word in the GNT by simply input the verse number, which is hyper-link with the PI’s Greek-Chinese Lexicon. The product allows its user to search for the lexical information of one biblical verse each time. For example, if the user selects Romans 2:8 (羅2:8), the database will show: A) the GNT text: τοις δε εξ εριθειας και απειθουσιν τη αληθεια πειθομενοις δε τη αδικια οργη και θυμος B) 7 content words of that biblical verse with their corresponding Chinese glosses: ἀδικία, ας, ἡ I. 不公正的行為；不正直的素質；不義的事情 ── 不公正的活動；違反正確品德規範的行動；惡行。 羅2:8 ἀλήθεια, ας, ἡ I. 事實真相；誠實；真理。 c) 真理；基督教的基本信息，指藉耶穌而帶來的上帝啟示，又或耶穌本身就等同於真理。 羅2:8 ἀπειθέω 過未完 ἠπείθουν；1過不定 ἠπείθησα 3. 名詞化用語： a) 不願意或拒絕服從(權力)的人。 羅2:8 ἐριθεία, ας, ἡ I. 1. 私心；對立；怨恨 ── 基於妒忌而怨恨起來，並含有「對立」的意思。 羅2:8 θυμός, ου̃, ὁ I. 1. 憤怒；暴怒；怒氣；盛怒 ── 極度憤怒的狀態，並含有「出於激情的爆發」的意思。 羅2:8 ὀργή, η̃ς, ἡ 2. 刑罰 ── 基於上帝對某人的憤怒審判而施行的神性刑罰。 羅2:8 πείθω 1過不定 ἔπεισα；將 πείσω；完 πέποιθα；過未完 ἔπειθον；1過不定 被動 ἐπείσθην；過完 ἐπεποίθειν；過未完 被動 ἐπειθόμην；將 被動πεισθήσομαι；完 被動 πέπεισμαι 3. 服從 ── 按照當權者或道理而行，以示屈從。 羅2:8 C) If users press the button for “detail information”, they will get all occurrences of a specific content word in New Testament immediately. As an example, the first content word was shown as following: ἀδικία, ας, ἡ I. 不公正的行為；不正直的素質；不義的事情 ── 不公正的活動；違反正確品德規範的行動；惡行。 路13:27； 16:8,9； 18:6； 約7:18； 徒1:18； 8:23； 羅1:18,29； 2:8； 3:5； 6:13； 9:14； 林前13:6； 林後12:13； 帖後2:10,12； 提後2:19； 來8:12； 雅3:6； 彼後2:13,15； 約一1:9； 5:17 This is a layman-accessible Database which will offer Chinese readers of the Bible the possibility to avoid sole reliance on the literal interpretation of the biblical text provided by the existing major Chinese biblical translations, thus promoting studies of the Bible informed by solid scholarly works on biblical Greek among Chinese-speaking scholars and students.

14411914.label: Major findings and research outcome
14411914.value: This database includes all entries of content words (i.e. nouns, adjectives, verbs and adverbs) in the PI’s Greek-Chinese lexicon, which offers lexical definitions and exhaustive lists of occurrences of all content words in the GNT. The lexical definitions of the PI’s Greek-Chinese lexicon, which will be re-assessed and updated with reference to recent scholarship on biblical Greek during the course of research. Users of the tailor-made search tool, whether they know Greek or not, will have easy access to the lexical information in Chinese about an individual Greek content word in the GNT by moving the mouse pointer to its corresponding verse number of New Testament, thanks to the hyper-link between the gloss and its corresponding updated entry in the PI’s Greek-Chinese lexicon. The impact of the proposed project will be far-reaching, as the resultant lexical database will be of service to both the scholarly community and the general public. The Bible is not simply a religious text. It is also a recognized world’s literary classics. Chinese-speaking literary scholars who do not know Greek will understand the Bible better by being informed of the accurate Greek lexical information about the New Testament. Even Chinese scholars in biblical studies will also benefit from the updated scholarship on the biblical Greek reflected in the lexical data. In addition, as a means of knowledge transfer to the general public, the resultant lexical database will have great potential to reach beyond the academia. Through the tailor-made search tool, all Chinese readers who are interested in the Bible will be able to acquire the lexical data of the GNT without knowing Greek. Being more informed about the Bible, both believers and non-believers will be able to minimize their misunderstanding of Christianity arising from distorted interpretations of the Bible. In the long run, this will facilitate dialogues between them, and between Christianity and other religions. Moreover, given that the New Testament is a major written work in Koine Greek, the resultant database will serve as an easily accessible reference tool for Chinese-speaking learners of the Greek language.

14411914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14411914.value: Building on the success of the two previous projects created by PI: The first one is the PI’s Greek-Chinese Lexicon of the Greek New Testament《新約希臘文詞典》, which was produced with the support from a CERG of the RGC in 1999 (CUHK 4010/99H). It was published by Hong Kong Bible Society in August 2015. And the second one is “Opening the Greek World to All: Creating a Chinese-Greek Lexical Database of the New Testament” was support by a GRF grant (CUHK/14411917) in 2014. A new GRF application for 2018/19 was submitted by PI which is aims at creating a layman-accessible e-learning interface for the Chinese-Greek New Testament. With the help of information technology, the interface will present the following lexical data related to the New Testament in user-friendly ways: 1) the Greek words of the verse selected by the user; 2) the Chinese text that is matched with the verse and constructed with the glosses provided by the PI’s Greek-Chinese Lexicon; 3) the Chinese definitions in the PI’s Greek-Chinese Lexicon of the Greek content words in the verse selected by the user; and 4) the occurrences of the Greek content words in the GNT listed under the Chinese definitions.

14411914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14411914.value: Realizing the limitations of a Chinese biblical translation as a representation of the Greek biblical text, many Chinese readers of the Bible would like to learn the Greek language so that they could study the New Testament more in-depth by getting access to the source text. Unfortunately, although they have such a desire, the Greek language is not easy for them to learn. Many existing Chinese resources and tools to learn biblical Greek required their users to have gained at least a very basic knowledge of Greek, if the users want to fully utilize them. The inconveniences to Chinese speakers in learning biblical Greek often discourage them to do so. The Greek New Testament (GNT) remains, to many Chinese readers of the Bible, a valuable yet inaccessible resource. In response to this problem, the project “Opening the Greek World to All: Creating a Chinese-Greek Lexical Database of the New Testament” aims at creating a Chinese-Greek lexical database of the GNT that can help Chinese readers to overcome the abovementioned language barriers with the help of information technology and the updated biblical language scholarship.
