To examine the effects and quality of school-based mentoring activities on the professional growth of mentor teachers;
To investigate influential factors which help mentor teachers develop their role as teacher leaders through mentoring practice.

14412214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14412214.value: Mentoring is an established process in the teaching profession by which novice teachers come to fit in as members of an educational institution and of the profession. Research in this area has traditionally emphasized the benefits of this process to mentees. The mentoring process, however, also provides a platform for mentor teachers to reflect on their own practice and hone their leadership as well as teaching skills. However, little research has been conducted into what mentor teachers need to help them perform their mentoring role effectively or how working with a less experienced colleague develops the mentor professionally. Studies in the area of mentor preparation are also rare. The key research question that guides this study is “What makes the growth of mentor teachers possible through mentoring practice?” It will identify the needs of mentor teachers, explore how they are currently prepared for the role, if at all, and will examine what mentor teachers learn through involvement in mentoring. It will assess the quality of existing mentor preparation programmes and suggest good practice so that induction programmes, and the wider school environment, can consistently contribute to the success of such schemes. This study will use a mixed method approach. Focus group interviews involving up to 30 participants from 30 primary or secondary schools will be used to identify mentor teachers’ views on their needs, their preparedness for the role, and what they learn through the mentoring process. Information gathered from them will help us to understand characteristics of mentoring practice and mentor preparation in primary and secondary schools as well as the environments in which such schemes take place. Based on the findings of these interviews, 500 questionnaires for mentor teachers will be administered to collect broader views regarding the existing quality of mentoring practice in relation to their professional development and school-based mentor preparation programme. Afterwards, 10 follow up individual interviews will be conducted to validate the issues emerging from the questionnaires. This investigation will be the first to identify what factors help mentor teachers not only perform their roles optimally, but also develop professionally as teacher leaders, thereby addressing a paucity of such information in the prevailing literature. Findings of the study will contribute to school-based mentor preparation programmes in Hong Kong by pinpointing key areas where the skillsets and knowledge bases of the participants need to be supplemented for maximum effectiveness.

14412214.label: Realisation of objectives
14412214.value: This study applied a mixed method approach to examine the professional needs and professional growth of mentor teachers when they engage in school-based mentoring scheme and take up their duty to help novice teachers have a smooth transition at an early stage of their career. The data collection process included three stages starting from 2014 and ending in 2017. Firstly, qualitative data gathered from interviews with 31 mentor teachers with varied mentoring experience from 30 primary and secondary schools were used to identify mentor teachers’ views on their needs, their preparedness for the role, and what they learned through the mentoring process. Information gathered from them helped us to understand the characteristics of mentoring practice and mentor preparation in primary and secondary schools as well as the environments in which such schemes take place. Secondly, a questionnaire based on the findings of these interviews plus several surveys regarding mentoring practice was designed. Questionnaires were administered to collect broader views regarding the current quality of mentoring practice in relation to the professional development of mentor teachers and their role transition, and the school-based mentor preparation programmes. 207 questionnaires from 25 secondary schools and 20 primary schools were collected. Thirdly, 10 follow up individual interviews were conducted to validate the issues emerging from the questionnaires. Based on the qualitative data collected at stage 1 via interview, four types of information were identified. Firstly, the professional needs of mentor teachers, namely structural and intellectual needs were obtained. Secondly, critical factors that affect learning opportunities of mentor teachers, such as mentoring practice, administrative support to mentoring practice from school leaders, school culture, resource allocation, external support and interpersonal relationship with fellow colleagues were identified. Thirdly, personal growth and the identity shift of mentor teachers when they engage in mentoring practice were described. Fourthly, the challenges mentor teachers encountered when they enact their role were provided. All these items served as the basis for the design of the questionnaire. This questionnaire further asked mentor teachers’ views on the “professional needs of being an effective mentor” and “when I enact my role as mentor, my professional needs have been matched”. Results collected from the questionnaires are consistent with the data collected in the stage 3 follow up interviews. Viewing the results of this study, the three stated objectives are all fully achieved. Details are explained as belows: Objective 1: Fully achieved Findings of Research question 1 “What are the influential factors of developing school-based mentor support and training in Hong Kong and what is their quality?” provided relevant information to respond to Objective 1 of this study. Results of this section show that the development and the quality of school-based mentor support and training are highly affected by the following: 1. The practice of mentoring has not yet been set as an agenda of school development 2. There is insufficient support on mentoring practice and lack of sharing among mentors and mentees 3. Official guidelines and related documentary support from the Education Bureau and schools are lacking 4. Teaching load are heavy 5. Mentor teachers lack time and opportunities to share their views among themselves 6. There is a lack of sharing from outside regarding the implementation of school-based mentoring schemes 7. Learning content seems to focus more on administrative issues of the schools rather than matching the knowledge needs of mentor teachers, such as career counselling and communication techniques, lesson observation techniques, understanding the psychological needs of novice teachers etc. 8. Mentoring practice has not yet been institutionalized The above eight factors have been shown to highly influence the development of school-based mentor support and the quality of mentor training programmes. Objective 1 of this study, therefore, has been fully achieved. Objective 2: Fully achieved The findings of Research question 2 “What do mentor teachers need in order to enhance their competency for undertaking mentoring responsibilities?” provided answers for Objective 2 of this study. Important findings which address the professional needs of mentor teachers when they engage in mentoring practice were generated from both qualitative and quantitative data. They are listed below: 1. Two types of professional needs of mentor teachers were identified. They are grouped as structural and intellectual needs. Items in the category of structural needs, together with their mean scores, are (i) “support of interpersonal relationship” (4.0); (ii) “school structure/ atmosphere” (3.8); (iii) “sufficient time and space for mentors” (3.7). The category of intellectual needs include (i) “Personality/Educational ideas” (4.2); (ii) “Administrative and professional development” (4.1); (iii) “Understanding community, school and mentees’ needs” (4.0); (iv) “Interpersonal communication and counselling skills” (4.0); and (v) “Mentoring related knowledge and skills” (3.7). 2. It emerged that administrative support has an impact on three factors: “school culture on mentor support”, “support of interpersonal relationship between mentors and mentees”, and “self-efficacy of mentor teachers”. 3. No significant differences between various types of schools regarding professional needs of mentor teachers were identified. 4. Professional growth of mentor teachers when they engage in mentoring practice takes several forms: (i) mentors have an increased of pedagogical knowledge and information technology knowledge during the mentoring practice; (ii) mentors with strong outside network have more opportunities to engage in transformative learning; (iii) mentors who have strong inside and outside ties seem to be able to have strong decisional capital when they encounter challenges. Viewing the findings stated above, the professional needs of mentor teachers and their professional growth when they engaged in school-based mentoring practice have been identified. In all, Objective 2 of this study has been fully achieved. Objective 3: Fully achieved Research question 3 “How do schools prepare their mentor teachers to perform their mentoring tasks and do they cultivate them as teacher leaders?” fully addresses Objective 3 of this study. After analyzing data related to the correlation of various items under the categories of “school climate and structure”, “administrative support to mentors”, “interpersonal relationship” and “self-efficacy of mentor teachers”, “self-perception on professional growth of mentor teachers” and “challenges mentor teachers encountered”, it was found that, in the role transition of mentor teachers to teacher leaders, the following factors were relevant: 1. School structure and climate have an impact on the growth of leadership skills of mentor teachers 2. Interpersonal relationships have an impact on the growth of leadership skills of mentor teachers. 3. Mentor teachers capitalize their leadership role through closing the gap between outside knowledge and internal practice. 4. Mentoring practice provides a context for mentors to grow or enhance their role as teacher leaders. The transformation to leadership role of mentor teachers has been identified as involving the growth of “policy implementation and management” (45.75%); the growth of “communication and decision making skills, and reflection” (40.7%), the growth of “self-efficacy” (29.6%), and the growth of “pedagogical skills” (22.5%) 5. Factors that contribute to the successful role transition of mentor teachers include (i) having sufficient information and learning programmes; (ii) developing counselling and/or career counselling skills; (iii) enhanced communication skills; (iv) improved pedagogical skills and pedagogical content knowledge; and (v) developing a sustainable and supportive learning community Findings stated above can help address the issue of role transition of mentor teachers when they engage in mentoring practice. Objective 3 of this study, therefore, has been fully achieved.

14412214.label: Major findings and research outcome
14412214.value: Based on both qualitative and quantitative data collected, major findings of this research project are presented as follows: 1. The development and the quality of school-based mentor support and training are highly influenced by whether the mentoring practices have been institutionalized and set as part of the school development agenda, and whether the mentors have been given resource allocation including time, sharing opportunities and external inputs on mentor training, and documentary support and guideline to help mentor teacher training. The relevance of the content of mentor training programmes is also important. 2. The professional needs of mentor teachers have been grouped as two types in terms of structural and intellectual levels. 3. Professional growth of mentor teachers appears to be threefolds. Firstly, most mentor teachers studied seem to gain a certain level of new pedagogical knowledge during the mentoring process. Secondly, mentor teachers who have strong external social capital tend to have more opportunities to engage in transformative learning. Thirdly, mentor teachers who act as boundary brokers are likely to develop their decisional capital. 4. The effects of role transition on some mentor teachers studied as teacher leaders have been identified. They gained knowledge and skills regarding “policy implementation and management”, “communication and decision making skills, and reflection”, “self-efficacy” and “pedagogical skills” all of which helped them to have successful role transformation. Others contributing factors to successful transition have also been found. The outcomes of this research project take three forms. Firstly, one referred journal article entitled “Why social capital is important for mentoring capacity building of mentors: a case in Hong Kong” was published in August 2018 in Teachers and Teaching: Theory and Practice which is one of the leading SSCI journals in the field of teacher education. Two more journal articles based on Findings 1, 2 and 4 are in the pipeline. The target journals for these two manuscripts are “Journal of Teacher Education” (Findings 1 and 2) and “School Effectiveness and School Improvement” (Finding 4) Secondly, three conference presentations, two of which were funded by the GRF grant were delivered. Each conference presentation addressed one research question of this research project. Thirdly, one Chinese technical report based on the findings of the questionnaires was completed and sent to each participating school of the research project. Suggestions on ways to improve the mentoring practice and the mentor training programmes were also proposed.

14412214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14412214.value: Two possible research directions could be further considered. Firstly, because the present findings show that mentor teachers who have an outside network can enhance their professional competency, schools need external inputs in order to facilitate their mentor training programmes. Given this, one possible focus of further research could be to study the possibilities of developing types of partnership schemes with outside experts that can maximize the professional competency of mentor teachers and improve school capacity. Such research could contribute to the knowledge development of school improvement through staff development. Secondly, because the findings show that many mentor teachers were able to capitalize their leadership role and successfully experience role transition to being teacher leaders, similar research may also be usefully applied to student mentorship in Hong Kong which is an field that deserves further attention. Taking up the role as a mentor may facilitate the personal and professional development of individual students when they help newcomers to be familiar with school culture.

14412214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14412214.value: Research on mentoring practice has put its key focus on ways to help novice teachers effectively function in their schools and contribute fully to school goals and objectives. Little attention has been paid to the professional development of the mentor teachers and how these mentors transit to teacher leaders as they work with their mentees. To address this research gap, this study focusses on “what mentor teachers learn and how they grow” by identifying the professional needs of mentor teachers, examining how they acquire new knowledge and leadership skills through their engagement in school-based mentoring practice and how their role transition is facilitated by practicing their leadership role during the mentoring process. Data gathered in this study help us to understand the characteristics of mentoring practice and mentor preparation in schools as well as the environments in which such schemes take place. Findings of this study contribute to school-based mentor preparation programmes in Hong Kong by pinpointing key areas where the skillsets and knowledge bases of the mentor teachers studied need to be supplemented for maximum effectiveness. More importantly, this study sheds further light on the global discussion on professional growth of veteran teachers by addressing their professional needs.

14412314.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14412314.value: 香港文學中的「六四」話語研究

14412314.label: Project Objectives
14412314.value: To study the literary representations of the June Fourth Incident by providing a comprehensive collection of the literary works published from June 1989 to June 1990, investigating what kind of immediate impacts are brought upon literature within a year after the incident in terms of themes, forms and language, and how China is conceptualized aesthetically in literature. To study the individually creative dimension of Hong Kong’s literary response to June Fourth by focusing specifically on portraits of the incident, recent development of the discourse and also examining related dialogues among different generations of writers. Combining the above two tasks, this study can generate a three-dimensional model for us to understand the June Fourth literary representations comprehensively, individually and inter-generationally. At a time when the issues of China-Hong Kong relations, social intervention of arts and political involvement of the post-80’s and post-90’s youngsters has attracted so much scholarly and popular imagination, the highest level of actual performance in literature cannot be overlooked but must be scrutinized within its specific aesthetic contexts.

14412314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14412314.value: The proposed research provides a pioneering study of the 'June Fourth discourse' in Hong Kong exemplified in literary works by writers and students. There are two main objectives: 1. Providing a comprehensive survey on literary works published in Hong Kong within the one year period of June 1989 to June 1990 with respect to the national identity discourse; and 2. Analyzing the 'June Fourth representations' in literature in the last 25 years after the incident by case studies of the Hong Kong writer Wong Bik Wan黃碧雲 (1961—); the youth writers' magazine Fleurs Des Lettres字花 (2006—); and poetry anthologies in the name of June Fourth. Combining the two perspectives, we shall able to learn more about the changing representations of the Tiananmen Incident of 1989 in the last quarter of century, as well as Hong Kong's initiatives on the incident, a subject where political reality and individual identity crisis meet, I believe this research will have a wide impact on our understanding of the complex relations between contemporary literature and politics as well as literature and social commitment. The actual vibrant society of Hong Kong has passed from pre-retrocession to post-retrocession, also offering us a new angle to study how literature manifests in different political status. This research will also provide unique case studies to understand the actual meanings, impacts, and ideological discourse reflected in the nuance of literary representations, which has become the burgeoning academic concerns in Hong Kong identity and the region's relation with China. 本計劃旨在探討香港對1989年6月4日「天安門事件」的文學回應與其「六四」話語之生成。具體研究目的有二︰1. 全面整理及描述1989年6月至1990年6月間的香港文學環境及其國族認同之轉變；2. 分析「六四」後二十五年間香港文學對相關事件之再現，研究重點包括香港作家黃碧雲（1961—）之小說、六四詩選及文學雜誌《字花》之相關專題。 從以上兩項分析中，將可見「六四」事件的文學再現（literary representations）在過去四分一世紀之轉變，同時亦見香港人對該事件作為政治現實與個人認同危機方面的意義。本研究可以為當代文學與政治的關係提供深化的實例，體現文學作為社會參與的可能。此外，亦展現從「回歸」到「後回歸」時期香港文學對不同政治身份的回應。最後，本研究亦為香港文學提供一個獨特的個案研究，在現時各種中港關係論述中，帶出機微的文學體制內如何反映實際的意義、影響與意識形態的轉變。

14412314.label: Realisation of objectives
14412314.value: 1. To study the literary representations of the June Fourth Incident by providing a comprehensive collection of the literary works published from June 1989 to June 1990, the project drew on the literary criticism of what was known as discourse analysis, espousing a view of literature and criticism based on the archival studies which held that literary works were embodiments of authorial consciousness. The objective was epitomized in the seminar given at Cambridge University in 2016, in which the PI undertook the task of examining a sum of 56 fiction, over 100 poems and over seven hundred days of literary supplements from newspapers, as well as nearly 1,000 articles collected from the National Archives, Japanese Diet Library and digital databases worldwide, so as to reconstruct the usual conception of ‘apolitical amnesia, as a collective, indifferent, bystander position of Hong Kong people. Yet if it read literary work to understand the vicissitude of literary life of June Fourth in Hong Kong, it also saw literary works as the expressions of writers whose relationship to the Chinese language and culture was never entirely stable. For the writing conveyed an aura of dislocation, hybridity and strangeness. No place on earth could represent the fate of lost and disorientation entailed from the June Fourth Incident better than Hong Kong, and no more ironic about the effort of trying to replace that condition with affiliation and accommodation. 2. To study the individually creative dimension of Hong Kong’s literary response to June Fourth by focusing specifically on portraits of the incident, the project viewed the ensemble of writing on the June Fourth incident as a discourse. Together the writings of Wong Bik-wan and Dung Kai-cheung composed a discipline by which Hong Kong managed and produced the ‘China’. Their writings expressed a will not only to understand what ‘non-Hong Kong’ was, but also to control and manipulate what was manifestly different. Although under the suggestions of scholarly critic Perry Link, he may considered Hong Kong writers’ stands as bystander, the project found that the precise diction and grasp of idiosyncratic Chinese used, the relationship to the Chinese language as an expression of China experience of exile, victims and even perpetrators. ‘An Experiment in Sinophone: A Reading of Wong Bik-wan’s Fiction after 1989’ considered the fact that the Hong Kong ‘bystanders’, as ‘the victims of victims,’ has become a crucial part of the history of the June Fourth incident. The paper argued that they must be acknowledged within this history under the concept of Sinophone literature, no Hong Kong literature can ignore the presence of the ‘China proper’. Such an approach was linked closely to strategies of ‘juxtaposition’ and ‘mutual recognition’ of the conflict between Hong Kong and China. As observed in the above mentioned paper, Wong Bik-wan was the first writer of any prominence to argue for the necessity of an affirmation of the limits between people outside and inside the incident. The works of her fiction ‘Of Tender and Violence’ 溫柔與暴烈 in 1993 and the long poem ‘Without a Hint’ 無所提示 in 2011 explains just as no one has been a direct victim of the incident, so too no one has been unmarked by it. Regarding the discursive mode of study of the project, if Foucault offered us a means of describing the relationship between knowledge and power over the country, Gramsci’s concept of hegemony provided a way of explaining how the influence of certain ideas about the June Fourth incident prevailed over others. The extensive influence of a particular idea, operated not through the brute application of force in Hong Kong (a non-totalitarian society), but by consent – a tacit, unwritten agreement often passed off as conventional wisdom or common sense. In ‘In Search of the Language Lost: Dung Kai Cheung’s Fiction after 1989’, it examines why the written language of Hong Kong literature received with such vicissitude during the colonial years and how is it that the urge on an ‘ideal language’ which writers pursue for are provoked after the June Fourth incident. The personification of language choices in Dung Kai-cheung’s fiction ‘The Rise and Fall of Wing Shing Street’ gives a vivid example of the futile ‘remaking’ of history and a trilemma of language search after 1989. The short story mirrors the difficulty of language choices over Cantonese (dialect Cantonese), Putonghua (vernacular modern Chinese) and an ideal artistic language of Nanyin 南音 (a combination of classical Chinese and Cantonese) which were personified by three female characters in the story. Although the literary language Nanyin was made as an ideal language, the ghostlike image of the character who personified Nanyin well expressed the haunted experience of the June Fourth incident. There is an urgent political need for such narration in the current situation. To testify to the very existence of the Hong Kong as a people and as people, with a history, a culture and a right to self-determination, was a radical and unsettling move for a culture that denied them all this, even refusing them the opportunity to represent themselves through the participation of the important historical moment of modern China. 3. Combining the above two tasks, this study can generate a three-dimensional model for us to understand the June Fourth literary representations comprehensively, individually and inter-generationally. At the time of this research took place, over 1,000 pieces of works of fiction, poetry and prose were collected and indexed for analysis. However, the PI found the development of Digital Humanities and related data analytical technology could benefit the project tremendously. For example, the founder of the Google Ngram Viewer tracked the uses of the words ‘Tiananmen’ and ‘天安门’ over the past decades in their English and Chinese corpus respectively for detecting censorship and suppression between the English publication and Chinese publication. (Michel, Jean-Baptiste, et al. 2011) However, what the study did not mentioned is that the use of 天安門 in Traditional characters--Chinese characters use in Hong Kong and Taiwan rather than the tested Simplified characters used in mainland China—projects no signs of censorship nor suppression, but an even more dramatic surge after 1989 and a sustainable level of attention than in the usage of the English corpus. The study made two cases in point. Firstly, the quantitative analysis of the text of millions of books resulted a new field of research and a groundbreaking tool to see answers to an array of otherwise intractable questions of the June Fourth literary corpus. Secondly, the results remarked that there is a big difference between the representations of Tiananmen written in simplified Chinese and traditional Chinese, i.e. in mainland China and Hong Kong. The incorporation of the methodology of digital humanities expanded the existing scope of the project which requires a book-length study to cover. The PI will accomplish the manuscript of it in six months with a publisher in Taiwan showed early interest in the book project. The three dimensional model in the objective will be fully covered in the last chapter of the monograph and the outline of the content could be referenced in the separate section concerning the outputs of the project. Michel, Jean-Baptiste, et al. “Quantitative Analysis of Culture Using Millions of Digitized Books.” Science, vol. 331, no. 6014, 2011, pp. 176–182. JSTOR, JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/40986490.

14412314.label: Major findings and research outcome
14412314.value: Despite the slightly outspoken essays, reticent tone, and sometimes parodic imageries, the literary works on June Fourth shows how remarkably consistent Hong Kong has been in its political and moral vision from the very outset. Hong Kong literature is asserted as being multicultural from the get go. No exclusivism can be found in the over 1,000 pieces of literary works examined, even to mainland China; rather we see that the same drive for coexistence that propel much of the literary writings about June Fourth. By detailing the slow emergence of an indigenous, Hong Kong resistance movement through the device of analysis and personal creativity, the Hong Kong literature experience is in fact narrating to us our own emergence as an engaged Hong Kong intellectual. It was also the first study wherein we juxtaposed the works by young poets born after 1989 to the long developments in the June Fourth literature. It engages the problem of authority in literature and politics, an issue that would find full expression later in the book length study. For the study of Tiananmen was not totally new; other scholars had addressed the subject before. But the current study differed markedly from its predecessors. It brought together the philosophies of aesthetics and archival science to challenge the authority on issues such as the ‘amnesia’ of the people towards the June Fourth incident and the Western knowledge about the comprehensive censorship of mentioning June Fourth in ‘Chinese media’. It examined an array of novelists, poets, essayists, the narratives of victims, as well as bystanders or even indirect perpetrators.

14412314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14412314.value: The traumatic affiliations remarking the June Fourth incident has frequently led critics to regard literary works on the issue more for its contribution to the rejection of mainland China than for its connection to both nationalism and self-determination. The project observed that for the Hong Kong writers writing about June Fourth, China was an ‘imaginary homeland’, the sort of place endlessly invented and reinvented by Hong Kong people who want to give a local habitation in words for it. The abundant corpus of literary works on June Fourth shows what the ‘local habitation in words’ look like. And with its fully digitized version downloadable in the near future, researchers can make use of the corpus and further explore the crucial issues of Hong Kong-China relations through the lens of June Fourth from the aspects of literature to sociology, politics and culture.

14412314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14412314.value: The project reinterprets the portraits of the June Fourth incident represented in high literary works in Hong Kong, away from the moral and comfortable canons of 'apolitical literature' or 'patriotic poetry', and into a grappling discourse of post-colonialism, nationalism and self-determination. It places Hong Kong literature within a tradition of other anti-hegemonic works, finding that all of them seek a cartographic sensibility with their literature, reclaiming, renaming and re-inhabiting their imaginary homeland of the democratized China with their literary works. Over 1,000 pieces works of fiction, poetry and essays on the topic were examined with qualitative close readings and quantitative archival science.

14413014.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14413014.value: 汶川震后規劃：走向韌性模式？

14413014.label: Project Objectives
14413014.value: To discern changes in China’s urban planning system resulting from the Wenchuan earthquake; that is, to understand the emerging concerns and innovative tools used by the system when facing a sudden occurrence with detrimental repercussion and to clarify how they differ from existing planning practice. In particular, the four key aspects of the planning system will be highlighted. To explore the use of ‘resilience’ as a theoretical construct in scrutinizing post-disaster planning. More specifically, this is to study the resilience of the planning system to natural disasters and to offer a new perspective to theorize China’s planning practice. To introduce a set of resilience attributes in planning and use them to evaluate the extent to which post-earthquake planning in Wenchuan is able to demonstrate resilience, even though this concept may not be overtly used by urban planners. To discuss planning outcomes from a 'resilience perspective'. Post-disaster planning in China is led by the central state but subject to local interpretation and the ever-changing post-disaster conditions. There are no specific standards and contents that are clearly defined. Many organizations and agencies are also involved in the processes of recovery and reconstruction. The interdependence of different agencies makes up a body of socially embedded, politically regularized and strategically selective forces in the planning process, forming another focus of our research. To critically analyse, evaluate and theorize on the results of post-disaster planning moving towards a resilience-based approach. This will allow us to make recommendations on how the planning system can be improved, resulting in resilient urban areas.

14413014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14413014.value: China is disaster-prone. It is a fragile territory exposed to many natural catastrophes. These take many forms and can lead to hazardous results, presenting enormous challenges in the way of reconstruction. The wide-ranging impacts of disasters, epitomized by the earthquakes in Tangshan in 1976 and Wenchuan in 2008, have gradually made government bodies, at various levels, aware that urban planning is an important tool for reducing vulnerability to natural disasters. As a result, there have been some attempts to establish a central state-led post-disaster planning system to address issues of recovery and reconstruction, as well as to build disaster-resistant communities. Although discussion is moving forward, its transformation into planning practice is slow. Ideas such as avoiding the use of land exposed to hazards sit uneasily with the emerging role of planning as a tool for capital accumulation. Little attention has been paid, at a more practical level, to post-disaster planning efforts nor to the processes by which planning policies in the aftermath of disasters are arrived at and contested at local inquiries. Though some scholars have investigated reconstruction planning, notably after the Wenchuan earthquake, there are no theoretical constructs in their interpretations and no systematic analysis of the post-disaster planning, which remains an area ripe for empirical study and further research. In this research, the PI will go some way towards meeting these deficiencies in academic inquiry. On a theoretical front, the discourse of ‘resilience’ will be introduced as a new construct to study post-disaster planning and to evaluate the capability of the planning system in the face of unexpected disturbances. Empirically, using two selected towns that were severely devastated by the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake as case studies, the research will assess to what extent the existing post-disaster planning system is able to cope with such sudden shock and detrimental repercussions and how far the ‘resilience thinking’ has been reflected in planning practice, even though the term is not explicitly mentioned. To this end, four aspects of the post-disaster planning system will be reviewed: they are (i) planning legislation, (ii) plans and the planning process, (iii) planning organization and (iv) implementation. This study will examine how these four aspects are critically engaging with resilience discourse. The result will have a significant impact on policymaking in terms of helping to decide what should be done to develop resilient responses to natural disasters in general and to earthquakes in particular. 中國是自然災害頻發的脆弱國度。不同類型的自然災害帶來嚴重損失，也讓重建工作面臨嚴峻挑戰。災害造成的影響，尤以1976年的唐山地震以及2008年的汶川地震為甚。在此背景下，各級政府部門正逐漸意識到城市規劃工作在減低災害分險方面的重要性。事實上，中央政府正在建立一套自上而下的災後規劃體系，以應對災后恢復、重建與抗災社區的建設工作。儘管相關討論取得了不少進展，但規劃實踐工作仍然緩慢。城市規劃通常被當作資本積累的工具，抗災思想（如避免將城市建設用地規劃在災害易發區）很難付諸實現。目前，很少有人關注災后重建規劃政策與決策過程。汶川地震後，部分學者已開始對重建規劃進行研究，但他們的研究大都不涉及理論框架的創建與規劃系統分析。所以，災后重建規劃仍然是亟待實證研究與學術探索的領域。 本研究將填補目前學術研究的空白。在理論框架方面，“韌性”理論會被引入，作為研究災後規劃的依據，以及評估規劃系統應對不可預測風險能力的工具。在實證方面，研究將以兩個在汶川地震中受毀嚴重的鄉鎮為例，評估災後規劃體系對於短期和長期災害影響的應對能力，並探究韌性思想在現有規劃實踐中的體現。為此，本研究將著重探討災後規劃體系的四個具體方面：(i) 規劃法規體系，(ii) 規劃文本及規劃過程，(iii) 規劃機構， (iv) 規劃實施。我們將檢討上述四個方面中體現的韌性思想，並作出批判性論述。希望研究成果能為災后公共政策提供借鑑，特別是如何才能以韌性的方式回應自然災害（如地震）帶來的後果。

14413014.label: Realisation of objectives
14413014.value: The research team has fully achieved the five stated objectives. Firstly, they have discerned the emerging concerns and innovative tools used by Chinese planners when facing disasters. Those planners mostly work in planning institutes, governmental planning agencies, and the planning schools of universities who were commissioned by local governments to prepare reconstruction plans. They have to work within the current planning framework set by the State Council and the responsible central ministry. Though devised through the state-mandated planning regime, the reconstruction planning demonstrates features not evident in regular planning practices. The first relates to the exceedingly high speed of planning process. This was made possible by the hierarchical state system, under which the superiors would hold government officials at every level accountable for quickly and diligently following the reconstruction plans. Second, planners were engaged with multiple agents, both state and non-state, territorial and extraterritorial. They worked in a web of diverse power relations. The third feature concerns a series of top-down mandated planning requirements for seismic zones, such as enforcing seismic building codes and applying geology-attuned regulations on the categories and scales of land uses. Finally yet importantly, adding to the complexities of reconstruction is the ‘pair assistance’ program (PAP), which contributed significantly to reconstruction, but also brought influential extraterritorial interests into the planning process. Yet, compared with normal planning practice, reconstruction planning has been more open to citizen participation in mobilizing a social base of support. This proved decisive in resolving disagreements. Nevertheless, the proliferation of interests also made it difficult for visionary plans to gain a foothold. Secondly, the research team has fully achieved the objective to explore the use of ‘resilience’ as a theoretical construct in scrutinizing post-disaster planning. In addition, they have gone beyond the resilience thesis written from Western perspective to offer a new way to theorize China’s resilience-building. Two points should be highlighted here. The first is that the team has identified three different approaches in incorporating resilient thinking into reconstruction planning, namely engineering, ecological and evolutionary approaches. Engineering approach finds resonance with the managerial and technical planning tradition, which highlights spatial equilibrium and structural resistance to disturbance for survival and quick return to the status quo. Ecological approach focuses on how a better future can be made through deliberation and vision setting. Evolutionary approach echoes recent planning inquiries which admit uncertainty of nature and highlight ubiquity of change, fluidity and the transformative potential of novelty. Traces of these different approaches have been found in the planning exercise of rebuilding Yingxiu and Weizhou – the two sites under investigation. The second point is that the research team has re-theorized the role of state in China’s resilience building. In most western contexts, the wide application of resilience in planning is said to lie in their ideological fit with neoliberalism. Underscoring the presence of disruptive forces and the need of adaptation, resilience bears parallels with the neoliberal worldview of a crisis-ridden economy and the neoliberal emphasis on individual and communities to pursue growth and competitiveness to weather such economic settings. It seems resonates well with the neoliberal mode of state-society relationship, which prefers bottom-up risk-taking and free choice over hierarchical government control. The research findings from this project oppose this hegemonic neoliberal mode in resilience building by illustrating that the practice of resilience is indeed path-dependent, such that it might depend on the active intervention and remaking of the state in places where the state has endeavored to maintain strong socio-economic control. Thirdly, the research team has fully fulfilled the objective to introduce a set of resilience attributes in planning and use them to evaluate the extent to which post-earthquake planning in Wenchuan is able to demonstrate resilience. They have identified eight major resilience attributes in planning, including built environment-related ‘physical attributes’ (robustness, efficiency, diversity, redundancy, and physical connectivity) which underpin engineering and ecological approaches to resilience, and ‘social attributes’ (social connectivity, capital building, flexibility and innovation) which stem from an evolutionary perspective of resilience. Together these attributes provide a multi-faceted framework for the team to assess the strengths and weaknesses of China’s local reconstruction planning in promoting community resilience. Fourthly, using the aforementioned resilience attributes framework, the research team has discussed the outcomes of reconstruction planning. They have found that signs of resilience are evident at varying degrees. There is an overarching emphasis on two physical attributes, robustness and efficiency, forming a classic checklist for engineering resilience. Robustness was achieved through structural resistance, actions of territorial prevention and tactics of protective buffering, while efficiency was attained through rapid planning responses and quick recovery of normalcy. Conversely, the signs of other three physical attributes conveying ecological resilience – diversity, redundancy and physical connectivity – are much less evident. For social attributes signifying evolutionary resilience, there are mixed achievements. Planners developed strong social connectivity with state agencies and engaged more frequently with local residents, but expressed concerns with working effectively with donor government unfamiliar with local needs. The central state’s engineering-minded planning framework drove planners to focus more on recovery and community vulnerabilities than on local capital building for adaptation to uncertainties. Its one-size-fits-all planning standards also discouraged flexible planning responses to site-specific needs. Reconstruction was seized by the central state as an opportunity to promote innovation in the socio-economic development trajectory of the affected communities, but some innovative attempts, such as earthquake tourism, fail to benefit the people as promised. In sum, reconstruction raised local capacity of risk management and helped local population to better cope with several secondary disasters after 2008. Local officials, planning professionals and residents became more aware of seismic risks, of where the causative faults are located, of how the ground behaves, of which zones and buildings are most vulnerable, of the need for strong social bonds, and of the odds of experiencing a damaging earthquake and mudslide. Throughout the planning process, all the players grew to understand the importance of disaster safety. Schools in Weizhou, for instance, have rescheduled their school terms to avoid rainy seasons when geological risks are high. Disaster drills have been established and saved lives in a few secondary disasters. Every responsible government official is equipped with a walkie talkie in case of urgency. Although difficult to measure, these are not insignificant achievements. Communities and individuals are increasingly enrolled in a state-mandated ‘frameworks of action’ to manage radical uncertainty. Finally, the team has sufficiently and critically analyzed, evaluated and theorized on the results of post-disaster planning moving towards a resilience-based approach. Theoretically, the major contribution of this project is to re-theorize the role of state in resilience building. Rather than simply playing a nudging role, the Chinese state becomes an active and unparalleled agent in the reconstruction of earthquake-stricken communities. Tasks such as relocating damaged communities, resettling affected residents, selecting future development path, and nurturing adaptive capacity of communities all require the inputs of the state, whose political authority to mobilize various socio-economic resources cannot be matched by other agents. Practically, the research team has explored the potential of using resilience as a framework to engage with practitioners. This can be evidenced by a number of invitations to the PI to give talks on post-disaster reconstruction by a few professional bodies.

14413014.label: Major findings and research outcome
14413014.value: Though the project has been completed in terms of RGC funding support, the PI is still continuing relevant research activities. She is still being invited to give keynote speeches and talks. In addition to these ongoing activities, she and her team have published three Chinese journal articles and four English journal articles. Two more articles (one English and one Chinese) are under review. Another English article has been fully drafted and will be sent out for review after some touch-up. The PI trained a PhD student, who wrote a dissertation entitled ‘Urban Resilience in China’s Post Disaster Reconstruction Planning: The Cases of Weizhou and Yingxiu Towns, Wenchuan County’. With a proposal based on this project, the PhD student was awarded a Research Excellence Award to do research in Waseda University in Japan. One result from this international collaboration is that the PI joined a professor from Waseda University to apply for a research funding in Japan. It was through this channel that the team was able to introduce the resilience building practice in Japan to Chinese mainland. In 2017, the PhD student successfully completed his research. He has worked in Shenzhen University as an Assistant Professor since 2018. Using the resilience framework derived from this research, he has been awarded a National Natural Science Foundation funding to conduct a new research in China’s Yangtze River Delta. The team has attended 8 international conferences and one workshop to present research findings. The PI has been invited by domestic professional bodies to give keynote speeches and talks to audience outside the university sector. The project has also generated a dataset with retention value through an online questionnaire survey with 57 planners who were engaged in the reconstruction process. In a less numerical term, the research has produced some important findings. Countering prevailing arguments, the research unravels that the practice of resilience is indeed path-dependent, such that it might depend on the active intervention and remaking of the state in places where the state has endeavored to maintain strong socio-economic control. In so arguing, the research is not denying the necessity for individuals and communities to make themselves less vulnerable to future catastrophes. What it emphasizes is the need to pay close attention to the important role of the state and the politicized nature of resilience. Through a questionnaire survey, the research also reveals that signs of resilience are evident in various planning practices.

14413014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14413014.value: The first two Chinese papers published by Urban Planning International succeeded in initiating debates among Chinese scholars and practitioners on the meaning and the translation of ‘resilience’. It is these two papers that drew the attention from outside the university sector. As a result, the PI and her team has been invited to give talks and produce papers for professional bodies. These activities will continue. Academically, the PI will continue to explore the role of state in building resilience. She will take advantage of various opportunities to engage with scholars in reconstruction.

14413014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14413014.value: The idea of resilience is commonly understood as the ability to survive and adapt in the face of uncertain disturbances, such as natural disasters. Although this concept is still evolving, scholars gradually come to agree that, instead of focusing on external threats, resilience emphasizes internal coping and adaptive capacity, and accordingly it invests in societal capacity building rather than mere resistant physical infrastructure provision. The notion of resilience is often associated with a belief that strong state intervention is not desirable. But is it necessarily the case? In a policy environment with strong state tradition, could the pursuit and realization of resilience still be possible? This intriguing question motivated us to conduct this research. Countering prevailing arguments, we unravel that the practice of resilience might depend on the active intervention and remaking of the state in places where the state has endeavored to maintain strong socio-economic control. In so arguing, we are not denying the necessity for individuals and communities to make themselves less vulnerable to future catastrophes. What we simply want to emphasize is the need to pay close attention to the important role of the state in building resilience.

14413214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14413214.value: We develop a semiparametric estimator for stated preference discrete choice models in this project. The rank-ordered logit model is applied to analyze stated preference data in a growing literature in environmental economics, transportation research, and health economics. Accounting for rankings of alternatives, the rank-ordered logit model is a more desirable model for ratings data than the multinomial logit model that only examines the chosen alternative. Yoo (2013) finds that the empirical regularity from the rank-ordered logit studies, which has been interpreted psychologically as evidence that decision makers are less certain about their less preferred alternatives, may simply reflect model misspecification. When the distribution function of the error term in the random utility function violates the rank-ordered logit model assumptions, the estimates tend to become attenuated in magnitude as more ranking information is incorporated into analysis. Yoo's findings, providing an alternative explanation to the empirical regularity, suggests the importance of developing a semiparametric estimator that does not suffer from the misspecification on the error terms. The proposed estimator is built upon Yan's (2013) smoothed maximum score estimator for multinomial discrete choice models. The new estimator utilizes the stated preference information as the rank-ordered logit model does, without making parametric assumptions of the error terms. We will establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator in this project, making statistical inference straightforward. Monte Carlo experiments will be provided to demonstrate the finite sample properties of the proposed estimator. We will apply the estimator to experimental data and compare its estimation results with the rank-ordered logit estimation results to avoid possible misinterpretation of the cognitive ability of respondents in survey data. 在這個項目中，我们提出一个新的半参数估计方法來研究敘述性偏好離散選擇模型。Rank-ordered logit 模型（ROL）经常應用于分析叙述性偏好数据。Yoo（2013）发现ROL的估計結果被心理解讀為人們對不太優選的替代方案有更大的不確定性的事實可能反應的只是模型設定的錯誤。當誤差項的分布函数違背了ROL模型中的假设，參數估计的結果趋于衰减的幅度隨著排名信息層次的加深而增大。因此，制定一个無需假設誤差項具体分布函數的計量模型是很重要的 在这个项目中所提出的估计方法是建立在Yan（2013）的平滑最高分估计在多项离散选择模型的基礎上。多项离散选择分析只可以观察到人们的选择决定。通過運用优先级排序的信息我们有可能获得更為精確的估计結果。 這個項目將會建立所提出的估计方法的大樣本性质，因此统计推断可以很容易地进行。蒙地卡罗实验将被用來評價该估计量的有限样本性质。我們会用試驗數據來比較新提出的估计量与ROL模型估计结果的差別。

14413214.label: Realisation of objectives
14413214.value: All the objectives are achieved and a working paper (coauthored with Hong Il Yoo) has been written based on the proposal of this project. Below I list how and to what extent the project objectives have been achieved in the working paper titled "semiparametric estimation of the random utility model using rank-ordered choice data". 1. In the paper, we propose two semiparametric estimators for estimating the random utility model using stated preference (rank-ordered) discrete choice data. The estimators are semiparametric in that the systematic component (or utility index) includes finite dimensional preference parameters but the error term follows an unspecified (or unknown) distribution, therefore they are robust to stochastic misspecification as long as certain monotonicity property holds. Our methods allow for a flexible form of heteroskedasticity across individuals. When complete rankings are stated, our methods also allow for heteroskedastic and correlated errors across alternatives, as well as a variety of random coefficients distributions. 2. The baseline method we develop is the generalized maximum score (GMS) estimator, which is strongly consistent but follows a non-standard asymptotic distribution. To facilitate statistical inferences, we make extra regularity assumptions and develop the smoothed GMS (SGMS) estimator, which is asymptotically normal. The parameters in the limiting distribution of the SGMS estimator can be consistently estimated, making statistical inference straightforward. A plug-in method is provided to choose the bandwidth in the smooth function for the SGMS estimator. 3. Monte Carlo experiments show the finite sample performance of the proposed estimators under a variety of stochastic specifications and different levels of stated preference rankings. For comparison with our GMS and SGMS estimates, we also compute maximum likelihood estimates using three popular parametric models, namely rank-ordered logit (ROL), rank-ordered probit (ROP), and mixed ROL (MROL). Six data generating processes (DGP) are considered, including the DGPs that coincide with the correct specifications of the ROL, ROP, and MROL models respectively and DGPs that allow for heteroskedasticity and random coefficients. As expected, a parametric estimator is consistent when the DGP happens to coincide with the postulated distribution assumption on the error terms. In the presence of error distribution misspecification, the parametric estimators often converge to different pseudo-true values when different levels of stated preference rankings are used in estimation, resulting unstable coefficients estimation using finite samples. The parametric estimators are also seriously biased under heteroskedasticity across individuals. The GMS and SGMS estimators perform well under the distribution specifications on the error terms imposed by the ROL and ROP models as long as certain monotonicity property is satisfied. When the complete rankings are reported, the GMS and SGMS estimators are consistent under the error distribution specifications of all three parametric models, heteroskedaticity across individuals and alternatives, and allow for random coefficients in utility functions. The efficiency gains for the GMS and SGMS estimators of using deeper rankings are substantial, what's more, the two estimators using complete stated rankings can accommodate the error structures of all three parametric estimators, just as the theory developed in the paper predicts. 4. The paper provides an illustrative empirical application of the GMS estimator and the SGMS estimator using a bank account choice data set. As in our Monte Carlo experiment, we compare the results with the maximum likelihood estimates of popular parametric models, rank-ordered logit (ROL), heteroskedastic ROL (HROL) and mixed ROL (MROL). Every customer in the data set faces 9 alternatives and states the complete preference rankings of the alternatives. The ROL, HROL and MROL estimators yield very different results from the proposed semiparametric estimators. Outside Monte Carlo settings, it is admittedly difficult to confirm whether the semiparametric estimates are indeed closer to the true parameters than the parametric estimates, yet the variation in estimation using different levels of stated rankings seems to be larger for parametric estimates than for semiparametric estimates.

14413214.label: Major findings and research outcome
14413214.value: This project develops two semiparametric estimators for the random utility model exploiting rank-ordered choice data. Compared with the existing parametric estimators that specify the distribution family of the error terms, the proposed semiparametric estimators leave the error distribution unspecified and allow for a flexible form of heteroskedasticity across individuals. In applied work, this feature allows the researcher to be agnostic about the form of interpersonal heteroskedasticity (or scale heterogeneity), which explains the difference between the proposed estimators and the maximum rank correlation estimator of Han (1987) and Sherman (1993) that rules out interpersonal heteroskedasticity. When complete rankings are reported, the two estimators allow for heteroskedastic and correlated errors across alternatives, as well as a variety of random coefficients distributions. They also accommodate all popular parametric models, delivering what empiricists may expect from the use of semiparametric methods. These attractive properties are relevant to empirical studies. The proposed estimators are consistent when the true data generating process consists of a mixture of different models such as rank-ordered logit and rank-ordered probit models using fully rank-ordered choice data. The empirical evidence from behavioral economics supports the notion that multiple models are required to characterize the observed choices. In the parametric framework, the motivation of using rank-ordered choice data is about efficiency gains from extra information on stated rankings. Interestingly, in the semiparametric framework, we find that using extra ranking information is not just a matter of efficiency gains, it is also a matter of robustness in the sense that using complete rankings allows the proposed estimators to be consistent under a wider class of stochastic specifications. For example, the (smoothed) maximum score estimator does not accommodate any error variance-covariance structure (i.e., the multinomial probit model) or random coefficients (e.g., the mixed logit model), but the proposed generalized (smoothed) maximum score estimator allows error structure of the multinomial probit model and random coefficients. This finding calls for a reconsideration of the conventional wisdom prevailing in the empirical literature. Several studies have suggested that in case the estimated using complete rankings diverge from those using only the best alternative, one should have more faith in the latter set of estimates and question the reliability of data on deeper preference rankings. But with our analysis, it is the former set of estimates that is consistent under a wider range of stochastic specifications or models.

14413214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14413214.value: There are several directions of further development of this project. First, the proposed methods apply cross-sectional data. We could consider extending this method for panel data, where we can incorporate other interesting issues such as state dependence and individual fixed effects. Second, this project extends the (smoothed) maximum score (MS) method from the multinomial choice setting to the rank-ordered choice setting. In addition to efficiency gains from using extra information on preference rankings, we find that the proposed estimators allow for a wider class of stochastic specifications than the MS estimator does, e.g., the multinomial MS estimator in general does not allow for random coefficients or heteroskedasticity across alternatives, yet the proposed estimators allow for them with complete rankings. A future step is to consider adapting other semiparametric multinomial choice estimators to the rank-ordered choice setting and check if they accommodate more stochastic distributions than their multinomial counterparts. Third, this project shows the performance of the semiparametric estimators under perfect ranking behaviors, i.e., individuals rank the alternatives according underlying utilities. In future research, we shall consider a method that works for rank-ordered data with "limited cognitive capacity", allowing a way to explicitly disentangle the stochastic misspecification from "limited cognitive capacity".

14413214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14413214.value: This project develops a new method for estimating the random utility model using rank-ordered choice data. The random utility model is widely used in economic applications when an individual faces a collection of discrete alternatives and picks the best one from the choice set, examples include choice of college and choice of transportation mode. Many estimation methods have been developed for the random utility model using multinomial choice data. A multinomial choice reports the individual's most preferred alternative, whereas a rank-ordered choice reports further about the individual's preference ordering such as her second and third preferred alternatives, allowing fewer individuals to be interviewed to achieve a given level of estimation precision. However, only a few methods are available in the literature for exploiting the rank-ordered choice data. Those methods also impose strong assumptions on the unobserved random utility components, ruling out many interesting economic applications. When those assumptions are violated, the estimations results become unstable using different levels of rankings. The proposed new method has weaker assumptions than the existing methods and can accommodate all the popular methods when individuals report the complete rankings, therefore it allows for applications of a much wider range of discrete choice problems.

14413314.label: Realisation of objectives
14413314.value: The five project objectives have been fully achieved in the following ways: 1. To answer the first research question, research has been done to review the role of emotional processes in teaching and learning, and to investigate the effect of emotional job demands and emotion regulation on teachers’ well-being. In specific, (1) Two review studies have been conducted to discuss (1) the significance of emotions in students’ mathematics learning and (2) the relevance of teachers’ motivational and emotional processes to their professional development. For the role of emotion in student learning, it is found that even in mathematics learning, enhancing students’ positive emotions would help reduce their extraneous cognitive load and anxiety, and facilitate the integration between students’ cognitive and affective development. Moreover, the knowledge about the role of emotion in mathematics learning would help improve teachers’ professional competency in regulating and utilizing emotions in classroom teaching. For the role of emotional labor in teachers’ work, it is revealed that teachers’ motivational and emotional processes, including emotion regulation and emotional labor, are closely related to a number of variables in education such as student motivation, educational reform, teaching practice and teachers’ psychological fulfilment and well-being. The findings have been published at Cogent Education and Educational Science Research: • Han, J., & Yin, H. (2016). Teacher motivation: Definition, research development and implications for teachers. Cogent Education, 3(1), 18 pgs. DOI: 10.1080/2331186X.2016.1217819 • Lin, W., & Yin, H. (2017). Mathematical affect: A new dimension of the senior secondary mathematics curriculum reform. Educational Science Research, (1), 70-75. (in Chinese) (2) A quantitative study, using multi-level analysis, has been conducted to investigate whether and how teachers’ emotion regulation strategies mediate the relationship between school-level job characteristics (including emotional job demands) and teacher well-being. The results indicate that school-level emotional job demands of teaching and individual-level suppression are positively related to teachers’ anxiety and depression. A positive relationship between emotional job demands and suppression is also found. These findings support the applicability of the job demands-resources model to school settings and indicate that reappraisal should be considered a personal resource and suppression a personal demand. The manuscript has been reviewing by British Journal of Educational Psychology: • Yin, H., & Huang, S. (under review). A multilevel analysis of job characteristics, emotion regulation and teacher well-being: A job demands-resources model. British Journal of Educational Psychology. (SSCI, IF: 2.403) 2. To answer the second and third research questions, Research has been done to investigate the display rules for teacher emotion in workplace and their relationships with the cultural context of Hong Kong. In specific, two studies have been conducted. (1) A quantitative study has been conducted examines the total moderation role that psychological capital plays in the integrative emotional labor model in which positive display rule perceptions predict emotional exhaustion both directly and indirectly via emotional labor strategies, i.e., deep acting and surface acting. The results reveal that psychological capital moderates the direct and indirect relationships between positive display rule perceptions and emotional exhaustion. Psychological capital also moderates the relationship between deep acting, but not surface acting, and emotional exhaustion. These findings suggest that psychological capital generally plays a positive role in the emotion regulation process. It is also noted that although psychological capital can reduce employees’ emotional exhaustion, employees with high psychological capital who practice surface acting may suffer increased emotional exhaustion. Suggestions are offered accordingly for organizations that aim to enhance teachers’ and employees’ psychological capital and to reduce the negative effects of emotional labor. The findings have been published at Current Psychology: • Yin, H., Wang, W., Huang, S., & Li, H. (2018). Psychological capital, emotional labor and exhaustion: Examining mediating and moderating models. Current Psychology, 37(1), 343-356. DOI: 10.1007/s12144-016-9518-z (SSCI, IF: 0.953) (2) A qualitative study has been conducted to explore the display rule perceptions of teachers and its possible relationships with the Chinese cultural context. It finds that the experience and expression of emotion are not only emotional matters but also results of rational operation. This means when teachers feel or express their emotions in some specific ways, they always calculate the cost and benefit of these emotions according to the situations, the norms for teaching, and the potential consequences of their emotional expressions. The Chinese teachers try to build a close, familial relationship with their students by releasing their positive emotions in the classroom, they also kept a professional distance from students by pretending certain unfelt emotions (e.g. coolness or anger), to make themselves look ‘‘mysterious’’ or even threatening. This paradoxical phenomenon indicate that teachers’ emotion regulation is moderated by cultural norms, and reflect the cultural influence on teacher–student relationships in Chinese cultural context. The findings have been published at Journal of East China Normal University (Educational Sciences): • Yin, H. (2017). Approaches to empirical educational research: A case study of teachers’ emotional labor. Journal of East China Normal University (Educational Sciences), 35(3), 47-56. DOI: 10.16382/j.cnki.10005560.2017.03.00 (CSSCI, in Chinese) 3. To answer the fourth research question, A quantitative study, based on Grandey’s integrative model of emotional labor, has been done to examine the relationships between Hong Kong teachers’ emotional labor strategies, the emotional job demands of teaching, trust in colleagues, and teacher efficacy. The results shows that surface acting plays a dysfunctional role, but deep acting and expression of naturally felt emotion facilitate teacher efficacy. Trust in colleagues is found to be an organizational resource for teachers that helps them to cope with the challenges brought about by the emotional demands of teaching. The results indicate that teachers should perform emotional labor wisely. The findings have been published at Teaching and Teacher Education: • Yin, H., Huang, S., & Lee, J. C. K. (2017). Choose your strategy wisely: Examining the relationships between emotional labor in teaching and teacher efficacy in Hong Kong primary schools. Teaching and Teacher Education, 66, 127-136. DOI: 10.1016/j.tate.2017.04.006 (SSCI, IF: 2.183) 4. To answer the fifth research question, a quantitative study, based on an adjusted Job Demands-Resources model, has been done to examine the relationships between two characteristics of teachers’ work environment (i.e., emotional job demands and trust in colleagues) and two indicators of teachers’ well-being (i.e., teaching satisfaction and emotional exhaustion) in the context of Hong Kong. In particular, the study focuses on how emotion regulation strategies (i.e., reappraisal and suppression) mediate these relationships. The results of structural equation modeling indicate that: (1) the emotional job demands of teaching are detrimental to teacher well-being, whereas trust in colleagues is beneficial; (2) both emotion regulation strategies mediate the relationships between both emotional job demands and trust in colleagues and teacher well-being; and (3) teachers who tend to use more reappraisal may be psychologically healthier than those tend to adopt more suppression. Implications for the improvement of school environments and teachers’ well-being are identified. The findings have been published at International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health: • Yin, H., Huang, S., & Wang, W. (2016). Work environment characteristics and teacher well-being: The mediation of emotion regulation strategies. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 13(9), No. 907 (16 pgs). DOI: 10.3390/ijerph13090907 (SSCI/SCIE, IF: 2.101)

14413314.value: The major findings include: • teachers’ emotional and motivational processes are closely related to a number of variables in education such as student motivation,teaching practice and teachers’ psychological well-being; • the emotional job demands of teaching are detrimental to teacher well-being, whereas trust in colleagues is beneficial; • the emotion regulation strategies adopted by teachers mediated the relationships between both emotional job demands and trust in colleagues and teacher well-being; • the emotional job demands of teaching positively related to surface and deep acting, and trust in colleagues positively related to expression of naturally felt emotion; • school-level emotional job demands of teaching and individual-level suppression are positively related to teachers’ anxiety and depression, whereas school-level trust in colleagues and individual-level reappraisal are positively associated with enthusiasm and contentment; • psychological capital moderates the direct and indirect relationships between positive display rule perceptions and emotional exhaustion. 14413314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14413314.value: Building on the PI’s this GRF project on the emotional labor of teaching and teachers’ efficacy and psychological well-being, further research can be conducted to explore (1) the relationship between school leadership and teachers’ emotional labor; (2) the effects of teachers’ emotional labor on student cognitive and social and emotional learning; and (3) the differences as well similarities in performing the emotional labor of teaching between Hong Kong teachers and their counterparts in other cultural contexts including mainland China. It will contribute to these underdeveloped areas in research literature by presenting, from a broader socio-cultural perspective, the relationships between school leadership, teacher emotion and student learning.

14413314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14413314.value: This project has contributed to the literature by proposing a multi-level investigation of the shaping effects of school-level job characteristics and trust relationships among teachers, and individual-level teachers’ emotion regulation and emotional labor on teachers’ sense of efficacy and psychological well-being in the context of Hong Kong. In general, it is found that the emotional job demands of teaching are detrimental to teacher well-being, whereas trust in colleagues is beneficial; surface acting negatively related to teacher efficacy, while deep acting and genuine expression positively related to teacher efficacy; teachers who tend to use more reappraisal may be psychologically healthier than those tend to adopt more suppression. These findings have generated suggestions that can guide teacher educators, school administrators and policy makers in establishing a supportive work environment for teachers, and help them to understand better the role of emotional labor in teachers’ work with the purpose to improve teachers’ well-being and effectiveness of classroom teaching.

14413414.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14413414.value: 中國的末代自梳女：一個區域傳統及其性別意涵與跨國視野再探

14413414.label: Project Objectives
14413414.value: In response to the call of the time for immediate efforts to record the life histories of the “last generation of Chinese spinsters,” this proposed project is designed to first conduct in-depth interviews of the surviving elderly spinsters in the south China region. The project is to supplement other spinsters’ life histories collected thus far and to study old and new cases with cross-generational and spatial comparisons. To situate the custom of sworn spinsterhood in the local socio-cultural context, interactions between spinsters and other village folks, men and women (including non-spinsters) will be observed. The project is to reveal the significance of migration to work abroad in the life experiences of spinsters who emigrated in their teens for southeast Asia working mainly as domestic servants before returning home for retirement. Field research will be conducted in Singapore and Malaysia, the host countries where most Cantonese spinsters-amahs spent their prime of life. This project is also to examine the role of spinsters and their sisterhood in forming emigrant communities in the south China region, supporting local livelihood and sustaining the tradition of migration for overseas jobs. Covered in the project are also spinsters’ return migration to their hometowns, their lives there after retirement, and their status and identities in local society. To enrich the present scholarship on the subject, this project intends to revisit the interrelated issues concerning the tradition of spinsterhood in the south China region while highlighting its gendered implications and transnational dimensions in order to shed light on the working of Chinese gender ideologies and relations in the formation of the tradition in the regional socio-cultural system and to contextualize micro case studies in the macroscopic perspective of gender, migration, and transnationalism.
