14413414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14413414.value: In recent years, the “last generation of spinsters in China” has become a popular narrative motif of the mass media, drawing even the attention of Hong Kong’s movie and television enterprises. Although Chinese sworn spinsterhood has been a research topic in the academic circles and spinsters as an “endangered species” in China today does stimulate ethnographic interest resulting in a body of scholastic publications, authors of these works tend to focus their studies on certain dimensions of the phenomenon, which actually concerns interrelated issues of spinsters’ subjectivities, customs of marriage resistant spinsterhood and sisterhood, the influence of religious beliefs, ethnic interactions, gender relations, social formation, migration, and even the transnational market for female labour. To enrich the existing scholarship, I propose to address the aforesaid issues, while highlighting the characteristics of this regional tradition, its gendered implications, and the transnational perspective as significant (yet under-explored) themes for an integral inquiry, in revisiting popular spinsterhood in the south China region where the age-old custom seems to have been tolerated by Chinese patriarchal society and further sustained by the opportunities for spinsters to work away from home or abroad. This proposed project has the potential to bring breakthroughs to the studies of the subject by verifying some of the hypotheses concerned with a cross-generational comparison of various old and new case stories from different locales in the region after in-depth interviews of the surviving elderly spinsters are conducted. An explanation for the disruption of the tradition in the late 1940s is also in order. Based on oral information and other kinds of materials including local documents, inscriptions, sources of material/non-material culture, etc., this project will contribute to the field by generating original analytical works, including one, for example, that details the negotiation between the spinsterhood tradition and the male-dominated mainstream culture. Studies of regional gender interactions of this kind may shed light on the features of Chinese gender ideologies and relations, especially that in this region under the rubric of Lingnan culture. In rounding off the effort to analyze as many spinsters’ life histories as possible, it is also expected that micro experiences and the regional socio-cultural system can be better linked up with the macro process of global migration when studying Cantonese spinsters as transnational migrant workers, their role in forming emigrant communities in south China, and the implications of their circular migration in the perspective of transnationalism. 「中國最後一代的自梳女」已成近年大衆傳媒通俗敍事的一個主題，牽引著香港影視業的注意力。雖然立誓不嫁的中國自梳風俗曾是個學術界的研究課題， 而自梳女作爲今日中國的「瀕危」一族，也刺激起田野調查的興趣，且已有好些學術出版物面世，其作者多集中研究有關現象的某些面相。這種現象卻其實關乎自梳女的主體性、抗婚自梳風俗和姊妹群、宗教信仰的影響、族群關係、社會形態、移民、甚至女性勞動力的國際市場等相互關連的課題。 為進一步充實已有的學術成果，本人建議在討論上述課題時，突顯這個區域傳統的特徵，及其性別意涵與跨國視野，作爲一個整體研究的重要(雖仍未充分探究）主題，以再探華南地區的自梳風。這個悠久的習俗似曾為當地的父權社會所容忍，且更因自梳女出洋工作的機會而持續存在。 透過深度採訪仍在世的年長自梳女後對該區不同地方的各種新舊個案作跨代比較，以驗證一些假説，這個建議有望能為有關課題帶來突破。是項研究也打算為自梳傳統在上世紀四十年代後期的中斷作出解釋。 以口述和他類資料包括地方文獻、碑刻、物質/非物質文化材料等為根據，本計劃也將為這個研究領域貢獻出具原創性的分析成果，如對自梳傳統與男性操控的主流文化之間的交涉所作的詳述即為一例。這類對區域内性別互動的研究，當能顯示這個以嶺南文化著稱的地域中的中國性別意識形態和性別關係的特色。 在盡量搜集更多的自梳女生命歷程史並作出總結分析的同時，本人也期望研究廣東自梳女作爲跨國移民勞工，她們對形構華南僑鄉所發揮的作用，以及她們的環程移徙在跨國視野下的意義時，能將她們的微觀經驗和區域社會文化系統與全球移民的宏觀過程勾連起來。

14413414.label: Realisation of objectives
14413414.value: Without extension permitted, the duration of the 22 months of my project was too short to achieve more than 60% of my planned work. Fortunately, now with intensive effort made in the year after retirement, I have successfully realized my research objectives in the following 7 areas: 1. In response to the call of the time for immediate efforts to record the life histories of the “last generation of Chinese spinsters,” I had applied for early start of my project and set off to conduct in-depth interviews of the surviving elderly spinsters of the last generation in the south China region. A research assistant with experience in oral history projects was hired to help me out in recording and processing the information collected. Another research assistant joined in later to take care of the logistics in field trips to towns and villages in the Pearl River Delta as well as the preparation of the transcripts of interviews. Information solicited in the field and from oral, material and written sources included oral stories, rituals, local documents, gazetteers, genealogies, inscriptions at temples and ancestral halls and so on. Visits to local cultural-historical research units, village and neighbourhood committees, etc. were also arranged. I also had exchange with local researchers and writers, staff at libraries and museums, and scholars at universities in Guangzhou. 2. Life stories newly collected are to supplement old ones for cross-generational and spatial comparison. Cases in Dongguan, for example, pose interesting contrast with those in Shunde, in terms of the degree of religious and ritual involvement in the custom of celibacy. And in Shunde, the sisterhood of spinsters of the last generation seems to be weaker in comparison with that of their predecessors who returned from their host countries in the late 1980s and early 1990s to create the golden age for empowerment in hometowns. 3. In order to situate the custom of sworn spinsterhood in the socio-cultural context of the Pearl River Delta region, interactions between spinsters and other village folk had been observed and my interviewees included both men and women (spinsters or not). As planned, local information was solicited to supplement documents in local archives, museums and cultural-historical research offices. 4. As one of the most crucial research approaches to the key issues of this project, field work overseas was conducted in Singapore and Malaysia, host countries of most spinsters who worked abroad as domestic servants or workers in other lines of service. In these two countries, as planned, I visited Chinese benevolent associations and places where Cantonese amahs used to assemble, such as townsmen’s associations, clansmen’s associations, and temporary hostels called “coolie rooms,” and temples that they liked to frequent, as well as collective graveyards for those who had stayed abroad for life. Visits to public archives such as the National Archives of Singapore were also very fruitful as oral-history records of female immigrants from China, including spinsters-amahs, have been well preserved there. For example, case stories with comparative value have been found in the section “Vanishing Trades” in its famous Oral History Interviews. I was also fortunate enough to interview elderly Cantonese spinsters who chose to retire in the host countries. A small number of them could still be found in public housing areas under the care of social workers. With extremely rare opportunities in both Singapore and Malaysia, I met a couple of former employers of spinster-amahs and conducted very touching interviews. In Singapore’s National Museum, I found a captivating video-recording made by a British doctor who had spent his childhood and adolescence under the loving care of a Chinese amah. All these on-site information and knowledge are hard to come by and very precious first-hand ethnographic materials testifying to the significance of migration and working abroad in the life experience of spinsters who spent their prime of life in the host countries. In this crucial part of my research, however, I encountered the same serious problem that I experienced in previous GRF projects, i.e., shortage of field research time, while serving as Department Chair. It was extremely hard for me to take “time-off” for overseas field trips, and as a result I needed to make follow-up visits to cities in southeast Asia especially those in Malaysia, as there are many of them, after my retirement using my own financial resources when the RGC funding had closed on time. 5. While ample evidences have verified the role of spinsters and their sisterhoods in forming emigrant communities in the south China region, supporting local livelihood and sustaining the tradition of migration for overseas jobs, the present project is to supplement previous studies on the issue of empowerment with more cases for comparison and to conceptualize the phenomenon by highlighting the significance of gender dynamics and interactions between spinsters and other community members. 6. For spinsters who returned to their hometowns for retirement after spending a considerable part of their lives working overseas, informants of the present project are mainly the last group of returnees whose cases are to be compared with their predecessors. As researchers on both generations, I manage to come up with a comparative generational study of return migration, life at their hometowns after living years overseas, and their status as well as identities in local society. 7. As demonstrated above, objectives of this project have been realized to a large extent resulting in a conclusive piece of work under preparation to revisit the interrelated issues concerning the tradition of spinsterhood in the south China region (such as spinsters’ subjectivities, custom of marriage resistant spinsterhood and sisterhood, the influence of religion beliefs, ethnic acculturation, social formation, etc.) while highlighting its gendered implication and transnational dimension in order to shed light on the working of Chinese gender ideologies and relations in the formation of the tradition in the regional socio-cultural system and to contextualize micro case studies in the macroscopic perspective of gender, migration, and transnationalism. My numerous trips to the Pearl River Delta region for interviews, observation, and field investigation have helped me grasp the gender relations in the local area and my several research expeditions overseas did work to sensitize me to the issue of transnational market for female labour and helped me understand how the opportunities for spinsters to work abroad facilitated the sustenance of their spinsterhood and sisterhood, and how the micro experiences and the regional socio-cultural system can be better linked up with the macro process of global and transnational migration when studying Cantonese spinsters as transnational migrant workers, their role in forming emigrant communities in south China, and the implications of their circular migration in the perspective of transnationalism. The long term significance of this projecct lies in its contribution to the reinterpretation of the Lingnan culture and the formation of emigrant society in south China, as well as a potential paradigmatic breakthrough in the study of gender and global transmigration. Indeed, as observed overseas, gender dynamics did play a crucial role in shaping the transmigrant communities in Singapore and Malaysia as well.

14413414.label: Major findings and research outcome
14413414.value: With the project objectives being fully achieved, the research outcome and major findings concerned include the following: 1. A monograph entitled Huaren kuoguo yimin shi de xingbie weidu (EnGendering the history of Chinese transnational migration) has been contracted to be published as a volume of the Series of New History of the Chinese Overseas to deliver the findings of my conclusive study centering round the thesis of popular spinsterhood as a regional tradition of south China, its gendered implication, and transnational perspective. (See attachment in Part C) 2. A paper entitled “Transmigration and Empowerment for Women: Cases of Celibate Spinsters’ Life Histories in Their Host Countries in Southeast Asia and Hometowns in South China” has been submitted to Research on Women in Modern Chinese History for review and publication. (See attachment in Part C) 3. Several chapters on the subject of spinsterhood in south China with updated information are to be published in my 2017 forthcoming book Kuayuexing de shixue tanjiu (Transborder historiography) as a volume of the Hong Kong Scholars Series. (See attachment in Part C) 4. A paper entitled “Engendering the History of Chinese Transmigration” was presented at the 2014 International Symposium on International Migration and Qiaoxiang Studies, Dec. 2014, Jiangmen. (See attachment in Part C) 5. I was invited to share my findings in a presentation entitled “Kuaguo yimin yu nuxing fuquan: Zishunu zai Huanan guli yu yidi shenghuo de gean yanjiu” (Transmigration and empowerment for women: Case studies of spinsters’ life in native towns in south China and strange land abroad) at the 1st Annual Meeting on Studies of the History and Culture of Lingnan, Nov. 2015, Xiqiao, Nanhai. (See attachment in Part C) 6. In December 2016, I attended the International Conference on Indigenous Experience and Diversified Paths of International Development of Oral History at Sun Yatsen University, Canton and delivered a presentation entitled “Nuxing kuaguo yimin koushushi shiwu jingyan zongjie (Oral histories of female transmigrants: A summary of practising experience). The written version has been solicited to be published in Shehui kexue zhanxian (The Social Science Front). (See attachment in Part C) 7. 14413414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14413414.value: Notwithstanding the title, this research project, especially its potential for further development, would not end with the production of outputs on the “last generation of spinsters in China.” In fact it has potential to lead to a series of studies promoted by me to engender the Lingnan culture, emigrant communities in China, as well as Chinese communities overseas, for instance. Another example is the comparative study of different ethnic groups of Chinese female transmigrants such as Spinsters, Sam Shui women, and Hakka women, in terms of their socio-cultural backgrounds, life and work at home and abroad, transmigrant experiences, and their role, status as well as identities in emigrant communities in China and Chinese communities overseas. Thus far I have been invited to give presentations on the related topics, moderate conference panels or organize conferences/book project workshops on the theme of engendering Chinese transmigration. Collaboration with other scholars is also expected to explore the possibilities for further development of the field. Indeed, the rich contents of this project would draw the attention of colleagues who are willing to work together for the promise of paradigmatic breakthroughs in the areas of history of the Chinese overseas, local history, women's/gender history, and so on.

14413514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14413514.value: 本項目研究香港兒童雙語發展中語言輸入所起的作用，主要考察幼兒期廣東話和英語的習得。我們將研究語言輸入的分佈如何影響語言優勢、非母語語言輸入的作用、父母及照顧者語碼轉換的影響。 以往的研究限於父母的母語分別是廣東話和英語的家庭，此項目將聚焦于父母雙方同時對兒童說兩個語言的情況。這種情形（一位家長-兩個語言）在香港社會越來越普遍，卻還未被系統地記錄和研究過。項目負責人的團隊將系統記錄在“一位家長-兩個語言”家庭中成長的兒童的語言發展，並將之與團隊以往研究過的“一位家長-一個語言”家庭中成長的雙語兒童進行比較。 本項目包含兩個研究目標： （1）縱向個案研究：我們將對6名雙語兒童進行18個月的錄影，所得的語料庫資料將按標準格式進行轉寫、數碼化並與音訊視頻檔相連結。這些資料將組成一個新的多媒體“香港雙語兒童語料庫”，供全世界的研究者使用。 （2）比較研究：將新的和現有的語料庫比較使我們可以看到兩類廣東話-英語雙語兒童在使用關係子句、與格結構和向右易位句等結構時的異同。 此研究的理論重要性在於幫助我們瞭解兒童如何在不同語言輸入條件下成為雙語使用者。它的創新之處在於它是對香港家庭中“一位家長-兩個語言”策略帶來的一種越來越普遍的雙語發展模式的第一個系統研究。研究發現對多個跨學科領域的專業人士有價值，這些領域包括雙語和多語習得、發展心理學、 幼兒教育、言語和語言障礙及治療。

14413514.label: Realisation of objectives
14413514.value: 1. Video-recording of 6 children interacting with care-takers in the home environment on a biweekly basis over 18 months. We recruited six children in the local community who met our selection criteria, i.e. the parents are native speakers of Cantonese who speak English as second language. The children’s interactions with parents and other adult speakers (domestic helper, research assistants) were recorded in regular sessions where the target language of interaction was English and Cantonese each for about 20-30 minutes. Video and audio files are available for most if not all of the sessions. The recording periods are as follows: Table 1 Subject information Child’s name Age No. of files (transcription) from to Eng Can A 2;10 4;08 (22mth) 22 20 H 1;11 3;05 (18mth) 18 19 G 2;00 3;06 (18mth) 22 22 Z 1;09 2;08 (11 mth) 10 12 N 1;05 2;11 (18 mth) 12 13 Y 1;03 4;04 (24 mth) 24 24 Total 108 110 Table 1 shows that the children were followed for 18 months except for one child (Z) who was not able to participate in the project beyond 11 months due to unforeseeable circumstances. In compensation, the recording of two children (A & Y) continued beyond 18 months because their parents were enthusiastic and requested continuation of the project. While the recording was conducted on a biweekly basis, an average of one recording per month was transcribed due to the limited resources available for the project as a result of substantial reduction of the funded amount. The target of one transcription per month was also suggested by one of the reviewers in the comments which we adopted and carried out. 2. Corpus data transcribed in a standard format, digitized and linked to audio and video files. The children’s speech data were transcribed in standard CHAT format. A total of 218 files (108 English and 110 Cantonese files) have been transcribed (see Table 1). While recordings were made on a biweekly basis, initially they have been transcribed on a monthly basis. There are more recordings than we can transcribe due to lack of continuity in engaging the same transcribers. Different student transcribers were engaged in transcribing the speech data at different stages during the project and the trained ones who had mastered transcription were unable to continue the task once they graduated. As a result a portion of the recordings remain untranscribed. By and large, we target at least one transcription per month for each child and in some cases two transcriptions per month are available. Privacy issues have been a major concern for the parents who are increasingly cautious about releasing their child’s images and information and their family life in the public domain. Some parents had reservations about releasing the videos and would not want us to release the transcripts linked to the videos. Efforts were made to reassure the parents that without their permission the videos will definitely not be released to the public and they will only be used for internal purposes by our research team. After some negotiation, they were willing to give permission to link the audio to the transcripts to preserve the privacy of the child, parents and family caretakers. 3. Analysis of language input and its relationship to the children’s development, addressing theoretical and empirical issues Input conditions we observed in the recording sessions include the following: i) free-play activities by the parents, caretakers and adult investigators ii) interactive picture-book reading activities Both are intended to reflect typical caretaker-child interactions at home. In a number of families, the parents undertook regular and intensive picture-book reading activities in English, which may account for their child’s robust development of English vis-à-vis Cantonese. While the parents of the children in the current study are all native speakers of Cantonese who speak English as second language with similar SES backgrounds, the proportion of Cantonese and English in the child-directed input varies. For example, while the majority of parents speak Cantonese more frequently to their children who show dominance in Cantonese, child A’s parents and caregivers tend to address her in English more frequently than Cantonese. Her development is thus skewed toward dominance in English. She shows strong English dominance throughout the period of study and consistent preference to speak English and even reluctance to speak Cantonese in the recording sessions. Our RA tried to spend more time interacting with her in Cantonese with the intention to boost her Cantonese but to no avail. Her Cantonese consistently shows protracted development relative to English. Such individual differences highlight the heterogeneity in bilingual development. Samples of caregivers’ input was captured, including domestic helpers in the home. This will allow further investigation of input from caregivers other than parents. There are a number of limitations in the present study. First, the sample size (N=6) remains relatively small and the language input conditions are more variable than anticipated, even though the families are from similar SES backgrounds in the Hong Kong community. Second, the measures used to divide children into dominance groups are limited and can further measures can be used. To further assess the validity of these measures for other samples, as well as the generalisability of our approach, future research should investigate different language dominance patters for different age groups and with different outcome measures. 4. Comparison of the development of children from one parent-two language families with those from one parent-one language families and their different language dominance patterns over time. In syntax, the development of wh-questions in English and dative construction with bei2 ‘give’ in Cantonese shows similar patterns in children under the two input conditions: children typically pass through a stage in the development of wh-interrogatives at which English wh-phrases are left in situ under the influence of Cantonese grammar whereas the word order of bei2 ‘give’ sentences as in the non-target order bei2 keoi5 lai5mat6 ‘give her gifts’ is influenced by English double object sentences. The early emergence of noun-modifying clauses is also observed which sheds light on the analysis of relative clauses (see last paragraph in section 6.1). These are characteristic features of children from one-parent-two language families just like children from one-parent one-language families. A number of grammatical properties such as verb particle constructions and null arguments await further investigation in order to achieve a more comprehensive picture of Hong Kong children’s bilingual development. The study of code-mixing (Yip and Matthews 2016) shows differences in the extent of code-mixing: under the one parent-two languages condition, rates of intra-sentential code-mixing were significantly higher than in the one parent-one language condition. There was evidence that individual differences in mixing rates reflected the mixing rates in the input from individual parents. One interesting finding is that regardless of dominance patterns and input conditions, all bilingual children are engaged in code-mixing to varying degrees and they are more likely to code-mix when speaking Cantonese than speaking English. Despite the prevalence of code-mixing in the adult input and children’s production, the children were able to develop bilingual proficiency in the two languages. Code-mixing does not have a negative effect on children’s bilingual development but allows them to better express themselves and construct more elaborate structure while pooling the resources of two languages together. However the relative proficiency of Cantonese and English varies as a function of the distribution of dual input that largely determines the dominance patterns of the children. This underscores the heterogeneity of bilingual development which can be achieved by the one-parent-two language strategy just as effectively as by the one-parent-one language strategy.

14413514.label: Major findings and research outcome
14413514.value: Language dominance of the children was assessed by a number of measures including language proficiency, input frequency and use. We have observed a non-linear relationship between bilingual children’s amount of exposure and absolute proficiency in each language, but our understanding of the relationship between language exposure and use and relative proficiency remains limited. Language of the environment is not necessarily an accurate indicator for language dominance. Language exposure at the individual level is a better predictor of the magnitude of cross-linguistic influence in bilingual children’s language production than language exposure in the community as a whole. Input frequency proved to be a powerful factor in shaping bilingual development and language dominance patterns. We have found ample evidence for effects of input in code-mixing. Code-mixing is widely practiced in many Hong Kong families, accepted as the norm in the subjects’ home environment. Whether the input contains code-mixing depends on the input conditions and parental discourse strategies. In some cases, code mixing is highly frequent and even welcomed by the parents: hence mixed utterances form part of the input to children developing bilingual competence. Regardless of dominance, children code-mix more frequently in the Cantonese contexts than in the English contexts, reflecting the norm in adult input, i.e. code-mixing occurs more frequently when adults speak Cantonese than when they speak English (Yip & Matthews 2016). There is evidence that the overall preference for mixing in the Cantonese context is modulated by language dominance. Both Cantonese-dominant and English-dominant children mix more elements from English into Cantonese, the English-dominant child Annette mixes more than Cantonese-dominant children in Cantonese contexts. All the children are influenced by the distribution of code-mixing in the input. Annette has further motivations for mixing when speaking Cantonese due to her familiarity of the English words which she can access faster and more easily than the Cantonese counterparts. An area of grammar on which the project has shed light involves noun-modifying constructions. The corpus data show that noun-modifying clauses where the noun has no grammatical relation with the modifying clause emerged as early as canonical relative clauses such as subject and object relatives. These constructions also undergo transfer to English. These findings cast doubt on the assumption that noun-modifying clauses are an extension of relative clauses, and suggest an alternative view whereby relative clauses may be a special case of noun-modifying clauses (Matthews and Yip 2017).

14413514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14413514.value: The corpus has potential for further development in the following respects:  Further qualitative and quantitative analysis of the individual children’s developmental data and the input can be conducted, for example , to determine whether there is correlation between the input in code-mixing and specific grammatical domains  Phonetic and phonological properties of bilingual development remain largely uncharted territory that can be looked at systematically. To tap the new databases more fully and to provide a comprehensive picture of how Hong Kong children develop bilingualism in English and Cantonese, it is essential to analyze the phonological development of the subjects. The proposed course of action to examine input effects in bilingual development is as follows:  Apart from course-grained measures such as MLU, apply more fine grained measures to determine the children’s developmental milestones and language dominance patterns;  To complement the present study on the role of input from home, investigate input from school, e.g. the distribution of input in the school curriculum.  More bilingual children can be recruited to address the issue of generalizability of the findings. The natural course of action is to conduct cross-sectional experiments engaging many more subjects at different ages.

14413514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14413514.value: The project recorded the speech of six bilingual children from 2 to 4 years old interacting with adults at home, documenting their development of bilingual proficiency in Cantonese and English. The study shows how bilingual proficiency naturally develops in early childhood in response to dual input. Being exposed to a greater proportion of language-mixing than children from one parent-one language families, children in one parent-two language families (where each parent uses both languages to the child) show a tendency to mix more in their production, even when the adult speaker makes an effort to stick to one language only. Code-mixing is shown to be a natural phenomenon that bilingual children engage in without affecting their language proficiency. The significance of the results lies in the success of the children in attaining bilingual proficiency in both languages in a one parent-two language situation which is increasingly prevalent in Hong Kong. Speaking both languages to the child is an equally effective option compared to the one parent - one language strategy. The corpus provides an important source of new data to inform researchers, educators, clinicians about how Hong Kong children develop bilingualism in terms of their lexicon, grammar and phonology.

14414014.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14414014.value: 中國農民工被害經歷的多層分析：檢驗社會排斥，日常行為以及社區解組理論

14414014.label: Project Objectives
14414014.value: To show the general patterns and levels of victimization among migrant workers in urban China using descriptive analyses. We also aim to identify significant types of offense, cohort, SES, occupation, and neighborhood differences as suggested by the three theories. Using logistic regression to test the effects of the individual-level factors (level of social exclusion and risky routine activities) on migrant workers' victimization. We will also rigorously examine the mediating effects of risky routine activities between social exclusion and victimization. Following the proposed integrative theoretical framework, we will apply HLM models to test the individual-level effects of social exclusion and risky routine activities and the community-level effects of social disorganization on migrant workers’victimization experience. Interacting effects among these factors will also be checked.

14414014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14414014.value: Using the 2012 and 2014 China Labor Dynamics Survey (CLDS), a multi-level national representative data set, this proposed project aims to: (1) examine the victimization patterns of contemporary Chinese migrant workers and, (2) test to what extent the migrant workers’ victimization can be explained by social exclusion theory, routine activities theory, and neighborhood disorganization theory. PI and Co-I have completed a two-year pilot study involving 58 in-depth interviews with migrant workers living in 11 urban-villages of Guangzhou, one of the major receiving cities of migrant workers in China. The results of our qualitative pilot study provide a solid foundation for this follow-up quantitative research using CLDS. Informed by the major findings of our pilot study and prior literature of both criminological research and migration/immigration studies, an integrative framework of social exclusion, routine activities and social disorganization will be adopted for analysis: first, social exclusion experienced by migrant workers will increase their risky routine activities and consequently lead to higher likelihood of victimization; second, neighborhood disorganization has both direct effects on migrant workers' victimization and interacting effects with social exclusion and routine activities. Such theoretical integration will be thoroughly tested through HLM models since the data set contains detailed information on social exclusion experienced in the receiving societies, routine activities, community characteristics, victimization, and sociodemographic information of the respondents and their families. This project will be the first national representative examination on victimization and its social correlates among Chinese rural-to-urban migrant workers, the population often ignored in previous Chinese victimization studies. The research will contribute to the rising policy need to understand the vulnerability of migrant workers, one of the most disadvantaged social groups in contemporary China. It will also have great potential for theoretical development by bridging and testing relevant Western theories in both criminology and migration/immigration fields with the most updated data from China. 通過分析2012年和2014年中國勞動力動態調查（CLDS），一項多層次的具有全國代表性的大型調查數據，本項目的研究目標包括：（ 1）探究現代中國社會中農民工的被害行為模式；並且（2）檢驗社會排斥理論，日常活動理論，以及社區解組理論對農民工被害行為的解釋力度。研究團隊之前已經完成一項為期兩年的初步研究，就上述問題在廣州（中國接收農民工的主要城市之一）11個城中村深入訪談了58位農民工。此項定性研究的成果為後續的大規模數據分析提供了堅實的基礎。根據訪談發現，並結合相關犯罪學以及移民領域的文獻，我們的定量研究將基於一個社會排斥、日常活動以及社區解組的綜合理論框架：首先，農民工的社會排斥經歷將增加他們的風險性日常活動，從而導致被害的可能性更高；第二，社區解組對農民工的被害有直接影響，也和社會排斥及日常活動存在相互作用。因為CLDS數據中包含了詳細的社會排斥經歷，日常活動安排，社區特徵，被害報告，以及受訪者及其家庭的社會人口信息，上述整合理論可以通過多層分析模型（HLM）得到較全面深入的檢驗。 這是首個具有全國代表性的考察中國農民工被害行為及其社會相關因素的研究。由於抽樣困難等各種原因，這一群體在中國過去的被害研究中常被忽略。從農村流動到城市的打工人群是現代中國最弱勢的群體之一，了解農民工面臨的問題及其根源已經成為日益上升的政策需要。本研究既有助於回應這種實際需求，也存在較大潛力運用中國最新數據整合並檢驗犯罪學以及移民學兩個相關領域的西方理論。

14414014.label: Realisation of objectives
14414014.value: 1. To show the general patterns and levels of victimization among migrant workers in urban China using descriptive analyses. We also aim to identify significant types of offense, cohort, SES, occupation, and neighborhood differences as suggested by the three theories. At the second stage of our project, we combined 2012 and 2014 China Labor Dynamics Surveys (CLDS). By reviewing the most recent literature, we find that migrant workers’ situations in China did not vary greatly between 2012 and 2014 and it is thus justifiable to combine the two years' data together so that we could obtain a larger sample size and more relevant variables with sufficient raw numbers could be analyzed. For example, in 2012 data set, based on strict criteria, we only got about 700 rural-to-urban migrant workers in the final sample; after merging the 2012 and 2014 data sets, the sample size of migrant workers could reach 1,381 (vs. 4,466 native urban workers). Based on this combined data set, we ran both descriptive analysis (means and percentages) and t-tests to compare migrant workers and their local counterparts in terms of their victimization and other relevant variables. In general, the first project objective has been achieved. As our first hypothesis predicts, victimization risks among migrants are significantly higher than those of urban residents (17.7% vs. 9.1%). We further find that compared to urban residents, migrants in fact have significantly greater risks of victimization for four types of offenses: assault, fraud, theft, and robbery. For both migrants and local respondents, males, younger ones and people with lower social status are more likely to be victimized, consistent with the predictions derived from the classical victimization studies. Moreover, this merged data set provides strong support to our hypotheses: migrants face more social exclusion, have more risky routine activities, and are more likely to live in disorganized communities than those local workers do. Compared to their urban counterparts, migrants report significantly less average years of education (9.5 vs. 12.5), less average number of local friends/acquaintances (2.5 vs. 2.9), a lower average level of local language proficiency (3.5 vs. 5), a higher percentage of working in a non-fixed place (13% vs. 9%) and a higher percentage of working overtime (74.3% vs. 38.8%). In terms of neighborhood contexts, the neighborhoods of native urban respondents have significantly better social cohesion (9.5 vs. 9.3) and lower mean proportion of migrants (21.3% vs. 44.9%) than the neighborhoods where migrant workers often live. Neighborhood segregation between migrant workers and local residents in China can be strongly supported. 2. Using logistic regression to test the effects of the individual-level factors (level of social exclusion and risky routine activities) on migrant workers' victimization. We will also rigorously examine the mediating effects of risky routine activities between social exclusion and victimization. Based on the combined 2012 & 2014 CLDS, we were able to achieve the second research objective. Previously we found that the indicators of routine activity theory in 2012 CLDS survey contained too many missing values and we had to give up this theory at the first stage of this project. After we combined the 2012& 2014 data sets, at least two variables measuring routine activities of migrant workers are valid and we could bring back this theory into our models. As we explained in our proposal, we developed an integrative framework of routine activity and social exclusion on the basis of extant criminological and migration/immigration research. The two further hypotheses are below: (1): levels of social exclusion among migrant workers are positively related to their risks of victimization; (2): The relationship between social exclusion and victimization is mediated by routine activities of migrant workers. In our individual-level regressions, we focus on the effects of social exclusion and routine activities on victimization among migrants, compared to those of a similar model for urban residents. The model for each group includes three social exclusion measures and two routine activity measures, plus three control variables. Variance inflation factor tests did not identify any multicollinearity problems among these variables. We ran both logistic regression and more advanced Rasch models to test these two hypotheses. The two statistical methods showed very similar results. Both hypotheses received empirical support. Specifically, institutional discrimination/exclusion targeting at migrants and low qualification to modern economy significantly increase their risk of victimization. To break the wall, migrants may need to go out more often to establish and maintain their local networks; they are then more likely to be victimized due to such risky activities. For these migrants, lack of education and local social network also lead to risky jobs (i.e. non-fixed workplace and longer working time) which would bring more risks of victimization. But local language proficiency is not that important when explaining migrants' disadvantages. 3. Following the proposed integrative theoretical framework, we will apply HLM models to test the individual-level effects of social exclusion and risky routine activities and the community-level effects of social disorganization on migrant workers' victimization experience. Interacting effects among these factors will also be checked. To achieve the third objective, we integrated the individual-level and the neighborhood-level factors by Hierarchical Linear Models (HLM). At the individual level, the model aims to address how social exclusion and routine activities may lead to migrant workers’ victimization. At the neighborhood level, the neighborhood contextual correlates (structural disadvantages indicated by poverty, rural migrant concentration, average collective efficacy perceived by residents in the neighborhood and level of disorder) might shape the micro level social processes and victimization among migrant workers. In addition, the same theoretical framework was tested across local workers so as to compare with distinctive disadvantages faced by migrant workers. Hierarchical linear modeling analyses have shown that neighborhood disorganization has direct positive effects on migrant workers’ risks of victimization and also interacts with social exclusion and routine activities at individual level. For migrants, once community-level variables are included in the model, the individual-level explanatory variables become nonsignificant except safe workplace. Specifically, living in a migrant-concentrated neighborhood (meaning more motivated offenders, more heterogeneity and less care from the government) will increase the likelihood of migrants’ victimization, while higher level of noise in the neighborhoods (indicating more guardians shown in that area) may be a protective factor for the migrants. Different from Western studies, collective efficacy in the neighborhood is only a protective factor of victimization for native urban residents but not for rural-to-urban migrants. The most important interacting mechanism we identified is that the neighborhood segregation between migrant and local workers will aggravate the positive relationships between migrants' social exclusion and victimization. However, similar to the results of recent studies on Hispanic communities in US, the migrant-concentrated communities in urban China actually provide some protections and reduce the positive effects of migrants’ risky routine activities on victimization.

14414014.label: Major findings and research outcome
14414014.value: Main findings: (1) With technology development and civilization, many societies, including China, violence and traditional types of property crime are in general decreasing, while new forms of property crime are increasing (see PI’s other publications in 2017 and 2018). However, due to long-term biased policies, rural-to-urban migrant workers in modern China have great disadvantages to find a decent job, foster a healthy lifestyle and living in a decent community. They face much higher risks of being victimized by street offenders compared to their local counterparts, especially in terms of certain types of offenses (assault, fraud, theft and robbery). (2) The levels of social exclusion among migrant workers are positively related to their risks of victimization. Such exclusion mainly can be categorized into two types: the first one is institutional discrimination making them difficult to interact with mainstream populations and then leading to the loss of valuable information and opportunities; the second one is migrant workers' low qualification to modern economy so that they are more vulnerable in the job market. (3) The relationship between social exclusion and victimization is mediated by routine activities of migrant workers. Due to social exclusion, migrant workers have limited access to regular jobs (they have to work longer, go home at night and earn cash instead of monthly bank payment), secured workplaces (they work on streets without sufficient guards) and local social capital (lack of ties/information for ensuring safety in urban area) so that they face high exposure to potential offenders, have less capable guardians, and make them more suitable targets. That is why they are more likely to be victimized compared to native urban respondents. (4) Neighborhood disorganization has direct positive effects on migrant workers’ risks of victimization and also interacts with social exclusion and routine activities at individual level. Contrary to the mechanisms shown in the models of local workers, neighborhood disadvantaged are more powerful than individual-level vulnerabilities when explaining migrants' victimization. Moreover, neighborhood segregation between migrant and local residents will aggravate the positive relationship between migrants’ social exclusion and victimization, while such migrant-concentrated communities in urban China at the same time provide certain protections and alleviate the positive relationship between migrants' risky routine activities and victimization.

14414014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14414014.value: We are preparing to submit two more papers using the CLDS data: one addresses the drinking and smoking behaviors of migrant workers (vs. native urban respondents) from a public health approach; one focuses on the changes of migrant workers' victimization with social development in China (using four waves of CLDS, from 2012 to 2018). Both of the papers aim to publish in top journals of sociology/criminology. This project targets at the adult migrant workers' victimization and the mechanisms behind it. Our research team would like to extend such victimization studies to the children of migrant workers, including left-behind children in rural China and migrant children who have moved to cities with their parents. The results would be compared with native urban students. One GRF proposal about migrant children's victimization would be submitted in Fall 2018.

14414014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14414014.value: Using the 2012 and 2014 China Labor Dynamics Survey, a national representative data set, this project aims to: (1) examine the victimization patterns of contemporary Chinese migrant workers and, (2) test to what extent the migrant workers' victimization can be explained by social exclusion they experienced (e.g. discrimination from urban mainstream societies), their own risky routine activities (e.g. working on the streets), and the problematic neighborhoods they are living in (e.g. neighborhoods received less protection from the government). Our multilevel data analyses provide strong empirical evidence to our integrative theoretical framework: first, social exclusion experienced by migrant workers increase their risky routine activities and lead to higher likelihood of victimization; second, neighborhood problems have both direct effects on migrant workers' victimization and interacting effects with social exclusion and routine activities. This project is the first national-level examination on victimization and its social correlates among rural-to-urban migrant workers, the population often ignored in previous victimization studies and migration research. It also has bridged the relevant theory gaps in criminology and migration/immigration fields with the most updated data. The research contributes to the rising policy need to understand the vulnerability of migrant workers, one of the most disadvantaged social groups in contemporary China.

14500514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14500514.value: Traditional economics relies heavily on the assumption that people are rational. This assumption is highly unrealistic, as nobody is fully rational. Economists, however, were reluctant to drop this unrealistic assumption because being irrational was deemed equivalent to being unpredictable. A recent revolution in behavioral economics changed this perception by showing that people in general are irrational in certain highly predictable ways. One of ways that people are predictably irrational is being dynamically inconsistent. In the last 20 years, economists have gained significant understanding of dynamic inconsistency, including how it generates various problems in our daily lives, and how various seemingly inefficient social institutions can actually be understood as devices to mitigate the dynamic inconsistency problem. However, the conventional wisdom (that is, until this proposed project) remains that dynamic inconsistency is a curse that we have to accept as part of our lives. This PI is the first economist to point out that dynamic inconsistency needs not be a curse, but can be a blessing sometimes, provided that we know how to make good use of it. The intuition, once explained, is actually very simple: dynamic inconsistency means that your future self does not share the same preferences as yours. But your future self is still the same person as you are, sharing all your information and secrets, albeit not necessarily your interest. S/he is hence your most formidable enemy, and the most capable candidate to keep you honest. With her/him looking over your shoulder, your various claims about yourself can gain a lot more credibility. This can give you a leg up in contractual relationships, when trust cannot be taken for grant. The objective of this project is to turn this deep insight into concrete advices for the general public, especially advices on how they should turn their own dynamic inconsistency problem into an advantage in contractual relationships. I plan to document these advices in at least one international refereed journal article, and present these advices in multiple conferences. The long-term significance of the project is that it will increase the welfare of the general public as we change the way we look at our own imperfection in general, and our irrationality in particular. It will also inspire a new research agenda, where economists search for ways to turn our other kinds of irrationality into our advantage.

14500514.label: Realisation of objectives
14500514.value: Objectives 1 and 2 have been 100% achieved. Objective 3 is almost fully achieved. In particular, findings in this project have been disseminated in a number of international conferences, and have been documented in a working paper ("How I Learn to Love Being Dynamically Inconsistent"), which is currently under review. However, due to the long time lag in publication in economics, this working paper still has not been accepted by an international refereed journal. As such, Objective 3 is slightly shy of 100% achieved. The first objective of this project is to identify various contractual settings where being dynamically inconsistent may help. I have successfully developed a fairly general theory of when being dynamically inconsistent may help. The theory is general enough that it nests many common contractual settings as its special cases. Examples include insurance, managerial compensation, franchising, weapon procurement, and exclusive licensing agreement, among many others. Given my general theory, identifying more such contractual settings boils down to checking the validity of two assumptions: the Sorting Assumption and the Assumption of Changing Tastes. I have successfully proved that these two assumptions are the two key sufficient conditions for dynamic inconsistency to be helpful. The second objective of this project is to turn the deep insight that being dynamically inconsistent can be a blessing instead of a curse into concrete advices in these contractual settings. This objective is achieved by a completely constructive general recipe provided in my working paper. The recipe is completely constructive, meaning that anyone can follow verbatim, even if he does not understand the proof of why it works. The recipe is also general, meaning that for anyone who wants to apply it, all he needs to do is to first describe a specific contractual setting using the unified language introduced in my working paper, and then map each step of the recipe (which is described using this unified language) back to the specifics of the contractual setting in question.

14500514.label: Major findings and research outcome
14500514.value: In this project, I developed a fairly general theory of how we can write contracts that take advantage of our own dynamic inconsistency. The theory is general enough to apply to many common applications, such as insurance, managerial compensation, franchising, weapon procurement, and exclusive licensing agreement, among many others. The common theme across all these applications is that a future self who shares all of your secrets but does not corroborate well with you is a very good instrument to keep you honest. By leveraging his incentives to betray you and expose your lies, you can gain credibility in convincing the others who you truly are. This major finding has been documented in my working paper "How I Learn to Love Being Dynamically Inconsistent", which is currently under review. Due to the long time lag in publication in economics, this paper still has not been accepted by an international refereed journal. This is the only reason why the the third objective of this project has not been 100% achieved. On the other hand, the finding of this project has been disseminated in a number of international conferences, and hence the third objective of this project has been largely achieved. Besides the major finding, this project has also uncovered a number of robustness results. First, the finding that a contractual party can benefit from his own dynamic inconsistency is robust to any prior probability distribution of that party's types. Second, it is also robust to small uncertainty on whether the party in question is indeed dynamically inconsistent. Third, it is robust to a small amount of naivety, where the party in question may not be fully aware of his own dynamic inconsistency. Fourth, the finding remains valid even if the type that is most eager to convince the others (the "high" type) is not dynamically inconsistent at all. This is because what is the most important is that the type that is most eager to lie (the "low" type) is dynamically inconsistent, and hence his future self can be brought in to expose such lies.

14500514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14500514.value: In this project, I considered only the case where an informed principal proposing a contract to an uninformed agent. It is in this particular case where I can prove that the informed principal can turn dynamic inconsistency into an advantage, in the sense that he can leverage his future self to help him credibly convince the others his true type. But I conjecture that the result can also be proved in a different setting, namely one where multiple uninformed agents compete in offering contracts to the informed party. Specifically, I conjecture that in the market equilibrium, these competing uninformed agent will offer exactly the same contract that the informed principal would have offered in the setting I have studied. Proving this conjecture requires one to take the approach of Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976), which I have not pursued in this project. I consider this pursuit as the most important next step in furthering this line of study.

14500514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14500514.value: Being dynamically inconsistent is mighty inconvenient. You cannot choose whatever plan of actions you like, but instead have to limit yourself to plans that your future self is willing to carry out. You procrastinate, and sometimes even preproperate. You have to give up flexibility, and are sometimes taken advantage by health clubs. In this project, I point out one benefit of being dynamically inconsistent, namely that it helps us to more credibly prove our hidden types to an untrusting party. The intuition is very simple: my future self, being the same me, share all of my secrets. If my future self does not share my preference, thanks to dynamic inconsistency, then he can be made a formidable enemy of mine, standing ready to betray me and expose any lie I may tell other parties. By leveraging on his incentives to betray me and expose any lie I may tell, I can hence more credibly convince other parties my true type, reducing certain contractual inefficiency that may otherwise arise from asymmetric information.

14500914.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14500914.value: 在什么样的情境下，家长式领导领导会更加有效？

14500914.label: Co - Investigator(s)
14500914.value: Prof Farh, Jiing-Lih Prof Liu, Jun Prof Qu, Qing Prof Yu, Guangtao

14500914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14500914.value: While previous studies have provided evidence on the influences of paternalistic leadership (PL) on employee outcomes, there remain two unresolved questions in the literature. First, do leaders’ personal characteristics impact the effectiveness of paternalistic leadership? Second, does the extent to which leaders and followers share the same organizational vision moderate the relationship between paternalistic leadership and employees’ voice behaviors (“speaking out and challenging the status quo with the intent of improving the situation”; LePine & Van Dyne, 1998, p. 853)? The purpose of this project is to answer these questions. PL is defined as “a style that combines strong discipline and authority with fatherly benevolence” (Farh & Cheng, 2000, p. 91). A three-dimensional (Authoritarian (A), Benevolence (B) and Morality (C)) model of PL has been used in research, but only the benevolence and morality dimensions have consistently been found to be positive, whereas the authoritarian dimension has been found to be both positive and negative (Farh, Liang, Chou, & Cheng, 2008; Li, Sun, & Jiao, 2013). This study focuses on Authentic (ABC: high on all three dimensions) and Selfless benefactor (aBC: high on BC but low on A) paternalistic leaders, two out of the eight possible types of paternalistic leaders (see Farh et al., 2008 for details), which we also found in our study (Qu & Fu, 2013). Using trust in supervisor as the influencing mechanism (e.g., Wu, Huang, & Chan, 2012), we argue that authentic paternalistic and selfless benefactor leaders will affect followers’ voice behaviors differently. We also hypothesize that any negative effects of authentic paternalistic leadership will be mitigated when the authentic paternalistic leader and his/her followers share the same organizational vision and that the positive effect of selfless benefactor leaders on followers’ voice behaviors will be strengthened by the leaders’ self-transcendent values. To test the two-level model governing these hypotheses, we plan to collect data from approximately 500~600 leader-follower dyads, using measures that have been validated with Chinese samples. We will also use our own indigenous Chinese Value Survey (CVS) instrument and will thereby contribute to the values literature. Hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) will be used to test the model. Our study will help clarify the mixed results and enrich the PL literature as well as increase knowledge on the values of the Chinese. The results will also provide practical suggestions to leaders to understand how to enhance followers’ voice behaviors to stay competitive in the marketplace. 许多研究都已表明，家长式领导 —一种有着父亲般的慈祥、威严和纪律的领导风格 -- 影响员工的工作绩效，但是仍有个问题亟待解决。首先，领导者个人特点是否会影响家长式领导有效性？其次，领导者与下属共享团队愿景的程度是否会调节家长式领导对员工建言的影响？本研究试图回答这两个问题。 在研究中，家长式领导通常有三个维度：威权、仁慈与德行。不过，只有仁慈与德行两个维度被发现具有稳定正向影响，而威权之效果却尚无定论。本项目聚焦于两种家长式领导组合：真实型家长式领导（三维度皆高得分）和无私型家长式领导（威权低得分，仁慈、道德高得分）。现有的研究，包括我们自己的，都已发现这两种家长式领导的风格。 本研究将下属对主管的信任作为影响机制，来解释真实型家长式领导和无私型家长式领导对员工建言产生的不同影响。我们假设当领导者与下属共享组织愿景水平较高时，真实型家长式领导对员工建言之负面作用会被削弱；当领导者具有较高水平之超越自我价值观时，无私型家长式领导对员工建言之正面作用会被加强。 为了检验以上跨层次假设，我们计划使用已经在中国样本被证实有效之测量工具，从大约80至100个小组（领导以及他们3-5个下属）中收集数据。我们将会使用自己开发中国人价值观工具收集信息，以对价值观文献有所贡献。我们将使用阶层线性模型分析数据、检验模型。在理论上，本项目将有助澄清家长式领导文献中之混杂结果，丰富家长式领导研究，以及增益中国人价值观研究；在实践上，本项目将为领导者提供促进员工建言之有效建议。

14501014.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14501014.value: 债权与股权的冲突、会计谨慎性与管理层薪酬

14501014.label: Project Objectives
14501014.value: To contribute to the literature on debt-equity conflicts and how governance structures can be used to address the agency problem. Prior studies focus generally on the role of debt covenants in protecting debtholders. I argue that compensation contracts can also be used to protect debtholders even if compensation is supposedly set by the board representing euqityholders, because the cost of debt can be prohibitively high if debtholders are not duly protected. To contribute to the literature on the use of accounting vs. stock performance measures in compensation contracts. Prior studies often focus on the relative informativeness of accounting and stock performance measures in explaining the relative weights these two measures take in executive compensation. I argue that another driving force could the demand arising from debt-equity conflict of interest. To contribute to the literature on accounting conservatism. Prior studies often argue that conservatism arises as a response to the demand of debtholders to protect themselves. However, the argument is typically from an ex post perspective in that by knowing bad news in a more timely fashion debtholders can take actions to stop their loss. I argue that by building conservative accounting numbers into compensation contracts, accounting conservatism can play an ex ante role to prevent risky projects from being taken in the first place. To contribute to the literature on debt contracts and compensation contracts. Positive Accounting Theory pioneered by Watts and Zimmerman (1985) treat these two kinds of contracts generally separately. I argue that the two can be related through accounting conservatism and debt-equity conflict.

14501014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14501014.value: Debtholders and equityholders have different preferences for risks. In particular debtholders cannot benefit from the upside of firm performance but would hurt from the downside, and the upside benefit would accrue to equityholders. Thus, equityholders have the incentive to take excessive risks at the expense of debtholders. This classical problem of debt-equity conflict implies that debtholders would impose higher cost of debt on the firm without proper mechanisms to protect themselves. It is to the benefit of equityholders to commit to some such mechanism in order to lower the cost of debt. Prior studies generally focus on the role of debt covenants in protecting debtholders. In this project I argue that executive compensation combined with accounting conservatism can achieve the same purpose. The argument is as follows. Risk-taking implies risky payoffs. Accounting is conservative in the sense that accounting is more timely to recognize bad news than good news. In a certainty world, there would be no demand for accounting conservatism. Accounting conservatism arises precisely to deal with risky payoffs. The asymmetric recognition of bad news vs. good news implies that risky projects tend to lead to lower earnings in the early years of the project. This is in contrast to stock returns which are forward looking and would react positively to projects with positive NPV regardless of the timing of gains and losses. Then, by tying executive compensation more to accounting performance than to stock performance, managers would be "punished" by taking risky projects due to lower compensation in the early years. As a result, they would be incentivized to staying away from risky projects, to the benefit of debtholders. Thus, my primary hypothesis is that: when debt-equity conflict is more severe, executive compensation puts more weight on accounting performance and less weight on stock performance. Additional hypotheses are: 1) The above effect is stronger when actual accounting is more conservative. This is because different firms have different practices of accounting conservatism for other reasons. The discouragement of risky projects works only with conservative accounting. 2) The above effect is stronger when debtholders are less protected, for example, there are less debt covenants, so that there is more reliance on the compensation mechanism. 债权人与股权人对风险有不同的偏好，具体说来，债权人在公司业绩出色时并不能从中分享好处，而公司业绩下滑时却承担损失，股权人则能享受出色业绩的收益。因而股权人有动因过于冒险而损害债权人。这个债权人与股权人之间冲突的经典问题意味着，债权人如果得不到适当机制的保护就会要求更高的利率，从而使举债成本增加。要想降低举债成本，股权人可以主动承诺某种机制来保护债权人。过去的研究基本上集中在如何通过债务契约来保护债权人，在本研究中，我提出将管理层薪酬与会计谨慎性结合起来可以达到同样的目的。道理如下： 冒风险意味着结果的不确定性。会计谨慎性原则是说在结果不确定的情况下坏消息在会计报表上的确认要早于好消息的确认。在一个无风险的世界会计没有任何必要谨慎。会计谨慎性原则的产生恰恰是用来处理不确定的结果的。会计上对坏消息和好消息确认上的不对称处理意味着风险性项目的盈余在早期较低。这与股票回报率形成鲜明对比，这是因为股票价格是前瞻性的，一个有风险的项目只要净现值是正的，则无论会计上损益确认的时间点如何，价格现在的反应都会是正的。由此，如果让管理层薪酬取决于会计业绩而不是股票业绩，那么管理层进行风险性项目时就会因为早期会计盈利较低而受到“惩罚”，他们就有动因远离高风险项目，从而有利于债权人。 根据以上道理，我提出的主要假设为：当债权人和股权人利益冲突越更严重，管理层薪酬放在会计业绩上的权重就越大，放在股票业绩上的权重就越小。另外我还假设：1）由于不同公司的会计谨慎性程度不一，以上效应在会计谨慎性程度高的公司里更大大；2）债权人在其它方面（如债务契约）得到的保护越少，则对薪酬机制的依赖越大，以上效应越大。

14501014.label: Realisation of objectives
14501014.value: 1. The paper finds that compensation contracts based on accounting performance measured from a conservative accounting system can be used mitigate the debt-equity conflicts. The objective is achieved. 2. The project finds that the weight on accounting performance in compensation contracts varies with firms' debt level after controlling for other known factors affecting the compensation weights. The objective is achieved. 3. The project finds that accounting conservatism works in favor of debtholders through the mechanism of compensation contracts rather than the traditional mechanism of debt contracts. The objective is achieved. 4. The project links debt contracts and compensation contracts through conservative accounting numbers. The objective is achieved.

14501014.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501014.value: The projects finds evidence supporting the argument that conservative accounting earnings can be used in compensation contracts to mitigate debt/equity conflict. In particular, CEO pay sensitivity to accounting return on asset is shown to increase with financial leverage, a proxy of the equity-debt conflict. Such higher sensitivity is primarily driven by the bonus portion of CEO compensation. In addition, the effect is more pronounced for firms with higher accounting conservatism and higher operational uncertainty, consistent with notion that protection of debtholders is most needed when the uncertainty level is high and most effective when the accounting practice is conservative. The research has produced a working paper, which was first circulated at a couple of international conferences in early 2017. After getting feedback and revision work based on the feedback, it was further presented at several international conferences and universities, and was used as the keynote speech or keynote speech theme at two other international conference/symposium.

14501014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501014.value: The paper has been presented at several international conferences (see detailed information provided) and universities (Rice University, Nanjing University, Southeast University, Southern University of Science and Technology, Tsinghua University) . It was submitted to a top academic journal but was rejected. It is now under further revision targeting at submission to another top academic journal. The main challenge is endogeneity that is difficult to completely address in this particular setting, although we already made some attempts. We are trying to do additional tests to further mitigate the concern of endogeneity.

14501014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501014.value: Debt holders and stock holders have different preferences for firms' risk-taking behavior. Debt holders are more concerned with the downside risk and stock holders care more about firms' upside risk. To protect debt holders' interest, we show that compensations contracts can put more weight on firms' accounting performance that are conservative. The reason is that risky investments tend to be treated as expenses initially, leading to lower accounting performance and discouraging such investments. In contrast, stock price could react positively to risky investments; compensation contracts based on stock price could encourage such investments.

14501314.label: Project Objectives
14501314.value: To study affective forecasting biases from a motivational perspective. To examine the ways affective forecasts and actual affective responses deviate and their consequences on goal pursuit.

To examine the ways affective forecasts and actual affective responses deviate and their consequences on goal pursuit.

14501314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14501314.value: 當作出決定，消費者經常會問自己在不同的場景：“我會覺得怎麼”。他們努力選擇行動，使他們感覺良好，並避免那些會讓他們感覺不好的選擇。然而，這些情感的預測往往是不準確的。例如，大學橄欖球球迷高估自己球隊的勝利將有多大影響他們的幸福。地鐵乘客亦傾向高估錯過車後，他們會有多遺憾。其他的研究表明，人們有時會低估他們的情感反應。 因為情感的預測經常出現錯誤，以這些預測作為決策基礎看起來是有害的。其他人也認為，在做決策時人們不應該考量預期的情緒反應。研究人員亦調查了如何可以改善預測的準確性。然而，我們認為情感的預測要準確才有用, 這一項假設並不一定有效。事實上，我們認為，當中的偏差很可能輔助目標追求。舉例來說，高估正面情感，可以增加決心和動力去追求該目標。另一方面，高估失敗可能帶來的負面反應，可激發精細的計劃，分析，和付出的努力，從而降低失敗的可能性。 總體來說，我們建議預期和實際的情感反應會出現偏差，是因為它們的差異是對目標追求有策略性意義。相比之下，情感預測偏差的修正可能會影響長期的目標導向。在這個項目中，我們打算測試相關的決定因素和情感預測的後果。在第一個方面，我們將測試預測誤差的大小，與人們對目標的經驗和專業知識之間的關係，同時這種變化是如何增強追求目標的動機（命題1）。在第二個方面，我們將測試，情感預測誤差可促進實際的目標導向行為，如規劃，奮鬥和目標修正（命題2）。如果這些命題都是有效的，他們將挑戰傳統的推定，即情感的預測要準確才是有用的。這一假設忽略了這些預測偏差可能帶來的潛在利益。也就是說，偏差可以帶來激勵效果，提升目標的實現。

14501314.label: Realisation of objectives
14501314.value: We have addressed the first objective of this project. In the past, many researchers have argued that people should not rely on affective forecasts to make decision because these forecasts are beset by errors (e.g., Dunn & Laham, 2006; Levine, Lench, Kaplan, & Safer, 2012; Walsh & Ayton, 2009). In the current research, we highlighted an alternative way to understand this issue. That is, the discrepancies between our predicted and actual feelings (i.e., the forecasting errors) can be beneficial to goal pursuit. That is, the forecasting errors can be motivational and help regulate people’s behavior to goal attainment. For instance, people are motivated to pursue goals that are associated with positive affect because this affect signals that the end-state is desirable (e.g., Higgins, 1997). Thus, an overestimation of the positive feelings associated with goal attainment could effectively increase the perceived value of a goal and hence the commitment and motivation to pursue it. Regarding the second objective, we collected empirical evidence showing that the ways predicted and actual affect deviate are systematic instead of being random. We also identified moderators of people’s predicted and actual feelings, which included expertise on a decision domain, importance of the goal, and the in-group versus out-group membership in the task context. The effects have been observed in lab settings and natural settings, with real and hypothetical consequences.

14501314.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501314.value: Central to our thesis, we found that affective forecasts often deviate from actual affective responses in ways that are beneficial to a goal pursuit. In the first series of studies, we found that novices and experts would make different kinds of affective forecasting errors. We found that novices are more likely than are experts to overestimate how happy they would feel if they succeeded a task; whereas experts are more likely than are novices to overestimate how disappointed they would feel if they fail a task. This differential pattern of results maps nicely with the previous finding that novices are mainly motivated by positive feedback whereas experts are primarily concerned with negative feedback. Hence, when the affective forecasts err in ways that correspond to the motivational drivers that people need, these misforecasts could enhance the chances of successful goal pursuit. These results have been replicated with expertise manipulated through hypothetical feedback and efficacy measured in academic settings. We also found that the magnitude of misforecast is related to goal importance. Specifically, we found that people’s affective prediction and responses are shaped by their ingroup versus outgroup membership in a task. Results showed that the affective prediction errors magnify when a person is completing a task together with ingroup members versus with outgroup members. This is because people often see the same task as more important when it is done with ingroup (vs. outgroup) members. Thus, when working towards an important goal, the more intense affective predictions would increase the effort to be spent and thus the chance of goal success. The above findings have been reported in major international conferences noted in part C. We received very encouraging comments from audience and journal editor during conference presentations. In the final phase of this project, we captured the downstream consequences of affective misforecasts. In a correlational study, we found that undergraduate students’ misforecasts were correlated with their exam performance. To make a more compelling package for journal submission, we are gathering causal support from longitudinal experiment. The progress of this experiment was slower than expected, because the task we used in the initial round was not sensitive enough. With modification, we ran the study again and have yet to reach our target sample size.

14501314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501314.value: One potential avenue for this line of research is to explore the application value of the findings. For instance, it may be possible to prime affective forecasts to be high or low through altering the response scale of a measure. It would then be interesting to see whether the primed affective forecasts would motivate people to work harder and increase their chances of goal attainment. Future studies may also explore and compare different ways to alter the magnitude of affective forecasts and their feasibility in real life settings.

14501314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501314.value: When making decisions, consumers often ask themselves “how will I feel” in different scenarios. They strive to select courses of actions that will make them feel good and avoid ones that will make them feel bad. However, because affective forecasts are often beset by errors, basing decisions on these forecasts might seem to be detrimental. In the present research, we question the validity of the assumption that affective forecasts need to be accurate in order to be useful. In fact, we found that the biases can be beneficial to goal pursuit. For instance, an overestimation of the positive feelings associated with goal attainment could effectively increase the perceived value of a goal and hence the commitment and motivation to pursue it. On the other hand, people’s overestimation of their negative reactions to failure could stimulate them to engage in more elaborate planning and analysis and to increase the physical effort they devote to the task at hand, thereby reducing the actual likelihood of failure. In sum, we propose that anticipated and actual affective responses deviate because their deviation is strategic to goal pursuit. In contrast, the correction of affective forecasting biases could interfere with long term goal-directed activities.
