14501414.label: Project Objectives
14501414.value: Examine tertius iungens practice as a behavioral solution for mitigating detrimental faultline effects on group processes and performance. Study the basis for surface-level and deep-level faultlines and their effects on group processes and performance. Explore the unique basis for group faultlines in a Chinese setting.
rows: Examine tertius iungens practice as a behavioral solution for mitigating detrimental faultline effects on group processes and performance.
Study the basis for surface-level and deep-level faultlines and their effects on group processes and performance.
Explore the unique basis for group faultlines in a Chinese setting.

14501414.label: Realisation of objectives
14501414.value: To realize the proposed objective #3 (Explore the unique basis for group faultlines in a Chinese setting), we interviewed 96 employees in 58 teams in seven Chinese organizations located in Beijing and Shanghai in 2015. Through these interviews, we found that both diversity and faultline were relevant in the Chinese context and group faultline was mostly perceived as detrimental to team processes and outcomes. Our respondents informed us about their perceptions of diversity and faultline bases. Demographic attributes, including sex, age, education, province and work tenure were highlighted. More interestingly, our interviewees reported four unique bases of faultline, namely personality, team characteristics, activities and hobbies, and leader preference, which were markedly different from the western focus of demographic attributes, such as age, gender, work experience, and education. Objective 3 was therefore accomplished and we presented these findings in Conferences #1, 2, 3 and 7. Despite our realization of objective #3, the interview findings fell short of informing us the faultline effects and potential remedies (objectives # 1 & 2). One possible reason is that the interviews were conducted at the work place of the interviewees and our interviewees were hesitant about sharing the detrimental effects of group faultline. To realize objective #2 (study the basis for surface-level and deep-level faultlines and their effects on group processes and performance), we decided to conduct another round of interviews. In 2016, we interviewed 21 team workers from 15 companies in Southern China. We used a snowballing technique and interviewed these team workers in coffee shops and other off-work venues. Findings from the second-round interviews confirmed about the unique group faultline bases we identified from the first-round interviews. In particular, leadership preferences, including strong leadership, leader power, leader behaviors (including tertius iungens practices), create new forms of group faultline and faultline mechanisms. One interesting finding is that group faultline, which is usually described as a group compositional pattern or group structure, can be actively created as a strategy. As proposed in the presentation for conference #6, we found that subgroups could be formed intentionally by group leaders or members for enhancing social influence or power. Promoting self-interest was mentioned as a major driver. Two implications can be drawn from this finding. First, power is a relevant basis for understanding group faultline effects. Recent literature on subgroups echo this line of finding that power is a relevant basis for faultline or subgroup formation (Carton & Cummings, 2012). Our interview findings further illustrated that power struggle mechanisms between leader and subgroups and among subgroups. Second, faultline is not a passive, given, social structure. Leaders or group members create group faultline for a purpose. These findings open up new research directions and potential new projects for understanding faultline dynamics and in partial fulfillment of objective 2. In addition, to understand about the effects of surface-level faultline in China (objective 2), we conducted a longitudinal survey study among new venture teams in the Chinese context. In this study, we examined the alignment effects of surface-level attributes, including gender, age, nationality, employment status, and location of study on new venture team advancement in a multiple-stage business idea competition (Output # 1). We found that team faultline strength has a negative impact on the performance of new venture teams. This finding illustrated that detrimental surface-level faultline effects existed in China, similar to what we know from the extant faultline literature. Based on the second round of interviews as well as the survey study on new venture teams, we found evidence of deep- and surface-level faultline and their effects on Chinese team processes and performance. In sum, objective 2 was accomplished. Objective 1 (Examine tertius iungens practice as a behavioral solution for mitigating detrimental faultline effects on group processes and performance) is outstanding. Our initial plan was to conduct a longitudinal survey among 100 teams in at least two different cities in mainland China. However, the data collection process was delayed because of two reasons. First, we need to wait for the results from the second round of interviews so that we can include the unique faultline bases as well as mechanisms in the survey. Second, the search for organizational sites took longer than expected. Finally, we found a collaborator in China and he assisted us in locating three companies in China and conducted the multi-phase and multi-referent survey study. Below is the detailed information regarding the survey data collection process. Company A Company B Company C City Shangdong Shanghai Shenzhen Ownership State-owned Private Private Size (employees) 1,595 65,000 2,565 Industry Tobacco Car accessories Electronics Sample size Teams 53 14 22 Participants 272 54 79 Data collection Time Points: Time 1 Time 2 Time 3 Company A April 2017 July 2017 October 2017 Company B May 2017 August 2017 November 2017 Company C June 2017 September 2017 December 2017 After the last round of data collection in December 2017, we continued to work with these companies regarding missing data. Finally, in late March 2018, the survey data was ready for cleaning and analysis. The focus of the survey was to examine the moderating role of tertius iungen practice (TIP) on the detrimental group faultline effects on group processes and performance. We have measured two TIP sources, supervisor and team member. We expect that they may have different impact on connecting the faultline-induced subgroup difference. While we are hopeful on the potential findings, we run out of time in completing the analyses. Looking back, we should ask for an extension of the project before the end of the project last year because of the need for the second-round interviews as well as the challenge in looking for organizational sites. We are now working on the data analyses and we plan to write a conference paper as well as a top-tiered journal article by the end of this summer. If possible, I would like to ask the panel member to grant us an extension of 6 -12 months so that we have time to report our findings and demonstrate the value of our project. In the meantime, we will keep the panel up-to-date about the progress of achieving objective #1. Carton, A. & Cummings, J. N. 2012. A theory of subgroups in work teams. 14501414.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501414.value: We asked two research questions. Is the concept of faultline relevant to Chinese teams? What are Chinese-specific faultline attributes and dynamics? In two rounds of interviews and a study on new venture teams, we found that group faultline was relevant and prevalent in China (Conferences #1, 2, 3 & 7). Interviewees were able to describe its nature, form, and effects. A study on Chinese new venture teams (Output # 1) replicated the detrimental effects of group faultline on group processes and outcomes, which were often found in studies of US and European teams. In terms of faultline bases, we found the both surface- and deep-level attributes were mentioned in the interviews. Similar to the extant faultline literature, many interviewees reported that sex, age, education, work tenure were faultline bases (Conferences # 1, 2, 3, 7). However, we noticed some important differences. First, provincial origin was mentioned as a way to distinguish between in-subgroup and out-subgroup members. Another interesting finding was education. Besides the level of education, overseas educational experience / exposure was reported as another potential faultline attribute. Employees who had been educated abroad, studied at local MBA programs but operated by foreign universities, had previous work experience in foreign-own firms were perceived as having different value systems and expectations, thus a relevant faultline attribute. Besides surface-level attributes, we also found unique deep-level faultline attributes in Chinese teams. Interview findings show that personality, work structure (whether they belong to similar departments), activities and interests (similar hobbies, for instance), and leader preference (whether leaders will create / endorse group faultline). These discoveries open up new possibilities in understanding deep-level faultline effects. In terms of faultline effects in Chinese teams, we have two major findings. For surface-level faultline, we found that group faultline, based on gender, age, nationality, employment status, and location of study, negatively affected new venture team performance (Output # 1). More interestingly we found that group mean of team members’ entrepreneurial passion mitigated the detrimental effects of group faultline while group diversity of team members’ entrepreneurial passion intensified group faultline effects. As for deep-level faultline, we found that faultline was not only a form of static social structure, it could be created intentionally for a strategic purpose (Conference # 6). Through intentional recruiting and decruiting, in-subgroups of loyal members were formed to enhance leader influence and bargaining power. Power struggle among subgroups become a critical group process for further examination.

14501414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501414.value: We see at least two potential directions for development. First, through the interviews, we realized the importance of leaders in Chinese teams, especially those with strong faultline. Many interviews quotes pointed to the exchange and relationship quality between leaders and team members. In other words, besides studying team-level effects, one potential direction is to study the dyadic level interactions, expectations, and their effects on employee attitudes and outcomes (Conference # 5). Second, the power dynamics in faultline teams are worth studying. While the extant faultline literature draws on social identity theory, Carton and Cummings (2012) has already proposed three different types of subgroup bases, identity, variety and power. While much has been studied about identity- and variety-based subgroups, power dynamics has received relatively less attention. Realizing this opportunity, my PhD student Qin Su chooses this topic as her dissertation thesis focus and will examine the power dynamics of group faultline at both group- and individual-level outcomes.

14501414.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501414.value: Group faultline refers hypothetical dividing line(s) that split a group into two or more subgroups based on one or more personal attributes. While the detrimental effects of group faultline has been consistently found in western teams, we are less certain whether this is the case for Chinese teams. We asked two questions. Is the concept of faultline relevant to Chinese teams? What are Chinese-specific faultline attributes and dynamics? In two rounds of interviews and a study of Chinese new venture teams, we found that group faultline was prevalent and had a similar negative impact on team performance. In addition, our studies revealed new and unique Chinese faultline bases and dynamics. For instance, Chinese team members perceive members from the same provincial origin as members of their own subgroups and those who do not belong to the same province as out-subgroup members. Provincial differences become a potential source of group conflict. Similarly, employees with overseas exposure, including overseas education or prior work experience with foreign-owned organizations, reported challenges in working with traditional Chinese managers who expect loyalty and obedience. These findings enrich the extant faultline literature and shed light on Chinese team management.

14501714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14501714.value: 近年來，新興市場國家企業的跨境兼並和收購已經進入了跨越式發展的階段。據中國的商務部統計，中國企業跨國並購的價值在2012年飆升至434億美元，占中國對外直接投資額的49.43％。鑒於這一現象日趨重要，我們從理論上和實證研究上急需探討那些在新興市場國家企業跨境並購背後的實際驅動因素。 在本研究中，我們將整合網絡信息理論和資源依賴理論構建一個新的理論模型，來解釋新興市場國家企業在哪裏進行跨國並購這一重要的戰略決策。理論上的整合可以對企業的行為有更全面的了解，並有可能對任何單一的理論所無法解釋的現象給出較為全面的分析。此外，本研究中理論的整合對新興市場國家企業尤為適合，因為這些國家的對外貿易依存度日漸增強，這些企業對國內巨大市場過度依賴，以及它們一直以來擅長使用社會網絡戰略。 資源依賴會導致企業對約束的吸收行為。我們把這個邏輯應用到新興市場國家企業的跨國並購中，並重點研究多重資源依賴將如何推動跨國並購的東道國選擇。同時，新興市場企業還可以從它們的網絡成員中已經用跨國並購管理特定國家的不確定性的經驗中獲益。此外，我們應用權變理論，認為網絡信息將會減少資源依賴性對跨國並購東道國選擇的決策影響。 這項研究將具有重要的研究意義。首先，從理論上，本研究將提升對新興市場國家跨國並購決定因素研究的理論基礎。其次，本研究將有助於進一步探索兩類重要的網絡參與者 （即集團內的兄弟企業以及聯盟中的合作夥伴）所傳遞的信息對核心企業戰略決策的不同影響。第三，本研究將有助於對約束吸收機制進一步了解，尤其是在確定這一機制的應用邊界和提升理論預測的精度上。 我們將建立一個中國上市公司跨國並購數據庫（2002-2012）來檢驗我們的理論假設。我們也希望通過本研究的理論發展和實證展示，能有助於對資源依賴和網絡信息理論的整合與應用，並更深入理解新興市場國家企業的跨國並購戰略。

14501714.label: Realisation of objectives
14501714.value: We have strictly focus on the four objectives set in the proposal. We have also made necessary changes to respond to the problems encountered during the grant period. In this way, we have fully achieved the objectives and the comments from our reviewers. To advance the RDT model of absorption. With regard to this objective, we have made progress in the following way. We extend the RDT model of absorption to the study on a firm’s geographic expansion from domestic to international markets. In particular, we build on the concept of mutual trade dependence to capture firms’ exchange environment in the global trade network. Mutual dependence is an important construct that explicitly combines the resource dependence logic and network methodology. Specifically, we highlight the effects of macro-level mutual trade dependence on the driving forces of cross-border M&As, which advances the RDT model of absorption in terms of the level of analysis and the scope of dependence absorption. To enrich the network information theory. With regard to this objective, we have made progress in three ways. First, we made necessary changes to focus on two prominent network information sources: joint venture partners and board interlock partners. Second, we extended the network perspective to include political capital, which is also an important information, legitimacy, and resource source for the international strategy of emerging market firms. This insight is used in the revision of some papers. Third, as any network is embedded in institutional environments, we extended this insight to include formal and informal institutions as well as institutional forces perceived by managers for the revision of some papers. To identify the boundaries of RDT. With regard to this objective, we have made progress in the following way. We made necessary changes to focus on the effects of firm-level network information and the moderating role played by country-level resource dependence. That is, we have advanced existing knowledge about how the interplay of network information and resource dependence affects firms’ geographic expansion. In particular, the influence of a firm’s network information can be bounded by the global trade network: when mutual trade dependence between countries is high, the positive effect of network information diminishes. To build a rich dataset. With regard to this objective, we have built part of the dataset on Chinese listed companies’ cross-border M&As during the 2002-2012 period for the current and future studies. In addition, we also developed a survey dataset on Chinese firms’ international strategy and Chinese listed companies’ OFDIs. For the purpose of testing our extended framework, we also developed a databased on the cross-border M&As of U.S. firms and global firms.

14501714.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501714.value: The major findings and research outcome can be seen from the papers developed from this project, which are summarized as below. In a paper (Gaur, Ma, & Ding, 2018, JIBS), adopting a mixed-methods design by combining the empirical findings of a survey of 212 Chinese firms with insights from interviews of senior managers, we find that both perceived government supportiveness and industry unfavorableness have positive relationships with OFDI. We further find that export experience positively moderates these relationships; and inward internationalization negatively moderates the effect of supportiveness, but not that of unfavorableness, on OFDI. In a paper (Zhu, Ma, Sauerwald, & Peng, forthcoming, JOM), using a multilevel analysis of a sample of 12,021 cross-border acquisitions involving 43 home and target countries between 1995 and 2003, we find that collectivism and humane orientation in home countries can exert positive influences on post-acquisition performance. Moreover, such effects are constrained by surrounding formal institutions when these formal institutions are incompatible with the prevailing informal institutions. In a paper (Xia, Ma, Tong, & Li, 2018, GSJ), using a sample of cross-border merger and acquisition (M&A) activities conducted by U.S. publicly listed firms, we find that although M&A experience of both interlocking and joint venture partners affects the focal firm’s global expansion, the effect of interlocking partners is more influential than joint venture partners. We further find that when mutual trade dependence between countries is high, the positive effect of network information from board interlocks diminishes. In a paper (Ma & Lu, 2017, APJM), with a sample of 1233 Chinese listed companies, we find that while business group affiliation has mixed direct effects, it moderates the effects of organizational traits and institutional conditions on firm value. Specifically, group affiliation aggravates old firms’ liability of oldness, but helps mitigate large firms’ liability of bigness. Besides, business group affiliation can reduce the liabilities that institutional voids bring about, as evidenced in its moderating effects on the relationship between regional under-development/industrial restriction and firm value. In a paper (Ma, Ding, & Yuan, 2016, JWB), with data from Chinese entrepreneurial firms, we find that the development of subnational institutional environments in the home country is related to firms’ degree of internationalization. Furthermore, while political capital with low-level governments enhances the effect of subnational institutions on internationalization, political capital with high levels of government has no such moderation effect.

14501714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501714.value: First, supplemental research will make our studies even richer by using different settings. For example, the frameworks developed in papers about Chinese firms’ international strategy (e.g., Gaur et al., 2018; Ma et al, 2016) or group affiliation (Ma & Lu, 2017) can be tested in other contexts; while the frameworks developed in a paper about U.S. firms’ cross-border M&As (Xia et al., 2018) might be tested by using firms from other countries. Second, it is theoretically interesting and practically important to identify the new boundary conditions of the main relationships proposed in these papers. For example, the effects of home country government supportiveness and market unfavorableness (Gaur et al., 2018) might be contingent on other firm-specific factors such as TMT’s political capital (Ma et al., 2016). Third, the new directions are the introduction of new dependent variables by looking at how the independent variables (e.g., supportiveness, unfavorableness, network, partnership, political capital, and home country institutions, etc.) could influence left-hand variables. Future studies may examine the effects on performance at different levels and along various dimensions. New theoretical lens might be adopted to examine these new issues, and additional data will be collected for future studies.

14501714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501714.value: This research project is largely around the drivers and outcome of firms’ cross-border strategies. First, our study of a sample of Chinese firms shows that whereas home country government supportiveness encourages firms to engage in OFDI by helping firms obtain resources and markets, home country industry unfavorableness pushes firms to engage in OFDI to escape. Firms’ international experience portfolio, including export experience and inward internationalization, also alters such relationships. Second, another study shows that U.S. firms can deal with this challenge by accessing relevant information from the M&A experience of interlocking partners and joint venture partners. While the information generated from interlocking partners is even more valuable and important than that of joint venture partners, the M&A experience of partners is particularly valuable for firms contemplating M&A activities in a country with relatively fewer buyer-seller exchange networks with their home country. Third, beyond China and U.S. settings, we further use a large sample of cross-border acquisitions involving 43 home and target countries. Interestingly, we find that collectivism and humane orientation in home countries can exert positive influences on post-acquisition performance. Moreover, such effects are constrained by surrounding formal institutions when these formal institutions are incompatible with the prevailing informal institutions.

14502114.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14502114.value: With the advent of the Internet and other forms of electronic communication, consumers communicate information to others in several ways. For example, they can have an oral chat via Skype, text message via Twitter, use mouse to click “like” on Facebook, or simply use a finger to touch what they want on an iPad or iPhone. In this proposal, we are interested in whether these different ways of communication will influence consumers’ decision making. This program of research will investigate three different aspects of this general concern. First, we will examine the effects of oral and written communications on consumer decision-making. We assume that consumers experience higher self-awareness when they convey messages orally than when they do so in writing. Consequently, they are more sensitive to the consistency of their decisions with social norm and are more likely to make decisions that are considered to be socially desirable in the former case than in the latter. Second, we will be interested in whether consumers will be more likely to accept the persuasion of the messages they mention orally than in writing. We assume that consumers will be more likely to perceive their voice as part of themselves and tend to attribute the messages said by them to their own motive instead of the influence of others. Consequently, if they are induced by others to talk about positive messages about a product, they will be more likely to be persuaded by these messages and choose this product than if they are induced to write those messages. Third, we will examine whether using different digital interfaces will affect the ways of communication which, in turn, may influence consumer decision-making. People respond to questions on a computer by clicking a mouse, but on an iPad by touching their choice. We assume that when exposed to a pair of hedonic and utilitarian food, consumers will spontaneously have an impulse to grab the hedonic food. If they use finger to touch the option on an iPad, this choice behavior mimics the simulated action of grabbing the food and, therefore, may enhance their impulse to take the hedonic food. Consequently, consumers should be more likely to choose hedonic food if they make a choice on an iPad than on a desktop computer. Our work will examine these assumptions and their implications for consumer behavior.

14502114.label: Realisation of objectives
14502114.value: Project 1: The Effect of Communication Channel on Consumer Behavior In this research, we propose that compared to those who discuss a brand by writing, consumers who discuss a brand orally tend to mention the self more frequently and generate more self relevant positive thoughts about the brand. Consequently, in the latter case, consumers feel more personally connected to the brand. This enhanced self-brand connection, in turn, generates downstream consequences such as the increased willingness to wait for a stock-out or the defense against any threat to the brand. We tested our proposed effect in a series of six studies. In study 1, participants either discussed their perception of a favorite brand orally or by writing an online review of it. They reported greater self-brand connection in the former case than in the latter. Studies 2 and 3 then showed moderators and the behavioral consequences of this effect. Those studies demonstrated that although discussing a brand orally could increase self-brand connection than by writing if participants were asked to discuss anything about a brand, this effect disappeared when they were either instructed to take first-person’s perspective while discussing the brand (study 2) or discussed another person’s perception of the brand (study 3). Furthermore, self-brand connection increases both the willingness to wait for a brand when it is out of stock (study 2) and the motivation to defend against an attack on the brand (study 3). Study 4 found that simply instructing communicators to focus on the interaction with the intended recipient mitigates the effect of communication channel on self-brand connection. This result builds on the findings of study 3 to provide convergent evidence for the critical role of interaction focus in driving the observed differences between speakers and writers in the context of brand communication. Study 5 provided further evidence for the mechanism by which communication channel influences self-brand connection. Conceptually replicating study 4, we obtained our usual effects (speech increases both the number of self-brand thoughts and self-brand connection as compared to writing) in default conditions; however, a heightened focus on interacting with the recipient attenuated the differences between speech and writing. Study 6 examined the condition in which discussing a brand by writing can benefit a brand more than by talking. We propose that when people have a goal to persuade others that a brand is good, they tend to construct messages in a more clear structure than when they simply share information about a brand with others. In the former case, since people have more time to deliberate on what they write, they are able to construct message about a brand more carefully and feel more confident about brand attitude. This feeling of certainty about brand attitude can also result in behavioral consequence associated with the brand. This project examines both objectives 1 and 2. In particular, studies 1-5 aimed to achieve the first objective, and study 6 investigates the effect of communication channel on persuasion, which addresses the second objective. We will run more studies in the future to examine the second objective more deeply. Project 2: Computer Interfaces and the “Direct-Touch” Effect: Can iPads Increase the Choice of Hedonic Food? Five studies were done to achieve the third objective. We examined whether consumers will be more likely to select hedonic product if they make a choice on a touch screen than on a desktop computer. In Study 1, participants used either the touch or nontouch interface to choose between two items that were pictorially presented on the screen. This initial study demonstrates our basic effect. Study 2 then showed the moderator of this effect. Specifically, Study 2’s findings suggest that the effect is less likely when the choice button is farther from (vs. closer to) the product picture (H3). Study 2 also shows that mental product interaction with the products mediates the direct-touch effect. In Study 3, we tested the alternative explanation that people deliberate to different extents when making food choices on an iPad versus a desktop. Our results show that the direct touch effect is independent of cognitive load. As such, the results do not support the amount-of-deliberation account. In Study 4, we introduced a new condition in which participants used a stylus to touch the iPad (giving us three computer interface conditions). The findings reveal that we did not obtain the direct-touch effect when participants used a stylus rather than a finger to indicate their decisions on a touch interface. In Study 5, we again show that touching a hedonic product (vs. clicking it with a mouse) on a laptop results in greater mental product interaction and subsequently higher purchase intention. Study 5 also demonstrates that the mere act of reaching toward and touching the choice button (for a purpose unrelated to food choice) can increase mental product interaction and, thus, purchase intention. All five studies support our hypotheses.

14502114.label: Major findings and research outcome
14502114.value: The first project merges insights from the communications literature with that on the self-brand connection to examine a novel question: how does speaking versus writing about a liked brand influence the communicator’s own later reactions to that brand? Our conceptualization argues that because oral communication involves a greater focus on social interaction with the communication recipient than does written communication, oral communicators are more likely to express self-related thoughts than are writers, thereby increasing their self-brand connection (SBC). We also assess the implications of this conceptualization, including the identification of theoretically derived boundary conditions for the speech/writing difference, and the downstream effects of heightened SBC. Results from five studies provide support for our predictions, informing both the basic literature on communications, and the body of work on consumer word of mouth. The second project focuses on the “direct-touch” aspect of touch interfaces, whereby users can touch the screen in an interactive manner. In a series of five studies, they show that a touch interface, such as that provided by an iPad, compared with a nontouch interface, such as that of a desktop computer with a mouse, facilitates the choice of an affect-laden alternative over a cognitively superior one—what the authors call the “direct touch effect.”

14502114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14502114.value: Future research can be done to examine the following issues: (1) show more evidence for how communication channel can influence the effectiveness of persuasion; (2) test whether consumers may use different processing styles to process information when it is presented on a touch (vs. non-touch) screen.

14502114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14502114.value: In the first project, we show that talking about a popular brand may make consumers discuss personal experiences about that brand, whereas writing about a brand may make them discuss the brand in an objective manner. Consequently, people may feel more connected to the brand when they talk about it than write about it. In the second project, we demonstrate that consumers are more likely to choose hedonic food such as cheesecake when they make a choice on a touch-screen such as iPad than on a desktop computer. This occurs because people can directly touch what they want on a touch-screen and may be more likely to engage in impulsive behaviour.

14502214.label: Project Objectives
14502214.value: Develop a two-sector dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model for a small open economy with news shocks, and characterize the impulse response of key macro-variables including output, investment, employment, consumption, saving and the current account. The empirical analysis will provide direct evidence on the relevance of the anticipation effect of news shocks. This project will make contribution to the literature of news shock in business cycle from both in theoretical development and new empirical evidence. Investigate the dynamic effect of news shocks on current account via investment and savings channels in a small open economy setting by using theories and empirical evidence. Provide an alternative approach to test the classical intertemporal approach on the current account by presenting direct evidence that the current account responds to changes in expectations about future output because of news shocks. Our analysis will have important policy implications, particularly for the global imbalance and the current account deficit in the United States. One objective of this study is to provide quantitative analysis on the effects of the recent US energy boom on the US current account.

14502214.label: Realisation of objectives
14502214.value: This project has achieved all the proposed objectives. It explores the effect of news shocks in open economies using worldwide giant oil and gas discoveries as a directly observable measure of news shocks about future output ̶ the delay between a discovery and production is on average 4 to 6 years. We first extend the Jaimovich and Rebelo (2008) small open economy model to include two sectors, where one sector is a resource sector with oil discoveries. We use this model to develop the macroeconomic predictions on the key macro-variables including output, investment, employment, consumption, saving and the current account for news about oil discoveries. In the empirical work, we construct a net present value (NPV) of the oil discovery as a percentage of GDP at the time of the discovery. We then estimate a dynamic panel distributed lag model over a sample covering the period 1970-2012 for up to 180 countries. Our empirical estimates of the effects of oil discoveries on key macroeconomic variables are largely consistent with the predictions of our model. In the years immediately following the discoveries, the current account decreases significantly as investment rises and the saving rate declines. Five years after the discovery, the average effect of giant oil discoveries on the current account turns positive and significant, as output and saving rise and investment declines. A peak effect is reached about eight years following the discovery after which the effect of giant oil discoveries gradually declines. Interestingly, employment rates decline after the news arrives and remain below normal for over 10 years. The unique timing characteristic of oil discoveries provides a methodological contribution to the identification problem of news shocks and the associated anticipation effects. Standard approaches in this literature rely on VARs or DSGE models, both of which require many untested identification assumptions and are thus subject to debate. Exploiting the natural lags between giant oil discoveries and the subsequent increase in production provides a unique way to directly measure news shocks about future output increase. In turn, that allows us to conduct a quasi-natural experiment that does not rely on identification using VARs or parametric DSGE models. Our approach provides direct evidence on how news shocks affect macroeconomic variables. This project also provides direct evidence for the classic intertemporal approach to the current account, by presenting a statistically and economically significant anticipation effect on the current account through both the saving and investment channels following the announcement of a giant oil discovery, supporting the view that expectations can be an important driving force for the current account dynamics. Our estimation results also shed some light on the effect of the so-called “shale revolution” on the U.S. current account. The regression estimates imply that a hypothetical discovery equal to the size of proven reserves (all considered at once) in U.S. unconventional energy would lead at its peak to about a 0.1 percent of GDP increase in the U.S. current account balance, and the long-run effect is negligible. The effect is small reflecting in part the relatively small size of those oil and gas discoveries in comparison to the size of the US economy but also partly due to the (negative) anticipation effect.

14502314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14502314.value: 在过去的20年，全球价值链在世界经济变得日渐重要。生产的全球化和细分化已经实质性地改变了国际贸易和资本流动。目前，大多数关于全球价值链的研究聚焦于它如何影响贸易计算和贸易政策。相对而言，研究全球价值链对宏观经济和全球经济的工作比较少。在本课题中，我计划把全球价值链引入一般的国际经济周期的模型。特别是，我将强调国家在全球价值链中的不对角色，并分析这种不对称如何影响外部冲击的国际传导机制。这个包含全球价值链的分析框架可以为我们了解全球经常项目不平衡和国际经济周期提供新思维。有鉴于中国经济的重要性，我也将定量研究全球价值链对中国经济的影响。不少关于中国经济的课题，也可以在这个框架下展开分析和研究。比如，全球价值链是否夸大中美贸易的不平衡？全球价值链是否影响中国的实际汇率？

14502314.label: Realisation of objectives
14502314.value: This project is motivated by the fast development of global production network with increasingly more intensive intermediate goods trade. More and more countries participate in the global value chain. The participation rate in global production increases from 43% in 1995 to 55% in 2007. Even after the financial crisis, there is still half of the world trade involved in the global production. How does the global value China affect the world economy? In this project, we intend to achieve three objects, the first and the most important one is how changes in trade patterns, in particular, greater trade integration through global value chain, lead economies to comove more? The second and third objects are to investigate if the position of countries along global value chain also matters for the global imbalance between China and advanced economies, like the US. A growing literature has studied the relationship between greater engagement in global production network and business cycle synchronization. However, the existing studies are silent on one important feature on global production: countries or sectors are specialized in different positions. For two countries or sectors, even they have same bilateral trade relationship captured by either value-added trade intensity, gross trade intensity or production sharing, their different positions could also matter for business cycle comovement or trade flow since the transmission of shocks along production value chain takes the time or needs inventory adjustment. In this paper, we first construct a distance measure based on an existing position measure: the upstreamness measure of a sector proposed by Antras and Chor (2013) and Fally (2012) and then apply it to a reduced-form panel framework. This measure captures position explicitly based on forward production linkage and enables us to focus on supply shocks' upstream transmission. To obtain country-level position measure, we weight sectoral-level position by the share of each sector's export in total gross export or the share of each sector's gross output in total gross output. The distance is defined as the absolute difference between two countries/sectors' positions. Data is taken from World Input-Output Database(WIOD) for 40 countries and 35 industries. World Input-Output Table from WIOD includes four-dimensional data information indexed by exporter, importer, sector-pair which allows us to examine the effect of distance from different dimensions. The major findings are reported in section 6.1. Our project is related to several strands of literature. The first strand of literature focuses on measurement of the global value chain. We first adopt measure developed by Fally (2012) and Antras and Chor (2013) in order to consider both intermediate goods and final goods production. The value-added based measure developed by Wang et al. (2017) is also considered for robustness check. The second strand of literature examines the effect of different degree of globalization and trade integration on business cycle comovement. Compared with existing literature, our research identifies a new channel through which trade linkage affect business cycle comovement - distance. We also focus on vertical structure but emphasize the role of distance, by separating distance and input intensity in vertical linkage and treating distance as an alternative mechanism for explaining business cycle correlation. Intuitively, when a shock hits an economy and spills over to other countries through production linkage, it has to go through all the production steps to arrive the impacting country/sector. The impact of shock could be weakened during transmission along the global value chain due to inventory adjustment, time lag or simply the use of intermediate goods. That is the moderation of the impact of the shock increases with the distance along the value chain. For different country pair/sector pair with same intermediate goods intensity, if their distance is longer, their business cycle might be less correlated. More importantly, this logic can be also applied to show that the distance matters for bilateral current account imbalance. For example, in our sample, in terms of upstreamness, China ranks the fourth which is far away from the final demand while the US is very close to the final demand. Finally, by emphasizing the role of distance, our study contributes to the common shock versus transmission mechanism debate and provides a guidance on the modelling of production structure and comovement. Ignoring the shock transmission along production stages in theoretical models could lead to misunderstanding about business cycle and global imbalance.

14502314.label: Major findings and research outcome
14502314.value: In this project, we first construct a distance measure based on an existing position measure: the upstreamness measure proposed by Antras, et.al (2012) and Fally (2012) and then apply it into a reduced-form panel framework. We document several stylized facts. (1) At the country level, resource-rich countries are in more upstream position. Asian developing countries are also in upstream position while European countries and US are basically downstream. At the sector level, the mining sector is in the most upstream position, followed by manufacturing, agriculture, and service. (2) The variation of distance is also large at country level and across different subsamples: North-North, South-South, and North-South. North-North sample on average has the shortest distance and largest output correlation. (3) Distance within the same sector is shorter than that between different sectors. We then examine the effect of distance at both country and sector level. For country-level analysis, we find that, in a panel framework and after controlling for country-pair fixed effect and year fixed effect, the distance along global value chain has a significantly negative effect on business cycle co-movement. That is, shorter distance increases output correlation. This finding is robust when different samples and alternative measures of output correlation are used. Our estimate is also economically significant. In the baseline regression, our estimated coefficient implies that if we increase the distance from its 10th percentile to 90th percentile, holding all other variables at their means, output correlation increases 0.116. This negative effect is still significant if we drop the financial crisis period. In particular, we find that the negative effect is larger in times of financial crisis than that in normal times. Moreover, we find that ceteris paribus, when one country is in relative upstream position, it leads business cycle. Finally, we test the effect of distance at sector level controlling exporter, importer, country-sector, country pair and sector pair fixed effect. We also find a negative relationship between sectoral distance and output correlation, however, the magnitude of the effect of distance is much smaller. Furthermore, we examine the effect of distance on output correlation within-sector (same sector across countries) and cross-sector (different sectors across countries). We find that the within-sector effect is much stronger than cross-sector effect. we have written a working paper including the above findings. The paper has been presented at a few conferences, currently is invited to submit to the Journal of Money, Credit, and Banking, which is a very decent academic journal in Macroeconomics.

14502314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14502314.value: This project can be extended in a few dimensions. First, we find robust evidence about the distances of countries along global value chains and international business cycle. Following the current research, we can think about how to incorporate the global value chain in a theoretical framework. Secondly, we can also investigate empirically whether the distance or position along global value chain can help explain other international macroeconomic puzzles.

14502314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14502314.value: Global value chains have been increasingly important in the global trade and production. Each country plays a different role along the global value chain. This project investigates the effect of distance along global value chain on business cycle comovement at both country and sector level using a comprehensive cross-country input-output data. We first show that there is large variation across countries and sectors. Resource-rich countries and mining sector are in the most upstream position. Asian countries located in more upstream position while European and US are in relatively downstream position. We then exploit the variation and show that the distance along global value chain has a significantly negative effect on business cycle comovement. The closer the two countries/sectors' distance, the more comoved their output is. At the sector level, we find that the negative effect between distance and comovement is stronger within sector than that cross sectors. These findings thus offer new insights regarding the international transmission of shocks and global imbalance.

14502514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14502514.value: Incidental similarities are chance similarities between individuals which create a sense of association between two people. Although incidental similarities can be triggered by trivial cues such as a shared family name or birthplace, they can have nontrivial consequences. For example, chance similarities to another person can increase compliance with a request to help this person (Burger et al. 2004) and, if the individual is a salesperson, can increase purchase intentions (Jiang et al. 2010). Existing research therefore suggests that incidental similarities lead to favorable reactions to the similar other. We propose that the effects of incidental similarities are not invariably favorable. Incidental similarities can elicit unfavorable effects, and can make an otherwise disinterested observer become involved in an exchange between a stranger and a company that (s)he merely witnessed. For example, a service failure involves the service provider and the suffering customer. From the perspective of an individual observing the failure, the nature of the effect of incidental similarities would depend on whether one feels a sense of association with the provider or the customer. Imagine a situation in which someone observes a customer being told that a table he had reserved is actually not available. If the observer notices that customer’s tie happens to be the same color as his own, he may be disposed to view the situation from the customer’s perspective and blame the provider for the failure. However, if the observer notices from the provider’s name tag that they happen to have the same surname, he may feel more similar to the provider and attributing him less responsibility for the failure. We also suspect this pattern will be stronger for observers with interdependent (vs. independent) self-construal, given they are more sensitive to interpersonal relationships. This is the first research to investigate the deleterious effects of incidental similarity in a service failure context. We attempt to illuminate the process through which incidental similarities can affect attribution and evaluation. We delineate two mechanisms through which the sense of connectedness can affect attribution: 1) a disposition to forgive if one feels a bond with the person at fault (the provider) and 2) empathy if one feels a bond with the person who is not at fault (the suffering customer). Our findings will not only contribute to an understanding of the effect of incidental similarities on perception and judgment but also will offer managerial insights into service failure and recovery. 人與人之間的巧合相似(例如相同姓氏，相同生日日期) 會令他們產生一種聯繫。以往研究指出這種微不足道的聯繫往往帶來意想不到的正面影響。例如人們大多願意幫助和他們有巧合相似的陌生人。亦會傾向願意購買和他們有巧合相似的售貨員的商品。 我們的研究提出這種巧合相似不一定會有正面影響，特別是在服務失誤的情況下，因為當中牽涉服務員及消費者兩方便。假如旁觀者發現他和那位不認識的消費者帶同一款顏色的領帶，這種巧合可能會讓他傾向怪責服務員。但若果他發現服務員的名牌寫和他同樣的姓氏，他可能傾向不怪責服務員。我們估計這情況會在相互文化的地域比獨立文化的地域更顯著。

14502514.label: Major findings and research outcome
14502514.value: Major findings: Observers’ (i.e., potential customers’) reactions to a service failure and their attributions of responsibility for its occurrence can depend on fortuitous characteristics of the protagonists that happen to draw their attention. Four field and laboratory experiments show that when observers have an incidental similarity to one of the persons involved in a service failure (the customer or the service provider), their attention is drawn to this protagonist, often leading them to construe the situation from this person’s perspective and consequently to blame the protagonist less for the negative event they observe. However, when an incidentally similar protagonist is rude or has an undesirable personal characteristic (i.e., obesity), observers’ greater attention to him or her increases their attributions of responsibility to him or her rather than decreasing it. These opposing effects of incidental similarity on attributions influence not only observers’ evaluations of the persons involved in the situation they observe but also their willingness to patronize the establishment. These effects occur both when observers actually witness a conflict offline and when they consider it online on the basis of reviews. The manuscript with the above findings was successfully published at the top tier marketing journal, namely, Journal of Consumer Research. We also presented the findings at three international conferences and one invited research seminar. Publication: Wan, Lisa C. and Robert S. 14502514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14502514.value: We think that more research works can be done on the topic of the role of observers in services consumption. For example, our conclusions assume that observers are not only incidentally similar to the persons they observe but also evaluate the similarity favorably. Individuals with a strong need for uniqueness may react negatively to indications they are similar to another. Moreover, both individual and cultural differences might exist in the general disposition to think about oneself in relation to others (Markus and Kitayama 1991). Participants in the present research were Asians, who may be particularly sensitive to the similarities between themselves and others and inclined to value social connectedness. Although the effects of incidental similarity have been identified in research on Western cultural samples as well (e.g., Burger et al. 2004), this difference could be a consideration in evaluating the generalizability of our findings.

14502514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14502514.value: “What a coincidence!” We have all experienced that mysterious sensation triggered by an unexpected connection with a person. This research suggests that these connections can affect observers of service failures to assign blame of the events to the provider or the customer. Our results indicated that the participants having the same last name as the customer would blame the service provider for the service failure, whereas those with the same last name as the service provider would blame the customer instead. Interestingly, this tendency will be changed if the service provider (or the customer) displaying a negative or undesirable quality (e.g., rudeness or obesity). In such scenario, participants sharing the incidental similarity with the provider were found to blame the service provider rather than the customer for the failure of service. This is because sharing an incidental similarity with the provider will increase an observer’s attention on the provider’s negative or undesirable characteristics, the observer will increase their blame on the provider in this case. Customer online complaints have increased 800% over the years between 2014 and 2015 (Causon 2015), capture many viewers’ attention. This research offers important implications for consumers’ reactions to the information conveyed on online websites.

14502814.value: Examine whether the finding of the audit fee premium for industry specialization in Goodwin and Wu (2013) holds in the match design employed by Minutti-Meza (2013). Examine whether partner-level industry specialization is associated with higher audit quality proxies, using both the match and fixed-effect model methods.

14502814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14502814.value: Auditor industry specialization (hereafter AIS) is an important topic in auditing research. Recently, Minutti-Meza (2013) argues that the auditor’s within-industry market share, a commonly-used proxy for AIS, could lead to the classic correlated-omitted-variable problem: client characteristics are correlated with the AIS variable and with audit quality proxies and audit fees. To address this potential problem, Minutti-Meza (2013) employs two rigorous research methods. The first involves matching clients of specialist and non-specialist auditors on determinants of clients’ choice of specialist auditors, and the second is the inclusion of client fixed-effects in models to control for unobservable client characteristics correlated with auditor choice. He demonstrates that there are no significant differences in audit quality proxies and audit fees between specialist and non-specialist auditors using both methods. Minutti-Meza’s (2013) study casts doubt on the validity of the within-industry market share specialization measure and challenges prior findings on the effects of AIS. In a related study, we (Goodwin and Wu 2013) show that industry expert partners charge higher audit fees and that AIS measured at the firm/office level is not associated with a fee premium. Most important, our finding of a partner-level fee premium for AIS holds when we control for client fixed effects. Since Minutti-Meza (2013) uses firm/office-level data and a client fixed-effect model as one of his research methods, our evidence suggests an alternative explanation for Minutti-Meza’s (2013) finding: the insignificant difference between specialist and non-specialist auditors could be due to the use of firm/office-level data, which are noisier in measuring AIS than are partner-level data. We propose two extensions to the partner-level specialization analysis. First, we will use Minutti-Meza’s (2013) matching method, which relaxes the linearity assumption of the fixed-effect model and accommodates time-varying client characteristics in explaining the outcome variables. Second, we will examine whether the audit quality of the clients of partner industry specialists is higher than that of non-specialists, an issue not yet examined in the abovementioned studies. The proposed study will shed light on the appropriateness of measuring AIS by within-industry market share. The partner-level evidence on how AIS influences audit quality will also advance our understanding of the nature of AIS. 審計師行業專長化(以下簡稱AIS)是審計研究中重要的課題。近來Minutti-Meza (2013)認為審計師行業內市場份額這一AIS常用的替代變數會導致遺漏變數偏誤：客戶特徵與AIS、審計品質替代變數及審計費用皆相關聯。為解決這一問題，Minutti-Meza (2013) 使用了兩種更嚴格的研究方法。一是將專家審計師的客戶與非專家審計師的客戶按選擇行業專長審計師的決定因素相配對；二是利用客戶的固定效應模型以控制客戶無法觀察、但與審計師選擇相關聯的特性。在這兩種方法下，他驗證了專家與非專家審計師在審計品質替代變數及審計收費下無顯著差別。Minutti-Meza (2013)這一研究質疑了行業內市場份額這一度量方法及以往關於AIS效應發現的正確性。 在相關的研究中，我們(Goodwin and Wu 2014)發現，擁有行業專長的合夥人審計收費更高，並且以事務所/分所層面計量的AIS變數與審計費溢價並無關聯。更重要的是，在控制了客戶的固定效應之後，我們這一合夥人層面上的發現依然存在。由於Minutti-Meza (2013)使用了事務所/分所層面的資料，且固定效應模型為其研究方法之一，我們的證據為Minutti-Meza (2013)的發現提供了一個替代性的解釋：專家與非專家審計師之間的無顯著差異可能是使用了比合夥人層面的資料更不準確的事務所/分所層面資料所致。 我們提議對合夥人層面的資料進行兩方面的拓展。首先，我們將採納Minutti-Meza (2013) 的配對方法，這放寬了固定效應模型中的線性假定，並可利用時變的客戶特徵來解釋後果變數。其次，我們將考察有著行業專長的合夥人在審計品質上是否優於其他合夥人，這一問題前述研究尚未涉及。本研究計畫書將會對以行業內市場份額度量AIS恰當與否提供見解。在合夥人層面上，AIS如何影響審計品質亦有助於我們理解AIS之本質。

14502814.label: Realisation of objectives
14502814.value: As noted in the previous Progress Report, we found a competing paper by Aobdia et al. (2016)*, who use proprietary data provided by the PCAOB† to examine partner-level industry expertise. Our proposed research overlaps with their paper to a large extent, and our findings are also consistent with theirs: industry experts earn significantly higher audit fee premiums but their audit quality is not better than others. Also, based on information reported by audit firms to the PCAOB, Aobdia et al.'s (2016) data are richer than ours. Specifically, their data include the average rate per hour and the number of audit hours for audit engagements. The granular data offer additional insight into the economics of fee premiums for industry expertise.‡ Given the competing nature of Aobdia et al.'s (2016) paper and the advantages of their data, it is likely that the academic value of our research would be discounted by reviewers or editors of high-quality journals. After careful consideration, we decided to overhaul the whole research project. Specifically, we now examine how auditor specialization in initial public offering (IPO) auditing business shapes IPO-audit practices. The change is motivated by the followings. 1. Although auditor specialization encompasses many dimensions, auditing research along this line has been dominantly concentrated on industry specialization. The paper will be the first to document auditor specialization by the types of auditing business. 2. IPO auditing engagements are more demanding than seasoned ones. Going public involves a host of complex financial-reporting issues and exposes auditors to higher risks. Meanwhile, IPO auditors are often under time constraint to complete the audits due to the clients' IPO market timing. 3. By turning IPO firms into long-term clients, IPO audit business can be audit firms' growth engine. Therefore, audit firms have strong incentives to develop IPO-auditing expertise. We attempt to answer the following research questions: 1. Do audit firms strategically assign partners with richer IPO-audit experience to perform IPO audits? 2. Do partners with greater IPO expertise provide better-quality IPO audits? 3. Do investors perceive IPO audits performed by partners with greater IPO expertise to be of higher quality? 4. Do partners with greater IPO expertise command an IPO audit fee premium? 5. Does IPO auditing expertise contribute to a functionally more efficient stock market? Now our research is fundamentally different from Aobdia et al. (2016). In fact, the revised study is even more exciting and promising—by looking at specialization by the types of audit engagements, we develop a new direction for auditor specialization literature (e.g., researchers can examine specialization in M&A, corporate restricting or other audit services). After careful data analysis, we find affirmative evidence for the above research questions. We have also written up the paper and submitted it to Journal of Accounting & Economics. Now the paper is under first-round R&R at this journal. * Aobdia, D., S. Siddiqui and A.G. Vinelli. 2016. Does engagement partner perceived expertise matter? Evidence from the U.S. operations of the Big 4 audit firms. Working paper, available at: http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2840332. † The PCAOB (Public Company Accounting Oversight Board), created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, is an organization overseeing the audits of public companies in the U.S. ‡ Specifically, Aobdia et al. (2016) find that both the average rate and the number of audit hours contribute to the expert-related fee premiums and interpret this finding as: a client is willing to pay a higher billing rate for access to an industry specialist partner; meanwhile, such a partner is also better able to shield his or her engagement team from client-driven or audit-firm driven time pressure, leading to a higher number of audit hours.

14502814.label: Major findings and research outcome
14502814.value: Consistent with the "learning-by-doing" knowledge acquisition mode in the auditing literature, we measure an partner's IPO expertise by his/her IPO auditing experience. We argue that engagement auditors with more IPO-audit experience should have a better understanding of IPO process and specific company's incentives and capacities related to financial reporting, and thus are better able to apply relevant accounting standards and required audit procedures, and make more accurate judgments and estimates during the IPO auditing process. Moreover, specialist auditors may be more independent to protect their reputational capital, which also results in higher-quality audited financial statements. We observe that audit firms tend to assign partners with more IPO experience, but not necessarily greater industry expertise, to IPO audit engagements. Partners' IPO expertise has a significantly positive effect on IPO audit quality. IPO companies audited by partners with deeper IPO expertise report lower discretionary accruals and are less likely to restate earnings downwards subsequently. IPO companies also benefit from hiring partners with more IPO expertise, as evidenced by the significantly positive association between partners' IPO expertise and open-market valuation of earnings. We also find that IPO expert partners charge 22.3% higher IPO audit fees than non-expert partners, all else being equal. Recognizing that there could be endogenous matching between IPO company characteristics and partners IPO expertise, we perform both two-stage least-squares (2SLS) and the propensity score matching (PSM) analyses. For 2SLS, we use the cross-region variation in the development of the public accounting profession (supply side) and the time-series of IPO activity level (demand side) as the instrumental variables. For PSM, we align audits performed by experts with those by non-experts by observable client and auditor characteristics. Our major findings are robust to both analyses. We have finished writing up the paper. Now the paper is under first-round R&R at Journal of Accounting & Economics.

14502814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14502814.value: The reviewer comments that "I found the paper to be generally well written and the setting is very interesting." He/she suggests that we can expand the scope of our investigation by further examining "dynamic aspect of the research setting." Following the reviewer's suggestion, we will include the following new analyses: (a) how audit firms coped with the lack of IPO expert partners in the early stage of capital market development; and (b) how the accumulation of IPO expertise helps to develop a well-functioning stock market by allocating capital to high-quality IPO firms. We are now intently revising the paper to strive for a favorable outcome at Journal of Accounting & Economics.

14502814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14502814.value: IPO audits are much more challenging than regular annual audits of public companies. We thus posit that partners with different levels of specialized IPO knowledge provide differentiated IPO audit services. We use Chinese data to test this supposition because the large size of the IPO market in China incentivizes auditors to specialize in IPO audits. Based on more than 1,600 IPOs during 1999–2012, we find that IPO companies audited by partners with greater IPO expertise are less likely to inflate earnings in the IPO prospectus, and their earnings are valued higher by the investors. In addition, IPO expert partners earn an audit fee premium. These findings support the hypotheses that partners build up their IPO audit expertise through leading IPO audits and such expertise enables them to provide higher-quality and more valuable IPO-audit services.

14502914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14502914.value: From the perspective of fiscal discipline, the importance of balanced budget rules is indisputable among both academicians and policymakers. Recent lively examples are the debates of fiscal cliff and debt ceilings of the U.S. economy. However, economists have reservation on balanced budget rules due to both their procyclical nature and the possibility of generating equilibrium indeterminacy. However, the existing literature arrives at this general conclusion in a real environment where monetary policy is absent and all agents are identical. Since the financial tsunami in 2008, central banks of developed countries have been active in pursuing easy monetary policy or quantitative easing together with balanced-budget fiscal rules. Also, with heterogeneous agents, different balanced-budget tax rules are expected to have different impact on them. Thus, this proposal reexamines the stability nature of different balanced-budget rules under alternative monetary settings of the macroeconomy when agents are heterogeneous. The findings of the project should have important implications for policymakers. 從財政紀律的角度看，平衡預算規則的重要性是不容置疑的。近期活生生的例子，首選美國經濟的財政懸崖和債務上限的辯論。 然而，由於其順週期的性質和產生不確定性均衡的可能性，經濟學家對平衡預算規則是有保留的 。然而，現有的文獻並未有考慮貨幣政策的影響 。自 2008 年金融海嘯，發達國家的中央銀行一直活躍在追求寬鬆的貨幣政策，其對平衡預算財政規則的影響不容忽視。因此，這項研究建議重新審視在不同預算平衡規則下，替代貨幣設置的宏觀經濟的穩定性質 。專案的調查結果應該對政策制定者有重要參考價值。

14502914.label: Realisation of objectives
14502914.value: We have already completed the first three objectives in the last two reporting periods. We are able to finish the last objective in this reporting period. For the research outcome of the second objective, we have mentioned in the progress report that it was under review at the Pacific Economic Review. Finally after a few revisions which are done in the current period, we are able to get it accepted for publication. For the newly completed objective, we are able to link the balanced-budget tax rules to the home production sector of the macroeconomy. We show that the presence of home production, which is a nontaxed sector, reinforces the intratemporal and intertemporal substitution effects of balanced-budget rules. As a result, it strengthens the destabilization effect of factor income taxes and weakens the stabilization effect of consumption taxes. Moreover, our calibration shows that the number of OECD countries’ tax-rate combinations that fall into the instability region rises when home goods account for a larger share of aggregate consumption, and hence persistent cycles can easily occur following a fundamental shock or a sunspot shock. The research outcome is just published in the Journal of Macroeconomics in 2018.

14502914.label: Major findings and research outcome
14502914.value: The major findings of this project are published in three academic refereed journals. 1. We examine the effects of constant-rate factor taxation on macroeconomic stability in a finance constrained economy. Our focus is on how the degree of factor substitution, as measured by the elasticity of factor substitution (EOS) in production, affects different balanced-budget tax rules. Analytically, we show that indeterminacy can occur under capital income taxation only when the EOS is very low, whereas indeterminacy under labor income taxation is not subject to the EOS restriction. This finding is robust when we tax all of the factor incomes with equal rates. Thus, in terms of macroeconomic stability, taxing capital income is preferred to taxing labor income. This is published in the Journal of Mathematical Economics. 2. In a real macroeconomic model, it is well established that a balanced-budget rule based on consumption tax can rule out indeterminacy. We show, both analytically and numerically, that such a balanced-budget rule induces indeterminacy and, hence, aggregate instability in a standard one-sector cash-in-advance economy. From a policy perspective, our results raise possible concerns that balanced-budget rules with endogenous consumption tax could have destabilizing effects under the current over-easy monetary environment. This is forthcoming in the Pacific Economic Review. 3. We examine the instability property of balanced-budget taxation on factor income and consumption in a two-sector real business cycle model with home production. We show that the presence of home production, which is a nontaxed sector, reinforces the intratemporal and intertemporal substitution effects of balanced-budget rules. As a result, it strengthens the destabilization effect of factor income taxes and weakens the stabilization effect of consumption taxes. Moreover, our calibration shows that the number of OECD countries’ tax-rate combinations that fall into the instability region rises when home goods account or a larger share of aggregate consumption, and hence persistent cycles can easily occur following a fundamental shock or a sunspot shock. This is published in the Journal of Macroeconomics.

14502914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14502914.value: To complete the last objective, we examine the instability property of balanced-budget taxation on factor income and consumption in a two-sector real business cycle model with home production. There we have not consider the marketization of the home services which is very common in a lot of developed economies. So we plan to extend the analysis to investigate how the stability effects of the balanced budget taxation can be affected by the size of the home sector, as well as the extent of the marketization of it. Some preliminary calculation has shown that the effects under marketization of the home sector can be very different from our research outcomes found in the Journal of Macroeconomics. we plan to write up a GRF grant proposal to investigate the relation between marketization, home production and economic stability.

14502914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14502914.value: From the perspective of fiscal discipline, the importance of balanced budget rules is indisputable among both academicians and policymakers. However, economists have reservation on balanced budget taxation rules because it has been shown theoretically that their presence is likely to generate more fluctuations. Nevertheless, the existing literature arrives at this general conclusion under some specific conditions. In this project, we have highlighted three important conditions: the absence of monetary policy, all agents are identical and there is only a single sector. Since the financial tsunami in 2008, central banks of developed countries have been active in pursuing easy monetary policy or quantitative easing together with balanced-budget fiscal rules. Also, with heterogeneous agents such as they have different income sources for taxation, different balanced-budget tax rules are expected to have different impact on them. Finally, when there is an additional home service sector, the between-sector allocation in response to the tax rules can lead to very different equilibrium outcomes. Our findings deliver the important message that balanced budget rules do not necessarily generate more economic fluctuations. The outcomes depend on many economic factors such as the financial and demographic structure of the economy.

14503114.label: Project Objectives
14503114.value: Introduce a variable of country-specific institutional environment to the relation between product market competition and financial reporting quality, thereby a new dimension to the information channel through which product market competition affects financial reporting quality. Build upon economic theories and evidence from prior research to analyze how country-specific institutional environment could lead product market competition to have a positive impact on firms’ financial reporting quality in countries with strong institutional environment but a negative impact in countries with weak institutional environment. 3.
