16101614.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101614.value: A revised manuscript is currently under review in Nature Communications. The original version of this manuscript has been deposited in bioRxiv [Cao Z, Hao Y, Lee Y Y, et al. Dietary fatty acids promote lipid droplet diversity through seipin enrichment in an ER subdomain. bioRxiv, 2018: 424663.]. Our manuscript reports the first characterization of the C. elegans seipin ortholog SEIP-1 and the conserved SEIP-1-enriched ER subdomain. Using single-copy transgenes and CRISPR mediated genome editing, we demonstrated that SEIP-1 is targeted to peri-LD cages that surround a subset of LDs. SEIP-1 promoted the expansion of associated LDs. Remarkably, human seipin was also targeted to peri-LD cages when it was expressed from a rescuing single-copy transgene in seip-1(-) worms. Heterologous expression of SEIP-1 in COS7 mammalian cells revealed similar cage structures upon oleic acid loading. Accordingly, SEIP-1 marked only a subset of LDs and supported their expansion. Ultrastructural analysis of peri-LD cages confirmed their identity as tubular ER subdomains. Genetic and dietary supplementation experiments further revealed the dependence of SEIP-1 targeting on polyunsaturated C18:3n6 (gamma linolenic acid, GLA) and bacterial cyclopropane fatty acids (CFAs). Attenuation of phosphatidylcholine synthesis enhances SEIP-1 targeting to peri-LD cages, possibly by reshaping the membrane lipidome on LDs or at the ER-LD contact sites. The effect of monounsaturated fatty acids on membrane fluidity is well documented. In contrast, the ability of GLA and CFAs in inducing phospholipid packing defects and membrane tensions have long been overlooked. Our data provides new insights on the specific requirement of polyunsaturated GLA and CFAs in sculpting a membrane environment that favors SEIP-1 engagement and LD expansion, which could not be readily studied in other models. CFAs are abundant in bacteria. Intriguingly, fatty acids harbouring cyclopropane rings, presumably from dietary source and gut microbiome, were also detected in human adipose tissue and plasma. Recent studies have clearly established a causal link of microbial metabolites in shaping the host lipid metabolism. However, the role of CFAs and their derivatives from the gut microbiome has not been previously studied. Our work is the first to show how CFAs can modulate cellular fat storage in eukaryotes. It provides a new framework for studying host-microbiome crosstalk.

16101614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101614.value: Our data has not yet established a direct causal link on how GLA and CFAs modulate the proper targeting of SEIP-1. Structural analysis will be necessary to gain further mechanistic insights. We propose to purify SEIP-1 in its native lipid environment. Native purification of SEIP-1 from a heterologous system (i.e. mammalian cells) could be performed. In heterologous COS7 cells, SEIP-1 was dispersed in the general ER network prior to oleic acid loading. Upon OA loading, SEIP-1 was sorted into tubular membranes adjacent to expanding LDs, which is distinct from the general ER membrane. Given the functional and morphological conservation of these cages, we expect that evolutionarily conserved peri-LD components can be identified through proteomic comparison between SEIP-1(+) and SEIP-1(-) LDs. We have established an immunoprecipitation-based method to separate SEIP-1(+) LDs from SEIP-1(-) LDs. We will proceed with the proteomic analysis and verify the candidates. We aim at identifying separate sets of conserved proteins that define SEIP-1(+) and SEIP-1(-) LDs. Our ultimate goal is to determine how LD heterogeneity correlates with LD cargoes and functions.

16101614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101614.value: In healthy individuals, the adipose tissue plays a crucial role in sequestering toxic lipid species from vital organs, thus offering protection against metabolic diseases. The development of adipose tissue involves complex reorganization of structures within dedicated fat cells. One of the key steps is the progressive formation of a giant lipid droplet, an organelle that contains neutral fat. In humans, mutations in the BSCL2 gene severely retard adipose tissue development, and cause congenital generalized lipodystrophy. The BSCL2 gene encodes seipin, a conserved protein that has been proposed to regulate lipid droplet formation and expansion. However, a consensus mechanism by which seipin promote fat storage is still lacking. In our report, we demonstrate in C. elegans and mammalian cells that seipin is enriched in subdomains of the endoplasmic reticulum, in close proximity of lipid droplets. Using genetic and dietary supplementation approaches, we further show that the localization of seipin is dependent on polyunsaturated fatty acids and microbial fatty acids that can be obtained from the diet. Mis-localization of seipin attenuates its ability to support lipid droplet expansion. Therefore, our work provides new insights into how dietary fatty acids can modulate cellular fat storage by steering key proteins to the right destination.

16101714.value: Extend our understanding of the link between NAADP-induced, TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release and the generation of Ca2+ signals in PMNs and SMCs during myogenesis in intact zebrafish embryos. 16101714.label: Realisation of objectives
16101714.value: Over the duration of the grant reporting period, we have extended our understanding of the link between nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP)-induced, two-pore channel 2 (TPC2)-mediated Ca2+ release and the generation of Ca2+ signals in the development and maturation of early neuromuscular activity in intact zebrafish embryos. Before the start of the project, we had characterized essential inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) and ryanodine receptor (RyR)-mediated Ca2+ signals generated during the differentiation of skeletal slow muscle cells (SMCs) in zebrafish embryos (Cheung et al., 2011). Thus, in the new project, our aim was to investigate the Ca2+ signaling pathways involved in SMC development in further detail and extend our focus to include the development of primary motor neurons (PMNs). At the start of the project, we showed that in addition to IP3R and RyR in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), TPC2 in the lysosomes also plays a crucial role in the differentiation and development of SMCs. Using our transgenic line of zebrafish that expresses the bioluminescent Ca2+ reporter, aequorin, specifically in the skeletal muscle, morpholino (MO)-based knock-down of TPC2 resulted in a dramatic attenuation of the Ca2+ signals and a significant disruption of myofibrilogenesis, whereas use of TPCN2-MO and a TPCN2 mRNA partially rescued the Ca2+ signaling signature and myogenic morphology. Embryos treated with trans-ned-19 or bafilomycin A1, a specific NAADP receptor inhibitor and vacuolar-type H+ ATPase inhibitor, respectively, also displayed a similar disruption of SMC Ca2+ signaling. TPC2, and the lysosomes were shown via immunohistochemistry and confocal laser scanning microscopy to be localized in perinuclear and cytoplasmic domains of SMCs, coincident with patterns of IP3R and RyR expression. These data indicated that TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release from lysosomes might act as a trigger to initiate the SR-mediated Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release essential for SMC myofibrilogenesis. This work was published in International Journal of Developmental Biology (Kelu et al. 2015). As, during the course of our project, the validity of using MOs to knockdown gene expression became a somewhat controversial topic due to their potential off-target effects, we also developed a line of mutant zebrafish where TPCN2 was knocked out using CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing. We demonstrated that use of this TPCN2 mutant line or inhibition of TPC2 with bafilomycin A1 or trans-ned-19, confirmed our MO-based data as they both also lead to a significant attenuation of SMC differentiation. For this reason, we continued to use the TPCN2-MO to knockdown TPC2 in a number of subsequent experiments. For example, we demonstrated that when morphants were treated with IP3/BM or caffeine, agonists of the IP3R and RyR, respectively, many aspects of myofibrillogenesis and myotomal patterning, as well as the Ca2+ signals generated in the SMCs were rescued. We mainly used normal confocal microscopy of fluorescently-labeled embryos or isolated SMCs to determine the localization of proteins (i.e., TPC2, IP3R, RyR, myosin or actin) in cells. However, in one series of experiments we used STED super-resolution microscopy, and showed that there is a close physical relationship between clusters of RyR in the terminal cisternae of the SR and TPC2 in the lysosomes. We propose that together, these data add to the accumulating body of evidence, which suggests that localized Ca2+ release via TPC2 might trigger the generation of more global Ca2+ release from the SR of SMCs via Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release. This work was published in Developmental Biology (Kelu et al., 2017) We were also very interested in investigating the role of TPC2 during the development of the early spinal circuitry in zebrafish. It is known that spontaneous Ca2+ transients in the PMNs are transformed from being slow and uncorrelated, to being rapid, synchronized and patterned. We demonstrated that in intact zebrafish, Ca2+ release via TPC2 is required for the establishment of this synchronized activity in the PMNs. Using the SAIGFF213A;UAS:GCaMP7a double-transgenic zebrafish line kindly provided by Koichi Kawakami (NIG, Japan), Ca2+ transients were visualized in the caudal PMNs (CaPs). To explore the possible role of TPC2-mediated Ca2+ signaling in the CaPs, Ca2+ imaging was performed following TPC2 attenuation via knockdown, knockout, or inhibition, as described above. We demonstrated that the disruption of TPC2 function resulted in a loss of both the normal ipsilateral correlation and contralateral anti-correlation of the Ca2+ signaling in the CaPs. There was also a reduction in the frequency and amplitude of the Ca2+ transients recorded from the CaPs, and a concomitant increase in the duration of the CaP Ca2+ transients. We also showed that the inhibition of action potentials with MS-222 resulted in a complete (but reversible) attenuation of the CaP Ca2+ transients, and also a decrease in whole-embryo NAADP levels. We suggest that these data indicate a novel function for NAADP/TPC2-mediated Ca2+ signaling in the development, coordination, and maturation of the spinal network in zebrafish embryos. This work was published in Developmental Biology (Kelu et al., 2018). Although we had demonstrated the requirement of TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release during SMC differentiation and motor circuit maturation in intact zebrafish embryos, the upstream trigger of TPC2/Ca2+ signaling during these developmental processes was unclear. NAADP is known to be a potent Ca2+ mobilizing messenger, which is suggested to target TPC2 in mediating the release of Ca2+ from the lysosomes. Thus, over the final few months of our project, we conducted molecular cloning of the zebrafish ADP ribosyl cyclase (ARC) homolog (i.e., ARC1-like), which is the putative enzyme for generating NAADP, and we characterized the expression of the arc1-like transcript and the NAADP level between ~16 hours post-fertilization (hpf) and ~48 hpf in whole zebrafish embryos. By fusing ARC1-like with either EGFP or tdTomato, we showed that it was localized in the plasma membrane, and associated with intracellular organelles, such as the lysosomes, Golgi complex and SR. Morpholino (MO)-mediated knockdown of arc1-like or pharmacological inhibition of ARC1 (via treatment with nicotinamide), led to an attenuation of Ca2+ signaling and disruption of SMC development. In addition, the injection of arc1-like mRNA into ARC1-like morphants partially rescued the Ca2+ signals and SMC development. We propose that these data suggest a link between ARC1-like, NAADP, TPC2 and Ca2+ signaling during SMC myogenesis in zebrafish embryos. 16101714.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101714.value: During the course of this project, we have acquired data indicating a novel role for TPC2-mediated Ca2+ signaling in the development of the neuromuscular circuitry required for the establishment of early coordinated locomotory behavior in zebrafish embryos. We utilized our line of apoaequorin-expressing transgenic fish to visualize Ca2+ signals generated in the skeletal slow muscle cells (SMCs), and the SAIGFF213A;UAS:GCaMP7a double-transgenic line of fish, to visualize Ca2+ signals in the caudal primary motor neurons (PMNs). We then knocked down TPC2 using a translation- or splice-blocking morpholino (MO); used CRISPR/Cas9-based gene editing to make a pan-embryonic tpcn2 knockout mutant zebrafish line; or pharmacologically inhibited TPC2 action via treatment with trans-ned-19 or bafilomycin 1A. Such disruption in TPC2 function resulted in significant attenuation of the myogenic Ca2+ signals and abnormalities in myofibrillogenesis. It also resulted in a loss of the normal ipsilateral correlation and contralateral anti-correlation of the Ca2+ signaling in the caudal PMNs. However, several aspects of the normal Ca2+ signaling signature in both cell types could be rescued with a tpcn2-mRNA. We also showed, via immunolabeling and confocal microscopy that in SMCs, TPC2 is initially localized in a nuclear/perinuclear domain, and it is subsequently distributed in a striated pattern associated with lysosomes in the cytosol, where it is coincident with IP3R and RyR in the adjacent sarcoplasmic reticulum. The inhibition of action potentials with MS-222 resulted in the complete (but reversible) attenuation of the caudal PMN Ca2+ transients, and a decrease in the whole-embryo NAADP levels. We cloned the zebrafish ADP ribosyl cyclase (ARC) homolog (i.e., ARC1-like), which is the putative enzyme for generating NAADP, and showed that the arc1-like transcript is expressed (and the endogenous NAADP is detected) in whole embryo extracts during the time window when the zebrafish myotome develops and is innervated by PMNs. We also showed that the pharmacological inhibition of ARC activity by nicotinamide and the MO-mediated knockdown of ARC1-like led to severe disruption in the myotomal patterning manifested by abnormal sarcomere formation. This indicates the importance of ARC1-like activity for SMC development. Furthermore, NAADP production was reduced after nicotinamide treatment, supporting the requirement of ARC activity in generating NAADP in vivo. Together, these data support the proposed action of an ARC1-like/NAADP/TPC2/Ca2+ signaling cascade in zebrafish during SMC development. This work has been published in four research articles (Part-C, Section-8, #7,10,14,15), and has been presented at 17 conferences (Part-C, Section-9, #1,5,10,11,17,21,27,29,31,35-42).

16101714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101714.value: We have recently applied for an RGC GRF grant to continue this exciting project. One goal is to generate lines of transgenic fish where tpcn2 is conditionally knocked out in a time- or tissue-specific manner. Thus, the effect of tpcn2 knockout on Ca2+ signaling and myofibrilogenesis can be investigated to a far higher level of temporal and spatial accuracy than has been previously achieved. We have already started to generate lines of TPC2 knockout fish via the Cre-loxP method. We would also like to identify the downstream targets of TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release via mRNA-seq and lncRNA-seq, followed by validation by qPCR and high-resolution imaging. Finally, we would like to extend our understanding of the precise location of TPC2 in the nuclear and cytoplasmic SMC compartments. This will involve the use of STED-based super-resolution nanoscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and electron tomography, as well as the application of complementary luminescence and fluorescence-based Ca2+ imaging techniques. We firmly believe that the more we discover about the function of TPC2, then the higher is the likelihood of novel treatment strategies being developed for the diseases that arise when the activity of TPC2 is perturbed.

16101714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101714.value: Two pore channels (TPCs) have recently emerged as a novel class of non-selective cation (predominantly Na+ and Ca2+) channels in endolysosomal organelles in cells. Of the three isoforms that have been described (i.e., TPC1, TPC2, and TPC3), only the first two are found in the human genome. Studies with TPC knockout, knockdown and/or pharmacological inhibition of their activity, have revealed that these channels participate in the regulation of multiple endolysosomal trafficking pathways, developmental events, and physiological processes. Dysregulation of the channels leads to/influences the development of a wide range of different diseases, including cancer and diabetes, as well as neurodegenerative, lysosomal storage, metabolic, and infectious diseases, an example of the latter being Ebola virus infection. Furthermore, evidence is accumulating to demonstrate that they help regulate important developmental processes, such as differentiation of skeletal muscle and neurons. Thus, gaining a better understanding of TPC function and dysfunction will have a long-term impact on human health.

16101914.label: Project Title(Chinese)
16101914.value: 探究Nme7（NM23-H7）在初級纖毛內的功能

16101914.label: Project Objectives
16101914.value: To characterize Nme7 in cilia and cilium-related functions We will examine the property of Nme7 in ciliated cells and evaluate its function in cilia and cilium-related events. To reveal the temporal and spatial characteristics of Nme7’s ciliary localization, imaging techniques ranging from immunofluorescence microscopy and time-lapse microscopy to electron microscopy will be employed. To investigate the function of Nme7, we will perform RNAi-mediated depletion of Nme7 in cell cultures and examine the potential effect in cellular activities related to cilia or ciliogenesis. These activities include hedgehog signaling and protein trafficking to cilia. In addition, we will investigate the function of Nme7 using zebrafish, an animal model well suited for studies of cilia and cilium-associated functions. We will carry out extensive characterization of Nme7 morphants and perform rescue experiments with the kinase-dead and ciliary localization-defective mutants of Nme7. Results obtained from the above experiments will demonstrate the function of Nme7 and also to facilitate the investigation of its action mechanisms in cilia and cilium-related events. To investigate the interaction of Nme7 with cilium-related proteins To understand how Nme7 exerts its function, we will initiate systematic search for cellular proteins that interact with Nme7 using proteomic technologies. Protein complexes of Nme7 will be isolated using affinity-based biochemical approaches and complex components will be identified by mass spectrometry. Demonstration of the identified interactions will delineate the functional networks in which Nme7 participates. Our preliminary studies have revealed the association of Nme7 with trichoplein and septins 2, 7, and 9, proteins that have been shown to regulate ciliary growth. We will carry out functional characterization of these identified interactions and reveal the physiological consequences of the interactions in specific biological processes. To identify phosphorylation events mediated by Nme7 in primary cilia To understand the kinase action of Nme7, we plan to identify its ciliary substrates. Ciliary proteins will be isolated and used for phosphorylation by Nme7; a control assay will use a kinase-dead mutant of Nme7 instead of the wild-type protein. His-phosphorylated proteins will be detected by immunoblotting with the anti-phosphohistidine antibodies in combination with two-dimensional electrophoresis and will subsequently be identified using mass spectrometry. In addition, the phosphorylation sites will be mapped by mass spectrometry. Next, we will validate the identified phosphorylation events in vitro and in cells and will investigate their biological roles using various approaches such as site-directed mutagenesis. We anticipate that the functional analysis of cellular phosphorylation mediated by Nme7 will inform how Nme7 exerts its actions.

16101914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16101914.value: 初級纖毛是一種進化上保守的細胞器，它們生長於脊椎動物大多數細胞的表面以感測細胞外環境、並協調多種信號傳導事件，纖毛的功能對動物發育和維持動物組織的穩態至關重要。初級纖毛的組織與功能上的缺陷與被稱為纖毛病的多種人類疾病和發育障礙緊密相關。在結構上，初級纖毛由從基體（中心體的母中心粒）延伸出的微管及其外披的纖毛膜構成。初級纖毛中有多種受體、離子通道和轉運分子，這與其作為感官細胞器的功能相一致。然而，我們目前對纖毛形成及其功能的認知仍然有許多懸而未決的問題。 本研究團隊一直專注於研究各種細胞活動中微管骨架的組織與調控。γ-微管蛋白環狀復合體是細胞內最主要的微管成核因子，我們最近在該復合體中發現了Nme7、並且闡明了Nme7在復合體中的功能。Nme7是被稱為NME的核苷二磷酸激酶和蛋白組氨酸激酶家族中一個未定性的成員。值得注意的是，nme7基因敲除小鼠呈現出以下缺陷：器官左右分布的不對稱性被破壞和纖毛病的特征。另外，在培養的細胞中抑制Nme7的表達損害了纖毛的功能。根據以上發現，我提出本研究計劃以致力於探究Nme7在初級纖毛中的功能。本研究計劃是以前次未資助提案為基礎、參考評審意見並基於我們最新實驗發現進行了廣泛修訂的結果。通過對人類細胞和斑馬魚的研究，我們發現Nme7是一個為纖毛生長所需要的纖毛蛋白。此外，Nme7具有激酶活性，並且該激酶活性是其纖毛功能所必需的。本研究計劃的特定目標是探明Nme7在纖毛中的功能、並闡明其在初級纖毛中作用的分子機理，這些關鍵問題將由涉及生物化學、蛋白質組學、分子和細胞生物學等技術的一系列試驗來解決。 這項研究有幾方面的重要意義，包括拓展我們對初級纖毛和NME家族激酶的認識，開發用於研究纖毛介導的細胞活動和動物發育的分子工具，並在分子水平上更好的了解纖毛病的發病機制。從該項研究中獲得的知識將有助於發現藥物靶標，以及開發預防和治療纖毛病的方法。

16101914.label: Realisation of objectives
16101914.value: We have fulfilled these objectives by characterizing Nme7 (also known as NM23-H7) in ciliogenesis. To investigate how Nme7 is involved in ciliogenesis, we examined Nme7 localization in cultured cells that ciliate upon serum starvation. When non-confluent cultures of hTERT-RPE1 (referred to hereinafter as RPE1) cells were subjected to serum starvation, short cilia appeared on the cells after a few hours of starvation and the cilia were fully grown after 48-72 h of starvation. Nme7 is a centrosomal protein and its centrosomal localization depends on its interaction with γ-tubulin ring complexes (γTuRCs). Indeed, Nme7 was detected on the centrosomes before serum starvation and on the basal bodies of the serum-starved cells. In addition, Nme7 appeared in the axonemes of primary cilia in a time-dependent manner: it displayed robust axonemal localization at the early stages of ciliogenesis (e.g. at 12 h of starvation), and the axonemal localization was reduced during cilium growth and became almost undetectable in fully grown cilia. These immunostaining analyses revealed a temporal pattern of Nme7 in the axonemes of primary cilia. We performed a sequence alignment of DM10 domains from Nme7 and several other proteins that exhibit localization in cilia or flagella, and identified conserved residues for a mutational analysis of Nme7. Lys48 and Arg49 are located in a cluster of conserved residues. Therefore, we created the double mutation K48A/R49A and examined the subcellular localization of the mutant. RPE1 cells transiently expressing the mutant or wild-type Nme7 were serum-starved for 18 h before fixation for immunostaining and imaging; under these conditions, the wild-type protein was readily visualized on the basal bodies and in the axonemes. The mutant displayed similar localization on the basal bodies as the wild-type protein, but was undetectable in the axonemes. These results indicate that Lys48-Arg49 is involved in the axonemal localization, but plays a dispensable role for the basal body localization. To investigate the role of Nme7 in ciliogenesis, we generated an nme7-/- line of RPE1 cells by using the CRISPR/Cas9 system and designed a guide RNA targeting exon 2 of human nme7. One of the selected clones contains a large insertion in exon 2, which disrupted the reading-frame after 18 residues of Nme7 and resulted in a premature stop codon. Before starvation neither nme7-/- nor the parental cells showed significant ciliogenesis. After 24 h starvation, the ciliation rates of the nme7-/- and parental cells were 35% and 50%, respectively. Therefore, ciliogenesis is impaired in the absence of Nme7. We performed anti-Nme7 immunoprecipitation and subjected the immunoprecipitates to protein identification by mass spectrometry. The identified proteins include trichoplein (TCHP), which has been shown to activate the kinase Aurora A on centrosomes, which inhibits ciliogenesis. To analyze the interaction with TCHP, we then generated an anti-TCHP antibody. The antibody detected a sole protein band, which was at the predicted size of TCHP. Moreover, this band was eliminated by RNAi-mediated silencing of TCHP expression. These analyses verified the antibody specificity. To confirm the interaction between Nme7 and TCHP, we performed reciprocal immunoprecipitations of Nme7 and TCHP. The immunoprecipitation of Nme7 robustly coprecipitated TCHP and vice versa. Quantitative immunoblotting showed that the precipitation of 88.6% Nme7 resulted in the coprecipitation of 89.1% TCHP from the cell extracts. By contrast, the immunoprecipitation of 92.7% TCHP coprecipitated 8.4% Nme7. These results revealed that most of the cellular TCHP exists in complexes with a subpopulation of Nme7. In addition, the majority of Nme7 does not associate with TCHP. We then conducted a binding assay using the purified recombinant proteins GST-TCHP and His-FLAG-Nme7, and the results verified the direct interaction between TCHP and Nme7. In an immunoblotting analysis, we found that the protein level of TCHP was ~87% lower in nme7-/- cells than in the parental cells. To verify this effect on TCHP, we silenced the cellular expression of Nme7 by using two siRNA sequences targeting to nme7. Transfection of either nme7-targeting siRNA effectively reduced the level of Nme7, which is consistent with the observations in our previous report. Remarkably, the RNAi-mediated depletions of Nme7 reduced TCHP to a minimal level, similar to the effect of nme7 knockout. By contrast, the silencing of TCHP expression by RNAi did not affect the Nme7 level. Collectively, Nme7 is required for maintaining the cellular level of TCHP, but not vice versa. Next, we wondered whether the down-regulation of TCHP involves proteasome-dependent degradation. To address this question, we inhibited the proteasome activity by cell treatment with MG132 after transfection of a control or nme7-targeting siRNA. In both control and Nme7-depleted cells, the protein levels of TCHP were significantly increased at 6 h of MG132 treatment and reached a plateau after 12 h of treatment, showing the involvement of the proteasome pathway in TCHP turnover. In addition, these data implied a dynamic turnover of TCHP even in the control-transfected cells. We noted that even after a prolonged MG132 treatment, the TCHP level was lower to a certain extent than that in the control-transfected cells under the same conditions. This observation suggests that TCHP may under degradation through other mechanisms in addition to the proteasome pathway. In our previous study, we identified a kinase-dead mutant (H206F) and a γTuRC-binding-deficient mutant (R322A) of Nme7, of which the mutant R322A does not show centrosomal localization. When transiently expressed, the mutant H206F was visualized on the basal bodies and in the axonemes in a pattern similar as the wild-type protein, indicating that the kinase activity is dispensable for the localization to primary cilia. By contrast, R322A localized neither to the basal bodies not to the axonemes. Therefore, the γTuRC association is not only required for the centrosomal localization of the protein, but also for the localization to primary cilia. Nme7 possesses a protein histidine kinase activity in an autophosphorylation reaction. Dr. Tony Hunter’s group (The Salk Institute for Biological Studies, U.S.A.) generated anti-phosphohistidine antibodies (Fuhs et al., Cell, 162:198-210, 2015). In collaboration with Dr. Hunter’s group, we used these antibodies to characterize the His-kinase actions of Nme7. In an autophosphorylation reaction using the recombinant protein of Nme7, the anti-phospho-His immunoblotting recognized the autophosphorylated Nme7. We then applied these antibodies in immunoblotting of ciliated nme7-knockout and parental RPE1 cells. However, the immunoblots showed a number of non-specific bands, but did not specifically detect any phospho-His-containing proteins from the parental RPE1 cells. We also conducted anti-phospho-His immunoblotting of γTuRCs isolated from parental and nme7-knockout RPE1 cells, but we could not detect any specific bands/spots of phosphorylated proteins. It is likely that the lack of detection of phospho-His-containing proteins was due to the insufficient specificity and sensitivity of the antibodies. Zebrafish is a commonly used model to study the impact of cilia defects on vertebrate development. We investigated the function of Nme7 in zebrafish by using splice-blocking morpholino oligonucleotides to knock down the protein. In zebrafishes injected with nme7-targeting morpholinos, we observed several phenotypes that are known as ciliopathies and these phenotypes include body curvature, hydrocephalus, and aberrant left-right asymmetry. nme7 morphants showed a reduction of cilia number in the Kupffer’s vesicle, which is composed of cells with long and robust monocilia and is crucial for zebrafish left-right patterning. Collectively, the phenotypes of nme7 morphants indicate that Nme7 is involved in ciliogenesis during zebrafish development.

16101914.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101914.value: Nme7 is an component of γ-tubulin ring complexes (γTuRCs) and required for γTuRC-mediated microtubule nucleation. It has been reported that nme7-/- mice develop ciliopathy symptoms, such as situs inversus and hydrocephalus. In addition, homozygous mutation of human nme7 is associated with situs inversus totalis. In this study, we characterized the functions of Nme7 in the assembly of primary cilia and demonstrated that Nme7 promotes primary cilium assembly both in cultured mammalian cells and by using zebrafish as a model organism. Cilium assembly in nme7-/- mammalian cells and in nme7 zebrafish morphants was impaired, and the ciliogenesis defects in the nme7 morphants caused ciliopathy phenotypes. To explore the mechanism by which Nme7 regulates cilium assembly, we identified that Nme7 localizes to the basal body and axoneme of cilia and is an important regulator of TCHP. Our study suggests that Nme7 is involved in ciliogenesis mainly through the following mechanisms: (1) Nme7 localizes to the growing primary cilia through the DM10 domain and the γTuRC-binding region; (2) Nme7 is associated with the γTuRC at the centrosome and promotes centrosomal microtubule nucleation; (3) cytosolic Nme7 binds to and stabilizes TCHP, a binding-partner of the kinase Aurora A. Taken together, we propose that Nme7 plays dual roles in cilium growth or function. The presence of several NME family members in cilia or flagella has been reported. However, the roles of these NME members in cilium assembly or function remain unclear. We demonstrated that the kinase activity is dispensable for the ciliary targeting of Nme7. Our work also demonstrated that Nme7 promotes ciliogenesis through its interaction with the γTuRC and TCHP and that the kinase domain B is the binding surface for both γTuRCs and TCHP. A single mutation in this domain disrupted the binding to γTuRCs and TCHP, and abolished the centrosomal and ciliary localization of Nme7. It has been shown that a homozygous mutation of human nme7, resulting in an in-frame deletion of 34 amino acids in the kinase domain B, is associated with situs inversus totalis. Therefore, our study suggested the molecular mechanism underlying the nme7-associated human ciliopathies. In summary, the above findings advanced our understanding of Nme7 in ciliogenesis and animal development. Several research articles have been published or are being prepared for publication based on the findings from this study along with the training of postgraduate students.

16101914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101914.value: In nme7 zebrafish morphants, we observed abnormal heart looping pattern and hydrocephalus, but we did not find cystic kidneys, which is a common ciliopathy phenotype. One possibility is that the Nme7 functions in ciliogenesis are organ- or cell-type specific. For example, Nme7 acts in ciliogenesis in the Kupffer’s vesicle, but not in that of kidney cells. In addition, the Nme7 functions might be required only at certain stages of animal development, and this is consistent with the observation that nme7-/- mice developed ciliopathy phenotypes, but showed physically normal cilia. We anticipate that the electron microscopy analysis of the ciliary pockets of primary cilia in zebrafish might provide information to enhance our understanding on the mechanisms of ciliogenesis and animal development. It has been known that TCHP functions in ciliogenesis and several other cellular processes. It would be interesting to identify the cellular activities in which TCHP-Nme7 complex or Nme7-free TCHP is involved. In addition, it would be important to understand the mechanisms that control the interaction between TCHP and Nme7 in these cellular events.

16101914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101914.value: Primary cilia are present on the surface of most cell types in metazoans and function as cellular antennae to mediate various signaling pathways, which plays important roles in embryonic development and adult organ homeostasis. In the present study, we demonstrated that Nme7 (alternatively named as NM23-H7) plays important roles in primary cilium assembly and animal development. nme7 knockout in cell cultures impaired the growth of primary cilia, and the silencing of Nme7 expression in zebrafish embryos led to impaired ciliogenesis and its associated fish developmental defects, such as aberrant left-right body asymmetry. To gain insights into the molecular mechanisms by which Nme7 functions in ciliogenesis, we revealed the spatiotemporal pattern of Nme7 in primary cilia and identified its interaction with trichoplein (TCHP), which has been known as a regulator of ciliogenesis. Furthermore, Nme7 stabilizes TCHP from protein turnover through the proteasome-mediated pathway. Collectively, these findings expanded our knowledge of the molecular principles governing the molecular assembly and function of primary cilia. Because defects in primary cilia cause a class of developmental diseases, which are called ciliopathies, knowledge derived from our study may provide new targets for developing therapeutic approaches for a number of human diseases.

16102414.label: Realisation of objectives
16102414.value: To achieve the aims we proposed, we utilized a temperature sensitive mutant zebrafish myd329 (referred to as puer herein after) with defect in microglia. By using microglia-specific markers, we showed that, when raised under the permissive temperature (24ºC), puer mutants contained normal number of microglia, but the number of microglia was drastically reduced 24 hours after switching to the restricted temperature (34ºC). We then went on to perform positional cloning and rescue experiment to demonstrate that the microglia defect in puer mutants is caused by a point mutation in the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptors nlrc3-like, a key regulator in inflammasome pathway. Subsequent biochemical analysis revealed that the single point mutation in puer mutants lead to self-aggregation of Nlrc3-like, which diminishes its restraint on apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a caspase recruitment domain (ASC) and results in the activation of inflammasome pathway. To further elucidate the cellular basis underlying the depletion of microglia in puer mutants, we performed high resolution time-lapse imaging analysis and found that, under the restricted temperature, the mutant microglia displayed a series of morphological chances including cell swelling and plasma-membrane rupture similar to that of necrosis and pyroptosis, suggesting that the loss of microglia in puer mutants is caused by the necrosis or pyroptosis of microglia. This notion was further supported by the finding that the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokine il1 was drastically induced in the mutant microglia under restricted temperature. In parallel, we generated a double transgenic fish, in which the neurons and microglia/microglia precursors are labeled by different fluorescents proteins, thereby allowing us to conduct time-laps imaging to track the behaviors of microglial precursors before and after they enter the brain. The time-lapse imaging analysis revealed that microglial precursors enter the brain via two specific routes. We further showed that the blockage of normal neuronal cell death significantly reduces the number of microglia in the brain. These results indicate that the brain colonization by microglial precursors are regulated by specific signals released by those dying neurons.

16102414.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102414.value: Microglia are tissue-resident macrophages resided in the central nervous system (CNS) and they play critical roles in removing cellular debris and infectious agents as well as regulating neurogenesis and neuronal activities. Yet, the molecular basis underlying the establishment of microglia pool and the maintenance of their homeostasis in the CNS remain largely undefined. In this proposal, we reported the identification and characterization of a mutant zebrafish puer, which harbors a point mutation in the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD) receptors, nlrc3-like, resulting in loss of microglia in a temperature sensitive manner. Genetic and time-lapse imaging analyses reveal that the loss of microglia in nlrc3-like deficient mutants undergo active cell death. We further show that the death of microglia in puer mutants is caused, at least in part, by the aberrant activation of inflammasome pathway. Our study indicates that the regulation of inflammasome cascade is critical for the maintenance of microglia homeostasis. This work is currently under review in the Journal of Genetics and Genomics. In addition, we also investigated the mechanics underlying the brain colonization by microglial precursors. We found that microglial precursors, which are born in the peripheral hematopoietic tissue, enter the mid-brain via two major routes: the lateral periphery between the eyes and brain and the ventral periphery of the brain. We further showed that the colonization of the mid-brain by microglial precursors is promoted by apoptotic neuronal death, which naturally occurs during neurogenesis. This work was later completed under the supported another grant and published in Developmental Cell (38:214-222, 2016).

16102414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102414.value: Many of the neurodegenerative diseases such as Multiple Sclerosis, Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases are caused by the progressive death of neurons in different regions of the nervous system. Although the precise molecular basis underlying these neurodegenerative diseases have not been fully defined, functional impairment of microglia, a population of immune cells in the central nervous system (CNS), has been shown to be closely associated with the onset and progression of these diseases. Thus, a comprehensive understanding how microglia pool is established in the CNS and how they function under physiological and pathological conditions will enhance our understanding of the development of various neurodegenerative disorders and may provide new therapeutic approaches for the treatment of these disorders. In our study, we used zebrafish, a tiny tropical fish, as an animal model to investigate how microglial precursors, which are born in peripheral tissue, colonize the CNS and subsequently maintain their population. We have found that microglial precursors enter the brain via specific routes and their subsequent colonization of the brain is regulated normal neuron cell death, which occur naturally during neuron development. We have further identified a key regulator important for the maintenance of microglia in the CNS.

16102914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102914.value: Autism is a neurodevelopment disorder characterized by impaired social interaction, problems in communication and stereotype behaviors. The cause and pathology of the disorder are not clear and currently there is no effective treatment. Studies suggest that malfunction of synapses could contribute to the pathogenesis of autism but the detailed mechanism is still elusive. A number of recent studies independently identified a region at chromosome 7p21 being duplicated in autism patients, but not in healthy control population. This duplication encodes a truncated ICA69 protein without its C-terminal domain. ICA69 is a BAR domain-containing protein and forms heteromeric BAR domain complexes with another BAR domain-containing protein PICK1. Through its interaction with PICK1, ICA69 controls the synaptic targeting and surface expression of AMPA-type glutamate receptors, which mediate the majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the brain and is important for synaptic plasticity, the cellular model of learning and memory. The identification of truncated ICA69 in autism patients raises the possibility that the truncated ICA69 could impair AMPA receptor function and contribute to the pathogenesis of autism. Here we propose to study the function of ICA69’s C-terminal domain and the potential abnormal function of the ICA69 truncation, with focus on the interaction with PICK1 and its role in AMPA receptor trafficking and synaptic plasticity. 16102914.label: Realisation of objectives
16102914.value: ICA69 (Islet Cell Autoantigen 69kD) is a major binding partner of PICK1 (Protein Interacting with C-kinase 1) in the brain. It comprises a BAR domain (Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs) and an ICAC (ICA69 C-terminal) domain. The BAR domain of ICA69 is crucial for its dimerization with PICK1 and its roles in regulating AMPA receptor trafficking and vesicular transport. However, the function of ICAC domain is largely unknown. In this project, we found that ICAC domain could not only block the PDZ binding of PICK1, but also inhibit the membrane association of PICK1 and ICA69 complex. Intriguingly, these findings also provided a potential mechanism for the known mutations of ICA69 in autism spectrum disorder. Autism is a neurodevelopment disorder characterized by impaired social interaction, problems in communication and stereotype behaviors. The cause and mechanism underlying the disorder are not known but studies found a strong genetic basis for the disorder. A copy number variation (CNV) at chromosome 7 was reported recently by several genome-wide studies of autism families. This CNV at 7p21 is a duplication that spans the genes NXPH1 (neurexophilin-1) and ICA69. Careful examination of the duplication revealed that this will lead to the production of a truncated protein of ICA69 without its C-terminus. Our data found that without the C-terminus, the truncated ICA69 mutant (ICAt) found in autism patient could no longer compete with AMPA receptor. While ICA69 disrupt PICK1’s clustering of AMPA receptors, ICAt form co-clusters together with PICK1 and AMPA receptors. In addition, ICAt interfered with the surface expression of AMPA receptors. In neurons, ICAt was found to concentrate in the cell body and redistribute the amount of PICK1 and AMPA receptors between cell body and dendrites. The redistribution of AMPA receptor could affect their function in the brain and contribute to the pathogenesis of autism.

16103014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103014.value: Biofouling refers to the undesirable growth of marine organisms on ship hulls, seawater pipelines, and other man-made surfaces. The attached organisms increase the weight, drag, and surface corrosion of vessels and block drainage pipelines, leading to increased maintenance costs and huge economic losses to maritime industries. In the past, toxic antifouling compounds such as tributyltin (TBT) were added to marine paints to prevent the attachment of foulers. However, the devastating environmental impact of toxic antifouling compounds led to the prohibition of their use and created an urgent need for environmentally friendly antifouling compounds. Many natural marine products have been identified as potential candidates for antifouling compounds. However, because detailed studies on their modes of actions are missing, there is no assurance if they will be safer than existing antifouling compounds to use. We recently developed a promising low-toxic antifouling butenolide derived from a marine bacterium. The acute toxicity of the butenolide in several non-target organisms, including micro-algae, crustaceans, and fish, suggested that it has a very low acute toxicity. Furthermore, we identified a thiolase, a key enzyme involved in energy production via lipid oxidation, as the potential binding target of the butenolide in one of the major fouling species, Balanus amphitrite. We hypothesized that the butenolide causes energy shortage in fouling organisms such that they cannot complete larval settlement and metamorphosis, which is an energy demanding process. We propose to further understand the effect of the butenolide in both target and non-target organisms using additional molecular tools. This study is divided into three parts. Part 1 aims to study the detailed mode of action of the butenolide in Balanus amphitrite. ‘Top down’ and ‘bottom up’ proteomics techniques will be applied to determine the mechanism of action of the butenolide and the site of interaction between the butenolide and thiolase. In part 2, we will study the effect of the butenolide in non-target organisms using proteomic profiling. In part 3, we will evaluate the toxicity of the butenolide in non-target organisms to propose candidate molecular targets for future antifouling screening efforts. We anticipate that our results will further demonstrate the effectiveness and low toxicity of the butenolide; enable us to compare the effect and molecular targets of the butenolide in both target and non-target species; and more importantly should our hypothesis be correct, establish a new screening platform targeting larval lipid oxidation to identify additional environmentally friendly antifouling compounds. 16103314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103314.value: Abstract The Hippo signaling pathway is an evolutionarily conserved pathway regulating a wide range of developmental and cellular processes including growth, differentiation, patterning and cell migration. Importantly, the Hippo signaling pathway is known to respond to regulatory signals from the actin cytoskeleton, consistent with the hypothesis that the Hippo signaling pathway might function to sense and interpret mechanical signals such as tissue shape, geometry and tension to coordinate cell behaviors in a multicellular organism. However, the mechanism of how the actin cytoskeleton regulates the Hippo pathway remains largely elusive. We identified beta-Spectrin as a protein required for Hippo signaling activity in a genetic screen for oocyte polarity defects during Drosophila oogenesis. Spectrins are known for linking the actin cytoskeleton to the plasma membrane. Our preliminary data allows us to form a hypothesis that mutations in beta-spectrin cause formation of stress-fiber-like actin structures that lead to loss of Hippo signaling activity. In this proposal we aim to elucidate the function of beta-Spectrin in regulating Hippo signaling activity. Elucidation of the beta-Spectrin function in the Hippo pathway will advance our understanding of the cytoskeletal control of the Hippo pathway, one of the key unanswered questions in the field. Mutations in beta-spectrin are linked to multiple developmental defects and diseases in mammals. Studies from this work will also likely shed new light on the understanding of the human diseases linked to abnormal spectrin function. Hippo信號通路是一條在進化過程中保守的信號通路，它在果蠅及哺乳類動物的生長發育調控中發揮廣泛的作用，維持器官組織的正常大小和形態。Hippo信號通路能夠在多細胞生物體中感知及讀取組織形態、幾何形狀和緊張度等力學信號來協調細胞行為。研究發現，Hippo信號通路受來自肌動蛋白細胞骨架的因子調節。然而，肌動蛋白細胞骨架如何調節Hippo信號通路的機理，目前仍然不清楚。 我們通過果蠅遺傳篩選鑒定出beta-Spectrin是一種維持 Hippo信號通路活性所必須的蛋白，而Spectrin是負責連接細胞膜和肌動蛋白細胞骨架的重要分子。 beta-spectrin的突變導致了壓力纖維狀的肌動蛋白結構的形成，這引起了Hippo信號通路的失活。 我們希望能夠闡明beta-spectrin調節Hippo通路的分子機理，這項研究將加深我們對細胞骨架控制Hippo通路過程的了解，這是該領域最重要的未知問題之一。在哺乳動物中，beta-spectrin的突變與多種發育缺陷及疾病有密切關系，此項研究亦有助於對與beta-Spectrin功能異常相關的人類疾病的認識。

16103314.label: Realisation of objectives
16103314.value: With the funding from this project, we, and two other research groups, have independently published that the spectrin network regulates Hippo signaling activity in a wide range of Drosophila and mammalian tissues (Deng et al., 2015; Fletcher et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015). These works provide important contributions for understanding how mechanical signals regulate tissue growth in living organs and have since been widely cited. Here I will provide a summary of main results from the original objectives and describe our new works derived from these findings. Objective 1. Dissect the relationship between the actin phenotype and the Hippo signaling phenotype in beta-spectrin mutant cells. We have found that the spectrin network has an essential role in organizing parallel actin bundles (Wong et al., 2015). The actin bundle organizing activity of spectrin was recently found to be conserved in C.elegans myoepithelial gonad cells (Wirshing and Cram, 2018). We found that other mutations affecting actin bundle formation, such as enabled (ena), also lead to abnormal Hippo signaling activity, consistent with recent reported roles of ena in tissue growth (Gaspar et al., 2015; Vaughen and Igaki, 2016). Objective 2: Examine whether beta-Spectrin functions to promote Merlin activation through beta-Spectrin/actin/Merlin interaction. We performed a series of experiments to test the hypothesis that beta-Spectrin regulates the interaction of Merlin and the actin cytoskeleton and promotes Merlin activation. In particular, we crossed a constitutive active form of Merlin, UAS-HA-Mer1-600, into the beta-spectrin mutant cells. The Hippo signaling defects in the beta-spectrin mutant cells cannot be rescued by the expression of the Mer1-600 construct, suggesting that merlin is not a primary target of beta-Spectrin/actin regulation of the Hippo pathway. Objective 3: Test whether increased tension in beta-spectrin mutant cells lead to Hippo signaling defects. We have found an elevation of myosin-mediated contractility in spectrin mutant cells, consistent with findings reported in (Deng et al., 2015). An elevation of myosin-mediated contractility through the overexpression of a constitutive form of myosin light chain (SqhEE) or Rok (RokCAT) has been shown to promote Yki activity (Deng et al., 2015; Rauskolb et al., 2014). Therefore, it is likely that the spectrin network regulates Hippo signaling activity through modulating myosin activity. Objective 4: Test whether the beta-Spectrin/actin/Hippo pathway link is conserved in human cells. We and others have independently found that the spectrin network also modulates YAP/TAZ activity in mammalian cells (Deng et al., 2015; Fletcher et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015). Together, these works suggest a regulatory pathway from the spectrin/actin network to Yki activity through modulating myosin activity, which is conserved in Drosophila and mammalian cells. Further work: Over the past decade, it has become clear that YAP/TAZ activity is mechanosensitive because YAP/TAZ activity in cultured cells can be dramatically modulated by mechanical manipulations as well as both pharmacological and genetic methods that affect the cytoskeleton (Panciera et al., 2017). Interestingly, only a handful of direct actin regulators have been identified with in vivo tissue growth-modulating mutant phenotypes, although a number of Hippo signaling regulators have been identified with links to the actomyosin network such as Ajuba and Zyxin (Gaspar et al., 2015; Rauskolb et al., 2014). These direct actin regulators include an actin capping protein a (cpa) (Fernandez et al., 2011; Sansores-Garcia et al., 2011), an actin capping protein b (cpb) (Fernandez et al., 2011; Sansores-Garcia et al., 2011), an actin nucleation factor Diaphanous (Dia) (Sansores-Garcia et al., 2011), and the spectrin network (Deng et al., 2015; Fletcher et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015). It remains unclear how many and which types of subcellular actin structures are critical for modulating Yki activity in vivo. Moreover, the mechanistic links between the actomyosin network and Yki activity remain puzzling. (1) Cell nucleus shape-mediated nucleocytoplasmic shuffling model It is recently shown in cultured cells that force-induced nucleus shape change can affect nucleocytoplasmic shuffling of YAP and thus modulate YAP activity (Elosegui-Artola et al., 2017). This study raises the possibility that the subcellular actin structures involved in maintaining cell nucleus positioning and shape are important for modulating Yki activity in vivo. We generated a single cell atlas of the wild type wing imaginal discs (unpublished results). The single cell data show that Hippo signaling target genes show quantitative distributions in the wing discs. Interestingly, among curated 329 cytoskeletal-related genes, only Msp-300 and Klarsicht, the only KASH proteins in Drosophila, show similar expression pattern to expanded, a well-established Hippo signaling regulator and target. The KASH proteins are the only known proteins mediating force transmission from the cytoplasmic cytoskeleton to the nucleus (Lele et al., 2018). We are currently testing whether the LINC complex function as a link between the spectrin/actin cytoskeleton and Yki nucleocytoplasmic shuffling, with our established imaginal disc live imaging system and a newly available live-imaging compatible Yki-YFP construct (Xu et al., 2018). (2) Adherens junctions (AJ) hub signaling model Another model has been raised that cytoskeletal tension-dependent Ajuba AJ localization promotes Wts AJ localization and inhibits Wts activity (Rauskolb et al., 2014). Moreover, Crumbs-mediated Kibra junctional localization has recently been shown to repress Kibra function (Su et al., 2017). We have previously examined Ajuba-GFP and Wts-GFP localization in spectrin mutant cells in fixed tissues and did not observe detects of Ajuba and Wts localization. However, it is noteworthy that quantitative differences would be hard to detect in fixed tissues. With the newly available live-imaging compatible Mer-YFP, Kibra-GFP, Ex-YFP, Wts-YFP, Hpo-YFP, and Sav-YFP constructs (Su et al., 2017), we are revisiting whether the spectrin network affects the AJ signaling hub in live imaginal discs. Additional work supported by reagents or methodology generated from this grant: 1. We have established a method to titrate the dosage of cytochalasin D to dissolve the strong actin fiber accumulation in beta-spectrin mutant cells in live egg chambers. Using this Cyto D titration method, we have shown that that the medial myosin pulses are critically dependent on the thin apical actin meshwork in the embryonic neuroectodermal cells (An et al., 2017). 2. We have established a single-cell transcriptome-based method to systematically examine the pattern of Yki targets in the wing imaginal discs from this study. Based on our transcriptomic data and analysis method, we have also contributed to a collaborative work on the interaction of Toll and Hippo signaling pathways in growth control (Katsukawa et al., 2018).

16103314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103314.value: The Hippo signaling pathway responds to mechanical forces such as actomyosin-based tension to regulate growth. How mechanical signals are transduced in the Hippo pathway remains largely unclear. Here we demonstrated that β-Spectrin is required in the Hippo signaling pathway in both Drosophila and mammalian cells. We also showed that β-spectrin mutations disrupt basal actin network in the Drosophila follicular epithelial cells and demonstrated a link between stress-fiber-like actin structures and Hippo signaling activity in an in vivo developmental context. This study uncovered a previously unknown function of the spectrin cytoskeleton and raised the possibility that the spectrin network can function as a tension-sensing system and feed into the Hippo pathway.

16103414.label: Project Objectives
16103414.value: The expression patterns of the host central carbon metabolism pathway genes after phage infection We want to address the question how the host central carbon metabolism pathway gene expression will be affected by cyanophage infection. As a preliminary result, we used massively parallel cDNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) to study the transcriptome dynamics of Prochlorococcus NATL2A infected by a T4-like cyanophage P-SSM2. Out of 2229 host genes, we identified 357 differentially expressed genes after infection. We found that both the host Calvin cycle genes rbcS/L (up to 12-fold) and the Calvin cycle inhibitor gene cp12 (up to 3-fold) have relatively higher transcript levels after phage infection. Cyanophage-encoded cp12 was also highly expressed (up to 48-fold of the host copy) and this may surpass the effect of a 12-fold change of the host rbcS/L transcript abundance in the infected host cells. In Prochlorococcus, transcript abundances may not be well correlated with their protein abundances (29). We plan to use Western Blot and tandem MS to measure host and phage protein abundances (rbcS/L, cp12) after infection and to see how they correlate with their transcript abundances. The interaction of phage CP12 with the host Calvin cycle enzymes PRK and GAPDH In plants and cyanobacteria, the Calvin cycle inhibitor CP12 shuts off the Calvin cycle by forming a protein complex with two key Calvin cycle enzymes PRK (phosphoribulokinase) and GAPDH (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase). We hypothesize that cyanophage-encoded CP12 can also form a protein complex with the host enzymes PRK and GAPDH. We will use the yeast two-hybrid system to verify the interaction of phage CP12 with host PRK and GAPDH in vitro. We will then perform co-immunoprecipitation assays to pull down the PRK-CP12-GAPDH complex in the infected host cells and to confirm the existence of phage-encoded CP12 in this protein complex. Finally we will use co-immunoprecipitation assays to see whether the cellular content of PRK-CP12-GAPDH increases during infection. The host carbon fixation rate and key metabolite levels after phage infection If the host Calvin cycle is shut off after infection there should be less carbon fixed in the infected culture compared to the uninfected control culture. We will add 13C labeled NaHCO3 (the preferred carbon source for Prochlorococcus) to the culture and measure the cellular content of 13C at different time points after infection. We will also measure the key metabolite levels to see if there is less metabolic flux to the Calvin cycle and more flux to the pentose phosphate pathway.

16103414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103414.value: The unicellular cyanobacteria Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus are the most abundant photosynthetic cells in the oceans. Three morphotypes of lytic cyanophages (phages infecting cyanobacteria) have been found to infect Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus: T4-like myoviruses, T7-like podoviruses, and siphoviruses. Differentiated by their ultrastructures and gene content, they are all double-stranded DNA viruses. In cyanobacteria, the light reactions of photosynthesis harness energy from the sunlight and split water to produce NADPH (electron carrier) and ATP (energy carrier), which are consumed by the Calvin cycle to fix CO2 and produce glucose 6-phosphate. Glucose 6-phosphate is oxidized in the pentose phosphate pathway to produce NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate, which can be used for nucleotide biosynthesis. Host-like metabolic genes involved in the light reactions of photosynthesis, photosynthetic electron transfer, pigment synthesis and pentose phosphate pathway are found in cyanophage genomes. Cyanophages don’t contain any Calvin cycle genes; instead, many of them have a Calvin cycle inhibitor gene cp12. We hypothesized that during infection cyanophages use these host-like metabolic genes to augment the light reactions of photosynthesis for phage DNA replication rather than carbon fixation. The objective of this proposed project is to test our hypothesis by directly studying the host central carbon metabolism after phage infection from different aspects: gene expression, protein interaction and metabolite level. The research proposed herein is designed to study the expression patterns of the host central carbon metabolism pathway genes after phage infection, examine the interaction of phage CP12 with the host Calvin cycle enzymes PRK and GAPDH, and investigate the host carbon fixation rate and key metabolite levels after phage infection. Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus are thought to be responsible for 50% of the total primary production in oligotrophic regions of the oceans and 20% of them are lysed by cyanophages every day. The research proposed here using them as a model system will deepen our understanding of the role of viruses in carbon cycling in the marine ecosystem. Since Synechococcus is abundant in the subtropical coastal waters of Hong Kong, our work will also help understand carbon cycling in the waters near Hong Kong. 單細胞藍細菌原綠球藻和聚球藻是世界上數量最多的的光合作用生物，它們的病毒（噬菌體）也在海洋中大量存在。藍細菌利用太陽光的能量進行光合作用，通過光反應途徑合成ATP和NADPH，這兩種物質之後在開爾文循環中被用來固定二氧化碳合成六碳糖。六碳糖在戊糖磷酸途徑裏被轉化為五碳糖，五碳糖之後可以參與核酸的合成。噬菌體基因組含有光合作用的光反應途徑基因和戊糖磷酸途徑基因，但是卻沒有開爾文循環基因，相反還含有開爾文循環的抑制基因。我們認為，當藍細菌被噬菌體侵染後，宿主的開爾文循環被抑制，光反應途徑所產生的ATP和NADPH被戊糖磷酸途徑利用以合成大量噬菌體DNA。本研究項目將從基因表達、蛋白質濃度和碳代謝產物濃度三個方面驗證我們的猜測。

16103614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103614.value: SynGAP, a small GTPase activating protein abundantly and specifically expressed in neurons, is target to the postsynaptic densities of excitatory synapses. SynGAP is essential for proper synapse development and for cognitive functions in all mammals including humans. Mutations of SynGAP are known to be associated with various mental disorders including autisms, schizophrenia, and intellectual disabilities. However, the molecular bases underlying synGAP’s physiological functions and mental disorders caused by SynGAP mutations are poorly understood. In this proposal, we aim to elucidate the atomic structure and cellular functions of a previously unrecognized trimerization domain of SynGAP located in the C-terminal half of the protein. We will also investigate the impacts of mutations within the SynGAP trimer region found in mental disorder patients on the structure and function of the protein. We also plan to dissect the structural basis governing the highly specific interaction between SynGAP and PSD-95, which is discovered here to be mediated by an extended PDZ-binding motif of SynGAP and the PDZ3-SH3-GK tandem of PSD-95. We will also study how formation of the SynGAP/PSD-95 complex can be regulated by calmodulin-dependent kinase II-mediated phosphorylation. The outcomes of the proposed study will not only provide mechanistic understandings to the physiological functions of SynGAP and its complex with PSD-95, but also be valuable for developing possible treatments for mental disorders caused by SynGAP mutations. 16103614.label: Major findings and research outcome
16103614.value: Despite the pivotal roles of the PSD in orchestrating synaptic structure and functions, our understanding of the mechanistic basis of its formation and dynamics remains rudimentary. Our slow progress in this regard is at least in part due to the PSD’s unique physical structure—an extremely large, chemically-inhomogeneous, densely-packed and yet somewhat mobile protein aggregate. For example, we do not understand exactly how PSD aggregates form and disassemble beneath postsynaptic membranes. Are a few selected proteins or are many proteins in the PSD collectively responsible for the formation of PSD aggregates? Does the formation of PSD aggregates affect the activities/specificities of enzymes found in the PSD? Although activity-induced protein modifications are known to alter protein-protein interactions, how exactly do neuronal activity changes alter the modes of PSD assembly? How do the PSD protein assemblies communicate with various protein machineries such as actin remodeling complexes and protein synthesis/degradation apparatuses? How do the mutations of synaptic proteins found in brain disorder patients affect PSD formation and function? In this project period, we discover that SynGAP, one of the most abundant PSD proteins and a Ras/Rap GTPase activator, forms a homo-trimer and binds to multiple copies of PSD-95. Binding of SynGAP to PSD-95 induces phase separation of the complex forming highly concentrated liquid-like droplets reminiscent of the PSD. The multivalent nature of the SynGAP/PSD-95 complex is critical for the phase separation to occur and for proper activity-dependent SynGAP dispersions from the PSD. In addition to revealing a dynamic anchoring mechanism of SynGAP at the PSD, our results also suggest a model for phase-transition-mediated formation of PSD. This work was published in Cell in 2016. In collaboration with Dr. Richard Huangir's lab, we also discovered that SynGAP can undergo synaptic activity-dependent dynamic exchange between PSD and cytoplasm of dendritic spines. The work was published in Neuron in 2015. During the project period, we have also systematically investigated how DLG family MAGUKs function individually and cooperatively are largely unknown. We discovered that PSD-95 PDZ3 directly couples with SH3-GK tandem in a PDZ ligand binding-dependent manner, and the coupling can promote PSD-95 dimerization and multimerization. We further demonstrated that PSD-93, but not SAP102, can also undergo PDZ3 ligand binding-induced conformational coupling with SH3-GK and form homo-oligomers. Interestingly, PSD-95 and PSD-93 may also form ligand binding-induced hetero-oligomers, suggesting a cooperative assembly mechanism for the mega-NMDA receptor synaptic signaling complex. This work was published in J Mol Biol in 2018.

16103614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103614.value: Our discovery of the phase separation of the PSD-95/SynGAP complex allowed us to propose that PSD may form via phase separation. We have developed this concept into a successful CRF proposal. We are happy to report that our concept of PSD formation by phase separation was supported by a paper just appeared in Cell in Aug. 23, 2018.

16103614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103614.value: All neurons in our brain are wired via a micron-sized connection unit called synapse, and each synapse contains a layer of densely-packed, protein rich compartment called postsynaptic density (PSD), which is responsible for brain signal processing and transmission. Mutations of genes encoding PSD proteins are a major causes of psychiatric disorders including autisms, schizophrenia, and depressions. While the existence of PSDs has been known to scientists for 60 years, how PSDs form and change in response to brain activities are poorly understood. During the project research period, we discovered that SynGAP and PSD-95, two abundance proteins in PSD that are known to cause autisms when mutated, can form an autonomously assembled network structure both in test-tube and in living cells. Most surprisingly, the SynGAP/PSD-95 assembly can form stable “oil-like” droplets in the midst of aqueous cytoplasm of living cells via a phenomena called phase-transition. This finding provides a possible answer for the long-lasting question of PSD formation in the field of brain science. Importantly, the HKUST team also found that defects of SynGAP or PSD-95 identified in autism patients alter the “oil-like” droplets formation of the complex and change the synaptic signaling activity of neurons. Our discovery was published in the journal Cell on August 25, 2016. In addition to providing a possible answer to how PSD might form in neurons, our work provides mechanistic insights into why mutations altering the SynGAP/PSD-95 interaction can contribute to various brain disorders including seizure, autism, and ID. Our discovery may also inspire new ways to develop therapeutic methods for these devastating diseases to human society.

16103714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103714.value: A central step in DNA replication initiation is the assembly of the pre-replication complex (pre-RC) at replication origins. The preRC consists of Cdc6, MCM, ORC, and Cdt1. Our group previously reported the solution NMR structure of Cdt1-Mcm6 complex, providing insights into the mechanism for the recruitment of MCM to replication origins by Cdt1 in human (12). There are approximately 10,000 replication origins in the human genome. However, the molecular mechanism for origin selection remains poorly understood. Recent studies suggest that human replication origins may be associated with G-rich sequences that have the potential to form G-quadruplex (G4) DNA (37). Previous work by others showed that human Orc1 binds G4 RNA (30). This work led us to investigate directly the role of G4 DNA in DNA replication initiation. Our group focused on the structure of G4 DNA and its interaction with known replication initiation proteins. Preliminary results showed that human Cdc6 binds G4 DNA directly supporting a role for G4 DNA in the recruitment of Pre-RC to replication origins. We also showed that G4 RNA binds both Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) and Cdc6 to form a nucleoprotein complex suggesting that G4 may also play a role in recruiting human pre-RC to the EBV replication origin. In analyzing the structure of G4 DNA that Cdc6 binds, we discovered a novel structural fold of G-quadruplex. In this proposal, we will investigate whether this novel G4-fold is specific for Cdc6 and vice versa. We will investigate the role of G-quadruplex as a structural landmark for the selection of replication origins in human and as an auxiliary factor in EBV replication through structural analysis. Detailed structures of the Cdc6-G4 DNA and the Cdc6-G4 RNA-EBNA1 complexes will provide insight on the molecular mechanism for origin selection in human and human viruses. EBNA1, an EBV encoded replication initiation factor is the only EBV protein expressed in all nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), a predominant cancer found in Hong Kong. We will collaborate with Prof Tsao (HKU), an expert in EBV and NPC, to study EBNA1 mediated DNA replication in NPC cells. In collaboration with Prof. Tye (Cornell), we will investigate the formation and genome-wide location of G4 DNA in vivo at different phases of the cell cycle. The outcome of this proposed research will provide fundamental knowledge about DNA replication in human and may have profound impact on our understanding of the molecular mechanism of EBV tumorigenicity. DNA復制是所有生命形式增殖所必需的。了解DNA分子於每個細胞分裂周期中如何復制是生命科學領域的重要科學問題。此領域目前的主要知識是由酵母，古生菌和細菌細胞模型得出的，其中仍然有許多尚未得到解答的問題，尤其是在人類細胞中的DNA復制。 復制起始的關鍵步驟是復制前復合物在復制起點的組裝。復制前復合物是由Cdc6，MCM，ORC和Cdt1組成的。最近我們研究組發表了Cdt1-MCM6復合物的精細核磁共振結構，這有助於我們闡明MCM是如何通過Cdt1被招募到DNA的復制起點，這一復制前復合物組裝的關鍵步驟。同時也有助於研究細胞周期蛋白Geminin是如何在人類細胞中阻斷這一步驟的（NAR 2012; PNAS 2012）。在人類染色體上大約有40000 個DNA的復制起點。然而DNA復制起點如何識別，以及DNA復制機器如何被招募到復制起點，這些問題的相關分子機制仍然知之甚少。 最近我們研究組取得了兩項關於了解人類DNA復制起始識別分子機制的重要進展：（一）復制前復合物可以直接結合人G-四鏈體結構DNA，從而招募復制前復合物到復制起點。 （二）通過由G-四鏈體的介導，EBNA1與復制前復合物相結合招募復制前復合物。這些發現表明人類染色體上潛在的3000個可能形成G-四鏈體結構的DNA序列的確能夠成為潛在的復制起點。 在潛伏階段的EB病毒DNA復制過程中，EB病毒通過由EB核抗原1(EBNA1)介導的對人復制前復合物的招募, 在人類宿主B細胞的每個細胞周期只復制一次。EBNA1是唯一在所有的鼻咽癌（NPC，香港的常見癌癥之一）細胞中都有表達的蛋白質。我們建議通過對復制前復合物/ G-四鏈體/ EBNA1復合物的結構研究，以及與香港大學的曹教授和香港中文大學的羅教授合作，對其在鼻咽癌細胞中的功能展開生化研究， 從而對這一病毒復制過程的分子機理有所認識。研究結果可能對EB病毒致病性以及人類細胞中DNA復制分子機制的理解產生深遠的影響，也可以提供抗癌藥物篩選和設計的潛在靶標。

16103714.label: Realisation of objectives
16103714.value: Object 1: Structural determination of Cdc6/G-quadruplex DNA complex by NMR (100%) To accomplish this objective, we need (1) to determine the structure of G-quadruplex, (2) to solve the structure of Cdc6 and (3) to measure the intermolecular NOEs for Cdc6/G-quadruplex structure calculation. Although we determined the novel chair type G-quadruplex structure of a human telomeric variant htel18T in 2014 by NMR, the referees from Nucleic Acids Research strongly criticized our approaches. After having successfully conducted all the suggested experiments in 2017, these referees started to question whether or not this telomeric variant htel18T has any biological function. In the beginning of 2018, we used bioinformatics methods to show that the telomeric variant htel18T DNA exists in human genome and finally we are able to publish this paper in Chem Sci (IF 9.1). Meanwhile, to rebuttal the critiques from the referees of Nucleic Acids Research, we used the double bromide substitution method to obtain the new type of wild-type human telomeric structures and developed a new NMR method to prove that this double bromide substitution was valid. With these new results, our crystal structure was published on Nucleic Acids Research (IF 11.5), a leading journal in the field. With the use of similar techniques, we were also determined novel structures of human G4C2 DNA repeats, which are believed to the genetic cause of the human ALS and FTD diseases which were published in 2015 and 2018 on the Journal of Scientific Report. With the successes of publishing novel G-quadruplex structures in high impact journals after unexpected struggles with biased referees, we started to solve the structure of Cdc6 and to measure the intermolecular NOEs for Cdc6/G-quadruplex structure calculation as described below. We have identified the interaction between Cdc6 (aa7-20) and the human telomeric variant G-quadruplex DNA, htel21T18 and solved their complex structure by NMR method. In the complex structure of Cdc6/htel21T18, the residues FPKRK bind to the bottom of htel21T18 through the hydrophobic and charge interactions. To investigate the specific recognition of htel21T18 by residues FPKRK, several mutants including S13E, F14E, F14A, P15E, K16E and R17E were created and titrated with htel21T18. The NMR results indicated that the FPKR are the key residues to bind with htel21T18 in which the mutations on these residues could abolish the interaction with G-quadurplex. Furthermore, we used different DNA sequences which can form different secondary structures such as single strand DNA (CATTCCCACCGGGACCACCAC), double strand DNA (GCTTTAAAAAGTAAGTT), G4-DNA of htel21T18 and RNA G-quadruplex formed by TERRA (UAGGGUUAGGGU) to titrate Cdc6 (aa 7-20). Our result indicated that Cdc6 (aa 7-20) can specifically recognize the human telomeric DNA/RNA G-quadurplexes. Especially, the titration of Cdc6 (aa 7-20) with chicken G-quadruplex showed no interaction by NMR implying the specifity of human Cdc6 in recognizing G-quadruplex. In summary, the structure of Cdc6/htel21T18 reveals the mechanism of Cdc6 recognizing the G-quadruplex. Our further study of the mutation in Cdc6 and titration with different DNA/RNA sequences demonstrated the specific selectivity of Cdc6 to G-quadruplex. Our results shed high light on development of specific probes and therapeutic drugs targeting on this G-quadurlex. These import results will soon be submitted to high impact journals as we did before. However, the abovementioned difficulties have the detrimental effects in slowing down our progresses for conducting researches on objectives 2-4. Especially, a large amount of addition experiments and sample making have quickly depleted the funding of this grant for carrying out structural and functional studies proposed in objectives 2-4. Currently, we are seeking other funding sources to support researches as stated in objectives 2-4. Object 2: Functional assay of Cdc6/G-quadruplex in DNA replication and cell cycle (60%) To accomplish this objective, we need (1) to find dysfunctional mutants based on the study stated in objective 1, (2) to knock down endogenous Cdc6, (3) to transfect with Cdc6 dysfunctional mutants and (4) to rescue DNA replication with the wild-type Cdc6. As described in Object 1, we were able to find dysfunction Cdc6 mutants. And we are currently working with Prof. Prioleau (Institut Jacques Monod, France) for the functional assays as in steps (2)-(4). These under achievements are mainly due to large numbers of additional experiments in objective 1 and depleting funding of this grant introduced by many additional expensive DNA and RNA samples Object 3: Structural determination of Cdc6/G-quadruplex RNA, EBNA1/G-quadruplex RNA and EBNA1/G-quadruplex/Cdc6 complexes by NMR (50%) In this objective, we need (1) to determine the G-quadruplex RNA, (2) to solve the EBNA1 and Cdc6 structures and (3) to measure intermolecular NOEs for structure calculation of Cdc6/G-quadruplex RNA/EBNA1 complex. Technically and financially, it turned out that determination unknown RNA G-quadruplex is a tremendous challenge. We decided to use a published RNA G-quadruplex for our study in the step 1 of the research. Next, we were able to obtain NMR samples for EBNA1 and Cdc6 peptides after long struggling in labeling and solubilizing the samples in step 2. As stated before in Objective 1, we ran out of money and time due to unexpected difficulty took place in objective 1 researches. We are continuing to working this important project and hopefully with additional funding. Object 4: Functional assay of EBNA1/G-quadruplex/Cdc6 in DNA replication in NPC cell lines (100%) We have conducted the functional test in our NPC cell lines. The result was not promising. As stated before, we ran out of funding and time to conduct this research. The student Mr. LEE TL working on this project graduated. However, we were able to publish a good paper on EBNA1 (Zha S et al (2018), Nanoscale, (IF 7.6)). However, as the paper is in collaboration with other people, we did know at which step of paper writing the acknowledgement of RGC was lost such that the paper did not acknowledge the funding support from RGC. In conclusion, though the grant size was small we have obtained numerous important results which opened a gold mine for our future study.
