16307214.label: Project Objectives
16307214.value: We plan to extend the concept of the Weil index to two dimensional local fields and prove the product formula for surfaces. We expect there to be two types of product formulas, the first is over all the curves passing through a given point, the second is over all the point in a given curve. Weil's product formula for the Weil index was proved for global fields, i.e., the function fields of curves over a finite field or number fields. We plan to generalize the formula to the functional field of curves over a local field. We plan to study the harmonic analysis on the adeles of an arithmetic surface with a goal to interpreting the Riemann-Roch-Faltings theorem on arithmetic surfaces as a representation theoretic result. We plan to study the symmetric spaces over loop groups and applications to automorphic forms.

16307214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16307214.value: The study of symmetry is systematized and formalized in the areas of mathematics called group theory and representation theory. Loop groups are among the most important infinite dimensional groups. The part of representation theory related to loop groups and their algebraic counterpart, affine Kac-Moody algebras, has been developing rapidly in last two decades. This project is a continuation of the two previous projects that study automorphic forms of loop groups. We plan to extend the concept of Weil index to two dimensional local fields and prove a product formula of the Weil index on surfaces over finite fields and arithmetic surfaces. We will also study harmonic analysis on adeles over surfaces and try to interpret the Riemann-Roch-Faltings theorem for arithmetic surfaces as a representation theoretic result. We will study symmetric spaces of loop groups and their applications to automorphic forms. 群論和表示論是系統化研究對稱性的數學領域。 圈群是最 重要的無窮維群之一。 圈群的表示論及其对应的仿射Kac-Moody代數的表示論， 在過去的二十多年里得到了迅速发展。 本項目主要研究圈群的自守型， 它是前兩個項目的发展和继续。 我們計劃推广 Weil 指數的概念， 使之适用于二維局部域； 并证明有限域上曲面和算术曲面Weil 指數的 乘积公式。我們也會研究的高阶adele 环的 调和分析， 并 試圖用之解釋算术曲面的黎曼 - 羅克 - Faltings定理。我們將研究 圈群的對稱空間，及在圈群的自守型中的应用。

And we proved a product formula for Weil index that generalizes the product for finite dimensional groups. 16400114.label: Project Title(Chinese)
16400114.value: 清代官员仕途之空间、时间、与社会网络影响因素研究：创建基于缙绅录的全国性数据库及其分析

16400114.label: Co - Investigator(s)
16400114.value: Prof Lee, James Z. Prof Ren, Yuxue

16400114.label: Project Objectives
16400114.value: Transcribe the Qing 缙绅录 (Jin shen lu) into a national database of postings of officials at specific points in time during the Qing. The Co-I, Professor Ren Yuxue, has already overseen the entry of 28,000 records covering northeast China. While the complete quarterly 缙绅录 consists of at least 209 quarterly editions with several million records, our initial goal will be to enter sets of editions from the mid-18th century to the beginning of the 20th that are adjacent or nearly adjacent to each other, and leave editions that are separated from others by long gaps for later. Our experience is that editions that are nearly adjacent to each other are easy to enter, because coders can copy over the previous ones and edit. By contrast, editions separated by long gaps are much more time consuming. As funding permits, we will fill in the gaps and enter the isolated editions. Develop and apply programs for nominative linkage to gather together records of the same official in different years and assign them a common identifier, thereby creating career histories. Experiments with northeastern data provided by Professor Ren suggest that on average, there are as many five records per unique name, suggesting that the database may provide data on as many as 500,000 distinct officials. However, there may be cases where there are more than one official with the same name. We will develop routines to make use of other data in the records to separate the records of officials who have the same name. Characterize key temporal and spatial patterns in the distribution of official postings during the Qing. This will include basic descriptive statistics on the numbers of officials by year, location, office (衙门/yamen), bureaucratic rank, ethnicity (民族), banner (旗分), and position. Characterize bureaucratic careers by analysis of linked records of the same official. We will produce basic descriptive statistics on the total number of years of service per official, and the number, variety, and geographic spread of assignments. We will examine trends and geographic patterns in these descriptive statistics to gain insight into changes in career trajectories over time and geographic differences. Examine patterns of movement between locations, offices (衙门/yamen), and positions by application of mobility tables to career data of individual officials. This analysis will focus on whether service in specific locations, offices, or positions had a consistent effect on the chances of attaining higher, more important positions. Examine the influence of social networks on subsequent attainment chances through application of social network techniques. We will investigate whether service at the same time in the same office with other officials generated systematic associations in subsequent career paths due to junior officials forming ties with more senior officials that benefited their subsequent careers, or because officials at the same level formed ties with each other that benefited them later. Assess the implication of the results for our understanding of the Qing bureaucracy, which currently is based heavily on case studies of specific locations or offices, or traditional institutional or legal history. While results are likely to reaffirm many existing generalizations about the Qing bureaucracy, we expect that because our approach is largely complementary to previous approaches to the study of the Qing bureaucracy, it will reveal novel patterns and trends that will hopefully inspire new lines of inquiry using more traditional methods.

16400114.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16400114.value: We propose to study spatial and social network influences on the career trajectories of Qing officials through creation and analysis of a database of 200,000 records of as many as 40,000 officials the Jinshen Lu (缙绅录). We will characterize key patterns in the promotion and assignment of officials during the Qing. We are specifically interested in how a bureaucrat’s place of origin, location and nature of initial and later assignments, and other characteristics shaped their career trajectories. In examining the influence of place of origin and location of assignments, we are specifically interested in the role of two types of networks. First, we will examine how the number and characteristics of officials from the same place of origin affected an official’s own career trajectory. Second, we will examine how the trajectories of other officials who served concurrently in the same location affected an official’s own trajectory. We will focus on whether there were coat-tail effects. Separately, we will also examine whether service in specific locations, or assignments that were considered especially difficult, were predictive of more favorable trajectories. We will create the required database of bureaucratic careers from surviving copies of the Jinshen Lu. During the Qing, the government distributed lists of active officials four times a year. These lists include names, place of origin, bureaucratic rank, current postings, and other information for all active officials. To create the database, we will begin by transcribing surviving copies of the Jinshen Lu to a database. This phase will build on work already done by the Co-I, Professor Yuxue Ren at Shanghai Jiaotong University, who in connection with her own ongoing research has already completed entry of records for officials who served in northeast China. Following a coding system that Professor Ren has already refined, we will enter the data for the rest of China. Drawing on the PI’s extensive experience with automated record linkage and creation of large, longitudinal databases, we will link the records of the same officials at different points in time to create the career histories that will be the basis of the analysis. To address the questions described earlier, we will apply latent growth curve modeling and other techniques that have been developed for studying determinants of career and other life course trajectories. We will also prepare the database for release so that other researchers can analyze it or link it to databases they are creating. 我们建议通过创建并分析由缙绅录中记载之有关多达40000名官员的200000项纪录所构成的数据库，研究空间与社会网络对清代官员仕途的影响。我们将描述有清一代官员晋升与任命的关键性模式。我们尤为关注官僚的籍贯、首次及之后历次所任的地点与职务性质以及其它特征如何形塑其仕途发展轨迹。在检视籍贯与任所的影响时，我们尤为关注两类网络所扮演的角色。其一，我们将检视同乡中出仕者的人数与特征如何影响官员自身的仕途发展轨迹。其二，我们将检视同在一处为官的同僚之仕途轨迹如何影响官员自身的仕途发展軌跡。我们将着重考察是否存在所谓“衣尾效应”。此外，我们也将检视任职于特定地方或出任被认为特别难做的职务，是否可作為預測日後仕途更為通達的因素。 我们将基于存世的缙绅录卷本创建所需的官僚仕途数据库。有清一代，清廷每年均會四度发布在任官员的名录。这些名录包括所有在任官员的姓名、籍贯、品阶、现职及其它信息。为创建这一数据库，我们首先将存世的缙绅录卷本转录为数据库。这一阶段将基于Co-I即上海交通大学任玉雪教授已完成的工作。任教授在其本人正在开展的研究中，已完成了对曾任职华北的官员纪录的输入工作。遵循业经任教授优化的编码体系，我们将输入余下来自中国其它地方的纪录。凭借PI运用软件进行纪录链接及创建大型历时数据库的丰富经验，我们将把同一官员在不同时点的纪录链接起来，从而创建作为我们分析之基础的职业史资料。 为了解答上述研究问题，我们将运用为研究职业与其它生命历程轨迹而发展起来的潜在增长曲线模型及其它分析技术。我们亦将整理该数据库以备发布，从而其他研究人员也可以分析或将其与他们正创建的数据库相链接。

16400114.label: Realisation of objectives
16400114.value: We have constructed a database from quarterly editions of the Jinshenlu (缙绅录) contained in the Qingdai Jinshenlu Collection (清代缙绅录集成) published by Tsinghua University Library, fulfilling the most important task of our objectives (Objective #1). At present it contains 2.78 million records of 300,060 officials. 2.25 million records of 184,613 officials are from the period 1850-1912, for which our database now has nearly continuous coverage. The remainder are from the mid-18th century to 1850. Complete longitudinal data on nearly all civil officials from 1850 to 1912 allows not only for the study of individual careers, but also the composition of central government ministries and agencies, and provincial and local administrations. We have made these data available to other researchers and the general public. We created a website where historians, genealogists and others interested in the career records of specific officials can search them by name: http://vis.cse.ust.hk/searchjsl/ The website has received 8893 queries so far. As described in section 11, we entered into a collaboration with the Institute for Qing History at Renmin University. We exchanged data with researchers led by Liu Cheng-yun at the Institute of History and Philology at the Academia Sinica. We also extracted data on specific counties for researchers at Sophia University, HKUST, and Xiamen University. We developed programs for nominative linkage (Objective #2) to produce unique identifiers to use in our analysis. For Han Chinese officials, nominative linkage was straightforward, since the combination of surname, given name, province and county tended to be unique. We wrote software to convert all the names to pinyin to account for characters replaced by homonyms. We also wrote software to harmonize different orthographies of the same character. For Bannermen (旗人), nominative linkage was challenging because most were not recorded with surnames or place of origin. Banner affiliation (旗分) tended to be stable, so we were able to use that to disambiguate Bannermen officials with the same name. We have characterized temporal and spatial patterns in the composition of Qing officialdom by producing descriptive statistics on the numbers of officials by year, location, office (衙门/yamen), bureaucratic rank, banner (旗分), ethnicity (民族), basis of appointment (出身) and position (Objective #3). Research output 1 in C8 presents many of these descriptive statistics, and research output 2 includes results on the geographic distribution of officials. Outputs 4-7 also present tabulations or other summaries of officials’ characteristics, focusing on the period between 1900-1912. We included basic descriptive results on trends in the composition of officials by basis of appointment, banner/civilian status, bureaucratic rank and other characteristics in most of the conference presentations in C9, and they are included in manuscripts we are currently preparing. To better understand trends and patterns in the composition of officials we initiated a collaboration with the Institute of Qing History at Renmin University. We initiated the collaboration with them because as analysis for Objective #3 began to yield results on changes over time and differences by region, it became clear that we would need to work with specialists in Qing institutional history to interpret these results. The Qing was a time of considerable change, especially in the last few decades, and it was very apparent that we would need a better understanding of the context in each period for us to interpret what was happening. We developed a collaboration in which we will work with the faculty at the Institute of Qing History to understand what is going on in specific periods, beginning with the New Government (新政) period between 1900 and 1912. Outputs 4, 6, and 7 in C8 are results of this collaboration. We produced output 4 on Banner and Imperial Lineage officials during the New Government Period, and collaborators at Renmin University produced 6 and 7 using data that we shared with them. We have additional manuscripts in progress on examination degree holders during the New Government period. We conducted analyses of careers (Objective #4) using the linked longitudinal data on individual officials produced in connection with Objective #2. Analysis has already revealed some basic facts about official careers in Qing China, for example, half of all officials served for less than four years, and only one-quarter of officials served for more than ten years. Length of service did not vary much by the basis of appointment, except that holders of the jinshi (进士) degree had slightly higher chances of serving longer. We have also calculated the chances of reaching high office (bureaucratic ranks 品级1-3), numbers of positions held, and numbers of locations served according to various background characteristics. We have presented results at major international conferences. The presentations are listed in section 9. We have focused on comparisons in careers according to basis of appointment, determinants of the career trajectories of examination degree holders, and determinants of the career trajectories of officials who were Bannermen. We are completing manuscripts and expect to submit them in the next year. Bijia Chen, our 4th year HKPFS PhD student, is also working on this for her dissertation, expected to be completed in 2019. As described in section 11, we have worked with Lawrence Zhang on the careers of officials who purchased the position. We have made considerable progress on the examination of patterns of movement between locations, offices (衙门/yamen), and positions (Objective #5). Some of the analysis are incorporated in the studies of careers that we are preparing in connection with objective #4, and other results are included in the papers on the New Government period that we and our collaborations at Renmin University have been writing. We are developing plans for new papers on the mobility of officials, including a study of mobility that we intend to write with Hu Heng at Renmin University. We made less progress on the analysis of social networks (Objective #6) because we only had enough data towards the end of the project period. We carried out exploratory work on whether the emergence of a major official from a county led to an increase in the number of other officials from the same province or county. For example, we have found that the rise of Zeng Guofan not only led to an increase in the number of officials from Hunan, but specifically to a sustained increase in the number of officials surnamed Zeng and from Xiangxiang county. We seek to scale this up and move from the study of individual cases to larger patterns. We are now in talks with a colleague at HKUST, Franziska Barbara-Keller, who is an expert on social networks in the contemporary Chinese bureaucracy and may collaborate on this analysis. Our results have yielded insights into the Qing bureaucracy (Objective #7). Outputs 1, 2, and 5 include results on the bureaucracy in general. We have been particularly successful in developing a better understanding of the period 1900-1912 as a result of our collaboration with the Institute of Qing History at Renmin University, and outputs 4, 6 and 7 include relevant results.

16400114.label: Major findings and research outcome
16400114.value: The most important research outcome is the creation of the database itself. By providing longitudinal, micro-level data on the careers of nearly all officials who served in the late Qing, and eventually in earlier periods, the Jinshenlu database will be a major resource for the study of Qing history, and bureaucracy more generally, and will support investigations of a wide variety of topics. It is also a tool for traditional historians conducting research on specific individuals, locations, or government offices, as apparent in the number of queries at the website (8893) and the requests for extracts for specific counties. We have shared our experience with this and other quantitative historical databases in an opinion piece (Output #8). Basic descriptive results from the database have provided important insights into the composition of the Qing bureaucracy. Output 1 presents some of the key findings. First, Bannermen, not Han civilians, numerically dominated the upper echelons of the Qing state. Analysis of the officials who worked in the Six Ministries in the central government shows that they were predominantly Bannermen. According to Table 6 of output 1, more than one-half of the highest-ranked officials (ranks 1-3) in the Six Ministries were Bannermen. This is important empirical confirmation of the effects of previously known Bannermen quotas in appointment and promotion. We have also quantified the shares of officials serving at different ranks according to the basis of their appointment. According to Table 7 in output 1, Bannermen and jinshi (holders of the highest exam degree) had the best chances of serving in high office, with just over 3% holding ranks 1-3. However, according to Table 8, Bannermen accounted for more than one-half of officials ranked 1-3, and jinshi accounted for less than one-fifth of officials. Among officials ranked 4-6, there were nearly as many holders of purchased degrees (jiansheng) as there were jinshi: 13.11% and 14.73%. We have also shown that civilian (non-Banner) officials were drawn from all over the country, with Jiangsu and Zhejiang overrepresented, and that the shares from different regions was stable over time (Figure 2 in output #2). Output #5 shows how the Qing state made use of its information about specific counties to rate them, and then use these ratings to assign officials. Outputs #4, 6 and 7 present detailed results on changes in the composition of government offices and positions during the New Government period.

16400114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16400114.value: Firstly, we are expanding the Jinshenlu database to contain editions that were not in the Tsinghua Library collection that was the basis of this project. We have already begun entering editions in the holdings of Harvard and Columbia libraries, and we are seeking access to others held at Peking University and the National Library. We expect that funding permitted, we will eventually have 5,000,000 records of approximately 500,000 officials from the mid-17th century to 1912. Second, with support from a GRF (16601718) awarded in 2018/19, we are collecting data on the family background of officials who held examination degrees so that we can assess intergenerational associations. Third, we are experimenting with linkage between these data and ancestry data for Republican-era university students collected in connection with two GRF supported projects (16602117 and 640613) to study continuity in elite composition from the Qing into the 20th century. Fourth, we are planning comparative projects. We are awaiting the outcome of an application for support from the ANR/RGC scheme for a comparison of the civil services of France and China, and in 2019 will reapply to a Korean agency for support for a comparison between the Choseon Korean and Qing Chinese bureaucracies.

16400114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16400114.value: We have created and analysed a new database of personnel records for civil servants in the late Qing that will be an important resource for the study of Chinese history in coming decades. Our results so far have illuminated the structure and composition of the Qing bureaucracy, including the roles played by Bannermen and civilians and the holders of exam and purchased degrees. Key findings include demonstration that Bannermen dominated the upper reaches of the Qing bureaucracy and that holders of the highest degrees (jinshi) accounted for only a small share of the highest officials. We have also shown that official careers were short, with half of the officials serving for less than three years, and only one quarter serving for more than ten years. Through collaboration with traditional historians, we have learned more about the New Government period between 1900 and 1912. Civilian officials were drawn from all over the country, though Jiangsu and Zhejiang were overrepresented. We have also made a searchable version of the database available online for anyone who would like to search for an ancestor or other person of interest: http://vis.cse.ust.hk/searchjsl/

16400314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16400314.value: Globalization brings people from different cultural backgrounds together. Although recent research has illuminated the advantages of multicultural exposure (e.g., Maddux & Galinsky, 2009; Tadmor, Hong, Chao, Wiruchnipawan, & Wang, 2012), intercultural contacts also bring about conflicts (e.g., Torelli & Cheng, 2011). Given that negotiation provides a means to resolve discordances (De Dreu & Carnevale, 2003), scholars have recognized the importance of being able to negotiate effectively across cultures (e.g., Adair, Okumura, & Brett, 2001; Imai & Gelfand, 2010). Negotiation is a social interaction through which individuals with shared and/or opposing interests communicate to resolve problems or conflicts. Negotiating across cultures has been shown to be particularly challenging compared with negotiating within culture because the negotiators might adopt and interpret information sharing and behavioral strategies differently (e.g., Adair et al., 2001; Gelfand et al., 2001). Building on research that focuses on cross-cultural differences in values, cognitive styles, and conflict management strategies, early studies on culture and negotiation took on a comparative approach to investigate differences in negotiation behaviors across cultures (see Gelfand et al., 2001); however, as Kray (2005) pointed out, “although researchers have identified a host of cross-cultural differences in styles and preferences, … knowledge about factors influencing the effectiveness of intercultural negotiations is sparse” (p. 159). The proposed research aims to fill this void. Specifically, going beyond the traditional focus of cross-cultural differences in negotiation, the proposed research investigates how lay people’s understanding of cultural differences colors their experiences in cross-cultural negotiation. It advances the cross-cultural negotiation literature by (1) proposing and testing two alternative theoretical perspectives in understanding how lay people’s beliefs about cultural differences influence intercultural dynamics, (2) dissecting the psychological processes underlying negotiation successes/failures, and (3) identifying the boundary condition that might enable individuals to harvest the most benefits out of their intercultural interactions. Aside from contributing to the negotiation literature theoretically and empirically, the proposed research also has important practical implications. Findings from the proposed studies will increase individuals’ awareness of how their understanding of cultural differences might color their intercultural experiences. Such meta-cognitive awareness could facilitate intercultural communication and enable individuals to manage conflicts effectively in the increasingly globalized world. 全球化促使來自不同文化背景的人聚集。儘管最近的研究已闡述了多元文化接觸的優點（例如，Maddux & Galinsky, 2009; Tadmor, Hong, Chao, Wiruchnipawan, & Wang, 2012），跨文化接觸亦帶來衝突（例如，Torelli & Cheng, 2011）。鑒於談判提供解決衝突的方法（De Dreu & Carnevale, 2003），學者們已確認研究跨文化談判的重要性（例如， Adair, Okumura, & Brett, 2001; Imai & Gelfand, 2010）。談判是一種社會互動，通過談判，持共同或相反利益的個體可以解決問題和衝突。跨文化談判與單一文化談判相比，前者具有較高的挑戰性，因為談判者可能對共享的信息有不同的詮釋，和採納不同的行為策略（如，Adair et al., 2001; Gelfand et al., 2001）。 基於過往的文獻著重研究價值觀、認知風格與衝突管理策略在不同文化之間的差異，早期有關文化和談判的研究一般通過用對比的方法來研究文化差異（見Gelfand et al., 2001）；然而，Kray（2005, p. 159）指出，“雖然研究人員已經識別了許多談判風格和偏好的文化差異，......有關影響跨文化談判成效因素的知識卻極為貧乏”。本研究旨在加深對此相關的知識。具體來說，本文超越過往探討文化差異的研究，去探索本質主義及社會認同如何影響人們在跨文化談判的經驗。本研究通過以下三點，豐富了有關跨文化談判的知識：（1）提出並驗證兩種理論視角，探討人們對文化差異的信念如何影響跨文化動力，（2）仔細分析影響談判成功或失敗的心理過程基礎，以及（3）識別在跨文化談判中可以使個人穫得最大利益的情況界限。 除了在理論和實證上對談判的文獻有所貢獻，本文提出的研究亦具有重要的實用意義。研究結果將增加個人對跨文化談判及跨文化談判成效因素的理解。在日益全球化的世界，此元認知的意識可以促進不同文化之間的溝通，使個人有效地管理的衝突。

16400414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16400414.value: This project proposes to study the social and cultural significance of documentary films about writers in Taiwan from the 1990s to the present. It aims to investigate, on the one hand, the cinematic engagement with literature, specifically, the participation of documentary in the canonization of modern Taiwanese literature, and on the other hand, the role that this cinematic production has played in the development of Taiwan’s mass culture in the last two decades. As this study involves intricate questions of screen representations of literary authorship and creative endeavor, it calls for a critical reflection of a host of interrelated cultural and theoretical issues pertaining to our culture’s pursuit of auratic experience. The project, while focusing on Taiwan, will also explore how Taiwan’s documentary films about its most respected writers provide a platform for us to revisit and rethink Walter Benjamin’s concept of aura, one of the most invoked terms in literary and media theories. Through the case of Taiwan, the project will examine the imagination of aura in our age of mechanical reproduction in an attempt to understand the relationship of our new media culture and literature from the historical and theoretical perspectives. 本研究計劃將以1990年間以至晚近的台灣作家紀錄片為對象，一方面討論以作家為主的紀錄片與文學經典化的關係，另一方面檢視此類紀錄片在大眾通俗文化發展中所扮演的角色。 本計劃將從文化研究、媒體理論與歷史分析角度，深入探討作家紀錄片的社會與文化意義，透過台灣的案例，考察大眾媒體想像與文學的深層互動。

16400414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16400414.value: The case study of Taiwanese documentaries has a range of implications for contemporary documentary culture in the global context, specifically, the transformation of documentary discourse and the impact of documentary on the mass culture in various periods under different circumstances and technical development. On the other hand, the methodology developed in my study has potential for more widespread application in the conceptualization as well as the performative dimension of a cultural product that we call “documentary” today.

16400414.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16400414.value: This research project cuts across literary studies and film studies. Currently there is a conspicuous lack of academic work in both literary and film studies that deals with the subject of literary biography in documentaries. Through the study of Taiwan’s documentary films about writers, this project fills the gap and conducts systematic research into various aspects and implications of this intriguing genre. The project contributes to our understanding of the multiple dimensions of the engagement of documentary films with literature and literary lives, and the cultural and visual connotations entailed by the production and reception of this documentary genre as a form of social practice and visual art.

16400514.label: Project Objectives
16400514.value: To shed new light on the work of well-known figures, such as Carl Schmitt, while at the same time broadening our understanding of Nazi-era international thought to encompass many other historically significant but understudied intellectuals, using both published literature as well as archival sources. To reconstruct the history and significance of Nazi-era debates over the meaning of neutrality, the concept of war, the theory of hegemony, and the concept of empire, and to contextualize them both within the tradition of German political thought and the immediate institutional and ideological struggles of the Third Reich. To demonstrate how the cultural memory of the Allied blockade of Germany between 1914 and 1919 shaped the theories of international law developed by German jurists between 1933 and 1945. To evaluate the ways in which intellectuals in Nazi Germany mobilized historical writing to critique the interwar international order and propagandize on behalf of the regime. To determine the degree to which German international thinkers in the Nazi period appropriated concepts and concerns from American contemporaries. To trace the reception of Nazi-era international thought among intellectuals in the United States between the 1930s and 1950s. To gauge the lasting impact and relevance of the German critique of liberal internationalism for contemporary political thought.

16400514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16400514.value: Conceived as a study in intellectual history, this project seeks to analyze and contextualize German theorizing about international affairs between 1933 and 1945. The Nazi dictatorship presided over a surge in publications on all matters related to international law, geopolitics, and international history, especially the history of empires and colonial expansion. This literature helped justify the regime’s foreign policy to its own citizens as well as to outside observers, and enabled German intellectuals of diverse ideological commitments to “work towards” what they envisaged as the regime’s goals. My aim is to produce the first monograph that gives a comprehensive account of the international theories that were produced in Germany under Nazi rule. It will focus on a broad range of figures including the geopolitician Karl Haushofer; the jurists Friedrich Berber, Werner Best, Carl Bilfinger, Viktor Bruns, Wilhelm Grewe, Norbert Gürke, Reinhard Höhn, Ernst Rudolf Huber, Hermann Jahrreiß, Günther Küchenhoff, Theodor Maunz, Paul Ritterbusch, Heinrich Rogge, Ulrich Scheuner, Carl Schmitt, Heinrich Triepel, Gustav Adolf Walz, and Ernst Wolgast; and the historians Paul Herre, Adolf Rein, and Christoph Steding. Three main approaches guide my research into the history of Nazi-era international thought. First, I seek to understand how the cultural memory of the First World War came to structure large parts of German international thinking. Many of the key concepts of Nazi-era international law and geopolitics, I hypothesize, can be traced back to wartime or interwar critiques of the Allied blockade of Germany. Second, I plan to investigate the role that grand historical theorizing played in the development of international thought in Nazi Germany. I am interested in understanding how German intellectuals mobilized the genre of international history as part of their larger attempt to justify—or otherwise come to terms with—the transformations to the international system wrought by Nazi Germany. Finally, I wish to investigate how American and émigré scholars interpreted the significance of Nazi-era international thought, and what lessons they drew for the possibilities of international order in the postwar world. In pursuing these questions, I hope to contribute to the history of the human sciences in Nazi Germany, to deepen our understanding of the critique of liberal internationalism that was developed there, and, more broadly, to shed light on some of the darker sources of modern international thought. 本課題旨於將德國政治思潮置於1933-1945年間的國際問題中進行分析。德國知識分子在第三帝國期間對基於政治地理的國際秩序有眾多著述，內容涵蓋國際法中日漸式微的中立原則、戰爭的定義、現代世界帝國的特性等。本課題力圖為全面回顧納粹統治下德國國際思潮的開學界先河。

16400514.label: Realisation of objectives
16400514.value: Objective 1: The initial focus of my study was the German jurist Carl Schmitt, the best known Nazi-era theorist of international relations. In addition to carefully studying Schmitt's published writings, I examined his personal papers in the state archive of North-Rhine Westphalia (March 2016 and March 2017), and collected a large amount of contemporary periodical literature which helped me put his writings in historical context (April 2015). I wrote two articles that deal with Schmitt’s relationship to lesser-known intellectuals who shared his ideas: a book chapter titled “The Idea of Thalassocracy in Nazi Germany: Carl Schmitt and Ernst Wolgast on Sea Power in History,” forthcoming (2018) in an edited volume published by Walter de Gruyter; and a manuscript of a book chapter titled “Modern Imperialism and International Law: Carl Schmitt and Ernst Rudolf Huber on the ‘International Legal Order’ of Great Spaces,” for an edited volume which is currently under review at Bloomsbury Press. Another focus of my research has been Ferdinand Fried, one of the most prominent economics writers in Germany during the 1930s and 1940s. During the Second World War, Fried devoted his efforts to articulating a vision of a postwar world order based on “great spaces,” continental blocs that would strive for semi-autarky but nonetheless engage in trade with each other. I examined Fried’s personal papers in the Federal Archive in Koblenz (February 2016 and June 2017), his Stasi file (June 2017), and his postwar interrogation reports in the National Archives in College Park, Maryland (September and October 2016). In the newspaper division of the Berlin State Library, I tracked down every piece of journalism he published between 1933 and 1945 (June 2017). I plan to submit an article manuscript about Fried to a major peer-reviewed journal of European history, such as the Journal of Modern History, in the summer of 2018. I have also investigated the career of Fried’s colleague, the journalist Giselher Wirsing, who similarly endorsed a postwar world order based on great spaces. I interviewed his daughter Sibille Wirsing in Berlin (February 2016), located his correspondence in the papers of Carl Schmitt, and tracked down documents related to him in the ministerial archives of the Federal Archive in Berlin (February 2016) and the East German Ministry for State Security (June 2017). After completing my article on Ferdinand Fried, I plan to write an article on Wirsing’s career in the Third Reich and postwar period. Objective 2 One of my goals in this project has been to reconstruct Nazi-era debates about international law and relations. During an early research trip to Germany (April 2015), I systematically worked through all the major journals on law and politics published in Nazi Germany. This groundwork helped me focus on one topic in particular: the German reception of the Tripartite Pact, the treaty signed between Germany, Italy, and Japan in September 1940 which pledged to recognize German-Italian hegemony in Europe and Japanese hegemony in East Asia. As I expanded my research on this topic, I examined the files of the German Foreign Office (July and August 2016) and collected all the diplomatic materials related to the signing of the Tripartite Pact. I also tracked down literature about the Tripartite Pact in the Federal Archive in Berlin and the Berlin State Library (July and August 2016). I visited the National Archives in College Park, Maryland, to view the captured records and interrogation reports of Japanese and German officials who had been involved in negotiating the Tripartite Pact (September and October 2016). I have written a draft on an article on this topic, which I plan to submit to a peer reviewed journal, such as Diplomatic History, in the fall of 2018, after I have conducted some final research in Germany this summer. Objective 3: I initially hypothesized that the cultural memory of the First World War blockade would play a major role in structuring German international thought. Some themes related to the blockade and maritime law are addressed in my forthcoming book chapter on “The Idea of Thalassocracy in Nazi Germany.” However, as I continued my research, I began to realize that the blockade was not the skeleton key to understanding German international thought that I thought it might be. My research and reading were useful in helping me to realize that this avenue would not be central to my broader project. Objective 4: The ways in which German intellectuals mobilized historical writing to critique the liberal international order has remained a major focus of my research. My book chapter, “The Idea of Thalassocracy in Nazi Germany,” discusses two German law professors, Carl Schmitt and Ernst Wolgast, who devoted their intellectual energies during the Second World War to examining the history of British sea power and its significance for the Third Reich. Objective 5: I have been keen to understand how Carl Schmitt read and appropriated contemporary American discourse about imperialism and the Monroe Doctrine. My book chapter under review, “Modern Imperialism and International Law,” focuses on Schmitt’s analysis of America’s foreign relations with Caribbean and Latin American nations at the turn of the twentieth century. I trace Schmitt’s evolving understanding of American imperialism, and the ways in which he altered his concept of imperialism to legitimate Nazi conquest during the Second World War. Objective 6: When I began my research project, I was interested in understanding how postwar American intellectuals and German émigrés appropriated ideas initially associated with German geopolitics and international law. Since then, Or Rosenboim’s study of wartime Anglo-American international theorists, The Emergence of Globalism (2017), has appeared, and Matthew Specter will soon publish a book titled Atlantic Realisms, which deals with Schmitt’s intellectual afterlife in the Cold War United States. The originality of my research project, I have come to realize, lies in its capacity to shed new light on a topic that many historians have thought they understood, but about which there is far more to tell: the foreign policy imagination of German intellectuals during the Second World War. I have thus decided to remove the question of postwar American reception from my study, and focus more specifically on the German side of the story. Objective 7: Since I began my project, its present-day relevance has become obvious in ways I hadn’t initially expected. One of Vladimir Putin’s closest advisors, Aleksandr Dugin, styles himself as a latter-day disciple of Carl Schmitt. Chinese legal theorists are engaged in vigorous debate about Schmitt’s vision of an “international legal order of great spaces,” and the One Belt One Road initiative has stimulated much discussion about the significance of “land and sea” in China’s foreign relations. The election of Donald J. Trump as president of the United States has raised, however briefly, the prospect of a grand partitioning of the world into spheres of interest among the great powers; his chief advisor, Steve Bannon, anticipated that the Trump presidency would be “as exciting as the 1930s.” As I write, the prospect of an international trade war that hobbles the liberal economic order is looming on the horizon. Though the German intellectuals I study may have lost some of their immediate relevance in the postwar decades, their longing for a nonliberal world order clearly exerts a powerful attraction for many thinkers today.

16400514.label: Major findings and research outcome
16400514.value: My research project has yielded all the materials -- and, in the form of finished manuscripts and works in progress, many of the constituent chapters -- for a book about the global imagination of German intellectuals during the Third Reich. When I began this project, I knew that the topic of international thought and the Third Reich was an important but understudied one, but I didn't yet know how to divide it into sub-themes or chapters. In the course of my research, I identified a group of intellectuals whose careers began in Weimar Germany, reached their apex during the Third Reich, and, in many cases, continued in the Federal Republic of Germany. They were among the first and usually most vocal proponents of a nonliberal world order to challenge the international order created at the Paris Peace Conference: it would be based on the partitioning of the world into Großräume or "great spaces," continental spheres of influence under the hegemony of leading powers, who would nonetheless -- as a totality -- constitute something resembling a stable global order. While Carl Schmitt is perhaps the best remembered of these thinkers, I have conducted detailed research on three other contemporaries--Ferdinand Fried, Giselher Wirsing, and Ernst Wolgast--whose ideas anticipated Schmitt's in important ways. I have also studied a number of debates--the reception of the Monroe Doctrine, the formation of the Tripartite Pact--which pull together the key ideas and protagonists of my study. I have also gained a much clearer understanding of the early twentieth-century background, and modern day relevance, of this wartime vision and its significance for the history of international thought. I now feel very confident about the direction of the book manuscript and the impact it may have on the fields of German history, global history, and the history of ideas.

16400514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16400514.value: Most of the research for the book manuscript has been completed; what remains can probably be accomplished in a number of short archival visits to Germany, one of which I will make in the summer of 2018. My major course of action is now to finish writing the article/chapter manuscripts that have emerged from the research. This process has taken somewhat longer than expected, primarily because it took a while to disaggregate a large body of material with many interconnections into a number of discrete sub-themes. Having now established the subject matter of each chapter, I feel that the writing process will accelerate, and that I will have completed an additional two or three article or chapter-length pieces of writing related to the project in the next year. I would like to submit some of these pieces for publication in peer reviewed journals, before ultimately including revised versions as chapters in my monograph.

16400514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16400514.value: This research project will yield the first intellectual history of Großraumdenken or "great space thinking," the peculiar vision of global order that flourished in Nazi Germany and provided much of the propaganda and legitimation for the regime's foreign policy. Even after Nazi Germany's defeat, the vision of a nonliberal global order based on continental spheres of influence continues to exert a powerful attraction on intellectuals all over the world. Much of the literature on this topic focuses exclusively on the exegesis of Carl Schmitt's legal writings. By examining a circle of important but lesser known contemporaries, many of whom anticipated Schmitt's ideas or offered alternative conceptions to his own, my research will shed new light on the history and significance of this current of international thought. So far, my research has produced a book chapter in press; a book chapter under review; and an article manuscript that is near completion. I expect the project to generate at least two more manuscripts for submission to peer-reviewed journals in the next year. Taken together, these pieces of writing will constitute the chapters of a monograph.

16400614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16400614.value: We study a repeated game in which players’ outside options are unknown to players. Each period, players can take an action to learn their outside options. If the realized outside option of a player is sufficiently high, then the player may prefer to choose the outside option over cooperating in the relationship. In some realizations of outside options, it is mutually beneficial to both players to take the outside options. Also suppose that if a player explores his/her outside option, there is a positive probability that the action is detected by the other player. The question is whether players should be allowed to explore their outside options in the design of an optimal relational contract. The tradeoff is that allowing players to explore their outside options on the one hand destabilizes the game and on the other hand allows players to reap the potential efficiency gain from discovering outside options which are potentially superior to the highest equilibrium payoffs from staying in the relationship. The first objective of this project is to characterize the precise condition under which it is mutually beneficial to allow one or both players in a relational contract to explore their outside options as the relationship progresses. In other words, we intend to characterize the optimal tolerance to cheating/infidelity. We believe this study will make an important contribution to the literature of relational contracts where the outside option is usually taken as exogenously given while in real life it is clearly not the case. We also believe that our model will provide a useful vehicle for analyzing a number of interesting questions which we'll elaborate in a later section. 我們研究了重複博弈中，參與人不知道自己和對手的外部選擇的情況。每一期，參與人可以採取行動來探索他們的外部選擇。如果參與人發現外部選擇足夠的吸引，他可能更喜歡外部選擇而終止合作的關係。在某些情況下（例如外部選擇足夠吸引），兩個參與人都選擇外部選擇是互惠互利的。 假定如果一個參與人探索她的外部選擇，其行動是有機會給對手發現的。現在的問題是最佳的關係契約是否應該允許參與人探索其以外部選擇。 讓參與人去探索的代價是合作關係的穩定性會被動搖，但另一方面這樣做可以容許參與人獲得更好的機會。該項目的第一個目標是找出在什麼的條件下，讓雙方學習他們的外部選擇是互惠互利的。我們相信這項研究將對關係契約的文獻作出重要貢獻。

16400614.label: Realisation of objectives
16400614.value: We have accomplished most of our originally stated objectives. Also, due to the support of this RGC grant, we have also written and published another paper in Economics Letters. Objective 1 is 100% completed. In the current, polished version of our paper, we have developed a model in which players play an infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma game and can choose to make investment to explore their unknown outside options. The actual outside option is stochastically determined. Objective 2 is 100% completed. We successfully characterized different types of equilibria. We also characterize conditions under which it is mutually beneficial to both players to allow the players with a stronger incentive to cooperate to explore her outside option, although doing so may risk causing the relationship to break up. Objective 3 is considered 80% completed. We originally conjectured that in the optimal equilibrium, the infidelity, or the extent to which players explore or invest in their outside options dynamically evolve overtime. As it turns out, the benefit of considering such dynamics is not apparent. In light of this discovery, we no longer consider the evolution of level of infidelity. Objective 4 is 100% completed. As pointed out in our report on Objective 2, we identify the exact conditions under which it is optimal for both players that the player less likely to cooperate refrains from search for his outside option, but the player with a stronger propensity to cooperate will search for her outside option every period. Our research project has been presented at the 2017 Asian Econometric Society Meetings. We have also published a paper at Economics Letters, titled "Liability and Reputation in Credence Goods Markets". The PI properly acknowledged the support of this RGC grant with Project Number 16400614 for both the conference presentation and the publication.

16400614.label: Major findings and research outcome
16400614.value: In many long-term relationships (e.g., business partnerships), partners choose to stay in the relationship and contribute to the relationship only if they find it in their long-term self interest to do so. The conventional wisdom is that improvement of the partners' outside options, i.e., payoffs of staying outside of the relationship, threatens the stability of the relationship. In our research project, we show that this conventional wisdom is not generally valid. When players' outside options are too low, they cannot credibly use the threat of termination of the relationship to deter cheating; following any partner's noncooperation, the partners end up staying in a sour relationship because they will be worse off if they break up with each other. We show that under some plausible conditions, by allowing the player who has a higher propensity to cooperate to explore or invest in her outside option, the other player will become more cooperative. More interestingly, both players will benefit from the more cooperative player's investment or exploration of her outside option. We have produced two research articles. The first article was presented at the 2017 Asian Econometric Society Meetings. The second article was published at Economics Letters. The PI properly acknowledged the support of this RGC grant with Project Number 16400614 for both the conference presentation and the publication.

16400714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16400714.value: 比较和可比性是一切社会科学比较研究的核心。但是，没有相似的方法和数据，精确的比较就不可能实现。近几十年来，社会人口学家，历史学家和经济史学家构建并公开了许多记录欧美历史人口的微观数据库。这些历史“大”数据的出现极大地转变了西方实证社会科学。在1986至1999这15年间，仅有100篇左右的学术著作引用了四个最具代表性的历史“大”数据库（IPUMS, Utah Population Database, Historical Sample of the Netherlands, and Scanian Economic Demographic Database）。而仅仅在2006至2010这5年间，引用相关历史“大”数据库的文献数量已经达到了2300余篇。这种新兴的学术研究范式不仅加深了我们对于许多人口行为及其历史根源的理解，更通过国际比较的视野促进了对这些问题全面深入的认识。麻省理工学院（MIT）出版社的“欧亚人口与家庭史系列著作(“Eurasian Population and Family History Series”Bengtsson et al 2004, Tsuya, et al 2010, Lundh, et al 2014)”就是一个很好的例子。 在中国以及亚洲，类似数据库的构建计划近年来也开始兴起。本研究项目将评测和比较东亚五个新的微观历史面板数据库，包括中国多代人口数据库－辽宁（CMGPD-LN）1749-1909、中国多代人口数据库－双城（CMGPD-SC）1866-1912、日本户口册数据库（NAC-SN）1716-1820、韩国多代人口数据库－丹城（KMGPD-TS）1678-1888、日治台湾户籍资料数据库（CTHRD）1906-1945。这五个数据库共包含半个世纪至两个世纪间居住在中国、日本、韩国和台湾特定地区1000个社区的61万人的370万条观测记录。我们研究计划的目的在于加深理解收集原始数据过程的主要特点和制度、由原始材料构建个人层面面板数据的后续过程、数据的具体局限与优势、以及与其他欧美历史人口相比这些数据在比较研究死亡、生育、婚姻、迁移等问题中的研究潜力。本研究计划的成果不仅将会大大推动东亚的社会科学“大”面板数据比较研究，还将促进东西方之间的新一轮微观比较。我们基于这些数据的比较人口学分析将会为加深理解过去的人口行为及相关动因贡献新的事实依据。同时我们会协调安排这些重要社会科学新数据的公开发布和用户培训，以推动亚洲和全球学界发展。

16400714.label: Major findings and research outcome
16400714.value: As proposed for the project, we have completed the five sets of objectives. Demonstrated by our 2015 Demography article, we have not only harmonized five different East Asian historical population panel datasets, but also evaluate and compare their data quality, concluding that they have high comparability and potential for comparative social science at a global scale. Our 2017 Evolution and Human Behavior article and Hao Dong’s PhD dissertation exemplifies such contribution of these new East Asian data to an important scholarship of international comparison. The new findings from the former paper highlight complex agency in kin and birth order effects on human reproduction, which has important implications to both comparative historical demography in East Asia and human evolution and behavioral ecology in general. The latter dissertation project further advances the comparative methodology in the field by melding all separate datasets and applying multilevel modelling for comparisons between populations and periods, which contributes to a better understanding of the similarities and differences between population and family behavior with new and first empirical evidence on the macro-micro interactions between patriarchy, family systems, household context, and individual demographic behaviors. Along with these research, we have also acquired much experience with constructing and analyzing big historical data and shared with the academia with our various other articles and presentations reported below. Hao Dong visited Reitaku University for six and a half months (mid-Jan to July) to work with another co-I Satomi Kurosu on expanding Japanese historical population data, understanding Japanese historical norms and institutions, and comparing behavioral patterns among East Asian historical populations. PI and all co-Is met at Reitaku University for this collaborative project. Under supervision and support of PI and other co-Is, Hao Dong conducted and defended his PhD thesis research, in line with the objective 4, analyzing how different data construction, institutions, and motivational traditions influence regional differences in family and individual population behavior in East Asia. James Lee and Hao Dong work with Tommy Bengtsson from Lund University on international comparative understanding based on the Eurasian Population and Family History Project (EAP) and the captioned funding project. This produces several conference presentations and seminars at Europe and mainland China in 2017, including a plenary talk at the European Society of Historical Demography conference at Leuven, Belgium.

16400714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16400714.value: The research led to new Big Historical Data comparisons within East Asia and with North American and European populations. It also strengthened connections with other researchers working with similar data for other East Asian and Western Europe societies, and inspired several new collaborative comparative projects to further study of the population and family behavior in East Asia and between the East and West. Additional manuscripts related to the project are currently in various stages of completion. These studies are the basis of many of the conference/seminar presentations listed in this report.

16400714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16400714.value: Our project successfully completes the tasks to construct, harmonize, and compare big data of 4 million records of 650,000 individuals in historical China, Japan, Korea and Taiwan. By so doing, we not only provide new sources for comparative social science that are comparable to similar Western data, but also improve our knowledge of how familial values and family context influence individual reproduction, survival and marriage and why such effects differ between spatial and temporal contexts. We develop new comparative methodology for the new era of increasingly available big population microdata, which, although similarly attempted by Western scholars for decades, has not yet been achieved in the field of comparative historical demography and sociology. As demonstrated by our interdisciplinary perspectives and publications, our project contributes to not only history, sociology and demography of East Asian societies in the past, but also evolution and behavioral science in general.

16400814.label: Project Objectives
16400814.value: Compare the structure of taxation at local level during the Southern Song, Yuan and early Ming periods Compare the expenditures of local government during these centuries Compare the modes of financial administration between Southern Song and Early Ming dynasty
rows: Compare the structure of taxation at local level during the Southern Song, Yuan and early Ming periods
Compare the expenditures of local government during these centuries
Compare the modes of financial administration between Southern Song and Early Ming dynasty

16400814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16400814.value: Based on a systematic collection and careful examination of financial data from local Chinese administrative units, especially that at the prefecture and county levels, this reaserch project demonstrates how political power in pre-industrial China operated in a fiscal dimension, say, how did money matter to Chinese local bureaucracy, how did local officials manage to collect taxes with/without the support of the gentry class, and most important, was there a linear relationship between taxation, development and welfare in rural communities. While the researcher focuses on the main thread(s) underneath changes in the sources and structure of taxation and public spending over the centuries, rich contexts of local society feature this exploration as well. This project targets primary sources, chiefly prefecture and county gazetteers, produced by Chinese local administrations, supplemented by quantitative information collected from other kinds of historical writings such as memorials, imperial edicts and state records. As a core of this project, I am going to reconstruct the tax sources and financial structures for 20 samples of prefectures or counties. 本項研究旨在利用現存南宋、元和明代地方志中保存的各種稅收數據來重建地方財政（包括其規模和結構），並進而對這一時期地方財政的結構性變化加以描述和解釋。宋元明時期府州及縣級方志編纂記錄了大量而珍貴的地方稅收資料，而以往研究者過於關注中央層次而重視不夠，同時這些資料由於展轉傳抄而頗有疏漏錯誤，必須加以仔細考證方能引用。本研究計劃立足於精心挑選的20個地方樣本，將其所反映財政狀況與當時地方政治和賦稅制度加以關聯比照，把握地方財政長達三四百年中表現出的特色與變化，以求深入瞭解傳統中國地方財政運作的複雜面貌。

16400814.label: Realisation of objectives
16400814.value: I have collected a large body of raw data on local public finance at the prefectural and county level. The historical data cover the years from 1150 to 1450, a transitional period from Southern Song dynasty to early Ming regime. Rich and systematic information reveals a dramatic change from a monetized tax structure that had prevailed before the Mongol conquest to a kind/labour-service-based one that dominated before 1450. In the nine case such as Huizhou Prefecture徽州, Suzhou Prefecture苏州，Changzhou Prefecture 常州, Huating County华亭/Songjiang Prefecture松江, Wenzhou温州, Anxi County安溪, Tingzhou Prefecture汀州, Fuzhou Prefecture福州and Fuzhou Prefecture抚州in Jiangxi, I am able to present all three benchmarks that clearly indicate the difference in sources and structures of public finance how dramatic changes occurred to the different sector of tax revenues related to changes in local institutions driven by political and military events. My ongoing book project (publication contract already signed with Brill), mainly the public finance data of the Song dynasty, will comprise the tax data at both the state and local levels. Quantitative information provided from the nine samples is sufficient to represent a typical image of local public finance of traditional China during this transitional period. For the other part of local public financial data, I am going to make them available at the website: these data are either incomplete or unclear due to poor preservation. The fruitful outcomes I achieved are more than I expected, but I still identify 5 per cent as unachieved because I need time to accomplish these two publication tasks. The study on the expenditure focuses first on the military expenditure. As revealed clearly in the cases of both Fuzhou and Wenzhou, for the Song dynasty period, because the soldiers stationed at the two prefectures were completely recruited from the market and paid monthly by cash and food, given their totals and professional ranks one can reach the totals of the payrolls. For the early Ming one needs to focus on the size and efficiency of military farms. Information other than the military expenditure such as irrigation, bridge-building, schooling is scanty yet even more meaningful. The collection of these ‘social history’ data are thus slow and I often adopt the case study method to interpret them. In the summary table I identify 85 per cen for what I have achieved for the research objective. Nonetheless it is a significant part of local governance that equally demonstrates the differences between the Song and the early Ming. In an up-coming workshop I will use the data on fire-reporting and fire-fighting preserved in the gazetteers of Wenzhou to argue how the local officials of the Southern Song were responsible to put out the fires that took place at cities under their administration. Therefore, we are able to find many records of unban fires in this period due to this reporting system. Fires surely continued to occur at the urban settings after the end of the Southern Song, but because urban-based taxes played only a minor role, if any, in the post-Song period, local administrators were no longer required to report fire-happening to the court. Despite that in comparison to the collection of tax revenue data, the study of the expenditures and financial administration are more related to the social contexts and necessarily examined case by case. This takes much longer time than expected, but this study highlights changes in the relationship between the state and local society during the transitional period and speaks to a wide range of historians and audience. I will keep on working on this area and continue to publish my case-based research outcomes.

16400814.label: Major findings and research outcome
16400814.value: The data collected from the nine prefectures mentioned above are ready to be incorporated into my book publication project. Together with the data on public finance at the state level, they will demonstrate a dramatic change from a monetized tax structure that had prevailed before the Mongol conquest to a kind/labour-service-based one that dominated before 1450. The examination of the financial data in the historical context has produced rich fruits. My current study on Wenzhou, a coastal prefecture, allows me to produce one published article (Liu 2017) and three conference papers on a variety of issues related to local governance and community development (see Part C: No. 7, 8, 9). I present all three papers at the international conferences held in China and Japan and plan to submit these papers in the coming year. I also use the tax and wage data to explore the complex relationship between the mode of public finance and long-term economic changes in late imperial China. I presented two papers on these findings at the XVIII WEHC Conference held this summer at Boston and received extremely positive feedback (see Part C: No. 5 and 6). I expect to submit at least one paper to the top economic history journals such as JEH and EcHR this year after revision. Previously I presented a couple of working papers on the nature and quality of historical economic data preserved at official records and proposed a tentative theory, namely, the military-fiscal state of the Song dynasty China (see Part C: No. 1, 2 and 4). These publications and presentations reveal that the study of local governance from a financial perspective can make an important contribution to Chinese history.

16400814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16400814.value: I plan to seek for a collaboration with Hong Kong scholars to expand the data sources into a more comprehensive one. Through my own research I find many interesting connections with other local historical dimensions and feel necessary to link financial data with quantitative information on social history such as individuals, genealogies schools, and networking, etc. This development can be achieved by a collbration fund supported from UGC and if the application is successful it will help to understand local government and elite in a deeply-rooted story. I also hope to develop the local public finance history into a global discourse/platform, say, a study of how to maintain local governance from a gobal perspective. After I have acquired rich experience in collecting and interpreting many local samples, I am ready to share my findings with scholars who are focusing on European public finance in the early modern period. A comparison of local governance, especially public finance, in imperial China and early modern Europe, can be achieved through such a dialogue/cooperation.

16400814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16400814.value: This study tells people that how a local government was necessarily operated to maintain order and for distribution of public interests even in traditional Chinese society. Yet the way to run the government had to be adjusted to the availability of resources and the background on which officials could exercise power in a stable way. During the three centuries from 1150 to 1450 we find Chinese local government differed much in ruling local communities in corresponding to significant changes of how to finance local governments and militaries.

16400914.label: Project Objectives
16400914.value: To describe the early origins and historical development of the belief in retribution for good and evil deeds in early and early medieval China. To document the interaction between Indian Buddhism and indigenous Chinese religious traditions (including Daoism and Chinese prophecy and apocrypha) and describe the process and features of indigenization and popularization of a new belief system in the period. To specify and compare the theoretical implications of the belief in retribution for good and evil deeds in the Chinese, early Christian and Islamic settings in the light of discussions of global ethics.
rows: To describe the early origins and historical development of the belief in retribution for good and evil deeds in early and early medieval China.

To document the interaction between Indian Buddhism and indigenous Chinese religious traditions (including Daoism and Chinese prophecy and apocrypha) and describe the process and features of indigenization and popularization of a new belief system in the period.

To specify and compare the theoretical implications of the belief in retribution for good and evil deeds in the Chinese, early Christian and Islamic settings in the light of discussions of global ethics.

16400914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16400914.value: This project proposes to explore, compare and interpret beliefs about reward and retribution for good and evil deeds in early and early medieval China. Most religious, cultural and ethical traditions make moral demands persuading people towards good behaviour. It was generally accepted among early Chinese schools of philosophy that a “general appetite to good, aversion to evil” could only be cultivated through endless learning and unremitting self-perfection. Yet such self-perfection could hardly be anticipated among the majority of Chinese. The “good deed brings fortune, bad deed brings misfortune” concept instead served to stimulate morality among the general public. Nevertheless, this idealized belief failed to gain traction because life was unpredictable, and good deeds were often followed by misfortune. From the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE, a concept of retribution for good and evil deeds that relied on a mechanical and deterrent design emerged in early Daoist doctrine. It soon grew into a popular belief and infiltrated Buddhist, Confucian and other popular cultural traditions which prevailed in Chinese society from the medieval to the modern periods. This study proposes to examine the early origins and historical development of this belief in early and early medieval China. The PI finds this belief deeply rooted in theory of the pre-Qin Moist School, in the theory of the Three Kinds of Fates that prevailed in the Warring States and Western Han periods, and in the chen prophecy and apocryphal discourse that predominated from the late Western Han to the Eastern Han. These connections have been noticed by few scholars, yet discussion has remained superficial and simplified. This study will also examine the interaction and interpenetration between Indian Buddhism and indigenous religious traditions, such as Daoism, Chinese Buddhist apocrypha and other popular religions, observe the process and features of indigenization and popularization of a new belief system as the cultural landscape of China underwent some fundamental changes. Interestingly, comparable beliefs can also be found in “The Shepherd of Hermas,” an early Christian text, and in the Quran. A comparison may reveal that diverse religious traditions in different parts of the world have concurrently developed beliefs sharing similar characteristics. The approach of this study is historical and comparative. it is expected to produce internationally refereed journal articles and presentations at international conferences and higher learning institutions. 善惡是普世性的基本價值範疇，各種宗教、文化的信仰或價值體系中，一般都有導人向善遠惡的道德訴求。但向善遠惡的道德素質絕非純粹發自內心、自然形成，必須經過持續的學習和不懈的道德自我完善才可能養成。先秦、秦漢的導人向善論述，一般以善福惡禍、善惡報應為誘因。然而天意難測、福禍無常,“善有善報，惡有惡報”的理想模式在現世人生中往往不能彰顯。 兩漢之際至東漢流行的讖緯學和早期道教，因而發展出鬼神伺察、奪算減年論述，以通俗易明的話語和意象，激發人們對鬼神等超自然力量的敬畏、對惡報的恐懼和對善報的期待。漢魏六朝期間，這一信仰與佛教的因果報應觀念曾有互動而彼此滲透。這種現世報式的、可以精確量化的善惡報應論述，以通俗易明的話語和意象，激發人們對鬼神等超自然力量的敬畏，強化了天道獎善罰惡的功利色彩。所謂“三尺頭上有神明”, “善有善報, 惡有惡報, 不是不報, 時辰未到”的善惡報應信仰，於是長期存活於中國人的生活和精神中,“成為民間尋求關乎個體生命價值的資源和支撐”。

16400914.label: Realisation of objectives
16400914.value: 1) This paper argues that the origin of Chinese concept of retribution derived from the principle of vengeance or blood feud prevailed in early stages of Chinese civilization. Then the concept developed further, within a moral and humanistic context during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, especially within Classical Confucian School, into a discourse which promoting general appetite to good and aversion to evil. From the 1st Century BCE to 3rd Century CE, a scheme of retribution deeds featured by a calculative, mechanical yet deterrent—constant divine witnessing and recording within human body or mind, instant reward or punishment for good or evil deeds by lengthening or shortening of a person’s giving life sanctioned by heavenly authorities based on the witnessing records—formulated in the chen prophecy and apocryphal learning and early Daoist doctrine. 2) This concept soon grew into a popular belief which was interacting with the belief of Karma of the imported Buddhism, and penetrated each other during the Early Medieval China. Consequently, the belief was comprised in Daoist, Buddhist and Confucian doctrines prevailed in Chinese society from medieval to modern China. The Karmic retributive logic and concept of cycles of samsara was well blended into the Chinese belief in divine retribution, as well as the Buddhist binary guarding spirits. 3) Ancient Chinese, Jews, Romans and Arabians all observed that the ideal of “Goodness has a good recompense and evilness has an evil recompense” repeatedly failed in real world. Mechanical and deterrent schemes were developed in Chinese, Christian and Islam traditions to ensure to their followers that justice would be served and divine retribution were promised. In early Christian and Islamic teachings, the concepts of divine retribution with angelic witnessing were characterized by the faith in the Last Judgment, Resurrection and the ultimate accountability of all human beings to God. In some Chinese Buddhist scriptures, the guarding spirits responsible for witnessing and registering human deeds appear to be two “angels” on host’s shoulders. Similar metaphor can be found in Christian tradition in which the guarding angels on shoulders symbolizing the binary division of good and evil in a soul. In Quranic teachings, the recording angels appeared from two to four. It is noteworthy that the Islamic Scribes have shown notable mercy on their hosts. It is well taken that concepts of divine retribution for good and evil deeds emerged in different socio-political contexts and developed in diverse cultural traditions around the world, yet we do see interactive exchange and mutual learning between different cultural traditions in the ancient and medieval world, regional and interregional. Ancient religious and cultural elites, both Chinese, Christian and Muslim, seemed to share the Graeco-Roman thinkers’ profound sympathy for human nature and have insight into the hearts of their peoples. This may be why they all accepted that the belief in divine retribution for good and evil deeds may well promote ethical or moral discipline among the general public and, at the same time, provide considerably positive energy for harmony and stability of societies.

16400914.label: Major findings and research outcome
16400914.value: Moral demands persuading people towards good are quite common in many religious and cultural traditions. Classical Confucians held that cultivation through persistent learning and unremitting self-perfection and consciousness of being watchful over oneself even when he or she was alone were upheld to encourage general appetite to good and aversion to evil. Yet such a moral cultivation would hardly be anticipated being achieved by the majority of Chinese. The retributive logic of give-and-take and the pragmatic pursue for material gain played crucial role in early and early medieval Chinese mindset. From the 1st Century BCE to 3rd Century CE, a scheme of retribution for good and evil deeds featured by a calculative, mechanical yet deterrent—constant divine witnessing and recording within human body or mind, instant reward or punishment for good or evil deeds formulated in the chen prophecy and apocryphal learning and early Daoist doctrine. This scheme attempted to stimulate veneration for spiritual and supernatural powers, increase fear of evil recompense, and promote anticipation for good recompense, with intelligible but heart-shocked expression and image, among the Chinese people. Consequently, the belief was comprised in Daoist, Buddhist and Confucian doctrines prevailed in Chinese society from medieval to modern China. Interestingly, comparable concepts of divine retribution for good and evil deeds can also be found in Christian and Islamic traditions. Mechanical and deterrent schemes were developed in Chinese, Christian and Islam traditions to ensure to their followers that justice would be served and retribution were promised which were guaranteed by divine witnessing and registering, and heavenly rewarding-punishing for good and evil, either with immediate effect or post-mortem eternal planning. It is well taken that concepts of divine retribution developed in different cultural traditions of the world each emerged in its own historical context and experienced its unique course of development. Yet, we do see interactive exchange and mutual learning between different cultural traditions in the ancient and medieval world, regional and interregional. From what we have explored in this paper, ancient religious and cultural elites seemed to share the Graeco-Roman thinkers’ profound sympathy for human nature and have insight into the hearts of their peoples. This may be why they all accepted that the belief in divine retribution for good and evil deeds may well promote ethical or moral discipline among the general public and, at the same time, provide considerably positive energy for harmony and stability of societies.

Three invited talks based on this paper were delivered and well received at the Chinese Taoist Association, Renmin University of China and Sun Yat Sen University (November, Guangzhou). The English draft of the paper has been presented on Special Theme Panel 25, “The Role of Religious Studies in the Understanding of Ancient History,” August 27 2015, the 22nd International Congress of Historical Sciences, Jinan, China. It is now under revision and will be submitted to a fine journal of religious and historical studies in 2016.

16401014.label: Co - Investigator(s)

16401014.label: Project Objectives
16401014.value: Investigate flows and spatial patterns of return migration based on a series of census microdata. What are the rate, distribution, and selectivity of return migration in China? How has it changed over the past two decades? Investigate the distribution of return migration by urban/rural settlement type. How important are village, township, town, county-seat and small city as returnees' settlement destination? What are the main differences between U- and R-returnees in terms of socio-demographics and occupation? Survey U-returnees and active labor migrants in the urban areas on their household information, socio-demographics, rural-urban linkages, and history of migration/ employment / entrepreneurial activities, and follow up a year after to see the changes. A complete sample of all subjects of return migration can be obtained by adding the urban sample of U-returnees and labor migrants to the rural sample of R-returnees and stayers. Investigate returnees’ rural-urban linkages in terms of household consumption, information, guanxi-social capital, employment and entrepreneurial activities across the two sectors. What are the main rural-urban linkages for return migrants to settle and/or invest in the township or urban strata? Explain in a nested logit model (1) labor migrants’ choice of return migration, (2) returnees’ choice of settlement type, (3) their choice of employment or entrepreneurial activities, and (4) their leadership effect on stayers’ choice of employment by (i) attributes and settlement conditions of the last urban destination, (ii) settlement conditions in birthplace, including housing, income level, employment and investment environment, (iii) personal and household factors, (iv) urban labor force experience, and (v) rural-urban linkages and local social capital interactions among subjects. What are the important factors for making a return migration, settling in an urban/rural stratum, and engaging in entrepreneurial activities? How strong and at what stratum is returnees’ leadership effect on the occupational change of rural stayers? Based on results and findings as well as indepth interviews with returnees and local officials, evaluate the impact of return migration on urbanization based on their preference for settlement in specific urban/rural strata and engagement in entrepreneurial activities there, along with its possible consequences of rising inflation and inequality. What are the main factors that help to maximize the returnees’ entrepreneurial potential and rural leadership effect without incurring many negative effects? Summarize our main findings and submit a policy report to the central government through our established connections, with respect to the future settlement of tens of million migrants at various urban/rural strata.
