17202114.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17202114.value: Wetlands are land areas that are saturated with water. They provide various important benefits for people and wildlife, and hence are often well-protected and carefully managed. Wetlands are in fact a mosaic of vegetated areas and shallow open water. Vegetation transpiration and open water evaporation, termed collectively as evapotranspiration (ET), accounts for significant water loss and can become a burden on our water resources. However, it is difficult to quantify ET and determine whether vegetation transpiration is higher than open water evaporation in wetlands. The complexity and the diversity of wetland conditions also make it challenging to generalize the factors that influence the relative rates of water loss. Moreover, previous ET studies mostly consider vertical water and energy balances, assuming horizontal fluxes to be negligible. However, vegetated areas and shallow open water in wetlands are intrinsically coupled and can exhibit significant horizontal water and energy exchange. The overall objective of this project is to accurately estimate the relative rates of vegetation transpiration and open water evaporation by accounting for the atmospheric, surface and subsurface exchange between the vegetated areas and the shallow open water of wetlands. This project will first perform ground measurements of water and energy fluxes in a wetland in Hong Kong. It will then analyze remotely sensed satellite data on the wetland for spatial variations in ET-related characteristics. Finally, it will combine both sources of information to examine the horizontal exchange of water and energy between the vegetated areas and the shallow open water, and to develop a mathematical model to derive generic insights and management guidelines. This project will help to resolve the relative rates of vegetation transpiration and open water evaporation in wetlands. It also aims to identify and generalize the factors that influence the horizontal exchange and thus the relative rates of water loss. It will address some important scientific questions with practical implications. For example, how does the open water level affect the surface water and energy exchange, and thus the overall wetland ET? What is the optimized vegetation arrangement to minimize the overall water loss? This project will improve our understanding of wetland ET and our management of vegetation and water resources in wetlands worldwide. It will further establish an innovative ET estimation framework that can be extended to other heterogeneous landscapes, and demonstrate the integrated management of vegetation and water resources with insights from the emerging discipline of ecohydrology. 濕地是帶有靜止和流動水體的淺水區，對人類和野生動植物具有重要作用，人類勢必要好好保護及合理利用。植被區域和開放水面鑲嵌組成了濕地。植被的蒸騰作用和水體的蒸發作用統稱為蒸散，是濕地能量和水分的主要消耗途徑，給濕地水資源帶來極大負擔。但是，計算蒸散量以及確定植被蒸騰和水體蒸發孰重孰輕的問題非常困難。濕地的複雜多樣性增加了研究者確定影響此相對率因子的難度。之前大量的蒸散研究僅僅考慮了垂直方向上的水體和能量平衡，而忽視了水平方向上的交互量。但是，植被覆蓋區域和開放水面本質上是相互關聯的，其之間水平方向的水體和能量交換不可忽視。這個項目的大體目標是通過測估二者之間空氣、表層及表層以下的交換來計算植被蒸騰和水體蒸發的相對率。首先，在一個位於香港的濕地，對能量和水體通量相關因子進行實地測量；其次，分析衛星遙感數據，得到蒸散量相關特徵的空間分佈；最後，建立數學模型對其模擬以發掘更深層次的意義及更加有效的管理方式。 本項目有利於解決濕地植被蒸騰和水體蒸發相對率的問題，也有利於確定和整合水平交換的影響因子。本項目還會探討其他具有實際意義的科學問題，比如，開放水體水位如何影響表面水體和能量交換，以及濕地整體的蒸散量？哪種植被規劃最有利於減少水體流失？這都將有利於增加對濕地蒸散量的理解以及為植被和水資源管理提供合理建議。本項目將建立一個新型的蒸散量測估模型，普及到其他不均一地表，並且透過水文生態學這一新興學科，表現出整合植被和水資源對濕地管理的重要性。

17202114.label: Realisation of objectives
17202114.value: Each of the project objectives is discussed below. Figures and tables are separately uploaded in the system. 1. Compare and contrast the ET-related characteristics (e.g., micrometeorology, surface parameters) of the vegetated areas and the shallow open water of a wetland Field measurements were performed using an eddy covariance system and an array of temperature and water-level sensors in the wetland within Mai Po Nature Reserve, as shown in Fig. 1. An eddy covariance system was used to obtain the energy budget of a vegetated area (i.e., reed bed) and the sensors were used to capture the temperature and water-level gradients across the interface between the vegetated area and the adjacent open water. Fig. 2 displays the temperatures and water levels at the different measurement locations in the reed bed and the adjacent water. The open water level was higher than those in the reed bed during most of the monitoring period, and the fluctuations of the open water level were also larger. Seasonal and diurnal variations of atmospheric parameters as well as the energy components in the vegetated area are shown in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4. Evapotranspiration (ET) fluctuations were consistent with that of temperature, but opposite to that of relative humidity. The latent heat induced by ET was the predominant outgoing energy term, which indicated the significant water loss through ET over the wetland. Hourly ET in summer was much larger than that in winter. Similarly, diurnal variation of energy components also fluctuated more significantly in summer than in winter. The peaks for Rn, H, LE appeared around noon. However, the maximum of ground heat flux appeared in the late afternoon. In winter, sensible heat flux was the largest term except Rn at noon, however, in summer, latent heat flux exceeded sensible heat flux. 2. Estimate the horizontal water and energy exchange between the vegetated areas and the shallow open water, accounting for atmospheric, surface and subsurface exchange First of all, footprint analysis was performed to confirm that the source area of the eddy covariance measurements was only the vegetated area. The influence of atmospheric exchanges was thus minimized. The surface lateral heat flux, which was mainly induced by precipitation and runoff, was estimated using the temperature of the runoff water, the open water temperature and the runoff coefficient which is a function of soil type, land use, drainage area slope, etc. Furthermore, the conductive lateral heat fluxes were estimated based on the temperature gradient between the reed bed and the adjacent water, the bulk thermal conductivity. Finally, the advective heat transfer was calculated based on the difference in water level between reed bed and the adjacent water, the temperature difference between the soil water temperature and water temperature, and the soil hydraulic conductivity. Fig. 5 (a) displays the conductive lateral heat fluxes between those different locations in the reed bed and the adjacent open water, which were of different magnitudes. The advective lateral heat flux was however small (Fig. 5b), on the order of 0.01Wm -2. 3. Deduce the influence of the horizontal exchange on the estimation of the relative rates of vegetation transpiration and open water evaporation. The influence of horizontal exchange on the estimation of the relative rates of vegetation transpiration and open water evaporation is related with the energy imbalance behind the eddy covariance system. To examine whether the horizontal exchange could be the potential reason behind the energy imbalance, the conductive and advective lateral heat fluxes were summed up and compared with the residual of the surface energy budget. As shown in Fig. 6, the horizontal exchange was relatively small compared to the energy budget residual, and the flux being an energy gain rather than an ‘‘unaccountable’’ loss in certain months. It was thus concluded that the horizontal exchange was not the main cause of the energy imbalance. Since the horizontal exchange was found to be insignificant in the study site, the sensitivity of the results to the variations of soil thermal and hydraulic conductivity was investigated. As shown in Table 1, the variation of the conductive lateral heat flux was relatively small at different thermal conductivities, but the advective lateral heat flux varied dramatically with the different hydraulic conductivities. Different soils can thus have different orders of magnitude of hydraulic conductivities and water fluxes. Therefore, although the advective lateral heat flux in the site of this study was not significant, it might not be negligible in other locations and might be one reason behind the energy imbalance. 4. Develop a mathematical model to accurately estimate vegetation transpiration and open water evaporation by accounting for the horizontal water and energy exchange Previous sections demonstrated that the influence of horizontal water and energy exchange was negligible at the site of this study, and it would not be the main reason behind the energy imbalance that influenced the estimation of vegetation transpiration and open water. Therefore, instead of developing a model to account for the horizontal water and energy exchange, this part of the project extended the research and made use of data from 150 FLUXNET research sites (http://fluxnet.fluxdata.org/data/fluxnet2015-dataset/) to examine the energy imbalance issue. It first summarized the temporal and spatial variations of energy balance closure (EBC) and its relationship with meteorological parameters. The data covered nine main land covers (Fig. 7): evergreen needle leaf forest (ENF), evergreen broadleaf forest (EBF), deciduous broadleaf forest (DBF), mixed forest (MF), shrubland (SH), cropland (CROP), savannah (SA), grassland (GRA), and wetland (WET), and five main climate zones: A: tropical area; B: dry area; C: mild temperate area; D: snow area; E: polar area. The median EBC of different land covers and climates are summarized in Table 2. The better EBCs were observed in SA, SH, and EBF, with values larger than 0.85. WET, MF, and DBF exhibited relatively poorer EBCs, with values less than 0.75. Also, there was an obvious decreasing trend from Köppen A to E. In Fig 8, the median EBC, air temperature (Ta), and vapor pressure deficit (VPD) show general decreasing trends from Köppen climate zones A to E. It also shows positive relationships between EBC and Ta and EBC and VPD. Fig. 9 displays the significant seasonal variations of EBCs in different months in some land covers, namely ENF, CRO, DBF, MF, and WET. Ta and VPD over most land covers displayed obvious seasonal variations, and there were positive relationships between Ta and EBC and between VPD and EBC (Fig. 10). The project further explored the potential bio-physiological link between energy imbalance and carbon uptake, and investigated the net ecosystem exchange (NEE), ecosystem respiration (RE), gross primary production (GPP). Their median daily values of each month are shown in Fig. 11. Generally, EBC decreased with the increasing NEE but increased with the increasing RE and GPP, which indicated that a better EBC corresponded with a larger carbon uptake. Finally, it investigated the relationships between the magnitude of seasonal variation of EBC (EBC_DIFF) and that of NEE, RE, and GPP (NEE_DIFF, RE_DIFF, GPP_DIFF), which were all positive (Fig. 12).

17202114.label: Major findings and research outcome
17202114.value: The field measurements conducted in the wetland of Mai Po mainly quantified the subsurface conductive and advective lateral heat fluxes between a reed bed and the adjacent open water, and examined their potential contributions to surface energy imbalance and wetland evapotranspiration (ET). The subsurface lateral heat fluxes were largest close to the interface of the reed bed and the water and decreased as the distance from the interface increased, as expected. However, the magnitudes of both the conductive and advective lateral heat fluxes were not substantial when compared to the other energy terms (e.g. sensible and turbulent heat flux), particularly the advective lateral heat flux which was in the order of just 0.01 W m-2. Moreover, the subsurface lateral heat flux was in phase with the energy budget residual only in some months but out of phase for most of the time. Therefore, the subsurface lateral heat fluxes could not account for the energy imbalance due to their small magnitudes and phase differences, and should not significantly influence the estimation of ET at the study site. Although the subsurface lateral heat fluxes were concluded to not exhibit significant influence on wetland ET, this study enhanced our understanding of the water and energy exchanges between a terrestrial biotope and its surrounding water, which might further generate some insights into the biochemical processes in the heterogeneous environment of wetlands. Through analyzing data from 150 FLUXNET research sites worldwide, EBC was found to generally increase with increasing Ta and VPD. Moreover, EBC was found to be not only constrained by atmospheric conditions but also influenced by vegetation physiology. Although the land covers with the four best EBCs (i.e., SA, SH, EBF, and GRA) showed high Ta and high VPD, the significant seasonal variation of Ta and VPD did not induce a large seasonal variation of EBC. Instead, the seasonal variation of EBC coincided with that of NEE, which indicated the potential connection between energy imbalance and carbon uptake. EBC generally decreased with NEE and increased with RE and GPP. The magnitude of seasonal variation of EBC displayed positive relationships with that of NEE, RE and GPP. These results could benefit the modeling and prediction of biophysical processes related to water, energy, and carbon fluxes from the leaf level to the ecosystem level. The enhanced understanding could further facilitate the implementation of eddy covariance techniques and the improvement of earth-system models.

17202114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17202114.value: The investigation of energy balance over the heterogeneous surface could be extended to the urban surface. The field measurements, however, would be challengeable due to the complex urban surface and turbulent characteristics in the urban boundary layer. The particular urban environment of Hong Kong, packed with high-rise buildings and people, would provide unique data regarding extreme urban influences. The influences from different urban characteristics (e.g., high aspect building ratio) on the eddy covariance measurements could be explored. The eddy covariance system could be installed within the roughness sublayer, and the fluxes would need to be carefully evaluated using three-dimensional footprint analysis. A feasible solution to assess the field measurements could be proposed under a non-ideal urban surface, yielding some insights that would be beneficial to the installation of eddy covariance systems in other cities.

17202114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17202114.value: Estimating the loss of water through evapotranspiration is important, but is particularly challenging in wetlands. This study measured and estimated the influence of water and energy exchange between vegetated areas and open water, and its potential influence to evapotranspiration in wetlands based on a local field site. It particularly examined the influence of subsurface horizontal exchanges which was always neglected by previous studies. It used eddy covariance techniques, temperature and water level sensors, and related analysis tools. This study further explored the potential reasons behind the energy imbalance behind the eddy covariance techniques using data from around the world. It examined the potential relationships between energy imbalance and meteorological variables as well as carbon uptake. Overall, this study enhanced our understanding of the water and energy exchanges between vegetated area and its surrounding water, which might further generate insights into the biochemical processes in the heterogeneous environment of wetlands. It further enhanced our understanding of the energy imbalance behind the eddy covariance techniques, which could further facilitate the implementation of such techniques and the improvement of earth-system models.

17202314.label: Realisation of objectives
17202314.value: We investigate a “thermal charging” phenomenon in Electrical Double Layer Capacitors (EDLC), which may open up a new and cost-effective route to harness low-grade heat by converting it into electricity and directly storing the electrical charges. It demonstrates an open circuit voltage of 80 to 300 mV by heating the supercapacitor to 65 oC via a prior electrical charge/discharge activation step. The charge generated at high temperature can be stored in the device after its returning to room temperature, thus allowing the lighting up of LEDs by connecting the “thermally charged” supercapacitors in a series. Electrical double layer capacitors (EDLCs) are charged by applying an electrical potential difference across the positive and negative electrodes (potential-dependent). In this study, the temperature-dependent characteristic of “thermally charged” voltage in EDLC are studied and possible mechanisms are discussed. The underlying mechanism is related to a thermo-electrochemical process which enhances the kinetics of Faradaic process at electrode surface (e.g. surface redox reaction of functional group, or chemical adsorption/desorption of electrolyte ions) at higher temperature. Thermally charging of supercapciators at low temperatures suggests potential of using electrochemical systems for converting heat into electricity. As low grade heat is abundantly available in industrial processes, environment, biological entities, solar-thermal, and geothermal energy, we believe that further optimization and searching for new materials with high temperature coefficient, fast kinetics, and low heat capacity will lead to new development and possibly practical deployment of electrochemical “thermal-charging” device that combines low-grade heat conversion and charge storage, which can be a game-changing technology.

17202314.value: In summary, we report a “thermal charging” phenomenon in EDLCs that the voltage of an EDL capacitor can be recovered much faster by heating. This “thermal charging” effect is related to the surface redox reaction of functional group or chemical adsorption/desorption of electrolyte ions resulting from the electrochemical reactions between the specific functional groups on the surface of activated carbon or/and electrolyte.

17202314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17202314.value: In the past few decades, low-grade thermal energy harvesting (< 130oC) has focused on the use of solid-state thermoelectrics and Stirling engines. However, these technologies are not very cost-effective at this temperature range, and are constrained by physical and material limitations. In addition, using the electricity generated from these conventional thermoelectric devices also requires energy storage devices, such as batteries and supercapacitors. The proposed thermal-charging supercapacitor provides a new approach to development of a rechargeable device that combines thermal energy conversion and charge storage.

17202314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17202314.value: It is a great challenge for efficiently converting low-grade heat (<100oC) to electricity. The proposed thermal-charging supercapciators at low temperatures demonstrates potential of using electrochemical systems for efficiently converting heat into electricity, which will lead to new development and practical deployment of electrochemical “thermal-charging” device that combines low-grade heat conversion and charge storage.

17202414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17202414.value: Future electrical power systems will feature high penetration of renewable power, energy storage and new loads as well as continuing growth in interconnections and stress levels, all of which makes power systems less robust to changes and faults. Recent blackouts taking place worldwide (e.g. American Queens and European blackouts in 2006 and the most recent blackout in July 2012 in India) are examples, which were triggered by instability of systems that worked under highly stressed conditions. Traditional stability analysis in power systems has not kept up with these changes and has some deficiencies that will prevent it from doing so as the new features accelerate. In particular, it did not pay enough attention to impacts caused by frequent changes in network structure, including at lower voltage levels, which play a significant role in determining global behaviour of power systems. For example, the analysis tools should be able to give rapid assessment of stability limits and their sensitivities to a large number of changes under greater uncertainty. The proposed research aims to establish a new framework for stability analysis and associated control in terms of network-based models and new computational methods to give foundations for the improved analysis and control. The research project will be based on a complete revision of the dynamical models to a network-based framework expressed to include the features of future grids. Then unsolved problems in stability analysis will be addressed, including study of the underlying mechanisms of instability of power systems in terms of network structure. By integrating the research areas of power systems and complex dynamical networks, we will exploit the relationship between stability properties and dynamic features and network structure in power systems. We will start from the transient stability analysis, and then extend to small disturbance stability and voltage stability issues as parts of the overall stability problem in power systems. With this basis, techniques for identification of modes of instability and stability sensitivity will be developed. Particular attention will be paid to the impacts that renewable power sources, storage and demand-side control (type, placement and size) placed at all voltage levels will have on stability of the system. New distributed controllers will be developed to prevent occurrences of instabilities and use the additional resources in future grids more efficiently. Systematic synthesis methods for these distributed controllers will be developed, which will strongly rely on the network-based representation of the dynamical issues.

17202414.label: Realisation of objectives
17202414.value: The background of the project consisted of prior work in power system dynamics (a subject dating back to 1930’s) and network science, a quite recent emphasis in science areas. The PI had actually made contributions in both these areas and proposed that they be fruitfully merged, a challenge that had been immediately taken up by some non-engineer scientists. But this work made dubious modeling assumptions in several key results. Further the overall subject of power system stability and stabilization had entered a new era with renewable power, distributed storage and demand-side control. This project posed four fundamental questions to be addressed using the network-based approach as follows: 1) After a fault has been cleared, under what condition the stability of the post-fault system will be preserved - stability analysis; 2) If instability occurs in the post-fault system, how and where will the power grid separate - instability mode identification; 3) What is the sensitivity of stability to changes, both continuous and discrete in node, network and controller properties including aspects of renewable placement, demand-side control and storage - stability sensitivity; 4) How to design a distributed controller to maintain stability and prevent loss of stability - distributed controller design. In hindsight, the scope of this project as originally described was much larger than could be accomplished with the funding for one GRF project. But within this project, student scholarship funding, a HKU PDF fellowship and a follow-up GRF, we can report that all these questions have been addressed comprehensively. In this GRF, the main attention was mainly on questions 1, 2 and 4 with contributions to question 3 made on the way. The specific results for these questions are briefly described below. Reference is made to research outputs listed separately in Sections 8 and 9 of this report. Stability analysis [Outputs 8.1, 9.1, 9.3] A major investigation was small-disturbance angle stability of power systems with emphasis on the role of power network topology, which sheds new light on the instability mechanism. A stability criterion in terms of a critical line-based matrix is established. It includes the existing results in the literature and applies to the unsolved cases where the critical lines exist but do not form cutsets. The concept of effective resistance arising from this work has application in areas other than power systems and has been further developed under this project and submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control. The theoretical deficiencies mentioned in the proposal in a new network synchronization-based approach were overcome in an associated project funded by the HKU PDF scheme and leading to a paper in SIAM J.Control, 2018. The network-based approach was then applied to the specific case of microgrids where special features arise. Transient stability of microgrids with radial topology from the line-based perspective rather than the bus dynamics perspective was studied. This method also helps to identify the topological weakness in the system. Moreover, optimization problems to measure the impact of power variations of renewables and loads on the stability level were given (sensitivity question). The local stability problem of DC microgrids from a network-based perspective was studied. New criteria in terms of the effective grounded conductance are established to check the positive definiteness of the Laplacian matrix of a loopy graph, and thus can be used to infer the local stability of DC microgrids. Network-based voltage stability could not be considered in this project and became the subject of a later GRF project. Instability mode identification [Outputs 8.2, 9.1] In this work, graph cutset properties are studied and applied to transient stability problems. First, we reveal that cutsets are intrinsically linked to cycles. Then, with the cycle constraint for the bus angles in power networks, we give a theoretical explanation of a common phenomenon in transient stability that the loss of synchronism initiates from the angle separation across the critical cutset in the underlying power network. An improved cutset index (ICI) is proposed based on these cutset properties. This index can better identify the vulnerable cutset and help to estimate the cutset-relevant unstable equilibrium points and critical energy for stability region determination. Some aspects of instability for microgrids were included in the papers on stability. Stability sensitivity Given the attention to stability theory, this topic received less direct attention than initially envisaged. However, the results all through the stability analysis work set up the tools for sensitivity studies and smaller case studies were done to illustrate this. Distributed controllers [Outputs 8.3-8.6, 9.4] In the first control result, a distributed framework is established to evaluate and improve the small-disturbance stability of a microgrid with inverter-based distributed generators (DGs). Moreover, the control actions for stability enhancement preserve the predefined economic dispatch and power sharing schemes. This work is highly significant in including the first distributed stability assessment tool for power grids. In prior work, a fast effective algorithm for adaptive coordinated voltage control scheme was presented. This was significant in allowing a system to avoid collapse after a sequence of major incidents that would normally cause collapse. The search space can be reduced into a limited area in which only effective control solutions are found. Within this reduced search space, a local search is then developed here to get an on-line control. Computational complexity analysis indicates that it is a very effective and fast way to achieve emergency voltage control. Subsequent work, not yet finished, is exploring a more completely distributed architecture for this algorithm. With the development of a new smart load device, the electric spring (ES) at HKU, the operation of distribution systems with high renewable penetration becomes more flexible. This work proposes a two-level voltage management scheme to optimize the voltage profiles of the network, especially at chosen critical buses. In the upper level, the tap positions of load tap changer and capacitor banks switching are optimized. In the lower level, the responsibility of maintaining the voltages of the critical buses is shared among the ES in a distributed way via consensus control. Given the importance of consensus control mechanisms in distributed control, a new prescribed-time distributed control method for consensus and containment of networked multiple systems was developed. Different from both regular finite-time control and the fixed-time control, the proposed one is built upon a novel scaling function, resulting in prespecifiable convergence time. Besides theoretical advances, the project looked at some specific more practical situations. This work aimed to provide an attempt to coordinate multiple groups of aggregated air-conditionings for providing supplementary primary frequency regulation service. Based on the thermal modelling of air-conditioning, the aggregation of such demand can be controlled as a virtual energy storage system (VESS). Following this project, the area of distributed control has developed at HKU into a large area of interest being pursued in follow-up GRFs and parts of a TbRS project. So certainly all the goals of the original proposal are being addressed fully.

17202714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17202714.value: The energy crisis and climate change concerns have been impelling the governments throughout the world to establish aggressive targets on renewable energy integration. Accompanied by tremendous benefit with renewables integration, essential variability and uncertainty associated with the massive penetration of renewable resources, such as wind and solar power, significantly challenge the current power system operating methodology. To accommodate variable resources as a part of bulk power systems, various flexibility requirements must be vitally satisfied. This proposed project addresses this critical issue. Flexibility is a critical prerequisite for accommodating large-scale variable renewables before a clean, efficient, reliable, resilient, and responsive smart grid can be established. To meet the wide and varied spectrum of flexibility requirements, the resources distributed at the periphery have been well identified as a promising new operating dimension. However, the systematic operating strategies to satisfy the flexibility requirement with the periphery resources have yet to be seen. With various variable resources, a comprehensive methodology should have the capability to assess flexibility, to establish sophisticated operating strategies, and to restore outage promptly. This project addresses the systematic operating strategies for the intelligent periphery cluster as flexibility resources in the context of a smart grid. A hierarchical architecture and some selected critical functionalities will be studied as three inter-related aspects. Flexibility assessment methods will be established first. According to the identified controllable region and the stochastic characteristics of renewables, the critical escaping time will be derived and used to evaluate operating points; and the system flexibility will be assessed by the proposed coherent security-region based risk indictors. The second task will address a hierarchical architecture and associated algorithms. With different properties of renewables’ prediction errors, stochastic models will be employed to establish operating strategies over a long time horizon and the deterministic set-based robust optimization methods will be used to construct the real-time strategies. Decisions on different time horizons are coupled with the proposed hierarchical architecture to satisfy the various flexibility requirements. Highly efficient algorithms will be developed to solve the proposed models. With the proposed architecture, the third task will tackle the coordinated restoration strategies for load pickup and renewables integration with realistic considerations. The proposed project is built on our past efforts and will carry the research a giant step future. In the long run, the accomplishment will represent a systematic methodology towards a flexible renewable-friendly smart grid. This project will also provide ample opportunities for students training. 為了應對能源危機和氣候變化，世界各國政府提出了積極的可再生能源利用政策，加速可再生能源的並網。在產生巨大效益的同時，風能、太陽能等可再生能源的可變性和不確定性也給電力系統的現行運行方式帶來了極大的挑戰。滿足各項靈活性的要求，是電力系統消納大規模可變性能源的前提。此項研究將關注這一重要的問題。 具有充分且多樣的靈活性資源，從而消納大規模的可再生能源是實現清潔、高效、可靠、有彈性，且具有自主相應能力的智能電網的先決條件。現在，為充分挖掘系統的靈活性資源，分佈在系統終端的靈活性資源的重要性已經得到廣泛的關注，且表現出了廣闊的運行應用前景，然而，尚缺乏利用這些靈活資源的系統化的方法。這一系統化的方法必須具備三個功能：1. 評估靈活性的資源；2. 制定可靠運行策略；3. 高效的故障的恢復。 在智能電網的背景下，本研究將致力于構建智能終端的運行策略，從而提供智能電網運行必須的靈活性。基於分層的架構以及智能電網的核心功能，本研究將主要涉及三個互相聯繫的研究目標。首先是靈活性資源評估的方法。根據可再生能源出力的不確定性以及系統的可控資源，基於擴展靜態安全域，對運行點離開安全域的時間作保守估計，並將這個時間作為一個指標，評估系統的靈活性。第二個問題是分層調度策略的構建以及相關的算法研究。根據可再生能源預測誤差的特性，在長時間尺度的問題上，將使用隨機優化方法產生運行策略。而实時運行策略，將使用基於確定性集合的魯棒優化方法。不同時間尺度的運行策略會在提出的分層調度方法中耦合，滿足不同的靈活性的要求。另外，還將開發快速、高效的算法求解提出的模型。基於以上成果，第三個方面將解決系統在遭遇大停電后的重啟動問題，主要關注重啟過程中負荷恢復和可再生能源的協調問題。 此項研究基於申請者過去的研究成果。長遠來看，研究成果將為構造可再生能源友好的靈活智能電網提供一個系統化的方法。此外，學生也將在參與這項研究的過程中得到大量的培訓機會。

17202714.label: Realisation of objectives
17202714.value: This project proposed a hierarchical robust operation methodology to construct a renewable-friendly. The resources at the periphery are fully utilized. All the project objectives have been accomplished and summarized as papers, reports, software, and monographs. We believe the findings of this project are critical for both theoretical study and power industrial practices. Specifically, the accomplishments include flexibility assessment, operating strategies considering uncertain renewables and different system components, coordinating methods for load restoration and renewables integration, and highly efficient algorithms to implement the required functionary requirements. All tasks have been successfully accomplished. With the support of this project, (1) the research accomplishments were summarized in 17 top-tier journal papers (16 papers have been published and one paper is under review) and 6 conference papers. Specifically, there are 5 papers in IEEE Trans. on Smart Grids, 5 papers in IEEE Trans. on Power Systems, 2 papers in IEEE Trans. on Industrial Informatics, 1 paper in IEEE Trans. on Sustainable Energy, 1 paper in IEEE Trans. on Power Delivery, 1 paper in IET Generation Transmission & Distribution, and 1 paper in IEEE Power and Energy Magazine. One paper on risk assessment was nominated as the best paper of 2015 IEEE PES General Meeting [Part C. Conference 2]. (2) Some highly efficient algorithms for large-scale power systems [Part C. Journal 2, Conference 5] were integrated into a project commissioned by Electric Power Research Institute, USA. An industrial level software module, SRN 5.0 was successfully developed and released by EPRI at the end of 2016. (3) The flexibility assessment [Part C, Journal 17] has been used in realistic Gansu Province power grid and reported to Ministry of Science and Technology of China. (4) Some accomplishments were summarized in a monograph: K. Sun, Y. Hou, W. Sun, J. Qi, “Power System Control under Cascading Failures: Understanding Mitigation and Restoration”, USA, John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. The accomplished objectives are: 1. Assessing flexibility for a system with renewable energy resources Flexibility assessment is a prerequisite to establish operating strategies. This project quantified the flexibility by a two-stage robust optimization model, where the operational flexibility region is determined by continuous perturbation on the renewables penetration level and forecast error. This method was tested in an IEEE standard system and a realistic system. The testing data were provided on the PI’s website. [Part C, Journal 17] Another critical prerequisite of a flexible power system is the state awareness ability. This project proposed a dynamic state estimation method for multi-area systems with PMUs’ measurements using an extended Kalman filter. A corrective strategy was proposed to estimate the corrective internal voltage and corrective rotor angle of each generator, which were employed to establish equality constraints for updating the dynamic states. The proposed method was tested in standard systems and China Southern Power Grid. The testing results are very encouraging. [Part C, Journal 3] The flexibility of the system can also be identified by system risk level. We proposed a risk evaluation method for power systems due to the lack of flexibility based on self-organized criticality. A judgment criterion for self-organized criticality state was given based on the failure sequences for different system states, and a risk evaluation metric was designed to check the self-organized criticality state for the system. A case study was provided to show the efficiency of the proposed evaluation. [Part C. Conference 2] 2. Hierarchical robust operation methodology to meet the flexibility requirements To meet flexibility requirements, a hierarchical architecture considering transmission/distribution, distributed microgrids and cyber-based control systems were proposed. According to the characteristics of uncertainties, robust optimization and stochastic optimization were employed for different purposes. The upper level of this hierarchical architecture focused on the transmission grids, in which the risk-limiting dispatch serves as the operational method. We proposed multi-period risk-limiting dispatch and risk-limiting unit commitment model to mitigate the operating risks through sequentially dispatching units. [Part C, Journal 10, 15]. Especially, the benefits of emission reduction were discussed [Part C, Journal 7]. The mitigation strategies for unfolding uncertain events [Part C, Journal 6] and components maintenance [Part C, Journal 1] were proposed. The lower-level of this hierarchical architecture focused on distributed microgrids. Electric springs (ESs) were integrated to implement responsive loads and enhance the system flexibility [Part C, Journal 12] and resilience [Part C, Journal 5]. The operational region was identified, and the additional flexibility from ESs was quantified and optimized considering renewables integration. A distributed control strategy was proposed with limited communication requirements [Part C, Journal 8]. The cyber-based control systems were also considered in this project. We proposed a cyber inference system against alter-and-hide attacks [Part C, Journal 4], and used a dynamic game-based model to determine preventive strategies for mitigating the risk of power outages when systems are under cyberattacks [Part C, Journal 9]. Additionally, we proposed a risk mitigation model with a partially observed Markov decision process to deal with cyberattacks on PMU-based grids [Part C, Journal 11]. 3. Robust self-healing method to coordinate load restoration and renewables integration In the high-level, load restoration was coordinated with the renewables integration in the transmission level. In the lower-level, the self-healing strategies for distribution systems were proposed. The restoration tools for realistic power systems were developed and reported in [Part C, Journal 14]. The load restoration was modelled as a multi-stage decision-making process. At each stage, a mixed-integer nonlinear load restoration (MINLR) model was formulated to maximize load pickup. A complete load restoration strategy was obtained by solving a number of MINLR models sequentially. A branch-and-cut solver was constructed to achieve efficiency. The optimal generation dispatch was modelled as a dynamic optimal power flow problem and solved by a direct solution method based on the interior point algorithm [Part C, Journal 2, Conference 5]. In the lower-level, we addressed the optimal allocation of Remote-controlled switches (RCSs) in the automating distribution systems (DSs). RCS allocation aims to minimize customer interruption cost, system average interruption duration, and maximize the amount of loads. Illustrative cases showed that a small number of RCSs can substantially enhance restoration capacity of DSs. [Part C, Journal 13]. 4. Highly efficient algorithms for the hierarchical architecture and prototype In each method, associated algorithms were proposed and tested. Generally, the system operation can be modelled as a sequential optimization problem, where we highlighted two development. Due to the non-convexity of OPF problem, convex relaxation serves as a bridge linking OPF formulations with efficient polynomial-time algorithms. Introducing redundant variables for bi-directional power flows and the products of bus voltages, the OPF was formulated into a non-convex quadratic programming (QP) model. Primal and dual convex envelopes for these terms were derived to convert the non-convex QP into a convex one. The tightness of primal and dual convex envelopes was validated via a spatial branch-and-bound framework. [Part C, Conference 5]. For large-scale calculation, graphics processing units (GPUs) is a powerful computing hardware. The enumeration method can be converted to a parallel computing structure, which can be accelerated effectively on the GPU platform. Using the enumeration method, we proposed a GPU based model predictive control strategy to determine the optimal switching time for a pumped storage unit to enhance operational flexibility and facilitate frequency regulation. To sum up, all proposed tasks have been successfully accomplished in this project.

17202714.label: Major findings and research outcome
17202714.value: This project provides essential components for the emerging smart grids with large-scale renewables and responsive loads. A hierarchical robust operation methodology for intelligent peripheries has been proposed and some methods have been established. The major findings are: (1) Flexibility assessment: Flexibility assessment for transmission systems includes variability and uncertainty of renewables, unexpected outages, and controllability of generation and loads. The indices quantify frequency, magnitude, and intensity of insufficient flexibility of a power system [Part C, Journal 17]. Dynamic state estimation method for multi-area systems provide system information for flexibility assessment [Part C, Journal 3]. Cyber systems can enhance physical systems’ flexibility. A cyber inference system can against alter-and-hide attacks [Part C, Journal 4]. A dynamic game-based preventive strategy mitigates the risk of power outages when a system is under cyberattacks [Part C, Journal 9]. A risk mitigation method was proposed with a partially observed Markov decision process when a PMU-based grid is under cyberattacks [Part C, Journal 11]. (2) Hierarchical robust operation strategies for the resources until the periphery to meet the flexibility requirements: A hierarchical architecture of a power system with intelligence periphery were constructed. The proposed risk-limiting dispatch for intelligence periphery covers the network constraints, multiple delivery periods, and unit commitment. Sequential dispatch method was proposed by updating prediction information for uncertainties [Part C, Journal 10, 15]. Sophisticated renewables operation can also reduce emission [Part C, Journal 7]. The unfolding uncertain events can be mitigated by sequential re-dispatch [Part C, Journal 6] and suitable components maintenance strategy [Part C, Journal 1]. Functions of intelligence periphery can be partly implemented by responsive loads. The operational region of electric springs can be identified with their controllability. They can enhance the system flexibility under normal conditions [Part C, Journal 12] and resilience under extreme events[Part C, Journal 5]. A distributed control strategy can coordinate their operation with limited communication [Part C, Journal 8]. 3. Robust self-healing method to coordinate load restoration and renewables integration The load restoration is a multi-stage decision-making process considering the operational constraints of generating units. Renewables are coordinated with different reserves. The convexification of power flow can enhance optimal power flow [Part C, Journal 2, Conference 5]. Allocating remote-controlled switches enables prompt restoration. The proposed strategy minimize load lost/interruption duration and maximize restored loads [Part C, Journal 13]. The GPU-based platform can accelerate the calculation [Part C, Journal 16]. The restoration tools for realistic power systems were developed [Part C, Journal 14].

17202714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17202714.value: This project established a hierarchical methodology for integrating uncertain and variable renewables. The resources until the periphery are used. Based on the preliminary results from this project future research should address extending the proposed methods to the normal and emergent operating scenarios. The resources at periphery provide the new dimension to enhance system flexibility, which is critical for accommodating renewables. A reasonable tradeoff between additional flexibility and utilities of the components at the periphery needs further identification. Highly efficient scenarios selection and reduction methods might be useful. Generating operating strategies to cover the selected scenarios may need parallel computational methods. The emergent operating conditions, especially operation strategies under extreme events, is worthy of in-depth study. Functionary requirements of different stages of extreme weather event should be carefully identified. Coordinating strategy for prior to/during/after the events should be constructed. Sequential operating strategy to mitigate the impacts is a critical research topic. Renewable contributions for different stages and associated algorithms should be developed. We believe the proposed sequential risk-limiting dispatch methods can be extended to meet the requirements. The methods to implement the proposed functionary should be studied. As a distributed resources, the distributed control strategy will be identified and tested.

17202714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17202714.value: Due to the aggressive penetration levels of renewable energy resources, flexibility is a critical prerequisite for constructing a clean, efficient, reliable, resilient, and responsive power grid. Due to the variability and uncertainty of renewables, all resources in a power system have to be used to provide enough flexibility. Since the conventional generators and loads are designed for the system with low adjustability, a new flexible dimension is critically needed. This project systematically addresses this problem. Power systems are essentially a multi-layer system. We designed a hierarchical architecture. The risks due to lack of flexibility were quantified and the risk sources were identified. For different risky sources, operation strategies were proposed under normal operating conditions. For large-scale systems, the operating strategies were adjusted with updating prediction information. For loads, a device was designed to adjust the unimportant load automatically to ensure the important loads. The security of the control systems was also studied. For outage scenarios, load pickup method was designed and coordinated with renewables integration. Some proposed methods have been implemented in realistic systems and obtained encouraging results. It is believed that the accomplishment of this project will provide a critical tool to implement system flexibility in the future smart grids.

17203014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17203014.value: Nano- and micron-sized metallic materials are increasingly being used in technological applications such as NEMS/MEMS, and there is thus a strong need to better understand the deformation behaviour of these small-sized structures. Dislocation plasticity, deformation twinning and martensitic transformation are the three major deformation modes in metallic materials. Most existing studies of small-sized metallic materials focus on the first two, and martensitic transformation has been investigated only in small-sized shape memory alloys. However, there is another type of transformation in small-sized metallic materials, i.e. face-centred cubic (fcc) austenite transforms to body-centred tetragonal (bct) martensite during plastic deformation, namely, strain-induced martensitic transformation. To the best of our knowledge, there are no published results in the literature related to this type of martensitic transformation in small metallic structures. The aim of the proposed project is therefore to investigate strain-induced martensitic transformation in small-sized metallic structures to obtain a better understanding of deformation behaviour in the nano- and micron-sized domain. The first step will be to determine whether a size effect exists for strain-induced martensitic transformations. An fcc alloy, Fe-9Mn-0.6C (wt%), will be used as the model material in this project. A preliminary study showed that strain-induced martensitic transformation can take place in micron-sized pillars fabricated from this alloy using focused ion beam milling. However, when the pillar size is decreased to the nanometre scale, martensite nucleation is likely to be reduced, as the dislocation sources become scarcer when the volume of strained material decreases. Therefore, martensitic transformation may be inhibited when pillar sizes attain the nanometre scale. In other words, a size effect may exist for martensitic transformation, a hypothesis that will be subjected to detailed investigation in this project. In addition to the size effect, other effects such as orientation and temperature dependence will also be studied, as well as strain-burst and strain-hardening phenomena in small-sized samples. Following these experimental studies, a 3-D phase field simulation will be carried out to simulate the experimental microstructures. In summary, the proposed project will involve systematic experiments and modelling carried out to improve our understanding of strain-induced martensitic transformations in nano- and micron-sized fcc metals. 微納米級的金屬材料越來越多地應用於各種技術領域，例如在NEMS/MEMS領域中的應用就是壹個很好的例子。我們非常有必要研究這些微納米材料的變形機理。金屬的材料的變形機理主要包含位錯、變形孿晶、馬氏體相變等等。目前對微納米尺寸金屬材料變形機理的研究主要集中在位錯和變形孿晶機理。目前馬氏體相變在微納米材料中的研究僅僅局限於形狀記憶合金。但是，除了形狀記憶合金中的馬氏體相變之外，還有另外壹種馬氏體變形機制，這就是應變誘導馬氏體相變。這種馬氏體相變的機理是面心立方奧氏體轉變為體心四方馬氏體。據我們所知，目前還沒有關於微納米晶體中應變誘導馬氏體相變的相關論文發表。本項目的目標就是彌補這方面的空缺，為進壹步完善微納米金屬材料的變形機理研究提供相關的實驗和理論依據。 本項目首先要研究應變誘導馬氏體相變是否存在尺寸效應。本項目采用壹種面心立方合金作為模型材料，該材料的化學成分為Fe-9Mn-0.6C (wt%)。我們的初步研究成果已經表明該材料的微米級單晶可以發生應變誘發馬氏體相變。但是，如果該單晶的尺寸降到納米級別，位錯源就會減少，很有可能導致馬氏體的形核點減小，使馬氏體相變更難發生，這就是所謂的尺寸效應。本項目的目標之壹就是要驗證這種尺寸效應是否存在。除此之外，晶體取向和溫度對馬氏體相變的影響、應變平臺、加工硬化等現象也是本項目的研究目標。除了以上的實驗研究計劃之外，本項目也計劃建立壹個三維的相場模型來模擬上述的實驗結果。總之，本項目預期獲得系統性的實驗和模擬結果，這些結果可以幫助理解微納米單晶中的應變誘導馬氏體相變機理。

17203014.label: Realisation of objectives
17203014.value: For objective 1, systematic experiments have been carried out to investigate the physical mechanisms responsible for strain-induced martensitic transformations in face-centered cubic (fcc) micropillars. It is found that the martensitic transformation can take place at the intersection of nanotwins or at the martensite embryos at the pillar surface. It is also found that large strain burst can be induced by martensitic transformation, and its magnitude depends on the orientation of pillars. Pillars with an orientation close to [10 0] show a much larger strain burst than the ones with an orientation close to [1 1 0]. This is because [1 0 0] pillars have a much higher fraction of transformed martensite to which the magnitude of strain burst is directly correlated. It can be concluded that the objective 1 has been achieved. For objective 2, a physical model is proposed to understand the critical stress for martensitic transformation in austenitic micropillars. By carrying our systematic experiments, it is found that the average critical stress for martensitic transformations in [100] micropillars (484 MPa) is much smaller than that in [110] micropillars (700 MPa). The deformation twins can be found in deformed [100] micropillars while the deformed [110] micropillars are free of deformation twins. The critical stress for twin divergence in [100] micropillars (480 MPa) is close to the corresponding critical stress for martensitic transformation. The theoretical critical stress for martensitic transformation in both [100] and [110] micropillars is estimated to be the same (750 MPa). The lower critical stress for martensitic transformations in [100] micropillars could be ascribed to the formation of deformation twins, which is confirmed by the microstructural observation that the martensite nucleates at the intersections of deformation twin bundles. Two martensitic transformation pathways, namely twin-assisted martensitic transformation and free-standing martensitic transformation are proposed to explain the orientation dependent martensitic transformation observed in the austenitic micropillars. These two pathways will be incorporated into the crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) simulations. To the PI’s understanding, comparing to 3D phase-field simulation, CPFEM is more suitable for simulating the strain-induced martensitic transformation in micropillars as both twins and dislocations can be incoported. Twins and dislocations can affect greatly the martensitic transformation. Therefore, the PI decided to carry out CPFEM simulation instead of 3D phase-field to simulate the strain-induced martensitic transformation in austenitic micropillars. The simulation results are expected in 2019. Therefore, this objective can be considered 50% achieved. It is expected that this objective can be 100% achieved in 2019.

17203014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17203014.value: Martensitic transformation in micropillars can provide excellent experimental validations for CPFEM simulations. CPFEM simulation on martensitic transformation has great potential for providing useful guidelines for design of new high-strength steels. 17203014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17203014.value: The present project carried out systematic investigations for understanding the strain-induced martensitic transformations in small-sized fcc metals. The effect of martensitic transformation on the strain burst is well understood. A larger volume fraction of martensite leads to a larger strain burst. The effect of orientation has been investigated. The critical stress for martensitic transformation is significantly reduced in [100] micropillars as martensite nucleates at the intersections of nanotwins. In addition, the role of martensitic transformation in the mechanical properties of high-strength steels has also been investigated, which can provide useful guidelines for the development of novel high-strength steels.

17203514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17203514.value: Concrete is made of cementitious paste and aggregate particles, wherein the cementitious paste, after hardening, bonds the aggregate particles together to give the concrete both stiffness and strength. The cementitious paste volume must be large enough to fill the voids between the aggregate particles for avoiding entrapment of air in the voids and to provide additional paste for forming paste films coating the aggregate particles to make the concrete workable during placing. Generally, to reduce the cementitious materials consumption, so as to reduce the cost and carbon footprint of the concrete production, the cementitious paste volume should be kept to minimum. However, for the production of high-performance concrete with high strength and/or flowability, the cementitious paste volume has to be increased. The increase in cementitious paste volume not only increases the cost and carbon footprint but also increases the heat generation and drying shrinkage, thus causing the concrete to be more liable to cracking. In fact, some engineers dislike high-performance concrete mainly because of the higher risk of cracking. There is therefore a need to minimize the cementitious paste volume in high-performance concrete. One possible way of reducing the cementitious paste volume is to increase the packing density of the aggregate so as to reduce the volume of voids to be filled. This can be done by dividing the aggregate into several (say, four) size fractions and adjusting the proportions of the various fractions to maximize the packing density. The PI has developed a wet packing test and a theoretical packing model for measuring and predicting the packing density of particle systems. Research using these tools would help to optimize the aggregate proportions for maximum packing density. Another possible way is to add a fine filler (treated as an additional aggregate portion) to fill into the voids between aggregate particles. If the filler has similar fineness as the cementitious materials, the filler would be intermixed with the cementitious materials to increase the total paste volume. By so doing, the cementitious materials paste can be reduced by the volume of filler added. The PI has been advocating the addition of filler as cementitious paste replacement to reduce the cementitious materials consumption. Previous studies by the PI revealed that this would also improve the dimensional stability and water resistance of the concrete. Further research on this topic as proposed herein would help to produce higher performance concrete with lower cementitious paste volume.

17203514.label: Realisation of objectives
17203514.value: The research project started in October 2014 and lasted slightly longer than three years. A PhD research student was recruited right at the start to work on the research project. To achieve the first objective, we developed a new aggregate classification system of classifying aggregate particles into fine aggregate with particle size < 1.2 mm, medium aggregate with particle size > 1.2 mm but < 5.0 mm, and coarse aggregate with particle size > 5.0 mm. Then, we studied the effects of the aggregate proportions on the packing density of the aggregate and the performance of the concrete produced as a self-consolidating concrete. It was found that with such classification into three classes instead of two classes, the aggregate particle size distribution could be better optimized to achieve higher performance. To achieve the second and third objectives, we developed a new strategy of adding limestone fines as cementitious paste replacement instead of direct cement replacement. It was found that this would increase the packing density of the particle system and thereby lower the cement consumption to lower the carbon footprint of the concrete for the production of green high-performance concrete. To achieve the fourth objective, we added different amounts of limestone fines as cementitious paste replacement and evaluated the effects of such addition of limestone fines on the general performance of the concrete produced. It was found that apart from lowering the cement consumption, this would also increase the strength, dimensional stability and robustness of the concrete produced.

17203514.label: Major findings and research outcome
17203514.value: 1. A new aggregate classification system of classifying aggregate particles into fine aggregate, medium aggregate and coarse aggregate has been developed. With this new system, it is now possible to better optimize the particle size distribution for achieving higher packing density so as to attain higher concrete performance. On this topic, two journal papers titled as "Adding ground sand to decrease paste volume, increase cohesiveness and improve passing ability of SCC" and as "Lowering paste volume of SCC through aggregate proportioning to reduce carbon footprint" are published. 2. A new strategy of adding limestone fines as cementitious paste replacement instead of direct cement replacement has been developed. By adopting this strategy, it is now possible to add limestone fines to increase the packing density of the particle system and thereby lower the cement consumption to lower the carbon footprint of the concrete for the production of green high-performance concrete. On this topic, one journal paper titled as "Adding limestone fines as cementitious paste replacement to lower carbon footprint of SCC" is published. 3. The effects of adding different amounts of limestone fines as cementitious paste replacement have been studied and the benefits of such addition of limestone fines in improving the general performance, strength, dimensional stability and robustness of the concrete produced have been evaluated and demonstrated. On this topic, two journal papers titled as "Filler technology for improving robustness and reducing cementitious paste volume of SCC" and as "Filler technology for low-carbon high-dimensional stability concrete" are published.

17203514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17203514.value: The newly developed aggregate classification system of classifying the aggregate into fine, medium and coarse aggregates and the filler technology of adding a filler as cementitious paste replacement in concrete are completely general and should be generally applicable. It is envisaged that these would maximum the packing density to increase not only the strength, but also the durability of the concrete produced. At least in theory, the newly developed methodologies could be applied to other types of fillers, other types of concrete and other performance attributes including the durability properties of concrete. Further researches along these lines are highly recommended. Moreover, if opportunity arises, trial application of these newly developed methodologies in actual concrete production should be attempted.

17203514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17203514.value: Two new technologies, namely: a more refined classification of the aggregate into three size fractions instead of two, and the filler technology of adding a filler such as limestone fines as cementitious paste replacement to lower the cement content, have been developed. Both these two technologies would enable better optimization of the particle system in concrete to maximum the packing density so as to lower the cement consumption to lower the carbon footprint, increase strength, increase performance as a self-consolidating concrete, improve dimensional stability (this would lower the risk of concrete cracking) and improve robustness (this would enhance the quality of concrete production). These technologies are completely general. In theory, they could be applied to other types of fillers, other types of concrete and other performance attributes including the durability properties of concrete. They are effective enabling technologies for the production of green high-performance concrete for sustainable development.

17203614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17203614.value: 泥石流具有流速高、出流距離大等特點，會造成生命和財產的重大損失。從微觀角度充分理解流體與顆粒的相互作用能夠加強對泥石流速度及深度的估計，這對泥石流隔柵設計的安全性、高效性和經濟性至關重要。以往，人們通常採用單相模型和雙相混合模型，將泥石流模擬為連續介質黏性流體。然而，這些方法無法顯式地模擬每個土顆粒的運動以及流體對土顆粒的作用力。 在這項研究計劃中，我們提出了一種能夠深入研究泥石流的計算模型，它以計算流體力學（CFD）和離散單元法（DEM）耦合，可以模擬散體材料與流體的力學作用。泥石流的流體部份將在CFD的構架下通過求解局部平均的納維─斯托克斯（Navier-Stokes）方程來模擬，顆粒運動由DEM求解。流體和顆粒相互作用則通過在DEM和CFD之間交換必要的信息來實現，比如拖拽力和浮力等相互作用力。泥石流的自由界面──這項研究最具挑戰性的部份──將通過流體體積法 (VOF)實現，它以每個流體單元中液體的體積分數作為該單元液體盈、空狀態的指示因子，以此定位流體（或泥石流）的自由邊界。本計劃提出的流體─顆粒耦合模型將結合模型試驗進行檢驗，試驗擬在香港理工大學進行。該模型還會通過與香港土力工程處（GEO）的合作應用於泥石流的現場研究。 本研究計劃的主要目的在於深入理解在幾何和地質參數（比如，黏度、流體密度、粒徑分佈、坡面傾角和河道粗糙度）影響下控制泥石流速度場分佈的微觀機理。本研究的成果將顯著提高對泥石流的理解，尤其是在微觀顆粒尺度的演變、物理特性和機理。這些新的理解能夠進一步幫助香港乃至全世界工程師進行更為安全、有效的泥石流隔柵設計。這種考慮自由邊界的CFD─DEM耦合方法不僅可以為研究泥石流提供新的思路，也可以運用在其他涉及流體─顆粒相互作用的領域。

17203614.label: Realisation of objectives
17203614.value: Task 1 Development of the coupled CFD-DEM model The development of an extended computational fluid dynamics and discrete element method (CFD-DEM) model is presented in a conference IS-Cambridge 2014 (Jing et al. 2014), and then published on International Journal of Numerical and Analytical Methods in Geomechanics (Jing et al. 2016a). The model incorporates volume of fluid (VOF) method to track free fluid surface. It is implemented based on open source library OpenFOAM, CFDEM and LIGGGHTS. More details about the governing equations and their numerical implementations can be found in Jing et al. 2016a. Task 2 Model validation Each component of the newly developed model has been validated carefully. In Jing et al. 2016a., a dam break case validates the CFD-component and VOF-component, particle sedimentation tests validate the CFD–DEM interaction at various Reynolds numbers, water-level rising tests validate the volume exchange among phases, and the porous sphere model is validated in both static and dynamic situations. Another core component of the model, i.e. the constitutive relation of fluid, has been validated against flume test experiments (see Task 3) that are carried out by ourselves. Three constitutive models are under examination, including Newtonian, Bingham and Herschel-Bulkley models, which cover a wide variety of fluid types encountered in natural debris flows. Task 3 Physical modelling Laboratory experiments of slurry and particles flowing down a small-scale flume have been performed in collaboration with Dr. Y.F. Leung at the Hong Kong Polytechnic University. A flume has been constructed, which consists a slope made by Plexiglas, with adjustable inclinations, a reservoir with a removable gate, and a horizontal runout plain. The flume is 1–2m long and 0.2m wide, the reservoir is 0.4m long and the runout plain is square, with length equals 1m. The fluid used is made of homogenous kaolin-water slurries. As a non-Newtonian fluid, its yield strength and viscosity increases with concentration. We measured both two rheological parameters as a function of concentration using a Brookfield rheometer (R/S SST200). These parameters, i.e. yield stress and viscosity, can be used directly as input for our numerical model (Jing et al. 2016b). Typical experimental results from our system include the flow profile on the channel, front position and frontal velocity, runout length and width, deposition shape and depth. The evolution of the channel flow, captured by video cameras, is post-processed with an OpticalFlow program (Matlab Computer Vision System ToolboxTM). Optical flow refers to velocity distributions of objects in an image, which can sharply delineate the free fluid surface. More than 50 (effective) flume tests have been performed, which systematically investigate the influence of slurry concentration, source volume at the reservoir, angle of inclination, base roughness, and fluid-particle interactions. The concentration, volume, and slope angle are designed in such a way that the Reynolds number of the flow falls in the same regime of debris flows in the field. In some cases where fluid-particle interactions are under examination, glass beads with numbering are added, whose diameters vary from 1cm to 3cm. In the cases with varying bed roughness, sandpapers are placed over the bottom of the flume. The results and their interpretation has been included in Jing et al. 2016b. Task 4 Characterization of micro and macro behaviour of debris flow Macro-perspective Macro behaviour of debris flows includes the flow depth, front velocity, runout distance, and deposit shape, etc. In experiments, these can be accessed by high-speed cameras and video cameras. Since the depositional mechanism is of great interest, it has been thoroughly studied in experiments and numerical simulations. It has been found that while viscosity mainly influences the flow velocity and the time scale of flow stoppage, yield stress determines the depositional mechanism of debris flows. Yield stress is a key character of slurry (and mudflows at real scale), because slurry behaves like a solid at rest and starts to flow beyond yielding. Therefore, the thickness and depth gradient of deposits are largely influenced by yield stress. Slurry tends to deposit with steep edges. In order to study the significance of yield stress and the different role played by viscosity in the course of deposition, we have adopted a viscous solution of Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) in laboratory and a wide range of combinations of yield stress and viscosity in numerical modelling. CMC solution has high viscosity but low yield stress. As a result, it exhibits very low flow velocity but its deposit is wide (semi-circular) and evenly spreading. This confirms that yield stress is essential to the accumulation of deposits. In numerical simulations, a phase diagram is established showing how yield stress and viscosity control the deposit morphology. More discussions are included in the paper published in JGR: Earth Surface. Micro-perspective One of the strength of extended CFD-DEM modelling is the microscopic information it can provide, which includes particle position, velocity, particle-particle and particle-fluid interaction, local flow velocity, flow shear rate, porosity and fluid pressure, etc. At present, we have taken this advantage to have a deep investigation of an important phenomena in debris flows, namely, size segregation (or reverse grading). We first use a representative element of granular flow to study the mechanism governing segregation. Parametric study is performed on varying slope angle, size ratio, concentration of large particles, and the coefficient of friction. We find that slope angle, which defines how much potential energy can be transferred into kinetics, mainly determines the time scale of the completion of segregation. Onset of segregation occurs at around 20 degree as slope angle increases, and the maximum extent of segregation rapidly converges beyond this critical angle. Similarly, the final degree of segregation is hardly influenced by size ratio and concentration, as long as they beyond certain critical values. On the other hand, friction plays a more important role in the final degree of segregation. Higher coefficient of friction promotes more rotation of particles, which may facilitate the occurrence of segregation. The work is published in Physical Review Letter (Jing et al. 2017). Another interesting use of DEM is to characterize the geometric roughness of an arbitrary surface made by spheres. In debris flows, base roughness is crucial to the flow kinetics, segregation and deposition. Basal effect in both mono- and bi-disperse flows has been studied in DEM simulations (Jing et al. 2016e). Furthermore, we propose a quantitative definition of base roughness, which takes into account size ratio of flow- to base- particles and the packing of the base layer. This definition is proven to be a good indicator of slip/non-slip condition in debris flows, and is expected to be much useful in the future study concerning boundary effect. Details of the definition and its application can be found in a manuscript submitted to Physical Review E (Jing et al. 2016f).

17203614.label: Major findings and research outcome
17203614.value: Our major contribution in the development of the coupled CFD-DEM model is twofold. First, a modified three-phase VOF model is proposed, which allows volume replacement between solid and fluid. The new advection equation in VOF ensures the conservation of phase fractions, and it governs the dynamics of free surface. Second, a porous sphere model is used to circumvent the grid-dependent problem encountered when the particle size is close to the mesh size. It well extends the applicability of traditional CFD-DEM schemes; a wider range of particle size distribution can be used in DEM, without sacrificing the resolution of CFD grids. Micromechanical origin of particle size segregation. Physical Review Letters The paper provides fundamental understanding of the physical process of particle size segregation in granular flows, which potentially enhances more accurate prediction of segregation. Published on one of the most prestigious journals in physics, the paper has been referenced more than 20 times in the past two years to support the most recent progress in relevant fields. It was reported in Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics by J.M.N.T Gray in 2017. A research group led by the Dean of engineering in Northwestern University is currently developing a segregation force model, incorporating the major findings in the paper. Runout scaling and deposit morphology of rapid mudflows. Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface Recently published on one of the top journals in geophysics, this paper contains a detailed dataset of numerical simulations and laboratory experiments for rapid mudflows and a scaling law that can potentially improve prediction of debris flow runout. An anonymous reviewer described it as “rather unusual and remarkable in science to have such a full work”. Part of the paper was presented in International Geotechnics Symposium in 2016 and awarded the Best Paper Award for Young Researcher by a judge panel chaired by Herbert Einstein from MIT. Extended CFD-DEM for free-surface flow with multi-size granules. International Journal of Numerical and Analytical Methods in Geomechanics. A mathematical model describing the dynamic free surface in coupled fluid-particle modeling is proposed, which is of great significance to engineering problems such as landslide and debris flow. The paper received great attention since its publication. It was awarded the most accessed article in 2016 and becomes the 6th highly cited paper of the journal. Both the free surface model and a porosity calculation approach presented in the paper have been employed in recent numerical studies of fluid-particle interactions.

17203614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17203614.value: More studies under Task 4 are ongoing. As observed in laboratory tests, frontal instability of slurry emerges under certain conditions that a successive wave overflows the initial deposit. This is referred to as roll wave in a more general sense. It is an important issue to address in debris flows, since the multiple surges may exaggerate their destructiveness. We have successfully reproduced this instability in numerical simulations and its condition of occurrence will be explored in next stage. In flume tests where glass beads are added, we find that the initial particle arrangements can influence the flow velocity (hence impact) and its final deposition. For instance, particles migrating on the edge of the flow may slow down the flowing mixture, as they increase the basal resistance of the front. And the mitigation of mobility is less significant when the particles are spreading more uniformly in the initial configuration, because there will be more particles left in the bulk of the flow, rather than transported to the edge. These findings inspire us to do more investigation under the framework of extended CFD-DEM, which will enhance the understanding of fluid-particle interactions in debris flows.

17203614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17203614.value: This study aims towards a thorough understanding of the fluid-particle interaction of debris flow at micro level with the use of an extended CFD-DEM computational method to consider granular flows with free fluid surface. Other fundamental problems relevant to dynamic granular flows, such as grain size segregation, are also studied. Flume tests will be conducted to calibrate the developed numerical tool, and the lab-scale debris flow events will be studied. The outcome will contribute to enhanced estimation of the velocities and depths of debris flows, which is essential for safe, efficient and economical barrier designs.

17203814.value: Develop new materials as gate dielectric with high dielectric constant (i.e. high-k) for the IGZO TFT's with high resistance to gate-metal diffusion, good thickness uniformity and low fixed charge density. Moreover, high-k dielectrics give high gate-oxide capacitance and hence high current drive. Develop an improved understanding of the nature of the IGZO/dielectric interface. Understanding the nature of the IGZO/dielectric interface is just as important now as it was for the Si/SiO2 interface system in the early 1960's. By performing extensive chemical, material, and electrical research, the stoichiometry and the bonding structures of the IGZO/dielectric interface, and their effects on the resulting electrical characteristics of the IGZO/dielectric interface (interface-state and fixed-charge densities) will be investigated. From (2), develop efficient IGZO surface passivation techniques for achieving smooth IGZO/dielectric interface, which is important for improving the carrier mobility and hence current drive. 17203814.value: The Information Age has entered the broadband wireless stage where the amount of data bombarding us is increasing at an enormous rate. As a result, today's electronic display devices have to operate very fast so as to deal with this data deluge, and often under low-voltage environment. In order to meet all these stringent requirements, worldwide research interest in the use of Indium Gallium Zinc Oxide (IGZO) for semiconductor applications has increased dramatically over the past few years. This interest has been stimulated by the many unique and outstanding physical and electronic properties of IGZO when compared with the most widely used semiconductors (amorphous silicon and polycrystalline silicon). These features make IGZO an ideal semiconductor material for making the low-voltage and high-speed electronic devices in the electronic display for a large number of high-impact consumer, industrial and military applications (e.g. HDTV, tablets and smartphones). But before all these benefits could be fully realized, it is of utmost importance to develop suitable material to act as an insulator inside the devices.
