17303714.label: Major findings and research outcome
17303714.value: The project aims to formulate the electronic transport of Dirac fermions in these emergent materials as two-dimensional materials and topological materials. We have published 8 papers relevant to the present project, including 1 in Physical Review Letters, 3 in Physical Review B, 2 in Nature Communications, 1 in New Journal of Physics, and 1 in Chinese Physics B. The major findings of this project are: (1). We developed a theory of high field magnetotransport in topological semimetals, and identified three scenarios in which the magnetoconductivity is negative. (Publication (1,6 )); (2). We developed a theory of weak antilocalization and localization in three-dimensional topological semimetals, and obtained the formula of finite-temperature conductivity and magnetoconductivity for Dirac fermions. (Publication (2,8)); (3). We found the anomalous phase shift of quantum oscillations in three-dimensional topological semimetals, which accounts for recent experiments in Cd2As3 and others. (Publication (7) ); (4). We found the parity of monopole charge determines the quantum correction to the conductivity in Weyl semimetal and proposed a scheme to detect the signature of the monopole charge (Publication (5)); (5). We applied the developed theories to analyze and fit the experimental data of quantum transport in Dirac semimetal Cd3As2, and Weyl semimetal TaAs. We identified the occurrence of weak antilocalization of three-dimensional Dirac fermions, and negative magnetoresistivity as a signature of chiral anomaly. (Publication (3,4))

17303714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17303714.value: In this project we have developed theory for the weak antilocalization and localization for the Dirac and Weyl fermions and the formula for magnetoconductivity in a strong field. However, there are still some unconventional transport properties, such as the extremely large and linear magentoresistivity and large negative magnetoresistivity in some topologiocal materials, which could not be understood very well in the existing theories. We shall continues our exploration along this direction and seek the supports from Research Grants Council.

17303714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17303714.value: The emergent phenomena were observed in novel two-dimensional materials and topological materials. The transport of Dirac fermions is distinct from conventional electron gases in many aspects. For example, the spin-momentum locking gives rise to a nontrivial Berry phase, which can drastically modulate the transport, leading to the absence of backscattering, weak anti-localization, and absence of Anderson localization. The project explores the theory of electronic transport in these emergent materials as the transport of Dirac fermions, focusing on the topics such as: the roles of electron-electron interaction and impurity in the quantum correction and fluctuation of conductivity, and the quantum transport of quasiparticles in topological materials. 17303814.label: Realisation of objectives
17303814.value: OBJECTIVE 1 Characterization of images of holomorphic isometric embeddings of the complex unit ball B^k of maximal admissible dimension into irreducible bounded symmetric domains, and related problems on geometric structures arising from examples of maximal dimension. Let Ω be any irreducible bounded symmetric domain of rank at least 2 and denote by M the dual compact Hermitian symmetric manifold. of the compact type. If the first Chern class c_1(M) is equal to p+2, by our previous results there are nonstandard holomorphic isometric embeddings from B^{p+1} into Ω (and also from B^k for k < p+1 by slicing). Images of holomorphic isometric embeddings of top dimension can be defined by an algebro-geometric object on M as follows. Let m be the complex dimension of Ω, and realize Ω as a bounded domain in the Euclidean space C^m by means of the Harish-Chandra realization. Let p be a regular boundary point on bΩ and W be the union of minimal rational curves (MRCs) on M passing through p, and write V for the algebraic subset of Ω defined as the intersection of W and Ω. Then, V is the image of a holomorphic isometric embedding of top dimension from a complex unit ball into Ω. In [1] we considered images of holomorphic isometric embeddings of B^k into Ω with respect to Kaehler-Einstein metrics normalized so that minimal disks for both B^k and Ω are of Gaussian curvature -2, and prove the general result that images are given by irreducible components of linear sections of M with Ω, where M is identified as a projective submanifold via the first canonical isometric embedding (e.g., Grassmannian by Plücker embedding). When Ω is the n-dimensional Lie spheres D_n, the noncompact dual of the n-dimensional hyperquadric Q_n, we completely classified holomorphic isometric embeddings of B^k into D_n. For k at least 2 the images S of such embeddings carry geometric substructures called VMRT sub-structures depending on the null dimension of the restriction of the canonical holomorphic conformal structure from Q_n to S. In particular, there exist hypersurfaces H in Q^n which are nonsingular hyperquadrics intersecting Ω, such that the intersection S of H and D_n is the image of a nonstandard holomorphic isometric embedding of B^{n-1}. S carries canonically a holomorphic conformal structure, as opposed to V defined by cones of MRCs, on which the holomorphic conformal structure degenerates. For Ω of rank at least 2 other than a Lie sphere, it is not known whether there exist nonstandard holomorphic isometric embeddings of B^{p+1} (where c_1(M)=p+2) other than those defined by cones of MRCs. In an unpublished manuscript, I introduced a method to tackle the uniqueness problem for nonstandard holomorphic isometric embeddings which exploits the duality of the pair (Ω,M) and the Gauss equation. Based on this method, a Ph.D. student of mine X. Yang wrote a thesis in 2017 entitled “Some rigidity results about holomorphic isometric embeddings from complex unit balls into bounded symmetric domains” in which the uniqueness problem was solved in a number of cases. Basing on some joint works with me and further work after his thesis, Yang and I are writing up an article in which we show that for any irreducible Ω of rank 2 not isomorphic to a Lie sphere, the cone of MRCs construction gives the only nonstandard holomorphic isometric embedding of B^{p+1} into Ω up to congruence. OBJECTIVE 2 Characterization, under certain dimension restrictions, of compact totally geodesic complex submanifolds S of a quotient manifold X = Ω/Γ of a bounded symmetric domain Ω by complex-analytic properties such as the holomorphic splitting of the tangent sequence, and related problems on subvarieties with excessive varieties of minimal rational tangents. We focused here on results where Ω is irreducible and of rank at least 2. In this case there is a decomposition of the symmetric square of the tangent bundle T(X) into an orthogonal holomorphic direct sum A + B, where A and B are nontrivial. Under the assumption that the tangent sequence 0 --> T(S) --> T(X)|S --> N --> 0 splits holomorphically over S, we have canonically a projection map from T(X)|S into T(S). From S^2T(X) = A + B and by Berger’s characterization of local symmetry in terms of holonomy groups, we obtained under certain dimension restrictions characterization theorems ascertaining that certain compact splitting complex submanifolds S in X are totally geodesic. An example of such a result is given in [1] as Theorem 2.2[1]: Let S be a compact splitting complex submanifold of X such that rank(S^2T(S))>max(rank(A),rank(B)) and dim(S) exceeds the degree of strong non-degeneracy of the bisectional curvature of X. Then, S is Hermitian locally symmetric of rank at least 2 and totally geodesic with respect to the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metrics on X. OBJECTIVE 3 Characterization of the Zariski closure on a mixed Shimura variety of the image of an algebraic subset of ΩxC^m under the uniformization map, and related problems including questions on equidistribution for finite-volume quotients of Ω. In [4] we prove the following major result proving the analogue of the Ax-Lindemann Conjecture for finite-volume quotients of B^n for arbitrary torsion-free lattices in Aut(B^n). Main Theorem [4] Let Γ be a torsion-free lattice in Aut(B^n), and write X:=B^n/Γ, which carries a canonical structure as a quasi-projective variety. Denote by p: B^n --> X the uniformization map. Let S be an algebraic subset of B^n. Then, the Zariski closure Z of p(S) in the quasi-projective variety X is a totally geodesic subset with respect to the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metric. The article [4] furnishes a transition from the study of purely geometric problems on bounded symmetric domains and their finite-volume quotients to problems in Functional Transcendence Theory. An intermediate result in [4] furnishes an important technique for the study of Zariski closures. For Main Theorem of [4] we prove the following intermediate statement ascertaining that the Zariski closure Z of p(S) is multifoliated by images under the uniformization map p: B^n --> X of leaves of some stratum of the universal family associated to some component of the Chow scheme of P^n. We have Proposition 3.2 of [4] Let K be an irreducible component of Chow(P^n), [W_0] be a member of K, S be a nonempty irreducible component of the intersection of W_0 and B^n, and S' be the tautological lifting of S to the universal family U of K. Let H be an Aut(P^n)-invariant subvariety of K such that, denoting by s: V --> H, n: V --> P^n the restriction of the universal family over K to H, a general point of S' is a smooth point of V. Here write X(Γ) for B^n/Γ. Then, denoting by n(Γ): V(Γ) --> X(Γ) the locally homogeneous fiber bundle over X(Γ) obtained by restricting V from P^n to B^n and passing to quotients modulo Γ, the tautological foliation F on V descends to a meromorphic foliation F(Γ) on V(Γ). Moreover, when Γ is a torsion-free nonuniform lattice the topological closure V"(Γ) of V(Γ) is projective, and F(Γ) extends to a meromorphic foliation F"(Γ) on V"(Γ). As a consequence, for any torsion-free lattice Γ of Aut(B^n) the Zariski closure Z of p(S) in X(Γ) is uniruled by subvarieties belonging to H. The link between the study of holomorphic isometries and Functional Transcendence Theory is explained in the article [3].

17303814.label: Major findings and research outcome
17303814.value: Our project focused on the study of bounded symmetric domains Ω and their quotient spaces X:=Ω/Γ by torsion-free lattices Γ in Aut(Ω). Ω is equipped with the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metric. We consider geometric objects on Ω and on X and characterize them in terms the geometry of the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metric. Our results break down into (1) the case where Ω is of rank 1, i.e., Ω is the complex unit ball, and (2) the cases where Ω is of rank at least 2. In Case (1), the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metric g on B^n is of constant negative holomorphic sectional curvature. Let Ω be any irreducible bounded symmetric domain of rank at least 2 and denote by M the dual Hermitian symmetric manifold M of the compact type. If the first Chern class c_1(M) is equal to p+2, by our previous results there are non-standard holomorphic isometric embeddings of the complex unit ball B^{p+1} into Ω (and also holomorphic isometric embeddings of B^k for k < p+1 by slicing). In the current project, we proved in [1] a classification of all holomorphic isometric embeddings of complex unit balls into n-dimensional Lie spheres D_n, which are the noncompact duals of n-dimensional hyperquadrics, and discovered underlying geometric substructures of images of such holomorphic isometries when k is at least 2. Exploiting the geometry of canonical metrics, we proved in [4] the Ax-Lindemann Conjecture for all lattices Γ of B^k for the uniformization map from B^k into X := B^k/Γ. For (2) Ω admits a canonical holomorphic G-structure captured by properties of the decomposition of curvature-like tensors with respect to the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metric. Using this, we showed in [2] that compact splitting complex submanifolds S of X are Hermitian locally symmetric under certain hypotheses on the dimensions of S. The overall findings reflect that the geometries of Ω and X are captured by two types of geometric structures, the projective structure in the rank-1 case and G-structures pertaining to a proper reductive linear subgroup R in the cases of higher rank. These two geometries are captured by properties of the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metrics, viz., constancy of holomorphic sectional curvature in the rank-1 case and properness and reductivity of holonomy groups (same as R) which we showed to have serious implications on splitting compact complex submanifolds of X under dimension restrictions.

17303814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17303814.value: Our result concerning the Zariski closure of images of algebraic subsets of B^n is a result in Functional Transcendence Theory related to the Ax-Lindemann Theorem. Let exp: C --> C* be the exponential map, and e:Cx…xC-->C*x…xC* be defned by e(z_1,…,z_n)=(exp(z_1),…, exp(z_n)). By the Ax-Lindemann Theorem (1970s), for an affine algebraic subset S of Cx…xC, the Zariski closure Z of e(S) in C*x...xC* is necessarily totally geodesic with respect to the quotient Euclidean metric on C*x…xC*. We dealt in particular with the analogue of the Ax-Lindemann Theorem in which the complex Euclidean space Cx…xC is replaced by B^n, C*x…xC* is replaced by the quotient of B^n by any lattice L and S takes the meaning of an algebraic subset of B^n. Our results showed that the Zariski closure of e(S) in X:=B^n/Γ is totally geodesic, yielding an analogue of the Ax-Lindemann Theorem for B^n. By this we opened up a new direction of research in Functional Transcendence Theory using methods of Complex Analysis, Differential Geometry and Algebraic Geometry. This direction of research was formulated into a research project and submitted in 2017 to the RGC for a GRF grant. The proposal was approved and the project is now ongoing.

17303814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17303814.value: Bounded symmetric domains Ω are model manifolds carrying special geometric structures captured by canonical metrics on them called Kaehler-Einstein metrics. (The naming of such metrics is inspired by Albert Einstein's theory of General Relativity.) ln this project we examined the nature of distinguished geometric objects lying on Ω or on their quotient spaces. Focusing on irreducible BSDs, the results break down into the cases where (1) Ω is of rank 1 and (2) Ω is of rank at least 2. For (1), i.e., the complex unit ball B^k, the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metric is of constant negative holomorphic sectional curvature. Exploiting this, we classified images of holomorphic isometric embeddings of B^k into Lie spheres and discovered underlying geometric substructures when k is at least 2. Using the geometry of canonical metrics, we proved the Ax-Lindemann Conjecture for all lattices Γ of B^k for the uniformization map from B^k into X := B^k/Γ. For (2) Ω admits a canonical holomorphic G-structure captured by properties of the decomposition of curvature-like tensors with respect to the canonical Kaehler-Einstein metric. Using this, we showed that compact splitting complex submanifolds S of X are Hermitian locally symmetric under certain hypotheses on the dimensions of S.

17304014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17304014.value: Laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (LDI-MS) is an important technique for direct analysis of samples in the solid state, ranging from semiconductors to biological tissues, forensic samples, and various types of daily life samples. A key to its success is the development of photo-absorption substrates/materials capable of absorbing laser energy in an effective way, and transferring the energy to analyte molecules in a controllable manner for the efficient desorption and ionization of analyte molecules. The LDI process is highly dependent on the physiochemical properties of the substrate. The introduction of nanomaterials as LDI substrates has attained certain success in the modulation and optimization of laser-substrate interaction for governing the laser desorption/ionization processes. However, nanomaterials consisting of single pure materials, such as silicon or graphite, could only have a relatively narrow range of physiochemical properties and, thus, might not have maximized the overall efficiency of LDI processes and the analytical performance of LDI-MS. In this proposal, we postulate, for the first time, that nanoalloys, formed by the mixing of different metal elements with different compositions and atomic lattice arrangements in nano-size, could have unique and tunable physiochemical properties favorable for the efficient desorption/ionization of analyte molecules upon laser irradiation. Specifically, we attempt to develop gold-based nanoalloys as efficient substrates for the modulation and optimization of their (a) laser energy absorption efficiencies, and (b) internal energy transfer efficiencies to analyte ions during the LDI processes. These two parameters are determining factors governing the efficiency of LDI-MS. By varying the different parameters in the physical and chemical preparation methods, Au-based nanoalloys with different chemical compositions, structures and sizes will be prepared. In addition, the physiochemical properties of the prepared nanoalloys, such as optical absorption efficiencies, electronic band gaps, surface plasmonic resonance energies, melting points, and surface binding properties, will be characterized. The effects of the respective physicochemical properties on the overall ion desorption efficiency and the extent of internal energy transfer in the LDI processes will be probed using the mass spectrometric survival yield method. This study will not only enhance our fundamental understanding of the complex LDI processes, but will also provide the basis for the rational design of more efficient LDI substrates for enhancing the detection sensitivity and specificity of LDI-MS for the analysis of a wide variety of chemicals and biochemicals. 激光脫附電離質譜法 (LDI-MS) 是一項重要的直接固體樣本分析方法。它的用途廣泛，已被應用於半導體、生物組織、法證樣品及各種生活常見物品的化學分析。LDI-MS方法成功的關鍵，在於能發展出一些能有效吸收激光能量的基質。這些基質不單能有效吸收激光能量，更能可控地將能量轉移給分析物作脫附和電離。基質吸收和轉移激光能量的效率，取決於它們的理化性質。近年，納米材料被引進成為新型的基質。納米材料的獨特理化性質，令它們能成功調節激光和基質之間的相互作用，從而優化LDI-MS方法（如更高的檢測靈敏度和特異性）。不過，常見的由單一純物質（如碳或矽）所組成的納米材料，理化性質的可調控範圍相對較窄。因此，這類納米材料未必能完全滿足LDI過程所需的基質條件，更可能局限了LDI-MS方法的分析表現。 在本研究項目中，我們率先提出發展納米合金作為LDI方法的基質，並以金作為納米合金基質的主要成份。通過添加不同貴族金屬、改變金屬組合比例、及改變原子晶格排列，製備一系列不同成份、結構和大小的納米合金，並調控它們的理化性質以優化LDI過程，從而提升LDI-MS的分析表現。我們會測量(I)各款納米合金的激光吸收效率，及(II)離子從納米合金基質脫附時的內能轉移(使用質譜法的Survival Yield方法)。這兩項參數對整個基質輔助LDI-MS的分析表現有關鍵性的影響。結合其他重要的納米合金鑑定數據，包括電子能帶距離、表面等離子共振能量、熔點、表面結合特性等等，可以比較和排列出納米合金各項理化性質對LDI過程和效率的影響。本研究項目不但探討了以納米材料作為基質進行LDI的機理，更可為新型納米材料基質的設計提供理論基礎和發展方向，從而開發出更有效率，更靈敏的「納米材料基質輔助LDI-MS方法」，擴闊LDI-MS方法對於不同類型樣本及化合物的分析應用。

17304014.label: Realisation of objectives
17304014.value: We have completely achieved the stated objectives. Overall, six research articles have been published in international peer-reviewed journals, and one manuscript has been submitted for the consideration of publication as a communication article. Three presentations were delivered in international conferences. The important findings are summarized. [Objective 1] & [Objective 2]: Protocols for the preparation of Au-based alloy nanoparticles, including preparation of bimetallic nanoalloys by argon ion sputtering and preparation of core@shell nanoparticles by wet chemical synthesis (i.e., successive reduction method), have been successfully established in our laboratory. After evaluation, Au-Ag alloy nanoparticles were found to have the best potential to be further developed for optical and mass spectrometric analytical applications. Morphology and size of the alloy nanoparticles were characterized using transmission electron microscopy. Optical absorption properties were characterized using UV-Vis absorption spectroscopy. Molecular dynamics simulation method was developed and successfully applied to estimate the melting point, boiling point, and threshold temperature for phase explosion of the alloy nanoparticles. Preparation protocols and characterization results for the Au-based alloy nanoparticles have been published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 2016, 8, 29668 – 29675 and Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, 2017, 19, 20795 – 20807. [Objective 3]: Important physiochemical properties of the alloy nanoparticles and their effects on the performance of surface-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (SALDI-MS) have been revealed. Using mass spectrometric survival yield measurement and molecular dynamics simulation, we found that phase explosion is a critical process to enhance the ion desorption efficiency of SALDI [Journal of Physical Chemistry C 2015, 119, 23708-23720; Journal of Physical Chemistry C, 2016, 120, 20368 – 20377]. We also found that alloying Ag with Au can lower the phase explosion temperature of the nanoparticles and further enhance the ion desorption efficiency compared with pure Au nanoparticles. Furthermore, we also discovered that incorporation of Ag into the nanoparticles would enhance the photoabsorption efficiency to capture more laser energy for the ion desorption. Moreover, the lower work function of Ag could initiate another mechanism, charge-driven particle explosion, to assist the ion desorption process [Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, 2017, 19, 20795 – 20807]. It is concluded that Au-based alloy nanoparticles would be a new class of tunable SALDI substrates to be optimized for different analytical applications. [Objective 4]: New analytical applications have been developed for Au nanoparticles, including chemical printing/in-situ extraction of biological tissues by gold nanoparticle-assisted laser ablation [ACS Omega, 2017, 2, 6031-6038], and direct analysis of over-the-counter drugs and herbal extracts by gold nanoparticle-assisted laser desorption/ionization without interfering infrared spectroscopy method [Analytica Chimica Acta, 2016, 919, 62-69]. For Au-Ag alloy nanoparticles, we carefully optimized their composition to achieve the best ion desorption efficiency for general small molecule detection by SALDI-MS [Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, 2017, 19, 20795 – 20807]. Also, we specifically optimized the Au-Ag alloy nanoparticles for optimal performance in both optical contrast and SALDI-MS detection sensitivity for latent fingerprint imaging [ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 2016, 8, 29668 – 29675]. Recently, we have also developed plasmonic Au and Ag nanoparticles as sensitive mass tags for immunohistochemical imaging of high-mass proteins in mouse kidney tissues [Manuscript has been submitted to a peer-reviewed journal].

17304014.label: Major findings and research outcome
17304014.value: In this project, we successfully prepared Au-Ag alloy nanoparticles of different sizes and compositions, in order to tune their physiochemical properties, for optimal SALDI-MS performance. There are several advantages of using Au-Ag alloy over pure Au nanoparticles, such as easier tuning (e.g., fine adjustment of composition) and wider tuning range (e.g., lower phase explosion temperature and better optical absorption efficiency) for the physiochemical properties, while retaining similar chemical stability. Furthermore, the fundamental studies of gold and gold-based alloy nanoparticle-assisted laser desorption/ionization revealed that phase-explosion of the nanoparticles played an important role in assisting the ion desorption. Moreover, the nanoparticles with high photoabsorption efficiency, weak binding interaction with analyte molecules, and low phase explosion temperature would be promising materials as SALDI substrates. We then developed and applied the Au and Au-Ag alloy nanoparticle-based SALDI-MS to bioanalytical (e.g., in-situ extraction and detection of metabolites from biological tissues) and forensic (e.g., optical and MS imaging of latent fingerprints) applications respectively. In essence, we have accomplished the followings: (1) Six publications in international peer-reviewed journals, including ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, Journal of Physical Chemistry C, Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, Analytica Chimica Acta and ACS Omega. One manuscript has been submitted and is under consideration. (2) Three presentations were delivered in international conferences. (3) We studied the fundamentals of gold and gold-based alloy nanoparticle-assisted laser desorption/ionization. The efforts not only helped identify the underlying mechanism(s), but also helped the design of new substrates with favorable physiochemical parameters [Journal of Physical Chemistry C, 2015, 119, 23708-23720 & Journal of Physical Chemistry C, 2016, 120, 20368 – 20377; Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, 2017, 19, 20795 – 20807]. (4) We developed gold-based alloy nanoparticles as a new class of SALDI substrates. Physiochemical properties which are critical to the analytical performance, such as photoabsorption efficiency and phase-explosion temperature, have been identified and could be tuned readily to deliver optimal performance for analytical applications [ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 2016, 8, 29668 – 29675; Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, 2017, 19, 20795 – 20807]. (5) We also developed new and interesting analytical applications, including in-situ extraction of biological tissues by gold nanoparticle-assisted laser ablation [ACS Omega, 2017, 2, 6031-6038], bridging SALDI-MS and conventional FTIR spectroscopy for the analysis of over-the-counter pharmaceutical products and botanical medicines [Analytica Chimica Acta, 2016, 919, 62-69], and developing plasmonic gold and silver nanoparticles as sensitive ion reporters for the immunohistochemical detection and imaging of high-mass proteins in biological tissues [manuscript submitted].

17304014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17304014.value: The current project helped develop our team’s competence in preparation of various bimetallic and core@shell metal nanoparticles, and studying their physiochemical properties and laser-induced responses via the combination of experimental and computation simulation approach. The results showed that physiochemical properties of Au-Ag alloy nanoparticles could be readily tuned to achieve desired analytical performance (e.g., color with high contrast and stability, high SALDI-MS detection sensitivity), and the alloy nanoparticles have been successfully applied to bioanalytical and forensic analysis. Based on these promising results, we have recognized the importance and direction of controlling the compositions and physiochemical properties of SALDI substrates. This project opened up the possibility of developing other Au-based alloy nanoparticles as potential substrates. We believed that combination of different nanomaterials (and their unique properties), for better harvest, more efficient conversion and more rapid release/transfer of the heat energy, can guide the design of new SALDI substrates with better SALDI-MS performance. Our team will continue to work on the development of new types of nanoparticle-based substrates and related SALDI-MS analytical applications.

17304014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17304014.value: Development of Bioanalytical Chemistry is one of the driving forces for the advancement of biological and biomedical science, such as discoveries of new diagnostic molecular biomarkers and therapeutic drugs. Surface-assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Mass Spectrometry (SALDI-MS) has been developed as a sensitive technique for small molecule analysis. The key to success of SALDI-MS is the choice of substrate materials, for efficient absorption and manipulation of laser energy to desorb/ionize trace analyte molecules for mass spectrometric detection. In this project, we have developed various gold-based alloy nanoparticles as efficient SALDI substrates, and studied their laser desorption/ionization mechanism(s). Based on these understandings, we developed some new SALDI-based analytical applications, such as sensitive imaging of metabolites in latent fingerprints, in-situ metabolite extraction from animal tissues, bridging FTIR and SALDI-MS for the analysis of over-the-counter drugs and herbal extracts, and amplification of ion signal for immunohistochemical imaging. The findings have been published in various peer-reviewed international journals. These accomplishments have laid a solid foundation for guiding the design of more promising SALDI substrates and leading to the development of better bioanalytical methods for the advancement of biological and biomedical sciences.

17304414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17304414.value: Quantum anomalous Hall effect and quantum spin Hall effect are two topological states of quantum matter, which possess chiral and helical edge states around system boundary. The chiral edge states produce quantum Hall conductance while the helical edge states produce pure spin Hall current and/or quantum conductance in a multiple-probe measurement. Experimental observation of quantum anomalous Hall effect in magnetically doped topological insulator thin film was reported recently. A quantum Hall conductance plateau is observed in a magnetic thin film by changing a gate voltage to tune the Fermi level, meanwhile the longitudinal conductance decays with temperature drastically, but does not vanish even at tens minikelvin in the quantum Hall regime. The measurement of quantum conductance of helical edge states InAs/GaSb quantum well was aslo reported. A wide quantum conductance plateau is measured in an electron-hole bilayer sample, and is robust under a perpendicular magnetic field up to 8T, and an in-plane magnetic field up to 12T. An in-depth analysis shows the discrepancy between the experimental data and theoretical predictions, which inspires the present proposal. The primary objective of this proposal is to develop a quantum transport theory for quantum anomalous Hall effect and spin Hall effect, to understand the stability of chiral or helical edge states in a strong magnetic field, and disorder effects in the formation of these edge states. This project will help us to understand physical properties of new topological states, enrich the knowledge of condensed matter physics, and explore possible applications of quantum anomalous Hall effect and quantum spin Hall effect in the next generation of quantum electronic devices. 量子反常霍爾效應和量子自旋霍爾效應是量子物質的兩種拓撲狀態，它們具有圍繞系統邊界手徵和螺旋邊緣態。手徵邊緣態會產生量子霍爾電導，而螺旋邊緣態會生產純的霍爾自旋流，和在多端口測量中得到量子化電導。在磁性摻雜拓撲絕緣體薄膜中，最近有報導實驗上觀察到量子反常霍爾效應。在磁薄膜中，通過改變柵極電壓來調整的費米能級觀察到一種量子霍爾電導平台，同時縱向電導隨溫度急劇衰減，但是在幾十毫K下也沒有完全消失。螺旋邊緣態的量子電導測量在砷化銦/銻化鎵量子井中也有報導。在電子- 空穴的雙層樣品中可測量到較寬的量子電導平台，並且在高達8T的垂直磁場和12T面內磁場下還是是穩定的。進一步深入分析表明，實驗數據和理論預測之間的差異，從而激發了本研究計劃。本方案的主要目標是發展一個量子輸運理論，了解手或螺旋邊緣態在強磁場中，這些邊緣態形成，穩定性，和無序的影響。該項目將幫助我們理解新的拓撲狀態的物理性能，豐富凝聚態物理的知識，並探討量子反常霍爾效應和量子自旋霍爾效應在下一代量子電子器件中的的可能應用。

17304414.label: Realisation of objectives
17304414.value: The primary objective of this proposal is to develop a quantum transport theory for quantum anomalous Hall effect and spin Hall effect, to understand the stability of chiral or helical edge states in a strong magnetic field, and disorder effects in the formation of these edge states. PI proposed to investigate the formation of chiral and helical edge states and quantum transport in these two physical systems, which are closely related, especially in a strong magnetic field. Over the past few years, PI has investigated the robustness of the edge states of quantum Hall effect and quantum spin Hall effect in topological insulator thin film, and examined the formation of quantum plateau of the Hall conductance. PI also investigated possible anonymous transport effect in two-dimensional systems. Totally 6 relevant publications arised directly from this research project, including 3 in Physical Review B, 1 in 2D Materials, 1 in ACS Nano, and 1 in Scientific Reports. The main results arising from this project is to illustrate the stability of the helical edge states in the external magnetic field, and the breaking of the edge state in the presence of the spin-orbital coupling and magnetic field. In the following, PI summarizes the main achievement of the present project. Robustness of quantum spin Hall effect: The edge states in the quantum spin Hall effect are expected to be protected by time reversal symmetry. The experimental observation of the quantized conductance was reported in the InAs/GaSb quantum well (Du et al., arXiv:1306.1925), up to a large magnetic field, which raises a question on the robustness of the edge states in the quantum spin Hall effect under time reversal symmetry breaking. Here we present a theoretical calculation on topological invariants for the Benevig-Hughes-Zhang model in an external magnetic field, and find that the quantum spin Hall effect remains robust up to a large magnetic field. The critical value of the magnetic field breaking the quantum spin Hall effect is dominantly determined by the band gap at the point instead of the indirect band gap between the conduction and valence bands. This illustrates that the quantum spin Hall effect could persist even under time reversal symmetry breaking. Edge states and integer quantum Hall effect in topological insulator thin films: The integer quantum Hall effect is a topological state of quantum matter in two dimensions, and has recently been observed in three-dimensional topological insulator thin films. Here we study the Landau levels and edge states of surface Dirac fermions in topological insulators under strong magnetic field. We examine the formation of the quantum plateaux of the Hall conductance and find two different patterns, in one pattern the filling number covers all integers while only odd integers in the other. We focus on the quantum plateau closest to zero energy and demonstrate the breakdown of the quantum spin Hall effect resulting from structure inversion asymmetry. The phase diagrams of the quantum Hall states are presented as functions of magnetic field, gate voltage and chemical potential. This work establishes an intuitive picture of the edge states to understand the integer quantum Hall effect for Dirac electrons in topological insulator thin films. Tunable interaction-induced localization of surface electrons: Recently, a logarithmic decrease of conductivity has been observed in topological insulators at low temperatures, implying a tendency of localization of surface electrons. Here, we report quantum transport experiments on the topological insulator Bi2Te3 thin films with arrayed antidot nanostructures. With increasing density of the antidots, a systematic decrease is observed in the slope of the logarithmic temperature-dependent conductivity curves, indicating the electronelectron interaction can be tuned by the antidots. Meanwhile, the weak antilocalization effect revealed in magnetoconductivity exhibits an enhanced dominance of electron-electron interaction among decoherence mechanisms. The observation can be understood from an antidot-induced reduction of the effective dielectric constant, which controls the interactions between the surface electrons. Our results clarify the indispensable role of the electronelectron interaction in the localization of surface electrons and indicate the localization of surface electrons in an interacting topological insulator. Renormalization group approach to stability of two-dimensional interacting type-II Dirac fermions: The type-II Weyl/Dirac fermions are a generalization of conventional or type-I Weyl/Dirac fermions, whose conic spectrum is tilted such that the Fermi surface becomes lines in two dimensions, and surface in three dimensions rather than discrete points of the conventional Weyl/Dirac fermions. The mass-independent renormalization group calculations show that the tilting parameter decreases monotonically with respect to the length scale, which leads to a transition from two-dimensional type-II Weyl/Dirac fermions to the type-I ones. Because of the nontrivial Fermi surface, a photon gains a finite mass partially via the chiral anomaly, leading to the strong screening effect of the Weyl/Dirac fermions. Consequently, anisotropic type-II Dirac semimetals become stable against the Coulomb interaction. This work provides deep insight into the interplay between the geometry of Fermi surface and the Coulomb interaction. Chiral anomaly and anomalous finite-size conductivity in graphene: Graphene is a monolayer of carbon atoms packed into a hexagon lattice to host two spin degenerate pairs of massless two-dimensional Dirac fermions with different chirality. It is known that the existence of non-zero electric polarization in reduced momentum space which is associated with a hidden chiral symmetry will lead to the zero-energy flat band of a zigzag nanoribbon and some anomalous transport properties. Here it is proposed that the Adler–Bell–Jackiw chiral anomaly or non-conservation of chiral charges of Dirac fermions at different valleys can be realized in a confined ribbon of finite width, even in the absence of a magnetic field. In the laterally diffusive regime, the finite-size correction to conductivity is always positive and is inversely proportional to the square of the lateral dimension W, which is different from the finite-size correction inversely proportional to W from the boundary modes. This anomalous finite-size conductivity reveals the signature of the chiral anomaly in graphene, and it is measurable experimentally. This finding provides an alternative platform to explore the purely quantum mechanical effect in graphene.

17304414.label: Major findings and research outcome
17304414.value: The aim of the present project is to understand the formation and stability of the helical and chiral edge states in quantum Hall system and quantum spin Hall system in an external magnetic field. Totally 6 relevant publications have been published directly from this research project, including 3 in Physical Review B, 1 in 2D Materials, 1 in ACS Nano, and 1 in Scientific Reports. The major finding of the present project are: (1) A theoretical calculation on for the quantum spin Hall system in an external magnetic field were carried out. It was found that quantum spin Hall effect remains robust up to a large magnetic field. The stability is dominantly determined by the band gap at the Gamma point. This illustrates the quantum spin Hall effect could persists even under time reversal symmetry breaking.This is in agreement with the measurement of the quantized conductance in a large magnetic field observed experimentally. (2) The Landau levels and edge states of surface Dirac fermions in topological insulators are studied under strong magnetic field. The formation of the quantum plateau of the Hall conductance are examined numerically and analytically. Two different patterns are found, the filling number covers all integers in one pattern while only odd integers in the other. This work establishes an intuitive picture of the edge states to understand the integer quantum Hall effect for Dirac electrons in topological insulator thin films, and how the quantum spin Hall effect breaks down when the time reversal symmetry is broken in the presence of the spin-orbital coupling and the external magnetic field.

17304414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17304414.value: In this project PI has studied the formation and the stability of the chiral and helical edge states of quantum Hall effect and quantum spin Hall effect. The two topological phases are still an attractive topic in condensed matter physics. For example quantum Hall effect has been observed recently a in three-dimensional topological Dirac material which quantum spin Hall effect was measured in several samples of 2D materials. We shall continue our exploration along this direction and seek the further support from Research Grants Council.

17304514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17304514.value: Water droplets dispersed in oil are often encountered in the oil and petroleum industries. These droplets need to be removed to avoid fouling and corrosion of the oil pipelines, and to enhance the quality of crude oil. Removal requires fusion of the water droplets, which is often induced by adding chemical demulsifiers as well as heating or electrically charging the water droplets. Of these approaches, the electrical-charging approach is considered the most energy-efficient. Besides oil recovery, charged water droplets also find uses in modern droplet microfluidic applications, where biochemical reactants are compartmentalized in water droplets with extremely small volume at the picoliter range. Miniaturization increases the quantity of compartments that can be analyzed at a given time, thus enabling high-throughput screening of efficacious molecules and cells for biomedical therapeutics and diagnostics at a significantly reduced cost. In these microfluidic applications, droplets are often electrically charged or placed under an electric field to enable their manipulation, including fusion. The practical importance of charged water droplets has motivated investigations into their dynamics and stability under electric field. Since additional chemical compounds are often present in the environment surrounding the charged water droplets, their effects on the droplet dynamics cannot be overlooked in such investigations. Among the additional compounds, amphiphilic molecules, such as surfactants, are highly prevalent in both oil recovery and high-throughput screening applications. These molecules modify the dynamics and stability of water droplets most, due to their tendency to adsorb to the interfaces. However, characterization of electrically charged water droplets in the presence of amphiphiles remains inadequate. The objective of the proposed project is to (1) investigate the interfacial phenomena relevant to charged water droplets by developing an electrical-charging-based device for studying the dynamics of electrically charged water droplets in the presence of common surfactants; (2) characterize the effects of different types of common amphiphile on the dynamics; and (3) demonstrate an electrical-charging-based device for screening the directed assembly of amphiphiles into bilayers at fluid-fluid interfaces of adhesive emulsions. In the short term, the study provides a fundamental understanding of the electrical charging effects on amphiphile-laden interfaces and a new technique for characterizing electrostatically induced fusion of droplets. In the long term, it will contribute to the development of emulsion-based formulations and advancement of fundamental interfacial phenomena involving emulsions. 在製油和石油工業中經常會遇到水滴分散在油中的情況。我們需要除去這些水滴以避免輸油管道結垢和腐蝕，並提高原油的質量。移除這些小水滴過首先需要讓水滴的聚並成大水滴，這常常通過加化學解乳化劑、對水滴加熱、電聚並等方法實現。在這些方法中，點聚並被認為是最節能的方法。除了採油，水滴的電聚並也適用於現代液滴微流體(droplet microfluidics)應用，在這些應用中不同的生化反應物以皮升範圍的體積被分開包裹(compartmentalized)在水滴中。 微型化技術提高了固定時間內可分析的液滴組份(compartments)數量，從而顯著降低生物醫學診斷和治療中高通量篩選出有效分子和細胞的成本。在這些微流體應用裡，液滴往往被通電或置於電場中，從而使對其的操縱包括聚並成為可能。通電水滴在實際應用的重要性已激發了對其在電場下的動力學和穩定性的研究分析。在此類研究分析中，額外的化學物質經常存在於通電水滴周圍的環境中，因此這些化學物質對液滴的動力學的影響是不容忽視的。 在上述的額外化學物質中，兩親性分子，比如表面活性劑，在油的恢復和高通量篩選應用中非常普遍。因為這些分子趨向於吸附至界面上，所以他們在改變了水滴的動力學和穩定性上有很大的影響。但是當下對有兩親分子存在的通電水滴的特徵分析仍然不足。 本研究項目的是： (1)開發液滴通電設備，研究關於帶電水滴的界面現象，從而研究有常見的表面活性劑存在的通電水滴的動力學； (2)表徵常見的不同類型兩親分子對水滴的動力學的影響； (3)演示一種基於通電來篩選兩親性分子組裝成液液界面雙分子層過程的設備。 在短期內，這項研究提供了通電效應會如何影響負載兩親分子的分界面的基本理解，以及用於表徵液滴電聚併的新技術。從長遠來看，這將有助於乳劑的配方開發，與涉及乳劑的分界面基礎現象的進一步發展。

17304514.label: Realisation of objectives
17304514.value: The objectives have been achieved: 1. We have investigated the dynamics of the charged droplets under different conditions, such as liquid velocities, surfactant concentrations and viscosity. We have interpreted the behaviors into different dimensionless numbers, such as electro-capillary number. We have also elucidated the behaviors in relation to the disjoining pressure between the interfaces. 2. We have characterized different types of amphiphiles, such as surfactants and other macromolecules. Our understanding has enabled the use of electrical charging effects to form membranes consisting of amphiphiles through interfacial assembly. Droplets that are formed or manipulated by charging have also been shown to have great potential to be used as micro-containers for biomedical applications. 3. We have demonstrated approach based on electrical charging to study the ability of amphiphiles to adhere to each other by both direct current, and alternating current. These result in measurements of the critical voltage and critical frequency for evaluating different aspects of the interactions between amphiphiles at interfaces. The works have also inspired new ways to form structures from components, such as proteins and particles. We believe this work has concluded that electrical charging is a promising way to build structures from amphiphiles with likelihood towards scale up.

17304514.label: Major findings and research outcome
17304514.value: - Understand how the dynamics of charging of water droplets relate to tunable parameters in micro-devices - Introduce new approaches to fabricate materials from amphiphiles based on droplets prepared by electrical charging - Widen the type of amphiphiles and macromolecules that can be processed by electrical charging - Extend the advantages of this electrical charging approach to biomedical applications. Most of the results have been presented in various international conferences (e.g. ASME International Conference on Nanochannels, Microchannels and Minichannels, APS Division of Fluid Dynamics etc.) and published in respected international journals (e.g. Journal of Materials Chemistry B, ACS Applied Materials and Interfaces, Soft Matter, Analytical Chemistry, etc.), as shown in Part C. While some papers have been submitted and are being reviewed, other results are being integrated with other applications and wrapped up for publication due to their potential for a greater impact.

17304514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17304514.value: Electrical charging is often a preferred means to controlling and manipulating objects, due to their excellent tenability. The manipulation of water droplets with and without amphiphiles represent a new area with outstanding potential for microscaled processing, such as materials fabrication and biomedical applications. In particular, membranes that are formed from assembly of amphiphiles are particular suited to using droplet interfaces as templates, due to their inherent bilayered nature. Hence the works have demonstrated promises for any applications that use membrane bound structures, including but are not limited to cosmetics and biomedical encapsulation. The ideas and tools may also benefit the development of artificial cells. The proposed course of action include publishing the remaining works, while discussing the attracting aspects with potential industrial and/or clinical collaborators who may look for either a formulation screening technique or a technique to form structures composed of amphiphiles. In addition, we also propose to explore the conversion of our lab-scale models into industrially manufacturable machines through collaborations with large companies or startups. These efforts will be facilitated by research grants, such as those from the Innovation and Technology Fund (ITF) of Hong Kong, and some other funding sources that connect the industries and academia in Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangdong province, where manufacturing is very mature. Some of the discussions and developmental plans have already started, with great interest from both scientific and industrial collaborators. Some of the project outcomes achieved are also benefiting other research projects indirectly.

17304514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17304514.value: Electrically charging of liquids have led to a variety of technologies, such as printing and fabrication of bioscaffolds. However, besides these current applications, liquid drops can also be charged electrically and lead to different dynamics with potential, particularly for assembly and manipulation of amphiphilic molecules, such as surfactants. Success in doing so will enable controlled stabilization and destabilization of emulsion drops, and new ways to assemble structures, such as membranes with amphiphiles as constituents. In this project, we developed a physical understanding of the dynamics of electrically charged droplets under different conditions, facilitating subsequent use of charged droplets in various applications. We also characterized the applicability of the electrical charging approaches to different amphiphiles, establishing the generality of these approach, and enabling new assembly strategies of droplet-based amphiphilic materials. We have also demonstrated devices that are based on electrical charging, with direct current and alternating current, for screening the stability of different amphiphile-laden interfaces. These results will provide the tools for evaluating the stability of interfaces with amphiphiles adsorbed, and inspire new applications of electrically charged water droplets, such as fabrication of drug delivery vehicles and biomedical containers for screening of compounds and cells. The approaches introduced have also demonstrated possibility for scaling up for industrial applications.

17304614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17304614.value: 金屬離子在生物學和醫學的作用是雙刃劍。一方面，它們作為酶的輔因子（如鐵和銅）和發揮對蛋白質的結構和功能有非常重要的作用;另一方面，它們也呈現出毒性，從而導致由其誘導的蛋白質功能障礙的各種疾病。儘管砷是無必需元素，其已成功用於治療急性早幼粒細胞白血病治療（ APL ;使用三氧化二砷， Trisenox® ） ，急性髓細胞白血病明顯的亞型，這可能源於砷礦物質，一個中國古老的傳統藥方。新的有機砷化合物(organoarsenical)正在開發和在對APL和其他癌症的臨床試驗。奇怪的是，砷被列為第一類人類致癌物和長期接觸，特別是含砷的飲水可導致多種癌症。 砷是一種典型的半金屬。作為“軟”的金屬，它結合蛋白質中的半胱氨酸（和組氨酸）; 而作為非金屬形成穩定的砷-碳鍵 (AS-C)。其準金屬的獨特特徵通常呈現在砷-蛋白質複合物中，例如可以觀察到半胱氨酸-砷-碳鍵。蛋白質和酶被認為是三氧化二砷（ATO）的目標，雖然甲基化也是一個重要的代謝物。作為砷（III）的已被證明直接結合的半胱氨酸殘基中的鋅指位於早幼粒細胞白血病蛋白（PML）的氮端RING結構域之內。但這樣的蛋白質相互作用誘導PML齊聚，從而提高SUMO化和降解。然而，似乎缺乏砷結合蛋白在（病理）生理學相關條件蛋白質組範圍的研究。 基於申請人砷的金屬組學和砷對其他類型癌細胞的細胞毒性初步數據顯示，申請人拟採用白血病細胞為例，開展砷結合蛋白的分子機制的綜合研究。申請人拟用整合的方法，包括自製的連續流動電泳和電感耦合等離子體質譜法（ GE- ICP-MS）系統結合蛋白質組學和結構生物學的策略。具體來說，申請人和合作者打算： （1）通過比較蛋白質組學和金屬蛋白質組學研究白血病細胞對三氧化二砷和砷的相關抗癌藥物，建立拟生理條件下砷結合蛋白研究的綜合方法。 （2）在敏感和不敏感的白血病細胞中，以及在不同的相位比較三氧化二砷-結合蛋白的分佈。 （3）進一步研究這三氧化二砷在生理學相關條件結合到某些關鍵蛋白（細胞）的熱力學和動力學。 （4）在蛋白質組範圍內建立三氧化二砷蛋白/基序結合的數據庫以及其合理化的依據。 所提出的研究將裝備我們用整合的方法來確定三氧化二砷和其他含砷化合物結合的蛋白質，從而將大大改善我們對三氧化二砷作用機制的認識。本研究的長遠目標是建立在金屬醫學和金屬蛋白質組學/金屬組學的領先的學術中心。

17304614.label: Realisation of objectives
17304614.value: Arsenic, a semi-metal, has long been in TCM and over ten years ago arsenic trioxide (ATO) was successfully used for the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL). New organoarsenical compounds are being developed and tested in clinical trials for APL and other types of cancers. Paradoxically, arsenic is classified as first class human carcinogen. As(III) binds to proteins at cysteines (and histidines) as a ‘soft’ metal, whereas forms a stable As-C bond as a non-metal. The unique feature of metalloid can commonly be observed in arsenic-protein complexes. Proteins and enzymes have been believed to be the targets of ATO although methylation is also an important metabolite. In this project, the PI (Prof. Sun) and Co-I (Prof. Tse) have established an integrated approach consisting of GE-ICP-MS and fluorescence for mining of arsenic-binding proteins under physiologically relevant condition (e.g. in cells). We examined responses of two leukaemia cells (NB4 and HL60) to ATO and related arsenic anticancer agents by comparative proteomics and metalloproteomics. To achieve it, we synthesized a new arsenic probe, which can rapidly enter cells to label and subsequently identify As(III)-binding proteins inside live cells. We found 38 and 32 As(III)-binding proteins in NB4 and HKL60 cells respectively. The up- and down-regulated proteins upon exposure of ATO (for 1 hr) were also examined and our combined data with bioinformatics (with the help of Volcano plot) clearly show that Hsp60 in mitochondrion is one of the important targets. Our further cellular thermal-shift assay (CETSA) of Hsp60 and bioassay of the Hsp60/Hsp10 refolding activity confirmed that As(III) binds Hsp60 and subsequently disrupts the function of the Hsp60, leading to the dysfunction of p53. This is the first direct evidence of anticancer activity of ATO by suppression of p53 through Hsp60, and part of the work was presented in international conferences (6th International Symposium on Metallomics, Vienna, 08/2017). A manuscript entitled “a selective fluorescent probe to track arsenic-binding proteins inside live leukemia cells” was submitted for publication and a patent is also in preparation. We then compared the profiles of ATO-binding proteins of ATO and ZIO-101 in NB4 and HL60 cells as well as at different phases of these cells. Different expression levels of aquaglyceroporin 9 (AQP9) and xCT, which are key regulators to facilitate ATO and ZIO-101 transport, are observed which only partially accountable for the observed differences in arsenic uptake across cell cycle, suggesting the presence of other importers for both ATO and ZIO-101. Furthermore, we show that the cytotoxicity of ATO and ZIO-101 on NB4 cells is also cell cycle dependent, with the highest cytotoxicity at S+G2/M phase and the lowest at G1+S phase. Our studies provide the first evidence on cell cycle dependent uptake and cytotoxicity of arsenic-based drugs at single cell levels, may have general implications for precise evaluation of other anticancer drugs by considering cell cycle phase. This part of the work was published (Sun and Tse etc, Anal Chem. 2018, 90, 10465). Certain proteins markers were analyzed by mass cytometer through quantification of proteins by a lanthanide-tag and will open a new horizon for single-cell metallomics and accordingly precision medicine. We further characterize both thermodynamics and kinetics of ATO binding to proteins such as RING and BIRD domains. We showed that RING of XIAP protein binds two arsenic (III) moderately with binding affinity of (Kd) of 18 μM. Binding of As(III) disrupts the dimerization of RING(XIAP) and subsequently affects its biological activity through conformational change. Our combined data indicated that ATO controls the fate of the XIAP by directly binding RINGXIAP finger domain, resulting in inhibition of XIAP’s self-ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. These data will be submitted for publication soon. Attempts have been made to crystallize As(III) protein complexes, however due to labile binding feature of As(III) to proteins (although thermodynamically stable), no crystals were obtained until recently (As(III)-RING). We also have built a data bank on ATO binding motifs/proteins at a proteome-wide scale for rationalization of ATO binding to proteins. Our study improves our understanding of the mechanism of action of ATO (and relevant compounds) and sheds lights into discovery of new drugs leads using new protein target(s). Certain parts of the work were published and a patent on mining of As(III)-proteome at proteome-wide scale is in preparation.

A manuscript was submitted for publication. We then compared the profiles of ATO-binding proteins of ATO and ZIO-101 in NB4 and HL60 cells as well as at different phases of these cells. Different expression levels of aquaglyceroporin 9 (AQP9) and xCT, which are key regulators to facilitate ATO and ZIO-101 transport, are observed which only partially accountable for the observed differences in arsenic uptake across cell cycle, suggesting the presence of other importers for both ATO and ZIO-101. Furthermore, we show that the cytotoxicity of ATO and ZIO-101 on NB4 cells is also cell cycle dependent. We provide the first evidence on cell cycle dependent uptake and cytotoxicity of arsenic-based drugs at single cell levels, may have general implications for precise evaluation of other anticancer drugs by considering cell cycle phase. This part of the work was published (Sun and Tse etc, Anal Chem). We further characterize both thermodynamics and kinetics of ATO binding to proteins such as RING and BIRD domains. We showed that RING of XIAP protein binds two arsenic (III) moderately with binding affinity of (Kd) of 18 μM. Binding of As(III) disrupts the dimerization of RING(XIAP) and subsequently affects its biological activity through conformational change. Our combined data indicated that ATO controls the fate of the XIAP by directly binding RING finger domain, resulting in inhibition of XIAP’s self-ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. We also have built a data bank on ATO binding motifs/proteins at a proteome-wide scale for rationalization of ATO binding to proteins.

17304614.value: We for the first time provide a As(III)-proteomes in both As(III) sensitive and insensitive cells, i.e. NB4 and HL60. The functions of those arsenic-binding proteins such as Hsp60 and Histone H3.3 are carefully analyzed. They may serve as a new drug target for cancer therapy.

17304614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17304614.value: Arsenic, a semi-metal, has long been in TCM and arsenic trioxide (ATO) was successfully used for the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL). New organoarsenical compounds are being developed and tested in clinical trials for APL and other cancers. Proteins and enzymes have been believed to be the targets of ATO although methylation is also an important metabolite. In this project, the PI and Co-I (Prof. Tse) have (i) established an integrated approach for mining of arsenic-binding proteins under physiologically relevant condition (e.g. in cells). (ii) We examined leukaemia cell responses to ATO and related arsenic anticancer agents; and (ii) compared the profiles of ATO-binding proteins in NB4 and HL60 cells as well as at different phases of these cells. We found that Hsp60 to be one of the critical targets (iii) We further characterize both thermodynamics and kinetics of ATO binding to proteins such as RING and BIRD domains. (iv) We have built a data bank on ATO binding motifs/proteins at a proteome-wide scale for rationalization of ATO binding to proteins. Our study provides new knowledge on the mechanism of action of ATO and as well as for development of new anticancer drugs.

17304914.label: Realisation of objectives
17304914.value: We have successfully addressed all proposed objectives, and beyond, due to the timely recruitment of research team, well-designed experiments and well-established collaborations with both researchers around the world and also with local oyster growers: Research team: We had FIVE full-time PhD and ONE full-time M Phil students to finish this project (see students list for details). Among those six students, the research thesis of THREE students are fully based on this project. They are: Dr Ko Wai Kuen (Ginger). She joined the project with Biotechnology background and graduated on time with PhD thesis (which was rated as an excellent, received best research award, and published 6 papers during her PhD). Her thesis work, rightly, as stated in the project objectives, addressed how the three aquaculture species of oysters along the coastal areas of China will respond to near-future climate change scenarios – i.e. who will be the winner or loser. After graduating from our lab, Dr Ko is currently working in Nature Conservancy. Her thesis was co-supervised by one of the Co-I’s of this project, Dr Yun Lam. Dr Yuan Meng: She has joined the project and our lab as PhD student with mechanical engineer (specializing in mechanics) background. This month, June, 2018, she has successfully defended her PhD thesis and successfully awarded (with “excellent comments”) PhD thesis. Using this multi-disciplinary project, Yuan has established several international and interdisciplinary collaborations to become a PhD scholar. Yuan’s multidisciplinary, cross-faculty (Science and Engineering) and cutting-edge research data have immensely helped this project to address all the three proposed objectives. Subsequently, Dr Yuan has just published very high quality papers (Papers 7, 8 and 13), and very much ready to join as faculty member in one of the top mainland universities. Importantly, all these papers clearly showing her interdisciplinary and international collaborative skills – involved authors from science, engineering and biomedical fields – and also multiple universities such as HKU, Poly U (Hong Kong) and University of Glasgow (UK). Experimental Plan: In the first part of this project, we have attempted to identify the winners and losers among the three oyster species that are intensely cultivated along the coastal waters of China for commercial aquaculture using a set of physiological traits as an index to assess their response to multiple climate change stressors. We have addressed this relatively challenging objective we have designed large-scale and long-term experiments. For example: The three species of oysters have been raised from embryo- to juvenile stage, at various treatment conditions, at hatchery scale experimental system using 500 L culture tanks; Our students went to oyster hatcheries in China. For example, oyster hatchery of South China Sea Institute of Oceanology (with Prof Ziniu Yu as collaborator) and done experiments in 2014 to 2018; also we went to Institute of Oceanology oyster hatchery during 2016 to 2018. All our experiments involved multiple measurements. For example, from a large-scale experiments involving multiple life stages, we took samples at multiple time points to study their physiological, developmental, and molecular and biomechanics levels. These multiple measurements, across multiple life stages of each species, were then comparatively examined to determine the winner and loser. Interdisciplinary collaborations: The project was successfully completed because our well established collaborations with FOUR institutes and oyster researchers from multi-disciplinary background – we all have co-authored papers (Papers 1-13). For example: Dr Yun Lam (YL) of City University, one of the CO-I’s of this proposal. YL is from chemistry background and intensively worked with the PI’s group and co-supervised one of the project students PhD thesis (Ginger Ko). YL has helped the project to successfully map most of the oyster shell proteins using modern proteomics tools, as proposed in the project proposal. This is one of the highly successful collaborations. Subsequently, both the PI and YL came up with new ideas for RGC collaborative research proposal and also unsuccessfully submitted to RGC in 2017. The 2nd Co-I, Dr Haimin Yao (HY), from Poly U of Hong Kong, is a mechanical engineer specializing in the analysis of biologically produced calcareous materials using nanoindentation and several modeling software tools. VT and HY have been working in collaboration for the past 4 years in this project. HY helped us to co-supervise Dr Yuan Meng’s thesis work in this project, which facilitated fulfill several objectives of this proposal. HY and VT have established strong collaborations and have received two GRF grants for individual projects on slightly related subjects. HY has provided advice on the application of various mechanical engineering tools. HY is currently co-supervising another PhD student working in PI’s laboratory. To what extent, we have achieved the proposed 3 objectives: Objective 1(“physiological vulnerability”) – We have fully addressed this objectives. Also, most of these results have been published in various journals (e.g. papers 1-2, 5-6). Meeting this objective was much challenging because culturing Hong Kong oysters from embryo to juvenile stage was extremely complicated and we were unsuccessful for couple of year and only managed to finish this experiment last year. On the other hand, culture of Pacific oyster and Portuguese oysters were much easier and therefore we have easily managed to finish those two experiments in first couple of years of this project. Nevertheless, we have managed to finish all the three species culture successfully now and quantified their physiological fitness response variable measurements, such as growth rate, respiration rate and developmental responses in response to various stressors such as ocean acidification, warming, hypoxia and reduced salinity. Objective 2 (“molecular mechanisms”) – Using the samples collected from the above experiments (in objective 1), we have intensively worked out the molecular mechanisms of multiple climate change stressor tolerance in three different oyster species. As genome of these oyster species have been annotated recently, we were able to complete this objective with great success. Briefly, using the newly annotated complete genome information from Chinese oysters, and OMICS (transcriptomics and proteomics) approaches, we have gained new insights into the mechanisms through which shellfishes might adapt or succumb to the projected coastal ocean acidification, warming and freshening scenarios. These results have been published in several papers (Papers 3 and 12) Objective 3 (“multi-nanoindentation mapping”) – This final objective was one of the most intensively studied subject in this project. The reason for this additional effort was due to the fact that this area of research is least studied in the entire climate change science and is fully interdisciplinary in nature. Therefore, we have recruited couple of PhD students from engineering background to study this objective. This truly interdisciplinary approach has paid off well. For example, the PI’s lab now has internationally recognized as interdisciplinary laboratory. Acidification, , warming, and freshening of seawater due to rising anthropogenic CO2 may collectively impair the calcification process and thus oysters is expected to form a shell with poor mechanical properties. Through an interdisciplinary collaboration with biological, medical and engineering faculties, we have successfully applied variety of mechanical engineering tools such as micro-CT scanning and nanoindentation to measure various mechanical properties of the calcified shells formed by three different oyster species. Consequently, we have modeled their shell strength using the engineering computational ABACUS model. These results have been published in various high impact factor journals (papers 4, 6-9 and 13)

17304914.label: Major findings and research outcome
17304914.value: Research achievements of this project are summarized in the abstract of 6 PhD students (attached) and 13 papers (attached) they published that are directly related to this project. These findings have been internationally recognized, e.g. the PI’ has been invited 12 times to present this project results in various international meetings as invited or key note lectures. Briefly, this project has come out with the following major conclusions: 1. We have managed to evaluate the interactive effects of three or four stressors (decreased pH, reduced salinity, hypoxia and elevated temperature) to various oyster species in a hatchery scale at physiological, molecular and mechanical levels. 2. Certainly, ocean acidification and other stressors will produce winners and losers among the three commercially cultivated oysters, the Hong Kong, the Pacific and the Portuguese oysters. The invasive oysters (Pacific and Portuguese) appear to be winners and they may have the capacity to invade and replace the native Hong Kong oyster. 2. We have successfully used the high-resolution shotgun proteomics technology (iTRAQ-2D LC–MS/MS) to understand how the Pacific oyster larval proteome was altered to cope with multiple stressors including ocean acidification, warming and reduced salinity. As the complete genome of this oyster species is available, we have identified thousands of oyster larval proteins with high confidence and also quantitatively mapped molecular pathways used by them to tackle climate stressors. 3. We show that Hong Kong oyster is able to withstand a significantly higher compressive force than Portuguese oysters. The higher compressive strength of Hong Kong oyster is coincident with a higher folia and lower chalk content as determined by micro-CT. The shells of Hong Kong oysters is softer and more elastic than Portuguese oysters which, combined with a lower chalk content, is likely to account for the higher compressive strength of Hong Kong oyster. These insights into the relationship between structural composition, crystallography and mechanical material properties provide an insightful context in which to consider the likely fate of a native and an invasive species in future climate change scenarios. 4. This project results, cumulatively, illustrated the trade-offs between the microstructural and crystallographic characteristics and the mechanical features in oyster shells of different species in near-future coastal oceans with ocean acidification, warming and freshening, which is not only surfaced the intriguing capability of oysters in biomineralization but also provided critical knowledge for forecasting the survival and production of edible oysters in the future ocean.

17304914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17304914.value: Unprecedented changing climates are exposing edible oysters to environments not previously experienced in recent years, leading to phenotype-environment mismatches and higher mortality and lowering the overall fitness. On organismal level, the ability to adapt and alter phenotype in response to rapid environmental changes may help to buffer against reductions in fitness. There has been increasing evidence that show epigenetic mechanisms, where heritable changes in gene functions are induced without altering underlying DNA sequence, can help to regulate the adaptive ability and phenotypic plasticity. To shed light on the role of the mechanisms in mediating adaption, we need to perform an exposure experiment using various different oysters’ species and genotypes that are cultivated along the entire Chine coastal area. Results from this, next-level, research will help to clarify the potential heritability of epigenetic traits in oyster, that are identified in this project, and provide insight into stress and adaptive mechanisms that help characterize the role of epigenetic regulations in response to these mechanisms that underlie oyster defenses against climate change. Next: The PI will explore both local (e.g. CRF) and mainland funding in collaboration with local and mainland oyster industry to find solutions for sustainable oyster aquaculture in a changing climate.

17304914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17304914.value: Oyster species are widely distributed throughout the globe and are well known to provide direct benefits to mankind as an ecosystem engineer, economic commodity and nutritious delicacy. This precious natural resource is, however, under threat due to climate change. This is a serious issue to China because >80% of world’s oyster are produced here. In this project, we have determined the winner and losers among three commercially important aquaculture oysters’ species along the entire coastal areas of China. Using various physiological, altered molecular metabolic pathways and shell mechanical models, we have comparatively analyzed various functional traits of present day and acclimated oyster species to near-future climate change scenarios, which will, allow an assessment of which species have very fixed physiological responses and may simply succumb to changing climates; and which can modify their physiological responses and may perform well under hotter temperatures; and enabled us predict changes in the distribution and success of these important species over the next 100 years. Our long-term, multi-species, multiple-stressor and multiple-life stage studies have identified that calcification, metamorphosis and growth of several oyster species will be negatively affected by coastal climate change stressors, threatening their viability, regardless of species.

17305114.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17305114.value: 新拓撲類形的無能隙邊界模式及其量子模擬

17305114.label: Project Objectives
17305114.value: We plan to construct a kind of one-dimensional (1d) topological lattice model whose Hamiltonian belongs to BDI-class with both the time-reversal symmetry (TRS) and particle-hoe symmetry (PHS). Based on our insight of boundary-bulk correspondence, we will elaborate that the corresponding gapless boundary-modes can be regarded as Fermi surfaces (FSs) on the boundary and are of Z-type. We intend to explore this model both analytically and numerically, and to manipulate a topological phase transition and a non-Abelian operation by tuning a controllable parameter. Moreover, we will try to simulate them with artificial-made quantum systems. We intend to propose a new D-III type of BdG-like 1d topological superconductor that has a pair of degenerated nontrivial Z2(2)-type gapless modes at each end-point with a fixed parity of fermion number, corresponding to the two orthogonal ground states. Based on this special feature, we aim to design a universal set of topologically-protected operations and simulate them quantum-mechanically, which may in principle make universal topological quantum computing possible, but it has never been achieved with the usual D-class topological systems of Z2(1)-type. We attempt to construct a novel CII-class lattice model that has a 2Z-type of nontrivial topological charges for the gapless boundary-modes.

17305114.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17305114.value: Research on the boundary-bulk correspondence of topological quantum systems has recently stimulated great interest. In particular, gapless boundary-modes of a kind of one-dimensional D-class topological superconductors as well as their quantum simulation have been paid much attention. However, as is known, not only it is extremely challenging to test experimentally the predicted non-Abelian statistics of these gapless boundary-modes in the D-class topological superconductors, but also it is in principle impossible to employ this type of boundary-modes to realize a set of universal quantum operations, while it is badly wanted for topological quantum computing. Motivated by this, in this project, we plan to construct several models with different topological classes and to search for some new topological types of gapless boundary-modes in the artificially-made topological superconducting lattices as well as to simulate them physically, which not only are of fundamental importance, but also possess a distinct advantage and potential for universal topological quantum computing in comparison with the D-class ones. It is expected that the proposed research will make a timely and valuable contribution to the interdisciplinary field related to condensed matter physics and topological quantum computing. 近來關於拓撲量子系統體－邊界對應的研究，特別是關於一類 一維D-型拓撲超導體及其量子模擬，引起了人們極大的興趣。 但是，實現D-型的無能隙邊界模式不僅實驗上具極大挑戰， 而且原則上不能進行普適的量子操控。 鑒於此，本項研究計劃 構造不同拓撲類的模型和在人造的拓撲超導晶格上尋找新拓撲 型的無能隙邊界模式， 並在物理上模擬它們。相關研究不僅有 重大的基礎意義，而且具實現普適量子計算的潛力和優點。 預期該項研究將對相關領域作出及時和有價值的貢獻。

17305114.label: Realisation of objectives
17305114.value: We proposed a lattice model of one-dimensional topological BDI-class Hamiltonian with both the time-reversal symmetry (TRS) and particle-hole symmetry (PHS), and then explored it theoretically. In addition, we also proposed a new D-III type of BdG-like 1d topological superconducting chain, and suggested a scheme to simulate it with superconducting quantum circuits, which may make a kind of universal topological quantum computing possible. Moreover, we also addressed topological gapless systems with other nontrivial anti-unitary symmetries like joint PT and CP symmetries. Finally, we also constructed a nontrivial CII-class lattice model that has a 2Z-type of nontrivial topological charges for the gapless boundary-modes. All of objectives have been achieved successfully.

17305114.label: Major findings and research outcome
17305114.value: We constructed an exotic class topological one-dimensional model with both the time-reversal symmetry and particle-hole symmetry. The corresponding topological gapless modes were found to be of Z-type. Besides, a new D-III class of 1D topological superconducting chain was proposed, and a feasible scheme was worked out with superconducting quantum circuits. The effects of disorder on various gapless topological systems were revealed. Moreover, a nontrivial CII-class lattice model that has a 2Z-type of nontrivial topological charges for the gapless boundary-modes was proposed and studied. Notably, a theory for Z2-type gapless modes was established for the first time, and a set of new topological classes with the PT and CP anti-unitary symmetries was classified and explored.

17305114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17305114.value: Our theoretical proposals and predictions on the D-III model and PT zero-modes may be emulated in superconducting quantum circuits. It is planned to make collaborations with experimental groups in other institutions on the matters.

17305114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17305114.value: Topological systems have recently stimulated a great interest as they are not only fundamentally important but also may have potential applications in robust quantum computing. In this project, we proposed several models with different topological classes and discovered new topological types of gapless boundary-modes. In particular, we elaborate how to simulate them physically in artificial superconducting lattices, which posses a distinct potential for realizing universal robust quantum computing. It is expected that our research would make a timely and valuable contribution to the interdisciplinary field related to condensed matter physics and topological quantum computing.
