17405014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17405014.value: In popular definition, the term ‘cybertext’ evokes the image of electronic literature written and read on digital platforms. In critical inquiry, however, the term covers a wide range of literary products, both printed and digital, that require the reader to undertake non-trivial actions during the course of reading. By ‘non-trivial action’, we mean the reader does not merely appreciate the contents of a literary work at an intellectual level, but also engages with its material medium and technology more physically. This type of literature is dynamic, as its outcome is determined, to a certain extent, by the reader's interaction with or manipulation of the textual material. In the Chinese world, creative works of literature that may be termed ‘cybertexts’ have been appearing over the past decade. However, the cybertext (and, more generally, experimental forms of literature) has not been fully recognized in mainstream Chinese literary criticism. This study is a first step towards filling this gap. It seeks to identify and analyze various modes of cybertextuality in contemporary Chinese poetics, including: (1) the printed poetry collection that allows the reader to configure disparate text segments at will to create new poems; (2) the computer hypertext that requires the reader to activate functional links in order to set a poem ‘in action’; (3) the interactive literary-art installation that generates poems based on textual input from the reader. As one of the first systematic studies of the Chinese cybertext, this project aims to conceptualize different modalities of experimental Chinese poetry as a dynamic spectrum. It focuses attention on an emerging form of contemporary experimental writing, with an eye to its structural and interactive features as well as the changing role of the reader vis-à-vis the author and the literary text. In doing so, the project lays the groundwork that will facilitate the research and teaching of this type of literature, which is presently marginalized in most literary curricula.

17405014.label: Realisation of objectives
17405014.value: All objectives set out have been realised. Specifically: I have analysed the proposed modalities of the cybertext with reference to contemporary Chinese poetry, and can now establish that these constitute different formations of the Cybertext Continuum, noting though that cybertext is not a closed category (Objective 1). These modalities have been found to be different from each other in terms of their structure and interactive potential; this relates to the role of the mode and medium and how these interact with the text in the production of literary experiences (Objectives 2 and 3). In each of these cases, I find that the role of the reader changes, for example, a reader can turn into a viewer-participant, even or a player/agent when encountering dynamic texts (Objective 4). The above themes are addressed in my research output accruing from this project (Objective 5; see below for details).

17405014.label: Major findings and research outcome
17405014.value: The research findings are published as follows: Research Outcome 1: "Translanguaging and visuality: Translingual practices in literary art", Applied Linguistics Review 2015; 6(4): 441–465. Major finding: Translanguaging operates in two visual art installations by the contemporary Chinese artist Xu Bing: transvisuality and transdiscursivity. In radical works of language art, translanguaging delineates borders while simultaneously interrogating them, creating liminal zones and articulating a politics of (mis)recognition, (un)readability, and (in)communicability. Research Outcome 2: "Cybertext: A Topology of Reading", in Modern Chinese Language and Literature, 29(1), forthcoming Spring 2017. Major finding: The creative geographies of the cybertext trigger a model of literary criticism that privileges the artifact of the text rather than the text itself. It also moves away from the dichotomous and oppositional relation between Author and Reader, treating both as co-participants in a holistic process of creating and unraveling a text-in-potential, a process capable of perpetual reiteration. At one level the cybertext resists against the myth of communicability. It asks: what if the entire point about a literary work is to not communicate? What if, to cite Susan Sontag, the whole point is to demonstrate “how it is what it is, even that it is what it is, rather than to show what it means” (Sontag 1994: 14; original emphasis)? I have suggested that the poems in Rub Ineffable, Pink Noise, and That Zebra need not, indeed must not, be read with serious intent, as if there were an underlying semantic core to be consumed, regurgitated, and digested. The issue here is not so much the question of form vs. content. It is the textual event, its ishness or suchness as manifested in the text artifact and all its attendant technologies, that comes to the fore, superseding a priori concerns about message and meaning. The text artifact is the message as well as the portal through which a reader enters into that message with the entirety of his/her body. Research Outcome 3: Translanguaging and Translation (monograph, with Mike Baynham), London: Routledge. Expected 2019. Major finding: Contract has been signed with Routledge, and research/writing is still underway.

17405014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17405014.value: There is potential to look at how creative individuals tap into social media and other forms of digital platforms to unleash the potential of translanguaging to create new virtual identities, including but not limited to literature.

17405014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17405014.value: This research project foregrounds the idea that a literary text does not belong solely to its author; it belongs as well to its reader. In unique formations of literature such as the cybertext, the reader is drawn into the creative process by virtue of his/her embodied engagement with the text. This means that the reader does not merely read or interpret the meaning of a text passively; s/he actively participates and intervenes in unravelling the text through his/her body and senses. In so doing, the identity of the reader changes to that of a viewer or even a player. The cybertext can thus be seen as a 'democratic' mode of literature wherein reader, author, and text (including its medium) interact to produce dynamic reading experiences.

17405314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17405314.value: Hong Kong launched the Pre-primary Education Voucher Scheme in 2007 to promote the affordability, accessibility, and accountability of early childhood education (Li, Wong, & Wang, 2010). This is a half-day voucher, which is calculated based on the average tuition of half-day programs. Thus, whole-day programs are under-subsidized. Many stakeholders urge the launch of a whole-day voucher, but there is little research on the relative benefits of half-day versus whole-day programs. To provide empirical evidence for theoretical development and practical improvement, we propose a three-year longitudinal study to compare the long-term effects of the two programs by following the development of a cohort of K1 students (aged 3). Specifically, we focus on the following questions: (1) Are there any significant differences in literacy, cognitive, and social development between half-day and whole-day kindergarteners? (2) How are the differences moderated by child characteristics, family background, parenting practice, and program quality? Stratified random sampling will be conducted to recruit 48 schools, representing 10% of the total 484 kindergartens that provide both half-day and whole-day programs (www.edb.gov.hk). One half-day and one whole-day K1 class will be randomly selected from each participating school, and 15 students will be randomly sampled from each selected class, yielding a total of 1,440 subjects. At the beginning of K1 (October 2014), and the end of each school year (June of 2015, 2016, 2017), the 1,440 students will be assessed with the Bracken Basic Concept Scale, Preschool and Primary Chinese Literacy Scale, and the Social Competence Scale. Their parents (N= 1440) will complete the Early Parental Involvement Scale and their teachers (N=96) will complete the Classroom Teaching Practice Report at the end of each school year. All the classes (N=96) will be assessed with the Early Childhood Classroom Observation Scale every March/April to evaluate the program quality. We will compare the student outcomes using hierarchical linear model with their family background and potential confounders, such as the family, school, and classroom effects, being controlled for. The comparisons matched by family socioeconomic status will be conducted within and/or between schools to control for sample selection bias. Those enrolled in two separate half-day sessions and/or switch from half-day to whole-day or vice versa will be analyzed separately as subgroups. This study will contribute to our understanding of the relative benefits of half-day versus whole-day kindergarten programs and provide much-needed empirical evidence to settle the theoretical debate and inform policy decisions. 香港2007年推出的學前教育學券計劃，幫助解決了幼教的可資付性、可進入性和可問責性問題（Li, Wong, & Wang, 2010)。但這個計劃只推出了半日制學券， 是基於半日制課程的平均學費來計算的。對於全日制課程來說，資助額明顯不足。因此，幼教界及本港社會各界均強烈呼籲政府推出全日制學券。但是，教育當局認為現階段半日制幼教課程“足夠而且適宜”，並沒有證據顯示全日制課程的相對優勢。因此，學術界有必要對全日制、半日制幼教課程的影響進行長期追踪研究，以解決這一重大教育決策中的基本理論問題。有鑑於此，本研究計劃旨在探討以下兩大問題：一是全日制、半日制幼教課程對幼兒認知、語言和社會發展是否有不同的影響？二是這些發展差主要是由幼兒自身因素、家庭和父母教育因素還是由學校教育因素造成的？ 為此，我們將在全香港經分層隨機抽樣以招募48所同時提供全日和半日制課程的幼稚園，約佔這類學校的10％。本研究將從每個學校中隨機抽取一個半日班和一個全日班。每班將隨機抽取15名學生，共計抽取1,440幼兒。將在學年開始和結束階段，對他們進行各項語言、認知及入學能力測試。而他們的父母（N= 1440）將完成家長問卷，他們的的老師（N =96）也需要填寫調查問卷。對此追踪研究數據，我們將進行多元方差分析、線性回歸分析和多元模型建構，以確定全日班和半日班對幼兒發展的不同影響，考察幼兒自身、家庭、學校等方面因素對此差異的決定性影響及其相互作用。 這項研究將有助於我們揭開半日班全日班孰優孰劣之謎，也為正在進行的幼教政策改革提供急需的實證數據，並為有關兒童發展與教育的爭論提供決策的依據和科學的參考。

17405314.label: Realisation of objectives
17405314.value: 1. Objective 1 is fully achieved. We investigated the impact of the whole-day versus half-day kindergarten program on children’s development using a sample of 364 children randomly sampled from 16 kindergartens in Hong Kong in 2015. Power analysis concluded that the sampling size was statistically significant at the 0.15 medium level (p = 0.5) (Cohen, 1988). Fifteen of the kindergartens were part of the Pre-primary Education Voucher Scheme (PEVS) and were included in the comparison group as PEVS-kindergartens must follow the Education Bureau’s strict regulations on education quality, the remaining kindergarten acted as a sub-sample. Children were assessed once every school semester, yielding a total of four waves of child assessments: Wave 1/Baseline (Autumn 2015), Wave 2 (Spring 2016), Wave 3 (Autumn 2016), and Wave 4 (Spring 2017). Children’s cognitive, language, motor, social and emotional development was assessed using standardized scales which have had good inter-rater reliability (r ≥ .7) and internal consistency (Cronbach’s alphas ≥ .7). Generalised estimating equations, the best statistical analysis method for longitudinal studies, thus, were used to investigate the long-term effect of the whole-day program impact regarding children’s development in language, cognition, pre-academic, fine motor, social-emotional, BMI, mid-arm circumference, skinfold thickness, balancing, tiptoe walking, and beanbag throwing, while controlling for their sex, family demographics (mother’s qualification, family income, existence of domestic helper, and extra-curricular activities), and school. No significant main effects of program type on children’s performances were found across all the developmental scores (e.g., in language; B=. 354, SE=1.14, χ2 =92.15, p=.756). 2. Objective 2 is fully achieved too. Generalized estimating equations were performed to analyze the effect of the predictor variable (whole-day versus half-day program attendance) on each of the child outcomes while examining the interactional effect of family characteristics (parents’ education, occupation, family income, and children’s experience of extra-curricular activities). Results showed that the moderating variables affected the outcome variables differentially. Family income, type of housing, and property right significantly interacted with program impact on children’s mid-arm circumference, pre-academic performance, externalizing of emotional and conduct problems. Father’s occupation moderated the relationship between program attendance and children’s balancing (with their preferred leg), tiptoe walking and hyperactivity problems, while both parents’ occupation moderated children’s performance in balancing (with their non-preferred leg). Children’s outside-school experiences did not assert too much variation except on their long jump performance. Results suggested that family socio-economic status only affected some of the children’s performances and this warranted further exploration of the two cohorts’ family differences. The quality of teaching and learning within the classroom was assessed with the Early Childhood Classroom Observation Scale (ECCOS), and as informed by our educator interviews, the kindergartens were very similar in terms of curricular, staffing, and pedagogies; in other words, the PEVS-kindergartens did not differ significantly regarding their quality of education. This is not surprising as the Education Bureau has always had strict regulations to control the curricular and educational aspects of kindergartens which receive funding from the government. This result again justifies our initial focus of PEVS-kindergartens only for the control of the quality of education. The debate on whether the whole-day or half-day kindergarten program will impact children more is a complicated social/educational/policy issue, aside from scientific investigation of their impact on children (objectives 1 and 2), attention must also be given to how local stakeholders view and anticipate the two program’s impact on not just children, but also on parents, educators, and kindergartens, especially in the midst of fierce public appeal for full subsidization of the whole-day program, and how policy refinement strategies could be advised. As a result, we included two additional lines of investigation – how do parents and educators of the participating children perceive the impact of the two programs on children, parents, and educators. The following section describes the findings on parents’ and educators’ perceptions. Parental perceptions on program duration impact: More than 70% from both parent groups perceived the whole-day program as more effective in fostering children’s independence, self-care, interpersonal, social skills as well as their adaptation to the whole-day-oriented primary school life. The whole-day program achieved the following advantages: (child-level) a structured lifestyle with optimum learning, greater development and school readiness; (parent-level) work-life balance; (teacher-level) learning enrichment and teacher-child/parent communication; and (school-level) educational efficiency and social responsibility. In terms of whether the whole-day program should be universalized, parents provided mixed results. Across the two years, more than 40% of whole-day parents believed in the universalization of the whole-day program whereas only around 20% of the half-day parents believed so. Support for the universalization was due to the advantages of the whole-day program, but reasons for opposition involved fear of a mechanical lifestyle with intensified academic and mind-body pressure, physical exhaustion after long hours at school, and decreased parent-child and leisure time. The two programs were found to suit families of different socio-economic background and concerns. Parents expressed the need to remain both programs as program choice should be based upon the wishes and needs of the family as well as the developmental level and adaptability of the child. Parents hoped for more government funding for more whole-day places to cater for the needs of dual-working families. Educator perceptions on program duration impact: My PhD student and I have published this section of the study, please kindly refer to Part C. (Below is an extraction of the abstract) The mixed methods study reported here adopted the Donabedian’s (2003) approach to explore this complex social-educational issue with reference to Hong Kong-Chinese educators’ perceptions of the benefits and disadvantages of the whole-day kindergarten program. In 2016, the authors surveyed 180 kindergarten educators from the main study’s 15 randomly sampled kindergartens, and conducted follow-up interviews with 30 of these educators one year later. The results showed that the whole-day program allowed for structural, curricular, and pedagogical improvement, enhanced the quality and quantity of children’s development, and eased the childcare concerns of working and single-parent families. The whole-day program, however, adversely impacted parent-child time and incurred heavier tuition fees for parents. The findings implied that no “best” program exists, only a better program “fit”; program selection should reflect family preferences and needs while ensuring high-quality learning opportunities and active parental involvement. The whole-day program is recommended to families that lack a stimulating home environment and childcare resources; the half-day program might fit financially able families with adequate childcare resources better. The authors argued that the supply of the free whole-day program should better match the demands of needy families. Journal submission plan: 1) The manuscript on the parent data will be submitted to a high quality journal in November; and 2) the manuscript on child outcomes will be submitted by the end of 2018.

17405314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17405314.value: Nature. This study assessed and compared the development of local Hong Kong children over a two-year period in order to establish if the whole-day or half-day kindergarten program could produce greater developmental and learning outcomes in children. Significance. This is the first empirical study in Hong Kong to scientifically investigate the effects of the whole-day versus half-day kindergarten program on Hong Kong children’s development and the perceptions of parents and educators of the two programs’ impact. Its significance involves: 1) contributing to the Western-normed research literature with Asian-focused empirical evidence; 2) the contextually and culturally relevant evidence facilitates the HKSAR government’s review measures of the Free Quality Kindergarten Education Scheme in terms of families’ affordability of and accessibility to the whole-day program; and 3) the practical suggestions given by professional educators could assist parents in deciding a suitable program for their child. Value. This is the first large-scale study in Hong Kong context, which provides empirical evidence to settle the debate on whole-day versus half-day kindergarten programme. The finding indicated that both types of programme have their advantages and disadvantages and should be fully funded by the HKSAR government. The valuable and comprehensive data could help with policy making and educational reforms in the long run.

17405414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17405414.value: This proposed research project studies a Catholic village in northeast China by focusing on the formation, negotiation and continuity of its Catholic identity under the historical periods of imperialism, republicanism, colonialism and communism from the nineteenth to the twentieth century. Founded by a few migrant Catholic families from other parts of China, the village under study is an ordinary yet representative Catholic community. The village came into being in the early nineteenth century, but official administrative order was not established in it until 1906. The early settlers developed and expressed their religious identity through the performance of Catholic rituals, strictly regulated by the local church founded by French missionaries in the mid-nineteenth century. Christian identity became critical for early immigrants in establishing their status, as loose imperial rule allowed the foreign missionaries and prominent Catholic families to govern the village in this early period. In the twentieth century, when different political powers (the late Qing, the warlords, the Japanese and the communists) intensified their control over society, the Catholic families developed social and political strategies to collaborate with them in order to maintain both their Christian identity and their elite status. The study of this village in the longue durée provides a concrete example for understanding the changing and intertwined relationships among family, community, the state and the Catholic Church. By examining the cultural, social and political forces behind the negotiation and persistence of multigenerational Catholic families, this project investigates how the mosaic of political forces under different rulers interacted with the local church to shape an indigenous Christian culture in the context of world history. I will rely on archival materials and fieldwork to document the public and private lives of Chinese Catholics in the village in different historical periods, especially during the early heyday of the Catholic Manchuria Mission (1840–98), the Boxer Rebellion and the late Qing (1900–11), the Republican period (1912–31), the Japanese Manchukuo (1932–45), and communist rule (1948–76), including land reform, the great famine and the Cultural Revolution. Focusing on a Chinese Catholic community, this study will illuminate a microhistorical perspective into how local experience is shaped by and fits into changing political discourses on religion and the state. 本項目聚焦中國東北一個天主教村莊的發展史，著重考察從十九到二十世紀，在晚清、民國、日據、以及共產黨統治等不同歷史時期中，該村莊如何形成并保持自己特有的天主教信仰及宗教傳統。 作為東北地區具有代表意義的移民村，該天主教村莊發源於從山東等地移民到此的幾戶天主教家庭。十九世紀初期當地已形成一個天主教家庭聚居區，但直到1906年該地區才有正式的官方建制。十九世紀中葉，法國傳教士在當地建立了天主教堂，早期的天主教移民，遵從本地天主堂規定，主要通過天主教儀式來建立和表達自己的信仰與身份。由於早期無官方建制，國家的控制尚未到達該地區，本地天主堂神父和顯赫的天主教家庭成為當地實際的管理人。天主教身份也成為早期移民在當地建立自己社會身份、地位、和聲望的重要社會資本。二十世紀，隨著不同的政治力量（晚清地方政府、軍閥、日本統治者、以及共產黨政府）不斷加強對地方社會的控制，當地的天主教家庭逐漸形成了不同的策略以便在政治變化中保持自己的天主教信仰和地方精英的社會地位。針對這一地區的長時段研究，將為我們提供一個實際的個案去更好理解在政治歷史過程中家庭、社區、國家和教會之間錯綜複雜的關係。通過對這些傳統天主教家庭何以維繫其宗教身份，及其背後的政治、文化、及社會網絡的考察，本項目力圖展示在變動的大歷史背景下，地方教會如何與不同的國家和政治力量角力互動，並由此塑造出本土的天主教文化。 本研究將依賴歷史文獻與田野考察去記錄與重現不同歷史時期地方天主教徒的公共與私人生活，尤其關注以下幾個時期：天主教滿洲教區時期（1840-98），太平天國及清末（1900-11），民國時期（1912-31），日據滿洲國時期（1932-45），以及共產黨時期（1948-76）包括土改、大饑荒、文化大革命等重要事件。本項目將從一個微觀研究的角度，探求地方經驗如何被塑造和融入經歷歷史變化的宗教與國家政治話語體系。

17405414.label: Realisation of objectives
17405414.value: This project is a historical study on Catholic communities in northeast China. It examines the formation, negotiation and continuity of Catholic identity in local society by focusing on a particular Catholic village under the historical periods of imperialism, republicanism, colonialism and communism from the nineteenth to the twentieth century. From the perspective of social history and religious history, it aims to reconstruct the formation of an indigenous religious experience in a Chinese Catholic community and to examine the continuity of its religious identity through ritual performance and political involvement under different regimes. Behind the historical changes, this project explores the power structures in local Chinese society and church-state relations at grassroots level. In methodology, this project tries to develop a microhistorical approach to the study of Christianity in China. During the course of 33 months of intensive research and writing, this project has made significant progress and achieved all proposed objectives. So far this project has resulted in a book manuscript (a monography in progress), an edited book volume (to be published by Brill), 2 journal articles, 2 book chapters, 9 international conference papers and an international conference I organized. The research outcomes listed in Part C will illustrate in details the contributions this project has made in Chinese history, particularly in the field of religion, state, and local society in late imperial and modern China. In the following sessions, I will summarize the realization of objectives and project achievements in two categories. Part I: Theoretical and Methodological contributions The first objective of this project is to write a new book on the history of Catholic communities in northeast China. The following two objectives aim to contribute to the study of Chinese local society, the church-state relations, and the history of Christianity in China. The last objective intends to make a methodological contribution by developing a microhistorical approach. All these objectives have been achieved in the form of publications. The major scholarly contributions of this project are in the following three interrelated aspects. 1. History of Christianity in China, indigenization and grassroots Catholic communities. This project examines the indigenization of the Catholic Church in a rural community. It focuses on the creation and persistence of the community’s resilient Christian identity under different political regimes. This identity, created and expressed through ritual performance, was originally an integral part of the local immigrant culture. After French missionaries founded a local church in the village in the mid-nineteenth century, they began to emphasize the strictness of Catholic ritual performance, which aimed to introduce the global Catholic church system into the local society. As a community founded by immigrants, the development of the local religious identity coincided with the formation of the local society. 2. The study of power structures in local Chinese society. The village under study grew from a cluster of a few immigrant Catholic families. The project investigates the public and private lives of these Chinese families and the ways in which they coped with dramatic political changes from the nineteenth to the twentieth centuries. I posit multigenerational Chinese Catholic families as a particular sphere in which religion played an important role in shaping family identity and private lives. 3. Religion, local governance, and church-state relations. This project studies the ways in which Christianity became a resource of local governance and the strategies used by local churches and prominent Catholic families to establish and maintain their religious identity. The local religious order in the Catholic communities survived until the mid-20th century and left a legacy that turned out to be extremely problematic in the post-1949 era. From a historical perspective, this study contributes to our understanding of contemporary outcomes for the Chinese Catholic population and the origins of China’s church-state relations at the grassroots level Part II: Archival Research, Data Collection and Production In terms of data collection, the most important contribution of this project is the discovery of a set of precious manuscripts. Alfred Marie Caubrière (1876-1948) was a French Catholic missionary from the Société des Missions Etrangères de Paris (MEP). He was dispatched to northeast China in 1899. Soon after arriving in the region, he was sent to a Catholic village near the provincial capital. He had spent the next twenty-seven years in that village until 1927. Caubrière wrote to his parents in France on a regular basis, usually several times a month. He left altogether 610 letters written in northeast China, dated from 1899 to 1940. 233 of these letters were written in the village under study where the first letter was dated on August 19, 1900, right after the Boxer attack on the village church, and the last one on January 27, 1927, describing the warlords chaos of the region during the Republican era. These family letters, with no intention for publication, provide a rare historical observation of a local Chinese Catholic community. It is valuable especially because very few Chinese documents about local religious communities, if any, survived the political chaos of the twentieth century. I have been working on the systematic church record preserved in the French MEP Archives for over a decade. I did not discover Caubrière’s family letters until May 2015. In the following months, I have managed to obtain photocopies of all 610 letters. In reading and analyzing these letters, I rediscovered another set of manuscripts I acquired in 2004 and finally proved that it was written by the same missionary. Briefly, these manuscripts includes: 1) The complete collection of a French Catholic missionary’s family letters dated from 1893 to 1941 (including those written in the village under study from 1899-1927). The missionary not only wrote about the village and the everyday lives of Chinese Catholics, he also drew. The over 100 illustrations in the letters vividly depict the daily life and religious experience of a local Catholic community that no other historical documents could demonstrate. These letters and illustrations greatly help historians to reconstruct the social life of local religious communities. 2) A thirteen-volume Chinese language study notes, “Documents de parler Chinois: Souvenirs de San-t’ai-tse [Documents of Speaking Chinese: Souvenir from Santaizi]”, which record word-by-word over two thousand entries of Chinese Catholics’ everyday conversions. A striking feature of the conversations lies in their extremely private and intimate contents, which contain the topics of pregnancy, childbirth, midwife and delivery, postpartum confinement (zuoyuezi), gift about a baby's completion of its first month (xianai), quarrels between husband and wife, complaints of in-laws and breaking up the family and living apart. A dutiful missionary and a meticulous ethnographer, Caubrière used his pen to open up a window for us to examine the ways in which Chinese Catholic villagers appropriated the traditions, languages, discourses and symbols that make up a religion and a local culture in everyday situations. Examination of these private writings also allow us to construct the family and private life in Chinese Catholic communities, to rethink the historical process of indigenization and the impact of Christianity in China on grassroots level. I am trying to publish these archival materials as a primary source collection.

17405414.label: Major findings and research outcome
17405414.value: This project has so far resulted in a book manuscript (a monography in progress), an edited book volume (to be published by Brill), 2 journal articles, 2 book chapters, 9 international conference papers and an international conference I organized. Please refer to Part C for the detailed information of these publications. In addition to the publications, this project has made a substantial contribution to the following two fields as mentioned in project objectives. 1. History of Christianity in China. One key issue in the history of Christianity in China is about indigenization. This project studies the establishment of Catholic Church in northeast China at the grassroots level. It examines the creation and persistence of local Catholic communities’ resilient Christian identity under different political regimes. This identity, created and expressed through ritual performance, was originally an integral part of the local immigrant culture. French missionaries systematically established churches in local communities and emphasized the strictness of Catholic ritual performance. The introduction of the Catholic Church system to rural Chinese society shaped the indigenous religious culture. Paradoxically, a Chinese church is at the same an integral part of the global Catholic Church. The monography and the edited book volume I am working on will illustrate this new argument about indigenization in full details. 2. Local society and Church-State Dynamics. Christianity has experienced explosive growth in contemporary China. However, the church-state relationship remains controversial. My study examines the formation and early development of Chinese Catholic communities in Northeast China and their models of religious governance. It argues that the widespread Catholic missions since the 19th century diffused not only religion but also notions of autonomy and models of local governance among Chinese Christians. The early development of northeastern Catholic communities was largely due to immigration and the absence of the state, which coincided with the formation of local society. Although the expansion of state power to rural society gradually eroded the traditional nexus of power at the village level, the local religious order in the Catholic communities survived until the mid-20th century. This religious autonomy left a legacy that turned out to be extremely problematic in the post-1949 era. From a historical perspective, this study contributes to our understanding of the origins of China’s church-state relations at the grassroots level.

17405414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17405414.value: During the course of this research, I discovered a body of new primary source of altogether over 600 family letters written by a French Catholic missionary to his family, among which over 200 were written in the Catholic village under study. This missionary, who has lived in this village over twenty-seven years, not only wrote about the everyday life in this Chinese Catholic community but also drew. He left us over 100 illustrations depicting the community, the villagers, and the religious life. In addition, this same missionary also left us a 13-volume unpublished hand written manuscript, a dictionary on spoken Chinese, which carefully recorded over 2000 conversations by local Chinese Catholic villagers. These materials open up a new window for us to explore the private sphere, family, and daily life of a Chinese religious community. Currenly I am editing these letters and manuscripts and looking for opportunities to publish them as a collection of primary sources, which will provide precious first-hand archival materials for historians, anthropologists, sociologists, and linguists to explore various aspects of religious and linguistic experience of local Chinese society and its interaction with the foreign language, culture and faith.

17405414.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17405414.value: This project examines the history of Catholic Church in northeast China by focusing on the formation, negotiation and continuity of Catholic identity in local communities from the nineteenth to the twentieth century. Founded by Catholic immigrants from other parts of China, many northeastern Catholic communities came into being in the early nineteenth century. The early settlers developed and expressed their religious identity through the performance of Catholic rituals, strictly regulated by the local church founded by French missionaries in the nineteenth century. Christian identity became critical for early immigrants in establishing their status, as loose imperial rule allowed foreign missionaries and prominent Catholic families to govern the community. In the twentieth century, when different political regimes intensified their control over society, the local churches developed strategies to maintain both their Christian identity and religious governance. By examining the cultural, social and political forces behind the negotiation and persistence of multigenerational Catholic families, this project provides a concrete example for understanding how the mosaic of political forces interacted with the local church to develop an indigenous Christian culture. It also contributes to our understanding of the origins of China’s contemporary church-state relations at the grassroots level.

17405714.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17405714.value: 網絡環境下合理使用與創造力之關係的比較研究

17405714.label: Project Objectives
17405714.value: 1. To gain the insights about how fair use regime had been employed to keep the copyright system balanced in the past by analyzing the interaction between technological development, legislative processes, and judicial decisions in various countries. 2. To identify new technologies being developed on internet, new works and rights being created by these technologies, and new right-holders and users of the works, and to explore the interaction, influences, and priorities among these factors. 3. To investigate the problems, applicability, and potential reforms of the current fair use doctrine in the Internet environment by studying new uses in practice and disputes involving uses in judicial decisions of different jurisdictions. 4. To study the compatibility between fair use and technological protection measures, and the possibility of adapting the copyright-complementary schemes such as Creative Commons into the existing copyright system to promote broader sharing culture. 5. Based on the accomplishments of the above objectives, to propose a new fair use regime that suits Internet environment so that creativity of all stakeholders can be unleashed rather than be constrained.
rows: 1. To gain the insights about how fair use regime had been employed to keep the copyright system balanced in the past by analyzing the interaction between technological development, legislative processes, and judicial decisions in various countries.

2. To identify new technologies being developed on internet, new works and rights being created by these technologies, and new right-holders and users of the works, and to explore the interaction, influences, and priorities among these factors.

3. To investigate the problems, applicability, and potential reforms of the current fair use doctrine in the Internet environment by studying new uses in practice and disputes involving uses in judicial decisions of different jurisdictions.

4. To study the compatibility between fair use and technological protection measures, and the possibility of adapting the copyright-complementary schemes such as Creative Commons into the existing copyright system to promote broader sharing culture.

5. Based on the accomplishments of the above objectives, to propose a new fair use regime that suits Internet environment so that creativity of all stakeholders can be unleashed rather than be constrained.

17405714.label: Realisation of objectives
17405714.value: 1. Through studying the history of the fair use system, the PI has gained the understanding that the fair use system has been essential to the balance of interests between original copyright holders and users. It fits very well to the environment of the pre-digital and Internet technologies that has identifiable authors and users by using analogue technologies for the limited distribution. 2. The project identified that the new technologies such as digital and Internet technologies have changed everything because they allowed unlimited use and sharing of the copyrighted works over the Internet. The former users have become remixers or creators, and the remix has become a dominant new form of creation, which are normally not for commercial purpose. 3. The project discovered that, under such a situation, the four factors of the fair use doctrine cannot be squarely applied to analyze the uses over the Internet because they are mostly non-commercial, non-transformative, and in a massive quantity. This has been found through case studies of the jurisdictions of the US, EU and China on the cases such as Google book project. The project also surveyed the reform of fair use systems in the UK, Canada, China and Hong Kong, and compared their pros and cons, and reached the conclusion that the current law reform concerning fair use, normally by adding new categories of works for fair use, is not sufficient to cope with the digital and Internet challenge. A new positive right, rather than fair use defence, should be created to allow users more freedom to create. 4. The project further studied the relationship between fair use doctrine and the technological protection measures (TPM) for copyright works, and concluded that they are incompatible because the former is designed to allow users to use the works, but the latter is adopted to restrict the use. When the TPM is employed, the use is totally prohibited, therefore the fair use doctrine becomes absolute. In other words, fair use doctrine become meaningless in the Internet era because most of the copyrighted works are protected by TPM. Therefore, a new scheme should be in place to protect users' right in using the copyright works and creating new works. The project found that the copyright-complementary regimes such as Creative Commons (CC) and compulsory licensing (CL) can be incorporated into copyright system to give users more space to use and create. Both CC and CL allow the users to use copyright works without getting copyright holders' permission to some extent, and CC also allows future users (or remixers) to use or remix under the same terms and conditions. This project adopted these features of the CC and CL, but in a way to make them into a positive and permanent right -- remix right -- that is belonged to the users/remixers and can be passed on to future users and remixers. This way, the uses cannot be restricted by TPM and creativity cannot be impeded. 5. Based on the above research and findings, this project concluded that the fair use doctrine, as it stands now, is not compatible with the characteristics of the digital and Internet technologies. The current efforts in reforming the fair use system, e.g., Canadian's adding UGC exception, have their limits and are largely unsuccessful. This project proposed to allow fair use system to exist to deal with the traditional copyright works, and in the meantime to create a new remix right for users/remixers for using massive and unidentified works over the Internet.

17405714.label: Major findings and research outcome
17405714.value: There are major findings from the following research outcomes: (1) "Taking Users’ Rights Seriously: Proposed UGC Solutions for Spurring Creativity in the Internet Age,"(co-authored with Weijie Huang) (Queen Mary Journal of Intellectual Property Law, Vol. 9, Issue 2, Feb. 2019, pp. 61-91, SSCI ranking: 136, Q4. SJR ranking for law: 449 out of 653, impact factor 0.147, Q3) This article argued that new technologies have empowered users to create user-generated contents (“UGC”), but the existing law entitles copyright owners to block users’ access to source materials and allows UGC platforms to exploit UGC freely. Supported by Austrian Federal Ministry of Science, Research and Economy for a joint project on “Prosumerism and IP”, this article proposes a two-pronged solution to better protect users’ rights: (1) an ex-post remuneration rule conferring UGC creators the right to use copyrighted work without permission but with remuneration; (2) a community-based approach imposing upon UGC platforms a common-law duty of monitoring infringement and adopting fair terms of use/service. (2) "The Age of Remix and Copyright Law Reform," (accepted for publication by Law, Innovation and Technology, Vol. 12, Issue 1, January 2020, SJR ranking for law: 131 out of 653, H Index 10, impact factor 0.613, Q1) This article argued that remix has emerged as a dominant force of creation in the digital age, but the solutions under the current copyright law have failed to adequately protect remix works and remixers. This research, sponsored by GRF grant, is the first in the field to call for the recognition of remix as a copyrightable work and granting remix right to remixers. It is also the first in the field to adopt some features of Creative Commons and compulsory licensing schemes into copyright system to solve attribution and licensing problems. This novel proposal will have a profound impact on world-wide copyright law reform. (3) Copyright, the Internet and the Balance of Rights (HKU Press, 2017) This book explores the issues of fair use of copyright in the Internet environment, the rights and status of users, the abuse and balance of rights, piracy and the responsibility of network service providers. It discusses the legislation and judicial reform for the above-mentioned issues in Mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, and explores how to achieve the best balance among parties and maximize social creativity under the internet environment.

17405714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17405714.value: Based one the current findings, more research could be done on the mechanisms that can be used to implement the proposed scheme. That is, how can the remixers (or future remixers) remunerate the original copyright holders for each piece of the works they use? And how the social media platforms and the remixers divide the profits earned from the contents provided on the platform. Specifically, the technology of blockchain and other private arrangements can be explored. PI will consider to submit a new research grant to carry out such a research project.

17405714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17405714.value: Through this project the PI made a significant discovery that fair use regime has become insufficient to cope with the challenges posed by the digital and Internet technologies because it is was designed for limiting copyright in the analogue world in which a use is normally deemed fair if it is in a small amount, for noncommercial and transformative purpose, and dose not substitute the market of the copyright holder. But these criteria have become inappropriate for the digital and Internet world that allow massive use of the copyright works, normally for noncommercial and non-transformative purpose, and can substitute copyright holders' market. In addition, the technological protection measures used by the copyright holders may block users from using their works completely, making the fair use doctrine inapplicable. Therefore, the existing fair use regime does not fit for the digital and Internet environment and a new solution needs to be found. The PI proposed to create a remix right and incorporated Creative Commons and compulsory licensing schemes into copyright, so that the users or remixers can have more freedom to create, and the interests between the original copyright holders, media platforms and users can be better balanced.

17406014.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17406014.value: 中國之南洋（東南亞）： 領域、殖／治民、文明與中歐關係

17406014.label: Project Objectives
17406014.value: This project aims at providing scholarly contribution and insight in China’s current trends of establishing a dominant position in the world (see objectives 2-5): International relations: to gain understanding on how dissimilar understanding of boundaries (of borders and subjects) affected state-to-state relations and East/ West relations. Trace the lineage of Chinese concept of territory: many studies in modern Chinese history concern the subjects of “Race” and “the Nation.” The proposed project, on contrary, will place “Territory” at the center of study. The purpose is to examine how Chinese concept of “Territory” has changed over time. Understanding the growth of present-day China: scholarship has shown that China’s territory and population grew by incorporating land and inhabitants under Chinese realm. These studies are limited to the imperial period, however. Studies with regards to the republican period are mainly analyzed from nation-based frameworks and seldom look beyond the confines of national boundaries. Data of my preliminary research material, however, reveal that China’s ambition to transcend its national borders was present. My goal is fill this missing link in scholarship. By studying China’s concept of territory in connection with European colonialism, this project therefore aims at gaining insight in the construction of what has become “the Chinese nation” within the context of international relations. Studies on the Chinese nation are mostly examined from a domestic perspective between revolutionaries and monarchists. Studying the topic from an international context (by taking British anti-Chinese policies into consideration) gives insight to the question: why the Chinese state, despite its intention to move beyond its territorial boundaries, did not succeed in establishing a prominent presence in modern Southeast Asia.

17406014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17406014.value: “Our countrymen were the earliest people that arrived in Nanyang [i.e. Southeast Asia]. If our country [i.e. China] had the political ability, it would have been our territory long time ago. But this is something that our ancestors were not able to complete… Therefore, now we have the task to bring it to completion. We have to spread and glorify the civilization of our country, so that our civilization would be planted and rooted in Nanyang.” (Quoted from Liang Qichao, Chinan Weekly, 13 January 1923; emphasis added by Oiyan Liu) “The Chinese were better off in Malaya before the English came: England from the West, and America from the East are crippling… We Chinese opened Malaya - it ought to be ours.” (Quoted from the Malayan Bulletin of Political Intelligence, 1 April 1925; emphasis added by Oiyan Liu) Why and under what circumstances did these words emerge in the 1920? This project looks at how the late Qing imperial state, early Republican state, Chinese intellectuals from Southern China, and Southeast Asian Chinese (Nanyang Huaqiao) viewed Southeast Asia in the last decades of European colonialism. It looks at the conflicting notions of political legitimacy to control Southeast Asian territory, its people, and Chinese and Southeast Asian Chinese views of “the European colonizer.” This research project seeks to understand the relationship between Chinese vis-à-vis Western notions of sovereignty on the one hand, and the tightening of border control, migration policies, and the changing definitions of the “colonial subject” on the other hand. Preliminary research findings reveal that Chinese claims of political legitimacy over Southeast Asia and British border and migration control peaked in the 1920s. Therefore, although this project covers the period from 1900 to 1928, it will focus on the discourse of sovereignty and territory in the second decade of the twentieth century. 二十世紀二十年代的檔案和報刊曾記載，認為東南亞地區應屬中國疆域而非屬於西方國家的領土。這論點源自華人移民史和管治能力。然而，當時大多數的東南亞國家都是屬於英、荷、法等已久的殖民地。既然如此，為什麼某些中國學者、當權者以及南洋華人會提出“中國之南洋”這一概念呢？ 本研究將探討這一概念產生的背景和語境。 研究將考察晚清和民國初期，中歐對東南亞領土、殖民、治民、主權以及國際關係等等方面的觀念衝突。除此之外，在歐洲殖民統治末期的東南亞，英、荷等帝國加緊了海上邊界和領土保護措施。除了當時東南亞民族為對抗殖民主義而提倡民族獨立運動外，這跟中國是否有意伸展到東南亞有關係嗎？本研究希望從歷史和歐亞關係的角度進行探索，以期對這些問題有進一步的瞭解。

17406114.value: 執行控制能力與父母管教因素為「窮思竭慮」的思想模式發展成因

17406114.label: Project Objectives
17406114.value: To examine the role of specific executive control functions (namely inhibition and switching abilities) and parenting factors (namely negative mood expression and intrusive/controlling parenting) in predicting rumination development in young Chinese adolescents using a systematic prospective design. To develop new experimental paradigms for assessment of rumination to supplement existing self-report questionnaire measures commonly adopted in the field.

17406114.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17406114.value: Different people use different ways to deal with their negative emotions when experiencing everyday stressful events. Some tend to distract themselves by being busy with other daily activities, whereas others tend to dwell on the roots of their negative emotion, analyzing its causes and implications. This latter coping strategy is commonly known as rumination. Since the introduction of this concept about thirty years ago, rumination has been a hot research topic in clinical psychology, largely due to its close connection with depressive risks. Specifically, many studies have demonstrated that ruminative coping increases a person’s chance of becoming depressed, intensifies the depressive mood symptoms and prolongs the duration of depressive episodes. Understanding the cause of rumination can hold a key to risk prevention for depression. Although many studies have been conducted on rumination, much remains unknown about why some people tend to adopt this emotion regulation strategy more readily. Moreover, as empirical studies to date have focused almost exclusively on adult or clinical populations, the developmental factors contributing to how ruminative preferences first emerge and consolidate remains unclear. When ruminating about a problem, the sustained focus on feelings of distress often makes the person become stuck in a cognitive loop – dwelling on the emotion aspects of the problem without finding an effective solution. Clinical scientists have begun to examine whether the disruption of a higher order regulatory system, known as the executive control system, is associated with the formation of ruminative copings. Previous research also suggests that parenting factors shape upbringing experiences pertaining to rumination development. To build on these new research directions, we propose a two-year longitudinal study to examine the role of executive control functions and parenting style in predicting rumination development. A large, representative sample of Hong Kong Chinese youths aged 10-12 years old will be recruited and tested on their executive control functions and family interactive styles at Time 1. The results will be used to predict their ruminative tendency one year later at Time 2. Findings from the study will provide a valuable scientific basis for understanding the predictors of a ruminative coping style in early adolescence – when clinical or subclinical depressive episodes are often first observed in youths. Outcomes of the proposed research therefore can have significant implications for depression risk prevention and effective treatment design.

17406114.label: Realisation of objectives
17406114.value: Objective 1: “To examine the role of specific executive control functions (namely inhibition and switching abilities) and parenting factors (namely controlling parenting) in predicting rumination development in young Chinese adolescents using a systematic prospective design.” This objective has been fully accomplished. The present project proceeded according to schedule and had successfully tested 250 local Chinese youths, aged between 10-14 and their parents (i.e. the primary carers), as planned. Upon receiving consents, participated youths and their parents completed several experimental tasks in Phase I data collection (baseline) including: i) a questionnaire packet for baseline measures (e.g., depression, rumination, parenting style); ii) two executive control tasks: the affective shift task (De Lissnyder et al., 2010) and the modified mixed antisaccade task (De Lissnyder et al., 2011); iii) three 10-minute family interaction tasks: a problem-solving interaction, followed by an event-planning interaction and a co-rumination interaction. Parent-youth discussions were video-recorded which were then coded according to the Dyadic Parent-Child Interaction Coding System (DPICS: Eyberg, Nelson, Duke, & Boggs, 2005) and the co-rumination coding scheme (Grimbos, Granic, & Pepler, 2013). The participated families were invited to take part in Phase II data collection again a year after. In this session, ruminative tendency of youths, as well as depression and anxiety measures, was collected using self-report questionnaires. The data were further processed and screened, and correlational and regression analysis were applied in examining the predictors’ interaction effects (please see 6.1 “major findings and research outcome” section for details). Objective 2: “To develop new experimental paradigms for assessment of rumination to supplement existing self-report questionnaire measures commonly adopted in the field.” This objective has been fully accomplished. Participated youths and their parents were invited to attend a laboratory session as mentioned. In the session, they were invited to join a behavioural observation task where they were presented with specific emotion-eliciting topics and situations and were asked to discuss among themselves how to solve these problems. The interactions were video-recorded and their ruminative behaviours and co-rumination patterns were subsequently coded. Validity of this observation method for assessing rumination was tested with reference to existing self-report questionnaire measures (please see 6.1“major findings and research outcome” section for details).

17406114.label: Major findings and research outcome
17406114.value: Local schools were widely contacted and 250 participants were recruited with both parental and youths' consent obtained. Their data were successfully collected for Phase I baseline assessment. The data had been inputted and coded, and were processed, screened and analyzed. Phase II follow-up data collection had also been completed successfully 1 year after. Overall, regression analysis on Phase I cross-sectional data suggests that parental overprotection moderates the relationship between youths' switching ability and rumination tendency (b = -.0004, SE = .0002, t = -2.1135, p = .0357). Overprotection explains a significant increase in variance in rumination tendency, ∆R2 = .0117, F(1,211) = 4.4668, p = .0357 (Objective 1). Also, global rating of observed co-rumination in a video-recorded family discussion task significantly correlates with self-report measures on co-rumination (r = .16, p = .087) (Objective 2). The analysis also extends to understand depressive risks associated with rumination development. For adolescents with low parental care in the prospective design, cognitive perseveration at baseline significantly increased with depressive symptoms 12 months later. Shifting deficits had no interaction with perceived parental overprotection in predicting depressive symptoms. In summary, our findings provided new insight in the individual and parental factors that contribute to the development of rumination and depressive risks in youths, and supports development of new experimental paradigms that assess ruminative processes.

17406114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17406114.value: The present research provides a good starting point for assessing rumination development in youths. The findings draws important impacts in youth mental health and are crucial to understanding psychopathological processes in relation to affect dysfunctions (e.g. depressive risks in youths). The project will be extended and developed in several ways. First, the present study provides a good solid database for building up further extensive longitudinal studies. Subject to future funding opportunities, the youth participants who took part in the study could be followed up all the way until young adulthood in examining the risks associated with development of mental problems (such as depression and anxiety disorders). Second, the new experimental paradigms developed (e.g. the set-switching task and co-rumination observation task) can be modified and applied in future research to test out specific contextual effects (e.g. trial sequencing effects, cognitive load effects) under various scientifically controlled conditions. Third, the present study also attracts international collaboration and the project will be further extended to test out cross-cultural comparison. Specifically, a new proposal examining the cross-cultural differences in depression and anxiety development across United Kingdom and Hong Kong Chinese youth samples is now underway and will be submitted.

17406114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17406114.value: The present project is the first to examine the developmental factors associated with rumination. Rumination is a coping strategy conceptualized as a repetitive thinking style focusing on individual’s negative mood, as well as the possible meanings and implications generated by this mood state. Specifically the present study systematically assessed the interplay between cognitive control functions and parenting styles among local youths (aged between 10-14 years old) in a two-year prospective longitudinal design. The findings indicated that high parental over-involvement and low parental care would interact with youths' cognitive abilities to impact on development of rumination and subsequent depressive risks. Scientifically, the findings address the important and fundamental questions of how some people gradually build up a tendency to adopt a ruminative thinking style. Clinically, a good understanding of how rumination occurs draws important implications to designing depression prevention programs in youths as well as enhancing psychological treatment effectiveness.

17406314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17406314.value: The proposed study examines the issues and challenges of children’s independent mobility and road-crossing ability. Child pedestrians are among the most vulnerable road users because of their small stature as well as their limited experience to judge the oncoming traffic. But children are a key pedestrian group which needs to be able to use the streets safely to go to school, to play, to socialize and to learn independence. The fear of road traffic injury is always a major concern among parents. Parents’ notion of the perceived risk of road trauma influences the mobility patterns of children. Many parents restrict their children’s mobility by removing them from the road environment. Children now have limited experience to draw on, especially in dealing with the ever-increasing traffic volume. The result of this has been associated with the overprotection of children and the declining walking intensity as a kind of physical activity for children. Promoting safe walking can have a wider impact on the health of children than simply the prevention of child pedestrian casualties. In compact cities like Hong Kong, various challenges and opportunities exist for further promoting independent mobility and safe walking among children. The proposed research project begins by examining the levels of independent mobility and walking habits of children in Hong Kong through a questionnaire survey among children (aged 6 to 12) AND their parents. Parents' perceptions on the road-crossing ability of their children will affect their decisions as to the modal choice of their children, whether they will be accompanied in their journeys, and who will accompany them. Moreover, a micro-scale assessment of the walkability of the children’s home and school environment will be made. In addition to the questionnaire survey, data related to different domains of children’s cognitive ability and inhibition control will be collected. Finally, the children will take part in some games/tests designed to understand their road-crossing decisions under different scenarios, and their overall ability of crossing roads safely without putting them at risk in a real road environment. With the above data, data analysis will be conducted to examine whether children’s road-crossing ability is associated with their individual, family and/or neighbourhood factors. This research project brings together a multi-disciplinary research team to address the key challenges and opportunities of children’s independent mobility and road-crossing ability in a compact city setting. 此項研究探討孩子的獨立出行與過馬路能力。一般來說，兒童身材較矮小及過馬路經驗不足等，是導致他們成為道路使用者中弱勢一群的主要原因。但兒童作為主要道路使用者，重要的是確保他們能安全地上學回家、外出玩耍、參加社交活動與學習獨立。一直以來，擔憂交通事故是家長非常關注的議題，而家長的焦慮無疑影響孩子的活動模式。許多家長因此限制子女出行和其它活動。但過度的限制，卻會使現在的孩子沒有具備足夠經驗來應付日益頻繁的交通。家長過度保護孩子除了會降低孩子的適應能力，還會減少他們的步行與運動量影響健康。由此可見，促進兒童行人安全，除了能減少傷亡外，還能替其身心帶來更廣泛的益處。 在人煙稠密的香港，充滿各種推動兒童獨立出行及安全步行的機遇與挑戰。研究首先向學童及家長進行問卷調查，探索孩子的獨立出行與步行習慣。父母對子女能力的評估，往往決定孩子们的交通模式，如會否陪同旅程及安排其同行者。除了問卷調查外，研究還會蒐集兒童的認知和抑制能力等不同領域的數據。在排除真實過路環境的安全風險下，研究團隊還會安排學童參加一些橫過馬路的电脑遊戲和測試，從而評估孩子們整體的過馬路能力。最后，研究項目還會對孩子們的居所和學校附近的步行環境作出微觀評鑑。 通過上述數據，研究將從學童個人、家庭和鄰里等各因素分析他們的過馬路能力。這研究項目匯集了跨學科的研究人員，以探究在這一個密集都市環境中，學童的獨立出行和過路能力面對的主要挑戰和機遇。

17406314.label: Realisation of objectives
17406314.value: All objectives have been fully realised. A brief summary is provided below: 1) To understand children’s mobility patterns and parents’ perceptions on their children’s road-crossing ability This objective was achieved through questionnaire surveys. The raw data for children’s travel behaviour revealed walking to be the most common travel mode to school, at 37%. Closely following this was school bus, at 35%. The rest were relatively evenly split across rail, other public transport and private car/ taxi, at around 9-10% each. Boys and older children were more likely to walk to school or take non-rail public transport to school, while girls and younger children were more likely to take the school bus or be driven to school. Rail was used primarily by older children but with little gender difference. Active journeys were rated by children as happier than motorised journeys, which concurs with current literature supporting the promotion of active travel for physical and psychological benefits. Regarding parental perceptions on their children’s road-crossing ability, parents were least confident in letting their child crossing at unmarked crossing locations, followed by zebra crossings, and finally by ‘green man’ signalised crossings. In fact, many parents had never let their child cross the road alone before and would start giving them the opportunity to cross alone (parents observing at a distance) only when they are ‘old enough’, which seemed to mean around 9-10 years old. Independent mobility does become more prevalent for children aged 11-12. 2) To examine different components of the road crossing decision and their relationship with the children’s physical and cognitive ability (100%) This objective was fully realised. Computation of whether the road-crossing decision is ‘correct’, ‘wrong but safe’, ‘wrong and unsafe’ and ‘critically wrong and unsafe’ involves the following components: reaction time, remaining time gap and walking times. The computer-simulated road-crossing experiment was used to obtain children’s road crossing ability, involving 18 main scenarios, with a variety of vehicle speeds (30 km/h, 50 km/h and 70 km/h), time gaps (2s, 4s and 6s, indicating the duration remaining before the vehicle’s arrival at the child’s vantage point) and side of lane (nearside and offside), plus 6 additional scenarios, which held the time gap and vehicle speed constant, but included distraction conditions). The focus was placed on ‘critically wrong and unsafe’ decisions, indicating that given the time taken for the child to make a decision (i.e. the reaction time), the child is unable to compensate for a ‘yes’ decision at a marginal crossing gap and fails to walk quicker to avoid the oncoming vehicle. The measure of the walking time is an integral part in understanding the relationship between the child’s road-crossing decision-making ability and physical ability. The time taken to walk across a regular two-lane road was measured by the ‘normal’ speed, where the child walks at their regular walking pace, and the ‘fast’ speed, where the child walks as if the ‘green man’ signal were flashing at a signalised crossing. A lower speed in the ‘fast’ walking condition was associated with a higher likelihood of critically wrong road-crossing judgments. Cognitive ability was measured using the Stroop Colour and Word Test for Children, testing information processing speed and inhibitory control. While there was not enough evidence to suggest that inhibitory control influenced road-crossing judgments, information processing speed was highly relevant, which indicates that at least one dimension of better cognitive ability is associated with better road-crossing decision-making. 3) To systematically analyse children’s road-crossing ability by individual, family and environmental factors This objective was fully realised. The individual, family and environmental factors affecting children’s road-crossing ability were systematically analysed using two binary logistic Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) models, with decision type as the binary dependent variable (i.e. ‘critically wrong and unsafe’ versus ‘not critically wrong and unsafe’). Both models found strong evidence regarding the importance of the road-crossing environment factors, that is the actual vehicle speed, distance, side of lane and distractions. Higher vehicle speeds, closer vehicles, vehicles on the offside lane and also visual distractions were found to significantly worsen children’s road-crossing judgments. Audio distractions – perhaps better described as auditory cues - actually improved road-crossing judgments compared to the no distraction condition. Individual factors also played a crucial part, in both physiological terms as well as psychological terms. Younger age, and children with a slower walking speed, were associated with poorer road-crossing judgments, as was poorer information processing speed measured by the Stroop Colour and Word Test for Children. Factors related to the children’s household and family were also examined. There was some indication that children residing in households where the parents who owned a car and parents who had, or knew of, no prior involvement in a near miss traffic accident were more likely to have children who made poorer road-crossing judgments. The analysis of these individual, family and environmental factors has shown that the road-crossing environment is highly significant in affecting the ability of children to make correct choices when crossing a road. Policymakers can draw insight from the findings to implement measures ensuring that road-crossing environments are safe for children to travel in. Furthermore, educational endeavours should target primary school children, especially those in the lower years, in order for children, from a young age, to understand the importance of safety in a live traffic environment as pedestrians. 4) To identify factors associated with poor road-crossing judgments among child pedestrians, and propose measures to strengthen these areas This objective was fully realised. We found that vehicles travelling at high speeds (at 50 km/h or above), as well as on offside lanes, are key factors associated with poor road-crossing judgments in child pedestrians intending to cross outside of the regular signalised crossings. The obvious measure to resolve this issue is to reduce speed limits at local roads where children may cross at non-signalised and unmarked crossings. This should be accompanied by the implementation of traffic calming measures, such as road-narrowing, footpath-widening and speed humps. Together, the measures are aimed at reducing vehicle speeds in these areas and create a safer space for children in the neighbourhood. Also, distractions at the road environment severely delayed children’s reaction times and hence led to significantly poorer road-crossing judgments. Visual distractions, whether it is a mobile phone game or something happening across the street, need to be taken seriously. They were shown to affect all children rather indiscriminately, regardless of age and gender. This indicates that educational measures need to clearly inform children the importance of staying focused and highly alert in a road-crossing environment, regardless of whether they are at a signalised crossing, zebra crossing, unmarked crossing or even just on the pavement. Finally, younger children performed poorer than older children in road-crossing judgments, as well as those with slower walking speed and poorer information processing speed. It is thoroughly reasonable for younger children to be accompanied and supervised, as they are also the ones who are least physically and mentally ready for travelling independently. Of course, while parental supervision is one important measure to counteract these factors inherent of young children, children must concurrently learn about safe road-crossing practices to enable them to navigate around different road environments as they grow up, which again underlines the significance of children’s road safety education.

17406314.label: Major findings and research outcome
17406314.value: Over one third of children walked to school, and another third took the school bus, while roughly 10% each used rail, other public transport and private car/ taxi respectively. Walking and public transport usage (except rail) was more prevalent for boys and older children, compared with girls and younger children. The contrary was true for school bus and private car/ taxi, and parents of these children were generally less confident in their children’s navigational and road-crossing abilities. Only 10% of children travelled independently to school, though this percentage increases with age. Binary logistic regression modelling showed that network distance from school was highly related with children walking to school, and there was also strong evidence showing that residing in neighbourhoods with a network of many road intersections, as well as a larger number of sports and recreation locations, increases the propensity for active travel in children. This relates to the compact structure of neighbourhoods being more conducive to walking behaviour. After all, neighbourhoods with a mix of land uses entails a variety of destinations that can be reached. Further analysis was conducted to explore the relationship between children’s mobility and wellbeing, which found that children who travelled actively for school rated these journeys happier than children who used motorised transport, which shows the promotion of active travel is not only good for the child’s physical development, but also has positive psychological effects. Regarding children’s road-crossing judgments, Generalised Estimating Equations modelling revealed that vehicles travelling at high speeds (at 50 km/h or above), as well as those on offside lanes, were key factors associated with children’s critical misjudgments of road-crossing situations. Also, visual distractions at the road environment severely delayed children’s reaction times and hence led to significantly poorer road-crossing judgments. Finally, younger children performed poorer than older children in the road-crossing experiment, and those with slower walking speed and poorer information processing speed also performed badly in comparison with their quicker counterparts. To publicise our findings to the community and wider academic circles on a regional and global scale, one full paper has been published, with another under review and two manuscripts being prepared for submission to peer-reviewed academic journals. The findings have also been presented at four major international conferences in Hong Kong and abroad in the past several years, with one more upcoming conference presentation at the Transportation Research Board 2019 Annual Meeting in Washington D.C.

17406314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17406314.value: Having suggested the importance of altering the neighbourhood environment to make road-crossing safer for children, it is also important to understand the effectiveness of road safety education on children in Hong Kong. Currently, road safety is taught under the ‘Moral and Civic Education’ programme of the regular primary school curricula. There are also various other initiatives and facilities that serve to improve children’s road safety knowledge, such as 1) Road Safety Towns, 2) the Road Safety Bus and also 3) various talks and seminars as part of publicity campaigns by different government departments. These initiatives and facilities have all been developed with the goal of helping children to become safe road users, but one key issue is whether these initiatives are actually helpful in improving road safety knowledge and road-crossing ability. A future course of action could be to investigate the effect of road safety campaigns longitudinally and follow up on children’s road safety knowledge and habits over the course of several years (perhaps until the end of their primary school studies), as well as how this relates with children’s travel behaviour and the relevant parental perceptions of the child and parental attitudes to road safety.

17406314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17406314.value: The research project has examined the broad issues and challenges in Hong Kong children’s mobility and road-crossing ability. The research project is significant because it has been able to uncover the types of challenges that children face when crossing a road, such as oncoming vehicles at a high speed and on the far side lane, as well as the many distractions that may occur before and during a crossing. Other important factors affecting children’s road-crossing decisions were also considered, including young age, slow walking speed and poorer information processing speed. The findings have much value in informing future policy direction in regulating and improving the built environment in the communities where children reside, beginning with the reduction of speed limits and implementation of traffic calming measures as a means to reduce vehicle speed, especially in communities where children frequent. Furthermore, there was concrete evidence that residing in compact neighbourhoods with many sports and recreation locations increases the propensity for active travel in children. This should form the blueprint in the planning of child-friendly, mixed-use, compact and walkable future neighbourhoods that children may begin to use, socialise and travel in and through them safely and happily.
