18404014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18404014.value: The study will investigate the effects of phonological awareness, trained by computer-assisted programs of Chinese pinyin GraphoGame and English GraphoGame, on reading development in both Chinese and English among Hong Kong primary school first graders. Three hypotheses corresponding to the study’s major goals have been developed. First, the GraphoGame interventions are expected to effectively improve overall phonological awareness in English, Mandarin, and Cantonese. Second, phonological awareness including syllable awareness and onset, rime and tone awareness at the sub-syllabic levels is expected to have a positive and retentive effect on reading development in Chinese. The invented pinyin spelling, as a more sensitive measure of phonological awareness in mandarin, is expected be have stronger relation to Chinese word reading, compared to traditional Mandarin phonological awareness tasks. Third, we hypothesize an overall positive effect of phonological awareness on reading development in English in the same group of Hong Kong children. By taking the computer-assisted intervention approach, employing longitudinal designs in Hong Kong’s unique language environment of “biliteracy and trilingualism”, the study will test the hypothesis of universal phonological principal (Perfetti & Tan, 1998) in reading a non-alphabetic script (i.e., Chinese) and an alphabetic script (i. e., English) in the same group of non-western children, and thus contribute to an increased understanding of reading development from a global perspective. 此項研究探討語音意識（通过普通话拼音GraphoGame和英文GraphoGame遊戲干預提升語音意識）對一年級兒童中、英文閱讀能力發展的影響。就此研究問題，我們提出三個假設。第一，GraphoGame遊戲學習可全面提升英文，普通話和廣東話三個語言中的語音意識。第二，良好的語音意識 (包括音節意識、聲母意識、韻母意識和聲調意識) 對中文閱讀能力的提高有持續的正面的影響。第三，整體語音意識的提升對以英文為第二語言的本地兒童的英文閱讀有正面的影響。本研究通過GraphoGame電腦輔助的干預方法以及縱向性追蹤的研究設計，借助香港兩文三語的語言環境的極好機會，可測試universal phonological principle（Perfetti & Tan, 1998）在非西方兒童同時學習非拼音文字（中文）和拼音文字（英文）的正確性，從而更完整的了解兒童早期的閱讀發展。

18404014.label: Realisation of objectives
18404014.value: All the objectives has been achieved. The project recruited 90, 100, and 90 students for the three groups (i.e., Pinyin GraphoGame, English GraphoGame, and control) respectively from two local government-supported schools. The intervention of the two GraphoGames were conducted in the participating schools’ computer rooms. Students played the GraphoGames 25 minutes each session for three sessions a week (in separate days) over a 12-week period. Trained research assistants were on-site setting up the computers and providing support and general encouragement to students in all the training sessions. The planned measures on word reading in Chinese, word reading in English, phonological awareness in Cantonese, phonological awareness in Mandarin, phonological awareness in English, nonverbal reasoning, rapid automatized naming, and vocabulary knowledge have been all successfully assessed in pre-test, post-test, and the two follow-up tests. Repeated measures ANOVA were conducted to analyze the effects of the two computer-assisted interventions (Pinyin and English GraphoGames) on phonological awareness in Cantonese, Mandarin, and English, comparing to the control group (Objective 1). This was performed with phonological awareness in Cantonese, phonological awareness in Mandarin, phonological awareness in English as the dependent variables, the group as the between-subject factor, the time as the within-subject factor, nonverbal reasoning, rapid automatized naming, and vocabulary knowledge as the covariates. The role of phonological awareness in reading development both in the same language (i.e., Chinese, English) and across different languages (i.e., transfer from Chinese as L1 to English as L2 and transfer from English as L2 to Chinese as L1) were examined in a series of regression analysis and in path analysis (Objective 2 & 3). Based on the data collected from the project, three papers were published in peer-reviewed journals in the field. One paper were presented in an international conference. Another two papers are in preparation.

18404014.label: Major findings and research outcome
18404014.value: The project investigated the effects of two computer-assisted GraphoGames (i.e., Pinyin and English GraphoGame) on phonological awareness and correspondingly reading development. For objective 1, the results showed that compared to control and English GraphoGame groups, the Pinyin GraphoGame group showed significant better training effect on Chinese phonological awareness, especially in tone awareness, even controlling for covariates (nonverbal reasoning, rapid automatized naming, and vocabulary knowledge), whereas no different training effect on Chinese phonological awareness were found between English Graphogame and control groups. In addition, both the English and Pinyin Graphogame groups showed significantly better training effect on English phonological awareness compared to the control group, whereas no different training effect was found on English phonological awareness between English and Pinyin GraphoGame groups for the sampled participants (in grade 1 of primary school at Pretest). For objectives 2 & 3, regression analysis showed that phonological awareness significantly predicted reading development in the same languages (i.e., Chinese as L1, English as L2) beyond nonverbal reasoning, rapid automatized naming, and vocabulary knowledge. In addition, the results showed that Chinese phonological awareness (L1) both directly and indirectly predicted English word reading (L2) through English phonological awareness (L2), demonstrating transfer effect from L1 to L2. However, the opposite pattern of transfer effect from English phonological awareness (L2) to Chinese word reading (L1) was not observed. In addition to the support of the hypothesis of the universal phonological principle, especially in early stages, the findings also provided support for the transfer facilitation model (Koda, 2007; 2008). Meanwhile, it also indicated that a certain threshold of L2 proficiency may need to be achieved for facilitative transfer from L2 to L1 to occur.

18404014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18404014.value: Future intervention studies with larger sample size and longer training period would be helpful in confirming and extending the present findings. In addition, it would be interesting to test the directionality and developmental mechanisms of cross-language transfer with different levels of L2 proficiency in longitudinal studies with more time points.

18404014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18404014.value: The current project found that training on Mandarin Pinyin can effectively improve phonological awareness in both Chinese (especially tone awareness) and English among Hong Kong local primary school grade 1 students (P1). Training on English phoneme and rime can effectively improve phonological awareness in English, but not necessarily phonological awareness in Chinese in Hong Kong P1 students. In addition, the project showed that phonological awareness in Chinese longitudinally predicted reading development in both Chinese and English. Theoretically, the current investigation of reading in a non-alphabetic script (i.e., Chinese) and an alphabetic script (i.e., English) in the same group of non-western children provided clear evidence supporting the hypothesis of universal phonological principle. Practically, the project suggests that explicit instruction in L1 Chinese phonology (such as teach Pinyin) may be helpful in learning both Chinese and English in young learners.

18404114.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18404114.value: Morphological awareness, defined as the “conscious awareness of the morphemic structure of words and their ability to reflect on and manipulate that structure” (Carlisle, 1995), has repeatedly been found important for learning to read in Chinese, mainly because of the characteristics of the Chinese language, such as the morpho-syllabic nature of the language and the large number of homophones. However, most extant studies in this area are still at the descriptive level, with the purpose of establishing or verifying the relationship between morphological awareness and reading development in Chinese. There is to date no study that focuses on interpreting that relationship with empirical data. In this proposal, in order to comprehensively unfold the function of morphological awareness in learning to read in Chinese, three research questions are posed, namely 1) whether morphological awareness can facilitate the organization of morphologically complex words in the mental lexicon, 2) whether the association between morphological awareness and Chinese word reading can be mediated by other factors, and 3) whether morphological knowledge can provide additional insights for learning Chinese compound words. The first two studies will follow a one-year longitudinal design with second graders as participants, in order to tap the causal relationship. It is proposed in Study 1 that morphological awareness tested in Time 1 may predict morphological sensitivity tested with a priming lexical decision paradigm in Time 2. In Study 2, vocabulary knowledge and semantic radical awareness are proposed as two mediators of the association between morphological awareness and Chinese word reading. In Study 3, a word learning task will be used with a brief intervention design with second and fourth graders as participants. It is proposed that, compared with the control group, the group which learn the words with a morphological approach as well as whole-word memorization should show better word learning performance. If funded, this project will be among the first to explicitly explore the mechanism of morphological awareness in facilitating reading development in Chinese, which not only clarifies the association among morphological awareness, morphological sensitivity, vocabulary knowledge, and semantic radical awareness in predicting Chinese word reading, but also demonstrates what types of words morphological knowledge can be more helpful for learning. Theoretically, this project contributes to our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of morphological awareness in reading development. Practically, the findings in this project can help educators design more effective instruction programs based on the concept of morphological awareness. 詞法意識被定義為對詞法結構的意識和操作能力（Carlisle, 1995）。該能力對中文閱讀習得的重要性已經被多個研究所驗證。但是目前的研究仍然停留在描述階段，即主要是去確定或證實詞法意識與漢語閱讀發展之間的關係是否存在。對於這個關係的具體機制目前還缺少實證性的研究。本研究將對詞法意識在漢語閱讀中的作用的原因進行探討。相應的，本研究有三個研究問題：1、詞法意識是否可以促進合成詞在頭腦中的組織；2、詞法意識在漢語閱讀中的作用是否可以部分的由其他因素進行媒介；3、詞法知識是否可以為學習漢語合成詞提供額外的線索。對前兩個問題的回答將通過一個以小二學生為研究物件的一年期追蹤研究來進行。我們預期：1、在第一時間點測試的詞法意識將會對在第二時間點測試的詞法敏感性產生預測作用；2、詞彙知識和漢字形旁意識可能是詞法意識與漢語詞語閱讀關係中的兩個媒介變數。對於第三個研究問題，我們會設計一個詞語學習任務在小學二、四年級兒童中實施。我們預期相對于控制組兒童，利用詞法意識方法進行詞語學習的兒童可能會表現出更好的對漢語合成詞的學習效果。如果成功申請，本研究將是第一批針對詞法意識在漢語閱讀發展的作用之機制進行具體實證研究的專案。本項目研究不僅可以進一步澄清詞法意識、詞法敏感性、詞彙知識以及漢字形旁意識在漢語閱讀發展中的作用，也可以幫助考查究竟詞法意識對哪一類詞語的學習更加有幫助。理論上，本專案研究可以幫助我們進一步理解詞法意識在閱讀發展中產生作用的具體機制。在實踐方面，本專案的研究成果也可以説明教育者根據詞法意識的概念設計更為有效的教學方案。

18404114.label: Realisation of objectives
18404114.value: Participants Two primary schools in Hong Kong (at Tseung Kwan O and Tuen Mun respectively) participated in this project. Both schools serve communities with low-to-middle SES. A total of 178 Hong Kong Chinese children were recruited as participants (86 girls, mean age = 8.06, SD = .42). One child was a Pakistani immigrant and thus the data of this child were removed. All remaining 177 children were native Cantonese speakers. No physical or mental problems of the children were reported by the schools or parents. The first round testing was completed in July 2015, lasted for two weeks. Twenty student helpers were well trained on administering the tasks and acted as testers. The second round testing was completed in June 2016, lasted for about one week. Another twenty student helpers were trained and acted as testers. One child did not attend the second round testing because he was absent at that moment. Therefore, the attrition rate is 0.6%. All tests were administered in the classrooms of the two schools. Measures As stated in the mid-term report, all children were administered with the following measures: Priming lexical decision task. In this task, participants were asked to judge whether the second word they heard matched with the picture presented on the left side or right side of the computer screen, by pressing the corresponding keys. When doing this task, children would first hear a beep sound and see a fixation on the center of the screen for 250 ms, which was followed by the prime word, pronounced by a female college student majored in Chinese linguistics after a 300-ms interval. Then after 150 ms, the target word was pronounced. At the same time, two pictures were presented on the computer screen, one matched with the target word, the other not. There was a 1500-ms interval between two trials. There were four conditions in this task: 1) Morpheme condition, 2) Semantic condition, 3) Homophone condition, and 4) Control condition. Morphological awareness. In the homophone identification task, children were presented with two disyllabic words aurally. Then they were asked to judge which of the two words contained a similar meaning with the word presented to them. There were 33 items in this task. In the compounding production task, children were asked to produce a novel word based on a novel scenario. Their answers were rated on a five-point scale. There were 30 items in this task. Phonological awareness. In the syllable deletion task, children were asked to take away one syllable from a three-syllable cluster orally (e.g., te2 kwang1 kaan2 without kaan2 should be te2 kwang1). In the onset deletion task, children were asked to take away the beginning phoneme of a Cantonese syllable (e.g., ciu1 without the onset should be iu1). There were 9 items and 22 items in these two tasks respectively. Vocabulary knowledge. In this task, children were asked to explain the words aurally presented to them. The task contains 32 test items and one trial item. Semantic radical function knowledge. In this semantic radical function-knowledge task, children were presented with a Chinese semantic radical and four pictures. Then, they were asked to select the picture that could properly indicate the meaning of the radical. There were two practice items, which were followed by 35 formal items. Chinese character reading. We designed a new Chinese character reading task based on the needs of the present study. A total of 216 Chinese characters were selected to construct this task, with grade (grades 1, 2, and 3 in primary school), compound/non-compound, character frequency, family size, and family frequency (i.e., the average of the frequencies of all words with a given morpheme) considered. Children were asked to read aloud the items one by one, and one point was given to each correct answer. Non-verbal intelligence. The non-verbal intelligence of the children were measured with Raven’s Standard Progressive Matrices (Raven, Court, & Raven, 1996). Only Sets A and B were administered. By conducting a one-year longitudinal study using above-mentioned measures, the first two objectives have been fully achieved. In order to further disentangle the role of morphological awareness on Chinese character learning, at the second round of testing, a new measure, namely the sensitivity to the semantic relation in Chinese compound words, was developed. The purpose of developing this measure is to try to achieve our third objective, considering the situation that we could not conduct the training study in the two schools, and we cannot find other schools to just participate in the training study. In addition to this measure, the family size of a Chinese character (i.e., how many words a Chinese character can make words with other characters) was introduced as well. Furthermore, an experimental study was conducted on 51 Hong Kong Chinese adults in order to investigate the influence of morphological information on memorizing Chinese compound words. In this experiment, during the Test Phase, the participants were presented with half of the Old words that they had previously seen during the Study Phase and a set of New words, which shared or did not share morphemes with the Old words, and were asked to determine whether they had seen these words in the Study Phase. Half of the New words shared the same compounding structure with the Old words (either subordinate or coordinative) and the other half did not. In the outcome section, more details on these three studies will be mentioned. The introduction to the measure of the sensitivity to the semantic relation (i.e., an expression-picture matching task) is as the following: Expression-picture matching task. The materials consisted of 32 item sets. Each item set contained a prime trial and a target trial. Each trial consisted of a compound, its corresponding audio, and two pictures. The compound always comprised an animate noun as the first constituent and a non-animate noun as the second constituent. For the pictures in the prime condition, one of the pictures was a matching picture that depicted either a POSSESSOR or a DESCRIPTOR relation in the compound, and the other picture was a non-matching picture that depicted either the head or the modifier of the compound word but not both. In the target condition, however, both of the presented pictures could be semantically related to the compound. One picture depicted the POSSESSOR relation, whereas the other depicted the DESCRIPTOR relation. Each target was preceded by two distinct primes with different relation interpretations, one at a time. To avoid repetitive priming, each prime-target pair shared neither the same head nor the same modifier. One trial started with the presentation of a fixation cross at the centre of the screen for 250ms, with a “beep” sound to remind the participant that the test was about to start. After a blank screen presented for 500ms, a compound appeared at the centre of the screen for 1200ms. Simultaneously, the participant heard the corresponding pronunciation. Then, after another blank screen was shown for 500ms, two pictures appeared on the left and right part of the screen. Once the pictures appeared, the participants were allowed to respond by pressing the “F” key on the keyboard to choose the picture on the left or the “J” key for the picture on the right.

18404114.label: Major findings and research outcome
18404114.value: Objective 1 related The processing of morphological information in both the first and second round of testing was examined by using the auditory priming lexical decision task. The linear mixed model (LMM) analysis was adopted for analyzing the data (Baayen, Davidson, & Bates, 2008). The same pattern of results was found in both rounds in this task. Namely, significant priming effects were found in both semantic and morphemic priming conditions, but not in the homophone priming condition. However, no significant difference was found between the semantic and morphemic priming condition. Such results have been discussed in the mid-term report. By using LMM, the relationship between children’s sensitivity to the morphemic information and their morphological awareness could be examined by controlling for both item-level (i.e., character frequency, semantic transparency) and subject-level (i.e., age and non-verbal IQ) variables. Interestingly, a significant positive interaction effect between the priming condition and homophone awareness (but not compounding structure awareness) was found, which indicated that children with better homophone awareness could better activate the morphemic information during lexical recognition. A relevant manuscript is being prepared. Objective 2 related In order to test the mediation effects of phonological awareness, vocabulary and semantic radical knowledge, regression analyses and mediation analyses using bootstrapping technique were conducted. A paper (Item 1 in Part C) related to this has been published. The findings have been introduced in the mid-term report. We conducted similar analyses among the measures using the longitudinal data. When we consider T1 morphological awareness as the IV, T2 phonological awareness, vocabulary, and semantic radical knowledge as the mediator, and T2 Chinese character reading as the outcome, the role of morphological awareness on Chinese character reading was found to be partially mediated by both vocabulary and semantic radical knowledge. Objective 3 related. The main goal here is to examine whether morphological awareness can provide clues for learning/memorizing Chinese characters. Although we encountered some difficulties in following the original plan in achieving this objective, three studies were conducted, and taken them together this objective has been maximally achieved (referring to the three publications listed in Part C, i.e., Items 2-4). Integrating the findings from the three studies, morphological information is activated during the memorization of Chinese compound words, children can rely on their morphological awareness to process the semantic relation information of Chinese compounds, and morphological awareness is more important for learning Chinese characters with small family size.

18404114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18404114.value: There are several potential directions to follow up this project. First, the interplays among morphological awareness, character reading and reading comprehension in Chinese children could be further investigated. There is a limited number of studies tapped the relationship between morphological awareness and reading comprehension in Chinese children, leaving the underlying mechanism not fully investigated. To draw a relatively comprehensive picture on the role of morphological awareness in the literacy development of Chinese children, it is necessary to systematically dig into the detailed mechanisms. Second, there are some other factors in different domains that have been found to be important for literacy development in Chinese. It could be a good way to integrate the findings and theories related to morphological awareness into this bigger picture, and explore the dynamic interactions among factors at different domains (such as ecological, psychological and cognitive/linguistic ones) in contributing to Chinese children’s literacy development. Third, some training programmes and related intervention studies can be developed accordingly. I have obtained two research grants, one from EdUHK and another from SCOLAR, about developing educational games for helping Chinese children improve their reading through training of morphological awareness; and I will conduct more studies in this direction.

18404114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18404114.value: In this project, the reasons why morphological awareness can help Chinese children learn single character are explored. Through a serials of correlational and experimental studies, the role of morphological awareness on learning Chinese characters was found to be mediated by vocabulary and orthographic knowledge, and moderated by the family size of a given character. Morphological information was activated during the processing of Chinese compounds, which can influence the memorization of the words and was moderated by homophone awareness. Theoretically, all these findings together can help us draw a clear picture on why morphological awareness can help children learn a single Chinese character. Practically, the findings in this project can help us design and implement literacy instructions based on Chinese morphology more precisely and more effectively. In addition, besides of morphological awareness, there are some other factors that have been found to be important for literacy development. However, studies focusing on the underlying mechanisms are still lacked. This project could also help researchers and education practitioners to think in more depth, with the purpose of refining the relevant theories and practices.

18404614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18404614.value: Since the first pilot project of integrated education was implemented in 1997 in Hong Kong, the number of students with SEN in inclusive settings has grown rapidly in the recent decade. Nowadays, students with different kinds of sensory, physical and cognitive impairments are learning together with students without disability in the same classroom. Throughout the development, one of the greatest challenges is the resistance from parents of students with and without disability. Parents of students with SEN may refuse inclusive educational placement because of their concerns about their child’s rejection by peers and teachers (Saylor & Leach, 2009), as well as the lack of support services for their child’s needs (Bennett et al., 1997; de Boer, et al., 2010). Parents of typically developing students may hesitate to support inclusive education (IE) because of their worry that their children would learn inappropriate behaviours from students with SEN (EOC, 2012; Rafferty et al., 2005). Since parents are the major stakeholders in education, their support and involvement is pivotal to the success of the implementation of IE (EOC, 2012; Gasteiger-Klicpera, et al., 2013; Palmer et al., 2001). While the topic of parents’ attitudes towards IE has received attention among education scholars in Western societies (de Boer et al., 2010, 2012 for a review), research on this topic is highly lacking in Asian settings. Given that there is evidence showing cultural differences in the practice of parents of students with SEN (e.g. Harry, 1992), it would be important to study what factors significantly predict parents’ attitudes towards IE in a Chinese cultural setting. Based on the constructed theoretical framework of analysis, the proposed study seeks to fill this gap by using an evidence-based approach to examine the predicting factors of parents’ attitudes towards IE. Quantitative and qualitative research methods will be applied to obtain triangulated evidence in this topic of interest. The findings of our study will be of practical value and help policy-makers to develop a better understanding of parents’ beliefs and concerns, and will therefore provide insights into the refinement of the policy of IE, as well as the development of parent education programmes to cultivate positive attitudes among parents in the community. It is anticipated that the outcome of this proposed study will facilitate an active collaboration among parents, teachers and other stakeholders so that students with and without SEN will finally both benefit from the inclusive learning environment. Hong Kong has started to implement the pilot scheme of integrated programs since 1997. Nowadays, students with different kinds of sensory, physical or cognitive impairments are learning together with students without disability in the same classroom. Throughout the development, one of the greatest challenges is the resistance from parents of students with and without disability. Parents of students with SEN may refuse inclusive educational placement because of their concerns of their child’s rejection by peers and teachers (Pivik et al., 1997), as well as the lack of support services for their child’s needs (Bennett et al., 1997; Fuchs & Fuchs, 1994). Parents of typically developing students may hesitate to support IE due to their worry that their child would learn inappropriate behaviors from students with SEN (Reichart et al., 1989). Since parents are the major stakeholders of education, their support and involvement is pivotal to the success of the implementation of IE (Palmer et al., 2001). While the topic of parents’ attitudes towards IE has received attention among prominent researchers in western society (de Boer et al., 2009), research study on this topic is highly lacking in an Asian setting. Given that there is evidence showing cultural differences in practice among parents of students with SEN (e.g. Harry, 1992), it would be important to study what factors significantly predict parents’ attitudes towards IE in a Chinese cultural setting. The proposed study seeks to fill this gap by using evidence-based approach to examine the predicting factors of parents’ attitudes towards IE in a Chinese setting. Quantitative and qualitative research methods will be applied to obtain triangulated evidences in the current topic of interest. The findings of our study will help policy-makers to develop better understanding on parents’ beliefs and concerns, and will therefore provide insights on the refinement of the policy of IE, as well as the development of intervention of parent education program to foster positive attitudes. It is anticipated that the outcome of this proposed study will facilitate an active collaborations among parents, teachers and other stakeholders so that students with and without SEN will both benefit from the inclusive learning environment. 香港自1997年起，已開展融合教育先導計劃。至今，很多有感官、肢體或認知障礙的學生，都可以與普通學生在課堂中一起學習。綜觀融合教育發展，特教生家長及普通學生家長是否接受融合教育的態度，是主要的挑戰。有特殊教育需要學生的家長擔憂孩子會受到同伴及教師的排斥 (Pivik et al., 1997)，以及學校缺乏對融合生的支援性服務 (Bennett et al., 1997; Fuchs & Fuchs, 1994)，因而拒絕融合教育安置。而普通學生家長因擔心孩子會從特殊學生中習得不恰當的行為表現，而不太願意支持全納教育 (Reichart et al., 1989)。家長是教育的重要持份者，他們的支持和參與是全納教育的成功關鍵 (Palmer et al., 2001)。在西方社會內，眾多知名學者已關注家長對全納教育的態度 (de Boer et al., 2009)，而這課題的有關研究，則在亞洲社會內，仍見欠缺。有證據顯示，特殊學生家長在實踐中存有文化差異性 (e.g. Harry, 1992)，在中國文化背景下，探討影響家長全納教育態度的因素，將顯得尤為重要。本研究旨在通過實證方法，檢視在華人社會內家長對全納教育態度的潛在影響因素，從以填補這方面研究的不足。研究人員將透過質性與量化方法，探索課題及引證各方面證據。研究結果將會協助政策制訂者，多了解家長的信念和擔憂，從而提升相關政策與服務；結果也會促使發展親職教育訓練項目，培養家長正向、積極的態度。本研究成果將會促進家長、教師及其它相關人員的合作互助，最終使融合生和普通學生都能從全納學習環境中互相受益。

18404614.label: Realisation of objectives
18404614.value: The objectives of this research project were fully achieved by quantitative and qualitative research methods. Our research team has performed extensive literature review on the questionnaire items for assessing people’s attitudes towards inclusive education. We finally selected items from the Parent Survey on Inclusion (PSI; Bennett, Deluca & Bruns, 1997). For the predicting factors of attitude, we assessed parents’ evaluation of the effectiveness of school inclusive measures, and psycho-social factors such as social support, mental health, and their child’s self-determination and school functioning. We believed that the effectiveness of school inclusive measures, students’ school functioning and psycho-social variables were predictors of parents’ attitude towards inclusion. A total of 1030 copies of primary school parents’ questionnaires and 925 copies of secondary school parents’ questionnaires were distributed. At the completion of survey data collection, a total of 1120 parents of students in primary and secondary school students (in the school year 2015/2016) completed and returned the questionnaires. Objective 1 The objective 1 “examining the current attitudes towards inclusive education among parents of children with and without SEN” was fully achieved with the questionnaire data collected. We examined the reliability of 4 questionnaire items selected for assessing attitudes towards inclusive education (Likert scale: 1= totally agree; 7= totally disagree). Lower mean scores indicate more positive attitudes. After excluding one item, the Cronbach’s alphas were .791 and .753 for secondary and primary school parents’ data respectively. Based on descriptive statistics, both primary school parents (M = 3.06, S.D. = 1.15) and secondary school parents (M = 3.30, S.D. = 1.14) demonstrated slightly positive attitude towards inclusive education. For primary schools, parents of SEN and non-SEN students were similar in their attitudes towards inclusive education (M = 3.17 vs M = 3.03 for SEN and non-SEN respectively, p > .05). For secondary schools, parents of SEN student (M = 3.09) were more positive towards inclusive education than parents of non-SEN students (M = 3.41). Objective 2 The objective 2 “identifying the potential predicting factors of attitudes towards inclusive education among parents of children with and without SEN” was fully achieved with the questionnaire data collected and analysed. We performed correlation analyses on primary school data. For parents of children with SEN, their attitudes towards inclusive education were highly correlated with their children’s self-determination (r = .233, p < .01), parents’ depression (r = .231, p<.01), and rating towards school inclusive measures (r = .398, p < .001). For parents of children without SEN, their attitudes towards inclusive education were highly correlated with their children’s school engagement (r = .114, p < .01), children’s self-determination (r = .238, p < .001), children’s mental health (r = -.134, p < .01), and rating towards school inclusive measures (r = .363, p < .001). Objective 3 The objective 3 “evaluating and comparing the differences in the current attitudes and predictors of attitudes towards inclusive education among parents of students with SEN and parents of students without SEN” was fully achieved by conducting the statistical analyses described below. First, we compared parents of children with and without SEN in their attitudes towards inclusive education using independent sample t-tests. There was no significant difference between parents of children with SEN and without SEN for primary school parents (p > .05) in their attitudes towards inclusive education. For secondary school parents, parents of children with SEN were significantly more positive than parents of children without SEN in their attitude towards inclusive education (p < .05). Second, we performed analyses to find out significant predictors of parents’ attitude towards inclusive education for primary school SEN and non-SEN students and parents. Based on some pilot data, exploratory analyses on the effect of demographic variables on parents’ attitudes demonstrated that male parents exhibited more positive attitudes towards inclusion than female parents; and parents of children at a higher grade level indicated less positive attitudes. Furthermore, factors were entered into a regression analysis to predict attitude towards inclusive education (AIE; dependent variable). For parents of SEN children, the predictors explain a significant amount of variance in the AIE (F(11,113)= 3.55, p < .001 , R2 = .51, R2 adjusted = .184). Rating towards school inclusive measures was the only significant predictor of attitude towards inclusive education (beta = .34, t(113) = 3.98, p < .001). For parents of non-SEN children, the predictors also explain a significant amount of variance in the AIE (F(11, 534)= 12.75, p < .001 , R2 = .46, R2 adjusted = .21). Parental involvement (beta = -.12, t(534) = -2.74, p < .01), parental anxiety (beta = -.12, t(534) = -2.09, p < .05), children’s self-determination reported by parents (beta = .16, t(534) = 3.73, p < .001), and ratings towards school inclusive measures (beta = .32, t(534) = 8.0, p < .001) significantly predict AIE. Finally, based on some pilot data, we evaluated the effects of knowledge and perceived social norms on attitudes towards inclusive education. A structural model describing the relationship between attitude, knowledge, and perceived social norm among parents of children with special needs. Results revealed that knowledge and perceived social norm were powerful predictors of parents’ attitudes towards inclusion and the two predictors were intercorrelated. Objective 4 The objective 4 “providing recommendations for improvement in policies and support services to both students with and without SEN, as well as their parents, in the Chinese community: Hong Kong” was fully achieved using quantitative and qualitative analyses of data. Based on the findings of our study, we suggest that in order to promote the support and positive attitudes toward inclusive education among parents of SEN and non-SEN children, more effort should be placed on improving the school inclusive measures, such as teachers’ professional knowledge and pedagogical skills in inclusive education, adaptation of curriculum, effective allocation of resources to inclusion by school management team, and extra resources for afterschool training or pullout lessons. For parents of non-SEN children, efforts may be dedicated to encourage the parental involvement, reducing their anxiety level, and promoting their children’s self-determination, in order to improve their attitudes toward inclusive education.

18404614.label: Major findings and research outcome
18404614.value: Based on the pilot questionnaire data collected, we evaluated the effects of knowledge and perceived social norms on attitudes towards inclusive education. A structural model describing the relationship between attitude, knowledge, and perceived social norm among parents of children with special needs. Results revealed that knowledge and perceived social norm were powerful predictors of parents’ attitudes towards inclusion and the two predictors were intercorrelated. The findings were published in the journal “International Journal of Inclusive Education”. Based on the data collected in this project, we also tested the relationships between peer social support, school social support, self-determination and school engagement of students with SEN. The results of structural equation modelling (SEM) analysis show that perceived school social support has a direct effect on the engagement of students with SEN. The variables examined in these analyses were initially considered the predictors of parents’ attitudes towards inclusive education. We found that additional information could be extracted from their inter-relationships to build a SEM model and reveal research findings in addition to the research questions proposed. A manuscript was submitted to the journal “Learning and Individual Differences” and is under review.

18404614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18404614.value: Based on the findings of the current study, parents’ attitude towards inclusive education could be improved by knowledge and perceived social norms. Further studies could be conducted to review the effectiveness of parental workshops and programs to equip them with the knowledge about underlying human rights issues and rationales of inclusive education, and the social norms in various cultures and countries. Another major finding of our project is that parent-perceived quality of school inclusive measures was a significant predictor of attitude towards inclusive education among both parents of SEN and non-SEN children. Particularly for parents of non-SEN children, those with greater parental involvement, less parental anxiety, and with more self-determined children were more supportive towards inclusive education. Further studies could examine whether there is any improvement in parental attitude towards inclusion with school’s efforts in improving the school inclusive measures, parental involvement, parental anxiety and self-determination of children with and without SEN.

18404614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18404614.value: This study examined factors predicting parents’ attitudes towards inclusive education. Questionnaire and interview data were collected from 1120 parents of students in primary and secondary schools. Results of analyses showed that parent-perceived quality of school inclusive measures was a significant predictor of attitude towards inclusive education among both parents of SEN and non-SEN children. For parents of non-SEN children, those with greater parental involvement, less parental anxiety, and with more self-determined children were more supportive towards inclusive education. The findings inform the education policy makers that in order to promote positive attitudes toward inclusive education among parents, more effort should be placed on improving the school inclusive measures, such as teachers’ professional knowledge and pedagogical skills in inclusive education, adaptation of curriculum, effective allocation of inclusive resources by school management team, and extra resources for afterschool training or pullout lessons. Moreover, for parents of non-SEN children, more efforts should be dedicated to encouraging parental involvement, reducing parental anxiety level, and promoting their children’s self-determination so that students without SEN could serve as supporters to SEN students who need extra social support to overcome their learning difficulties.

18405014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18405014.value: A review of the current literature on developing students’ critical response to visual arts reveals a heavy reliance on using art criticism models in schools. The learning of art criticism is generally seen as an engagement of students in various language tasks, such as describing, analysing, interpreting and evaluating. Geahigan (2002) disagrees with the view that the learning of art criticism is a discursive practice and conceptualises it as a process of inquiry. Building on the theory of Geahigan, the present study aims to develop, field-test and evaluate an inquiry-based model for learning art criticism. Using ‘design research’, a systematic and rigorous method of seeking out tested improvements in learning situations, as the principal methodology, the study will develop and test a pedagogic model that will enhance students’ critical ability in art criticism. The study will be conducted in three phases. Phase 1 will involve the preparation of eight teacher participants in the understanding of various art criticism models and the development of inquiry-based art criticism curriculum plans. Phase 2 will focus on the implementation of the curriculum plans. The investigators will observe three to five lessons and advise on the refinement of the plans. In Phase 3 the effectiveness and outcomes of the inquiry-based art criticism teaching on students will be investigated. Data will be obtained from interviews of teacher participants, classroom observations, video-recorded lessons, and the pre-testing and post-testing of student performance in written texts of art criticism. The data collected will be examined in relation to current theories on learning art criticism, and used to develop a pedagogical model which is theoretically and practically sound, taking into consideration the Hong Kong context. Addressing the gap between the theorisation, development, and implementation of inquiry-based art criticism learning, the project is important at this time, when the Senior Secondary Curriculum and the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education Examination are being launched. Both the new curriculum and the examination place a strong emphasis on art appreciation, criticism and inquiry. The development of a critical audience has also become particularly important since the first phase of the West Kowloon Cultural District project will be coming to realisation as early as 2015. The study will represent a timely effort to answer many of the questions raised by the community, schools, teachers and students about the development of the critical ability of our next generation. 從新近有關發展學生視覺藝術批判回應的文獻中發現，學校相當依賴藝術評論模式的運用。一般而言，藝術評論的學習被視為學生透過語言來達成任務，例如運用語言對藝術作品作出描述、分析、詮釋和評價。吉伊根(Geahigan, 2002)不認同藝術評論的學習乃一以語言論述為實踐的說法；反之，他認為藝術評論的學習是一個探究的過程。以吉伊根的理論為基礎，本研究旨在發展、實地試驗和評價以探究為本學習藝術評論的方法。本研究以「設計研究」為主要硏究方法。此方法有系統而慎密，是一種在學習情境下尋求測試改善的研究法。本研究將發展和測試一個能夠增強學生藝術評論批判能力的教學方式。 本研究分為三階段進行。首階段為準備階段，共有八位教師參與認識各種不同藝術評論模式的工作坊，並發展出以探究為本的藝術評論課程設計。第二階段將集中在課程設計的實施上。研究者將視察三至五個課堂，並提出對課程設計的修改建議。最後階段則為探究為本藝術評論教學的成效和成果的研究。研究資料將由教師的訪談、教學觀察、課堂錄影，以及學生在藝術評論寫作的前測和後測表現而獲得。所獲取的資料將以新近學習藝術評論的理論作檢視，並加以運用發展出符合香港情境，且兼具理論與實踐的教學模式。 本研究有其迫切性意義，它填補理論、發展和實施探究為本藝術評論學習之間的缺口，尤以在新高中課程和香港中學教育文憑考試實行之際。誠然，新課程和考試兩者均強調藝術欣賞、批評和探究。此外，由於西九龍文化藝術區計劃的首階段將於2015年實現，故發展出具批判能力的觀眾顯得更為重要。本研究為關心我們下一世代批判能力的社會、學校、教師和學生們，提出適切的解答。

18405014.label: Realisation of objectives
18405014.value: Objective 1: To develop an inquiry-based art criticism learning model based on the tenets proposed by Geahigan. Based on the theoretical tenets and practical suggestions proposed by Geahigan, a curriculum framework was created and disseminated to the experimental group teacher participants at the two-day workshops. Each teacher then developed a school-based curriculum plan that actualized inquiry-based art criticism teaching and learning. Each plan covered a 9-month period of the 2015-2016 school year and engaged students in personal response, research, and aesthetic skill and concept acquisition activities. During the period of the development of the curriculum plans, the researchers visited each teacher participant two to three times and provided suggestions for improvement, such as the formulation of thematic topics, the design of relevant teaching activities, the selection of artworks for in-class discussion, etc. Objective 2: To field test and refine curriculum plans using an inquiry approach at the senior secondary level. The curriculum plans developed by the teachers were field tested in eight schools. The participants included teachers, students and independent raters. Two groups of secondary school teachers and students were invited to participate as the experimental group and the control group. The teacher participants were recruited through the Professional Learning Community for Secondary School Visual Arts, a group formed by the Hong Kong Curriculum Development Institute. The student participants (aged 17-18) were Secondary Five students who took visual arts as their examination subject. They were the students of the teacher participants. Both groups of students were required to write an art criticism essay before and after the implementation of the curriculum plans. In total, there were eight teachers and 85 students in the experimental group, and seven teachers and 82 students in the control group. For the independent raters, six serving or former secondary visual arts teachers were recruited to mark the students’ essays. Objective 3: To identify the ways in which teachers translate inquiry-based art criticism into practice. Each teacher participant was interviewed before and after the implementation of inquiry-based curriculum plans. Two video recordings of teachers’ art criticism lessons were conducted at the beginning and the end of the curriculum year. The interviews and video recordings were transcribed. Teachers were interviewed on their expectation of student learning, ways to realize inquiry-based learning in their design, difficulties in implementation, and the changes of students’ performance in class and art criticism writing. Interview data was organized into themes articulating teachers’ ways of putting theory into practice. Objective 4: To investigate the effectiveness of inquiry-based art criticism and related learning activities in enhancing student learning of art criticism. An experimental design was set up to examine the effectiveness of inquiry-based art criticism approach on two comparative groups. A pre-test and post-test were administered to student participants before and after the implementation of the curriculum plans. A rubric developed by the researchers, namely, the Art Criticism Assessment Rubric, was used to assess students’ essays in eight domains. An inter-rater reliability test was conducted and the results indicated that it is a rubric with acceptable reliability. Two t-tests were conducted to analyze students’ results in the pre- and post-test. Within Group Comparison between Pre-test and Post-test A paired-samples t-test was conducted to compare the pre- and post-test scores within the same group. There were statistically significant increases in all domains for both groups. A large effect size, i.e., the relative magnitude of the differences between means, for all of the domains in the experimental group was observed. Varied effect sizes (mainly from moderate to large) for all the domains in the control group were observed. Across Group Comparison between Pre-test and Post-test An independent-samples t-test was conducted to compare the mean difference between the pre- and post-test scores across the two groups. It was found that the improvement of the experimental group was significantly greater than the control group. There were significant differences in the improvement of scores for the experimental group compared to the control group in all domains except Description. The magnitudes of the differences in the means varied mainly from small to moderate. The domain of Formal Analysis is the one with a large effect size. Objective 5: To evaluate the impact and outcomes of inquiry-based art criticism and related learning activities on student learning of art criticism. The impact and outcomes of inquiry-based art criticism and related learning activities on student learning were evaluated by comparing the scores of the experimental group and the control group, supplemented with data collected from teacher and student interviews, and observation of lessons. The impact was concluded in terms of three aspects: use of research materials, broadening of art viewing strategies and improved analysis and judgment of artworks. More Use of Research Materials Use of Researched Materials was the domain with the largest improvement in both groups (experimental group: 73%; control group: 35%). There are two possible explanations of the results. First, the scores of both groups in this domain were the lowest among all the others in the pre-test (experimental group: 3.58; control group: 3.62). There was therefore a lot of room to gain improvements in the post-test. Second, the poor performance in the pre-test may become a motivation for both groups to improve. In the pre-test, little evidence of research could be found in most of the students’ essays. The students might not have taken this domain seriously and most of them did not have experience of using researched materials in their essays. But in the post-test, for example, one student studied the historical background of the work and the preference of the artist in that period. Broadening Students’ Art Viewing Strategy Application of Aesthetic and Contextual Knowledge was the second most improved domain. The improvement of the experimental group (34%) in this domain was twice that of the control group (16%). The broadening of students’ art viewing strategy may be ascribed to the well-constructed teaching unit and the emphasis on aesthetic concept and skill acquisition in the whole inquiry-based learning method. In each unit, teacher participants were required to focus on certain aesthetic theories or concepts which were delivered through in-class discussion of selected artworks. This ensured that those theories and concepts were clearly illustrated through concrete examples. On the side of the students, some of them began to pay more attention to the context, such as why and how a work was created. Improved Analysis and Judgment of Artworks In the domains of Formal Analysis and Judgment, the improvements of the experimental group (31% and 34% respectively) were three times more than those of the control group (9% and 10% respectively). The effectiveness of the inquiry-based approach may be attributed to its emphasis on student’s personal response and research activities in the learning process. In the interviews, some students mentioned that they began to compare their views with other students in the personal response activity. With regard to engagement in research activities, the students expressed that there were more opportunities for them to learn the contextual knowledge and to consider the various points of view of an artwork. Having broadened their perspectives in viewing and gained useful contextual information, the students were better equipped to develop an informed analysis and judgment of an artwork.

18405014.label: Major findings and research outcome
18405014.value: Major findings It was found that inquiry-based model was an effective strategy for improving students’ performance on art criticism writing. The mean score of the experimental group increased from 52.48 to 67.92 (29.4%), compared to that of the control group from 50.20 to 56.92 (13.4%). The inquiry-based model is capable of producing significant improvements in different domains of art criticism writing. The scores of the experimental group increased by 1.61 (31%) on Analysis and 1.73 (34%) on Judgment, while those of the control group increased by only 0.5 (9%) and 0.49 (10%) respectively. The underlying assumption that art criticism is not a discursive practice but a process of inquiry proves to be effective for teachers and students. Inquiry-based art criticism teaching and learning has impacted in four major areas: 1. Encouraged reflections and exchange of views: The students were encouraged to begin their responses to artworks with their personal experience. They learned to reflect on their own responses and to accept others’ views. 2. Well-constructed unit plans: The three types of teaching activity formed a structure for the teachers to develop their unit plans. Each unit plan focused on certain aesthetic theories or concepts and was fully illustrated through in-class discussion of selected artworks. 3. Facilitation of multiple perspectives: The learning of aesthetic and contextual knowledge enhanced the students’ capacity to explore an artwork from multiple perspectives and move beyond considering artworks solely on the basis of feelings and emotions. 4. Construction of personal knowledge: Having broadened their perspectives in viewing an artwork and gained useful contextual information through research activities, the students were better equipped to develop informed analysis and judgment of a work of their own. Research outcome 1. Publication: Three papers were published in Research in Arts Education (2016) and The International Journal of Art & Design Education (2017; in press). 2. Presentation: Two papers were presented in the 8th Annual International Conference on Visual and Performing Arts (Athens, May 2017) and the 35th InSEA World Congress (Daegu, August 2017). 3. Website: A website ‘Learning and Teaching Art Criticism’ (www.artcrit.eduhk.hk) was launched in April 2018 to share the project results. As at June 2018, 206 teachers and 356 students have registered as members and 48 inquiry-based unit plans have been shared. 4. Workshop: One half-day seminar (May 2017) and a 3-day workshop (June and July 2017) have been organised for 90 and 29 secondary school teachers respectively.

18405014.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18405014.value: The project revealed that strategies of questioning and engaging students in art criticism dialogues are needed for guiding students’ personal response activities. According to the teacher participants, this was a challenging task and a lot of preparation is required. Therefore, developing a holistic questioning and dialogue engagement strategy for teachers is a much-needed direction in future research. In response to this pedagogical concern, an application of GRF project entitled “An investigation of the use of group dialogue and questioning strategies with primary school students learning visual arts in museums and schools” was made. The project was funded and was launched in January 2018. Art making and responding to art are two closely related areas in the learning of visual arts. However, the design of related art making activities had not been a focus of the present study. A full practice of inquiry-based learning should take into account the ways in which art criticism is connected to art making. This is a question for future studies in visual arts education. In the dissemination of project results through the website, a column will be created exploring different strategies in which teachers integrate responding to art with making art.

18405014.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18405014.value: The teaching of art criticism in schools has been influenced by art criticism models that emphasize observation and linguistic practices. Instead of asking students to observe an artwork and make verbal or written statements, George Geahigan proposed an inquiry-based art criticism learning model that engages students in personal response, research, and aesthetic concept and perceptual skill acquisition activities. Using inquiry-based art criticism as a foundation for curriculum development and connecting the model to authentic situations in schools, the present study investigated the effectiveness of the model on student learning. Fifteen secondary school teachers were invited to participate. Eight teachers taught the experimental group (85 S5 students) with inquiry-based curriculum plans and the other seven teachers taught the control group (82 S5 students) with their own school curriculum plans. Students of both groups were asked to write an art criticism essay before and after the implementation of the plans. The results demonstrated that the overall improvement of the experimental group after one academic year was significantly greater than that of the control group. It was found that the inquiry-based approach was a successful strategy in improving students’ skills in analysing, judging and using aesthetic and contextual knowledge in art criticism writing.

18405414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18405414.value: Since Hong Kong preschoolers with special needs were placed in kindergartens with integrated programmes in 2001, enrolment figures for children with special needs have been rising in kindergartens. Children with special needs being physically included in kindergartens may not necessarily mean that they are socially adjusting well. In the proposed study, social inclusion is assessed on four dimensions: peer preferences for children in the class, each child’s number of friendships, peers’ perception of children’s social roles in the classroom and the extent of each child’s social engagement. The study is designed to answer the following questions: To what extent are children with special needs socially included in these preschool settings? To what extent and how do teachers facilitate social inclusion in these inclusive classrooms? The answers to these questions have implications for the successful implementation of inclusive education in kindergartens. The study uses a multivariate analysis of variance group comparison design to test whether children with and without special needs differ in terms of their social inclusion in their classroom learning environments. About 180 children will be recruited from 20 integrated kindergartens for the proposed study (i.e., 90 children with special needs matched with 90 children without special needs matched in age and gender in the same classroom from a total of 20 kindergartens) using convenience sampling. Sociometric testing techniques (through which children are interviewed about the children in the class) will be used to assess the first three dimensions of social inclusion, namely, peer preference, friendship and peer perception of social roles. The fourth dimension of social inclusion, that is, social engagement by children with special needs, will be assessed during classroom observation. Using correlational analyses, we will also examine the relation between learning environment and social inclusion. Learning environment will be assessed based on teachers’ classroom behaviour using classroom observational assessment and scoring approach, through which teachers are rated on the domains of emotional support, instructional support and classroom organisation. Anecdotal records of the learning environment will also be examined specifically from the aspect of social inclusion, which is most related to learning environment. This knowledge will help teachers to structure their classroom environments for the promotion of social inclusion in Hong Kong preschool settings.

18405414.label: Realisation of objectives
18405414.value: In order to meet the four stated research objectives, the Principal investigator (PI) underwent the following venture for the project: In the Preparation Phase from January 2015 to March 2015, a full-time senior research assistant was employed. The contact list of potential participants from integrated kindergarten was prepared. The assessment forms were designed. In the pilot study phase from April to August 2015, seven integrated kindergartens were contacted via phones, emails and direct on-site visits. Invitation information letter and consent form were sent to parents and teachers. As a result, a total of 53 children with special needs and 204 typically developing children from the seven integrated kindergartens participated in this study. We tried out the research procedure in one kindergarten and with the school consent, we videotaped the class observation. From September to December 2015, we employed some part-time research assistants as the assessment of child interviews and observation ratings following individual target child was very labour intensive. Using the videos from the pilot study, we trained them to rate the children interactions using our assessment protocol until the inter-rater reliability reached 80%. The main study started from January and completed in June 2016 when we collected data from the remaining six kindergartens. For Objective 1: to compare preschool children with and without special needs in terms of their social inclusion in the classroom, assessed in terms of social preference, friendship, peer perceptions of social status, and social engagement, the investigators completed the data collection by carrying out peer nomination test and sociometric class activity observation. Each participating child was interviewed one-on-one during their school break time using the Peer nomination test. In addition, class teachers were interviewed and given a questionnaire to fill in for each participating student in their class. The sociogram consisted of three parts: observation of the nature and frequency of children's initiations and responses, children's engagement with peers in the classroom, and the quality of the children's interaction with peers in the classroom. The raters recorded down the number of occurrence in every 5 minute interval during their 30-minute free-play sessions. For Objective 2: to compare the learning environments of Integrated and Mainstream classrooms, the investigators completed the data collection by using Individual Child Engagement Record-Revised (ICER-R) to measure the engagement frequency and quality of interactions between peers and teachers. For Objective 3: to identify specific aspects of the learning environmental factors associated with the social inclusion of preschool children with and without special needs, and Objective 4: To identify the specific aspects of the learning environmental factors associated with the social inclusion of preschool children with and without special needs, the investigators collected data using the CLASS, a classroom observational measure on which teachers' behaviours are noted as qualitative data and coded as quantitative data on 31 items grouped in 8 dimensions: positive climate; negative climate; teacher sensitivity; regard for student perspectives; behaviour management; classroom organization; instructional styles; and social communication modelling. In June 2016, the project entered the Data editing and analyses phase. The full data consists of at least four different data sets, namely, the analysis of (1) sociometric nomination data, (2) free play observation of social interaction, (3) classroom observation of teacher-child interactions and (4) classroom climate. Data analysis for each set and each level will take two months each. So it took about 9-12 months to complete the entire data analyses. The project duration was extended to another five months until 31 May 2017. The student behaviors recorded in each video was coded and the categorized data went through various statistical analyses such as ANOVA and linear regression. The principal investigator started to write manuscripts for submission to international conference papers and peer-reviewed journals.

18405414.label: Major findings and research outcome
18405414.value: On 17-18 June 2017, the PI presented the project findings, entitled as "An investigation of the extent of social inclusion for kindergarten children with special needs in Hong Kong" at the international conference, First Australia and New Zealand Conference on Advanced Research (ANZCAR-June 2017). The project results were also reported in local seminars at the Integrated Wellness (iWELL) centre of Education University of Hong Kong on 16th January 2018 and at the Support Unit of Special Educational Needs (SuSEN) centre on 17th July, 2017 respectively. One article was published, entitled as, “A systematic review of classroom interventions: To promote social inclusion for preschoolers with special needs in inclusive educational settings” (Tsang and Cheng, 2017) was published in Emerging Trends in Educational Research and Policy Studies, Volume 8, issue 2. Another two manuscripts were being submitted to peer-reviewed journals, namely, “Parent-Implemented Interventions for Young Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review of Fidelity Assessment” by Kam & Tsang, and, “Social inclusion of children with special needs in Hong Kong preschools” by Tsang, Hsueh, Chow, Chan & Fung. In sum, Objectives 1-4 have been completed by May 2018 and achieved the following deliverables: (i) 1 article was published in peer-reviewed journal; (ii) 2 manuscripts are being submitted to peer-reviewed journals this month; (iii) 3 presentations for local and international conferences; (iv) 1 PhD student was admitted doing longitudinal study on the GRF project; and 2 more EdD students have been admitted doing related studies under my supervision as principal supervisor.

18405414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18405414.value: Our findings challenge the current focus in social inclusion intervention. Conventional social inclusion intervention programs target at the ‘normalization’ of child behaviors by social skills training (Otero, Schatz, Merrill, & Bellini, 2015). These programs aim to help child develop prosocial behaviors, such as how to share, imitate, ask for help, greet, and respond to conversation while playing with toys (Frostad & Pijl, 2007). More emphasis is placed on social skills training, rather than social participation in social inclusion programs. Hence, although the social skills training approach enhances SN preschoolers’ age-appropriate social skills, opportunities to put those skills into practice in the classroom may be limited (DeMonchy, Pijl & Zandberg, 2004). Our findings direct us to rethink the design of our social inclusion interventions, that is, to shift the focus from improving child’s social behaviors to fostering interpersonal interactions through social participation in the classroom (Skinner & Pitzer, 2012). Hence, more peer-mediated and parent-mediated strategies should be adopted to promote social participation in children with special needs. Further studies on this shifted intervention focus is warranted and will be realized by my doctoral students who show interest to commit their research along this direction in their proposals on social inclusion studies.

18405414.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18405414.value: The current study aims to compare the social inclusion status of preschoolers with and without special needs in inclusive Hong Kong preschool classrooms. Social inclusion was measured in terms of social acceptance (peer nominations for liking), mutual friendships (peer-child nominations for mutual liking), and social participation (four observational measures). The convergent validity of these six measures of social inclusion was also tested by examining their relationships with one another. Findings showed that compared to their typically developing peers, children with special needs were less socially accepted, had fewer mutual friends, and showed more passive participation. Furthermore, social acceptance and mutual friendships were significantly correlated with several measures of social participation, in particular, passive non-participation. Our findings suggest that social inclusion interventions should not only aim at training specific social behaviors for children with special needs, but also educating children with and without special needs to socially participate together. This sheds light on the importance of teachers’ or parents’ roles in designing learning environments that can foster active participation as well as social participation in children with or without special needs in the classroom.

18406214.label: Realisation of objectives
18406214.value: Realization of objectives In line with the funded proposal, the realization of the five objectives was achieved through the following channels: (1) construction of a culturally sensitive instrument for data collection and analysis; (2) the dissemination of the findings through the project schools, local and international audiences in academic conferences and academic exchanges; and (3) the submission of scholarly outputs for publication. Objectives 1 & 2 were fully realized in the following ways: The research team theorized the structural relationships among the demographic and contextual factors on a foundation of three areas of scholarship: Subjective Well-being (Huebner, 2001; Fisher, 1999); Academic Engagement (Appleton et al., 2008) and Civic Engagement (Schulz et al., 2008; Yuen, 2013 & 2014; Yuen & Lee, 2013). An integrated questionnaire combining both well-being and engagement with school and society was pilot-tested and revised. We conducted the survey with 31 secondary schools including one international school, collecting over 15,000 valid student samples. The large sample size has provided a very useful database for all interested researchers for ongoing related studies. Findings have been disseminated in both local and international seminars, conferences and journals. Objectives 3 & 4 were fully realized in the following ways: In line with the proposal, a range of dissemination channels was explored by the project team. First, individual school reports were made available to all participant schools. The student demographics vary from school to school. Specific attention was therefore applied in mapping the pathways with well-being and engagement of students in the school-based data with reference to the overall sample data. This was especially useful when PI - Yuen was invited to share the school findings and policy recommendations for addressing student well-being and engagement at school staff meetings. These proved effective in creating a direct impact on school personnel towards being more responsive to their students' multiple needs. Second, as arranged by RGC, PI - Yuen delivered two public lectures, one in the Central Library and the other in the Science Museum to disseminate the project findings and to generate data-driven recommendations for public policy with regard to society. Third, to increase the societal impact of the project and to increase awareness of the differentiated needs of different student groups, a press conference was held on 7 June 2016 at the PI-Yuen's former institution, the Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK). The findings were widely covered by the local press and media such as RTHK & Commercial Radio Hong Kong. Public debates on the "unexpected" results of mainstream, Chinese immigrant and ethnic minority students were aroused. For example, why the mainstream Chinese youth are less happy or satisfied with life than their ethnic minority counterparts? And, what could be done to help the Chinese immigrant students to be more engaged in the society? PI-Yuen has made available the insights of the project results with the media both before, during and after the press release. Fourth, our team continues to engage the society in relevant debates. For example, with reference to the findings, PI-Yuen makes active contributions to the RTHK's Teacher Blog on the prevailing obstacles and success factors affecting positive well-being and academic engagement across mainstream, working class, immigrant and minority youth in Hong Kong. This is a good indicator of the perceived need of the society in this area as acknowledged by the local media. Fifth, as academics and scholars in higher education, our team members have prepared and are currently working on a number of international journal articles using mainly the quantitative data as reported in the output lists. In addition, PI-Yuen has successfully secured an English book contract from Routledge (London) to disseminate mainly the qualitative findings. The book, entitled "Multiculturalism, Educational Inclusion and Connectedness in Hong Kong: Wellbeing, Ethnicity and Identity among Chinese and South Asian Students" (expected January 2020), will be used as one of main references in the field and as a main text for undergraduate students in Hong Kong. Another Chinese book titled “Destiny vs Happiness: Stories of Floating Youth” (命定與福祉：漂流少年) (Expected 2019) has also been completed and accepted for publication by Breakthrough Ltd. (突破出版社). Our writing commitments and research endeavours show how the findings have been and will be widely disseminated among local and international researchers, policy makers and research students. Sixth, the scholarship has benefited both experienced and emerging young researchers. Aware of the issues, inquiries from international bodies and research students about the instrument and concerning research collaboration opportunities have been received throughout the duration of the project and beyond. Moreover, two of the PI-Yuen's doctoral students are currently engaging in student well-being and academic engagement as a consequence of this project and the prior research of PI-Yuen. Seventh, to put theories and findings into practice, PI-Yuen submitted a proposal for the Knowledge Transfer Fund by the Chinese University of Hong Kong shortly after joining the University. Motivated by the project study, the proposed title is "Enhancing intercultural community engagement of mainstream low-income, Chinese immigrant and ethnic minority families". The aims are: (1) to respond to needs of the parents of low income from diverse cultural backgrounds; (2) to provide differentiated community support to different cultural groups in Hong Kong; (3) to expose university students to the real-world situation and be prepared to offer culturally sensitive assistance to the target children and families; and (4) to create a more equitable and harmonious society. The result of application will be released in January 2019. Objective 5 was 80% realized in the following ways: This is a challenging and an important objective to be achieved. At this stage, we have conducted comprehensive analysis of the data set according to our theoretical framework. A validation paper is currently under review to test the prediction of school engagement with regard to civic engagement: A study of Hong Kong mainstream youth (International Journal of Educational Research). Another validation paper is under preparation. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) that seeks to test the following hypotheses: Spiritual Health (SH) and Subjective Well-Being (SWB) are positively associated with civic participation. In this it is proposed the association between SH and civic participation is partially mediated by Academic Engagement (AE) and subsequent civic knowledge and civic attitude. SEM analyses were employed to determine the segmented differences among the ethnic minority (mainly South Asian students) and Chinese immigrant students as compared to the mainstream student group. In this regard, we aim to submit working papers by the summer of 2019. On a different note, to advance the theory of segmented and differentiated engagement and to make the study sustainable and to create greater and longer-term impacts, we have taken the theoretical framework into the next level. PI-Yuen is grateful to have received generous funding support for her continuing and on-going GRF project Ref. No. 18606717 (Transition from Secondary to Post-Secondary Education: Access, Obstacles, and Success Factors of Immigrant Minority and Low Income Youth in Hong Kong.) The remaining 20% will be fully realized in 2019 when all the validation papers and the works under-preparation are published.
