21500714.label: Major findings and research outcome
21500714.value: The major findings of this project were apeared in the PI's research publications. The PI has published 4 conference papers, 1 book chapter (SCOPUS indexed), and 3 journal articles (1 SSCI indexed, 1 SCOPUS indexed, and 1 peer-reviewed journal articles). The major findings are as follows: 1. The results showed that psychological distance was the main determinant of job performance and that the different dimensions of objective distance increased psy-chological distance in a nonlinear fashion. The results showed that interaction effects exist between each dimension of objective distance. That is, the different objective distances increased the psychological distance in a non-additive way. We found that neither cultural nor temporal distance by themselves increased psychological distance but cultural and temporal distance interacted with spatial distance to produce greater psychological distance than did the simple combination of the two dimensions of the objective distance. 2. The results of this research show that technology and job characteristics jointly induce virtual workers' psychological states, which in turn reduces their job satisfaction. The results also indicate that the manner in which technology and job characteristics influence virtual workers’ technostress varies depending on the intensity of virtual work. By discussing the magnitude of the different factors that determine virtual workers’ psychological states and their job performance, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of virtual workers’ challenges in collaboration. The study provides insights and prescriptive guidelines that will help managers and companies develop strategies to maximize the benefits of virtual work implementation.

21500714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21500714.value: Despite many intriguing findings derived from this project, the limitations of this project could turn to be future research topics as an extension of this project. First, the samples may have been biased because the survey respondents were limited to one country (South Korea) only. Given that most Korean companies expect a great deal of physical presence and long work hours, the results may reflect the particular workplace experience of this country, potentially limiting the generalizability of the findings. Accordingly, future results may vary depending on sector-specific or country specific contexts. An expansion of the models developed in this project to include other task characteristics and cultural factors would be a valuable extension of this research. Second, although this project disentangled the mixed effects of the virtual workers’ psychological states induced by technology and their network ties, allowing the PI to explain the different magnitude of each factor that determine the workers’ job performance, this project did not fully explain when or where the specific functions of technologies would induce more serious negative influences on virtual workers’ psychological states (including psychological distance). Future research would benefit from specifying the different types of communication and collaborative technologies and linking them theoretically with job-related outcomes (e.g. job performance, job satisfaction, and turnover intention).

21500714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21500714.value: Technology-enabled and physically dispersed virtual teams have emerged as a critical organizational form for structuring work on a global scale. Despite the great potential benefits of virtual teams, many virtual workers report negative experiences—such as communication depersonalization, conflict, feelings of isolation, and lack of shared knowledge—which may negatively influence the virtual worker’s job performance. Given that virtual teams are becoming more ubiquitous and commonplace in business, it will be of value to academia and industry to address these challenges and thus increase virtual workers’ job performance. Despite the increased attention to virtual collaboration from research and practice, the operational conceptualization of psychological distance remains equivocal; research findings regarding its roles on work outcomes are inconsistent and often appear conflicting. To fill these gaps in understanding, this study addresses the following questions: (1) How is the psychological distance between virtual workers formed? (2) How does the psychological distance between virtual workers influence their job performance? Drawing on construal level theory, this project conceptualizes psychological distance and then develops and tests a nomological network to explain the relationship between objective and subjective distance and virtual workers’ job performance. By precisely disentangling the effects of different dimensions of objective distance on psychological distance, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how virtual workers construct their perceptions of psychological distance, how it can be measured, and how it influences individual job performance in a virtual team.

21501014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21501014.value: Online labor markets are Internet platforms that facilitate Buyer-Determined (BD) auctions, in which buyers can identify and hire service providers who bid to offer their services. Marketplace platforms such as eLance and Freelancer opened new venues for companies to source services globally and have been growing rapidly. Critical to the success of these marketplaces are the use of BD auctions. Despite the growing significance of the new marketplaces and the critical role online BD auctions play therein, few empirical studies have investigated the impact of auction design in the context of online labor market. To fill this gap, this research studies the impact of BD auction design, specifically bid visibility (i.e., open bid BD auction versus sealed bid BD auction) on service providers’ bidding behavior and consequently on outcomes of BD auctions in online labor market. There has been extensive interest in understanding online auction mechanisms in Information Systems and Economics literature. As a new form of online auctions in the emerging online labor market, online BD auctions present nuances that call for additional empirical investigations that extend the discussion in current auction literature to the new context. To achieve this, I leverage on a unique proprietary dataset collected from a leading marketplace to carry out empirical investigations about (1) the impact of bid visibility on service providers’ bidding behavior (bid anchoring, learning and bid revision) and (2) the impact of bid visibility on auction outcomes (bid price/quality, buyer surplus, contract probability and project performance). In the research, I will implement alternative empirical models and estimation methodologies to ensure the robustness of the research findings. Specifically, I will explore natural experiment conditions created by exogenous changes to the price of auction design features and quasi-experiment conditions generated by matched samples. I will also implement an integrated model of bidding behavior and compare the estimation results to reduced form analyses. In later stage of this project, I will seek for collaboration from the site vendor in conducting field experiments. The proposed research intends to make contributions to the information systems literature on online auctions by empirically studying the impact of bid visibility on bidding behavior and auction outcomes in the context of online labor market. The unique observational data enables empirical comparison of user behavior and auction outcomes under different BD auction design. The study will generate import practical insights for both site vendors and participants in online labor market. 線上勞動力市場（也成為眾包網站）是一種新型的機遇互聯網平台的勞動力交易方式。在這樣的線上平台中，勞動需求方（例如公司）通過賣家決定式拍賣機制（Buyer-Determined Auction）從勞動供給方（例如軟件工程師）獲得服務。英語環境中，規模較大的平台包括eLance，Freelancer，中文網站方面，則有豬八戒網和威客網等網站。隨著這種跨越傳統地域限制的勞動力交易模式的發展，越來越多的公司開始嘗試眾包模式。線上勞動力市場的成功離不開有效的競價機制。基於賣方主導的市場特點，線上勞動力市場一般不同形式的採用賣家決定式拍賣機制。拍賣機制的具體形式直接決定了市場的有效性和用戶體驗。本研究著力於通過實證研究的方式探索不同的拍賣機制的形式對於市場參與行為和項目拍賣結果的影響。特別的，我將通過對於實際市場項目拍賣數據的分析發現競拍形式（明標或是暗標）對拍賣結果的影響。這一研究將得益於與市場平台公司的研究合作。通過合作，我可以獲得實際市場運行的數據，並觀測到市場發展過程中發生一些自然變化。通過對建立針對這樣的自然變化的實證模型，我可以獲得更穩健的理論估計。在本項研究中，我還會嘗試通過研究合作進行實地實驗性的研究，已提供更充分的理論支持。儘管業界對於這一新興勞動力供給模式非常推崇，關於市場機制的實證研究仍然比較匱乏。本項研究力圖填補之一理論空白，並為線上勞動力市場中的機制設計提供具有實證基礎的指導建議。

21501214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21501214.value: Although creativity is a truly desirable and often scarce commodity in organizations, its moral implications have not been fully explored. Thus, this proposal seeks to amend the research on creativity by taking a new approach to investigate the relationship between creativity and morality. A common, intuitive view of the dark side of creativity suggests that creativity can implicitly or explicitly encourage unethical behavior because morality is conventional and creativity is unconventional. We provide new theoretical perspectives that are different from this logically incomplete and questionable view. Because many mundane unethical actions are truly unoriginal and do not require any creativity, they are unlikely to share anything in common with creativity. In addition, when moral rules or norms are wrong, creativity can actually lead to novel and unconventional practices with higher morality, e.g., the civil disobedience movement of Gandhi (Wolpert, 2002). Thus, we suggest that creativity is more related to moral innovations instead of moral routines. Because creativity often serves as a pragmatic tool, people are likely to use creativity to search and discover new moral middle grounds to pragmatically solve traditional moral problems. The resulted moral solutions can be contextual because creativity can lead to either creative/moral behavior or creative/immoral behavior. But these creative, pragmatic solutions are often ingenious circumventions instead of blatant violations (regardless of whether the violations are moral or immoral) because creativity often balances different moral motives and at least obliquely respects for basic moral or social values. As noted by Csikszentmihalyi (1996), for example, “it is difficult to see how a person can be creative without being both traditional and conservative and at the same time rebellious and iconoclastic” (p.71). Because creativity, as a double-edged sword, may have different moral implications, we also seek to explore potential solutions to dampen its unintended negative effects on moral decisions. We suggest that employees’ positive mood and organizations' value-based ethics programs will help reduce creativity’s negative effects without inhibiting creativity. This is because with strong value-based ethical programs, happy employees are more sensitive to the negative emotions associated with unethical behavior. Thus, employees are more likely to use creativity to pursue good instead of bad courses when they are happy and when strong value-based ethics programs are in place. We propose three complementary experimental and field studies to test these propositions and explore the relationship between creativity and morality in organizations. 創新在組織中是珍稀的資源，但是創新的道德含義並沒有得到足夠的研究。一種通常的，直覺性的觀點是因為創新通常是非傳統的，但道德是傳統的，所以創新會鼓勵不道德的行為。當前這個研究項目認為這個觀點是存在問題的，因此作者提出了新的理論觀點。首先，很多不道德的行為往往是乏善可新的，因此它們並不要求任何創新，也難和創新有任何的交集。此外，在當前的社會的道德規範存在道德問題的時候，創新實際上可以導致新穎的，非傳統的，但是具有更高的道德水準的行為（例如，甘地發起的非暴力不合作反抗運動）。 因此，當前的這個研究項目使用一種新的方法來研究創新和道德之間的關係。具體的講，本文作者提出人們更可能利用創新來探索和發現一個新的道德中間地帶，並以此來實用性地解決傳統的道德問題。這些創新的解決方案可能是一把雙刃劍，因為它們既可以導致創造性的有道德的行為，也可以導致創造性的但缺乏道德的行為。現在的這個項目主要研究創新所涉及的這些重要的道德議題。除此之外，作者也希望探討可能的解決方式來降低創新對於道德決策可能的負面影響。

21501214.label: Realisation of objectives
21501214.value: I have achieved most of the objectives that I originally planned. Specifically, my research takes a new approach to investigate the relationship between creativity and morality. I suggest that creativity does not necessarily increase immoral behavior such as outright violations of moral rules or norms, especially when the immoral behavior is unambiguously unacceptable. Instead, people often use creativity to craft original solutions that balance different moral motives and, at least obliquely, respect basic moral laws and values. In particular, creativity may lead people to explore novel, and previously untapped moral possibilities to pragmatically tackle difficult moral problems (Dewey, 1981; 1987; Fesmire, 2003). In addition, I propose that the flexible logic of moral creativity should increase people’s inclinations to support morally debatable behavior rather than morally wrongful behavior because the former involves new but conflicting moral values and the latter is clearly an unoriginal and ostensibly offensive moral violation. These new perspectives are important because they go beyond the intuitive view that morality is conventional and creativity is unconventional. They also provide new insights into the moral implications of creativity by more accurately connecting the nature of creativity with morality. I used a triangulation of methods to include both experimental and survey studies to test my predictions. The four complementary studies operationalized creativity in two different ways: the first three lab and online experimental studies used different psychological approaches (e.g., Brendl, et al., 1995; Roney, et al., 1995, Vohs, et al, 2006) to either explicitly or implicitly prime people to be momentarily creative; the last survey study measured the degree of creativity that employees’ work required chronically. Specifically, Study 1 showed that creativity primes did not increase direct violations of the rules; instead, they stimulated people to take advantage of systemic loopholes to ingeniously circumvent the rules. Study 2 and 3 demonstrated that priming creativity led people to exploit a systematic loophole in both moral and immoral ways. In addition, both studies showed that creativity increased the likelihood that people would approve of moral rule circumvention more than immoral loophole taking. Finally, Study 4 used the data of 4,833 managers and business professionals from 20 countries to show that job-required creativity was positively related to people’s support of behavior whose morality some might question (e.g., abortion and euthanasia) but was not related to behavior that is clearly wrong and/or immoral (e.g., cheating and accepting a bribe).

21501214.label: Major findings and research outcome
21501214.value: My research investigates creativity as a moral tool, predicting that creativity generates pragmatic solutions by stimulating both unethical rule circumvention and ingenious escapes from immoral rules. The results have shown that creativity, as a pragmatic moral tool, can have substantial but malleable effects on moral judgments and decisions, and that these effects depend on the context of an individual’s moral decision. Although creativity and morality may conflict when a creative decision violates acceptable moral rules and norms, the relationship between the two can also be compatible when individuals use creativity to avoid immoral rules or laws. In both situations, creativity leads to resourceful rule circumventions rather than any blatant moral or rule violations. This result suggests that people use creativity to pragmatically solve moral problems by searching and locating a middle moral ground to balance different moral motives. In addition, although the effects of creativity can be contextual and malleable, people generally approve more of creative and moral behavior instead of similarly creative but morally questionable behavior. Specifically, the results from four complementary studies are as follows: Study 1 showed that when people were creative, they did not violate rules directly; instead, they were more likely to ingeniously use loopholes to circumvent the rules. Studies 2 and 3 showed that when people were creative, they circumvented moral and immoral legal ordinances for different moral motives; they also approved of moral rule circumvention more than similarly creative but immoral rule circumvention. Finally, Study 4 suggested that experiencing more workplace creativity was related to justifications of morally debatable issues (e.g., euthanasia and homosexuality) but not justifications of clearly immoral issues (e.g., bribery and cheating).

21501214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21501214.value: The current research primarily investigates creativity as a general mindset; however, there are different types of creativity (Kirton, 1976; Oldham & Cummings, 1996). For example, creativity can be characterized as incremental or radical. Similarly, individuals may have different creative styles (e.g., innovative versus adaptive style, Kirton, 1976; 1994). It is unknown from the current research whether different types of creativity or creative styles may have different moral implications. Additionally, because creativity and morality are complex and may vary in different contexts, investigating a number of different boundary conditions to better understand the relationship between creativity and morality might be helpful. For example, Study 4 compared people’s moral perceptions instead of their workplace decisions in right-right versus right-wrong dilemmas. The complexity of these moral issues opens up a variety of new research questions. For instance, do the effects of creativity vary in interpersonal and organizational contexts? Do right-right and right-wrong moral issues co-vary with creativity across contexts? How does creativity affect the behavior and perceptions of oneself versus those of others? I hope that this paper will stimulate future research on these and other related and important questions.

21501214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21501214.value: The current research has several implications for creativity and moral problem solving. First, it challenges the common, intuitive view that the originality and divergence of creativity (Guilford, 1956) is contrary to conventional morality. My results suggest that creativity does not necessarily encourages these mundane, unethical activities (Runco, 2009; Wang & Murnighan, 2015). Instead, it seems to selectively motivate original moral alternatives that people would otherwise rarely attempt especially when they are uncreative. Second, the current results suggest that creativity can be a double-edged sword, with both positive and negative moral consequences. When a creative mindset is activated, people often use it as a tool to search for new moral alternatives to existing moral problems. Because of its pragmatic orientation, creativity seems to have its greatest effects in the middle of the moral continuum, where moral flexibility is possible. Finally, the good news from the current research is that, as a double-edged sword, creativity seems to only increase moral flexibility for morally debatable issues but not for positions that are clearly immoral. Thus, if correctly guided, creativity may have more positive than negative effects on moral judgments and decisions because people tend to avoid choices that are clearly wrong and immoral.

22100014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22100014.value: 赤芝Ganoderma lucidum和紫芝G. sinense同作靈芝使用。一直以來,因為靈芝酸類化合物對癌細胞具有細胞毒作用，所以被普遍認為是其有效成分，也是有關質控研究的焦點。但是最近的研究表明，只有赤芝含有靈芝酸，而紫芝卻沒有。由此，這一常用中藥的品質控制面臨著緊迫而嚴峻的挑戰。另一方面，作為主要成分，紫芝和赤芝多糖均有明顯的免疫調節作用，並能顯著抑制腫瘤生長，理應成為質控的重點。然而目前的研究多集中在粗多糖的層面，僅偶有赤芝純化多糖的報導,對紫芝多糖更是知之甚少，整體研究缺乏系統性，作用機理也不甚清楚。本項目旨在使用系統的提取分離結構解析手段，以及抗腫瘤、免疫調節、心肌細胞保護等多個活性研究平臺，對紫芝和赤芝多糖（分總多糖、中性/酸性組分和純化多糖）的化學結構、生物活性及其分子靶點進行多層次、多方面的比較研究，從而揭示二芝共有的活性物質基礎，為其品質控制和研發提供科學依據。

22100014.label: Realisation of objectives
22100014.value: Both Ganoderma lucidum (GL) and G. sinense (GS) are used as Lingzhi in China. Their functions are assumed to mainly derive from triterpenes and polysaccharides; however, the two species have very different triterpenes profiles, if this was the case, then the bioactivity of these two species should differ. Instead, could the polysaccharides be similar, contributing to the shared therapeutic basis? In this study, two main polysaccharide fractions from different batches of GL and GS were systematically compared by a series of chemical and biological experiments. The results showed that the polysaccharides from two species shared the same structural features in terms of mono-/oligo-saccharide profiles, molecular size, sugar linkages, and IR/NMR spectra. In addition, these polysaccharides showed similar tumor-suppressive activity in mice. Further study on RAW264.7 cells indicated that these polysaccharides exhibited similar inducing effects to macrophages, as evaluated in the phagocytosis function, NO/cytokines production, inhibition against the viability and migration of cancer cells. Mechanistic investigation revealed the identical activation via TLR-4 related MAPK/NF-κB signaling pathway and gut-microbiota modulatory effects. In summary, GL and GS polysaccharides presented similar chemical features, antitumor/immunomodulating activities and mechanism; this establishes polysaccharides as the active principles and supports the official use of both species as Lingzhi.

22200014.label: Project Title(Chinese)
22200014.value: 基於降維的多維大數據相關性學習

22200014.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22200014.value: 大數據是機器學習領域的一個活躍研究課題，對於許多傳統和新興的應用有著及其深遠的意義。大多數的現實數據是多維度的，如圖像，視頻和功能磁共振成像序列。多維大數據往往非常的高維，有豐富的結構，且是高度冗餘的。 降維是一種通過把高維數據映射到低維空間中來提取有用信息（特徵）的一種方法，在計算效率和精確度方面影響顯著，對大數據應用至關重要。此外，許多數據集是相關的，找到這些關係可以大大幫助信息採集和決策。 典型相關分析是一種經典的學習兩組數據間相關性的方法，但其使用向量表示數據，已經無法滿足多維大數據的要求。該項目旨在開發高效和有效的降維算法，通過多維度的張量表示來學習多維大數據集之間的相關性。 該項目的成功將極大地推動大數據分析，並提供新的機器學習工具。隨著大數據對於香港工商業界變得越來越重要，此項目的研究成果將能極大得幫助和提高他們的知識發現和決策過程。

22400214.label: Project Objectives
22400214.value: To examine the impact of various natural and man-made disasters on policy, institutions, and governing practices in contemporary China, and to explain the contexts, actors, and processes that give rise to different types of changes. 22400214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22400214.value: Disasters are often thought to stimulate learning and bring about change. However, when thorny political issues arise in this process, the prospects for learning and change become obscure. This project seeks to understand the impact of various natural and man-made disasters on policy and governing practices in contemporary China. Have policymakers and bureaucrats taken advantage of the window of opportunity that the various disasters had tended to open, and if so, how? How did the political structure affect the outcomes? Particular research attention will be paid to 1) intragovernmental relations in reconstruction, 2) different modes of post-disaster management, e.g., reactive or preventive, stagnant or developmental, myopic or hyperopic, 3) the role played by nonstate actors like NGOs and civic groups in the process of recovery, and 4) the impact of an increasingly integrated international community on China’s practices. Two major tasks are expected to be accomplished at the end of this project: First, a database of China’s post-disaster management since 2000 will be built; Second, in-depth analysis of eight cases from four regions in China will be conducted for identifying the micro processes and causal chains that have led to different types of post-disaster change in policy and governance. This proposed study will contribute to our understanding of the “constructive” force of disasters which constantly reshapes human society. Moreover, through examining the strategies as well as difficulties of the Chinese government in coping with stressful conditions, this research will provide a fresh interpretation of the “resilience” of the regime and account for the adaptation endeavors by the government in a new world milieu featured by globalization and ever-advancing communication technologies. 這項研究試圖理解各種類型的自然和人爲災害如何影響當代中國的政策和管治。政策制定者和執行者是如何利用災害打開的機會之窗？政治結構如何影響災難和災后建設的結果？研究會特別關注以下問題：1）災后建設中的政府内部關係；2）不同的災后處理模式，比如被動反應或是主動預防，停滯或是發展式的，短視或有遠見的；3）災后恢復中非政府組織、公民社會所扮演的角色；4）國際社會對中國治理的影響。

22400214.label: Realisation of objectives
22400214.value: The project objectives have been completely achieved through field research, archival research and data-set building. Between 2015-2018 the PI conducted multiple field trips in Mainland China to investigate the impact of various natural and man-made disasters on policy, institutions, and governing practices, and the Chinese government’s strategies and adaptations in coping with stressful conditions and new circumstances. 1) May 2015, Sichuan: The PI conducted interviews and collected data on the development of NGOs in that area after the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake. 2) August 2015, Shanghai: The PI conducted interviews with informants on post-disaster management by government after the 2010 Shanghai Fire. 3) November 2015 and February 2016, Hong Kong: The PI took the opportunity of field research in Hong Kong to train the qualitative research skills and research ethics of her MPhil student. The MPhil student recruited with this grant has great research interest in how natural/man-made disasters in Hong Kong affect local party and electoral politics. The PI and the MPhil student observed the electoral campaign and voting behavior during the District Council Election and Legislative Council By-elections after the incident of lead in drinking water. 4) May 2016, Sichuan: The PI conducted interviews and focus groups with government officials and the representatives of various civil society organizations (CSOs) to understand the CSOs’ development trajectories and changing roles in post-disaster local governance. 5) May 2017, Sichuan: The PI visited various regions to study people’s observation and evaluation of different aspects of post-earthquake local governance: policy innovation, political trust, CSO development, contentious politics, etc. 6) June 2017, Beijing: The PI interviewed the representatives of NGOs and private foundations to explore how grassroots NGOs developed after/from disaster relief have experienced with the government’s purchase-of-services contracting and private foundations’ grant schemes, and how the transforming funding game has reshaped NGO strategies and their relationships with the local state. 7) August 2017, Shanghai: Same as 6) 8) May 2018, Sichuan: Same as 5). In each field trip, the PI visited different sites, conducted interviews and focus groups with various informants (disaster victims, officials, CSO representatives, scholars, journalists). In some research sites, the PI also conducted participant observations of government meetings, CSO operations and community activities. Although the PI initially encountered unexpected difficulties in finding informants and getting them to discuss the incidents in detail, the problems were solved through long-time rapport building and snow-balling strategies. In total, over 180 in-depth interviews and 6 focus groups were conducted. The PI also set up a team to build a database of the media reports of China’s post-disaster management since 2000. The database includes all reported disasters in China during that period. For each case included, information on the following aspects has been collected: 1) time and place of occurrence, 2) casualty and losses caused, 3) type of the disaster (natural, man-made, or natural disasters in which human errors aggravate devastation), 4) media attention, and 5) management practices. The PI trained the team in basic research skills for media content analysis and data-set construction. The PI presented her research findings of this project at several important international conferences: 1) (June 2016) “Navigating My Way to Help: Development of Social Work NGOs after the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake”, 2016 AAS-in-ASIA Conference in Kyoto, Japan. 2) (March 2018) Round table: Wenchuan Earthquake: A Decade of Changes and Continuities, 2018 AAS (Association for Asian Studies) Annual Conference, Washington, DC (co-organizer and discussant). 3) (July 2018) “How Chinese Grassroots NGOs Cope with the New Funding Game”, 2018 AAS-in-ASIA Conference, New Delhi, India (panel co-organizer and paper presenter). The PI will co-organize a conference on “Politics, Societies, and Disasters: China and Beyond” in Copenhagen, Denmark in June 2019. The conference was originally scheduled in June 2018 before the completion of this project. However, it was postponed to June 2019 due to the time conflicts of some co-organizers. Therefore, part of the Conference budget was unspent. (Note: The Conference budget is for the PI’s travel expenses. The conference on “Politics, Societies, and Disasters: China and Beyond” will be funded by 2018 Comparative Perspectives on Chinese Culture and Society Programme Grant (US$25,000) from the Chiang Ching-kuo Foundation).

22400214.label: Major findings and research outcome
22400214.value: This research has helped illuminate the evolution of local state-society relationships in post-disaster management in contemporary China. It finds that after the disasters many Chinese local governments become more willing to embrace the third-party management model and a more open associational environment. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether Chinese civil society organizations (CSOs) can flourish and contribute to the rise of a civil society in the western sense of the term. In fact, most of these CSOs have limited aspirations that do not extend to promoting civil society as a political space: they simply wish to avoid trouble and complement the state in serving populations in need. Moreover, the narrowing of funding sources has caused anxiety and driven CSOs to compete for the favour and patronage of donors. Newly established CSOs are likely to become government- or business-like organisations before they can demonstrate their unique value. Post-disaster CSO development has transformed from a grassroots-driven, relatively organic, and untamed process, first into a rather fluid and dynamic situation, and then into a top-down managerial set of procedures. Still, not everything is lost. The new funding game that sees the coexistence of government and business rationales, as well as recent developments like the facilitated channels for philanthropic public fundraising and CSOs’ versatile strategies for self-sufficient growth, may open new windows of opportunity for Chinese CSOs. The research also finds that local officials have progressively pursued clientelistic strategies towards civil society organizations (CSOs). A series of policy changes have strengthened local officials’ incentives and abilities to play the role of both entrepreneur and gatekeeper in CSO development. Controlling vast resources and possessing overriding management authority, local officials, with the aim of reducing risks and maximizing personal gains (not necessarily material), seek and nurture ‘reliable CSO working partners’ whose resources, personnel and expertise can be appropriated for the officials’ own purposes. The state resources for advancing the CSO sector’s overall development and its effective participation in social service delivery have thus been gradually channelled along patron-client lines. Over time, personalistic bonding increasingly ordinates local state-society relationships. However, this domination is highly fragmented and transforming the state agents involved, which may inhibit the Chinese state from achieving coherent, integrated domination over the rising CSO sector.

22400214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22400214.value: Upon completion of this ECS project, the PI has moved on to a new project, “Grassroots Party Building in Urban China in the Reform Era” (GRF-12607217). Two major parts of the new project are developed based on this ECS project: 1) How do Primary Party Organizations (PPOs) contribute to crisis management in terms of their competence in coordination, mobilization, disciplining, and public service provision? 2) What are the actual effects of Party building in civil society organizations? The PI is also developing a new line of scholarly inquiry which is inspired by this ECS project: the relationship between crisis management and social memory and trust. The first step is to design a comparative study of how food safety problems are handled and perceived in different Chinese societies (mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao). These regions share a similar food culture and experience of late industrialization. Case studies comparing them may show how different regulatory challenges and public opinion about food safety in different societies are shaped by the distinctive development trajectories of governance systems and civil societies. After conducting some preliminary research, the PI will apply for GRF support for the new project in 2019.

22400214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22400214.value: This project is situated at the interface of three different bodies of research: post-disaster management, policy change following disasters, and China’s modes of governance. It examines the long-term effects of various disasters on China’s policy, institutions, and governing practices, and seeks to explain when and how well-considered recovery endeavours can take place, and what cause hasty and poorly designed reconstruction. It tells a story of how intergovernmental relations, state-society relationship, and international engagement can shape the recovery and reconstruction processes and outcomes. It also gives an account of China’s state capacity in coping with stress and adapting to new circumstances: In particular, how has the Chinese government’s governing logic been reshaped by new opportunities and constraints? In which way has it adapted its modes of governance?

22400414.label: Realisation of objectives
22400414.value: 1. To contribute to the development of the scholarship on portfolio assessment through an in-depth analysis of how teachers implement portfolio assessment in the sociocultural context of Hong Kong; The first objective was achieved by way of in-depth, exploratory case studies conducted in six local secondary schools within slightly more than a one-year timeframe. The seven case studies involve extensive data collection procedures including pre- and post-observation interviews; telephone interviews; two to three classroom observations; analysis of instructional materials/school documents, and finally a detailed questionnaire on classroom-based writing assessment. These data sets helped the PI to analyze the extent to which the macro-level (system, culture and policy), meso-level (school, classroom and parent) as well as micro-level factors (teacher belief, knowledge and practices) would come into play when individual teachers attempted their own portfolio-based programme at diverse school contexts, namely high-performing vs. low-performing schools, public vs. direct subsidy scheme schools, English as medium-of-instruction vs. Chinese as medium-of-instruction schools and so forth. In addition to the above research procedures, the PI invited the seven case study informants to compose a narrative frame, which captured what, how and why they introduced the portfolio system in their work contexts. The narrative frame was supposed to be one highly personalized data source which provided the PI with an invaluable insider perspective when analyzing and reporting the data. The challenges to achieve the objective no. 1 and attempts to overcome them will be discussed together with the objective no. 2. 2. To explore how secondary-level teachers manage the relationship between assessment of learning and assessment for learning in the writing classrooms; The second objective was achieved by analyzing data gathered from individual teacher interviews, classroom observations and the questionnaire. Based upon the literature, teachers, including our participants, are familiar with evaluating their student writing summatively, yet they may not be as proficient as we anticipate when it comes to assessing writing formatively, namely providing commentary for text revision and encouraging reflection for learning enhancement. Although the interview and questionnaire data could reflect how teachers managed the relationship between assessment of learning (AOL) and assessment for learning (AFL), classroom observations served as accurate evidence to triangulate with student self-reported data. Through observations, the PI was able to clarify whether the teacher participants understood the theoretical rationale behind AOL and AFL, how much they managed both assessment purposes concurrently and the extent to which they were pedagogically ready to utilize AOL to inform AFL-related practices for improving student learning. The challenge to achieve the objectives no. 1 and 2 is twofold. First, it is demanding to recruit sufficient case study participants who are willing to trial writing portfolio assessment, since Hong Kong teachers are infamous for overworking such as additional administrative duties and heavy marking loads owing to a book inspection culture. Second, despite improved teacher qualifications, the PI is well aware that a majority of participants are not knowledgeable about second language writing assessment in general and portfolio assessment of writing in particular. This issue would affect successful application of portfolio assessment in the classroom contexts. Attempts to overcome the first and second challenges included a recruitment of teacher participants through the PI’s personal connection, such as his former and current students, and provision of fundamental language assessment training for the participants, namely in-house seminars and workshops. 3. To analyze how teachers develop a set of instructional strategies that guide them to set up an effective portfolio programme at the classroom level; To achieve the objective no. 3, the PI thoroughly analyzed all interview and narrative frames data to tease out what instructional strategies the participants have adopted. Apart from these formal channels, I have been contacting the teacher informants via a number of informal ways like social media platforms, e-mails, WhatsApp, phone calls. While I did not include these informal channels as data collection and analysis procedures, this first-hand information updated me of how the teacher participants formulated, adapted and eventually applied pertinent instructional strategies when trying out diverse versions of writing portfolio assessment in classrooms. In retrospect, the major challenge to achieve this objective was that the teacher participants had lots of brilliant ideas, but these ideas tended to be discredited by a range of institutional and/or systemic constraints, such as exam-driven instruction, disapproval from the English panel chair, etc. To get through these barriers, the PI gave expert advice to the participants to fine-tune their portfolio systems in order to be more contextually appropriate for actual implementation, provided that a ‘strong’ version of portfolio assessment might not be accepted by students, parents and colleagues immediately. Also, the PI shared with the participants some examples of using the product-based portfolio systems in his previous research study as reference. 4. To investigate student reaction (i.e., affect) to the implementation of portfolio assessment and whether they have actual writing improvement after the exposure to this assessment innovation. The fourth objective was achieved by student focus group interviews, analysis of student writing samples kept in the portfolios, student reflective pieces, and individual teacher interviews. Regarding the aspect of affect, the PI relied on both student and teacher interviews. Thus far, a majority of students showed interested in keeping their portfolios and liked the idea of self-reflection, as it helped them become more conscious of their current and desired writing abilities. Yet, some student participants had concerns about the technical procedures involved (i.e., workload) and its sustainability (short-term vs. long-term implementation). To measure student growth in writing, the PI has analyzed the writing samples (N = 180) by particularly looking at the use of vocabulary, length of paragraphs, grammatical accuracy, clarity of contents, and originality before and after student participation in the portfolio programmes. The major challenge to collect student data was timing and validity. First, both teacher and student participants were busy. More often than not, the PI could only interview the student participants after school within a very limited timeframe as the students had to attend extra-curricular activities or tutorial schools. Second, because of the power relation, the student participants might not tell the PI of their true feelings and portfolio experience for fear of upsetting their teachers unless their identities were hidden. However, anonymity could not be done as the teacher participants nominated who would be interviewed by us. Because of this, the PI had randomly talked to some non-participants in order to elicit their candid views about portfolio experiences.

22400414.label: Major findings and research outcome
22400414.value: Objective 1: We have classified the teacher participants into three categories, namely proactive innovators, compliant executors, and visionary game changers when they trailed portfolio assessment. In PI’s (2018) book chapter, he reported how two teachers have introduced the portfolio approach, with one being a visionary game changer and the other a compliant executor. This publication implies that teacher application of portfolio assessment was hindered by meso- and macro-contextual factors. Teacher readiness to implement writing assessment practices is equally significant. To make contributions to portfolio assessment scholarship, PI’s (2017) paper in Assessing Writing has suggested ways to narrow the research-practice gap. Objective 2: Our questionnaire has shown that a majority of teacher respondents have sound knowledge and understanding of AOL and AFL, but not assessment as learning (AAL). Almost a decade entering the curricular reform, it appears that teachers have a much clearer idea of managing AOL and AFL to support learning of writing. Yet, AAL remains a novel pedagogical approach, so teachers found the idea unfamiliar and have seldom ventured into reflective practices in their classrooms. These data were reported in the PI’s (2018) paper at the 53rd RELC Conference and his forthcoming refereed paper. Objective 3: Classroom data have indicated that select teacher participants have attempted diverse strategies to initiate their portfolio programmes, including use of dialogic journals in single-drafted composition classes; collaborative portfolio compilation by writing workshops; the whole-school approach to end-of-unit and end-of-year reflection; the showcase portfolio approach with limited teacher scaffolding. These pedagogical strategies were reported in the PI’s (2017) paper presentation at the 52nd RELC Conference and his 2017’s EdUHK invited talk on issues in writing portfolio assessment. They were also presented as individual case studies in the PI’s (2018) authored book. Objective 4: Student participants were generally positive about portfolio keeping experiences. The junior-form students enjoyed autonomy to select representative works for grading. With that said, some senior-form students (those in Willy’s case) expressed concerns about the effectiveness of reflection and self-assessment (Lam 2018). Considering student affect, portfolio assessment did motivate learners to improve writing and metacognitive skills. Since the teachers adopted diverse scoring methods, it is difficult to compare student actual writing gains. Yet, the PI has analyzed all student writings by Faigley and Witte’s (1981) taxonomy and found that select students have improvement in essay length, ideas and use of advanced vocabulary but not in coherence and organization.

22400414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22400414.value: Drawing upon the major findings of the project, the PI has recommended the following ways forward for future investigations of writing portfolio assessment in regional and global classroom contexts: 1. In addition to measuring student linguistic gains, it is more significant to look into how students manage the processes of portfolio keeping. We can examine student beliefs, motivation and composing behaviours when they engage in the construction of writing portfolios. These process data will shed new light on how to maximize the learning-oriented properties of portfolio assessment. 2. As portfolio scoring remains problematic, another potential area for development is to formulate a framework or system regarding how to evaluate student portfolios impartially, consistently and accurately. After all, assessing student portfolios is a complex endeavour, involving in making professional judgments on multiple written genres and reflective pieces. 3. To follow the twenty-first century educational trend, the advent of digital portfolios appears to become another line of research which is worthy of empirical investigations. It is because digital portfolios may advance students’ linguistic, metacognitive and technological skills to maintain competitiveness for their future study careers.

22400414.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22400414.value: The research project investigated secondary-level teacher trial of diverse portfolio assessment approaches and student responses to portfolio keeping experiences. It adopts a mixed-method approach, utilizing individual teacher interviews, classroom observations, student focus groups, a questionnaire on assessment literacy, documentary analysis and teacher narrative frames. The significance of the study is threefold. First, little has been done to examine how the portfolio approach can promote teaching and learning of writing in Hong Kong classrooms and beyond. Second, synergizing teaching and assessment of writing by an alternative assessment approach aligns with the current curriculum reforms worldwide. Third, the trial of writing portfolio assessment equips students with the twenty-first century study skills - reflection and self-assessment in learning writing. The impact of this project has generated seventeen pieces of research output, which extensively disseminate the idea of classroom-based portfolio assessment internationally. Another impact is that second language (L2) writing teachers could flexibly fine-tune their portfolio approaches even in the product-based writing environments via a range of adaptation strategies derived from the research outcome. In brief, this project showcases how the experimentation of portfolio assessment empowers teachers and students to advance their knowledge base on English L2 writing assessment.

22400514.label: Project Objectives
22400514.value: To complete a refined and formal presentation of the Counterfactual Reference Theory of Names and Empty Names (CR). To conduct foundational studies on underlying philosophical issues related to the nature of possibility and modal logic.
rows: To complete a refined and formal presentation of the Counterfactual Reference Theory of Names and Empty Names (CR).
To conduct foundational studies on underlying philosophical issues related to the nature of possibility and modal logic.

22400514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22400514.value: This research project aims at making a formal presentation of a novel theory called the Counterfactual Reference Theory of Names and Empty Names (CR) and investigating some related problems regarding the nature of modality. CR tackles particularly the problem of empty reference, namely, how sentences containing non-denoting terms (such as ‘phlogiston’ and ‘Sherlock Holmes’) are meaningful even when no objects are denoted and thus no facts are possibly represented by such sentences. It avoids all common approaches, including the denial of names, the postulation of non-existent objects and abstract entities, and the appeal to pretence. Instead, it proposes to explain an empty name by what concrete objects it could refer if it were used as a non-empty term. For example, if the Sherlock Holmes stories were told as history, then ‘Sherlock Holmes’ could refer to some person, even though in our actual language it is fictional. CR uses this characteristic to work out a full account for all standard semantic properties of names including rigidity, individuation and truth-conditions of sentences containing them. CR was regarded as ‘novel and ingenious’, ‘ambitious’ and ‘certainly worth developing’ by internationally leading scholars Professors Dorothy Edgington (Birkbeck College London and the University of Oxford) and Manual Garcia-Carpintero (the University of Barcelona). It has been presented at nine conferences and seminars at major universities around the globe, receiving wide attention and enthusiastic discussions. CR raises some interesting questions about the nature of modality. For example, counterfactual referents are possible objects, yet what kind of possibility is involved? What are the differences among physical, metaphysical, conceptual and epistemological possibilities, if any? Are possible worlds real? Could a name counterfactually refer to something logically impossible? These questions do not threaten CR’s validity. However, they are significant and at the forefront discussions of philosophical logic in general. I thus propose to conduct a systematic study to examine them and see how CR would contribute to the current debates. I divide the enquiry into three sub-categories to which rigorous conceptual analysis and critical arguments will apply. Literature review and textual exegesis on classical works of major theoretical traditions will be sought. So will extensive examples from ordinary usage and linguistic practices. The theories will be then tested on typical examples and be assessed according to their relative explanatory power, metaphysical commitment, and internal coherence. The project aims at producing two journal articles on the nature of modality and one book on the CR. 本研究項目之目標在為一全新之專名及空名理論―「反事實指涉論」(簡稱CR) ―提供形式化的表述, 並研究與模態性質相關之理論問題。CR特別處理空指涉的問題, 即含有非指謂詞項(例如:「燃素」和「福爾摩斯」)的句子, 在沒有指涉對象, 即也沒有表述的事實下, 如何能成為有意義的句子。它不採取一般的進路, 如: 否認空名為名稱之類屬、接受有所謂非存在的或抽象的物體存在作為空名的指涉對象、或訴諸偽裝。相反, 它提出以空名若用為有指涉時有可能指謂的具體事物, 來解釋與空名有關的種種語意表現。例如: 假如福爾摩斯故事是作為歷史來傳述, 則「福爾摩斯」這名字可能指涉某人, 即使事實上在我們的語用中, 「福爾摩斯」只是虛構的名字。CR用此意念構造一個能應用傳統上所有有關專名的性質於空名的理論體系, 包括: 固定意指、名稱之區分和句子的真值條件等。CR也會用上一些二維語意論的邏輯工具。l CR提出一些有關模態性質的有趣問題, 例如: 反事實指涉物是具體的可能存在, 這裏牽涉的是何種可能性? 物理上的可能性、形上學的可能性、概念上的可能性、還是認知上的可能性? 以上種種可能性之間又有否真實而清楚的差異? 此外, 可能世界是真實的嗎? 空名可以反事實地指涉邏輯上不可能的事物或事態嗎? 這些問題不影響CR的有效性, 但它們是哲學邏輯中一些基礎和重要的課題, 本項目也會對這些問題作有系統的討論。 本項目將分成數個子項作出嚴格的概念分析及批判論證, 考察各主要理論傳統之經典著作, 亦會應用大量日常生活的例子和語言習慣, 測試理論之相對解釋能力、形上學預設和內部融貫性等。

22400514.label: Realisation of objectives
22400514.value: This project has two objectives. Both objectives have been fully achieved. For objective (1), I have presented a refined account of the Counterfactual Reference Theory of Names and Empty Names (CR). Briefly, the main contribution of this endeavour is to link CR to a causal theory of names and in doing so supplement CR with an account of intentionality in order to answer the question of how an empty name can be named. I explicitly distinguish the what-question of reference from the how-question. I also spell out a view on the ontology of fictional characters, thus presenting CR as a third approach to the existing polemic poles of theories of names (direct referentialism vs. descriptivism) and those of empty names (object theories vs. pretence theories). To give more details, I state clearly that the two-dimensional matrix is meant as a semantic account to indicate truth-values of a proposition given each context of utterance. This reading answers the question of what a term refers, leaving the question of how a term comes to refer to a certain object to be determined meta-semantically. In the case of names, including empty names, the how-question is to be explained by casual processes. For example, a baptiser directs attention onto an object and associates it with a sign while other users follow their predecessors in using the name with an intention to co-refer. A baptiser may not indeed intend to name a real thing, but just to introduce a fictional name. However, had the baptiser’s intention been changed, the same procedure could associate an existent thing with a name. Hence, we can use these counterfactual situations to explain how an empty name is formed. They represent shifts in context of utterance. I call possible objects to be referred in a different context of utterance counterfactual referents. Counterfactual referents are not referents. They do not indicate any actual semantic relation between a name and reality. However, a set of counterfactual referents closest to the actual world would indicate the cognitive condition of the users of an empty name. Most empty names, like non-empty ones, are not descriptive names. Information association with an empty name will shape representations of various counterfactual referents in different user’s minds. That explains how, for instance, different readers of a novel may have similar, though not necessarily identical, mental representations of its characters. Theories of empty names are dominated by object theories and pretence theories. CR belongs to neither. It is not an object theory because it stresses that an empty name literally does not refer to anything, not even an abstract entity created by human activities, a view held by Creationists such as Kripke (2013) and Salmon (1998). A set is an abstract entity, but fictional characters are not something that come to exist as Creationists held, so the dispute is not verbal. Fictional characters have concrete properties such as running, eating, loving, killing, etc. Abstract objects do not and cannot have such properties. Our thinking of an object does not make them real or come into existence; neither can thoughts of fictional characters do. Thinking them just mean we establish intensional relations with them and can communicate with other agents about them. CR gets the ontology right, clarifies the confusions and avoid asserting entities beyond necessity. CR is not a pretence theory either because it does not seek to explain semantic function through speech acts. On the contrary, it believes that only by specifying to what objects an empty name counterfactually refers would it become clear what it means to pretend to be something, if such pretence happens. A pretence theory is ineffective if it does not spell out what it is to pretend and CR does exactly that. For objective (2), the investigation involves three foundational issues: (a) Are possible worlds real? (b) Are there impossible worlds? (c) What are metaphysical and epistemological possibilities? I started with the study on (c) first. I focused on various interpretations of the two-dimensional matrix. While philosophers do not dispute that the horizontal dimension characterises metaphysical possibilities, they vary over interpretation of the diagonal proposition. Chalmers (2006) and Jackson (1998) believed it represents epistemological possibilities. Stalnaker (2006) believed it is meta-semantic. Some even favoured a Kaplanian (1977) semantic understanding. Different readings represent different philosophical agendas. For my purpose, I adopt a semantic reading to two dimensional matrix; yet I argue why a certain object is associated with a name in a certain context of utterance is to be determined meta-semantically. Referents of a name do not vary across context of utterance out of linguistic principles like in the case of indexicals. However, it is possible that a name is linked to other objects before a convention is established. I use this understanding to support CR. Epistemological possibilities are not broader than metaphysical possibilities because knowledge aims at truth and one cannot know anything that is not true. However, imaginability or conceivability can be broader than metaphysical possibilities construed in the Kripkean way. We can imagine things by shifting either contexts of utterance or contexts of evaluation. When we do the former, only our language is changed, not the world. Jackson described this as an error theory. If this is right, contrary to Chalmers (1992), conceivability does not entail metaphysical possibility. Taking conceivability this way, we don’t need to worry about impossibilities in fiction because they are not metaphysical. A frog does not really change to a prince; it is a prince all the time, we just change our language and regard him as a frog at some point of time (say, under a spell). Indeed, what motivates the discussions of impossible worlds in (b) are something stronger and more serious like logical paradoxes and contradictions which require breaking away from classical logical laws. (b) is a question that goes beyond this project which concerns fiction only. It requires more logical tools such as familiarity with paraconsistent logic. I would like to develop related new projects on that in the future. For (a), Lewis (1986) argued for advantages of modal realism in explaining a variety of philosophical issues such as causation, the metaphysics of particulars, events and persons, etc. Kripke (1980) preferred a stipulated view of modality which regards ‘possible world’ as an instrument of thought. I think CR is compatible with either because it only needs to appeal to something independent of language; it does not matter whether they belong to the realms of reality or the mind. However, Kripke used object (referent) as the principle for organising information around a name and this allows him to demarcate meaning-giving from reference-fixing. Given names and empty names are subject to a unified account and CR uses possible worlds to explain empty names, if we want to construct a parallel argument between semantic theories of names and empty names, then it is better that possible worlds and the actual world share the same ontological status. This line of thought provides a semantic incentive to modal realism.

22400514.label: Major findings and research outcome
22400514.value: The project has refined a theory of empty names called the Counterfactual Reference theory (CR). It stands as an alternative to the present polemic poles, direct referentialism and descriptivism. A major refinement of the theory is to distinguish the what-question from the how-question of reference and link the latter with a certain causal theory of naming as the metasemantic background for reference determination. Direct referentialism may stay as the paradigm for answering the what-question, while we employ the metasemantic linkage to explain cognitive profiles of a name without jeopardizing the what-question of reference. A typical metasemantic linkage to names (including empty names) is the causal history of name uses. Employment of such linkage also allows continual employment of objects as principle of organisation of information even though when the objects (counterfactual referents) are not the object referred. As such it relocates the problem of empty reference and release theoretical tension for direct referentialism. Moreover, this outcome also paves for an argument for compatibility with modal realism, though it does not exclude other possibilities either. A book manuscript is output and a publication contract is signed. The project has led to the development of another GRF research project which was scored 4.5 and successfully funded by the RC for three years (project no. HKBU 12612217). It also triggers many research ideas about which papers have been prepared for conference presentations and journals in the future. For example, I had presented in three conferences during the project period. I have also submitted another conference abstract based on the ideas on two-dimensionalism mentioned above and was accepted. I will present in another conference about naming processes of empty names in the near future, too.

22400514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22400514.value: The distinction of the what-question and the how-question of reference has provided insights to organise many entangled and inter-related problems related to reference theories. I have developed this idea and submitted another research project proposal, entitled ‘How Proper Name Refers: Is Causal Descriptivism Defensible?’ The proposal received excellent reviews from external reviewers and was scored 4.5 in last year’s GRF assessment. It was awarded a funding of $322,500 (project no. HKBU 12612217). The project has commenced since 1 January 2018 and will run for three years until the end of 2020. That project aims to build a general account of how a name comes to associate with objects. It uses empirical surveys in additional to theoretical debates to support its conclusion. On top of this, I have obtained an internal funding to continue exploring and writing a journal article on logical problems related to impossibilities, a theme related to the project here. The question of impossibility has gained more and more attention in the philosophy circle thanks to discussions by logicians such as Graham Priest. Other themes will be explored and developed in the future. I shall attend a conference in July in which speakers will talk about related issues, such as the nature of modality and the ontology of possible worlds.

22400514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22400514.value: Philosophy of language studies the relations between language, mind and reality. Names are commonly considered representation of objects in reality. Indeed, a dominant reference theory holds that the semantic function of a name is exhausted by its having a bearer. Empty names provide a challenge to this view because empty names do not have bearers yet they do not seem to be semantically dysfunctional. This project refines a unified account of names and empty names, called the Counterfactual Reference Theory (CR). CR refutes the dominant view, solves the problem of empty names yet retains some important insights proposed by the dominant view such as that a name once established always refers to the same object that it purports to refer. The biggest refinement this project generates is to link CR with a causal theory of names. Different causal chain would indicate alternative contexts of utterance should an empty name becomes denoting. The set of these alternative contexts represent the cognitive profile of an empty name and differentiates it from other empty names even though no object is referred. The outcome helps to distinguish clearly the what-question from the how-question of reference and show what problems the latter is responsible to answer.

22400614.label: Project Title(Chinese)
22400614.value: 電力用戶及低碳未來: 智能電網發展在日本及中國的比較研究

22400614.label: Project Objectives
22400614.value: To systematically examine, evaluate, and explain the processes, mechanisms, achievements, and limitations related to engaging consumers in the process of smart grid diffusion in Japan and China. To develop a theoretical model to conceptualise the interrelationship between consumer engagement and smart grid diffusion, and to examine how such relationships are conditioned by the interactions of government action and market mechanisms. To provide insights into possible cross-national socio-economic and political factors that may influence smart grid diffusion. We will examine whether there is a distinctive Asian model and, if so, how and to what extent the Asian model differs from the experiences that have been observed in the Western context. To provide policymakers and the business sector with practical guidance and recommendations on the development of consumer engagement tactics for the diffusion of smart grids.

22400614.label: Realisation of objectives
22400614.value: The work done so far is well in line with the research objectives. Major research tasks conducted: (i) we conducted about 50 interviews with key stakeholders in five field trips which took place in five cities in Japan and China (Tokyo, Kyoto, Beijing, Guangzhou, and Foshan) during this project period; (ii) we organised and implemented two pilot deliberative pollings (DPs) in Guangzhou and Kyoto in early 2016 and early 2017 respectively, each with 47 undergraduate participants), (iii) we organised an international energy conference on smart grids in Asia in Hong Kong Baptist University in November 2015 – which was titled “The First Asian Energy Conference: Smart Grids, Sustainability Transition, and Innovation in Governance’- held in Hong Kong Baptist University with about 70 participants. This project resulted in three sets of outputs. The first set of outputs relate to publications. These include: (i) a paper published on Energy Policy in 2017 – the paper is titled “Explaining the role of incumbent utilities in sustainable energy transitions: A case study of the smart grid development in China” ; (ii) a manuscript submitted to Journal of Cleaner Production in March 2018 – which is titled “Understanding undergraduate students’ perceptions of dynamic pricing policies: An exploratory study of two pilot Deliberative Pollings (DPs) in Guangzhou, China and Kyoto”; (iii) a manuscript under preparation – which is titled “State-market dynamics in energy transitions: A comparative study of smart grid developments in Japan and China”; (iv) three working papers published in 2015, 2016, and 2017 – on the themes “the roles of incumbent utilities”, “business model innovations for smart grids”, and “two pilot Deliberative Pollings in Guangzhou and Kyoto” respectively; (v) two briefing documents – which were published for the pilot deliberative pollings that we conducted in Guangzhou and Kyoto; and (vi) three presentations made at international conferences. The second set of output relates to the creation of a new, large body of empirical data derived from (i) approximately 50 in-depth semi-structured interviews, (ii) quantitative questionnaire data from about 100 participants in the two pilot DPs, and (iii) qualitative transcription data of the two DPs. The third set of output relate to the strengthening of an international, interdisciplinary research partnership between six institutions in Hong Kong, the Mainland China, the US (Stanford), Japan (University of Kyoto) and France (Sciences Po) that can sustain the team’s high-impact long-term research in this emerging field of energy governance. This project has largely fulfilled the objectives as follows: In relation to Objective 1, we conducted qualitative study (data collected mainly by face-to-face semi-structured interviews) and specified the five critical functions of state and market interactions which are conducive to the deployment of smart grids [Relevant outputs: three conference presentations]. In addition, we conducted quantitative and qualitative analysis on the two pilot DPs in Guangzhou and Kyoto. We provided a better understanding of how undergraduates in these two cities changed their perception of alternative pricing options and made difficult trade-off decisions. We also shed light on the limitations that relate to engaging consumers in smart grid diffusion by in two ways: (i) we provided a better understanding of the tensions between incumbents and new market players [Relevant output: our published paper], and (ii) we shed light on the complexity of how the undergraduates may react to trade-off decision in energy transitions, and discussed the policy implications that relate to public acceptability and public engagement [Output: our manuscript under review]. In relation to Objective 2, the project has developed a conceptual framework which provides a better understanding of the changing roles of state and market in energy transitions. The framework specifies five critical functions which are created by state-market interactions. These functions are market building, market regulation, managing public goods, networks and partnership building, and policy learning. We applied this framework in the two case countries. [Relevant research output: three conference presentations; and a manuscript which is under preparation, and is planned to be submitted to Environmental Policy and Governance (a SSCI journal)] In relation to Objective 3, our comparative study found that these two countries have their distinct models, and a single Asian model that can fit all does not exist [Relevant outputs: conference presentations, and a manuscript under review]. In addition, our pilot DPs found that some important national level contextual factors (e.g. public distrust, familiarity with market logics) which may explain the differences of the participants’ responses across these two countries (a manuscript under review). In relation to Objective 4, practical policy recommendations on the development of enhancing public acceptability and consumer engagement approaches were given by the Project Team through: (i) exchange between the Project Team and power companies and other stakeholders at the 2015 international conference; (ii) sharing research findings between the PI and senior executives of utilities in Japan, China, and Hong Kong in research/ policy meetings. Examples of those meetings and the participating utilities’ are include: (i) meetings with a senior executive of Kansai Electric, Japan, in January 2017 and February 2018; (ii) meetings with senior executive of the Smart Grid Institute of China Southern Grid Company. Reasons for under-achievements: There are challenges that affected the fulfillment of some of the objectives. First, there was a project delay of the Kyoto Pilot DP. To a large extent because of funding constraints, our local collaborator in Kyoto experienced difficulties in recruiting participants, moderators, and student helpers. As a result, the tasks of recruitment, transcription, and data analysis were all delayed. Second, there was a delay in publications. At present, although a paper has been published on Energy Policy alongside with the publications of a number of working papers and briefing documents, two manuscripts are either under review or preparation. Attempts to overcome problems: Efforts were made to address the challenges. First, the team successfully sought an internal grant from the Faculty of Social Sciences in HKBU to conduct a study on the pilot DPs in Japan – which greatly helped ensure the pilot DP in Japan was sufficiently funded. Second, a manuscript which was derived from the findings of the two pilot DPs was submitted to Energy Research & Social Sciences in September 2017, but was rejected in February 2018. Reviewers raised concerns over (1) the justification of focusing on undergraduate students only; (2) the lack of both internal and external validity of the findings as the sample size is small. A major revision on the manuscript was done. The revised manuscript is titled “Understanding undergraduate students’ perceptions of dynamic pricing policies: An exploratory study of two pilot Deliberative Pollings (DPs) in Guangzhou, China and Kyoto, Japan” was submitted to Journal of Cleaner Production in March 2018, and is currently under review. In order to address concerns raised, this revised manuscript explicitly states that the study is exploratory in nature and yet still can make important contribution to the literature; and provides strong justifications for focusing undergraduate students as a target stakeholder group in our study. The PI has gained invaluable experience in conducting and managing interdisciplinary and multi-method research from this project. This experience will be transferrable to the PI's large projects work in the near future, including the recently granted GRF which is a comparative study of energy transitions in China, South Korea, and Japan.

22400614.label: Major findings and research outcome
22400614.value: This project resulted in three sets of findings: The first set of finding relates to the theoretical and empirical findings of the changing roles of state and market in the smart grid deployment processes. (i) We have developed a conceptual framework of the functionality of state-market dynamics. It specifies five critical functions of state and market interactions which could facilitate the deployment of smart grids: market building, market regulation, managing public goods, networks and partnership building, and policy learning [Relevant research outputs: three presentations made at conferences]. (ii) We found that China and Japan have adopted distinctive models of smart grid deployment which differ with each other, and may also differ from those found in the western context. We found that there exists an incumbent led model in China (Output: a published paper), and this work complements our earlier publication in 2013 which characterisied the Japanese model as a government-led and community-oriented model. (iii) We created a body of new empirical data in the non-western contexts of energy transitions. The second set of findings relates to a better understanding of the roles of two key agents of change, namely incumbent utilities and the young generation, in energy transitions. (i) Tensions between incumbent utilities and new market players impeded the development of SGs in various ways [Relevant research outputs: a published paper, a manuscript under review, and three conference presentations)]. (ii) Participating undergraduates’s perception on pricing options (which may subsequently affect the effectiveness of public engagement in demand-side energy management programmes through smart grids) did change after they participated in deliberative processes. Our findings confirm with the literature that deliberation is conducive to empower the public to make informed, thoughtful, and responsible energy-relation decisions. In addition, we found that national level contextual factors may explain the differences in the smart grid development pathways across these two case countries [Relevant research output: the manuscript which is under review]. The third set of findings is derived from the two pilot DPs. We found that the normative mechanisms of DP can be applied beyond the West to the Asian context. Outcomes: (1) We created a new body of theoretical and empirical knowledge about engaging consumers in smart grid deployment in two major Asian countries. (2) We developed and tested a conceptual framework of state-market dynamics in Asia. (3) We tested the application of deliberative polling as an innovative method to engage the public in making complex energy decisions. (4) We provided policy recommendations.

22400614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22400614.value: The findings of the project suggest that there is potential for further research development in the four following areas: 1. We can extend this China-Japan comparative study to a larger comparative study to include western (e.g. the UK, France) and southeast Asian countries (e.g. Philippines). A future large scale international project can enhance the generalisability of findings and the global impacts. 2. We can also a larger study that may test the conceptual framework in the contexts of other energy technological options such as solar energy, wind power, nuclear power, and electric vehicles. 3. We can develop a study that focuses on the stakeholder perspectives of energy transitions. This research has shed light on the roles of incumbent utilities and the young generation. Our findings suggest that the changing relationships between the government, incumbent utilities, and electricity end-users are an important area of future research. 4. We can replicate the pilot DPs of dynamic pricing in universities in other major cities such as Sydney, Paris, and Stanford through the PI’s existing research network. In combination of the existing dataset of the DPs in Kyoto and Guangzhou, we can compare and explain the similarities and differences of undergraduates’ responses across these major cities.

22400614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22400614.value: Technological innovations in smart grid technologies have the potential to create new opportunities to engage electricity consumers as a way to ensure sustainable energy future. This comparative study of smart grid developments in Japan and China aims to identify the essential elements of and the barriers to effective consumer engagement in smart grid diffusion from an Asian perspective. Based on about 50 qualitative interviews conducted in five cities in Japan and Asia, and quantitative and qualitative data derived from two pilot deliberative pollings conducted in Kyoto and Guangzhou, this project has several key findings relate to the theoretical and empirical findings of the changing roles of state and market in the smart grid deployment processes. We paid particular attention to the roles of incumbent utilities in influencing niche accumulation and regime shifts in energy transition, as well as the roles of the young generation (undergraduates) in offering public inputs for making difficult trade-off energy decisions.

22400914.label: Project Title(Chinese)
22400914.value: 從法律視角重新審視明清易代（1619-1740）之政制、社會與經濟變遷

22400914.label: Project Objectives
22400914.value: To identify and evaluate the institutional and socioeconomic changes that took place during the Ming-Qing Transition from the early versions of the Great Qing Code and relevant judicial cases. To refute the established opinion that the Qing legal system directly copied the Ming form, and thereby demonstrate the unique characteristics and specific concerns of the Qing system. To discover the discontinued elements of the Ming legal system, and recognize the trends interrupted during the course of Chinese legal developments. As an original investigation of the effects of institutional changes and economic recessions on local society as well as the judicial apparatus in case studies, to provide an analysis that may help to understand similar issues in China today. To build a Historical GIS of casebooks from the Ming-Qing Transition which will facilitate future spatial and jurisprudential research on these underestimated social and legal materials.
