24300114.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24300114.value: The discovery of the Higgs particle at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations, and the awarding of the Nobel Prize in Physics 2013 to Professors Peter Higgs and Francois Englert, have demonstrated clearly the potential and importance of particle physics research at the energy frontier. Also, the strong participation of Hong Kong institutions in the Daya Bay Reactor Experiment constitutes a solid foundation for the creation of the Joint Consortium for Fundamental Physics in Hong Kong (JCFP), which will join the ATLAS collaboration at CERN. The Large Hadron Collider is the highest energy particle accelerator in the world, and the ATLAS detector is the largest particle detector ever built for collider physics. After the successful 2011-2012 period, which brought about the discovery of the Higgs particle, these experimental facilities are now in a shut-down period expected to last until early 2015. Significant maintenance and upgrade activities during this shutdown period will allow the center-of-mass energy of the proton-proton collisions to be raised from 8 TeV (its maximum value so far) to about 14 TeV; i.e., an increase of up to 75%. This large increase in energy will significantly improve the reach of several searches for new physics, and the expected precision in the measurement of the properties of the Higgs particle. This shut-down period also provides an excellent opportunity for the Hong-Kong group to contribute to the ongoing ATLAS work to get ready for the next LHC run, both in terms of the hardware development and in terms of the preparation of the physics program, to be ready in time for the new data-taking period at 14 TeV. This project is aimed at strengthening the JCFP physics program, specifically through work on the following areas: 1. Study and update of muon identification using information from the Liquid Argon calorimeters, 2. Study of the properties of the Higgs boson, specifically its width and couplings, and 3. Search for new physics in Exotic Physics channels, specifically targeting some of the potential final states of Dark Matter particles. These areas are designed to avoid overlap with the objectves of the JFPC proposal and, to the maximum extent possible, to complement them to build a complete and solid physics program from Hong Kong institutions, with a significant impact and a long-term contribution to LHC Physics.

24300114.label: Realisation of objectives
24300114.value: All objectives were achieved. They are described in more detail below. It may be worth clarifying that the original objectives were written when the center-of-mass energy of LHC Run 2 collisions was expected to be 14 TeV; instead, after a technical assessment of the conditions of the machine, the acceleration division of CERN decided to set it to 13 TeV, but this change did not affect the objectives. Objective 1. We studied and characterized the performance of the algorithms used in ATLAS to identify muons using only tracking and calorimeter information. To this end, we analyzed a large number of simulated proton-proton (pp) collision events of three relevant types, described below; on each sample, events underwent full simulation of the interaction of final-state particles with the ATLAS detector. We produced three types of samples: Z to dimuon samples (Z boson production from pp, which subsequently decays to a muon pair), top-antitop production (from pp, with a subsequent decay of the top quarks to lighter particles), and a set of single-particle samples where each event consists initially of a single particle (a muon or a pion) produced at the interaction point and moving in a random direction in the detector, with definite energy values. The latter, single-particle, samples allow us to study the detector response to particles of different momenta and direction in an extremely clean environment. We used large Z to dimuon and top-antitop samples already available (produced earlier by the ATLAS Collaboration), and we produced new single-particle samples, consisting of 25,000 events for each of 19 values of transverse momentum, plus 25,000 events for each of 19 values of total momentum, using the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid; the ATLAS MCP group provided storage space for these samples, which were made available to other groups to study muon identification and reconstruction. Using these samples, we measured efficiency and fake rates of the CaloTag muon identification algorithm (one of two algorithms used in ATLAS for this goal), and studied the variables used to build its main discriminant. We identified a number of modifications that maintain or increase the muon identification efficiency for all values of transverse momentum with a slight or moderate increase in fake rates. These modifications were presented to the ATLAS Muon Software group and, after evaluation, were adopted in the ATLAS reconstruction software. Objective 2. We worked on several aspects of the study of the properties of the Higgs boson, both with data from Run I (at 7 and 8 TeV) and from Run II (at 13 TeV), in close collaboration with the ATLAS Higgs Working Group, and the ATLAS group in charge of the four-lepton analysis. Previous ATLAS results on coupling strengths of the Higgs boson used the complete dataset from Run 1 of the LHC. They have been extended and updated including additional Higgs decay channels (to dimuons, pairs of tau leptons and pairs of b quarks). In close collaboration with other Hong Kong institutions, we contributed to these results focusing mainly on the study and validation of selection procedures, the estimation of the expected number of background events in the final selection, and the study of systematic uncertainties. The results were published and used for a joint ATLAS-CMS measurement of Higgs boson production and couplings. The ATLAS Collaboration also published an initial measurement of the tensor structure of the Higgs couplings in Run 1; in this publication, based on 25 fb-1 of pp data at a center-of-mass energy of 7 and 8 TeV, an Effective Field Theory approach called the Higgs Characterization Model was used to describe the mixing between CP-even and CP-odd states; the analysis used ratios of BSM to SM tensor couplings. Combining the statistical power of two Higgs decay channels (to pairs of Z bosons and to pairs of W bosons), a large range of parameter values was excluded at a 95% CL. The non-excluded intervals are compatible with the Standard Model predictions. Our group played a mayor role in the preparation of these results. We continued to work on refining and extending these results using the Run 2 dataset, at a center of mass energy of 13 TeV, and contributed significantly to this work through our work on the decay of the Higgs boson to four leptons, continuing the work described above for the 7 and 8 TeV measurements (i.e., the study and validation of selection procedures, and the estimation of the expected background level in the final selection). The project also resulted in the development of a technique that can reduce drastically the computing resources needed to produce full-detector simulation samples corresponding to BSM scenarios. The tensor structure of the Higgs couplings can be described by the coupling strengths of 12 new-physics contributions (in the Higgs Characterization model); to explore this parameter space, a large number of sample points needs to be used; however, a straightforward simulation of all these points would be prohibitively expensive in terms of both CPU-time and storage requirements. Instead, a small number of samples from this parameter space, combined appropriately, can accurately reproduce the samples that would be obtained for any other point. Objective 3. Building upon the experience with muon and electron reconstruction gained in the analysis of the decay of the Higgs boson into four leptons, we focused our work on the study of Exotic Physics channels with the search for electron-muon resonances in Run II. We contributed to several aspects of this search, studying its selection procedures and a number of alternative selection criteria to improve the sensitivity of the procedure. The results for 3.2 fb-1 were made public by the ATLAS Collaboration in a conference note, setting 95% CL limits on the mass of an SSM Z’ boson, on the threshold mass for quantum black hole production. These results were published in the European Physics Journal C. I would like to clarify here that ATLAS Conference notes do not include an author list; as a result, neither individual ATLAS members, nor funding agencies, are explicitly listed. This is the reason for the lack of an explicit acknowledgement to RGC in this item in section 8 of the Electronic System (Part C: Research Output). However, the link to the corresponding publication is also given; in the publication, RGC is acknowledged. Objective 4. Train Hong Kong students and postdocs for research in the forefront of fundamental physics. One postdoctoral research associate, two PhD students (Haonan Lu and Tak Shun Lau), three MPhil students (Yun Sang Chow, KaWa Tsang and Wing Sheung Chan) and five undergraduate students (Mak Sze Ning, Chi Wing Ng, Heng Fai Chang, Man Yat Chu and Zihui Wang) contributed to this project. This allowed them to fully benefit from the close interaction with colleagues from other ATLAS institutions (located both in Hong Kong and overseas), from learning several of the tools used for research in High Energy Physics, and from working with the most recent data and Monte Carlo simulation from the Large Hadron Collider, on searches and measurements at the energy frontier.

24300114.label: Major findings and research outcome
24300114.value: 1. Segmenting the solid angle covered by the calorimeter components into a large number of sub-regions allows a much finer control of the performance and a better selection of the operating point (in the rejection vs efficiency plane). In some regions, the modified set of cuts allowed an increase of about 20% in muon efficiency for large transverse momentum of the muon candidates. 2. The coupling properties of the Higgs boson were studied in the four-lepton decay channel using up to 36/fb of proton-proton collision data from the LHC at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV collected by the ATLAS detector. Cross sections were measured for the four main production modes of the Higgs boson in several exclusive regions and were interpreted in terms of coupling modifiers. Its inclusive cross section times branching ratio were measured and found to be in agreement with the Standard Model expectation. Also, initial constraints were placed on its potential non-standard-model couplings. Several studies were done in common with the teams studying the spin and parity of the Higgs boson. Results are included in publications listed in part C.8 as #1, #2 and #6. 3. A search was performed for a heavy particle decaying into different-flavour dilepton pairs using 3.2 fb−1 of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. No excess over the Standard Model prediction is observed. Limits at the 95% credibility level are set on the mass of a Z′ boson with lepton-flavour-violating couplings at 3.0, 2.7 and 2.6 TeV, and on the mass of a supersymmetric sneutrino with R-parity-violating couplings at 2.3, 2.2 and 1.9 TeV, for eμ, eτ and μτ final states, respectively. The results are also interpreted as limits on the threshold mass for quantum black hole production. Results are included in publications listed in part C.8 as #3, #4 and #5.

24300114.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24300114.value: There are several areas for potential refinements and improvements. Regarding the muon identification procedures, the implemented segmentation can be subject to two types of optimization: (a) in terms of the boundaries used and (b) it can be separated in bins of transverse momentum of the muon candidates. Also, this segmentation can be applied to the other calorimeter-based muon identification algorithm in use (based on a likelihood ratio instead of cuts). For the Higgs analysis, many developments are currently under way, both on the theory side (with different decompositions of the SM Lagrangian in terms of operators that may be especially sensitive to BSM contributions) and in terms of experimental techniques; one example is the use of Machine Learning techniques in parallel with trying to minimize the sensitivity to potential BSM physics when trying to measure the cross section of the main production modes of the Higgs boson. Finally, for the dilepton searches in lepton-flavor violating channels, the use of Machine Learning techniques can be expected to bring a significant improvement, both when applied at the level of physics objects (specifically in the identification of tau leptons) and at the level of signal extraction.

24300114.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24300114.value: This research project contributes to our understanding of the fundamental processes of Nature from three fronts: (a) our measuring tools, (b) the role and characteristics of the Higgs boson, and (c) searching for phenomena that is not expected in our current theories. These objectives are pursued through the analysis of proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN in Geneva, Switzerland. There, protons travel almost at the speed of light; when they collide, they can transform into any particle allowed by the laws of Nature. Our current description of these laws (the “Standard Model”, or SM) provides very precise predictions for the possible outcomes of these collisions, but we know that the SM is incomplete, so we are making a systematic search for phenomena not contained in it. We aim specifically to (a) improve the identification of muons, because muons constitute one of the best tools to reconstruct what happened on each particle collision; (b) learn as much as we can about the Higgs boson, which was discovered very recently (in 2012) and whose interactions with other particles may unveil unexpected new phenomena; (c) search for particles that would violate one of the predictions of the SM.

24300214.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24300214.value: This project aims to explore a wide range of emergent phenomena in strongly correlated electron systems using pressure as a tuning parameter. These phenomena, including diverse types of magnetism, unconventional superconductivity and metal-insulator transitions, are not only of theoretical interest, but are also of growing technological significance. The properties of strongly correlated electron systems are sensitive to the interaction strength among electrons. This interaction strength can be varied elegantly using hydrostatic pressure, which directly changes the distances between the electrons. Unlike chemical doping which donates or removes electrons, the application of hydrostatic pressure does not introduce chemical disorder that can potentially mask the intrinsic physics of the system. Therefore, hydrostatic pressure has been regarded as a valuable tuning parameter for modern condensed matter physics research. In order to reach the pressures that are high enough to observe new and unconventional states, we will design, develop and optimize a unique magnetic induction technique to detect and study novel quantum phases under pressure. An extremely tiny sensing coil will be carefully introduced into the high pressure region of the Moissanite anvil based pressure device where the sample is placed, thereby achieving a large coupling between the sample and the coil. This approach will enable the detection of novel phases and hence the construction of the ‘pressure phase diagram’, which serves as a guidance for detailed microscopic exploration. Next, we will use quantum oscillations, a powerful probe that has recently been applied to understand the Fermi surface of copper oxide high-temperature superconductors, to study the dynamics of electrons in these systems at ambient and high pressures. Of particular interest are systems which can be driven to straddle a quantum critical point, which is a zero-temperature singularity in the phase diagram where a second-order quantum phase transition between the order state and the disorder state takes place. We will be able to track the fate of the electrons across the quantum critical point. The successful completion of this project will contribute a powerful high pressure tool for routine magnetic investigations of correlated electron systems and deepen our understanding of the physics of quantum criticality, particularly a structural quantum criticality, and its interplay with other competing states. 這項目旨在探索強關聯電子系統下以壓強作為調整參數的廣泛的突發現象。這些現象，包括多種類型的磁特性、非傳統的超導電性和金屬 - 絕緣體轉變，不僅是科研人員感興趣的理論研究，也有著日益提高的技術價值。強關聯電子系統的性能對電子間的相互作用力猶其敏感。藉由更改靜液壓強能直接改變電子間的距離，這種相互作用力也可以隨之改變。有別於運用化學摻雜來捐贈或刪除電子，靜液壓強的應用不會引入化學無序，引致系統的物理特性被掩蓋。因此，靜液壓強一直被視為現代凝態物理研究的一個重要調整參數。為達到這個足以觀察到新的和非傳統的狀態之高壓，我們將設計、開發和優化獨特的磁感應技術來探測和研究在壓強下異常的量子相位。一個極其微小的感應線圈將被小心地引進放著樣品的碳矽石砧壓強裝置，從而實現樣品和線圈之間的大型耦合。這種方法將使得異常的相位和“壓強相位圖”能被探測，並將引導詳細的微觀勘探。接下來，我們將使用量子振盪（即最近被應用到理解的氧化銅高溫超導體的費米面的強力探測工具）來研究這些系中在周遭和較高的壓下電子的特性。特別令人感興趣的是其可以被驅動到跨越量子臨界點，這是一個在相位圖下的零溫度奇點，有序和無序狀態之間的二階相變也在此發生。我們將能夠在整個量子臨界點附近看到電子的命運。成功完成此項目將作成一個強大的高壓工具來研究電子關聯系統的常規磁研究和加深理解量子臨界，特別是晶體結構的量子臨界的物理特性，也增加與其他國家的相互交流。

24300214.label: Realisation of objectives
24300214.value: In the first stage of this ECS project, we have made rapid progress in the construction of a new and modern laboratory capable of reaching the extreme conditions needed. The nature of the project allows us to explore a wide range of topics in correlated electron systems. Objective 1 of this project seeks to develop the capability to detect phase transitions under pressure. We have placed particular emphasis on optimizing our detection sensitivity as soon as the project started. With this capability we have reported the pressure dependence of the superconducting transition temperature in TlNi2(Se,S)2 and FeSe1-xSx; the discovery of a quasilinear magnetoresistance in pressurised CrAs; the discovery of isotropic superconductivity in WTe2 at ~9.8 GPa; and the pressure dependence of a ferroelectric-like structural transition in LiOsO3. These results were published in peer-reviewed journals including 3 x Phys. Rev. B (Rapid Comm.), 2 x Nature Commun. and 1 x Appl. Phy. Lett. Objective 2 is specifically related to a material system with R3T4Sn13 stoichiometry (R=rare-earth or alkaline-earth, T=transition metal). Here, we have also made progress in the construction of the temperature-pressure and temperature-composition phase diagrams in (CaxSr1-x)3Rh4Sn13, the heat capacity measurement across the entire series (CaxSr1-x)3Rh4Sn13, the construction of a universal temperature-tuning parameter phase diagram for R3T4Sn13 with different transition metals, the report of the Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in Sr3Ir4Sn13, and the investigation of the T* transition in La3Co4Sn13. Results related to this objective have been published in Phys. Rev. Lett. (1 paper) and Phys. Rev. B (3 papers, including one as Rapid Comm.). Finally, with the research capability developed in this project, we also investigated ScSb and heterostructure of Bi2Te3/FeTe. The ScSb project is interesting because of the large magnetoresistance, which is related to our work on CrAs. The heterostructure work involved the measurement of the upper critical field, which is a topic our group is always interested in. The ScSb and the Bi2Te2/FeTe results are published in Phys. Rev. B and Sci. Rep., respectively.

24300214.label: Major findings and research outcome
24300214.value: This project directly results in 12 journal articles [2 Nature Commun., 1 Phys. Rev. Lett., 1 Appl. Phys. Lett., 1 Sci. Rep., 4 Phys. Rev. B (Rapid. Comm.) and 3 Phys. Rev. B], as listed in Part C. In CrAs, we used pressure to explore the phase diagram. We detected the superconducting state under pressure, consistent with previous reports. Furthermore, we discovered that the normal state of CrAs features an anomalous, quasilinear magnetoresistance. With band structure calculations and symmetry analysis, we attribute the quasilinear magnetoresistance to the fact that a tiny Fermi pocket at the Y point of the Brillouin zone reaches the extreme quantum limit at several teslas. In (CaxSr1-x)3Rh4Sn13, we constructed the temperature-x phase diagram (x=Ca content) that shows the the structural transition temperature T* can be driven to 0 K at x~0.9. We proposed that, if the T* transition remains second-order at x~0.9, a structural quantum critical point can be realised. We measured the heat capacity across the entire series, and reported an enhanced electron-phonon coupling strength in the vicinity of x~0.9. Therefore, strong-coupling superconductivity can be realized in the vicinity of the structural quantum critical point. We also investigated the sister compound Sr3Ir4Sn13, in which we detected Shubnikov-de Haas quantum oscillations, allowing the construction of the Fermi surface. Furthermore, we studied the T* transition in La3Co4Sn13 using electrical resistivity, heat capacity, X-ray diffraction and bandstructure calculations. Our results indicate that T* transition in La3Co4Sn13 is a continuous transition, and further tuning of this transition may result in a quantum critical point, analogous to the (Ca,Sr)3Rh4Sn13 and (Ca,Sr)3Ir4Sn13 series. Other findings include the discovery of an isotropic superconductivity in WTe2, despite its layered crystal structure; the weakening of the diamagnetic shielding in FeSe1-xSx under pressure near the pressure where Tc is substantially enhanced; and the construction of the temperature-pressure phase diagram for ferroelectric-like metal LiOsO3, in which the non-polar to polar transition temperature can be substantially enhanced under pressure.

24300214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24300214.value: With the infrastructure well-established, we can apply the same strategy to a wide range of materials. The materials to be studied are not limited to correlated electron systems. For instance, a newly awarded RGC project will investigate topological semimetals under multiple extreme conditions. With regards to R3T4Sn13 series, we plan to have a deeper study of the lattice dynamics, and we hope to find other systems with similar phase diagrams which show the interplay between structure instability and superconductivity.

24300214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24300214.value: The ability to understand and control the behaviour of electrons in solids remains one of the chief goals in condensed matter physics research. With fine controls, we can study the physics underpinning the material properties systematically, and materials with useful functionalities can be realised. In this project, we use hydrostatic pressure as the knob to control various interaction strengths in solids. For example, superconductivity in certain material systems can be induced with the application of pressure. Hence, the ability to subject a given material system under extreme conditions offers the opportunity to discover new phases, and/or to perform detailed studies of the existing phases via microscopic probes (such as quantum oscillations). This strategy, developed and optimised over the course of this project, will be employed to study a wide range of materials.

24300314.label: Project Objectives
24300314.value: Experiments on the initial condition parameter space: B fields have to be assumed dynamically important in the initial condition, otherwise field lines will be tangled by turbulence and appear random in orientation, which is inconsistent with observations. With a dynamically dominant B field assumed, simulations only with gravity result in an elongated structure perpendicular to the field lines, and simulations only with turbulence result in clouds aligned with the fields. This is because the contraction (due to gravity) and expansion (due to turbulent pressure) are both channeled by the field lines. The reality is that both orientations are observed (Li et al., 2013). We will fine-tune the initial conditions so that both types of clouds will appear in the simulations with comparable populations. Sub-regional physical properties that define the cloud orientations: From the resulting bimodal clouds in "1", we can trace back in time to study what the main different properties are between the sub-regions that bring out different cloud orientations. ‘Super-critical’ mass: ‘Super-critical’ means that the density is high enough such that self-gravity can overcome internal turbulent and magnetic pressure (the thermal pressure is usually much smaller and it will not be dynamically important in molecular clouds). Gravitational contractions and turbulent shocks (both mainly along the field line when the B field is dynamically important) are the major mechanisms for increasing local densities. Only the super-critical sub-regions of a cloud can contract in all directions and so be capable of affecting the SFE.

24300314.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24300314.value: Inspired by our latest observations, we propose numerical studies to improve the understanding of the physics behind star formation. While it is widely observed that galactic spiral arms break into molecular clouds which then further fragment into stars, the physics behind this process is still vigorously debated. The role played by magnetic fields (B fields) is especially mysterious, owing much to the difficulties both of observation and simulation. Open questions remain at every stage of star formation. For example: are galactic spiral B fields strong enough to anchor into molecular clouds? and, if so, how can the B fields affect star formation efficiencies (SFE; the ratio of stellar mass to parent cloud mass)? Very recently, a series of our surveys have shed light on the first question: galactic B-field directions are found to be preserved in molecular clouds (Li & Henning, 2011; Li et al., 2009) and they can shape clouds to have bimodal orientations: these are either parallel or perpendicular to local B fields (Li et al., 2013). Moreover, we found that the parallel cases have an SFE typically twice as large as the perpendicular ones, which inspires a brand-new direction for tackling the second question. The fact that galactic B-field directions anchor in molecular clouds suggests that B fields are dynamically important compared to gravity and turbulence during the cloud formation process. This means that gravitational contraction and turbulent velocity are channeled by B fields and thus should be anisotropic. We propose that the bimodal cloud orientation is a consequence of these anisotropies (Li et al., 2013). Here we will first show that this model can also qualitatively explain the difference between the SFEs. We propose to then carry out experiments which use numerical magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations in order to study this model in detail. In particular, the simulations will answer: what is the initial condition parameter space that leads to the bimodal cloud orientation?; how will the probability density function (PDF) of the gas density be different between the two cloud types?; and what is the mass fraction that is dense enough to collapse against turbulent and magnetic pressure (super-critical)? By answering these questions, we will be able to estimate the SFE difference under the assumption that B fields are dynamically dominant in the processes of cloud formation and fragmentation. Comparing this prediction with SFE observations will offer a crucial test of the role played by B fields in star formation. 星系的旋臂如何碎裂成分子雲? 分子雲如何進一步碎裂, 坍縮成恆星? 一直是天文學家致力解決的問題。其中又以磁場在恆星生成中所扮演的角色最令人費解, 因為磁場既難直接觀測又難作數值模擬。分子雲仍保持著星系旋臂磁場嗎？ 分子雲磁場能影響恆星生成的效率（ＳＦＥ）嗎？ 本組最近的觀測解答了第一個問題：一個對 30 個分子雲的survey發現分子雲仍保有星系磁場方向 (Li & Henning, 2011; Li et al., 2009). 本組也發現分子雲的長軸頃向平行或垂直於磁場 (bimodal orientation; Li et al., 2013), 且兩類分子雲有不同的 ＳＦＥ. 這個發現啓發了一個研究, 解答ＳＦＥ的全新方向. 分子雲能保有星系磁場方向是因為磁場的能量高於重力場及湍流. 因此重力坍縮和湍流速度都應呈各向異性. 本組提出正是此各向異性導致分子雲的 bimodal orientation. 在此我們進一步指出此各向異性亦能定性解釋兩類分子雲不同的 ＳＦＥ. 基於此論述我們計畫用數值模擬的方法來定量地研究兩類分子雲的 ＳＦＥ. 更確切地說, 我們想回答下例問題: 何種初始條件能導致 bimodal orientation? 兩類分子雲密度的 probability density function 有何不同? 兩類分子雲各有多少比例的subregion能坍縮? 藉由回答上述問題, 我們能預測SFE以和觀測作比較, 進而了解強磁場的論述是否正確.

24300314.label: Realisation of objectives
24300314.value: This is a very productive project. Besides achieving most of the objectives, a few new research directions are inspired by this project. This is the first grant awarded to the then one-year-old group led by a PI had no experience in numerical simulations. The strategy is to work on an open, well-tested code, ZEUS, with an experienced postdoc (Frank Otto). Within less than half a year, a simple simulation had helped us publish a set of observational data to Nature (2015), which is impossible without the help from the simulation. The later simulations inspired several observational works; two has been published: one (objective #1) made to the Nature Astronomy cover story (Aug. 2017); the other (objective #3) is just accepted by Astrophysical Journal (ApJ 2019). Three other works have been submitted and still under review. Frank Otto led the first publication in numerical simulation (objective #1; ApJ 2017) and the second one (objective #3), led by a graduate student (Z.T. Guo), will be submitted late January 2019. While ZEUS is extremely helpful for our research, it, however, cannot effectively trace the detail gas redistribution, which is why objective #2 is not 100% finished. We have recruited a research assistant professor, H.H. Wang, to lead a couple of graduate students to improve the code. The modification has been finished and is under testing. The new code will not only fully achieve objective #2, but will equip our team with a unique ability in numerical simulation!

24300314.label: Major findings and research outcome
24300314.value: The grant helped our young team build a solid foundation of numerical experiments, which led to the following discoveries, and counting. 1. Cloud field strength gradually changes with mass-to-flux ratio; there is no sharp turning as expected in the literature (e.g., Crutcher et al. 2010). The work is published in Nature (Li et al. 2015). Though this work is submitted before this grant is awarded and is not related to the objectives, the simulation enabled by this grant played a crucial role in convincing the referees to accept this work. The simulation is published in the appendix of this paper. 2. The correlation between cloud-B field alignment and star formation efficiency (Objective #1; Nature Astronomy 2017) 3. The relation between Alfven Mach number and turbulence velocity anisotropy (Objective #1; ApJ 2017) 4. The relation between scales and B-field orientation in super-critical and super-Alfvenic cloud cores (Objective #3; accepted for ApJ 2019)

24300314.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24300314.value: The numerical simulations from this project inspired many other works that are undergoing: 1. The relation between cloud-B flied alignment and cloud fragmentation: One graduate student, Chi Yan Law, is looking for the signatures of B-field orientation on cloud fragmentation. He got one paper submitted to MNRAS and another two in prepare. 2. Velocity anisotropy analysis of molecular cloud at various densities: One postdoc researcher, Hongli Liu, is leading this direction; one paper submitted. 3. New models for the B field-density relation tested by Bayesian analysis: Collaborated with the CUHK Statistics Department; one paper submitted. 4. The Objective #2 is not 100% completed, because the current numerical code, ZEUS, cannot dependably trace the contracting gas back. We are developing a new code with test particles that is able to better trace the gas flows.

24300314.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24300314.value: The project equipped our young team with the ability to do numerical experiments, which have unlimited possibilities for future development. So far, the experiments on how magnetic fields can affect cloud dynamics and star formation have already made significant impact to the field and been published in best journals, e.g., Nature and ApJ.

24300414.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24300414.value: 質量均衡的研究對格陵蘭冰川在氣候變化下的響應以及對全球海平面變化等議題至關重要。現有的研究主要關注格陵蘭在幾十年或更長時間內的線性變化。但鮮有觀測研究格陵蘭注出冰川在進幾年內的短期的非線性變化。 本項目以三個格陵蘭冰川為切入點，利用多種衛星大地測量（包括合成孔徑雷達干涉InSAR、全球衛星地位系統GPS、衛星重力、以及衛星測量）來量化研究最近三到五年內這項個別冰川的季節性和年際性質量均衡。我們將結合包括冰川流速、地殼形變、冰面高程變化等不同物理量，來細化地表質量均衡和冰川動力學這兩個過程對冰川總體質量變化的貢獻。 我們還將研究這些冰川短期變化後的物理機制。 本項目將彌補冰川短期變化的研究空白、有助於完善冰原模型及基於模型對於格陵蘭未來變化和其對全球海平面的影響的預測。本項目將培養一名博士研究生和兩名本科生、并在本港建立一個有關極地變化的研究教育基地。

24300414.label: Realisation of objectives
24300414.value: I have completed all the proposed research tasks and realized all three objectives as per the original application. Objective 1: To collect and analyze high-frequency geodetic data obtained by various satellites during the past three to five years at three representative outlet glacier systems in Greenland. We have collected and analyzed the following geodetic data to investigate glacial changes at Upernavik Isstrøm, Jakobshavn Isbræ, and the entire Greenland Ice Sheet: a. Three-dimensional displacements measured by Global Positioning System (GPS) mounted on bedrock (known as the Greenland network) to quantify and investigate loading-induced deformation at annual and inter-annual scales from 2003 to 2017. b. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images from TerraSAR-X satellite to map glacial velocities and their changes using the speckle-tracking algorithm. c. Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) data from 2007 to 2017 to calculate mass changes and the loading deformation. d. Altimetry measurements from NASA’s Airborne Topographic Mapper (ATM, 2006-2017), the Ice, Cloud and land Elevation Satellite (ICESat, 2006-2009), and the CryoSat-2 satellite (2010-2017) to estimate the rate of ice volume changes. Objective 2: To quantify non-secular mass changes by combining multiple geodetic observables and separate individual components due to surface mass balance and glacial dynamics. We have built a comprehensive framework to combine multiple geodetic observations for quantifying glacial mass balance at seasonal and inter-annual time scales and to separate individual components due to surface mass balance and glacial dynamics. The key steps and components of this methodologic framework include: a. Modeling non-ice loading deformation due to changes in atmospheric pressure, ocean bottom pressure (non-ocean tidal loading), and continental water storage; and removing them from the GPS measurements to obtain 3-D displacements only due to ice loading/unloading. b. Converting GRACE-measured gravity fields into vertical displacements using loading theory and Love numbers. c. Applying the multichannel singular spectral (M-SSA) analysis to the combination of GPS and GRACE-derived vertical displacements to identify and fully utilize the spatial correlations from these independent data sets d. Performing fluxgate calculation using ice velocity time series and ice thickness, taking account the temporal changes of glacial front and ice thickness at the front. e. Distributing total ice flux spatially across glacial catchment based on the inferred spatial pattern of dynamic mass loss, which is the difference between the total mass loss and the surface mass balance (SMB) as output by regional climate models (RACMO and MAR). f. Calculating time series of loading displacements using the SMB models and distributed dynamic mass loss. We applied this framework to Upernavik and Jakobshavn, robustly extracted transient variations in glacial mass near both glacier systems, and quantitatively analyzed the relative contributions from dynamically induced mass loss and SMB. We revealed that at Upernavik, the 2008-2011 transient mass change was due to both SMB and glacial dynamics; the 2011-2014 transient was mainly due to abnormal SMB. Near Jakobshavn, SMB is the dominant contributor to the seasonal and transient displacements at three out of four mid-field GPS sites. While, at the near-field GPS site that is 2 km to the glacier, the contributions to the transient displacements from SMB and glacier dynamics are comparable. We also applied a similar work to the entire Greenland Ice Sheet, with a focus on quantifying inter-annual variations of the ice sheet, which is dominated by SMB variations. We have shown that the transient mass changes were characterized by a sustained mass gain from late 2007 to early 2010, a sustained mass loss from early 2010 to early 2013, and a mass gain from early 2013 to mid-2015. Our regional assessment revealed that the central-west, southwest, northeast, and southeast regions display similar time-varying patterns as we found for the entire ice sheet, but the north and northwest regions show different patterns. Objective 3.: To investigate the processes that control non-secular changes and their relationships with long-term changes. Using the Community Ice Sheet Model (CISM), we have designed and conducted a series of numerical simulations to investigate the potential factors and mechanisms that control temporal variations in glacial velocities at Upervavik. The numerical experiments have been performed with varying ice temperatures and surface mass balance rates, as well as user-defined large-scale calving events. We found that increasing ice temperatures can lead to higher glacial velocities with greater fluctuations in magnitude. More importantly, our simulation results suggest that large-scale calving could lead to an abrupt increase in velocity and the magnitude of this velocity increment is related to the size of ice calved away. For Jakobshavn, our comprehensive investigations revealed that: a. The calving front position change has a strong influence on the ice discharge: the significant ice front retreats in 2012 and 2014 (advances in 2011 and 2015) were coincident with the accelerated (decelerated) mass loss of the upstream. b. The retreat of the calving front into an overdeepened basin whose bed is retrograde may have accelerated the retreat after 2011, while the inland-uphill bed slope behind the bottom of the overdeepened basin has prevented the glacier from retreating further after 2012. c. The transient SMB changes were mainly caused by abnormal ablation with little contribution from abnormal accumulation. d. The widespread thickening in 2016–2017 was caused by glacier dynamics: a decrease of ice flow velocity near the frontal portion during 2016–2017 caused the thickening. e. The transient signals were mainly caused by the inter-annual variations of the ice discharge while the seasonal signals were largely influenced by the seasonal retreat and advance of the calving front. For the entire Greenland ice sheet, we found that the runoff anomalies dominated the transient mass changes of the ice sheet from 2007 to 2016. Future spatial analysis shows that during 2007-2016, runoff contributed more to the transient mass change than precipitation in the north and southwest regions in terms of the summation of the absolute anomalies, less in the northwest and northeast regions, and comparably in the central-west and southeast regions. We also explored the climatologic mechanisms for the observed transient mass changes by using two atmospheric indices: the Greenland Block Index (GBI) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) index. We found that GBI correlates more directly with runoff changes than does the NAO index. High-GBI-associated high temperature was one of the main reasons for the transient mass loss of the entire ice sheet during 2010-2012 while low GBI can explain the transient mass gain during 2013-2015. Contrasting behaviors of precipitation anomalies in east and west Greenland under abnormally high or low GBI conditions may explain the different patterns of the transient mass change in the northwest and the rest of Greenland. Lastly, we evaluated the impact of inter-annual variations of ice mass on the estimates of acceleration in Greenland ice mass changes. We proposed a new time series model to better describe the mass change patterns of Greenland. This new model consists of two parts, the deterministic part including a constant, a rate, a quadratic term, and seasonal terms, and the stochastic part including a First-Order Gauss-Markov process to represent the irregular interannual variations. Our new model estimates an acceleration of 1.8±0.9 Gt/yr2 in mass loss from 2003 to 2016. This is significantly lower than the one without explicitly accounting for inter-annual variability, which is 7.5±1.5 Gt/yr2.

24300414.label: Major findings and research outcome
24300414.value: The project has produced six research papers on Greenland glacial mass balance and two papers on an innovative use of GPS reflected signals. Please refer to Part C for detailed citation information and the full papers. Below I summarize our major findings as reported in the Greenland papers. Examining the vertical displacements measured at two GPS stations near Upernavik Isstrøm, Liu et al. (JGR, 2017) found that (1) atmospheric pressure loading contributes to half of the GPS vertical displacements at annual periods, (2) annual vertical displacements at these two coastal stations are sensitive to ice mass over 85% of the ice sheet, and (3) differential verticals between stations are useful to constrain ice mass changes within 120 km. Applying the multichannel singular spectral analysis to the combination of GPS data and GRACE data, Zhang et al. (JGR, 2017) identified two transient signals in ice mass variations during 2008 and 2014. They showed that the transient change starting in mid-2008 was due to the combined contributions from dynamically induced mass loss and SMB. The transient change starting in mid-2011 was mainly due to ablation. Zhang et al. (EPSL, 2018) used multi-source geodetic measurements to study the short-term mass changes of Jakobshavn Isbræ. They revealed that that (1) Jakobshavn underwent three episodes of transient mass changes from 2007 to 2017, (2) SMB was the dominant contributor, (3) Ice discharge and calving contributed differently to dynamical ice mass changes, and (4) Jakobshavn underwent widespread thickening along its main flowline since 2016. Ran et al. (TC, 2018) identified a seasonal mass anomaly throughout the GRACE record that peaks in July at 80–120 Gt and interpreted to be due to a combination of englacial and subglacial water storage generated by summer surface melting. Zhang et al. (EPSL, 2019) determined the transient mass changes over Greenland over the decade of 2007 to 2017. Northwest Greenland showed different change patterns from the rest Greenland. Atmospheric circulation anomalies as measured by the Greenland Blocking Index are able to explain most of these transient anomalies. Zhang et al. (TC, 2019) applied a deep learning architecture to multi-temporal SAR images towards automatically delineating the calving front positions of Jakobshavn Isbræ. Demonstrating through this successful case study and due to the transferable nature deep learning, this methodology can be applied to many other tidewater glaciers both in Greenland and elsewhere in the world, using multi-temporal and multi-sensor remote sensing imagery.

24300414.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24300414.value: 1. Better estimation of acceleration by accounting for inter-annual variations. We have proposed a new time series model to better describe the mass change patterns of Greenland. More work is needed to evaluate the robustness of this method and the significance of the newly estimated and lower-than-reported acceleration in Greenland mass loss. 2. Understanding the links between Greenland ice mass balance with changes in atmosphere and ocean circulations. We have shown that changes in atmospheric circulations as represented by the Greenland Block Index can explain most of the observed ice mass variations. Further inter-disciplinary studies in collaboration with atmospheric and ocean scientists are needed to exam the coupling between the inter-annual glacial changes with atmospheric fluctuation (e.g., the Northern Atlantic Oscillation) and ocean circulation (e.g., the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation). 3. Automatic delineation of glacial front in Greenland. As it has become increasingly labor-intensive and time-consuming to manually delineate glacial fronts a large number of remote sensing images taken over decades and over large areas, it is desirable to deep learning to automatically extract glaciological features from these big data. Building on our successful case study on Jakobshavn, we plan to develop a research proposal to pursue this direction.

24300414.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24300414.value: Most research that has analyzed the ice mass changes of Greenland ice sheet has focused on detecting linear rates and accelerations at decadal or longer periods. The transient (short-term, non-secular) mass changes show large variability, and if not accounted for properly, can introduce significant biases in estimates of long-term ice mass loss rates and accelerations. Our series of studies have filled in research gaps regarding the short-term changes in glacier mass balance and helps to constrain glacier/ice-sheet models and improve the projection of future changes of the Greenland Ice Sheet and its contribution to sea level rise. Overall, our studies provided quantitively insight into the spatio-temporal variations of the transient mass changes over Greenland during the past decade and proposed potential climatological mechanisms for explaining these changes. Importantly, we pointed out that surface mass balance, instead of glacial dynamics, played a key role in controlling the transient mass changes of the entire ice sheet. Our studies highlight the need to improve our understanding of the relationship between atmospheric circulations and short-term Greenland mass balance.

24300514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24300514.value: 本計劃目的是建構一套統一的方法在偏誤取樣(Biased sampling)情況下對半參數加速失敗模型(Semiparameteric Accelerated Failure Time Model, AFT)進行參數估計和統計推論。 生存分析在過去數十年一直是統計學的熱門研究課題。其研究成果被廣泛應用在各個不同的領域，包括公共衞生(Public health)、生物醫學(Biomedical studies)、信度(Reliability)、工程學(Engineering)和金融(Finance)等。傳統方法旨在分析從簡單隨機抽取出來的樣本作生存時間的估量；如在臨牀試驗試驗中檢驗隨機抽樣的治療組別(Treatment group)和參照組別(Control group)的生存時間長度是否有明顯差別。因為是簡單隨機抽樣，所以每個實驗對象在這些數據裏都各自帶有相同權重。 可是在實際應用上，並非所有的數據都是如上述情況般在機率一致的設定下獲得。相關例子包括病例世代研究(Case-cohort study)。為了節省收集大量病人共變量(Covariates)的金錢和時間，一些罕有疾病研究(Rare disease studies)只會對所有病發的個體和部份被刪失(Censored)個體作數據收集。在這個設定下，每名被刪失（沒有發病）而又被選中的個體實際上帶有相較更多的權重，籍以代表整體沒有病發的組別。類似的徧誤取樣比比皆是，典型例子包括抽類機率與生存時間成正比的長度徧誤取樣(Length-biased sampling)和只有樣本生存時間長於某特定臨界值才被抽樣的左截斷抽樣(Left-truncation sampling)。 現有參考文獻中只有對個別偏誤取樣作參數估計和統計推論的結果：絕大部分的研究的設定都只能應用於單一的偏誤取樣上而不容易延申至其他的偏誤取樣。本計劃除了提供一套統一的統計推論方法外，亦會發展其他（於臨牀試驗上）常見實用而又未被考慮的偏誤取樣；對其他研究方向，包括變量選擇(Variable selection)亦會作分析和提供答案。

24300514.label: Realisation of objectives
24300514.value: The three objectives of the project have been achieved in this proposal for various projects. 1. One publication output entitled "A Unified Approach to Semiparametric Accelerated Failure Time Model under General Biased Sampling Scheme" (see Publication #1 in Part C) proposes a generic framework for inference problems of the accelerated failure time (AFT) model based on biased censored data. Traditionally, there are separate methods/techniques in handling individual biasedness of data, either due to design of occurs naturally for the AFT model. Typical examples include length-biasedness (in which larger/subjects with longer survival times tend to be more likely to be collected), case-cohort sampling (in which subjects with observed failures are all collected while censored subjects are sampled with a predefined, fixed probability in order to save data collection time/cost) and generalised case-cohort (where the case-cohort sampling mechanism is further generalised so that subjects with events and censored subjects are both sample with certain known probabilities that can be dependent on attributes of individuals). This paper first constructs an estimating equation for the simple case with Gehan weight in order to correct the sampling bias obtain an unbiased point estimate for the parameters of interest. Based upon these point estimates of the model parameters, we can also obtain a non-parametric estimate for the unknown baseline cumulative hazard function. The corresponding asymptotic normalities of our proposed estimators are also established. The point estimates yielded can also serve as an initial value for a more general weight including log-rank weight that is commonly adopted for the AFT model in order to improve estimation efficiency. The first objective is, therefore, achieved for this work. Since solving our estimating equation directly may encounter numerical issues, the procedure proposed also transforms this root-finding problem into a convex optimization problem, whose maximisers can be more easily to be obtained. This enables our inference procedure can be more stably implemented and our second goal is also achieved. Finally, in terms of numerical accuracy and feasibility, this paper considers four different types of biasedness and presents our results that demonstrate very decent performance. The point estimates are virtually unbiased and the corresponding empirical coverage probabilities of the confidence interval constructed based on bootstrap are generally very close to the nominal values. Two datasets are also analyzed in this paper with conclusions that are consistent with previous findings. This further verifies the reliability of our proposed method as well as its versatility in terms of being able to handle some new types of biasedness including length-biased on censored data with case cohort sampling. The third objective of this project is also achieved. 2. Another publication output entitled "Estimation and Inference of Quantile Regression for Survival Data under Biased Sampling" (see Publication #3 in Part C) considers also a generic framework for inference problems of censored quantile regression. One may view this project as an extension to the previous work as the AFT model can be regarded as a special case under the censored quantile regression framework. However, the censored quantile regression is a more flexible model that captures not only the mean behaviour of the failure time distribution but instead its distribution. Along a similar direction, we first propose an estimating equation for estimating the parameters of interest based on biased samples. The complexity of this model originates from the fact that we are interested in estimating the quantile regression parameters as a function of the quantile values. We then establish its uniform consistency as well as its weak convergence to a Gaussian process. Together with the aforementioned types of biased sampling mechanisms, we also extend the framework so that both types of length-biased sampling (censored first, length-biased afterwards and length-biased first, censored afterwards) can both be properly handled by this model. The first objective of the proposal is also achieved for this project. Since the variance of our proposed estimator based on its limiting distribution does not have a closed-form representation, we need to seek an alternative approach to provide a reasonable estimate for it standard error. While traditional bootstrap procedure can be a legitimate candidate, it can be potentially time consuming as it involves repeated solving of the objective function, which is again a translated problem that provides the same (or very close) solution as solving for the root of the estimating equation. A modification of Zeng and Lin (2008, Biostatistics) is considered in the paper to reduce the computational time. The new proposed method extends the scope of Zeng and Lin (2008)'s and applies it to estimate the variances of the regression parameters evaluated at different quantile values as a process. This paper also discusses an extension of using generalised method of moments (GMM) strategy to improve the efficiency of the estimation. The second objective of this project is reasonably achieved. Finally, similar to Publication #1, the paper includes an extensive set of simulations in order to demonstrate the benefits/performance of our point and variance estimation procedures. Two datasets are also analysed in the paper with some new findings that are not discussed in previous literature. 3. The three objectives are also achieved for another paper entitled "Value at Risk Simulation for High-dimensional Portfolios" (see Publication #6). In the field of finance/risk management, value-at-risks (VaRs) have been frequently adopted as an effective tool for calculating risk capital reserve as required by international banking regulatory bodies including Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). VaR is in fact defined as the quantile of the change in the value of the portfolio concerned over a pre specified investment period. With our experience in handling quantile estimation in the previous work, in this paper, we leverage the powerful tool of variable selection including LASSO to provide a more objective and accurate approach for VaR estimation. The framework considered involves a regression-based simulation procedure. Under mild regularity conditions, we can establish the model consistency as well as convergence results of the VaR estimates. The additional LASSO component allows a substantially larger set of basis functions to be included in the model so that the influential variables can be included in the estimation procedure, thus yielding more accurate VaR estimates. The computational burden is negligible compared with some existing procedures. Two simulations and a real data analysis are also presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of this new proposal. 4. For other projects, we also consider separate yet relevant issues that are related to either survival modelling or risk management applications. All these works involve careful analysis on the problems of interest justified by numerical examples/illustrations. The three objectives of the project are also expansively covered.

24300514.label: Major findings and research outcome
24300514.value: The main focus of this research project is to develop proper treatments for handling various biased samples under different semiparametric models. Existing methods tend to handle individual types of biased sampling with separate methods. To provide a unified solution, we have developed an estimation equation based approach for solving such a problem for the accelerated failure time (AFT) model, which is a competitive alternative to the Cox proportional hazards model; see Publication #1. Furthermore, due to the fact that quantile regression can provide a more flexible tool for modelling censored lifetime data, we also developed the corresponding treatment for such a rich class of models. In addition, we also investigated issues related to efficiency of the proposed estimator. These results are presented in Publication #3. Our study them on survival data also motivated us to investigate issues due to delayed treatment effects. A publication on such research is yield; see Publication #2. Noteworthy, although Publications #1 - #3 were submitted prior to the commencement of the grant, there was substantial work involved afterwards in order to address issues raised by referees. Not only a considerable number of new numerical results were produced, the structures of these papers as well as the technical arguments provided were extended significantly compared with their initial, preliminary versions. Upon success in developing a feasible treatment for quantile regression model, we also considered a relevant problem which that is related risk management. Specifically, we attempted to offer a variable selection procedure for estimating value-at-risk (VaR), one of the gold standard risk measures since its introduction in 1996 that has been widely adopted. Our framework is constructed upon the celebrated Longstaff and Schwartz (2001) model, a simulation, regression based approach for pricing. With the modern techniques developed for variable selection, we proposed also a simulation, regression based method that can more accurately estimate VaRs for complicated portfolios with nonlinear payoffs, which has been a challenge for the respective audience. In particular, we proved the asymptotic properties of our LASSO-based estimator and justified its effectiveness via extensive numerical examples. This work presented in Publication #6. Along this direction, we also studied some other issues including unit root properties of VaRs under various model, with the results published in Publication #4. Also, a paper on probability bounds for boundary crossing, which can also be applied to risk modelling, was also published; see Publication #5.

24300514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24300514.value: Our experience for biased data for the AFT and censored quantile regression models motivates us to connect these two models from a different perspective. This observation inspired us to come up with a new model that attempts to connect the AFT model with the quantile regression. Since the efficiency of quantile regression model parameter is also of great interest to both researchers and practitioners, with the translation from the quantile regression model to the AFT model, we proposed a more efficient method for censored quantile regression models. This work is an on-going project for another GRF grant proposal, which has shown some promising results. Furthermore, we may also connect biased sampling with importance sampling, which is a typical strategy for improving efficiency for estimating risk measures. This is of great concern of the modellers because a more accurate and efficient estimates of various risk measures allows institutions to better leverage the capital without being too aggressive in terms of risk to pursue any extra potential reward. Our work on VaR estimates encourages us to work along this direction. A manuscript on this has been prepared and is going to be sent out for review in a near future.

24300514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24300514.value: This research project enables researchers/end users to have unified methods to reliable estimate covariate effects of various models which are commonly applied in medical studies and/or financial industry. The occurrence of biasedness, either naturally arisen or by design, further complicates the statistical inference procedure. Without proper correction for these biased data, the conclusions made can potentially be misleading. In addition, this project also leverages recent techniques developed for variable selection to provide an objective and computationally fast solution for estimation of risk measures. The results can be applied for more accurate capital reserve calculations from which a higher level of safety can be ensured for financial institutes and hence the financial market. Other miscellaneous results that are related to quantile or mean estimates for various settings are also yielded under the generous support of this research grant.

24300614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24300614.value: The proposed research aims to investigate how the detrimental effects of ozone air pollution on ecosystems may influence air quality and climate through various physical, chemical and biological feedback mechanisms. Outdoor air pollution is among the most pressing environmental concerns today, and one of the most significant air pollutants is surface ozone, due to its harmful effects on human health, natural vegetation and crop productivity. While the major contributor to surface ozone is anthropogenic emissions of ozone precursors, both climate conditions and land surface characteristics are shown to substantially affect surface ozone concentration. A realistic assessment of future ozone air quality, which is necessary for sustainable urban planning, thus requires a better understanding of its complex interactions with emissions, climate, and the biosphere. A major uncertainty for future ozone projections is associated with the biogeochemical feedbacks involving vegetation. Physiological and biochemical changes in plants induced by chronic ozone exposure would modify several biosphere-atmosphere processes including the exchange of water vapor, emissions of organic gases from plants, and deposition of ozone and other gas molecules onto leaves, constituting important feedbacks between ozone, the biosphere and concentrations of aerosols and other greenhouse gases. Ozone-vegetation interaction is shown to significantly influence the hydrological and carbon cycles, but its impacts on atmospheric composition are largely unexplored and potentially significant, with ramifications for air quality and climate. To address this gap of knowledge, we will implement a new set of ozone-vegetation schemes into the Community Earth System Model that simulates the immediate interactions and feedbacks between climate, atmospheric chemistry and biosphere in a fully coupled configuration. We will conduct full-response, control and sensitivity simulations to quantify the impacts of ozone-vegetation feedbacks on atmospheric composition under changing emissions, climate and CO2 for the present (2000) and future (2050) following IPCC AR5 scenarios. Taking biogeochemical feedbacks into account, we will derive more reliable future projections for concentrations of ozone and other air pollutants, which are then used to evaluate the impacts on human health, agriculture and climate. Such findings are crucial for better policy formulation concerning air quality, land use and climate management. We also aim to develop a simplified ozone-vegetation parameterization scheme for use in stand-alone chemical transport models used in air quality assessment. This makes the inclusion of biogeochemical feedbacks in high-resolution regional models more computationally affordable for historical and future simulations, and represents an important contribution to geoscientific model development. 該研究項目旨在探討臭氧空氣污染對生態系統的破壞如何通過各種物理、化學和生物的反饋機制來影響空氣質素和氣候。室外空氣污染是當今最迫切的環境問題之一，地面臭氧更是其中一種最重要的空氣污染物，對人類健康、自然植被和農作物生產等均有嚴重損害。人為排放雖是臭氧污染的主因，但氣候條件和地表特徵均可顯著影響地表臭氧的濃度。要對未來臭氧空氣質量作出切實的評估，需更深入了解它與排放、氣候和生物圈之間複雜的相互作用，這是可持續城市規劃所必需的。未來臭氧預測的一個主要不確定因素來自涉及植物的生化反饋作用。長期暴露於高臭氧當中，會引致植物產生生理及化學上的變化，從而改變某些大氣生物圈過程，如水氣交換、有機化合物的天然排放、氣體在葉上的沉積等，構成臭氧、生物圈和其他溫室氣體或氣溶膠之間的重要反饋。科學家已發現臭氧與植被的相互作用對水和碳循環有著顯著影響，但仍未了解其對大氣成分、以至空氣​​質素和氣候的潛在影響。 有鑒於此，我們將會在CESM地球系統模式內實施一個新的臭氧植被機制，在完全耦合的配置下模擬氣候、大氣化學和生物圈之間的直接相互和反饋作用。我們將因應IPCC現在(2000年)及未來(2050年)各情況下排放量、氣候和二氧化碳濃度的改變，進行不同的模擬實驗，以量化臭氧植被反饋對大氣成分的影響。充分考慮生物地球化學的反饋，將幫助我們對臭氧濃度和其他空氣污染物作更可靠的預測，有助評估對人類健康、農業和氣候的影響，以在空氣質素、土地利用及氣候管理等方面制定更有效的政策。我們並會研發一個簡化的臭氧植被參數化方案，以使用於獨立運行的大氣化學模式當中，有助提升高析度區域大氣模式在模擬生物地球化學反饋時的計算效率，對地球科學模式的發展作出重要貢獻。

24300614.label: Realisation of objectives
24300614.value: The research plan and activities set forth in the proposal have been followed closely and conducted accordingly, and the three objectives have been achieved to a highly satisfactory extent. The findings of Objective #1 and #3 have already been published in three papers, while an additional publication on the findings of Objective #2 is currently under preparation. Objective #1 has been successfully achieved by using a global earth system model to examine the impacts of ozone-vegetation coupling and feedbacks on present-day atmospheric composition and ozone air quality. Indeed, the meteorological feedbacks (in addition to the biogeochemical feedbacks) we have found in this study are very strong and influential, representing an exciting, new finding that we did not expect in the original proposal. Our results have been published in a top-ranking journal in the atmospheric and climate sciences: Sadiq, M., Tai, A. P. K., Lombardozzi, D., & Val Martin, M. (2017). Effects of ozone-vegetation coupling on surface ozone air quality via biogeochemical and meteorological feedbacks. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 17(4), 3055-3066. Objective #3 has also been successfully achieved by using a land surface model to parameterize how leaf area index (LAI) responds to ozone exposure, and implementing the parameterization in a chemical transport models. The findings of this part of the project have been published in a top-ranking journal in the atmospheric and climate sciences: Zhou, S. S., Tai, A. P. K.*, Sun, S., Sadiq, M., Heald, C. L., & Geddes, J. A. (2018). Coupling between surface ozone and leaf area index in a chemical transport model: strength of feedback and implications for ozone air quality and vegetation health. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 18(19), 14133-14148. In relation to Objective #3, we have also tried to parameterize how ozone concentration may respond to changes in LAI (thus closing the two-way feedback loop) using mostly a chemical transport model. The results have been published in a high-ranking journal in the atmospheric and climate sciences: Wong, A. Y. H., Tai, A. P. K., & Ip, Y.-Y. (2018). Attribution and statistical parameterization of the sensitivity of surface ozone to changes in leaf area index based on a chemical transport model. Journal of Geophysical Research-Atmospheres, 123(3), 1883-1898. Objective #2 has also been achieved to a satisfactory extent. The model experiments and simulations for various future scenarios of anthropogenic emissions over the 21st century have been carried out successfully to quantify how ozone-vegetation coupling may affect both public health and vegetation health in the future. The findings are currently being finalized and prepared into a manuscript intended for publication in a high-impact journal.

24300614.label: Major findings and research outcome
24300614.value: Plants play significant roles in modulating atmospheric chemistry via biogenic emissions, dry deposition and transpiration, and all of these are closely tied to physiological functions such as photosynthesis and stomatal aperture. As ozone damages plants, these functions can be greatly altered, leading to potentially important but unexplored feedback effects on air quality. This research project has been the first to study such feedbacks between ozone and vegetation. By implementing in an earth system model a scheme to account for ozone damage on plants, we created the first framework that can allow ecosystem structure and ozone concentration to coevolve dynamically within a model, and found that ozone-induced reductions in dry deposition and transpiration and the resulting temperature rise could substantially increase simulated ozone, representing a strong self-amplifying effect of ozone via ozone-vegetation coupling that is previously unknown [Sadiq et al., 2017]. We further focused on the dynamic interactions between ozone and leaf area index (LAI). We developed and implemented into an atmospheric chemical transport model (CTM) a new statistical parameterization for ozone-LAI relationship, so that, for the first time, ozone-LAI coupling could be dynamically simulated in a CTM. We found that the large ozone-induced decline in LAI alone could already lead to a strong positive ozone-vegetation feedback [Zhou et al., 2018]. We further examined the effects of ozone-vegetation coupling on 21st-century air quality and vegetation health, and found that in the ever-increasing anthropogenic emissions can generate more air pollution than previously predicted due to the self-strengthening effect of ozone-vegetation interactions, but active pollution mitigation measures as well as forest resource protection can yield the double-benefit of securing both public and ecosystem health. Overall, our findings highlight the need to consider two-way ozone-vegetation interactions in models to derive a better understanding and future predictions of air quality and ecosystem health especially under simultaneous climate and land-use changes. Our studies often point to the difficulty in diagnosing the relative importance of different plant-mediated pathways that affect ozone. To tackle this, we systematically performed a series of CTM experiments and used the outputs to build a statistical model that can predict the effect of any LAI change on surface ozone, and diagnose the contribution from different pathways, thus providing a useful tool for scientists and practitioners to evaluate the effects of land cover change on air quality [Wong et al., 2018].

24300614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24300614.value: We have successfully proven that ozone damage on plants can initiate a cascade of feedback mechanisms that ultimately affect climate and air quality, but the projections still suffer from large uncertainties mostly due not to the mechanisms per se but to the input parameters concerning plant ecophysiology. The sensitivity of different plant types to ozone damage can vary substantially, and even the same plant type may respond differently to ozone under varying conditions especially as soil water availability fluctuates on synoptic timescales and soil nitrogen content changes on interannual timescales. These are active topics of research in our research group now, all stemming from this research project. A particularly important direction is to integrate global observations and field experimental results to better constrain plant-ozone relationships for a greater variety of plant types and under varying conditions, so that the large uncertainty in simulating and predicting ozone-vegetation interactions on multiple spatial scales can be reduced. To further examine how soil water stress and nitrogen content may interfere with plant-ozone relationships (with a special focus on integrating experimental data), research funding is currently being sought from various sources.

24300614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24300614.value: Plants play significant roles shaping air quality through absorbing various air pollutants, emitting organic compounds that participate in atmospheric chemistry, and regulating the water vapor content in air. Meanwhile, ozone is a significant air pollutant with harmful effects on both human and plant health. As ozone damages plants, all the above functions can be greatly altered, leading to potentially important but unexplored self-strengthening or self-weakening “feedback” effects on ozone air quality. Our research was the first to study such feedbacks between ozone and vegetation. By implementing in computer models various numerical schemes to account for ozone damage on plants, we created the first modeling framework that fully represents the two-way ozone-vegetation interactions, and found that ozone damage can reduce the ability of plants to absorb pollutants and increase surface temperature, both leading to further enhancements in ozone levels. This represents a strong self-amplifying effect of ozone through ozone-vegetation coupling that is previously unknown. Such “positive feedbacks” could lead to even worse ozone pollution than previously predicted for the coming 21st century, and call for more active pollution mitigation measures as well as forest resource protection to safeguard both human and ecosystem health.

24300714.label: Project Objectives
24300714.value: Improve the rational genus bound of knots in three-manifolds and establish the rational four-ball genus bound in the corresponding product four-manifolds. Relate these genus bounds to the genus problem in four-manifolds. Investigate properties of Floer simple knots, L-spaces and their connections to fundamental group. Apply the rational genus bounds to study one-sided Heegaard splittings, the complexity of three-manifolds and other related classical questions in low-dimensional topology.

24300714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24300714.value: This project studies invariants from Heegaard Floer homology and their applications in topological and geometric objects in low-dimension. Heegaard Floer homology is a (3+1)-dimensional topological quantum field theory that has close ties to gauge theoretical invariants originated from mathematical physics. It is an infinite dimensional version of Morse theory which has been used to construct various invariants of knots, three-manifolds and four-manifolds. Floer homology and the associated invariants are some of the most useful tools for classifying and detecting properties of three- and four-dimensional manifolds, on which the shape of our universe is modeled. In this project, the PI aims at achieving a deeper geometric understanding of certain classes of knots (Floer simple knot, simple knot) and three-manifolds (L-spaces, multi-point strong L-spaces) that naturally arise from Heegaard Floer homology. We examine their connections to other aspects of low-dimensional topology such as rational genus, fundamental group and one-sided Heegaard genus. This in turn brings in new insight and may lead to significant progress in complexity problem in three-manifolds, genus problems in four-manifolds, and other related classical problems in low-dimensional topology. 此课题研究Heegaard Floer同调群之不变量及它们在低维拓扑和几何上的应用。 Heegaard Floer同调群源起于数学物理中的规范场论，属于（3+1）维的拓扑量子场理论。它也可类比成无穷维的Morse理论，并由此构造各类三维、四维或纽结不变量。这些不变量对于三、四维流形的分类和性质的研究有重要帮助。 在此课题中，项目负责人希望能更好的理解某些Heegaard Floer同调中某些特殊纽结（如Floer简单结...)及三维流形（如L-空间...)，同时探索它们和低维拓扑中的有理亏格、基本群以及单边Heegaard亏格的联系。 这些都将有助于我们在三维流形复杂度问题，四维流行的最小亏格问题等经典低维拓扑问题取得重要进展。

24300714.label: Major findings and research outcome
24300714.value: In addition to achieving the original 3 objectives, we defined a concordance invariant nu+ that results to a (arbitrarily) better bound of slice genus than the classical tau invariant of Ozsvath and Szabo. In some sense, this is also the strongest concordance obstruction that one can possibly extract from the Heegaard Floer theory. In addition, we obtained a cabling formula for nu+ in certain ranges.

24300714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24300714.value: There are several potential projects on nu+ invariant: such as, the relationship of unknotting number and nu+ invariant of a knot; the nu+ equivalence relation, etc. With new techniques on bordered immersed curve recently developed, more output may be produced regarding Floer simple knots and L-spaces.

24300714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24300714.value: The PI wrote 4 journal papers and 1 proceeding paper under the support of this grant. Among them, the work on nu+ invariant is particularly interesting and is playing an important role in the field of knot theory and low dimensional topology, particularly in areas relating to the cobordism and concordance group. Due to the significance and influnce of this work, the PI was invited to give a Keynote Speech at the Eleventh East Asian School of Knots and Related Topics. Since then, it has inspired many further collaborations and work among researchers.

24300814.label: Project Objectives
24300814.value: Study the size effect of magnetic dopants in a model material system, Bi2Se3. The study will cover the dopants of magnetic metal elements. We plan to calculate the stresses and lattice deformations induced by most of the magnetic metal dopants. Also, for each magnetic dopant, we will calculate its size effect on ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states. Based on this knowledge, we will have an overview of the stresses induced by them. Also, we’ll calculate the dopant formation energy of each dopant and check the relationship between the dopant induced volume change and the dopant formation energy. Apply the external strains to enhance the magnetic dopants concentrations and control magnetic properties. Based on our results of the first step, we can apply external strains intelligently to the TI lattice and check how the dopant formation energies change with external strains. At the same time, we’ll also calculate the magnetic moment of each dopant under external strains. We expect that the external strains may largely change the crystal field splitting and exchange splitting of the dopant and change the electron occupation on each energy level and the spin state of the dopant. We’ll especially focus on how the strains will control the spin ordering, magnetic ordering, electron orbit ordering, and their interactions. We will find the critical strain value for each dopant that would change the dopant from low spin state to high spin state. Some codoping pairs will also be studied.
