28400214.label: Major findings and research outcome
28400214.value: We found multiple subtypes of math difficulties among Chinese children. In particular, we identified 4 subtypes of math difficulties in Grade 1 (i.e., number sense deficit, numerosity coding deficit, symbolic deficit, and mild difficulty) and 5 subtypes in Grade 2 (i.e., number sense deficit, numerosity coding deficit, symbolic deficit, working memory deficit, and mild difficulty). About 62% of the children were consistently classified into the same deficit group in both grades, suggesting reasonable stability in the subtypes of MD across time. The findings were accepted for publication in Journal of Educational Psychology (Impact Factor=4.433; 96 percentile in educational psychology; see Part C 8.2), and presented in the Association for Psychological Science Annual Convention (see Part C 9.3). Based on the data collected, we did additional analyses regarding the relation between visuospatial working memory and math achievement. We identified the mediating roles of numerical magnitude representation and problem representation. The findings were published in Learning and Instruction (Impact Factor=3.967; 94 percentile in educational psychology; see Part C 8.1). Further analyses on the data also found that place-value concept predicted children’s math achievement well. The result was presented in Annual Conference of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education (see Part C 9.2). We also developed an intervention program for elementary school children with math difficulties to help them to learn place-value concept. Using a pretest-posttest design, we found that children who attended the place-value program showed better understanding in place-value concept afterwards than their counterparts who did not attend the program. The findings were presented in the 40th International School Psychology Association Conference (see Part C 9.1). The intervention program is now freely downloadable on the website of Education Bureau for teachers to use in their teaching (see Part C 12.1).

28400214.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28400214.value: Based on the findings on the cognitive profiles of subtypes of children, we can do follow-up assessment with the children to trace their development in different domains of math, so as to gain better understanding of the cognitive development of these children. We have attempted to do follow-up assessment with them in Grades 3 and Grades 4 and will try to trace their development in the coming years. For the place-value intervention program, we have submitted an application to an internal grant (Knowledge Exchange Fund) from the University of Hong Kong to further improve the program (e.g., make it more child-friendly) and develop it into a mobile app so that children can learn it at their own time and pace.

28400214.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28400214.value: The project has found that children who have mathematical difficulties can be classified into subgroups with different cognitive deficits. In particular, we identified 4 subtypes of math difficulties in Grade 1 (i.e., number sense deficit, numerosity coding deficit, symbolic deficit, and mild difficulty) and 5 subtypes in Grade 2 (i.e., number sense deficit, numerosity coding deficit, symbolic deficit, working memory deficit, and mild difficulty). About 62% of the children were consistently classified into the same deficit group in both grades, suggesting reasonable stability in the subtypes of MD across time. These findings help us better understand the underlying cognitive challenges faced by children with mathematical difficulties. To help these children in learning mathematics, we have developed an intervention program on place-value concept and arithmetic skills. An evaluation study has provided support for the effectiveness of the program. The program is now freely downloadable from the website of Education Bureau for local teachers to use.

28400614.label: Project Objectives
28400614.value: to investigate the relations between poverty status and learning outcomes including language and cognitive ability among Hong Kong kindergarten pupils in a two-year longitudinal study; to investigate the role of parental educational expectation and investment as a mediator between family income and learning outcomes including language and cognitive ability among kindergarten pupils in Hong Kong; and to investigate the role of family stress and parenting style as a mediator between family income and learning outcomes including language and cognitive ability among kindergarten pupils in Hong Kong.

28400614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28400614.value: According to the 2011 Hong Kong Population Census, 275,360 children aged 17 or below were living in households with income falling below the newly established poverty line. Despite receiving better welfare protection relative to their counterparts in developing countries, underprivileged children living in an affluent society like Hong Kong often experienced additional harm as a result of their relatively disadvantaged position in society. Education used to be an important means for these underprivileged children to achieve upward social mobility and to break the cycles of intergenerational poverty. Nevertheless, recent developments in Hong Kong show that education inequality is replicating social stratification which is causing concern whether education remains an effective means to help underprivileged children to escape poverty. In order to introduce target intervention to break the link between poverty and poor educational outcome, one has to understand the mechanism in the process. Since the mechanisms that mediate the relationship between poverty and learning outcomes has been little-researched in Hong Kong, our proposed two-year longitudinal study aims at examining the roles of parents’ educational expectation, educational investment, parental stress and parenting style as potential mediators to the relationship. 300 five-year-old children attending the final year of kindergarten education (K3), with half from disadvantaged families, will be recruited via stratified random sampling and followed through until their second year primary education (P2). The children will undertake Raven’s Standard Progressive Matrices test to measure their non-verbal cognitive ability. They will also undertake standardized language tests in both Cantonese and English which will indicate their readiness for literacy instruction in their first and second language. With respect to the home mediating variables, we will interview children’s parents during baseline assessment as well as the two-year follow-up assessment to collect data on parental educational expectation, educational investment, parental stress and parenting style, and assess their relative importance in mediating the impact of poverty on children’s learning outcomes. All these measurement and tests will be done at the baseline assessment and the two-year follow-up assessment. Results from the study will inform policy makers on the nature of intervention that will empower children living with poverty to compete with their peers from more advantageous backgrounds on a level playing field. 根據2011年的香港人口普查，現時全港共有275,360名17歲以下的貧窮兒童。相比起落後地區的兒童，香港的貧窮兒童雖然有較好的社會福利保障，但卻因在貧富懸殊的香港社會環境中處於弱勢，他們的成長同樣受到限制。教育一直被視為向上流動及防止跨代貧窮的主要途徑，但近年香港社會的發展出現因家庭社經地位差距而引伸的教育機會不平等，令人憂慮教育能否繼續幫助低下階層兒童脫貧。為使有效改善貧窮對兒童教育的負面影响，我們希望通過是次研究了解兩者關係的內在機制。這次研究將會追踪300名來自不同社會階層的兒童，通過一些智力及語言測試了解他們從幼兒班高班(K3) 到小學二年級(P2) 這段期間的學習能力發展。我們亦會訪問學童的父母，了解在這段期間家長對子女的教育期望，教育方面的投資，家長精神壓力及教育方式對他們的學習能力的影响。這些測試及訪問將會在研究的初期和末段進行以作比較。這次研究的結果將有助制定適切的政策幫助香港的貧窮兒童，使他們能在一個更公平的環境下成長。

28401514.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28401514.value: 許多人類行為背後的心理過程都是隨著時間而變化的動態過程。對於這種動態過程的研究需要心理學者採用對同一組受試群體進行多次採樣的追蹤研究。潛變量曲線模型是追蹤數據分析方法中被廣泛應用的統計方法之一。從概念上來講，潛變量分析模型是採用結構方程模型作為架構對個體發展過程進行分析的一種統計方法。這種分析方法使得研究者可以評估個體心理在某一特定時間段的發展或改變及心理過程發展是否存在個體差異 常用的潛變量模型假設個體的心理發展過程在所觀察的時間段內具有齊性。意思是對所有被試在同一時間點進行所有的測量，並且所有個體在所有測量階段的間距都是相同的。然而，考慮到實際條件的限制比如時間，人力，受試者的心理過程的發生點的不同等，在很多情況下，要所有受試者在同一天或同一時間點完成所有測試，對研究者來說是非常困難或是不可能的。目前常用的潛變量模型並沒有很好的解決數據的時間相關性這一問題。因此，當所有測量齊性這一假設不能滿足時，應用當前的常用潛變量模型對存在時間依存問題的數據進行分析可能會導致不准確或有偏頗的結果。 雖然目前還有其他的分析方法可以對存在著時間依存問題的數據進行分析，但當前的結構方程模型分析方法不是操作起來技術上難以實現，就是很少有結構方程模型軟件能支援對這種對存在時間依存關係的數據進行分析的方法。因此，當前研究的最主要的目的是研究出更佳和更靈活的分析程序，利用傳統結構方程模型的框架發展出可以用於分析時間依存追踪數據的分析方法。這種結構方程模型分析方法將讓研究員能更靈活地對追踪數據進行分析。 眾所周知，用於對發展過程進行分析的不同的統計方法具有不同的內在的統計假設，並且這些方法在不同建模過程中具有不同的表現。然而，具我們所知，目前並沒有研究曾系統性地分析和評估過這些不同的方法對時間依存追踪數據進行分析的不同的表現。因此，此研究的另一個目的將會比較我們所提出的研究方法和傳統的方法在分析對時間依存追踪數據進行分析的結果表現的異同。這一研究結果不僅會幫助研究者在對時間依存數據進行分析時怎樣選擇合適的統計方法提供有用的參考，同時也能驗證我們所提出的新方法在哪種情況下分析時間依存數據有最佳的表現。

28401514.label: Realisation of objectives
28401514.value: Objective 1 “To develop a better method for applied researcher to analyse growth curve model with time-dependent observations under the traditional SEM framework” was well achieved as evidenced by the new model that we have developed in this project for conducting latent growth curve analysis. In this project, we have used the model reparamterization technique to develop a new model for latent growth curve analysis in structural equation modeling (SEM). This newly developed model is better than the traditional latent growth curve model for analysing longitudinal data in at least two aspects: 1. Our new model can handle longitudinal data with time-dependent observation. Traditional latent growth curve model in SEM captures the variable of time as fixed parameters (i.e. factor loadings on the growth factor) in the model. This implies that researchers must assume all participants to begin the study at the same time and the time interval between measurements must also be the same for all individuals. If this assumption is violated, the estimation and the test of parameters will be biased. Our new model has overcome this constraint and incorporate the time variables as observed variables in the model. This feature allows researchers to take the inter-individual heterogeneity of time of measurement of each observations into account. Using the new model, researchers can handle longitudinal data with time-dependent observations easily. 2. Our new model is a general model for modeling different growth patterns. Traditional latent growth curve model requires researchers to presume the growth pattern and specify the factor loadings according to the hypothesized growth pattern (e.g. 1, 1, 1, … for linear pattern, and 1, 4, 9, … for quadratic pattern) before conducting the analysis. In other words, the model specification varies with different types of growth pattern. In contrast, our model is a general model for studying different growth patterns. The growth curve pattern is modelled as a free parameter in our model and is estimated based on the data instead of specifying by the researchers. This reduces the burden on the researchers as it helps to avoid specification error and provide more flexibility for the researchers when they have no idea about the pattern of growth. The validity and efficiency of the newly developed model has been tested by using computer simulation study. Results from the simulation study has provided empirical evidences to support the accuracy and adequacy of the new model for analysing longitudinal data with time-dependent observations. Hence objective 1 was achieved. Objective 2 “To provide recommendations for the applied researcher about the conditions at which the proposed method works best by comparing the performance of different approaches for the analysis of growth curve model with time-dependent observations under different model conditions” was also well addressed. In order to provide recommendations for applied researchers about when our new method works best, we have run a series of simulation studies to compare the performance and efficiency of our new method, the definition variable approach (an alternative SEM method for latent growth curve analysis), and the multilevel modeling approach for handling longitudinal data with time-dependent observations under different model conditions including sample size, number of waves, variation in time of measurement, homogeneity of error variances, and types of growth pattern. Based on the results of the simulation study, the recommendations for the applied researchers can be briefly summarized as follow: 1. A minimum sample size of 200 is usually recommended. 2. When the assumption of homogeneity of error variances is violated, both our method and the definition variable approach are recommended. 3. When linear growth curve pattern is assumed, all methods perform satisfactorily in terms of model estimation and testing. However, if researcher has lack of knowledge about the growth curve pattern, our method works best and is highly recommended because researcher do not need to presume any pattern of growth when he/she is specifying the model, whereas the model specification of the other two approaches presume a specific growth pattern and parameters will be estimated poorly when the presumed pattern is violated. 4. Non-convergence of our method can usually be solved by setting better start value. These recommendations for applied researchers have been disseminated in international conferences and workshop. During the project period, the PI shared the project findings at two large-scale international conferences (31st International Congress of Psychology and 29th Association for Psychological Science Annual Convention). A Structural Equation Modeling Workshop on Latent Growth Curve Analysis was organized on 28 December 2017 (see details in Section 12). The project team is working on journal publication which will further promote the method and recommendations to more researchers in various disciplines. Hence, objective 2 was achieved.

28401514.label: Major findings and research outcome
28401514.value: In this project, we have developed a new SEM method for latent growth curve analysis. The new latent growth curve model allows researchers to analyze the individual trajectory of change and differences in individual trajectories even though individuals have their own metric of time and observations are measured at different time points (Kwan, 2016; Kwan & Chan, 2017; Kwan & Chan, 2018). Through a series of simulation studies, we have tested the efficiency and performance of the new method (Kwan & Chan, 2017) and have compared its performance with other alternative approaches for growth curve analysis with time-dependent observations. First, results from the simulation study have supported that our method performed satisfactorily in parameter estimation with relative bias in estimation as small as 0.01% for some parameters. Under all model conditions except when sample size is small (N = 100), the method had good control in Type I error rate (i.e. close to the nominal Type I error rate of 5%) and achieved a statistical power of over 0.9 for the test of growth-related parameters such as mean intercept, mean slope, variance of intercept and variance of slope (Kwan & Chan, 2017; Kwan & Chan, 2018). Second, compared with the definition variable approach, both methods showed comparable performance under all model conditions except in conditions with quadratic growth pattern. The model specification under the definition variable approach requires researchers to presume the growth pattern whereas our method is a general method, of which the model specification is invariant to the growth pattern. Therefore, parameters were poorly estimated in the definition variable approach when model with a quadratic growth trajectory was fit, whereas our method continued to performance satisfactorily. The results of the simulation study support our method as a better method in term of its flexibility to evaluate different types of growth pattern using a unified model specification. Finally, compared to the multilevel modeling (MLM) approach, our methods also outperformed the MLM approach in term of parameter estimation when the homogeneity of error variances and linear pattern could not be assumed. Under other condition, both methods performed similarly (Kwan & Chan, 2018). In conclusion, the findings of this project have showed that our newly developed method is a valid and reliable method for analyzing longitudinal data with time-dependent observations. The method provides a better alternative for applied researchers to conduct latent growth curve analysis under traditional SEM framework.

28401514.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28401514.value: Further development of the research can be focused on two areas. The first area is the application of the new method in theoretical study. The new method is particular useful to research that make use of longitudinal data with time-dependent observations. For example, in a public health study, visitors of health center have irregular visits throughout a period of time, and the health records of these visitors are time-dependent in nature. Therefore, our method can be applied to study the health trajectories of these visitors. Future studies may explore the usefulness of the method in Big Data analysis that involves public health or clinical data. The second area is the novel use of model reparameterization technique in SEM. This project has demonstrated how to use the model reparameterization technique to develop a new model that overcome the limitation of traditional method for conducting latent growth curve analysis. Future studies may investigate how this technique can be used to overcome other model limitations as set up by the traditional methods in SEM.

28401514.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28401514.value: A new latent growth curve model has been developed in this project for studying change across individuals. Latent growth curve analysis (LCA) is a statistical approach for modeling individual trajectory of change within the structural equation modeling framework. It helps researchers to estimate the change over time and test the differences in change across individuals. Since many human behaviors are dynamic in nature, LCA becomes one of the most common methods for studying change in psychological research. Nevertheless, traditional LCA method assumes the timing of observations to be the same across all individuals and may lead to biased results when this assumption is violated. Hence, this assumption imposes a limitation on the method because it is sometimes impractical to collect all data at the same time due to various constraints in longitudinal studies. The significance and value of our new method is that it overcomes this limitation and take the individual differences in the time of measurements into account. The method can accurately estimate the change and difference in change across individuals even individuals have their own metric of time. Our method undoubtedly provides a better and more flexible alternative for applied researchers to conduct LCA analysis with time-dependent observations.

28401614.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28401614.value: 香港性小眾/同志學生在學校是否受到平等對待仍然面臨挑戰。研究性小眾歧視的學者認為性小眾在社會受到歧視是因為人们對非異性戀者抱有偏見。在各種消除學校歧視和偏見的策略中，性/别多元化教師培訓是一個有效的方法消除歧視和偏見。 本計劃的目標是： 1)發展一套本地化的性/别多元化教師培訓課程; 2) 評估上述課程的成效。與此同時，本計劃將探討相關的教育策略/政策，以達到平等共融的教育理念。

28401614.label: Realisation of objectives
28401614.value: Objective 1 To identify training themes through qualitative study. Objective achieved through the following tasks: Through document analysis and literature review, we found that heterosexism and genderism against sexual minorities persist in most Asian Chinese societies, including Hong Kong, where protective and anti-prejudice policies and support programs for students and teachers were nonexistent or insufficient. Heteronormative socio-cultural climate in Hong Kong makes it difficult to establish support programs without initiatives from the government. Based on this review and other community observations in public forums, we realized the challenges of facing prejudice as research team members and the difficulties in recruiting informants under heteronormative atmosphere. Strategies were used to overcome the challenges, such as obtaining institutional supports, offering individual in addition to group interviews; prolonged engagement, and persistent community observations etc. to maintain collaborative relationship with stakeholders, so as to collect information-rich data. By using these strategies, we were able to recruit 85 informants, and such sample size has surpassed the originally proposed size by 70%. We learnt from informants on how they perceived sexual diversity, sexual prejudice, sexual minority students’ experiences, and how sexual prejudice has been constructed in the society and in school settings. We were informed about the narratives of diverse sexual/gender identities, including those with fluid, non-binary, and multiple identities on the sexual/gender variant spectrum, in addition to those whose sexual identities fall within cisgender, and binary spectrum. They faced multiple stigma by not being acknowledged of their sexualities and gender identities in schools, families, and communities in their everyday life. We also learned that informants in the education sectors faced dilemma/institutional barriers in understanding diverse sexualities of sexual minority students. Community support programs run by organizations with LGBQ-friendly and rights-based perspective filled in the gap left by the education sector. Training themes, cultural limitations, and strategies in conducting sexual diversity training were informed by the informants. Objective 2 To examine the effectiveness of the training program with validated tools. The following tasks were completed to achieve the objective: Related to informants’ suggestions from qualitative interviews, we modified the recruitment and sampling method, as well as training content and format to better engage informants to join the training workshop outside the school contexts. Training location was suggested to be changed to professional organizations and training institutes; non-random sampling was adopted instead of random sampling; the contents focused on 1) attitudes/awareness - how cultural factors had constructed sexual prejudice; 2) updated concepts and research studies on sexual diversity; 3) Narratives and panel sharing were adopted as strategies to illustrate key issues faced by sexual minority students in Hong Kong. The training used workshop format instead of small groups. We validated tools to measure attitudes, knowledge, and behaviors of the participants, and the tools yielded good to excellent internal consistency. 327 participants participated in the training sessions from the education settings were divided into control group and two different experimental groups, which was education-only, and combined education-contact format (with additional face-to-face dialogue between participants and sexual minorities). Results from one-way between-group ANCOVA showed that there were significant differences between the control and both experimental groups (education-only and education-contact) on attitude and knowledge scales.

To examine the effectiveness of the anti-sexual prejudice teacher training program in improving teachers’ attitudes, knowledge, and anticipated professional behaviors to support sexual minority students.

28401614.label: Major findings and research outcome
28401614.value: Literature review found that sexual and transprejudice persist in Asian cities, where anti-prejudice policies and support programs are nonexistent or insufficient. Heteronormative and cisgender-centered socio-cultural climate in Hong Kong makes it difficult to set up school-based support program without government initiatives. Semi-structured interviews with 85 informants found that there were gaps observed between educator and sexual minority informants on the attitudes to and knowledge on sexual diversity. Majority educator informants adopted concepts of binary sex /gender, feeling uncomfortable to talk about gender variant and non-binary sexualities/gender identities. Specifically, they had limited understanding on students with multiple stigmatized identities. On the other hand, sexual minority informants felt more comfortable and well-informed about sexual diversity knowledge based on their lived experiences and initiatives to seek knowledge around sexuality concerns. Informants in both groups indicated that cultural forces, such as religious values and Confucian family belief, contributed to the manifestation of sexual prejudice in school context. Educator informants faced institutional barriers in addition to individual level barriers. A subgroup of educator informants engaged in self-reflexivity to explore their value dilemma when they encountered conflicts between personal and professional values. Informants found that even if they were equipped with knowledge and with supportive attitude, they were still reluctant to support sexual minority students formally for fear of being targeted. Schools appeared to them as unsafe to openly support sexual minority students and to participate in training. Thus, out of school community support services played essential roles in filling the educational and training gaps. The following training themes emerged: To start teachers’ training officially; Awareness of cultural factors in constructing/contesting sexual/transprejudice; Holistic perspective and updated perspectives of sexuality; Engaging trainees with cultural competent skills. Due to the heteronormative climate in school, training format and contents should address cultural realities of educators’ context, to ensure a safe space for them to discuss barriers/dilemma, and to protect them from sexual prejudice. Based on the themes, teacher training workshops adopting an experimental intervention-control-group design were carried out with 327 participants. Scales examining the training effectiveness were validated with good to excellent internal consistency. Results from one-way between-group ANCOVA showed that there were significant differences between the control and both experimental groups (education-only and education-contact) on attitude and knowledge scales, but not the behavioral scale, indicating that the training was found in improving teacher's attitudes and knowledges to support sexual minority students, but not in improving their intended behaviors.

28401614.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28401614.value: Based on this research, we found that gender minorities, such as gender variant, gender non-binary students, and gender and sexual minorities who fell within the disability group (such as students with special educational needs) suffered multiple marginalization in the school system. Two projects will be carried out to understand transgender prejudice and community support experience of gender variant and gender non-binary individuals. A pilot project will be started in August 2018 on community and family supports to gender minorities. Another project proposal on transgender prejudice has been submitted. A postgraduate student under the PI’s supervision has started a project on exploring sexuality experience of disability students.

28401614.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28401614.value: The study is of significance by reporting the difficulties, dilemma, and professional training themes of educators in supporting sexual minority students in Hong Kong schools. It also reveals and acknowledges the existence of diverse sexual and gender expressions/identities of sexual minorities, including those most invisible ones with fluid, non-binary, and multiple stigmatized identities on the sexuality spectrum, in addition to those whose sex, sexual orientation, and gender identities fall within cisgender, and binary spectrum. Validation of the Chinese translated scales to measure attitudes, knowledge and intended behaviors of educators to support sexual minorities has contributed to the advancement of quantitative measurement for researchers in Hong Kong or other Chinese-speaking regions. Qualitative study was adopted to understand teacher training themes, and the cultural barriers to implement the training in Hong Kong. Quantitative study has confirmed that the training is effective in enhancing teacher’s attitudes and knowledge to support sexual minority students, but not their intended behaviors. Both quantitative and qualitative study demonstrated that educators, even equipped with supportive attitude and essential knowledge on sexual diversity, appeared to/might have reservation and difficulties to step forward with supportive behaviors to support sexual minority students in school context. This gap warrants further investigation.

28401714.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28401714.value: Emotionally competent children fare better across multiple domains of adjustment. Therefore, the socialization of children's emotions is a topic of great interest to both scholars and practitioners. Most prior research, however, has focused on the direct links between mothers’ emotion socialization practices and child outcomes, and little is known about (a) whether socializers other than mothers play a unique role in children’s emotional development; (b) how parents’ socialization beliefs may affect their emotion socialization practices; and (c) how parents’ emotion socialization practices may interact with children's characteristics to affect child adjustment. Moreover, nearly all existing studies on parental emotion socialization are based on European American families – the situation in other countries, including China, remains underexplored. Grounded in theories of fathering, gender socialization, and differential susceptibility, the goal of the proposed study is to fill some of these gaps in the literature by examining (a) whether fathers’ and mothers’ emotion socialization practices independently contribute to children’s emotional competence; (b) how parents’ gender attitudes may shape their emotion socialization practices for sons and daughters; and (c) how child temperament, particularly fearfulness and emotional negativity, may moderate the links between parental emotion socialization practices and child emotional outcomes in a sample of Chinese families. The proposed study will employ a two-wave longitudinal design, and collect data from about 300 second-year kindergarten children, and their fathers, mothers, and class teachers, for 2 consecutive years. Local kindergartens will be classified into three strata (i.e., high, middle, and low) based on the median household income of the districts where the kindergartens are located, and invitation letters will be sent until two kindergartens in each stratum are recruited. Twice in the study, children will be interviewed during class periods and given tasks on knowledge about emotion display rules, emotion understanding and perspective taking abilities, and emotion regulation; parents will be sent separate questionnaire packages on their own emotion socialization practices and gender attitudes and their children’s temperament; and class teachers will be asked to rate the expressivity, understanding, and regulation of emotions for each participating student in their classes. On a theoretical level, the proposed study will add to the literature by illuminating the potentially important roles of fathers, parental gender attitudes, and child temperament in understanding emotion socialization processes; on an applied level, it will provide insights for designing effective programs by elucidating what parents can do to promote their children’s emotional competence. 情緒智商較高的孩子，在行為、社交和學業方面都有較好的表現。所以，家長對子女情緒智商的社教化，一直受到學者和教育工作者的重視。可是，現存的相關硏究，大多著重母親的社教行為對子女的直接影響；我們對於（a）父親的影響、（b）家長的想法如何影響他們的社教行為和（c）家長的社教行為對不同特質的孩子的特殊影響，認識並不深切。另外，現存的相關硏究大多於歐美國家進行，我們對其他國家的情況，包括中國，幾乎一無所知。這項硏究以父親教養理論、性別角色社教化理論和兒童氣質理論作基礎，嘗試在香港這個中國社會中，探討以下三大問題： （a）父親對子女情緒智商的社教化，是否扮演獨特的角色？ （b）家長對性別角色的看法，會否影響他們對兒子和女兒情緒智商的社教行為？ （c）子女的人格氣質，尤其是驚恐和負面情緒的敏感度，會否調節父母社教化對他們的影響？ 這項硏究將追蹤大約三百個二年級的幼稚園學生，並從這些學生本身，和他們的父母和班主任，獲取數據。我們將把本地的幼稚園，按照地區的社經情況分為高中低三個階層，並在每一階層邀請兩間幼稚園參與硏究。我們將在上課時間訪問學生，了解他們對情緒表達、情緒認知和情緒控制的能力；家長則會填寫問卷，就自已對子女情緒智商的社教行為和性別角色定型，以及子女的人格氣質提供資料；班主任亦會填寫問卷，為班上每一位參與硏究的學生，提供有關情緒智商的資料。在理論層面，這項硏究將闡明父親的參與、家長的性別角色定型和子女的人格氣質，如何幫助我們了解家長對子女情緒智商的貢獻。在應用層面，這項硏究將幫助教育工作者設計有效的課程及家長工作坊，幫助家長在日常生活中，提升子女的情緒智商。

28401714.label: Realisation of objectives
28401714.value: This project examined the importance of socioemotional competence in the preschool years. It also examined the roles of parental beliefs (objective 2) and practices (objective 1), as well as child temperament (objective 3), in child socioemotional development. Important features of this project included the use of both qualitative and quantitative methods, and the reliance on multiple informants, to address several related questions on child socioemotional development. Our research outputs thus far addressed these questions by showing that (a) child socioemotional competence is important for other aspects of child adjustment, (b) parental beliefs shape parental practices related to child socioemotional development, (c) both fathers and mothers play an important role in promoting child socioemotional competence, and (d) child temperament moderated the relationship between parental socialization practices and child socioemotional competence. Our project showed that child socioemotional competence, such as in the form of behavioral control and attention shifting, may contribute to child academic development. Our quantitative data, collected through structured tasks with preschool children, showed that children’s abilities to inhibit impulses and direct attention were uniquely linked to their reading and writing performance, even controlling for general language and visual-motor skills (Chung, Lam, & Cheung, 2017). In Hong Kong, parents, teachers, and community members place great importance on academic development. In order to promote socioemotional learning, it would be useful to demonstrate how socioemotional competence may help children to learn in classroom settings. This study has been published advance online in Reading and Writing (2016 Impact Factor: 1.49; Q2 in Education and Educational Research). Our project indicated that parental beliefs, particularly those about child developmental levels, are important in directing how they socialize their children. Our qualitative data, collected through focus group interviews with parents of preschool children, showed that parents adjusted their expectations for and practices with their children when their children grew up (Kwong, Lam, Li, Chung, Cheung, & Leung, under review). For example, parents helped their children to regulate negative emotions (by “patting their backs, humming a familiar tune, or helping [their] children reappraise the situation in a more positive light”), and to manage peer conflict (by helping their children to use self-talk and, again, reappraise the situation) in earlier years. However, when their children grew older, parents expected their children to more independently deal with negative emotions and peer conflict. In other words, some parents are highly aware of their socialization roles, which transit from participating in co-regulation of emotions and co-management of conflict to promoting self-regulation of emotions and self-management of conflict. This idea about transition in parenting practices could be used for parental education, particularly for parents who are overprotective, or who provide “helicopter” care regardless of the developmental levels of their children. This study has been revised and resubmitted, for the third round of review, to Early Childhood Research Quarterly (2016 Impact Factor: 2.44; Q1 in Education and Educational Research). Our project demonstrated that both fathers and mothers play unique roles in shaping child socioemotional competence. Our quantitative data, collected through questionnaires from fathers, mothers, and teachers of preschool children, suggested that paternal and maternal hostility were independently predictive of decreases in child socioemotional competence over time (Lam, Chung, & Li, under review). Despite an emerging literature on fathering, the contributions of fathers to child socioemotional competence remained underexplored. Our work expanded the theoretical literature by highlighting the potentially complementary roles of fathers and mothers in understanding child socioemotional development. Practically, our work pointed to the utility of targeting both parents in efforts to promote child socioemotional competence. This study received a revise and resubmit decision from Frontiers in Psychology (2016 Impact Factor: 2.32; Q2 in Psychology, Multidisciplinary). Our project found that child temperament moderated the relationship between parental socialization practices and child socioemotional outcomes. Our quantitative data, collected through structured tasks with preschool children and questionnaires from their parents and teachers, identified child negative affect as a moderator of the association of coparenting cooperation with child socioemotional outcomes (Lam, Tam, Li, & Tam, under review). Consistent with a dual risk hypothesis, children who were high on negative affect and exposed to low coparenting cooperation showed particularly low levels of peer acceptance, social cognition, and social competence. Worth mentioning is that, in order to isolate the unique impact of coparenting cooperation, we controlled for individual parenting practices and marital relationships in our analyses. These findings addressed our research objectives in two ways. First, they illustrated the multiple ways through which fathers may contribute to their children’s development. On one hand, fathers’ cooperation with mothers matters. On the other hand, as shown in the aforementioned study on paternal and maternal hostility (Lam, Chung, & Li, under review), fathers’ negative parenting, in itself, matters. Second, these findings indicated that the impact of caregiving environment (e.g., coparenting cooperation) on child development (e.g., child socioemotional comptence) is best understood taking into account child temperament (e.g., negative affect). On a practical level, our findings pointed to the importance of helping parents, especially those with temperamentally difficult children, to work cooperatively toward their childrearing goals to promote child competence. This study was revised and resubmitted, for the second round of review, to Journal of Family Psychology (2016 Impact Factor: 1.74; Q2 in Family Studies). To recap, this project used both qualitative and quantitative methods, and data from children, parents, and teachers, to address important questions on child socioemotional competence. Collectively, the one study published, and the three other studies under review, showed that child socioemotional competence is important for child adjustment, and that parental beliefs, parental practices, and child temperament are crucial factors to consider when examining and promoting the development of child socioemotional competence in early childhood.

The overarching goal of our project is to examine the importance of child socioemotional competence, as well as the roles of parental beliefs and practices and child temperament in understanding and promoting child socioemotional competence. Our findings showed that child socioemotional competence, such as in the forms of controlling impulses and directing attention, is important for academic learning in classroom settings (Chung, Lam, & Cheung, 2017). In order to promote child socioemotional competence, we may target parents’ beliefs about child socioemotional competence. For example, parents tend to hold different expectations for younger and older children in the domain of socioemotional development, expecting younger children to co-regulate emotions and co-manage conflict with the assistance of adults and older children to self-regulate emotions and self-manage conflict independently (Kwong, Lam, Li, Chung, Cheung, & Leung, under review). Moreover, both fathers’ and mothers’ parenting practices are important in promoting their children’s socioemotional competence (Lam, Chung, & Li, under review). For example, fathers’ and mothers’ hostility were uniquely linked to decreases in their children’s socioemotional competence over time. It is noteworthy that child temperament may moderate the relationship between parental socialization and child adjustment. For example, children with high negative affect are particularly affected by less-than-optimal cooperating experiences (Lam, Tam, Li, & Chung, under review).

28401714.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28401714.value: The PI will explore the possibility of incorporating the findings based on this project into a parental intervention programme that promotes child socioemotional competence in a preschool setting. For example, parents can be taught about the importance of child socioemotional competence, and coach on how to adjust their expectations for their children, control their hostile language and behaviors, and take into account their children’s temperament. A possible future research direction involves testing whether a programme of such kinds can really bring a positive impact on parents and children. The PI will teach a professional development course, titled “Promoting Socioemotional Competence: Family and School Practices,” for local teachers beginning from the academic year of 2017-2018. He would use the findings based on this project to inform teachers of the best practices to promote socioemotional competence among preschool children.

28401714.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28401714.value: This project examined the importance of child socioemotional competence, and how parents may promote their children socioemotional development. Findings showed that child socioemotional competence, as a set of foundational skills that allows children to understand instructions, follow rules, and make friends, is important for academic learning in classrooms. Both fathers and mothers are important in promoting their children’s socioemotional competence. For example, fathers’ and mothers’ hostility predicts deceases in their children’s socioemotional competence over time. Parents should learn how to control their own negative emotions, and manage their children’s misbehaviors using non-hostile methods, such as induction and time out. The socialization practices of parents seem to be particularly important for children with difficult temperament, such as those who show sustained negative emotions in response to new environments.

28401814.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28401814.value: 漢代（公元前206年–公元220年）器物研究，隨著近數十年來大量漢墓的發現及豐富的漢代文物出土，而有長足的發展。然而，過往這方面的研究多集中以個別器物或墓葬為探討對象。同時，考古材料多視為輔助文獻性質。而此研究則嘗試另闢蹊徑，提出不同的觀點，以「仿製」為主題，探索和重新思考漢墓中各種出土文物之間的關聯、特性與角色，以至箇中所揭示的漢代社會、文化和信仰的面貌。 古往今來，當不同物料之間存有價值的差異，仿製便會出現。古代中國亦出現不少相關的例子，如陶鼎、木璧等等，這以廉價的材料(陶、木)，來仿製原來以貴重材料所製作的器物(青銅器、玉器等)的情況並不難理解，亦相當普遍。然而，在漢代墓葬中所出現的仿製情況並非如此單一。比如以玉仿製價值相對低廉的物料製器，便違悖了上述的邏輯。此外，當時這種仿製的概念，亦展現於實物與圖像之間。 此研究期望能梳理各種豐富的原始資料，包括考古出土材料、考古報告、博物館藏品、圖錄、文獻史料等，以將相關的漢代文物資料系統化。同時，透過跨學科的研究方法，探討一些被忽略的漢代器物仿製的情況，由此闡釋箇中的因由與動機，以及背後所隱含的社會和文化意義。除了以傳統歷史學方法整理文獻史料，這項研究將會依據大量考古學資料為基礎，並使用藝術史學的風格分析以至社會科學的理論方法作統合剖析。當中亦突顯物質文化研究作為進深了解漢代的信仰觀念、以至社會歷史的重要性。

28401814.label: Realisation of objectives
28401814.value: For objectives: 1) to collect and examine primary material of Han scattered in various museums and archaeological institutes in China and overseas; 2) to compare and review the textual information with substantial ordinary artifacts of the Han period; and 3) to build a preliminary electronic archive of the primary material for studying Han material culture. These three objectives had been achieved respectively by the following actions and outcomes. First of all, substantial data (including images, statistics, textual material, etc.) have been collected from a wide range of primary materials, encompassing archaeological reports, scholarly periodicals, monographs, classical literatures, books and catalogues, etc. for building a definitive database with texts and images. An initial research electronic database has been developed, and the collected data have been analysed and reviewed from time to time. Based on the initial collected data, comparing the objects with textual documentations, the PI identified significant objects that required further in-depth analysis, and conducted field research for first-hand study of the target artefacts and accessing relevant ordinary archival data in different mainland and overseas museum collections, including Changsha Museum, Hunan Provincial Museum, Changsha Bamboo Slips Museum, Museum of the Western Han Dynasty Mausoleum of the Nanyue King, Capital Museum, National Museum of China, Nanjing Museum, The Oriental Metropolitan Museum, Hepu Han Dynasty Cultural Museum, The Museum of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, The Yale University Art Gallery, The Penn Museum, British Museum, Victoria and Albert Museum, The Fitzwilliam Museum, Guimet Museum, Cernuschi Museum, Fukuoka City Museum, Itokoku Historical Museum, and Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties, etc. By visiting these museums and institutes, questionable object items had been examined and clarified, moreover, high-resolution images of objects, and related archival documentations, such as archaeological reports, provenance records, etc., were collected and further contributed to and enhance the electronic database. Afterwards, the collected date sets were analysed and synthesized, and generated in forms of tables, charts, and maps, and these data and information became highly useful and effective tools to analyses and illustrate different relevant issues of this research project, for example, to chart the distribution and development trajectory of a certain type of ritual objects (such as bi disc, sheng, etc.) during Han dynasty. Eventually, these data sets were disseminated in forms of tables, charts, and maps, and were integrated into and published on different research papers (as shown in Part C-8), conference papers (Part C-9) and different public talks and seminars (Part C-12). In order to respond and achieve the following four objectives: i.e. 4) reexamining our general understanding of imitation of material in ancient Chinese society; 5) tracing the changes of the hierarchy of material in the Han burial context; 6) addressing a relatively new perspective to understand Han society; and 7) broadening the scope of understanding the religious ideologies of Han through rethinking the materiality and identity of different objects and materials in the tomb context; Four peer-reviewed academic papers (Part C-8) were produced, and the PI participated in refereed international scholarly conferences to present six research papers (Part C-9) yielded from this research project. On the basis of the electronic database developed in this project, specific ritual objects were identified and selected as case studies for in-depth examination and addressing objectives 4 to 7. For example, bi disc was chosen as one of the major case studies, this type of object was believed to have the power for communicating with Heaven in ancient China, by studying different forms and representations of this type of object, it reveals the complicated situation of imitation practice (objective 4) and the hierarchy of material in different status Han burials (objective 5). It also provides a different approach (biographical approach) and alternative perspective to look at the situation (objective 6), and helps us understand further about the religious ideologies during the times (objective 7). Relevant and detailed findings, discussion and analyses are documented and published in two academic paper, i.e. a book chapter entitled “Dynamic between form and material: the bi disc in Western Han noble burial ritual” published by the Cambridge University Press (Part C-8.1); and an article “Representation of heaven and beyond: the bi disc imagery in the Han burial context” published by the journal Asian Studies (Part C-8.2). Another study focuses on jade dragon pendants, another prevalent ritual object used during ancient China. This study analyses different jade dragon pendants unearthed from a Western Han princely tomb of Chu at Shizishan, and an interesting situation that imitation existed among the dragon pendants from this tombs. This study seeks to investigate the motives driven the practice (objective 4), and provide alternative perspective to rethinking the materiality of the object in the context (objective 7). Details of the relevant findings and discussion are documented in the academic paper, “A Collection of Dragon Pendants from the Tomb of Prince of Chu at Shizishan in Xuzhou” (Part C-8.3), which was submitted to and currently under reviewed by Wenwu, a preeminent international archaeological journal. Other case studies on the issue of imitation, include the iconography of sheng and the Queen Mother of the West, lacquered head covers, etc. were also adopted to address the Objectives respectively. Relevant findings and discussions were written as conference papers and presented in different referred international conference. During this research period, six different research papers were accepted and presented in different international scholarly conferences, they are: “The Jade Disc and Its Representations in Han China Burials”, “Jade Vessels in the Western Han Mortuary Context”, “Antiquarianism and Displays of Ancient Materials in Pre-modern China”, “From Mythology to Representation: Sheng and Its Iconography in Han Burial Ritual”, “The Sheng and Its Representation in Early China Burials”, and “A Study of Lacquered Head Covers in Han Burials” (Part C-9). In addition, the findings and outcomes of this research project were also disseminated to and discussed with the public as public talks and seminar in different academic and public arenas, including art museums, the Fine Arts Department of the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and the Cattle Depot Artists Village (Part C-12).

28401814.label: Major findings and research outcome
28401814.value: Major findings of this research project are as follows: 1. Although many objects made of inferior material are generally perceived as less precious imitations of valuable originals, this research indicates the situation was neither simple nor linked only to the availability of valuable material. 2. Even in elite tombs, many non-jade version of bi disc objects were used and presented as mingqi as part of the owners’ property, and in this case, the significance of object was manifest in the form of disc, not the material of manufacture. 3. By the Western Han, beliefs about the form of disc and its original material of jade diverged and, therefore, their trajectories became entirely different and complex. 4. In ordinary Han tombs, the use of imagery imitation of jade disc is a hybrid continuity and development of the elite tombs in the South and noble mountain tomb of the East. 5. The imitative practice of disc in ordinary Han tombs, revealed the protective purpose was no longer sustained by bi disc image, but the significance of image was enriched and became a symbol represented heavenly world. 6. Imitation of a rare archaic object occurred in noble tombs context, it reveals imitation as a method to retain the distinction of owner. 7. Although jade imitation was a case of reverse logic of using inexpensive material to imitate objects made of valuable material, different examples of this practice were found from Shang dynasty through Tang dynasty. Outcomes includes a preliminary electronic archive of primary data and images for studying ancient Chinese material culture has been established, and the database material together with the above mentioned findings are thoroughly analysed, addressed and compiled in 4 different academic papers respectively: “Dynamic between form and material: the bi disc in Western Han noble burial ritual” a book chapter published by Cambridge University Press (Part C-8.1); two journal papers “Representation of heaven and beyond: the bi disc imagery in the Han burial context” (Part C-8.2) and “A Collection of Dragon Pendants from the Tomb of Prince of Chu at Shizishan in Xuzhou” (Part C-8.3); and the sections “Ancient jades” and “Medieval jades” in the article “Carvings (stone and jade) in pre‐modern China” (Part C-8.4). Moreover, the major findings were addressed and illustrated in 6 different referred conference papers (Part C-9). In addition, the findings were shared and discussed with the public in 4 public talks (Part C-12).

28401814.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28401814.value: On the basis of this research, future studies can consider looking into different media or material that have not been duly discussed in current project, such as glass, ceramic, lacquer, etc., since the current research primarily focuses on studying different types of ritual objects rather on a specific medium of material. Moreover, the study period can move beyond Han dynasty, for example, the study period of glass imitation can either expend to earlier Eastern Zhou period, or later to Tang Dynasty, as glass was more prevalent used during the periods. In addition, the regions for investigation can also consider expanding to East Asian or Southeast Asian areas, such as Vietnam, Korea and Japan, so as the entire picture of material exchange and development of the region in ancient time can be more clearly revealed and illustrated. To realize the mentioned aspects, beside carrying out research projects, publishing research papers, it can also consider making integral use of scientific analysis results of some of the studied artifacts and material, such as bronze and glass, and therefore collaboration with scientific professionals can be considered in future.

28401814.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28401814.value: This is an in-depth research with emphasis on the phenomenon of imitation, a practice that was prevalent and constant in the material world, once distinctions of value began to occur among various materials. It was popular and understandable to use inexpensive material to imitate objects made of valuable primary material, such as gold and jade, however, the authentic situation of imitation was conceivably far more complex in the Han Dynasty. For example, the existence of jade imitation was a case of reverse logic. Moreover, imitation not only occurred among various materials, but also between genuine objects and image representations. This research explores and examines the intricate incentives for the practice and selection of material, in order to reveal the embedded cultural and social values in the materials and objects per se of the time. More broadly, this research also demonstrates the importance of studying material culture, which is an alternative way to enhance our understanding of the development of society and religious beliefs of ancient China.

28401914.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28401914.value: Parental involvement encompasses a broad range of parenting practices, and it has been widely associated with positive child outcomes. Although many studies on parental involvement have been conducted, a systematic examination of parental involvement investigating its antecedents, changes, and influence on young children’s outcomes during the early school transition is lacking. Therefore, the present two-wave longitudinal study will use the mixed-methods and multi-informant approaches to examine parental involvement during the transition to primary school in Hong Kong. Three major research questions will be addressed: (1) What are the relationships between parental involvement and school adjustment? (2) What are the changes in parental involvement during the transition to primary school? (3) What are the factors that influence parental involvement in early childhood and primary education? Stratified random sampling will be used to recruit three kindergartens in each of the three strata developed based on the median monthly household income of the districts. Within each of the nine kindergartens, two upper kindergarten (K3) classes with children aged five to six years will be randomly selected. All participating kindergarten principals (N1 = 9), the lead kindergarten class teachers (N2 = 18), and one randomly selected parent from each class (N3 = 18) will participate in the individual interviews at Time 1 to explore the factors that influence parental involvement. The 18 parents will also participate in follow-up interviews at Time 2 to examine the changes in and the influencing factors of their involvement after their children have entered primary school. Approximately 360 children (N4 = 20 × 18 classes) and their parents as well as their lead class teachers will complete a series of tasks at each time point. The parents as well as the kindergarten (Time 1) and primary school (Time 2) lead class teachers will report on parental involvement. The teachers will also rate the children’s school adjustment. At both time points, the child interview will be conducted to assess parents’ involvement and children’s school adjustment. The investigation of the proposed model will extend the principal investigator's previous work on parental involvement and contribute to the theoretical understanding of the influences of and changes in parental involvement as well as the complex associations between parental involvement and school adjustment. The findings will also lay the foundation upon which further support can be built in both the local and international communities to facilitate parental involvement from the early education years. 本計劃將以為期兩年的時間，採用混合研究方法及運用不同的資料提供者，重點分析: 1) 家長參與與幼兒入學適應的關係; 2)家長參與於幼小銜接前後之變化; 及 3)影響家長於早期教育之參與的因素。本研究將根據地區家庭入息中位數，分層隨機抽樣共九間受訪幼稚園。每間受訪幼稚園之兩班高班學生及其家長將被邀請參與本研究。為探索影響家長參與的因素，幼稚園校長(N1=9)、班主任(N2=18)及家長(N3=18)會參與第一階段的個人訪談。該十八位家長亦會在第二階段參與跟進訪談，從而分析他們在兒童升讀小學後，其參與角色的轉變以及影響其參與程度的因素。同時，共有約360位兒童(N4=20x18班)及其家長，聯同他們的班主任，將完成一系列的評估。其中家長將於第一及第二階段評估自己的參與行為及子女的入學準備。另外，幼稚園(第一階段)及小學(第二階段)的班主任均會就家長的參與程度及兒童在學校中的適應表現作評核。在每一階段，兒童訪談亦會用作評估家長參與的程度及兒童的入學適應表現。此調查將延續筆者有關家長參與的研究，並有助理解及促進家長於早期教育的參與。

28401914.label: Realisation of objectives
28401914.value: The present study was carefully designed and successfully conducted to examine the three objectives stated. This study contributed to a theoretical understanding of the influences and stability of parental involvement as well as the complex associations between parental involvement and children’s school adjustment. The achievement of the objectives lay the foundation upon which further support can be built in the community for facilitating parental involvement from the early education years. Below is the summary of how the project objectives have been fully achieved. Objective 1 & 2: Study 1 was designed to achieve Objectives 1 and 2 of this project, in which multi-informant and longitudinal approaches were employed to examine both the influence of parental involvement on children’s school adjustment as well as the changes of parental involvement across the transition to school. Specifically, a two-wave longitudinal design with a 8-month interval was conducted. Time 1 was done in March and April 2015, whereas Time 2 was done in November and December 2015. The participants were children (mean age: 70.39 months at Time 1 and 76.98 months at Time 2), mothers, fathers, and kindergarten and primary school teachers from 324 and 247 Hong Kong middle- and upper-middle-class families at Time 1 and Time 2, respectively. Class teachers and parents received their questionnaires approximately three months before the end of the kindergarten school year. During the same period, the research assistant (RA) and student research assistants (SRAs) visited each kindergarten to conduct the child assessment sessions. The RA and SRAs received training on research protocols and data collection before administering the assessments. A pilot study involving a convenience sample of preschool children and their parents and teachers was conducted to ensure the clarity and validity of the questionnaire items and the instructions for the child assessments, and for training purposes. The RA and SRAs remained blind to the research hypotheses. All of the measurements conducted at Time 1 were repeated at Time 2. At Time 2, the participating children and parents were invited to a research session either at the kindergartens their children attended, the university, or their homes. During the research session, the children and parents completed the tests and questionnaires, respectively, in separate rooms. Over the course of the study, 77 families (24%) dropped out. Therefore, we were able to conduct follow-up assessments with 247 children (126 girls, 121 boys) and their parents (237 mothers, 210 fathers). The attrition was mainly due to parents no longer wishing to participate, migration, and illness. During the follow-up research session, the parents were also asked to provide consent and contact information so that the research team could obtain their children’s primary school teachers’ ratings of parental involvement and the children’s school adjustment. Of the 247 children who participated in the follow-up assessment, 241 parents granted approval to contact their children’s primary school teachers. Some of the participating children were in the same primary school classes. As such, some of the primary school teachers completed more than one survey (i.e., two teachers had five children, five teachers had four children, seven teachers had three children, 27 teachers had two children, and 136 teachers had one child in their classes). Phone calls were made to 177 primary school teachers in 119 primary schools to explain the study. The information letter, consent form, questionnaires, and return envelope were then sent to all of the teachers. A total of 198 (82%) completed questionnaires were received from 148 primary school teachers. To examine changes in parental involvement over time (Objective 1), two sets of mixed models analyses were run: one set for the self-reported parental involvement variables serving as the dependent variables and one set for the two teacher reports on home-school conferencing serving as dependent variables. The independent variable for these analyses were timepoint. On the other hand, to examine the degree to which changes in parental involvement and child outcomes predicted one another over time (Objective 2), cross-lagged panel analyses were run involving a series of structural equation models with SPSS AMOS, Version 24. Separate analyses were run for mothers and fathers for parental involvement for each of the child variables. All of the autoregressive and cross-lagged paths between Time 1 and Time 2 were also included in the model. The control variables in the analyses were child sex, child age, and parent education. Objective 3: Study 2 was designed to achieve Objective 2, in which in-depth individual interviews with different stakeholders were carried out to understand the factors influencing parental involvement in early childhood years. In particular, two upper kindergarten (K3) classes with children aged five to six years were randomly selected from each of the nine kindergartens. All participating kindergarten principals (N1 = 6), the lead class teachers (N2 = 12), and one randomly selected parent from each class (N3 = 12) participated in the individual interviews. Based on a review of the literature and interview questions developed in previous studies in the Chinese context, main interview questions were developed: 1) What are school’s philosophies toward home-school collaboration? 2) What are your attitudes toward home-school collaboration? 3) What are some home-school collaboration activities available in your school? 4) What are some school resources available for facilitating home-school collaboration? 5) What are some difficulties associated with home-school collaboration? Apart from the above five questions for all participants, one additional question was designed for principals and teachers: 6) How does home-school collaboration affect your work as a principal/teacher? All interviews were conducted at the kindergarten approximately four months after the commencement of the school year. Interviews were conducted by the prinicipal investigator and the research assistant (RA). A semi-structured interview protocol was used to help ensure consistency across participants while allowing the exploration of new issues. Several techniques were also used by all interviewers across interviews, such as avoiding leading questions, utilizing probing techniques, and letting the informant lead). Each interview took approximately 30 minutes. All interviews were audio-taped and later transcribed by student assistants for analysis. The constant comparative method of the grounded theory approach were used. Specifically, the method of comparing and contrasting the respondents’ responses to each interview question were used to form categories, assign codes to the categories, summarize the content of each category for developing themes, and find negative evidence. Every interview was carefully studied to examine the internal consistency of individual interviews. As soon as more than one interview has been completed, comparisons between interviews within the same kindergarten were conducted. Upon the completion of all within-group analyses, between-group comparisons were conducted with regard to the experience of home-school collaboration to validate the story told by one group. Different aids (i.e., memo writing, close reading and rereading, and coding) were used to facilitate the identification of relevant quotes and to support the systematization of the analysis process.

28401914.label: Major findings and research outcome
28401914.value: In Study 1, results revealed that among the six dimensions of parental involvement, parent-child discussion and school-based parental involvement increased over time during the transition to primary school. In other words, the Hong Kong parents who participated in this study engaged with their children more in conversations about their schooling, communicated more with teachers, and became more involved in the school context to gain information about their children’s education and about the primary schools’ practices and policies. Results also revealed that the mothers’ involvement in language and cognitive activities during kindergarten predicted better school adjustment after school transition. On the other hand, the mothers were more involved at their children’s primary schools when their children demonstrated lower cognitive skills in kindergarten. Altogether, the findings highlight the importance of examining different dimensions of parental involvement over time during the transition to primary school and the bidirectional relations between parental involvement and children’s school adjustment. In Study 2, responses from interviews with principals, teachers and parents provided evidences about the factors that influence parental involvement in early childhood education and primary school. Specifically, the lack of time and low levels of self-perceived parental efficacy were identified by participants as major barriers in parental involvement. For instance, most of the participants suggested that work and childcare responsibilities are major reasons of their unavailability. The participants also discussed parents’ frustration and feeling of incompetence in parental involvement, as the learning activities of young children are getting more challenging and complex these days. The findings deepen our knowledge and understanding of the various factors that influence the involvement of parents for identifying strategies that facilitate high-quality parental involvement both at home and in school to foster a smooth school transition for family and children.

28401914.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28401914.value: First, the results provide evidences that Chinese parental involvement translates into significant gains in their children’s school adjustment. One practical value of our findings would be to encourage schools to not only support parents by increasing parental involvement in school, but also by supporting parental involvement at home through various means, such as designing parent-child learning activities, before school transition. Second, the finding that children’s lower cognitive skills predicted higher levels of parent-teacher communication suggests that teachers should encourage involvement from the early years, particularly when children are experiencing adjustment difficulties, by engaging in frequent communication with parents about their children’s needs and giving parents precise instructions on how to teach specific concepts at home. Finally, the findings of the influencing factors of parental involvement, namely parents’ lack of time and feeling of incompetence, provide insight about strategies to support parental involvement. For example, schools should invite parents for participation by considering their availability as well as by informing them ahead of time to facilitate parents’ arrangement. Schools should also provide clear instructions and parent education opportunities to increase parents’ skills and motivation for involvement.

28401914.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28401914.value: This study found that parents engaged in higher levels of involvement over time during the transition from kindergarten to primary school. Also, parental involvement during kindergarten predicted better school adjustment after school transition. Furthermore, parents were more involved at their children’s schools when their children demonstrated lower levels of adjustment in kindergarten. Finally, this study found that parents’ involvement in general is limited by their time and parental efficacy. As the new free quality kindergarten education policy in Hong Kong places heavy emphasis on the enhancement of parental involvement for improve the quality of kindergarten education, our study provides timely insights for practical implications in the local context. Specifically, our findings suggest that schools may respond to parents’ needs by providing more opportunities for parents to become involved in their children’s learning both at home and in school. Doing so would help parents obtain information about school expectations and their children’s learning progress. This may further increase parents’ discussions with their children or impart knowledge and strategies for teaching specific concepts at home, thereby facilitating a smooth school transition.
